Roundup: Surging natural gas prices add to Germany's gas supply concerns
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:15:55 CST
07:15:55 KST

FRANKFURT, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European natural gas prices have hovered near multi-year highs as the heating season approaches, raising concerns in Germany over energy costs and low gas storage levels.
Dutch TTF front-month futures, the benchmark for European gas, were trading at around 80 euros (92 U.S. dollars) per megawatt-hour (MWh) on Wednesday, slightly down from around 83 euros (95.5 dollars) on Monday, the highest level since December 2022.
Natural gas prices in the European Union (EU) have more than doubled since the outbreak of the Iran war. The surge has coincided with hikes in oil and other energy prices amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Meanwhile, Germany's natural gas storage inventory was around 56 percent full, the lowest level ever registered for September since the tracking started in 2011, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Germany's more than 40 gas storage facilities remain barely over half full as the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz adds pressure to an energy system that has undergone major changes since the Russia-Ukraine conflict erupted in 2022 and Germany moved to reduce its reliance on Russian energy supplies.
Traditionally, operators could fill natural gas storage facilities during the summer when demand and prices are relatively low and sell it during the higher-demand winter months. However, the sharp rise in gas prices has weakened the economic incentive to replenish storage facilities.
The Iran war and resulting disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for international oil and natural gas shipments, have driven gas prices sharply higher, making summer storage less attractive to market participants.
"At the same time, the situation of German storage facilities is worsening due to the turbulence on the energy markets," FNB Gas, an association of gas transmission operators in Germany, said in a report
The combination of high prices and relatively low storage levels has fueled concerns among some politicians and market participants about gas supplies and affordability this winter.
During a Bundestag debate last week, Alice Weidel, co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, cited the low storage levels and argued that replenishing gas inventories must be a top priority. She warned that a cold winter could force Germany to make costly emergency gas purchases or resort to rationing, dealing a heavy blow to businesses and households.
As the Iran war drags on and tensions in the Red Sea flare up, experts have warned that EU natural gas prices could rise further to 100 or even 120 euros (115.1 to 138.1 dollars) per MWh if supply disruptions worsen. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: China's auto innovation creates opportunities for global suppliers: Bosch executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:15:53 CST
07:15:53 KST

HANNOVER, Germany, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's rapid advances in automotive technology are creating new opportunities for global suppliers, while Chinese automakers' growing international ambitions are reshaping the global auto industry, a senior Bosch executive has said.
"Every time we visit China, what is most important for me is to see lots of innovations being demonstrated," Markus Heyn, deputy chairman of the Bosch board of management and chairman of the Bosch Mobility business sector, said in a recent interview with Xinhua at IAA Transportation in Hannover.
At one of the world's largest gatherings for commercial vehicles and transport solutions, Heyn noted that Chinese automakers have strengthened their position in the domestic market while increasingly expanding overseas.
Heyn sees this shift as an important development in the global automotive industry. "You can only have a leading position in the industry if you are leading in more than one country," he said. "If you are good in China, then you also have to be good in Europe or other regions of the world."
The growing global ambitions of Chinese automakers are also changing their relationship with suppliers such as Bosch. "Cooperation with Chinese customers has become faster and more open," Heyn said.
Bosch's sales in China reached 149.8 billion yuan (22.47 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up 4.9 percent year-on-year, according to the company.
Bosch has 38 manufacturing sites and 28 research and development centers in China, Heyn said, adding that the country is not only an important production base for Bosch but is also becoming an increasingly important source of innovation.
The rapid development of Chinese automakers, particularly in electrification and intelligent driving, is creating both competitive pressure and new opportunities for global suppliers, he said.
"I think it creates more opportunities," Heyn said, adding that cooperation with automakers and other industry partners provides a basis for innovations and new products.
For Bosch, those opportunities extend beyond passenger cars, making commercial vehicles a major area for future growth.
At IAA Transportation, Bosch showcased a range of technologies for commercial vehicles, including electric motors, inverters and other electrification solutions, as well as fuel-cell power modules. The portfolio reflects Bosch's strategy of developing different powertrain paths as the commercial vehicle industry undergoes a broad transition.
"The heavy-duty commercial vehicle business is a key growth area for us. We aim to double our sales in this segment by the mid-2030s," Heyn said.
Bosch expects global truck production to grow by about 1 percent in 2026 to around 3.3 million vehicles and reach about 4 million units by the mid-2030s. Based on that outlook, the company sees the potential to double its sales of heavy-duty commercial vehicle technology from more than 4 billion euros (4.6 billion U.S. dollars) currently to around 8 billion euros (9.2 billion dollars) by 2035.
Electrification will be an increasingly important part of that growth, Heyn said, although the pace of the transition varies across regions. "Batteries are also becoming the lead technology in commercial vehicles," he said.
However, Heyn said the transition would not follow a single technological path, particularly in heavy-duty long-haul transport.
"Achieving the world's climate goals in the transport sector isn't an 'either-or' proposition. We have to use every technology that helps us transition away from fossil fuels," he said, adding that hydrogen and alternative fuels would continue to complement battery-electric technology in long-haul transport. ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Fed announces 1st interest rate hike in over 3 years as inflation stays sticky
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:15:48 CST
07:15:48 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its target federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent to address persistent inflation, marking its first interest rate hike since July 2023.
"Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little," said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in a statement.
In support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, "the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent," the FOMC said.
The committee reaffirmed "its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system."
"Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability," it reiterated.
All 12 FOMC members voted in favor of the rate hike.
In conjunction with the FOMC meeting held on Sept. 15-16, participants also submitted their projections of the most likely outcomes for real GDP growth, the unemployment rate and inflation for each year from 2026 to 2029 and over the longer run.
The Fed's Board members and Federal Reserve Bank presidents projected median U.S. GDP growth of 2.3 percent in 2026, up from the June projection of 2.2 percent. The median unemployment rate was projected at 4.1 percent in 2026, down from the June projection of 4.3 percent.
For 2027, participants raised their GDP growth projection to 2.4 percent from 2.3 percent and lowered their unemployment rate projection to 4.1 percent from 4.3 percent.
As for inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, FOMC participants projected it at 3.7 percent in 2026, up from the June projection of 3.6 percent. The projection for 2027 remained unchanged at 2.3 percent.
The participants defined "appropriate monetary policy" as the future path of policy that best satisfies their interpretation of the statutory mandate to promote maximum employment and price stability.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference after the FOMC meeting. He has said that the risk is that people's inflation expectations become "unanchored," which means people lose faith that inflation may return to normal.
"The Committee's unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis," Warsh said.
"Inflation is the problem," he reiterated. "Stable prices have been the problem for more than five-and-a-half years."
Warsh put a very positive spin on the interest rate hike, saying a robust and resilient economy can handle a quarter-point hike.
He failed to say whether an aggressive rate-hiking cycle is on the way. "I'm not in the forward guidance business," he said.
As for AI's potential economic impact, Warsh said the Fed has created a task force to study that.
Responding to a question about U.S. President Donald Trump's demands for interest rate cuts, Warsh said Fed independence is a "two-way street" and Fed officials "stay in our lane."
In early September, Trump threatened to completely stop trade with countries running trade surpluses with the United States should the Fed fail to cut rates, triggering the Fed independence issue. ■

The strike came after disputes over compensation for night work. Unions say air traffic controllers at Charleroi receive no specific compensation for night shifts and are seeking better conditions, but Skeyes has rejected the demand. The two sides have held several rounds of talks since late July but failed to produce an agreement.
BSCA said the internal labor dispute at Skeyes has affected passengers, airlines, airport staff and other businesses operating at the airport, while also hurting economic activity in Wallonia.
The airport called on Skeyes management and workers' representatives to resume talks and find a solution. It also advised passengers to check their flight status with airlines before traveling to the airport. ■

“Interest Rates in the United States should be 1 per cent, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World – BY FAR,” he wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform.
“LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” he concluded.

“I ... talked to Kevin,” Trump said, appearing to confirm an interaction with the Fed chief that Warsh himself has so far declined to corroborate. 
“And I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing.”
Trump, as he has in recent social media posts, also appeared to connect persistent US trade deficits with the borrowing costs set by the central bank, even though the two are largely unrelated.

Trump’s screed came shortly after Fed policymakers unanimously agreed to raise rates by 25 basis points to 3.75 per cent to 4.00 per cent, an action that Warsh described at a subsequent press conference as “a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision”.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said.
And rates are likely going still higher.
New policy projections showed 16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-percentage-point hike by the end of this year, with only two of them seeing rates remaining stable from here.
Warsh said again on Sept 16 that he is opposed to sharing forward guidance and did not submit a projection.
Trump tapped Warsh in January to succeed Powell, whom Trump nicknamed “too late” for taking a more cautious approach to rate cuts last year than Trump wanted.
Warsh, for his part, took office with a pledge to maintain the Fed’s independence on setting monetary policy while at the same time working in greater concert with the White House on other matters.
Since Warsh took office in June – after a Senate confirmation that was nearly derailed by a federal investigation into Powell and renovations of the Fed headquarters building – he initially steered Fed officials to holding rates steady, although not all policymakers agreed with the approach in the face of inflationary pressures.
On Sept 16, he said the time had come for the central bank to take action.

Asked at his press conference if he planned to meet Trump to explain the Fed’s decision, Warsh demurred.

“The president is making clear he disagrees with the policy without explicitly saying Warsh is personally to blame, giving him a nickname, or threatening retaliatory action against the Fed,” said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. 
“Instead he’s redirecting his ire toward trading partners, which have little to do with the monetary policy decision.” REUTERS

US Fed hikes rates in search of ‘timelier’ drop in inflation

While US President Donald Trump had promised to lower prices on his watch, the combined impact of his global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom has kept price pressures intense enough that the Fed felt it needed to raise its benchmark overnight interest rate by ¼ of a percentage point to the 3.75 to 4 per cent range.

Satellite data shows major ice losses for Greenland and Antarctica
New research based on satellite data going back to the 1970s has documented major polar ice losses in Greenland and Antarctica — home to Earth’s two great ice sheets — that have contributed to rising global sea levels.
Between 1979 and 2023, according to data from 27 satellite missions, Greenland and Antarctica lost a combined 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice, adding 3.14cm to the worldwide sea-level rise.
The study, employing the longest satellite data record of changes in ice sheets ever gathered to give the most complete account to date of ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica, was conducted by the Ice Sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise team, an international group of polar scientists.

OpenAI announced a new framework on Wednesday for how it publicly discloses AI misalignment incidents, which the company says it hopes will help inform similar standards across the industry. The company is also releasing new information about several examples of AI model misalignment it identified in the past year.
“As models advance and become more widely deployed, decisions about AI development need evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine,” Kai Chen, OpenAI’s newly appointed head of alignment research, tells WIRED. “We don't believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed.”
In a briefing with WIRED, an OpenAI official said the company previously disclosed misalignment incidents too infrequently. The official, who agreed to the briefing on the condition of anonymity, said the new framework is designed to make it easier for OpenAI to quickly inform the public when it discovers that its AI models are behaving in unexpected ways, even before it can fully investigate, explain, or mitigate the behavior.
The framework outlines methods for OpenAI employees to report misalignment incidents to the company’s senior safety and alignment leaders, who will then determine whether further investigation is needed. OpenAI says it plans to develop more objective disclosure criteria in collaboration with other AI developers, external researchers, industry standards bodies, and regulators. The company says it’s actively working on proposed reporting mechanisms for disclosing safety, security, and misalignment incidents to the US federal government.
“At the moment, there is no industry-wide framework with explicit standards for how AI developers should disclose examples of misalignment in their models,” OpenAI said in a blog post. “We hope that the framework we’re outlining today is a first step toward creating such standards, setting out which misalignment instances developers should disclose and what their reports should contain.”
OpenAI is releasing the framework at a critical juncture for the AI industry. Last weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman signaled support for Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s proposal for the tech industry to coordinate on slowing AI development. The call to action came just days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and subsequently went viral for warning the public that the race among frontier labs to develop increasingly advanced AI was putting humanity’s safety at stake.
The calls for an AI slowdown have been met with resistance by President Trump’s administration, which has argued that the industry does not need new laws or regulations to ensure its technology is safe.
Two of the misalignment examples OpenAI shared on Wednesday involved the company’s internal, unreleased AI models, which OpenAI says uploaded files to the internet despite not being instructed to do so.
One of the incidents happened in October 2025, when OpenAI says it was testing one of its models on its ability to cite publicly available data in its answers. But when the model couldn’t find the information it needed, it uploaded a file to a temporary file hosting service, which it then later tried to cite in its answer. The company says this appeared to be an attempt to exploit an automated grading system used to assess the model’s proficiency on the benchmark.
In another example from April of this year, OpenAI says a group of agents was tasked with completing a “workbook” together using only local files. When the agents struggled to share files with one another, one of the agents uploaded them to the public internet and shared a link with the other agents.
In another incident, which OpenAI says it discovered last month, an unreleased version of its GPT-6 Astra AI model appeared to give itself “jailbreaking-like instructions.” In several scenarios, the model essentially prompted itself to ignore developer instructions, take on a new persona, or limit how long model responses could be. While these jailbreaking-like attempts happened rarely and were effective to varying degrees, OpenAI says the behavior raised concerns internally. In the training run for the version of Astra that was released publicly, the company says it has not observed any instances of the model trying to jailbreak itself.
OpenAI also shared more detail on Wednesday about the message board its agents developed in a package manager, Artifactory. While this incident was discovered in May of this year, OpenAI says its agents would use a similar mechanism to coordinate the Hugging Face hack months later. In this incident, the company says its agents did not exploit any vulnerabilities to exchange messages. OpenAI says it now uses alignment monitors, evaluations, and red-teaming efforts to ensure its agents are not covertly communicating with one another.
Cybersecurity professionals previously told WIRED that the Hugging Face hack came down to human errors, and modern-day security practices could have prevented the incident. Chen notes, however, that OpenAI is trying to take a well-rounded approach to AI safety that accounts for the rising capabilities of AI models and doesn’t depend on a secure environment.
“We want to make sure the models are aligned regardless of what environment they’re deployed in,” Chen said. “When people are pointing fingers and saying this is a security issue and not an alignment issue, I think it doesn't really make sense, because you want the model to be well-behaved all the time.”

Muhammed Yasin Gungor
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The US military must urgently adapt its forces to operate and prevail in contested environments extending from the ocean floor to the gravitational space between Earth and the Moon, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine said Wednesday.
"Our task, my friends, is to adapt right now, so the Joint Force is prepared to fight, endure and win in global contested environments, from the seabed to cislunar space," Caine said at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in the US state of Maryland.
Reiterating that "today's modern battlefield operates from the seabed to cislunar space," Caine said future conflicts will dismantle long-held assumptions of uncontested logistics, secure sanctuary areas, or safe resupply routes. He warned that frontline formations must assume they will be "hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum and tracked in real time."
"In the future fight, advantage will go to the side who can see first, who can understand first, decide first and act first," he said, urging the joint force to deliver massed lethality using an agile, optimized "high-low mix of combat capabilities."
His warnings follow Monday's disclosure by Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, who confirmed that the Space Force operates on-orbit "space control weapons" capable of defending joint forces against hostile adversary actions. The announcement marked the first formal public acknowledgment of armed US platforms in orbit amid intensifying orbital competition with China and Russia and the development of the "Golden Dome" missile defense network.
China denounced the US deployment, saying that Beijing opposes turning outer space into a "war zone" and urging Washington to halt its orbital military buildup.
While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits placing nuclear weapons or weapons of mass destruction in orbit, it does not explicitly ban conventional weapons in space
Caine identified digital autonomy as the primary catalyst transforming modern combat dynamics, outpacing all other military technologies.
"No factor is accelerating change as fast as artificial intelligence and advancing cyber capabilities," he said, adding "AI is here now, and it’s already changing the way militaries see, sense, decide and act."
To illustrate how algorithmic integration is redefining military operations, he highlighted an incident in June near the coast of Oman, where an autonomous vessel guided by AI recovered two US soldiers after their Apache attack helicopter went down.
"Taken together, these examples from the Strait of Hormuz to the front lines in Ukraine show how quickly technology is changing the character of war," he said.

New AMC Boss Open to Unmanned Next-Gen Tanker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:06:28 UTC
07:06:28 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The new head of Air Mobility Command said Sept. 16 he wants to explore an unmanned option for the service’s next-generation aerial refueling system.
As the service pursues its first fleet of semi-autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft, Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley said he is open to looking at emerging technologies for a future unmanned or optionally manned large aerial refueling aircraft. The service is preparing to sign a deal for 75 additional KC-46 Pegasus tankers, but it continues to search for a long-term answer to replacing its Eisenhower-era KC-135 Stratotankers, the bulk of today’s tanker fleet.
To field a next-generation tanker in the mid-2030s, the Air Force is pursuing an analysis of alternatives, looking at everything from an innovative blended wing-body aircraft to more KC-46s to a stealthy and possibly uncrewed refueling platform.
“Thinking beyond the current KC-46 buy and the program extension, whatever that next tanker looks like—our advanced tanker system—it’s got to be connected. It’s got to be able to defend itself, but it begs the question: does it need to be manned? Could it be optionally manned? It could be autonomous, or is there a family of solutions maybe that would answer that question?” Tulley, who took command of AMC in early August, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
“I do not believe that it has to be a manned future air refueling solution,” Tulley said. “I think you’re seeing that with the MQ-25 and the Navy’s work,” Tulley added, referring to the Navy’s development of the uncrewed MQ-25 from Boeing, an unmanned tanker capable of transferring 14,000 pounds of fuel to aircraft like the F/A-18 Super Hornet and the F-35 at a distance of 500 miles from a carrier in highly contested airspace.
That airplane is much smaller than Air Force requirements, however; a KC-46 can carry 212,000 pounds of fuel, more than 15 times the capacity of the MQ-25.
Solving that problem is what Tulley is after. “How do we, the U.S. Air Force, bring that to bear in scope, scale, and range?” he asked. “An optionally manned or an unmanned tanker at the ranges we need to operate at is a very large aircraft.”
Currently, the Air Force is not yet “employing fully autonomous large aircraft, but the technology I would say [is] … rapidly getting there,” Tulley said.
Boeing’s large civilian airliners can take off with very little help, fly on a programed route, and land with autopilot, “but we don’t employ [aircraft] that way,” Tulley said.
The market for autonomy in large aircraft is a military market, so “establishing the requirement and then supporting the requirement with the right technology” will be key, he said.
“There are some companies out there who have offered to develop things where they can bring a carry-on kit on KC-135s and other aircraft,” he said. “But we haven’t seen them test those successfully.”
Meanwhile, the Air Force and Boeing unveiled an agreement in mid-May to resolve critical deficiencies with the Pegasus that currently stand in the way of the service signing a pending contract for 75 additional KC-46s. The service is also working to add connectivity and active defense systems on both the KC-135 and the newer KC-46.
“We are going to be recapitalizing tankers for decades, and in the interim, the same dedication to bringing on new platforms is necessary to sustain those that we have,” Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue, deputy commander of Air Mobility Command, said during the conference. “The last KC-135 pilot has not been born.”

UN chief calls for global cooperation to address AI threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:04:24 UTC
07:04:24 KST

The United Nations chief has urged global competitors in artificial intelligence (AI) to cooperate in addressing threats from the technology, warning that "the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety."
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Wednesday that concerns raised by those on the frontlines of AI technology that its development "is racing ahead of our understanding of the risks" can't be ignored.
Governments must assume their first responsibility to protect civilians from AI threats, which means "national action is essential," Guterres told UN reporters. "But global coordination is also indispensable."
"We need guardrails to build trust — and that makes AI safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the centre."
Guterres was referring to a proposal from Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, to ensure AI safety by coordinating a slowdown in its development by leading technology companies and governments.
OpenAI's Sam Altman, SpaceX AI's Elon Musk and other prominent industry leaders have said in recent days that AI’s development needs to slow down. But Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg distanced the company Wednesday, saying every AI company has to ensure its technology is safe.
There are other obstacles to a coordinated effort on AI, including domestic and global competition, especially from China, and profit motivations. And there has been pushback from President Donald Trump, who this week called threats that AI might destroy humanity "a HOAX" and claimed efforts to limit the technology are part of a "SICK conspiracy."
'Runaway AI'
Guterres has praised the enormous potential of AI, including to accelerate economic development and education and to strengthen health systems. But he has also warned of the "existential" threat of "runaway artificial intelligence."
He said AI will be a major topic in his discussions with world leaders at their annual gathering next week for the high-level session of the UN General Assembly.
"The United Nations will continue to explore practical ideas and approaches in the immediate days ahead," Guterres said. "We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure and responsible development of AI — while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards, or additional measures to manage potential risks."
At Guterres' behest, the General Assembly established the first global scientific body on AI in 2025.
In its preliminary report in July, the 40-member panel warned that the rapid, unchecked use of AI at scale risks harm to the mental health of users, "potential use as a destructive tool, impacts on social, economic and environmental systems, and challenges associated with controlling the technology."
The secretary-general told reporters he is aware that geopolitical divides might pose problems. But he said countries "that have the highest capacity in the frontiers of AI" should establish contact, exchange information and agree on some common guardrails "to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at global level."
Guterres responded to a question asking whether next week's meeting of top officials from the UN's 193 member nations wouldn't be the perfect opportunity for a summit on curbing the excesses of AI. He said there wasn't time to properly prepare a meeting.
But he said, "I think it makes full sense at the right moment to have a serious international summit on artificial intelligence." And at a summit, he said, "it is absolutely essential to have everybody on board" — governments, companies, scientists and civil society — "and I hope that this will be possible."

The shape of a leader’s face might predict their likelihood of starting a war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:00:24 UTC
07:00:24 KST

Does the shape of a world leader’s face predict their likelihood of starting a war? New research suggests that leaders with wider facial proportions tend to be more prone to initiating international military conflicts, especially during their first years in power. The findings, published in Politics and the Life Sciences, provide evidence that subtle biological cues might offer a window into the psychological tendencies that shape global politics.
The facial width-to-height ratio is a physical measurement of the human face. It is calculated by dividing the distance between the outer cheekbones by the distance from the top of the upper lip to the middle of the brow. Over the years, evolutionary psychologists have proposed that this specific facial metric serves as a biological signal of a person’s underlying predisposition toward dominance and physical formidability. In ancestral environments, wider faces may have reliably signaled fighting ability, teaching humans to subconsciously read these proportions as indicators of aggression.
Earlier research discovered that wider facial proportions correlate with aggressive behavior in everyday situations. For example, a 2008 study found that men with larger facial width-to-height ratios tended to act more aggressively in laboratory experiments and professional hockey games. Later research showed this pattern held for political leaders making military decisions. A 2022 study found that United States presidents with wider faces were more likely to use military force abroad.
Citizens also seem to respond to these cues. As indicated by a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, people who perceive an ongoing threat of conflict between groups are more likely to prefer political leaders who look and act dominant.
The new research expands this line of inquiry globally. “One of the real world problems that interests me is why some leaders are more conflict-prone than others,” Ross Miller, an associate professor of political science at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, told PsyPost. “Even within the same states, leaders that confront similar security issues respond differently to threats. Why?”
While traditional political science often points to factors like a country’s economic power or strategic rivalries to explain wars, decisions to deploy military force fall to individual leaders. Past attempts to measure a leader’s aggressive tendencies usually relied on analyzing their speeches or biographies, which takes immense time and limits the number of leaders scientists can study. By using the facial width-to-height ratio, Miller sought to evaluate the aggressive predispositions of over a thousand world leaders to see if physical traits could predict international conflict across different cultures and eras.
“Traditional approaches emphasize important contextual factors – like power,” Miller explained. “For example, consider a traditional approach to this question: Why did Russia invade Ukraine? Because they are significantly more powerful than Ukraine, and figured they could force Ukraine to change its policy of joining NATO.” While these structural explanations are valid, he noted, his approach highlights that “it is also useful to take into account leaders’ qualities.”
To investigate this, Miller analyzed a massive dataset of 1,761 leaders from 174 countries over a 63-year period, from 1947 to 2010. This sample included nearly every major world leader from the post-World War II era. The idea to apply this metric to global conflict actually emerged from a parenting moment when Miller issued an empty threat to his daughter about throwing away her toys.
“That was a big threat, which I immediately regretted, because my daughter simply studied my face, checking to see if the resolve was there,” he recalled. “In class an idea formed: is there a literature on faces and conflict.” This realization led him to previous research on facial proportions and aggression, prompting him to spend his time during the COVID-19 pandemic compiling photos of world leaders.
To measure facial proportions, the researcher collected high-quality photographs of these leaders where they were facing the camera directly with a neutral expression. Using digital imaging software, Miller measured the width and height of each face to calculate the exact ratio. These facial measurements were then compared to a historical database of militarized interstate disputes.
This database records instances where leaders threatened, displayed, or actually used military force against another country. To ensure the results were not simply capturing other political dynamics, the analyses controlled for a variety of alternative factors. These included the country’s military power, geographic proximity to adversaries, whether the state was a democracy, and the leader’s age and gender.
The results indicated that leaders with higher facial width-to-height ratios were more likely to initiate international conflicts than leaders with narrower faces. Specifically, this effect was highly dependent on how long the leader had been in power. In the first year of their tenure, leaders with wider faces were roughly three times more likely to initiate a conflict compared to their peers with narrower faces.
“In my reading, the key takeaway from this work is that there seems to be an association between the [facial width-to-height ratio] of elected leaders and, particularly in their early tenure, the likelihood of initiating an international conflict,” said Alex Jones, an associate professor at Swansea University who was not involved in the study.
“Conflict is a rare event in IR [international relations], so the statistical, observation models often have difficulty making strong predictions because of that rarity,” Miller explained. “My results indicate that high-FWHR leaders are over three times as likely as low-FWHR leaders to initiate conflict. But we have to place that in context that we are starting from a low baseline – a low probability event. Tripling a small probability still leaves a pretty small probability. Just because a high-FWHR leader is in place does not mean automatic conflict initiation.”
While a relative threefold increase sounds substantial, the absolute number of conflicts initiated remains very small. Because full-scale military actions are so uncommon, minor shifts in probability can appear magnified when expressed as relative percentages.
Jones agreed that the actual increase in risk is slight. “The graphs highlight a change in probability of something like .02,” he told PsyPost, noting that in extremely large samples, almost all comparisons become statistically significant. “I’d assume that such a small effect probably doesn’t mean much in practical terms.”
This surge in aggression early in a leader’s time in office aligns with the idea that new leaders often use military force to establish their reputation and show adversaries that they will not back down. Once their aggressive tendencies become known to the international community, the need to prove themselves diminishes. Opposing countries may also actively avoid provoking leaders they know to be highly aggressive. As a result, the influence of facial proportions on conflict initiation faded the longer a leader remained in power.
“I was surprised that the latitude to initiate conflicts that leaders enjoy early in their tenure declines so rapidly,” Miller said. “By year three in power there is not much difference between low- and high-FWHR leaders. I expected it to diminish as other states adapt, but not that quickly.”
The findings are in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which questioned the validity of the facial width-to-height ratio as an evolutionary marker of dominance. That earlier study found that, when adjusting for body size, men in the general public did not actually have larger facial width-to-height ratios than women. However, it is worth noting that the earlier research focused on anatomical differences between sexes in the general population, whereas the new study specifically measures behavioral outcomes and conflict decisions among elite political leaders.
Jones also pointed out that “the assumption that [facial width-to-height ratio] is related to testosterone… has been tested a few times with not much support.” He warned against assuming a direct biological pipeline. “I think the clear painting of the results and a first reading is that the causal chain goes something like ‘hormones -> appearance -> behaviour -> conflict’,” he said. “I don’t think this provides good evidence for that.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. First, the facial width-to-height ratio is just one single physical characteristic. It does not account for other facial cues that people use to judge aggression, such as the width of the chin or the shape of the eyebrows. Second, measuring facial proportions from photographs can sometimes be inexact, though the researcher took steps to standardize the measurements by using multiple photos when possible.
This measurement challenge is significant, according to Jones. “[Facial width-to-height ratio] is a notoriously tricky measure,” he noted. It is “affected by all sorts of simple things like distance to the camera, head orientation, and so on.” He explained that his own 2025 research found the metric is highly sensitive to the vagaries of photography. “With a ‘wild’ dataset like this, it’s surely unstandardised and injects a lot of noise,” Jones added.
There is also a possibility that countries facing severe security threats purposefully select leaders who appear more dominant and aggressive. If a nation is already on the brink of war, voters or ruling elites might naturally elevate a leader with a wider face. This makes it difficult to completely separate the leader’s inherent aggression from the country’s existing path toward conflict.
“One reason I find these results interesting is that they complement work showing that people become more attracted to dominant-looking leaders when they perceive greater intergroup conflict,” Adi Wiezel, an assistant professor of psychology at Elon University, told PsyPost.
“Taken together, these findings raise interesting questions about the relationship between conflict, whom people select as leaders, and how those leaders subsequently behave,” continued Wiezel, who directs the Wiezel Behavior, Opinions, and Relations between Groups (BORG) Lab and was not involved in the research.
This potential bias in impressions means that a finding like this could emerge even if there is no inherent biological link between a leader’s appearance and their actual behavior. If a restless, conflict-prone nation intentionally chooses an intimidating leader, the environment itself may be the true cause of any subsequent wars.
“Whether that leader initiates action is due to a lot of factors, and if there’s no link between behaviour and appearance, then this finding might emerge as a function of the bias in impressions,” Jones said.
Wiezel cautioned against drawing definitive causal conclusions from observational data. “Facial appearance can shape how other people perceive and respond to us, and those reactions can themselves influence behavior and opportunities over time,” she explained. “The study identifies a provocative association across a very large historical sample, but it cannot isolate which of these possible pathways produced it.”
The dataset also lacked controls for the race or ethnicity of the leaders, as comprehensive historical data on these factors across 174 countries does not currently exist. Different populations can have varying average facial structures, which could influence the broader patterns. Future research might explore how these facial metrics interact with a leader’s personal history, such as whether they experienced childhood trauma or served in the military.
Wiezel would like to see future research examine how a leader’s age and gender affect this relationship. While the new study found no difference between men and women, she noted that “the relatively small number of conflicts initiated by women limits how definitive that conclusion can be.” Age could also be an important factor, she added, because “some of the theory linking facial characteristics to aggression emphasizes physical formidability and intrasexual competition. This raises the possibility that such processes may matter more among younger men.”
For his part, Jones suggested using a bottom-up cognitive psychology approach that decomposes facial images into various sources of variability. “I’d like to see a more holistic approach to examining facial appearance and its link with behaviour undertaken,” he said, which “opens up novel theory driven approaches.”
Additionally, scientists hope to examine whether wider-faced leaders are less likely to engage in international cooperation and peace-building, providing a more complete picture of their foreign policy behaviors.
“I am working on another paper on U.S. interventions in conflicts guided by FWHR,” Miller said.
The study, “Looks that kill: Facial metrics and international conflict 1947–2010,” was authored by Ross Miller.

Thousands Protest in Malta as Alleged Mastermind Walks Free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:56:00 UTC
06:56:00 KST

Reported by
Outrage spilled onto the streets of the Maltese capital on Wednesday evening as demonstrators gathered at the heart of Valletta, shifting from vigils to protests to demand political accountability following the acquittal of the alleged mastermind behind the 2017 assassination of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
For 107 consecutive months - on the 16th of every month since Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb outside her home - civil society groups held silent vigils. But the Sept. 2 acquittal of Yorgen Fenech, a prominent businessman accused of orchestrating and financing the plot, transformed that quiet grief into open defiance.
Chanting “Mafia! Mafia!” and “Injustice!”, thousands of protesters marched from the Parliament building to a memorial standing directly opposite Malta’s Law Courts to lay flowers and light candles before Caruana Galizia’s portrait. Banners carried by the crowd called for the protection of journalists and democracy, declaring: “The Trial Has Ended. Our Work Has Not” and “Impunity Ends Here.”
“Justice has not been served,” Rebecca Gauci, a protester told OCCRP. “The people who carried out the murder are still running free, and something has to happen.”
She added that justice was essential both for the Caruana Galizia family, who have “been through hell and back,” and for the country as a whole.
“This can impact anyone… I’m here because this should concern everyone in Malta – this concerns us all and we should all be angry at this.”
Organized by the civil rights groups Repubblika and Occupy Justice, the demonstration was framed as a direct challenge to the nation's political establishment.
“We will not accept that the search for the full truth ends here,” the groups said in a joint statement, asserting that leaders “have failed Malta for far too long.”
Pia Zammit, a founder of Occupy Justice, urged authorities to pass “effective laws against the mafia” and follow the financial trail to reclaim illicit funds for the public. “It’s not calling out the mafia that gives Malta a bad reputation - it’s the mafia that ruins Malta’s reputation,” Zammit told the crowd.
Fenech, 44, the former chief executive of the Tumas Group, a major Maltese business conglomerate and investment company operating primarily in real estate, hospitality, and energy, was cleared of complicity and criminal association after a nine-member jury deliberated for eight hours following a landmark 55-day trial. The jury voted eight to one on both charges to acquit him.
Prosecutor Anthony Vella, whose team is expected to appeal the verdict, had argued that Fenech paid 150,000 euro ($170,000) to a middleman to engage hitmen and subsequently funneled leaked police intelligence to the killers. The trial laid bare the ties between Fenech and Malta’s governing elite, revealing WhatsApp exchanges with former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, regulatory chiefs, and the deputy police commissioner who initially led the murder investigation.
While five men have been convicted for their roles in the bombing - including hitmen serving up to 40 years and two men sentenced to life for supplying military-grade explosives - Fenech’s acquittal leaves the plot without a convicted mastermind, fueling fears among activists that political complicity will go unpunished.
Manuel Delia, a co-founder of Repubblika, insisted the acquittal should not cause the public to surrender. He called for sustained solidarity with Caruana Galizia’s family, who he noted turned their private grief into a broad public crusade, “fighting for journalists they did not know and institutions that failed them.”

UNITED NATIONS, September 17. /TASS/. Russia favors a comprehensive approach to Afghanistan, which envisages a trust-based dialogue with its authorities and is free from the language of pressure and blackmail, Russian Permanent Representative to the UN Vasily Nebenzya said.

ISIS-K member sentenced to 20 years in prison in case tied to Kabul bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:49:32 UTC
06:49:32 KST

ISIS-K member sentenced to 20 years in prison in case tied to deadly 2021 Kabul airport suicide bombing
A member of an Islamic State affiliate in Afghanistan was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization, which took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 U.S. service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the American military's chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the affiliate, known as ISIS-K. But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on Aug. 26, 2021.
U.S. troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a lone suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah's role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai International Airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that President Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress. Sharifullah was captured in early 2025 by Pakistani intelligence and the CIA near Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, and was extradited to the United States.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a "dedicated terrorist" who expressed no remorse for the "unfathomable" grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of the U.S. service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children's sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families. Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps Lance Cpl. Jared Schmitz.
"They may have taken his life, but they'll never take his legacy," Schmitz said. "A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for."
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, Army Staff Sgt. Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was "forever changed" by the attack.
"No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart," she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers say he was never an ISIS-K leader and has not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
"He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial," defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that "from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to ISIS-K, Sharifullah's carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans."
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISIS-K, but did not reach a unanimous decision on whether any deaths at the airport "resulted from" that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had decided that question.
In a statement Wednesday, Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said Sharifullah "spent nearly a decade at the heart of a horrific campaign of terror, providing critical support for attacks against civilians around the world and, ultimately, contributed to the deaths of 13 U.S. servicemembers and dozens of others at Abbey Gate."
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to "catch and kill the crusaders" from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. They said Sharifulla aided in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people, and a 2016 suicide bombing that targeted security guards at the Canadian embassy in Kabul.
His role in those ISIS-K attacks, the Justice Department said, included providing surveillance, transporting suicide bombers or weapons and communicating with attackers.
Ahead of the 2021 Kabul airport bombing, Sharifullah surveilled a route to the airport to watch out for Taliban checkpoints, prosecutors said. He "communicated to ISIS-K leadership that the route was clear," and hours later, an ISIS-K operative named Abdul Rahman al-Logari detonated the suicide bomb, the Justice Department said.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the U.S.
His lawyers also said in a sentencing memo that Sharifullah was not an ISIS-K leader, but was instead a "conduit for messages passed between different actors in the organization."
"No evidence at trial linked Mr. Sharifullah to the [Abbey Gate] attack, besides his own statements made while his family was detained by Pakistani authorities known to torture detainees," his attorneys said.

US troops must prepare to fight around the moon, Trump’s top military adviser says
The comments by Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, come soon after the US revealed that it has deployed weapons in space
American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth’s orbit but around the moon, President Donald Trump’s top military adviser said on Wednesday, looking ahead to a new frontier in warfare after the US revealed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.
General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told service members and industry figures at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference outside Washington that the US military should adapt now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”.
Space Force, the newest military service, which was created by Trump in 2019, is preparing to fight in space and around the moon because “humanity is advancing deeper into space – the Space Force’s job is to help be prepared to defend US interests,” Lieutenant General Gregory Gagnon, head of the force’s Combat Forces Command, told reporters separately.
The announcement that the US military is ready to fight in the area between high Earth orbit and the moon itself comes days after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed at the same conference that the US has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons”.

One Nation volunteer previously promoted neo-Nazi ideologies
Unknown

One Nation faces questions over volunteer that tribunal once linked to neo-Nazi group
In short:
A man who volunteered for One Nation during a West Australian by-election was previously named in a federal tribunal ruling as someone who promoted neo-Nazi ideologies.
David Donis handed out how-to-vote cards and attended the party's victory event, sparking questions about One Nation's vetting processes.
What's next?
WA's One Nation leader Rod Caddies appears to have pre-empted the revelation, saying if an extremist had infiltrated the party, they would be expelled.
A man who volunteered for One Nation during the party's successful West Australian by-election was previously named by a federal tribunal for promoting neo-Nazi ideologies.
David Donis handed out how-to-vote cards for One Nation in the state seat of Secret Harbour last month, sparking fresh questions about vetting months after Pauline Hanson revealed the party had shut branches she said were "infiltrated by extremists".
Mr Donis was a founding member and president of the Society of Western Australian Nationalists (SWAN), a now-deregistered organisation the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) found was a racist extremist group.
The tribunal's comments about Mr Donis were made in a 2023 case concerning an army reservist's security clearance.
Mr Donis was identified by other political volunteers at the Singleton Primary School polling booth on August 27 and later pictured standing near the stage at One Nation's victory party that night.
Two people told the ABC there was an incident during the day where Mr Donis yelled at a voter leaving the polling station, prompting other volunteers to intervene and calm the situation.
A One Nation spokesperson said the individual the ABC identified as David Donis was "not a member of One Nation".
"Our party does not condone extremist views, and where such issues are identified they're acted upon swiftly by the party," the spokesperson said.
It is understood Mr Donis was a volunteer rather than a formal member and would not be permitted to continue associating with One Nation.
A Liberal source told the ABC that Mr Donis had previously been a member of the party as a teen but ultimately left when it became known his views were "not welcome".
Mr Donis has previously denied promoting neo-Nazi ideologies, but in 2023 the AAT said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members had done so.
One Nation's vetting has previously come under scrutiny, with Senator Hanson revealing in June that the party had shut down four branches.
"I'm being infiltrated by these extremists, so it's all the time happening with One Nation; they set us up all the time," she told Nine papers.
One senior West Australian Liberal told the ABC that One Nation has had "years of warnings" about problems with candidates and people associated with the party.
They said background checks should be "second nature".
"That includes basic vetting to ensure people publicly representing the party do not have verifiable links to neo-Nazis, white supremacists or organisations advocating political violence," the Liberal said.
Man adhered to "neo-Nazi ideologies"
In mid-2023, the AAT accepted evidence Mr Donis was a member of SWAN, which it determined was a "nationalist and racist extremist group".
Mr Donis denied the allegation, but the tribunal said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members "adhere to, and promote, racist and neo-Nazi ideologies" and supported politically motivated and communal violence.
The findings about Mr Donis emerged in a case in which the AAT upheld ASIO's decision that an army reservist posed a security risk and should lose his NV1 clearance.
The AAT said the reservist had close ties to Mr Donis and SWAN, which the tribunal accepted was a nationalist and racist extremist group after hearing "closed evidence" — classified material that could not be disclosed publicly.
The case noted SWAN came into existence around 2018 or early 2019, with Mr Donis as a "founding member and president".
Incorporation documents show SWAN members voted to voluntarily deregister the organisation due to "inactivity" in October of 2023, three months after the AAT findings.
One Nation WA pre-empts volunteer revelation
West Australian One Nation leader Rod Caddies appeared to pre-empt potential controversy over a party volunteer last week in a video shared on social media.
Mr Caddies criticised state Liberal MP Anthony Spagnolo for submitting a series of questions on notice to the Labor government "probing some tie" between One Nation's "Secret Harbour campaign and neo-Nazis".
He accused Mr Spagnolo of taking a page out of the "radical left playbook" by "trying to take One Nation down and tie us to Nazis".
"I don't know what sad little 'gotcha' the member thinks he has. I suspect it's something about some low-level volunteer or some link like that,"
Mr Caddies said if that were the case it meant the Liberal Party would have to own "everything their volunteers have said or done".
"The next time someone loosely affiliated with the Liberal Party has a shady background or says something crazy, I'll make sure every one of their members are set to the same standard you set," he said.
Mr Caddies then said even if the Liberals did "uncover something" it would not prove anything.
"If it turns out some idiot has managed to weasel his way into One Nation, we'll expel him; that's simple. If an extremist has infiltrated One Nation, it's by hiding their extremism," he said.
Volunteer witnessed shouting at voter
Mr Donis initially attracted the attention of volunteers from other political parties at a Secret Harbour by-election polling booth last month after he yelled at a voter.
One witness said it was before midday when they saw Mr Donis interact with a mother and daughter leaving the venue after voting.
They overheard Mr Donis wish the pair a "good day" before adding he hoped they had put One Nation "first" and Labor "last" on the ballot paper.
The witness said the woman replied she was more likely to put One Nation last, which prompted Mr Donis to accuse her of supporting abortion and setting a "bad example" for her daughter.
They said the woman gave a dismissive response, but Mr Donis kept yelling as she walked away across the car park.
The witness said the One Nation "booth captain" at the school intervened to try and quiet Mr Donis, as did a nearby Liberal member who urged him to "settle down".
They said there were no further incidents at the booth involving Mr Donis that day.
Later in the evening, Mr Donis was spotted at an event for supporters of One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen.
The ABC has been unable to contact David Donis.

Israel and Morocco have agreed to open embassies in their respective countries following trilateral talks between their senior diplomats and the United States ambassador to the United Nations in New York.

Diplomatic elevation

Officials from both governments confirmed following Wednesday's discussions that a series of economic agreements will be finalised before the end of the year.
The Israeli statement added that "high-level reciprocal visits between the two countries will take place in the coming months."

How Democrats Are Mobilizing to Counter Potential Election Interference Amid Trump Concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:38:45 UTC
06:38:45 KST

With the midterm elections less than two months away, Democrats are training thousands of volunteers on how to respond to any potential incidents of voter intimidation at the polls in November.
The New Battlefield Project—an initiative that is being coordinated by the Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), which operates under the Democratic National Committee (DNC)—involves training at least 10,000 volunteers so that they’ll be equipped to counter interference or intimidation at polling locations across the country if such situations arise, says Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC.
The on-the-ground team—dubbed the “Democracy Protectors”—will be wearing blue to distinguish themselves, and will be trained in de-escalating conflicts and documenting any potential “bad actors and bad behavior.” Information about such incidents would then be passed along to the state party and the DNC to take action where necessary. Kleeb says the volunteers will also be helpful resources to voters—for instance, they can help direct people to the right polling locations. The trainings, Kleeb adds, are based on constitutional observer trainings that the Minnesota Democratic Party coordinated amid Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in the state.
In addition to the Democracy Protectors, the New Battlefield Project includes teams that are focused on encouraging citizens to register to vote and to vote early, as well as on dispelling any misinformation or disinformation spreading online ahead of Election Day.
The DNC musters an election protection program every year, and states sometimes train volunteers to perform similar tasks. But this year’s effort is larger in its scope and is being coordinated nationwide.
Kleeb says Democrats were spurred to launch the initiative because of speculation and concerns they were hearing from voters, candidates, and elected officials that President Donald Trump could send federal agents to polling places.
“About six months ago, state parties really started to put in place a program that we thought would address the threat of Donald Trump and what we think his allies are doing this cycle,” Kleeb says. “We heard Trump and Steve Bannon talking about how they could potentially be sending the National Guard, the military, or ICE agents outside of polling locations.”
“We take them very seriously,” she continues.
Trump Administration floats sending federal agents to the polls
The Justice Department announced last month that its Civil Rights Division would be “monitoring polling sites in Florida and Wyoming for the states’ primary elections to ensure transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law.”
On Tuesday, FBI Director Kash Patel also indicated that he was not opposed to the idea of dispatching federal agents to voting locations.
Separately, Trump has deployed the National Guard to cities across the country, including Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., with the stated goal of helping combat crime, though the data indicates that crime rates in many of those cities have been falling for years. When asked in May if he would send members of the National Guard or ICE officers to the polls, Trump replied, “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”
The troops’ presence, as well as comments from the President and his allies, has raised concerns from some Democrats that the military could be sent to voting locations. Members of the military are prohibited under federal law from being sent to “any place where a general or special election is held,” however. And in August, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin in a letter that the “Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections. Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said earlier this month that ICE—which has also ramped up enforcement in cities around the U.S. since Trump returned to office—“isn’t there to patrol the polling places.” But he added that “We’re there to enforce specific threats,” a comment that exacerbated fears among Democrats, advocates, and voters that ICE agents may show up at the polls in November.
When asked about the possibility of ICE agents being stationed at the polls during the midterms, then-White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said earlier this year that that was “not something [she has] ever heard the President consider.”
“I can’t guarantee that an ICE agent won’t be around a polling location in November,” Leavitt said in February. “I mean, that's frankly a very silly hypothetical question. But what I can tell you is I haven’t heard the President discuss any formal plans to put ICE outside of polling locations. It’s a disingenuous question.”
Kleeb says that Democrats wanted to be prepared just in case.
“Maybe nothing will happen,” Kleeb says. “Maybe they don’t send anybody anywhere. Maybe that’s going to be true. But as the Democratic party … we do not want to wake up the next day after Election Day, saying to ourselves, ‘Damn it! They said that they were going to do this, and we didn’t believe them,’ or ‘We thought that it was just them thumping their chest.’ We’re taking them seriously.”
When asked by TIME about the New Battlefield Project, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement that “the only ‘fears’ Americans have about our elections are being fueled by extreme liberal Democrats who refuse to support commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections and other basic election security measures like Voter ID.”
Bis’ comment appeared to be referring to the SAVE America Act, the restrictive voter ID bill that the President has forcefully championed during his second term that has been met with vocal backlash from Democrats and voting rights advocates. The measure passed the House, but Senate Republicans have said they don’t have the votes required for it to pass the upper chamber.
‘An air of menace’: Experts express concerns over Trump Administration’s actions
Experts have expressed concerns about potential election interference in the November midterms, in light of recent actions taken by the Trump Administration.
“The Trump Administration has been progressively trying to regulate and interfere in elections in ways which are not constitutional,” alleged Pippa Norris, a lecturer in comparative politics at the Harvard Kennedy School and founding director of the Electoral Integrity Project. “Most of his actions haven’t actually succeeded, but they have sown confusion, and therefore there’s been problems because they can undermine public trust in the system.”
She cites, for instance, recent reports that the Trump Administration has directed federal agents to comb through voter rolls, which are overseen by the states, in a quest to find non-citizens. Research overwhelmingly shows that voter fraud is extremely rare.
Richard Briffault, a professor at the Columbia Law School, says that Trump “has been consistently complaining about fraud and misconduct at the polls, always without evidence.” Trump has repeatedly falsely claimed that the 2020 election was “stolen” from him.
Briffault adds that the Trump Administration has dispatched federal officials—such as those from the Justice Department, the National Guard, and ICE—to various places, which could be sparking concerns among local elections officials and voters about potential conflicts at the polls. He also points to the Trump Administration’s effort to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots—a move that was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, which the President railed against on social media this week.
“It is not surprising that many people are nervous that [Trump] might do something to try and disrupt the election if he feels it’s going against him,” Briffault says. “We don’t know what he’s going to do.”
“There’s kind of an air of menace that the Administration has generated,” he continues. “Whether they do anything, we won’t know until Election Day or the lead-up to it and after.”
Norris says that the practice of sending people to polling places to counter intimidation is often used in other countries during contentious elections. But she cast doubt that the New Battlefield Project was “the most effective thing which the DNC can do,” expressing concern that there isn’t enough time before the November midterms to effectively train volunteers in recognizing and responding to potential issues and that that could raise the possibility of “disputes” or conflicts at polling places, particularly if Republican organizations also dispatch volunteers to those locations.
Training for the volunteers started about three weeks ago, according to Kleeb. She adds that Democrats are taking the concern of potential conflict “very seriously;” a critical part of the training, she says, is teaching volunteers how to de-escalate tense situations while making it “very clear” that they should not engage if any violence erupts.
Briffault says it’s not clear yet if the initiative will be effective at countering potential intimidation, but that it could foster “a level of comfort” for voters at the polls. He notes, though, that there are so many polling places across the U.S. that it’s not possible for the New Battlefield Project to have a presence at all of them.
“I do think it’s important for people to know that there will be other people there looking out to make sure the election goes smoothly and without disruption,” he says.
Kleeb says that the volunteers won’t be at every polling place in the country, but each state party will decide the locations that have the most need for them. In Nebraska, for instance, Democrats think the second congressional district is “the most flippable congressional seat” in the state, so the party plans to station volunteers in high-traffic precincts in that area. In some states, the party may look to dispatch volunteers to polling places in areas with high immigrant populations or with many young people who may be voting for the first time, she adds.
“Our elections are safe and secure,” Kleeb says. “The Democracy Protectors Program is put in place to ensure that voters have a friendly face outside the polling location to make sure that their vote is counted.”

Walla said protesters gathered outside Tzur’s parents’ home to denounce her and co-director Yuval Abraham, with some accusing the filmmakers of portraying Israeli soldiers as “murderers” before the world. 
Activists linked to Ben-Gvir’s party
Israel Hayom, citing unnamed sources, reported that organizers of the demonstration and many participants were activists and campaign staff associated with the Jewish Power party led by far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The newspaper said messages circulated on social media ahead of the protest included explicit calls for violence.
The demonstration came shortly after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would advance two bills targeting people he accused of defaming Israeli soldiers, remarks that referred in part to the “Naza” documentary.
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir on Monday instructed the military prosecutor to examine possible legal action against the filmmakers, while Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar on Wednesday asked Shin Bet chief David Zini to open an urgent investigation into the documentary, according to Israeli media.
The film, directed by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Abraham and Tzur, includes accounts from Israeli military personnel who said they witnessed actions in Gaza, including the burning of residential areas used as shelters and the killing of people during food distribution.
“Naza” is an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike, according to the filmmakers.

AI rivalry hangs over Trump-Xi talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:38:05 UTC
06:38:05 KST

AI rivalry hangs over Trump-Xi talks
WASHINGTON, Sept 16 - The race for AI supremacy is set to hang over next week's meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Washington and Beijing view advances in AI as critical to their economic and military competitiveness, but they remain at odds over access to advanced chips, allegations of technology copying and regulation of the AI industry.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend to discuss AI-related issues before the leaders' summit. Here are some of the key talking points and disputes.
MILITARY ATTACKS
An AI system that interfered with a nuclear command network or launched a military cyber operation could leave either government with minutes to decide whether the other government had attacked.
U.S. and Chinese security experts are urging both governments to prepare for such scenarios. They have proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyberattacks, and a hotline for incidents involving autonomous AI.
Open questions include how to stop an accident from being mistaken for an attack, which military decisions machines should never make and how nuclear-armed rivals communicate when technology behaves unexpectedly.
COPYING U.S. TECHNOLOGY
Copying U.S. technology through a technique known as “distillation” has become a flashpoint in the battle over AI model development.
Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.
The U.S. government accused six Chinese companies in September of maliciously copying American AI products using distillation, with law enforcement officials saying in a statement that the firms did so "likely with Chinese government awareness.”
The U.S. made a similar accusation in April ahead of Trump's visit to Beijing. The Chinese embassy in Washington called the allegations “baseless.” CHIP EXPORTS TO CHINA
Chinese access to key U.S. technologies underpinning the artificial intelligence boom is a point of friction between the two countries.
Since 2022, the U.S. has imposed sweeping restrictions on shipments of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China.
There is evidence of advanced AI chips being smuggled into the country, though the scale is unknown.
The U.S. has been considering restrictions on the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access data centers in other countries to prevent those firms from benefiting from Nvidia’s advanced chips.
There have been some exceptions to this effort. Late last year, Trump decided to allow sales of Nvidia’s H200 AI chips. H200s are not the most sophisticated chips available, but their sale prompted concerns from China hawks in Washington who argued the chips could bolster China’s AI capabilities. REGULATION
The two leaders have fundamentally different perspectives on how involved they should be in the AI sector.
Trump has brushed aside calls for new federal AI rules, saying on Monday that the U.S. only needs a strong president, which the country has "in spades." He said calls from AI executives for regulation of the technology are a "hoax."
The Chinese government has rules governing AI algorithms and the data used to train them, including requiring content generated by AI to be clearly labeled.
US VS. CHINA AI DEVELOPMENT RACE
The estimates U.S. officials typically give put Chinese AI models just a few months behind their American counterparts, although industry leaders increasingly describe them as neck and neck.
In 2025, then-White House AI adviser David Sacks said China was likely three to six months behind the United States on AI development. Earlier this year, the U.S. Commerce Department put DeepSeek V4 Pro about eight months behind frontier models.
Many in the industry say the gap is shrinking quickly. Last month, Hugging Face Chief Executive Clement Delangue said China was winning the race as far as open-weight models were concerned — and likely was not far off in terms of frontier models either. Frontier models are the most advanced AI tools and open-weight models have publicly accessible core elements that can be downloaded, inspected and modified.
“I wouldn’t be surprised if they start dominating at the frontier either by the end of this year or next year at the rate of progress,” Delangue told broadcaster CNBC on August 3. REUTERS
