Houthi's Bab el-Mandab gains expose Saudi failures in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:35:42 UTC
06:35:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthi's Bab el-Mandab gains expose Saudi failures in Yemen
The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandab Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of US protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced U.S.- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the United States nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defence coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
Allies collapse, partners hesitate
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declined to directly intervene militarily.
Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt said Riyadh wanted Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source said MbS asked President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
A Saudi source said the meeting was scheduled long before the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February and "while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss."
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandeb — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilise the region via a détente with Iran, has unravelled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defence coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
The Yemen Trap
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and U.S. strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen."
(Reuters)

aston martin and brough superior turn their track superbike into a road machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:33:09 UTC
06:33:09 KST

Aston Martin and Brough Superior introduce the AMB 002 Roadster, their first motorcycle designed and certified for use on public roads. The new model follows the track-only AMB 001, unveiled in 2019, and the AMB 001 Pro of 2022, extending the collaboration between the British marques beyond the circuit. Developed from scratch rather than adapted from either predecessor, the AMB 002 is limited to 300 individually built examples, with first deliveries scheduled for the third quarter of 2027.
The roadster combines compact proportions with sculpted carbon fiber bodywork shaped by the Aston Martin Design Studio. A smooth carbon fiber fuel tank rises toward the rider, while crescent-shaped openings carved into the side fairings channel cooling air around the engine. Automotive references appear throughout: Aston Martin’s side strake passes through the fairing and wraps around the headlamp, twin oval exhausts reference the Vanquish, DB12 S and DBX S, and blade-like rear lights recall the Vulcan, Valkyrie and Valhalla. Keyless operation, a backlit ignition button and leather saddle pads add details more commonly associated with the company’s road cars.
the AMB 002 is built for public roads | all images courtesy of Aston Martin
A FIVE-KILOGRAM TITANIUM FRAME HOLDS THE NEW V-TWIN
At the center of the AMB 002 is an all-new 1,083cc four-stroke water-cooled V-twin, producing 130 bhp and 110 Nm of torque. Developed for stronger low- and mid-range response on the road, the engine is machined and assembled in-house at Brough Superior’s headquarters in Toulouse, France, including CNC-machined billet engine cases developed to reduce weight. It sits within a titanium backbone frame milled from a solid billet that weighs just five kilograms and contributes to a 50:50 weight distribution.
Carbon fiber body panels and fuel tank help keep the motorcycle’s overall weight to 190 kilograms, while concentrating mass low within the chassis. Up front, Brough Superior’s double-wishbone Fior fork separates steering and braking forces rather than relying on a conventional telescopic fork. Evolved from the system developed for the AMB 001 Pro, the suspension is intended to maintain the bike’s geometry under braking and reduce dive, particularly when braking while leaned into a corner.
sculpted carbon fiber shapes the roadster’s body
FROM TRACK-ONLY EXPERIMENT TO ROAD-LEGAL ROADSTER
The AMB 002 marks a shift in a collaboration that began with motorcycles conceived primarily as collectible track machines. The first AMB 001 paired Aston Martin styling with Brough Superior engineering, while the subsequent AMB 001 Pro pushed the partnership further toward circuit performance. For the new Roadster, the brands instead focus on making the same combination of lightweight materials, mechanical detailing and limited production usable beyond the racetrack.
Each AMB 002 will be hand-built by Brough Superior in Toulouse, combining carbon fiber, titanium and machined components with hand-finished leather details. Production remains capped at 300 motorcycles, continuing the limited-edition approach of its predecessors while significantly increasing the number that will reach owners. Aston Martin and Brough Superior have not announced pricing for the Roadster, but orders are already being accepted ahead of deliveries beginning in Q3 2027.

Left on brink of victory in Swedish election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:32:18 UTC
06:32:18 KST

Sweden's Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson speaks in Stockholm on election night on Sept. 13, 2026. | Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images
Social Democrat Leader Magdalena Andersson is on course to become Sweden’s next prime minister as her left-wing bloc holds an unassailable lead over the right and far right with 99.9% of results declared.
By 10.30 p.m. on Wednesday night, Andersson’s four-party grouping was three seats ahead of Ulf Kristersson’s alliance of the right and far-right parties in the race to control the 349-seat parliament.
The Swedish Election Authority is set to confirm the “preliminary” result when all the votes have finished being counted, expected on Thursday.
Advertisement
The election is one of the closest in recent Swedish history, and offered voters a sharp choice between electing a new left-wing government or allowing far-right ministers into power for the first time.
Swedish public broadcaster SVT called the election for Andersson’s side on Wednesday night. Her Social Democrats are Sweden’s biggest party and have enjoyed the loose support of three other opposition parties who are seen as her likely coalition partners: The Greens, the Center Party, and the Left Party.
Kristersson’s conservative Moderates have been campaigning alongside the Christian Democrats, the Liberals and the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. His allies do not expect him to concede defeat until Andersson wins a vote in parliament to prove she can command a majority. That vote won’t happen before Sept. 29 at the earliest.
Coalition negotiations will begin in earnest once the final outcome is confirmed. In theory any combination of parties can form into a government but in reality, the two-bloc system is likely to hold, meaning Andersson will seek to govern with some or all of her left-leaning partner parties.
Andersson’s Social Democrats stand on 99 seats, with her most natural allies in the Greens on 22. But that still leaves her 54 seats short of a majority and with a potentially difficult task persuading the other two parties in her bloc to cooperate with each other.
The Left Party, which has a historic association with communists, is emboldened by increasing its seat tally at this election to 30. And it has said the price of supporting a government will be gaining ministers inside the new top team.
Advertisement
But the Center Party’s leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has said she cannot support this, because the “fringes” must not dominate the next government. Thand Ringqvist, whose party is set to take 25 seats — enough to get Andersson’s bloc a majority — ideally wants to form a new centrist administration without either the Left Party or the far-right Sweden Democrats. But the parliamentary numbers do not add up to a majority for such a grouping.
The Center Party has said it will start talks with Andersson’s Social Democrats. Thand Ringqvist was clear on Wednesday night that Kristersson’s rightwing bloc had “lost their government mandate.” But she told SVT that “at the same time, the election result, as it stands, does not give a mandate for a political left turn.”
Kristersson had promised to elevate representatives of the far-right Sweden Democrats into ministerial positions in his government if he won. In the end, while his Moderates party increased their vote share, the SD fell backwards, bucking the recent trend that had seen far right populists gain ground elsewhere in Europe.

Why women in China are still at risk of abduction and forced marriage
The latest incident has exposed many failings in local authorities’ work in a country where a mindset of favouring sons over daughters still exists
One stormy night last month, a driver surnamed He saw two tall men get out of a car in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen and pull a young woman off the street and into the vehicle. During the struggle, her umbrella fell to the ground.
She did not appear willing. Suspicious, He followed the vehicle and later reported the incident to local police, supplying them with footage he had recorded. Thanks to him and the police, the abducted 18-year-old was rescued from a forced marriage.
According to media reports, the teenager, originally from Lanzhou, Gansu province, had been promised to a man by her parents without her knowledge or consent. After receiving the agreed price from the prospective groom’s family, her parents forced her to drop out of school.
The teenager sought help via online posts and eventually a non-profit organisation found her a job in a Shenzhen coffee shop. But her parents, intent on marrying her off, tracked her down and sent a team to stake out her workplace and ambush her, driving her over 20 hours back towards home before they were stopped by the police.

Argentina court orders halt to Sea Lion oil project off Falkland Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
An Argentine federal court on ordered the suspension of work Wednesday linked to the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falkland Islands, involving Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and British firm Rockhopper Exploration, according to Argentine media
Federal Judge Mariel Borruto, based in the Rio Grande in Tierra del Fuego province, granted a preliminary injunction ordering the companies to refrain from starting or continuing work needed to develop the offshore oil project,
The order covers drilling, subsea installations and the start of commercial oil production, according to details of the ruling reported.
The Sea Lion project is located 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands, an archipelago administered by the UK but claimed by Argentina. Navitas and Rockhopper made a final investment decision on the project in late 2025.
The ruling came after a lawsuit was filed by the Center of Ex-Combatants of the Falkland Islands in La Plata, and an environmental lawyers’ association seeking to stop the project on environmental and sovereignty grounds.
Borruto ordered the suspension until an environmental impact assessment is carried out before the relevant Argentine authorities.
The judge also ordered the companies to provide information on the status of the project, its schedule, wells, floating production facilities, contractors, financing sources, insurers and environmental studies.
The court said the measure is provisional and does not constitute a final ruling on the companies’ responsibility or on all issues raised in the main case.
Argentina has stepped up legal and diplomatic action against oil companies operating around the Falkland Islands.
President Javier Milei’s government has opposed the development, arguing that the islands and surrounding maritime areas are part of Argentine territory.
The UK has administered the islands since 1833 and rejects Argentina’s sovereignty claim. London also supports economic activity on the territory.

Britain has reaffirmed its "firm support" for Kosovo’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity following a war crimes verdict against former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci earlier Wednesday.
In a statement, British Minister for Europe Lord Wood of Anfield expressed that the UK respects the independence of the Court and its judicial process and remains committed to justice, accountability and reconciliation across the region.
"The UK remains a close friend and partner of Kosovo, firmly supporting its sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, as well as peace across the Western Balkans," he noted.

The minister underlined that at this important moment, political leaders and public figures have a responsibility to promote calm, ensure any reactions remain peaceful, and put people’s safety first.
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention committed as top commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army during the country's break from Serbia in the 1990s.
Born in 1968, Thaci became the first prime minister of Kosovo from 2008 to 2014 and served as president from 2016 until his resignation in 2020.
Kosovo declared its unilateral independence from Serbia on Feb. 17, 2008, but Serbia still sees Kosovo as its "own territory."

Ukrainian Parliament Passes Key First-Reading Reforms for Parcel Tax and Small Business Bankruptcy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:09:29 UTC
06:09:29 KST

The Verkhovna Rada on Sept. 16 passed two significant draft bills in their first readings, advancing key fiscal and business reforms required under Ukraine’s international funding commitments.
Lawmakers backed Draft No. 16051-1, with 273 votes, to introduce a 20% value-added tax (VAT) on cross-border e-commerce parcels valued at under €150 ($170).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the proposed rules, foreign online marketplaces and digital platforms would be responsible for calculating and remitting the tax directly.
Personal non-commercial shipments worth up to €45 ($52), unaccompanied luggage worth up to €150 ($173), and imported goods designated for military and energy needs will remain tax-free.
The passage follows almost a year of political pushback: parliament had previously failed to pass the parcel tax twice, despite appeals from Serhiy Marchenko, the finance minister, and Serhii Koretskyi, prime minister, before President Volodymyr Zelensky directly urged lawmakers to support it.
The legislation aims to generate around Hr.10 billion ($224 million) annually for a dedicated state budget fund to support Ukraine’s armed forces, while leveling the playing field between domestic and foreign retailers.
The reform is one of several structural benchmarks under Ukraine’s updated IMF program, required to release an upcoming $692 million tranche.
The parcel -tax measure was included among commitments signed in November 2025 and is also linked to progress toward €3.7 billion ($4.27 billion) in EU macro-financial assistance.
Ukraine Plans War-Risk Insurance Fund, Considers 1% VAT Increase to Cover Business Losses
During the same session, parliament approved No. 15024 with 270 votes to institute simplified, lower-cost insolvency procedures for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).
The measure limits proceedings to a maximum of 180 days, without extensions; safeguards employee wages; and harmonizes national law with EU Directive 2019/1023.
The bill fulfills one of several indicators under the Ukraine Facility plan needed to secure €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) in EU funding.
To take effect, both measures still require approval in a second reading, alongside key amendments to the Customs Code.
According to the August 2026 Monitoring Report published by the RRR4U consortium, Kyiv is navigating critical bottlenecks across three major donor pipelines, creating severe risks for the national budget despite recent policy breakthroughs.
Ukraine still faces 13 unfulfilled reform indicators from late 2025 through mid-2026, leaving around $4 billion in macro-financial assistance for 2026 frozen. Koretskyi told lawmakers that Ukraine is counting on $30 billion from partners this year, contingent on parliament delivering the reforms it promised.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says he'll be watching the home affairs minister's migration announcement today with "absolute fascination".

Speaking to Channel Nine, Joyce says the migration policy sounds like One Nation's and has labelled Tony Burke "the greatest no-show since Amelia Earhart" for delivering his speech six weeks late.
One Nation has unveiled its plan to slash immigration by 750,000 places over three years. Essentially, student visas would be capped at about a third of current intake, and visas for the families of skilled migrants would be cut to zero.
Asked by Channel Nine whether his party will do any modelling on its policy, Joyce has suggested One Nation would be happy for economists to look over it.

Former Labor Party strategist and RedBridge pollster Kos Samaras says the government's plan to slash Australia's net overseas migration intake could alienate diverse voters.

"What's motivating Australians voting is the state of the economy. Immigration, only for a third of One Nation voters, is the number one issue. Among other voters it's 12 per cent," he said.
He said many culturally diverse Australians are feeling uncomfortable about the tenor of political debate.
"They are witnessing a live debate about them and their place in this country and so my message to the political class is whether it's Labor, Liberal or One Nation: don't ignore [migrants], they will determine a lot of seats."
Plibersek brushes aside questions on cabinet discussions over migration overhaul
Tanya Plibersek has brushed aside questions about whether there was disagreement in cabinet over a proposal to overhaul migration.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke will be announcing an overhaul of Australia's migration system at the National Press Club today.
The speech, which was expected to announce a drastic cut in migration, was scheduled for six weeks ago but the ABC understands the measures were internally contentious.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Plibersek says senior government members have had "very constructive discussions".
"I don't talk about what happened in cabinet but I can say to you that it is a very constructive discussion that focused on the real issues here. Which is making sure that our immigration system is fit for purpose, that it meets the needs of our country, and that and by the way, that we continue to celebrate the contributions that migrants to this country make today and have made for many, many years," Plibersek says.
Migration target 'bad idea', says expert
An immigration expert has told the ABC political debate about net overseas migration is "numerical theatre about the wrong number" as he urges policymakers to focus on addressing temporary migration instead.
Australia's net overseas migration number, or NOM, measures all migrant arrivals minus all migrant departures, with two-thirds of the current 306,000 figure comprising temporary visa holders like working holidaymakers and students.
Professor Alan Gamlen from ANU's Migration Hub says Labor's plan to limit the NOM to 225,000 by 2028 would be a pointless exercise.
"I would say having a net migration target is a bad idea. If you have a target it's always going to be missed," he said.
"Missing those targets leads to a lack of confidence in the government to control migration, which is what happened in the UK before Brexit."
While Labor's plan appears largely focused on regulating temporary visa holders like students and backpackers, Gamlen says the NOM also accounts for Australian citizens and permanent residents, whose movements can't be controlled.
"Other countries to which we compare ourselves have abandoned this idea a long time ago. Canada targets just temporary migration."
Universities Australia worried migration overhaul will do 'lasting damage' to sector
Universities Australia chief executive Luke Sheehy says he's "deeply worried" about Labor's upcoming overhaul of migration.
The home affairs minister will announce an overhaul of migration at the National Press Club today, six weeks after it was abruptly postponed.
The ABC understands the announcement could include an effective ban on international students bringing family members to Australia.
But Sheehy has told ABC News Breakfast any move to cut international students would leave universities with a funding gap.
The chief executive says successive governments have for decades encourage universities to attract international students.
He says the universities sector relies on skilled researchers, half of which he says come from overseas.
"I'm going to look at the detail but the question is fewer international students means a bigger gap in how we fund our world-class university system. And the next question for the government is, are you going to step up and pay for it?" Sheehy says.
"I think this is going to do lasting damage. We've already seen the world's highest visa application fees. We're sending the wrong signals at a time when international students can help turbocharge not only our universities, the way we operate, but our skills base for the future."

Russian Oil Profits Surge as Middle East Conflict and Kremlin Cash Counteract Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:06:30 UTC
06:06:30 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Oil Profits Surge as Middle East Conflict and Kremlin Cash Counteract Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Despite a relentless campaign of Ukrainian drone strikes that has knocked out roughly a fifth of Russia’s oil refining capacity, Russian refineries are raking in unprecedented profits, The Moscow Times reported on September 16.
According to data from Rosstat , the refining sector earned a staggering 938 billion rubles ($11.13 billion) in the first half of the year, a 16.2% increase from the same period last year. Financial analysts expect third-quarter profit margins to surge even higher, marking an era of extraordinary profitability for the domestic segment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This windfall of “super-profits” is being driven by a combination of record-high wholesale prices on the St. Petersburg exchange and massive state subsidies through Russia’s fuel “damper” mechanism, The Moscow Times noted. Wholesale prices for petroleum products began climbing in March following the outbreak of war in the Middle East.
By July, exchange prices hit record highs, with AI-95 gasoline reaching 82,600 rubles ($980) per ton and diesel at 77,600 rubles ($921). In September, the price of AI-92 gasoline set a new all-time high of 73,100 rubles ($868) per ton.
To prevent these wholesale spikes from fully passing to consumers, the Russian government pays oil companies directly from the state budget. These “damper” payouts ballooned to nearly 350 billion rubles ($4.15 billion) per month during the second quarter, and reached 500 billion rubles ($5.93 billion) across July and August, The Moscow Times wrote.
For giants like Gazprom Neft, these state payouts and price surges have more than compensated for the reduced refining volumes caused by drone attacks and unplanned repairs.
However, this corporate windfall is being directly funded by the Russian public. Since the beginning of the year, retail gasoline prices have surged by 21.2%, while diesel has jumped 18.4%.
The Moscow Times reported that, while major oil companies can artificially hold down prices at their branded stations using state subsidies, independent gas stations are forced to buy fuel at inflated wholesale rates and pass the costs onto everyday drivers.
While the Kremlin tightly guards the exact financial toll of the Ukrainian strikes, the damage remains immense. The Ukrainian General Staff previously estimated that drone attacks have inflicted $13.5 billion in damages to the Russian oil industry since August 2025.
According to the Russian insurance broker Mains, direct losses to the oil and gas sector from drone strikes exceeded 100 billion rubles ($1.19 billion) last year, with total indirect costs and lost profits surpassing one trillion rubles ($11.87 billion), The Moscow Times added.
In addition to striking onshore refineries, Ukraine is also targeting the maritime logistics network Moscow uses to export its petroleum. As part of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces' “MoLoChKa” campaign to cut off shadow-fleet revenues, a Ukrainian naval drone recently maneuvered past a pursuing Russian interceptor helicopter to strike the sanctioned oil tanker Armada Leader off the coast of Sochi.
Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi reported that the operation has successfully targeted 285 Russian-linked vessels over 10 weeks, culminating in 16 ship strikes.
While Ukrainian strikes on refineries and shadow-fleet vessels have constrained Russian petroleum exports, the current global fuel crisis is primarily driven by a massive supply shock due to war in the Middle East. Severe transit restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz have slashed Persian Gulf fuel exports by roughly one million barrels per day.
Combined with Russia’s drone-induced outages and self-imposed export limits, this unprecedented squeeze has drained 1.6 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil from the global market, sending international prices soaring past the equivalent of $200 per barrel.

What’s Really Behind the Global Diesel Shortage—and How Much Is Actually About Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:06:18 UTC
06:06:18 KST

- Category
- World
What’s Really Behind the Global Diesel Shortage—and How Much Is Actually About Ukraine?
Global diesel supplies are tightening as Persian Gulf exports collapse and Russian refinery output falls. So what is really driving the shortage—and how much of it is actually about Ukraine?
The global diesel shortage has increasingly been linked to Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, but market data shows that the larger supply shock began thousands of kilometers away—in the Strait of Hormuz, where severely restricted shipping has slashed fuel exports from the Persian Gulf.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the International Energy Agency’s September Oil Market Report, Gulf countries and Russia together exported 1.6 million barrels per day less diesel and gasoil in August than in February, when they accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade in the fuels.
The IEA said Gulf diesel and gasoil exports alone had fallen to just 390,000 barrels per day—slightly more than one-quarter of their pre-war level.
That means the Gulf lost roughly 1 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports, making disruption in and around the Strait of Hormuz the larger component of the combined Gulf-Russia decline.
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli strikes at the end of February, Reuters reported, cutting Europe off from roughly one-quarter of its diesel and jet fuel supply and helping push fuel inventories at Northwest Europe’s main trading hub to their lowest level in 12 years.
Traffic through the chokepoint remains heavily restricted. According to Reuters on September 16, only four vessels were visibly recorded crossing Hormuz the previous day, compared with a 10-day average of 18. Some ships are believed to be making so-called “dark” crossings with their tracking systems switched off.
The IEA has described the Middle East disruption as the largest oil supply disruption in the history of the global market, noting that around 15 million barrels per day of crude and another 5 million barrels per day of oil products normally passed through Hormuz.
The agency said restoring transit through the strait is the single most important measure for easing pressure on global oil and fuel prices. Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have added another significant supply loss.
The IEA said disruptions to Russia’s refining system and the near-halt in product exports following intensified Ukrainian strikes compounded the decline from the Gulf.
Reuters reported on September 15 that six of Russia’s leading diesel-producing refineries—which together account for roughly half of the country’s diesel production—had reduced or halted output following drone attacks.
Russia has also removed additional supply from the international market through its own policy decisions. Moscow has restricted diesel exports as it tries to protect its domestic market amid refinery outages and fuel shortages, and is preparing to keep restrictions in place through October.
According to Reuters, not all of the Russian diesel missing from the global market reflects refinery outages alone. Moscow has also restricted diesel exports in an effort to stabilize domestic fuel supplies following disruptions at Russian refineries.
Meanwhile, the scale of the Middle Eastern disruption remains larger. The IEA estimates that refined-product and LPG exports from Gulf producers remain almost 60%, or 3.7 million barrels per day, below February levels, while nearly 3 million barrels per day of Gulf refining capacity has been shut because of attacks and limited export routes.
The consequences are now visible worldwide. US diesel and gasoil prices exceeded the equivalent of $200 per barrel in early September, according to the IEA, while Asian diesel refining margins reached a record of more than $87 per barrel on September 16.
Industry executives also warn that there is little spare refining capacity available to replace the missing barrels. Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said in September that the global market was missing large volumes of refined products from both Russia and the Middle East, while US refineries were already operating close to maximum levels.
The figures therefore point to a broader picture than Ukrainian refinery strikes alone. Those attacks have reduced one major source of global diesel supply, but they hit a market that was already severely constrained by the collapse in Persian Gulf fuel exports following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. And for now, the Gulf remains the larger part of that supply shock.

NASA has discovered the largest recent impact crater in the Solar System on the Moon
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:02:26 EEST
06:02:26 KST

NASA has discovered the largest recent impact crater in the Solar System on the Moon
Kyiv • UNN
The crater, 222 meters in diameter, formed about two years ago after a piece of space debris crashed into the Moon. NASA confirmed the discovery in early 2026.
A new crater approximately 222 meters in diameter and up to 43 meters deep has been discovered on the Moon. It was formed by the impact of a fragment of an asteroid or comet approximately two years ago. It has become the largest known modern impact crater in the Solar System, Associated Press reports, according to UNN.
Details
The crater was recorded by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spacecraft on the Moon’s near side in May 2024, shortly after the impact. However, the relevant images were found only in August 2025 among the enormous volume of data collected.
In the autumn, the spacecraft took more detailed photographs of the area, and in early 2026, scientists confirmed the discovery. The new crater is approximately three times larger than the previous record holder, discovered by LRO about 10 years ago.
Such impacts occur approximately once every 132 years
According to researchers’ estimates, an impact of this scale is extraordinarily rare. Scientists called it "a truly unique, once-in-a-lifetime observation."
The impact altered the Moon’s surface across an area of more than 100 km around the impact site. Another study also found a cold region approximately 7 km wide near the crater, whose formation is associated with the mixing of the upper layer of lunar soil.
The crater was named after the late director of the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston, Thomas McGetchin. The research findings were published in the scientific journal Science Advances.

Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA documents how mass civilian deaths were routinely built into Israeli targeting decisions in Gaza.
The film, which won a major prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected "collateral casualties" and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers.
It has drawn a backlash in Israel, with the military examining potential legal action against those involved in it. But it has also played into the charged political atmosphere ahead of Israel's October 27 election, which public opinion polls show Netanyahu's right-wing coalition could lose.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu accused some of his election rivals of failing to take a tough stand against the documentary, saying this made them unfit for office. And on Wednesday, he pledged to advance two bills that he said aimed at addressing the "immense damage" done to Israeli soldiers.
"The first, to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames (Israeli) soldiers, and the second to hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times," Netanyahu said in a social media video.
"We will hit them both in their pockets and in their citizenship, as their place is not with us."
Netanyahu cited three incidents in proposing the bills: "the recent film NAZA which portrayed (Israeli) officers and soldiers as war criminals"; 2025 remarks by left-wing ex-general turned politician Yair Golan that "a sane country does not kill children as a hobby"; and a military legal officer's 2024 leak of a video showing soldiers abusing a Gaza detainee.
Reuters could not immediately reach the NAZA filmmakers for comment.
In 2022, Israel's Supreme Court upheld a law that permits stripping citizenship from Israelis who carry out actions that constitute a breach of trust against the state. Any new legislation would likely face similar court challenges.
The NAZA filmmakers say they believe it is important that Israelis watch the documentary and grapple with the narrative it presents.
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel's military campaign that has left much of Gaza in ruins.

====================================================================================================

Washington Won't Be Regulating AI Anytime Soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.
But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.
White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.
But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.
Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.
Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.
In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.
Independent Auditors
The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.
As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.
But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.
The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.
There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.
Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.
To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.
But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.
Kill Switches
There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.
There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.
Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.
The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.
So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.

Rachida Dati in court: French ex-minister on trial over Renault-Nissan corruption case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:58:12 UTC
05:58:12 KST

Former minister and MEP Rachida Dati is on trial in Paris in the Renault-Nissan case, accused of corruption and influence peddling after taking €900,000 from a group subsidiary for counseling. Carlos Ghosn is being tried in the same case in absentia.
The trial of Rachida Dati opened on Wednesday afternoon before the Paris criminal court. The former justice and culture minister is facing charges of passive corruption, passive influence-peddling, and concealment of abuse of power and breach of trust.
At the heart of the case are the €900,000 she received between 2009 and 2013 from a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan, while she was serving as a Member of the European Parliament.
The opening day was marked in particular by the absence of Carlos Ghosn. The former head of Renault-Nissan, who has been in Lebanon since fleeing Japan in 2019, is also being prosecuted, notably for active corruption and influence-peddling.
Tried in absentia, he asked in a letter to the court for the hearing to be postponed, arguing that he had not been properly served. He said he was willing to take part in the proceedings via videoconference.
Over six half-days of hearings, up to 28 September, the court is to examine the relationship between Rachida Dati and Carlos Ghosn and, above all, the nature of the services said to correspond to the €900,000 paid by RNBV, the Dutch subsidiary of the Renault-Nissan alliance.
Fees at the heart of the proceedings
Rachida Dati maintains she worked as a lawyer for the group and denies any lobbying activity in the European Parliament. Her lawyers denounce what they call an "intellectual construct" by the prosecution and insist their client has "exclusively" carried out legal work.
The prosecution, by contrast, argues that the fee agreement signed in 2009 was used to conceal lobbying activities. Investigating magistrates noted the paucity of documents that could, in their view, establish the reality and scope of the legal services provided. They also consider that the remuneration was "totally disproportionate" to the work for which evidence has been found.
Investigators are looking in particular at several interventions by Rachida Dati in the European Parliament, including three questions submitted in 2012 and 2013 relating to the automotive sector. The prosecution believes her parliamentary activity may have been influenced by her professional ties with Renault.
Rachida Dati faces up to ten years in prison and a €450,000 fine, as well as a possible ban on holding public office. She remains presumed innocent until the court reaches its decision.
Carlos Ghosn, for his part, will therefore not be in the dock. The former executive, who disputes the allegations against him, remains in Lebanon. His absence adds a particular dimension to a trial that is expected to help the court determine whether the €900,000 paid to Rachida Dati did indeed correspond to legal services or whether it concealed lobbying activity, which was banned at the time for MEPs.

According to Spencer, the conflict with Charles concerned, among other things, the participation of 15-year-old Prince William and 12-year-old Prince Harry in the funeral procession behind their mother’s coffin.
In 2017, both princes said in the BBC documentary "Diana, 7 Days" that the decision regarding their participation in the procession had been made jointly by the family. Harry later said that he was glad he had taken part in it.

Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:46:28 UTC
05:46:28 KST

Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
American political scientist John Mearsheimer has claimed that the Ukraine conflict can’t be resolved diplomatically because the two sides’ goals remain irreconcilable and it will ultimately be settled on the battlefield. 
 Mearsheimer made the remarks during a visit to Moscow in an interview with Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Presidium of the Council on Foreign and Defense Policy and editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs.
 Fyodor Lukyanov: John, if a time machine brought great diplomats like Metternich and Talleyrand into the present day, what would they do to stem the bloodshed and bring today’s conflicts to an end? Would they succeed?
John Mearsheimer: Well, they were definitely skilled diplomats. And if we talk about the Ukraine-Russia war, they would go to great lengths to try to solve that. But I think that they’d be unable to do it. I don’t think that war, the Ukraine war, can be settled diplomatically. I think it’s going to be settled on the battlefield.
Now you say to yourself, why do I think it can’t be settled diplomatically? It’s because Russia’s goals are unacceptable to Ukraine, and Ukraine’s goals are unacceptable to Russia. For example, Ukraine wants the territory that Russia has annexed returned to Ukraine.
It views the Donbass, Zaporozhye, and Kherson as sacred territory. And from Ukraine’s point of view, it’s completely unacceptable that Russia be allowed to annex that territory. Furthermore, Ukraine, given what’s happened, wants a security guarantee, either from NATO or from the United States, to protect it moving forward.
This is unacceptable to the Russians. Furthermore, it’s unacceptable to the Russians to give up the territory that they’ve now annexed. So how can you have a diplomatic agreement between the two sides when there are such stark differences? Ukraine is simply unwilling to give up those four oblasts and Crimea, which Russia has annexed.
And Russia is unwilling to allow Ukraine to have that territory back. Furthermore, Ukraine wants a security guarantee from the West. It wants to be part of NATO, which is understandable from Ukraine’s point of view. But Russia certainly doesn’t want Ukraine in NATO. That was the principal cause of this war to begin with. So you see that the Russians and the Ukrainians are directly at odds on key issues where they’re unwilling to compromise.
So the question is, how do you get a diplomatic solution? And the answer is, you don’t. And this one will be fought out on the battlefield. And the final solution will be determined by who wins the war.
Fyodor Lukyanov: All right, then what would victory actually look like? Would winning the war mean eliminating Ukraine as such?
John Mearsheimer: I don’t think that the Russians are going to eliminate Ukraine. I think that’s almost impossible. I think what the Russians are going to do is they’re going to take a substantial portion of Ukrainian territory. They already have taken probably about 20%, and I think they’ll ultimately try to take considerably more territory from Ukraine. But they will not conquer all of Ukraine.
Furthermore, Ukraine will be, when this war is over, a dysfunctional rump state. And the Russians will have a vested interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state, so that it can’t join NATO, and so that it doesn’t present a threat to Russia. So I think what you’re going to get here at some point is a frozen conflict, not altogether unlike what you have in Korea.
The Ukrainians will never accept the idea that Russia has conquered all this territory. The Ukrainians and the [Western] Europeans, for that matter, will not accept the new status quo. They’ll want to go back to the borders, the pre-2014 borders.
And the Russians, of course, will want to make sure that doesn’t happen, because the Russians live in fear that Ukraine will become part of the West, and it will become a Western bulwark on Russia’s borders. So what you see is that once you get this frozen conflict, Russia will have a deep-seated interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state.
This is one of the reasons I think the Russians are likely to try to take Odessa and to take the Black Sea coast away from Ukraine, because the Russians will see that as an important way of weakening Ukraine in the future. And again, Russia will have a vested interest in weakening Ukraine.
And from Ukraine’s point of view, it makes perfect sense to see Russia as an existential threat, to want to have help from the West to deal with Russia, and to want to get its sacred territory back. I fully understand how the Ukrainians think, but that’s unacceptable to the Russians. So if you have these two parties to a conflict, one, the Russians, and two, the Ukrainians assisted by the Europeans, who have irreconcilable differences, there’s no diplomatic way out.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Does it mean that all efforts made by the Trump administration, Kushner, Witkoff and others are just a waste of time?
John Mearsheimer: I think that’s basically correct. I mean, in the case of the Trump administration, I think that it’s important to emphasize that President Trump himself has the right instincts. He wants to settle the war, the Ukraine war, and he wants to establish good relations between the United States and Russia. There’s no question that his instincts are right on this issue.
But there are two problems. One is the structural problem that I just described to you, the fact that the warring parties have irreconcilable goals. That’s point number one. And point number two is that President Trump is an inept or poor negotiator. He views himself as somebody who is brilliant at cutting deals, and he can easily shut down the Ukraine-Russia conflict in his own mind.
But exactly the opposite is true. He’s a ham-fisted, inept diplomat, and he hasn’t even come close to shutting down this war as a result of his ineptitude.
Fyodor Lukyanov: We have just marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Looking back a quarter of a century later, how would you assess their significance from the perspective of great-power politics?
John Mearsheimer: Well, 9-11 has nothing to do with great power politics. It’s just very important to understand that. 9-11 took place during the unipolar moment, when the United States was the only great power on the planet, and there was no great power politics, because you didn’t have rival great powers that could compete with each other.
And what happened with regard to 9-11 is that a small group called Al-Qaeda, which hated US Middle East policies, found a way to attack the United States and cause serious damage, and then led the United States to launch the global war on terror, which led to a number of the forever wars that we became involved in, especially Afghanistan and Iraq. And both these wars were disasters. Our response to 9-11 was badly mistaken. There was no need to launch a global war on terror. We just got ourselves into even more trouble.
But it had nothing to do with great power politics.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Could that moment be seen as the beginning of the end of the unipolar world, as some argue?
John Mearsheimer: I think that you can make that argument. I think that the 1990s were the heyday of the unipolar moment. But Russia was in terrible shape during the 1990s. And remember, Putin comes into power in roughly 2000, right? The end of ‘99, Putin comes into power. And I believe Putin resurrects the Russians from the dead.
But during the 1990s, Russia was badly weakened. And China hadn’t grown significantly by 2001. In fact, it’s not until 2001 that China joins the WTO. And when China joins the WTO, its economic growth really takes off.
So I think you can see that throughout the 1990s, up to around 2001, 2002, the United States is an incredibly powerful country. And the unipolar moment, except for what happened on 9-11, looks like it’s going very well. But after 9-11, things tend to go downhill pretty quickly. And I think the most important event here is the 2008 financial crisis, which hurt the United States badly. And then by about 2017, the Russians had come back from the dead, and I think Putin had created a situation here in Russia where Russia was once again a great power, by about 2017. And at the same time, China was also a great power in roughly 2017. So it’s around 2017 that you transition away from unipolarity to multipolarity.
And that’s a fundamental change that has drastically altered international politics. The United States was much freer to intervene around the world during the unipolar moment because there were no great power competitors, and it was free to get itself into all sorts of trouble in places like Afghanistan and in Iraq.
But then came multipolarity, and now the United States has to worry above all else about rival great powers.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Why do you single out 2017? As far as I can see, nothing particularly significant happened that year. In 2014, there was Crimea; in 2015, Syria. So why 2017?
John Mearsheimer: Well, what I’m concerned about is the balance of power. And the question is, when you look at Russia in the 1990s and in the very early 2000s, it has hardly any meaningful military power. Its military has really been wrecked. And what you see around 2015, 2016, 2017, is that the Russian military is much more effective than it had been in the previous decade and a half.
And I think this is largely the doing of Putin. I think Putin went to great lengths to help restore the Russian economy. And as the Russian economy began to flourish, the Russians were able to translate a lot of that economic might into military might.
So, by about 2016-2017, most assessments from places like the RAND Corporation about the Russian military say that Russian military power is now quite formidable. Obviously, the Russians in 2017 were not as powerful as the Soviet Union was at any point during the Cold War.
But the Russian military by 2017, and this of course is true of the Chinese military as well, looks like a quite formidable instrument. See, my argument is if you’re going to talk about going from unipolarity to multipolarity, you’re basically asking yourself the question, when do countries like China and Russia become great powers?
And for me, a great power is a country that has sufficient military power to put up a good fight against the most powerful state in the system. And of course, this is the United States. And again, I think by 2017, most security analysts in the United States believe that the Russian military was a quite formidable instrument and was quite well positioned to put up a serious fight against the United States.
And given that military power, the restoration of military power in Russia, I think that was the basis that people used to make the case that Russia was once again a great power. And just to say one more thing on this, I think everybody understood that Russia was and still is today the weakest of the three great powers.
I think the United States remains the most powerful state on the planet. I think the Chinese are now a close second. And I think there is a danger moving forward that China could overtake the United States.
And I think the Americans or most American foreign policy elites or the American foreign policy elite is very worried about that possibility. So China, in a very important way, is the real peer competitor, not Russia.
But Russia is still a great power, I think that everyone recognizes that. And I think that’s why the United States cares so much about the Ukraine war. And I think the reason that President Trump is interested in stopping or ending the Ukraine war and having good relations between Russia and the United States is because Trump understands that Russia is a great power.
And from an American point of view, it would make much more sense for the United States to be allied with Russia against China, or at least have Russia neutral, rather than create a situation where we have, in effect, driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
I mean, if you think about living in a multipolar world where there are three great powers, if you’re the United States and this is China, you want Russia on your side of the ledger. But instead, because of our foolish policies regarding Ukraine, we’ve driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
And again, I think Trump’s basic instincts about the importance of settling the Ukraine war and getting Russia on good terms with the United States is driven in good part by his insight or his belief that China is the real threat for the United States.

Russia’s veterinary watchdog finds live pseudorabies virus in a dog vaccine batch linked to mass deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:38:44 UTC
05:38:44 KST

Russia’s veterinary watchdog finds live pseudorabies virus in a dog vaccine batch linked to mass deaths
Russia’s federal veterinary watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, detected live Aujeszky’s disease virus in samples from batch No. 20 of the Multikan-8 vaccine, according to TASS.
The samples were collected in Russia’s Yaroslavl region. “This confirms a causal link between the mass deaths of dogs and their vaccination with Multikan-8 from batch No. 20, which was contaminated with an extraneous virus fatal to dogs,” Rosselkhoznadzor said in a statement.
Aujeszky’s disease, also known as pseudorabies, is an acute viral disease that affects the central nervous system in domestic and wild animals and is fatal in most cases.
In mid-August, dog owners began reporting in large numbers that their pets had died after receiving the Multikan-8 vaccine. The first reports came from the Yaroslavl region. The vaccine’s manufacturer, Vetbiokhim, recalled four batches. Rosselkhoznadzor ordered that batch No. 20, comprising 60,000 doses, be removed from circulation and destroyed. Vetbiokhim prepared settlement agreements with the affected owners. The company did not acknowledge a link between the dogs’ deaths and the vaccine but offered compensation to the owners of dogs that died.

AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Sept 16 to pass a law to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames Israel’s soldiers, his latest threat against the Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about soldiers’ killing of Gaza civilians.
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA alleges that mass civilian deaths were routinely built into Israeli targeting decisions in Gaza, something Netanyahu and the military reject.
The film, which won a major prize at the Venice Film Festival on Sept 12, takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected “collateral casualties” and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers.
It has drawn a backlash in Israel, with the military examining potential legal action against those involved in it. But it has also played into the charged political atmosphere ahead of Israel’s Oct 27 election, which public opinion polls show Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition could lose.
On Sept 15, Netanyahu accused some of his election rivals of failing to take a tough stand against the documentary, saying this made them unfit for office. And on Sept 16, he pledged to advance two Bills that he said aimed at addressing the “immense damage” done to Israeli soldiers.
“The first, to revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames (Israeli) soldiers, and the second to hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times,” Netanyahu said in a social media video.
“We will hit them both in their pockets and in their citizenship, as their place is not with us.”
Netanyahu cited three incidents in proposing the Bills: “the recent film NAZA which portrayed (Israeli) officers and soldiers as war criminals”; 2025 remarks by left-wing ex-general turned politician Yair Golan that “a sane country does not kill children as a hobby”; and a military legal officer’s 2024 leak of a video showing soldiers abusing a Gaza detainee.
Reuters could not immediately reach the NAZA filmmakers for comment.
In 2022, Israel’s Supreme Court upheld a law that permits stripping citizenship from Israelis who carry out actions that constitute a breach of trust against the state. Any new legislation would likely face similar court challenges.
The NAZA filmmakers say they believe it is important that Israelis watch the documentary and grapple with the narrative it presents.
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel’s military campaign that has left much of Gaza in ruins.
The war was triggered by Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel which killed 1,200 people, most of them civilians, according to Israeli tallies. REUTERS

US stocks end midweek lower as Fed raises rates for first time in over 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:36:10 UTC
05:36:10 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
US stocks closed mostly lower on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years and Chair Kevin Warsh warned that inflation remained persistently high.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 631.33 points, or 1.21%, to 51,461.78.
The S&P 500 declined 33.92 points, or 0.45%, to 7,551.81, while the Nasdaq Composite was nearly flat at 25,978.43.
The Fed unanimously increased its federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4%, marking its first rate hike since July 2023. Policymakers also projected one additional quarter-point increase this year.
Equities initially responded positively to the widely anticipated decision but reversed course as Warsh emphasized persistent price pressures during his post-meeting news conference.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” Warsh said, adding that inflation readings during the summer did not indicate a meaningful improvement in underlying trends.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note climbed back above the psychologically important 5% threshold, trading around 5.02%.
Banking shares led the decline amid concerns that further rate hikes and elevated borrowing costs could weaken lending and economic activity.
Shares of Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Citigroup fell around 3%, while JPMorgan Chase lost around 1%.
Intel shares rose on reports that the US chipmaker was holding talks with South Korean memory producer SK Hynix about manufacturing semiconductors in the US, helping limit losses on the technology-heavy Nasdaq.
The US dollar index gained around 0.6% to 100.21, its highest level since late July.
Gold futures fell 0.6% to $4,266 per ounce, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude dropped 3.7% to $101.87 per barrel.
European stocks close higher
European stock markets, meanwhile, ended on Wednesday higher, led by gains in technology shares ahead of the Fed’s policy announcement.
The STOXX Europe 600 index rose 0.46% to 637.09 points.
Britain’s FTSE 100 advanced 0.28% to 10,688.47, Germany’s DAX gained 0.53% to 25,537.75 and France’s CAC 40 increased 0.62% to 8,140.59.
Italy’s FTSE MIB recorded the strongest gain among the major European indices, rising 0.8% to 51,969.12, while Spain's IBEX 35 also gained 0.41% to end at 19,635.80.

film stills leave the screen and become elaborate makeup compositions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:35:59 UTC
05:35:59 KST

Emerald Vysions turns the face into a cinematic stage
For Toronto-based makeup artist Emerald Vysions, the face becomes a small-scale stage for images, emotions, and cinematic memories. Working on her own face, the artist reinterprets film stills through saturated pigments, graphic lines, metallic textures, rhinestones, feathers, and highly constructed lashes. Vysions extracts the visual language of movie scenes and compresses it into eye looks that can be read in a single glance.
A film normally exists at a distance, projected onto a screen, framed by a rectangle, and experienced through the collective act of watching. Emerald Vysions relocates fragments of that spectacle onto the body. The screen becomes the eyelid; production design becomes color and texture; costume can become an arrangement of rhinestones or an exaggerated lash.
Pierrot le Fou (1965) | all images by Emerald Vysions
from screen to skin
Cinema is one of the starting points for Emerald Vysions, but her makeup does not try to reproduce a film scene exactly. The artist picks apart what makes an image stick: a particular color combination, a costume detail, the shape of a gesture, or the mood of a scene. These elements reappear across the face as pigment, crystals, unusual lashes, painted shapes and other small details.
Seen alongside the film stills that inspire them, the difference in scale is striking. A whole scene, its actors, costumes, interiors and lighting, is reduced to the area around the eyes.
One example draws on the rich reds and feathers of Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), translating the excess of the original scene into red pigment, jewels and pale feathered lashes. Other looks pick up on the strong blues, yellows, greens and pinks of their respective references. Vysions seems to pull individual details out of the scenes and give those details a new life.
Vysions’ work lives in the gap between the original image and what she does with it. The film still gives her a starting point, but the makeup does not always follow it literally. A color might become more intense, a detail might be enlarged, or something almost incidental in the original scene can become the focus of the makeup, resulting in something familiar without being immediately legible. You recognize the mood before you recognize the reference.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Daly Cherry-Evans has arrived at the end of forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:32:41 UTC
05:32:41 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Ahead of his last NRL games, Daly Cherry-Evans has finally reached the end of forever
Years ago, when Daly Cherry-Evans was merely in his early 30s, he'd say that he was going to play forever and he was only ever half-joking.
Every time he'd be asked about his future, be it at the beginning of a season or at the end, he'd grin widely and assure whoever wanted to know that he, in fact, would never, ever stop.
Most of the time it felt like a gag, a way for one of the slickest operators in the NRL to disarm the inquiry and Cherry-Evans follow with all the usual patter we hear from the greybeards — that he'd play as long as his body held up or as long as he was still enjoying it.
Plenty say that but Cherry-Evans has lived it. He lived it long enough that he reached the end of the "lifetime" deal he once signed with Manly, long enough that younger men than him succumbed to the ravages of age and long enough that maybe the joke was on us the whole time for not believing him in the first place.
It is only now, a few months before he turns 38 years old, that Cherry-Evans has finally arrived at the end of forever.
Win or lose, the Sydney Roosters sudden-death semifinal against Cronulla on Saturday is the beginning of the last days, the ones that seemed like they would never arrive.
A defeat will mark Cherry-Evans's final NRL match before he links with Hull FC in Super League next year where's he's odds on to, at least once, play with or against someone a full two decades younger than him.
A win will push the Roosters into a preliminary final against the Dolphins and keep the dream of a farewell premiership alive.
If the Tricolours do manage to go all the way, Cherry-Evans will break Lote Tuqiri's record for the longest gap between grand final wins by one season.
That premiership back in 2011 is still definitional to Cherry-Evans and what he's been for all this time.
In becoming the first rookie halfback to win a grand final since 1978 and because he was one of Manly's best through the finals and on the big day in their win over the Warriors, Cherry-Evans was able to transcend many of the slings and arrows launched during the rise of franchise playmakers.
Instead of the typical hero journey most halfbacks endure, with its peaks and valleys and rises and falls, Cherry-Evans's success as a rookie gave him a kind of instant validation.
There was never any talk of what he might be one day once he matures, or what he would eventually become once he developed this part of his game or not.
There was no debate whether he would one day be enough to lead a team to glory because he had already done it. It was instant proof of concept.
So many of young halfbacks are defined by their future, the possibility of what they might be, but ever since that first season, Cherry-Evans has instead existed in a blissful and seemingly eternal present.
His game has changed in subtle ways since that first year with Manly but through a bird's-eye view the similarities of his 16-year career is remarkable.
This season was the 15th of those years where he managed at least 20 games and he has as many try assists this year at age 37 as he did the year he turned 25.
Old halves are supposed to run less but his return in that part of his game this year (51 run metres per game and five line breaks from 24 matches) is not miles away from his return as a rookie (57 per game and 11 line breaks from 27 matches).
They're meant to be worse at defending as well, but this year Cherry-Evans has had the third-best tackle efficiency of his career.
That's not to say there hasn't been some ups and downs for Cherry-Evans through his long career, but because of where he started and how long he's been there it was always easy to ride out the downs because, even as he reached his mid-30s, he had more time.
A bad option or a poor game or a sprayed kick, as rare as they were, or even a season where his team didn't make the finals were easier to accept because there was always more to come. He could always come back to what he had always been.
The end of that reality was put into stark relief in Sunday's qualifying final loss to Penrith even as, at the end of all things, Cherry-Evans can absolutely still cut it in a game of such quality and intensity.
It was only a month ago that he scored both tries in a 12-6 Tricolours win over the Panthers that remains their best performance of the season.
This time, with Sam Walker sidelined, Cherry-Evans slotted back into halfback and taken the lion's share of the kicking game and his field position chess match with Brian To'o as he hunted a 40/20 in the second half was a highlight.
In the end, two kicks Cherry-Evans got wrong cost the Roosters badly.
First it was a screwball torpedo of a thing with ten minutes left that he launched from his own 40 metre line that found the grass and seemed perfect until it took one bounce too many and trickled dead.
It was unfortunate and nothing more. Not even someone as experienced as Cherry-Evans, who will likely bring up his 450th first class game next year, can predict how a ball bounces.
Penrith rolled up the field on the seven-tackle set and took the lead through a Nathan Cleary one-pointer but it was not necessarily a death blow given Cherry-Evans is the modern day field goal king.
He's kicked 31 of them in his career, the most of anyone in the NRL era.
He's kicked them to cap off big wins and to break stalemates at the last second — seven of them came in golden point extra time and his most recent match-winner was just a few weeks back against Newcastle.
He's kicked them off both feet, in howling gales and monsoonal rain.
He's never met a way he couldn't do it and he's met all the ways it can be done.
But this time his only attempt, from inside 20 metres and right in front, was a shank the likes of which we've rarely seen during his career.
Even the best can get it wrong, but both moments brought into stark relief just how things have changed for Cherry-Evans.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson was circumspect about it after the match, pointing out that Cherry-Evans had iced games before for the Roosters and would do so again.
The former is a fact but the latter is closer to a prediction than a guarantee.
There might still be a next week for Cherry-Evans, but it only might be. There will not be a next year.
On Saturday night against Cronulla, with Walker still out, Cherry-Evans must become the system once again.
He will play sharp and smart, like he always does, like he always has, and maybe it will be enough to earn another day.
But after seeming ageless for so long, he is running out of tomorrows. He has reached the end of forever and after seeming immune to time for so long it is coming for him at last.
The story might not have its final chapter against the Sharks or the Dolphins, but the last page is nigh and the final days of Daly Cherry-Evans in the NRL are a reminder of how the present, after seeming fixed for so long, becomes history wholesale — not at all and then all at once.
