Zelensky Signs Law Targeting Scam Call Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:31:14 UTC
05:31:14 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky signed the law that introduces criminal liability for the organizers and participants of scam call centers, after Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, approved tougher penalties for electronic fraud earlier on Wednesday.
In his evening address, Zelensky said the Verkhovna Rada had passed the legislation alongside other bills linked to Ukraine’s commitments to international partners. The measures are needed to help close the state-budget deficit Ukraine is currently facing and, by doing so, sustain Ukraine’s resilience during the fifth winter of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I just signed this law. It is important that there is a vote for laws that are in Ukraine’s obligations to partners,” Zelensky said, expressing gratitude towards the parliament for today’s “effective vote.”
“It is important that they supported criminal liability for fraudulent call centers,” he continued.
The measure comes amid Ukraine’s wider effort to address corruption and improve criminal law as it works towards its EU accession.
New penalties – up to 12 years in prison
The decision No. 10190, newly adopted Wednesday morning, adds a separate provision to Ukraine’s Criminal Code covering organized groups that use electronic communications to obtain property or property rights through deception.
It applies to groups of at least three people who act according to a coordinated plan and divide tasks among members. The offenses may include acquiring, storing, processing or using personal data, banking information, authentication codes or other payment details to facilitate fraud.
Ukraine Plans War-Risk Insurance Fund, Considers 1% VAT Increase to Cover Business Losses
Under the legislation, creating or leading such groups can carry a prison term of seven to 12 years, along with confiscation of property if convicted.
Participants who knowingly take part in the group may face five to 10 years in prison, with or without asset confiscation.
Additionally, recruiting others into such networks may carry a sentence of three to five years, rising to five to 10 years for repeat offenses.
At least 313 lawmakers voted to support the decision, which came after an alleged protection scheme for the scam centers that involved Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General.
According to Ukraine’s anti-graft agencies; National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), Kravchenko allegedly protected the scam centers and helped launder millions in wealth, acquiring high-end real estate, expensive vehicles, and other luxury assets.
In the wake of the incident, Kravchenko resigned from his post.
He later left the country in haste and published a video message announcing notices of suspicion against officials from anti-graft agencies, though they were never officially served.
On Tuesday, Sept. 15, Verkhovna Rada dismissed Kravchenko.
Seven bills awaiting their first reading
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky said lawmakers were also considering seven bills tied to Ukraine’s obligations to international partners, most of which were still awaiting their first reading.
“Some of these measures may be difficult, unpleasant, and unpopular,” Zelensky said, noting that Ukraine must adopt them regardless, as Kyiv is facing a defense funding shortfall of about $27 billion (€23 billion).

The president also praised the soldiers fighting on the front lines, calling their “courage and devotion” an example for the entire nation.
“Your choice and your will shall once again show that millions of people stand behind our fighters; that we are a united people, bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland; and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” Putin said.
“I urge you to exercise your constitutional right and make a considered, responsible decision, so that the election results demonstrate the maturity and resilience of Russian society. This will be our shared response to those who seek to weaken Russia, hold back its development, and deprive us of our sovereignty and our right to determine our own destiny.”
The 2026 parliamentary elections will take place September 18-20, with a total of ten parties contending for 450 seats in the lower house of the Russian parliament.
In July, Putin accused Kiev of seeking to destabilize Russian society through “terrorist attacks” targeting civilian and energy infrastructure. ZHA rethinks benghazi’s urban growth through a digital planning hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:20:33 UTC
05:20:33 KST

BENGHAZI 2050 BUILDS AN ADAPTABLE FRAMEWORK FOR THE CITY
Benghazi, the historic port city on Libya’s Mediterranean coast, is looking toward 2050 with a new planning framework developed by a consortium including A&O TEC, Prior+Partners, Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA), Homa, Buro Happold, Systematica and Fichtner. Conceived amid a period of urban growth, infrastructure investment and renewal, Benghazi 2050: Next Generation City Plan sets out to coordinate future development while reconnecting the city with its waterfront, historic center and expanding neighborhoods. Rather than defining a single architectural intervention, the proposal combines a spatial vision with a digital platform intended to guide projects across the metropolitan area over the coming decades.
The Vision and Spatial Strategy begins with an analysis of Benghazi’s existing character and collective memory, proposing what the team describes as an adaptable framework based on connection rather than fragmentation and restoration rather than demolition. Public transport and pedestrian routes would link the historic core and shoreline with residential neighborhoods and metropolitan centers, while new employment and knowledge districts accommodate future growth. Zones of nature are also integrated into the strategy to support water management and ecological diversity, allowing urban expansion to develop alongside environmental systems rather than independently from them.
benghazi 2050 maps the city’s long-term growth | all images courtesy of ZHA
DIGITAL DATA FORMS THE FOUNDATION OF A CITYWIDE TWIN
At the center of the proposal is the Benghazi 2050 Digital Planning Hub, conceived as a shared evidence base for understanding the city and testing its future development. The platform brings together information on existing urban, socioeconomic, environmental and infrastructural conditions within a common spatial interface. Its datasets range from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and three-dimensional urban models to population and land-use information, transport networks, infrastructure, environmental resilience studies, ongoing developments and future planning scenarios.
This accumulated information provides the foundation for a dynamic digital twin of Benghazi. As new data is added, the system is intended to evolve alongside the city, allowing proposals to be considered in relation to their broader urban context rather than as isolated developments. In this sense, the Digital Planning Hub extends the spatial strategy beyond the format of a conventional static plan, creating what the team describes as a living environment for collaboration between authorities, local communities, planners, designers and investors.
the proposal coordinates growth across the metropolitan area
ZHA SHAPES THE SPATIAL VISION AND DIGITAL PLATFORM
The multidisciplinary consortium divides the project across different layers of urban research and design. Prior+Partners leads regional and urban planning, economic strategy and governance; Homa focuses on land use, built form and socioeconomic strategy; Systematica develops transport and mobility; Buro Happold addresses the natural environment and utilities; and Fichtner contributes energy and infrastructure expertise. ZHA is responsible for the spatial vision and scenario design, while also leading the interface design and technology integration of the Digital Planning Hub. Web services, deployment and hosting are developed by Silicon Shore.
Together, these elements frame Benghazi 2050 not as a finished image of the city, but as a system through which its transformation can continue to be measured, evaluated and adjusted. The concept proposal brings baseline research, growth scenarios, spatial planning and computational tools into a single process intended to connect Benghazi’s identity with its long-term development. The Vision and Digital Planning Hub were presented as part of the Next Generation City Plan at the Global Competitive Urban Planning Initiative – Benghazi, held from September 6–8, 2026.

US House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:20:17 UTC
05:20:17 KST

For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump’s ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The vote took place late Tuesday, and for a third time, the US House voted to end the war in Iran, attempting to cut President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action.
The roll call, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Democrat Representative Seth Moulton, who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it’s time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."
Republican Representative Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.
Mast said Trump is against "forever wars, and that is what he is ending" — the decades of hostilities from Iran.
"They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States," Mast said. "Enough is enough."
Last war powers vote before midterms
The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched on 28 February has dragged on, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.
Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.
Voters are confronting high prices, particularly for gas at the pumps, as the conflict disrupts the flow of oil resources through the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday that the war has cost more than $38 billion (€33 billion), as of 1 August, and is projected to be costing between $2 billion (€1.74 billion) and $3 billion (€2.62 billion) monthly, depending on the intensity of the fighting. The budget office projected inflation will be 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027 due to the war.
Trump himself had promised not to involve the US in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House, and his actions against Iran are weighing on the Republican Party that controls the House and Senate. Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to an AP-NORC poll in July.
In the previous House actions, four Republicans voted to halt the war in Iran, but that number rose to seven in Tuesday’s war powers vote, including GOP lawmakers from battleground Iowa, Representative Zachary Nunn and Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and retiring Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina.
They joined GOP Representatives Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky voting in favor of the war powers resolution, with all Democrats.
War powers put to the test
Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration’s military action remain a long shot so long as the president is able to fend off or veto the measures.
The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but GOP senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.
While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also gives the president authority as the commander in chief to engage in some military actions. The War Powers Act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.
House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged at a press conference Tuesday the need to bring gas prices down.
But the Republican speaker said he believes the Iran conflict is entering a "new phase" as allies step up to help stabilize the region. When that happens, he said, "you’re going to see, as the president said, anytime gas prices will go down again, the cost of groceries will as well."
Johnson said Trump expects the shift after the election, and the speaker added, "I’d love it to happen today."

Russia Exploited Migrants and Refugees for Ukraine War Recruitment, Amnesty International Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:13:08 UTC
05:13:08 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Exploited Migrants and Refugees for Ukraine War Recruitment, Amnesty International Reports
Russia has used deceptive, coercive, and exploitative practices to recruit foreign nationals into its armed forces and send them to fight in Ukraine, a pattern that in many cases amounts to human trafficking.
This was reported by Amnesty International in a briefing published on its official website on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking," Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International's Secretary General, stated, adding that the practice fits the definition set out in the UN's Palermo Protocol.
The Palermo Protocol is the UN's 2000 anti-trafficking treaty and the source of the first internationally agreed definition of human trafficking. It sets out a three-part test: an act of recruitment or transport carried out through coercion, fraud, or abuse of vulnerability for the purpose of exploitation.
Under its terms, a victim's consent is void once deception or coercion is used, which is why signed contracts do not shield the recruitment from the trafficking label.
Amnesty International's research documented how recruiters lured individuals into the Russian Armed Forces under false pretenses and exploited the precarious circumstances of migrants and refugees already inside Russia. Those targeted came primarily from low-income countries in the Global South .
The briefing drew on interviews conducted at two Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps between 2024 and 2026, with individuals from Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Somalia, and South Africa.
Amnesty International also gathered testimony from foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces, their families, lawyers, and journalists.
According to the organization, recruiters typically presented military service as a non-combat role, such as work in a military kitchen or as a driver far from the front.
Two Sri Lankan men believed they had been hired as cooks but were sent to the front lines and captured within weeks. "The scale of fighting is unimaginable. You do not see Ukrainian soldiers, only drones. Drones everywhere," one recounted.
Amnesty International reported that misleading online job advertisements and local agents deceived recruits in their home countries with false promises of civilian work and expedited Russian citizenship.
A South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was instructed to fly to Moscow, where his documents were seized. "He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he was becoming a soldier," his wife told the organization.
The briefing detailed severe restrictions imposed once contracts were signed. Recruits from Brazil and Sri Lanka described having passports and mobile phones confiscated before deployment.
Pedro, a Brazilian IT professional recruited under the pretext of a well-paid tech job, recounted asking his commander to leave and being told, "If you try to escape, you will either go to jail or we will kill you."
Amnesty International noted that most enlistees were deployed to active combat zones after roughly two weeks of training, with little regard for combat readiness.
The organization emphasized that recruiters weaponized irregular immigration status and pending criminal charges, presenting enlistment as an alternative to detention and deportation.
Amnesty International called on Russia to end the abusive practices immediately and urged states whose nationals are at risk to issue public warnings and pursue accountability.
The organization also directed a series of recommendations to Ukrainian authorities regarding third-country nationals held as prisoners of war.
Previous reports indicated that by mid-August 2026, at least 2,982 recruits from 37 African countries had been documented, roughly 486 of whom had been killed, with Kenya, Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria among the largest sources.
Foreign nationals from more than 40 countries have since been identified in Russian ranks, many funneled in through deception after traveling abroad in search of civilian work.

Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:08:50 UTC
05:08:50 KST

Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
Discontent is testing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
Syria’s parliament has voted to abolish an al-Assad-era “terrorism” court and nullify the legal effects of its rulings, in one of the first significant legislative moves by the country’s new assembly.
The vote on Wednesday formalised the abolition of the court, which Syria’s new authorities had already treated as defunct, state-run Al-Ekhbariya TV reported.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Explosion at depot storing weapons left from Syria war kills 14
- list 2 of 3Kurdish YPJ women fighters face exclusion from Syria’s new army
- list 3 of 3At least seven killed in fire at prison in northern Syria
The Counter-Terrorism Court, established in 2012, was used to prosecute thousands of Syrians for offences deemed “terrorism-related” under ousted former President Bashar al-Assad.
Wednesday’s vote came during the opening weeks of the first parliament formed since al-Assad was toppled. The chamber convened for the first time in July.
In June 2025, President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served in what he described at the time as the “abolished Counter-Terrorism Court”.
Syria’s March 2025 constitutional declaration had also called for abolishing the effects of what it described as unjust rulings issued by the court, including returning confiscated property.
The United Nations Human Rights Committee said in 2024 that the 2012 law establishing the court failed to adequately provide key judicial guarantees and raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, and the court’s independence.
The vote is among the assembly’s first major legislative decisions after it spent its initial sessions establishing its internal rules and committees.
The 53-year-long rule of the al-Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after a lightning 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise. With it ended a brutal police state, notorious for its use of torture and disappearances.
Kurdish discontent amid government integration deal
Hundreds of oil tanker trucks were stranded in northeastern Syria’s Kurdish region on Wednesday after demonstrators blocked a major highway near the town of Tal Tamr in protest over rising fuel prices.
Discontent has been building in the Kurdish region amid a push to integrate a once-powerful Kurd-led armed force – the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) – into Syria’s army and bring them under the control of the central government.
The integration agreement with the SDF, minted in August, has been widely regarded as a victory for al-Sharaa’s government, but discontent is testing the president’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
Kurds, who made up about 10 percent of Syria’s population of 23 million before the civil war began in 2011, were long marginalised under the country’s al-Assad dynasty. During the war, they carved out a de facto autonomous zone in the northeast.
When northeast Syria – including its oilfields – was under the SDF’s control, fuel was heavily subsidised. After the central government took control, it removed those subsidies, leading to a price hike.
Syrian Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir is scheduled to be questioned in parliament on Thursday over the increase in fuel prices.
On Sunday, the government further hiked petrol prices by about 30 percent and diesel by 40 percent, citing rising global fuel prices due to the US-Israel war on Iran as well as repair work at the Baniyas refinery on the country’s coast.
Demonstrators shut down the M4 highway near the town of Tal Tamr, blocking trucks bringing oil from the Qamishli and Rmeilan oilfields, and announced that they would only reopen the route if the price increases were reversed.
Additionally, students in the cities of Qamishli and Hasakah staged mass protests in recent weeks over a government decree that makes Kurdish an official language of instruction for the first time in Syrian history but only provides for three classes a week in the language. By contrast, Kurds had set up a school system teaching mostly in Kurdish.
With the new post-war government reasserting control over the northeast, Kurdish communities have been anxious about losing the rights they had under self-rule. Al-Sharaa has promised constitutional protection for Kurdish language and political rights.
In January, the integration deal reached between the central government in Damascus and the SDF halted weeks of fighting. While some Kurdish politicians hail the integration as a door for the Kurds to participate in building the new Syria and to demand their rights through the constitution, others consider the step a result of pressure from Turkiye and the United States and potentially harmful for Kurdish interests.

Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calls it a 'red line'

Saudi Arabia, a US ally which has been the target of large-scale Houthi strikes since early September, declared Mecca a “red line” as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city, as the region responded with condemnation Wednesday but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key US ally, declared Mecca a “red line” as slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
With the world’s biggest oil exporter under fire from the rebels backed by the Saudis' regional adversary, the kingdom needs a safe outlet for its crude as well as military assistance. There's no clear path to either.
A crucial Saudi pipeline has been shut down, reportedly for weeks, after an attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Houthis have been targeting infrastructure in the kingdom and its shipping on the Red Sea, where they have seized several islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometres (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Mohammed.
The attacks are the first test of a new defence pact among Saudi Arabia, NATO member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan. But officials from Turkey and Pakistan told The Associated Press they have not received a Saudi request for support in response to the Houthis' escalation.

Final results were declared Wednesday in the southern Philippines' majority-Muslim Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, following the region's first-ever parliamentary elections.
The Regional Board of Canvassers (RBOC) of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) said 2,018,478 voters cast ballots, with an 84.34% turnout in Monday's elections, according to a statement from the Bangsamoro government.
The 80-member parliament consists of 40 regional parliamentary party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
For the Regional Parliamentary Political Party (RPPP) seats, the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured 16 seats, followed by the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15. The BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) had eight and the Raayat Democratic Party secured one.
For district representative seats, the BFP won 15, UBJP nine, Serbisyong Inklusibo Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP) six, while the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party (PBP) and Al Ittihad-UKB won one each.
In the sectoral races, Yul Adelfo Olaya and Mary Ann Arnado won seats representing settler communities. Aida Silongan, Sulffy Abbas, Muhammad Nadzir Ebil and Marjanie Mimbantas-Macasalong represented the women, youth, ulama and traditional leaders sectors, respectively.
The Teduray and Lambangian communities selected Jo Glenna Jover and Leticio Datuwata, respectively, as their Non-Moro Indigenous People representatives under customary laws.
The BFP is led by Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua, while the UBJP is headed by former interim Chief Minister Murad Ebrahim, who is also the leader of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Officials will assume office Oct. 30 and will elect the region’s chief minister.

How growing up in East Germany affected cognitive health in later life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:00:21 UTC
05:00:21 KST

Older adults who lived in socialist East Germany before the 1989 reunification show better cognitive health and slower mental decline today than their West German peers. This unexpected advantage seems linked to the former East German educational system, which featured longer compulsory schooling and widespread early childcare. The findings were recently published in the journal Research on Aging.
Following World War II, Germany was split into two distinct nations with opposing political and economic models. The German Democratic Republic in the East operated as a socialist state with a planned economy. The Federal Republic of Germany in the West developed as a capitalist, liberal democracy.
When the countries reunited in 1989, citizens merged into a single legal and economic system. This unique history provides researchers with a natural experiment to study how entirely different societal structures affect human development over a lifetime.
The contrast between East and West Germany represents a rare situation where culturally similar populations were separated by completely different modes of governance. The East German welfare state prioritized collective investments, aiming to build a highly productive workforce through extensive health and education services.
Previous research has consistently shown that East Germans suffered worse physical health and lower life expectancies compared to West Germans. These physical disparities are largely attributed to differences in health behaviors, economic development, and cardiovascular health.
Sociologist Ariane Bertogg at the University of Konstanz and gerontologist Jeffrey E. Stokes at the University of Massachusetts Boston wanted to see if these political systems left a similar footprint on the aging brain. They tested two competing ideas about cognitive aging.
One theory suggested West Germans would perform better on cognitive tests in later life because they enjoyed stronger economic growth, better nutrition, and more civil liberties. Another theory proposed that East Germans might have an advantage due to their state funded educational system.
East Germany mandated ten years of compulsory schooling, compared to eight or nine years in West Germany. The East also provided universal early childcare and a less socially divided school structure.
Educational exposure early in life is a primary driver of cognitive reserve. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to build dense neural connections, which helps it compensate for age related damage and delay the onset of memory loss.
To find out which societal effect dominated, Bertogg and Stokes analyzed information from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. They looked at a large sample of 5,231 older adults who lived in either East or West Germany in 1989.
Participants were at least 50 years old during the study and were interviewed multiple times over an average of four years. The survey included four standard tests used to evaluate brain health and predict dementia.
Working memory was tested by asking participants to recall a list of ten words. Executive function, which involves planning and focusing attention, was measured by having people name as many animals as they could in a set time.
Orientation was scored based on whether participants correctly knew the current date and day of the week. Finally, numeracy was tested by having participants repeatedly subtract the number seven from one hundred.
The researchers used statistical models to map each person’s cognitive trajectory over time. They adjusted the results for factors like childhood health, household income, and overall educational attainment.
To account for early life conditions, the researchers utilized a special retrospective module of the survey. Participants provided detailed histories regarding their childhood health, their perceived math and language skills relative to peers, and the number of books in their childhood homes.
The data revealed that individuals who lived in East Germany before reunification performed better across all four cognitive tests. They also showed a slower rate of cognitive decline as they aged.
West German residents experienced a steady decline in immediate memory and verbal fluency over the course of the study. In contrast, East German residents maintained stable scores or even slightly improved in these areas.
East Germans also demonstrated less steep declines in their orientation and numerical abilities. The researchers noted that these advantages were especially pronounced in men.
The results present an unusual paradox in aging research. Usually, populations with poorer physical health and lower life expectancies also suffer from worse cognitive aging.
Despite East Germans having higher rates of cardiovascular disease and earlier mortality on average, their aging brains remained more resilient. This suggests that the early benefits of an egalitarian, intensive education system can offset some of the physical wear and tear associated with a lower standard of living.
Next, Bertogg and Stokes examined whether a person’s age at the time of reunification influenced their cognitive outcomes. They wanted to know if experiencing the transition during a specific life stage altered the trajectory of mental aging.
They found that the gap in memory and verbal fluency was widest between East and West Germans who were in their forties when the Berlin Wall fell. West Germans in this age group showed relative disadvantages compared to their Eastern counterparts.
For numeracy and orientation, the East German advantage was highest among those who experienced reunification in their twenties. The cognitive differences between the two populations were largely absent among people who were already nearing retirement age in 1989.
The researchers interpret this as evidence of critical periods in adult development. Entering the workforce during reunification may have helped young East Germans maximize the benefits of their schooling within the new, larger economy.
Conversely, West Germans navigating reunification in their forties may have faced intense economic competition and family stress. Mid adulthood is often a period of high financial responsibility, making individuals more vulnerable to the mental health impacts of economic shifts.
The two nations differed in many ways beyond education and economics. West Germans faced higher exposure to environmental toxins like lead from gasoline, simply because car ownership was much higher there.
Social and psychological experiences also varied wildly depending on the side of the border. West Germany fostered a more open civil society, while East Germany relied on secret police and informants, which negatively impacted social trust.
The dataset did not allow the researchers to measure the direct impact of these specific social and environmental stressors on brain health. Future investigations will need to look at similar differences across other post socialist and capitalist European countries to see if the pattern holds.
Future studies will also need to track clinical diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, rather than just test scores. High performing individuals sometimes hit the maximum possible score on cognitive tests, which can mask early signs of decline.
Cognitive test performance does not capture the full reality of living with a neurodegenerative disease. Tracking actual medical records over time will clarify how these early life educational advantages translate into real world dementia prevention.
The study, “Is There a Cognitive Footprint of Political Systems? The Case of Separation and Reunification of East and West Germany and Its Association With Later Life Cognitive Health,” was authored by Ariane Bertogg and Jeffrey E. Stokes.

Greenland and Antarctica lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:58:00 EEST
04:58:00 KST

Greenland and Antarctica lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice
Kyiv • UNN
Between 1979 and 2023, the ice sheets lost 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice. This raised global sea levels by 3.14 centimeters.
A new study based on satellite data collected since the 1970s recorded significant losses of polar ice in Greenland and Antarctica — the regions home to Earth’s two largest ice sheets — contributing to a rise in global sea levels, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Between 1979 and 2023, according to data from 27 satellite missions, Greenland and Antarctica lost a combined 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice, causing global sea levels to rise by 1.24 inches (3.14 cm).
This study, which used the longest satellite data record to date on changes in ice sheets to provide the most comprehensive picture of ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica, was conducted by the Ice Sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise team.
According to scientists, the findings provide new evidence of the consequences of human-caused global climate change.
"To better visualize the scale of this enormous figure: 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice is enough to form a cube 23 kilometers (14.3 miles) high," said climatologist Inès Otosaka of Northumbria University (England), the lead author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Data.
Of the total ice loss recorded in the study, about 60% occurred in Greenland and 40% in Antarctica, despite the fact that Greenland’s area is only about one-eighth the area of Antarctica.
"When ice sheets melt, this contributes to rising global sea levels. And for every additional centimeter of sea-level rise, 2 to 3 million people are put at risk of annual coastal flooding. At present, ice sheets are one of the main contributors to sea-level rise, accounting for about 25% of the total increase in this indicator," Otosaka explained.
El Niño may become the strongest in decades - UN03.09.26, 14:31 • 5166 views
"We extended the time span of our satellite data to cover the period since the 1970s, and this confirms that ice loss began in the 1990s and has increased since then. Our estimate indicates that the rate of ice loss quadrupled between the 1980s and the 2010s," Otosaka added. The study recorded a slowdown in the rate of ice loss between 2020 and 2023, although scientists said this was likely a short-term fluctuation rather than a change in the long-term trend. They noted that exceptionally heavy snowfall in East Antarctica provided enough ice accumulation to offset some of the losses from glaciers in other parts of the continent, while a relatively mild summer in Greenland significantly reduced surface ice melting.
About 84% of the ice loss was caused by glaciers rapidly flowing into the ocean, rather than by surface ice melting; this indicates that the long-term trend is driven by the ice sheets’ response to ocean warming, Otosaka explained.
The researchers noted that although the overall sea-level rise resulting from ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica may appear insignificant, it puts between 6 and 9 million people worldwide at risk of coastal flooding and soil erosion.
"These findings have important implications for coastal development planning and demonstrate the urgent need to develop plans to protect coastal communities around the world from the consequences of melting ice sheets," Otosaka concluded.

Lithuania to Build CAESAR Maintenance and Repair Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:56:12 KST

Lithuania will establish a center for the maintenance and repair of French CAESAR self-propelled howitzers.
To that end, Lithuania’s Ministry of Defense has signed an agreement with French defense company KNDS France, LRT reported.
Investment in the new infrastructure and the purchase of specialized equipment will amount to €12 million.
Lithuania will become the first country in the world to receive technological expertise from France to repair the electronic and hydraulic components of CAESAR self-propelled howitzers.
This will allow Lithuania’s defense industry to maintain the artillery systems independently instead of sending them to France for repairs.
Lithuania signed a contract to purchase the French artillery systems in December 2022. The agreement provided for the purchase of 18 CAESAR Mark II 6×6 wheeled self-propelled howitzers.
Under the contract, the first howitzers are scheduled to be delivered to the Lithuanian military in 2026, with the full order to be completed by 2027.
The Lithuanian Army has not yet received any CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, as the systems are still undergoing production and testing.
All 18 CAESAR Mark II howitzers ordered will eventually become part of the artillery battalion of the Žemaitija Infantry Brigade, replacing the outdated 105 mm M101 towed howitzers.
In August 2025, Estonia received six French 155 mm CAESAR self-propelled howitzers. The Baltic states are seeking to standardize their artillery systems to reduce maintenance and repair costs.
The Lithuanian Armed Forces have also deployed medium-range NASAMS air defense systems on the approaches to Vilnius.
Lithuania currently has two batteries of these air defense systems, with a third scheduled to arrive in the country in 2028.

Modi’in project with Rochester Jewish community turns fallen soldiers' stories into memorials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:54:57 UTC
04:54:57 KST

“I feel so bad taking all this blood, Imma [Mom],” said Yonah Brief, the wounded Duvdevan medic who was receiving a transfusion. “I just want to give it back.”
Several months after the October 7 massacre hero’s death on November 25, 2024, Yonah’s wishes became a reality: The Brief family set up a national Duvdevan blood drive that collected 480 gallons of blood in the first year.
Yonah, from Modi’in, spent 417 days in the ICU. After being hit by 13 bullets, 11 bouts of pneumonia, two amputations, and catastrophic liver and kidney failure, his impact lives on.
Yonah is one of 35 soldiers from the Modi’in community laid to rest since the October 7 massacre. Today, their memories adorn the paths all over Modi’in’s public landscape thanks to the support and involvement of Rochester’s Jewish community.
The initiative was facilitated by the Modi’in-Rochester Partnership, also known as Partnership2Gether (P2G), which celebrated its 23rd year in August.
A singular goal: To work together and create communal depth
After the October 7 massacre, P2G collaborated with Mayor Haim Bibas and the Modi’in Municipality to create misholim, a series of paths and public markers bearing the names and stories of Modi’in’s and Rochester’s fallen.
Featuring a QR code linking the soldier’s story, the placement of paths are deliberate.
Eden Zimri, who served as a commander in the Artillery Corps’ drone unit, was killed on October 7. She is commemorated on the IDF Nahal Oz outpost’s path, which runs between her home and the community pool, where she once swam.
Eitan Auster, a commando squad leader in the Egoz special unit, is commemorated on the path to the synagogue.
The path commemorating Brief, who was active in Bnei Akiva, leads to the local youth group’s center.
Families are approached on their own timeline and allowed to grieve before any public honor is offered. The proposal was extraordinary for David and Hazel Brief, Yonah’s parents.
“Many other bereaved families have to struggle against their city or town to even name a bench in their son’s name,” they said in a statement.
The paths have become a part of daily life in the community. Today, families of the fallen sing, dance, and celebrate around their loved ones.
Some families feel closer to their loved ones by the path than by other conventional places, Avni said. For example, on Remembrance Day, Eitan Auster’s mother chose to honor her son by the path rather than going to Mount Herzl Military Cemetery.
The initiative also honored the greater Rochester community in Upstate New York. Yonatan Dean Chaim, an oleh (new immigrant) and convert who moved from Rochester to Ramat Gan to serve in the IDF, was killed during Operation Swords of Iron, the Israel-Hamas War. In response to a request in Summer 2025, P2G facilitated the construction of a path in his memory.
For Zigi Avni, a member and chairman of the partnership, misholim demonstrates exactly how P2G is unique among the other 44 Israeli-American city partnerships.
The program’s projects emphasize in-person relationships over online alternatives, and both communities engage with efforts to connect, he said. The initiative now boasts at least five different programs, he added.
According to Dr. Hila Hadas, CEO of mental-health organization Enosh and co-founder of P2G, the goal “is to create depth in each community and work together.”
The Journey for Identity, where youth from both communities come together to learn and reflect on their unique Jewish identity through a three-week summer trip to Rochester, Poland, and Israel, directly encapsulates this vision.
Zoe Linnett, 18, from Modi’in recalls the culture shock of experiencing Rochester’s community. She said the trip “sparked an ember... that Israel fanned into a flame” after touring Israel and the October 7 massacre sites.
Long conversations about identity brought the cohort closer to each other and to Jewish pride, Linnett said.
Hadas said: “We aren’t trying to make anyone more religious or make aliyah.”
The question that continues to permeate every conversation until today, she said, is: “What does it mean to be a Jew in today’s world for me?”
Sixty percent of US adults hold an unfavorable view of Israel, according to a Pew Research study conducted in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.
Nevertheless, even when once unquestionable support and fundraising falter, the partnership remains steadfast in answering this question, Hadas said.
P2G’s involvement with misholim and the Federation of Rochester’s $350,000 donation recognized an ever-evolving need.
“A few years ago,” before October 7, “just donating money was enough,” Avni said. “It’s not the same anymore.” Now we need “the spirit, the ideas, the partnership.” Money “is not everything.”
Martin Zand, a professor and the target of a pro-Palestinian poster on Rochester University’s campus, said he actively defends and empathizes with his brothers and sisters in Israel. That comes from “recognizing that we are fighting different battles – one a physical battle, and the other an equally existential battle.”
Despite the different traumas and lived experiences, through efforts to understand and accommodate each other, Israeli and Diaspora communities continue to prove how we are indeed our brothers’ keepers, he said.

Netanyahu US trips: $13,000 for hair and makeup, $500 smoking fee, $125 traffic ticket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:54:47 UTC
04:54:47 KST

Documents released by the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) on Wednesday following a Freedom of Information request revealed a long list of expenses recorded during Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visits to the United States in 2025, including more than $13,000 for hair and makeup during one trip, a $500 "smoking fee," $295 to repair an embassy door, and $125 for a traffic ticket.
The documents were provided to attorney Elad Mann of the Hatzlacha organization following a request filed under the Freedom of Information Law. They include billing tables, delegation lists, and schedules from the prime minister's visits.
Some details were redacted on national security grounds. The PMO also clarified that in some cases, the process of reviewing the bills has not yet been completed.
During Netanyahu's visit to Washington in February, one of the most prominent entries in the expense report was a $6,772 charge for a makeup artist, alongside $6,747 for a hairdresser, totaling $13,519.
That visit also included a $25,000 charge for the prime minister's suite, $511.50 for food in the suite, and approximately $298 for laundry.
One of the smaller entries, however, stands out: $500 listed as a "smoking fee - conference room, press conference with the prime minister."
The report also lists additional expenses for lighting and photography, transportation, work rooms, refreshments, and equipment the delegation used during the visit.
Over $6,000 spent for makeup artist and hairdresser
Charges for a makeup artist and hairdresser appeared again during a visit in April. This time, $3,036 was recorded for the makeup artist and another $3,036 for the hairdresser, for a combined total of $6,072.
The same report includes $1,228 for "printers + toners" and approximately $240 for a "whiteboard + corkboard."
The largest charge during that visit was $51,661 for Washington's Watergate Hotel, while the total itemized charges in the report came to approximately $128,900.
In the report covering Netanyahu's July visit, a particularly large charge of $172,701.60 appears for the Willard InterContinental hotel in Washington.
Among the many entries, however, is a far smaller one: $295 to a locksmith company, described as "repair of embassy entrance door - malfunction during prime minister's visit."
The documents also include purchases from Amazon, Costco, Target, and Staples, as well as expenses for refreshments, office equipment, vehicles, customs, and overtime.
The July visit's expense report totaled approximately $373,700.
Another unusual entry appears among the expenses from Netanyahu's trip to New York and Washington in late September: $125 under the description "traffic ticket - prime minister's visit 09.25."
During that trip, the prime minister's suite at the Loews Regency in New York cost $5,999 per night, for a total of $41,993.
The PMO explained in the documents that the visit took place during the UN General Assembly, when demand for hotel rooms in New York is particularly high, and rooms are booked far in advance.
The schedule attached to the documents shows that the visit included, among other events, meetings with the presidents of Paraguay, Serbia, and Argentina; an address to the UN General Assembly; a meeting with the United Arab Emirates foreign minister; and an interview with Fox News.
Netanyahu later flew to Washington, where he met US President Donald Trump at the White House.
The highest nightly price for the prime minister's suite among the documents released was recorded during an end-of-year visit to Florida: $10,000 per night, for a total of $50,000.
According to the table, a regular room for members of the delegation cost approximately $250 per night on average.
The official schedule shows that during the visit, Netanyahu met, among others, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Trump, and spoke by phone with Vice President JD Vance.
The visit later included interviews with Fox News and Newsmax, a meeting with Steve Wynn, dinner at Larry Ellison's home, meetings with evangelicals and elected officials, and Netanyahu and his wife attending a New Year's event at Mar-a-Lago.
The delegation list for the Florida visit includes dozens of names and positions from the PMO, the public diplomacy apparatus, foreign relations, and logistics, alongside additional officials whose details were redacted.
PMO: Figures do not necessarily represent final bills in every case
Despite the extensive detail, the PMO cautioned that the figures do not necessarily represent final bills in every case.
In its response to the Freedom of Information request, the office said that the prime minister's overseas visits are not paid for directly by the PMO, but through the Foreign Ministry and its missions.
Before a visit, an estimated cost is transferred, but suppliers' invoices and receipts are collected only after the trip ends.
According to the PMO, the process can take "many months," and payment is transferred to the Foreign Ministry only after the expenses have been reviewed.
Among the hundreds of thousands of dollars spent on hotels, flights, and logistics, it is the smaller entries in the documents that provide some of the most unusual glimpses into the expenses behind the prime minister's trips: a makeup artist, a hairdresser, a smoking fee, a faulty door, and a single traffic ticket.

Hebron’s Jewish community finishes restoring tomb belonging to ancestors of biblical King David
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:54:29 UTC
04:54:29 KST

Hebron’s Jewish community completed a four year restoration of the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth atop Tel Hebron in the West Bank on Tuesday.
The work was spearheaded by the community’s international spokesperson, Yishai Fleisher, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
He also serves as a member of the Efrat Local Council, and is a widely recognized English-speaking voice for Israel abroad, with his YouTube channel having more than 300,000 subscribers.
The tomb is believed by Jewish sources to be the burial place of the biblical King David’s father, Yishai, and his great-grandmother, Ruth the Moabite.
“The location of the site in Hebron, city of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the first acquisition of the Jews in the Land of Israel, made by our forefather Abraham, carries important spiritual significance,” explained Fleisher. “There is a connection between the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth and the Cave of the [Patriarchs].”
“The sources state that there are four 'wheels' in the Chariot of the G-d: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David. Why specifically David? Because David is the one who fulfills the dream of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the dream of a united and strong people in their land, living in holiness."
Bringing Safed to Hebron
Fleisher, working closely with a team of historians and artisans, drew up a design drawing on the turquoise color usually associated with Safed, departing from the site's traditional browns and greens.
"We wanted to bring the sanctity of Safed's turquoise into the heart of Hebron," Fleisher said.
The graves of Yishai and Ruth themselves were redesigned using stone, calligraphic inscriptions, a Star of David, and a wheat motif to represent Ruth's biblical story.
Renovations for the tomb, as well as the establishment of a new synagogue and study hall at the site, were completed using mainly local Hebron stone, wrought iron, and wood.
The project cost roughly one million dollars fundraised by Fleisher from donars around the world.
Connecting site to younger generations
Additionally, a chamber dating back to the Byzantine and medieval periods was restored and converted into a a working studio, where a scribe writes on parchment using traditional methods, in view of visitors.
The completed site also includes shaded seating areas, water fountains, restrooms, a small event hall, a courtyard, parking, and direct access to the Tel Hebron archaeological park.
"If young people saw the place as it used to be, they wouldn't connect to it, and they wouldn't feel that this is a place of holiness,” Fleisher stated. “My view is that these places we love, places that are our heritage, need to be beautiful, need to expand the heart, to believe that this is truly something great.”
“I'm looking forward to applying my experience in beautifying Hebron to beautifying the whole Land of Israel through the Knesset.”
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Reminder
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine supported strengthening liability for electronic communications fraud and the activities of scam call centers. The relevant Law No. 10190 was adopted in its entirety on September 16.
According to the explanatory note, the law provides for amendments to the Criminal Code of Ukraine by adding a new Article 1901, "Electronic Communications Fraud," which establishes liability for electronic communications fraud, that is, the unlawful collection, storage, processing, and use of personal data and information containing banking secrecy, including individual account information, payment instrument details, payment card details, and authorization codes, with the aim of taking possession of another person's property or acquiring rights to property through deception or abuse of trust using electronic communications and/or technical means of electronic communications.
The Criminal Code of Ukraine is also supplemented with new articles:
-  Article 2554 ("Creation of, management of, or participation in an electronic communications fraud organization");  
-  Article 2555, "Recruitment for participation in an electronic communications fraud organization," establishing new liability for the actions of such fraudulent organizations and participation in them.

Tips for consumers hit with a debt collection notice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:59 UTC
04:41:59 KST

How to make sure you are not impacted by misleading debt collection notices
This year has been a perfect storm for financial stress.
With three interest rate hikes, rising cost of living, and a Middle East war driving up fuel prices, more Australians are falling behind on their debt repayments.
And that has led to a 12 per cent spike in the number of people calling the National Debt Helpline.
In fact, an additional 20,000 people contacted the organisation for debt advice in the year to August, taking the total to 187,905.
About 15,000 of those were directly related to debt collection.
Adding to the stress is the fact that debt collectors are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to ramp up their efforts to claw back money from debt-ridden consumers.
One woman was sent repeated legal threats, trying to force her to pay a claim she was never liable for, which legal experts described as the "worst kind" of bullying.
It comes as the ACCC takes ARMA Group and Force Legal to federal court, alleging that between them they sent 320,000 debt enforcement notices to individuals that were allegedly misleading.
So how is a debt collector meant to engage with an individual, and what rights does one have in the process?
What rights does an individual have?
The coordinator of the National Debt Helpline, Vicki Staff, said the first thing to do was work out if the debt was valid.
"For example, you may have already paid the debt … I recommend writing to the debt collector and letting them know that you have paid it in full and provide any copies of records if you have something to prove that the debt is repaid," she said.
If the debt is more than three years old in the Northern Territory, and more than six years old elsewhere, that means it is statute-barred, meaning the legal time limit to start court proceedings has expired.
"If it's an unsecured debt and you've not made a payment, you've not acknowledged the debt in writing, and there's no court judgment that's been entered against you, you're in a good position to be able to challenge it," Ms Staff said.
But if the debt was valid, she said "crunch the numbers" to see what was realistic for repayment.
"Get your ducks in a row first [and] get an agreement from the debt collector as to an affordable payment arrangement," Ms Staff said.
Under the National Credit Code, an individual may be able to change the terms of their consumer credit contract to allow them to pause or reduce payments for a period of time.
If you're not happy with the process, Ms Staff said there were other avenues.
"Check to find if your debt collector is actually registered with an external ombudsman, [and] you can make a complaint," she said.
There's also the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
"If the creditor is a financial services provider, you can take a complaint to [AFCA]," Nicola Howell, senior law lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology, said.
"Financial services providers should have an internal dispute resolution process as well that you can go to and seek to resolve the matter."
Expectations of a debt collector
Just like other industries, debt collector conduct is governed under Australian consumer law.
That means there are standards and expectations in place when looking to recover costs.
"Being proactive and being open to affordable hardship arrangements for people … communicating really clearly with customers around what was expected," Ms Staff said.
Dr Howell said if a debt collector did not act appropriately, there were consequences.
"The prohibitions against misleading and deceptive conduct or unconscionable conduct apply to businesses that are engaging in trade or commerce," she said.
"There's no carve-out for lawyers in terms of how they're conducting their business in that interface with consumers."

====================================================================================================

'Mobilisation of fear': The deeper strategy behind One Nation's immigration policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:41 UTC
04:41:41 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Jyoti has called her migration agent three times this month. Each time, she asks the same question: Has there been any update?
Her application for a Skilled Independent visa, a pathway to permanent residency, has been sitting in the queue for months. It has felt like a long wait for Jyoti, who has lived in Australia for the better part of a decade. In recent months, that uncertainty has taken on a new urgency.
The 43-year-old is a secondary school teacher who lives in an outer northern suburb of Melbourne with her husband and their two children. She arrived from Punjab, northern India, eight years ago as an international student and is now in Australia on a work visa.
She asks that only her first name be used because she fears speaking publicly could affect her family's visa prospects.
I feel like the axe is going to fall on people like us before anyone else.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"International students, temporary visa holders ... we would be the first to lose our livelihoods and our place here if Pauline Hanson comes to power, or if her party keeps gaining momentum," she tells SBS News.
Jyoti says she is watching the lead-up to Victoria's November election closely. To her, the election will be an early test of how far One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's momentum could travel and what that could mean for her family's future in the only country her children have really known. It's a fear, she says, that everyone she knows in her position is carrying right now.
One Nation wants to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders from Australia over three years. Not one of them will get a say in whether the party succeeds.
"Our fate is being decided by political parties whose fate we have no say in," Jyoti says.
Australia is home to roughly three million temporary visa holders, including students, graduates and skilled workers.
As One Nation pushes for sweeping cuts to temporary migration, it raises a harder question about political power: are people with the least ability to influence an election also the easiest to target?
Who One Nation's visa cuts would hit hardest
One Nation's plan would tighten the student and graduate visa systems, restrict family members from accompanying temporary skilled workers, and close off "visa hopping" — the practice of extending a stay by switching between visa categories rather than leaving the country and reapplying offshore.
According to the policy announced on Monday, international students and graduates would absorb the biggest cuts.
The student visa population, including accompanying family members, would fall from about 590,000 to 350,000, and the graduate visa population from about 270,000 to just 40,000 over three years.
Family visas linked to temporary skilled workers would be phased out entirely, a change expected to shrink that cohort from about 263,000 to 160,000 over the same period.
"Tinkering around the edges will not fix the damage," Hanson said in the media release.
"This is about giving Australians breathing space by drastically cutting the stock of temporary migrants, restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia."
Speaking with ABC's Radio National on Monday morning, Environment Minister Murray Watt said One Nation's policy would trigger economic disruption.
"One Nation's policy is a recipe to destroy the Australian economy and drive the Australian economy into recession," he said.
For people already living that reality, the question isn't abstract. Jyoti says the proposed changes have made getting permanent residency feel less like the obvious next step in her journey and more like a race against time.
They are looking at us as just numbers, but there are actual lives and people behind these numbers.
Not everyone would be affected equally, says Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration. Much depends on a migrant's professional skills and experience.
"Temporary entrants with skills in strong demand tend to secure permanent residency much faster than others," he tells SBS News.
For instance, a nurse's pathway to permanent residency looks nothing like that of a graduate in a field with weaker demand. For the latter, the road can be far longer, and far less certain.
One Nation has confirmed it would maintain a net overseas migration (NOM) ceiling of 130,000 a year once its proposed three-year reset is complete.
Rizvi says that target leaves the policy with nowhere else to land.
"Taking into account the fact that One Nation has said it wants to quarantine WHMs [Working Holiday Makers] and PALM [Pacific Australia Labour Mobility] visas from any cuts; cannot lawfully reduce places for partners and dependent children; can't easily reduce numbers of NZ citizens contributing to NOM and wants to maintain a flow of tradies and health workers, it leaves no room for students and temporary graduates," he says.
Essentially, One Nation policy would mean abolishing the international education industry.
"That would have massive consequences for university budgets and staff. Possibly 50,000 jobs would be directly affected. More indirectly."
The political cost of having no vote
Temporary entrants have never had voting rights in Australia and "never will", Rizvi says.
But it's a dynamic that has shaped migration policy for longer than many realise, says Emily Foley, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Canberra who studies social democratic and centre-left political parties.
She says temporary migration has quietly created problems over many decades that successive governments have had little reason to confront.
"For years, policymakers and governments knew there were significant issues with the temporary migration program essentially creating an underclass of exploited and marginalised workers," she tells SBS News.
"And yet, precisely because this cohort are not voters, there was minimal political incentive to actively discuss the policy area, particularly when migration was such a salient and politicised election issue."
One Nation is not alone in pushing for tighter controls on temporary migration. Labor has already moved to amend parts of its policy, including restricting visa hopping, shortening Temporary Graduate visas, raising the income threshold for temporary skilled migration and introducing managed limits on new international student commencements.
The Coalition has also promised to reduce migration by linking NOM to the number of homes built. It has separately proposed making compliance with an Australian Values Statement a universal visa condition, with breaches potentially leading to visa refusal or cancellation.
But One Nation's proposal goes considerably further, targeting the temporary migrant population with sharp reductions in student and graduate numbers and restrictions on accompanying family members.
Foley says the party's focus is consistent with its longstanding position on immigration.
Attacking temporary migrants is therefore not surprising.
"This cohort, despite many being Australian taxpayers, are without the civil, political and economic rights and privileges of Australian citizens and permanent residents. It is easy for parties like One Nation to attack and marginalise temporary migrants precisely because they have so little recourse."
Benjamin Moffitt, a senior lecturer in politics and international relations at Monash University, is more blunt about the electoral calculus.
"It removes the one thing that usually keeps rhetoric in check: the people it hits getting a vote on it," he tells SBS News.
"Temporary visa holders and prospective migrants can't punish a party at the ballot box, so there's no electoral cost to going as hard as you like on them.
"That's true of migration policy generally, not a One Nation quirk, but it's a big part of why this is the one area where the inflammatory rhetoric can run so far ahead of the actual policy detail."
But he stops short of saying One Nation is deliberately targeting temporary migrants for this reason.
What can be established, Moffitt says, is that the groups One Nation has identified most precisely — including international students, working holidaymakers and skilled visa holders — are among those who cannot vote.
"Whether that's a deliberate strategy of picking targets who can't retaliate, or simply where the populist radical right's usual scapegoating logic lands by default, isn't something you can necessarily tell apart from the outside."
One Nation did not respond to SBS News' request for comment on whether the lack of voting rights among temporary visa holders is a consideration in its immigration policies.
What temporary migrants contribute
Temporary migrants make up a significant part of Australia's workforce and international education sector. Their contribution extends beyond the visa system, with international students alone generating almost $55 billion in education export income in 2025.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, international students and their families accounted for 82.4 per cent of non-residents eligible to work in Australia in June 2025.
Andrew McKellar, CEO of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told reporters on Monday that cutting temporary migration to the degree proposed by One Nation could have a significant economic impact.
"You know, if you're going to cut overall visa levels by 750,000 over a three-year period and drive net overseas migration into negative territory, that's a COVID-level shock to the Australian economy," he said.
One Nation has pointed to Canada's recent cuts to temporary migration as evidence that immigration can be reduced without crashing the economy.
McKellar said the focus should instead be on the potential impact of the proposed cuts on Australia's growth.
"What the debate cannot be about is it cannot be about arbitrary targets. We can't have solutions which are extreme, which would cause very significant damage to the Australian economy."
Why immigration works for One Nation
Tiziana Torresi is the program director of the School of Society and Culture at Adelaide University and studies normative political theory and the governance of migration. She says immigration sits within a broader populist strategy that divides society between an "authentic" Australian public and groups portrayed as threatening to its interests.
"Anti-immigration rhetoric has been central to One Nation's political discourse from its emergence," she tells SBS News.
Torresi says the party's appeal taps into economic and social anxieties.
"The mobilisation of fear is a key strategy of populist far-right parties, enabling them to present themselves as the only true voice and defenders of an authentic national community threatened by 'outsiders'," she says.
Moffitt says this extends to issues such as housing, jobs and infrastructure. He describes this approach as 'nativism', where social and economic problems are attributed to outsiders, particularly migrants.
"Nativism doesn't identify a housing crisis and then, separately, decide migrants are to blame; it needs a scapegoat for social and economic ills, and the migrant is the figure built to supply one," he says.
The result is a message that can speak to voters worried about the cost of living, housing and population growth, while also tapping into deeper concerns about Australia's changing social and cultural identity.
Torresi says this allows One Nation to present itself as the party willing to restore a sense of control to voters who believe established political parties have failed them.
One Nation can exploit these various anxieties by claiming that 'ordinary Australians' are being left behind or displaced.
That is where the politics of temporary migration becomes more complicated. The people most directly affected may have no vote, but the issue is being used to speak to millions of people who do.
Beyond the ballot box
Torresi says the absence of a vote does not mean migrants are politically disconnected.
"Migrants are embedded in families, workplaces, neighbourhoods, unions, community organisations, and broader social networks, creating relationships with citizens who do possess electoral rights," she says.
Those relationships can give migrants an indirect political voice through the citizens around them, who can respond at the ballot box.
"Consequently, political attacks on migrants may have effects that extend well beyond the migrant population itself."
But temporary migrants may have fewer connections to Australian citizens who can advocate for their interests, Torresi says.
"Temporary migrants may be doubly vulnerable to anti-immigration politics because they can lack both direct and indirect forms of political influence."
Back in Melbourne, Jyoti says the fear she feels is being mirrored back to her.
"It's not just me. Everyone I know in this situation feels the same fear," she says.
We've built our lives here, and none of that means we get a say in what happens to us next.
Her migration agent still doesn't have an update. She'll call again next week.

Japan just hit a new longevity milestone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:37 UTC
04:41:37 KST

Humans are living longer and longer. Now Japan has broken a new record for longevity: more than 100,000 people in the country are centenarians—some 107,677 of them are at least 100 years old.
Japan has one of the highest life expectancies in the world. Researchers believe this national longevity is likely linked to low rates of obesity, healthy diets, widespread health screenings and affordable health care, which lead to lower mortality rates from heart disease and cancer.
“I am very happy that so many people have been able to stay active for so long,” said Japan’s health minister Kenichiro Ueno at a news conference announcing the milestone in Tokyo on Tuesday.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Japan is “exactly where you would expect to see this first,” says Jay Olshansky, an epidemiologist at the University of Illinois Chicago. But he expects more countries to follow as large birth cohorts hit the 100-year mark and medical advances continue.
“Most people at older ages now are living on manufactured time—time that was created for us by our physicians and by the public health community,” he says.
But more people living long lives isn’t all good news. Japan also has one of the lower birth rates in the world. And its lower fertility rates and smaller working-age population are squeezing public resources and making caring for its older populations more difficult. Additionally, a long life can be “a potentially dangerous scenario unless it’s accompanied by good health,” Olshansky says.
Japan’s oldest known person, Fuyo Kumamato, is 114 years old. (The oldest living person in the world, Ethel Caterham in the U.K., is 117 years old.) Researchers around the world are studying supercentenarians, people older than age 110, in hopes of keeping more people healthy for longer.
“What’s really critical about this is quality of life,” Olshansky adds. “Just living longer should not be the primary goal of medicine and public health anymore. It should be health extension or health span.”
