AfD, the far right, and the lessons Germany's mainstream forgot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:29 UTC
04:41:29 KST

Breadcrumb
AfD, the far right, and the lessons Germany's mainstream forgot
On 6 September, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a landslide victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, securing nearly 44% of the vote and 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats. The result marked the first time since the Second World War that a far-right party has won a state election in Germany.
The party fell just three seats short of an outright majority, meaning it cannot govern alone and will need support from another party or lawmakers to form a government. However, other MPs, specifically from the Büdnis Sahra Wagenknecht Party (BSW) will most likely give the AfD the seats it needs to run the state.
The election should not be viewed in isolation. It is the latest and perhaps most alarming indication of how Germany’s political mainstream has increasingly adopted positions once associated primarily with the far right, particularly on migration, asylum and national identity.
Their 258-page manifesto, titled Das Land Zuerst (The Country First), details a fundamental shift in the country’s immigration system. It promises large scale deportations of immigrations and asylum seekers, and advocates for a “remigration program,” that might even affect German resident holders or those who do not sound or look German.
AfD leader Alice Weidel has been explicit about the party’s intentions. She has said that if elected to government, their first 100 days would bring about the deportations and a closed German border, adding that “if it has to be called remigration, then let it be called remigration.”
Years in the making
The AfD’s policies range from encouraging Germans to have more children through financial incentives, such as a €2,000 birth bonus (although only applying to German citizen heterosexual families), to bringing back coal mining, and restoring friendly relations with Russia to provide cheaper access to energy.
They also want to change their school curriculum to focus less on the Holocaust and more on the country’s history pre-World War Two, and severely restrict abortion access.
While many attribute the AfD’s rise to worsening economic conditions, including rising energy prices, fewer job opportunities, and stagnating wages, these factors alone do not explain the party’s growing support. The political conditions that have allowed the AfD to flourish have been developing for years.
Last year, many of us warned that the mainstream parties’ shift towards increasingly anti-migrant and xenophobic rhetoric could ultimately backfire. Rather than isolating the far right, mainstream politicians have increasingly attempted to compete with it by adopting policies that restrict migrants’ rights and treating migration as the defining political crisis of the country.
Under the former Socialist Democrat Prime Minister Olaf Scholz in January 2025, the German Bundestag passed the Repatriation Improvement Act, one of the most significant recent efforts to accelerate deportations by extending maximum deportation detention from 10 to 28 days, as well as significantly reducing the benefits of refugees and asylum seekers.
Meanwhile Freidrich Merz, while claiming that he and the Christian Democratic Party must isolate the AfD so they do not “carry out an ethnic cleansing of the country,” Merz’s own government representatives admitted that they needed to be even tougher on migration.
“Perhaps it was also a mistake by the CDU that in recent years it had not addressed the issue [of migration] enough,” Minister President Sven Schulze said.
The politicisation of migration became emboldened especially following the December 2024 attack on a Christmas market in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, in which six people were ultimately killed and around 300 injured. The suspect was a Saudi national who had lived in Germany for years and had publicly expressed strongly anti-Islamic and far-right views, including support for the Alternative for Germany (AfD).
Despite the attacker being an anti-Islam, AfD supporter himself, the media, political parties and AfD themselves became emboldened with anti-Muslim, anti-migrant rhetoric.
Weidel declared that “Magdeburg would not have been possible without uncontrolled immigration” and called for “a restrictive migration policy and consistent deportations.” AfD supporters subsequently gathered in Magdeburg, with protesters reported chanting “Deport, deport, deport.”
Integration
Instead of attempting to rectify emboldened far-right ideologues, Merz presented his policy platforms to revoke German citizenship from dual nationals, especially pro-Palestinian demonstrators, people he considers “terror supporters,” and those who he believes commit severe crimes.
And in fact, some months later a naturalised Palestinian man, Abdullah A., had his citizenship revoked over alleged support of Palestinian fighters on his social media.
Now, directly after the AfD win, the CDU is reportedly moving to tighten citizenship rules even further. According to a recent report, senior CDU figures are drafting proposals that would effectively reverse key elements of the citizenship reform introduced by the previous government, including the normalisation of dual citizenship.
This follows a historic 2025 total of 332,500 naturalisations in Germany, after a 2024 citizenship reform under Olaf Scholz reduced the standard residency requirement to five years and allowed naturalised citizens to retain their previous nationality.
The reported plan includes renouncing previous citizenship, passing a language examination, covering living costs entirely from their own income, and disavowing “all forms of antisemitism."
Already, this country’s politicians are looking for ways to make it harder for individuals to integrate into German society by forcing people to give up their passports from their country of origin.
The danger does not stop with only the AfD winning elections, as we are already seeing dangerous signs that the far-right party is willing to use the machinery of the state to escalate violence where it deems necessary.
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, gave the people a glimpse of his viciousness when he did not condemn building arms manufacturers in his state because he wants to reserve the arms for his own “remigration offensive.”
Inspired by Trump’s America
I am reminded of the United States, of the armed, masked ICE officers abducting immigrants from their homes, on their way to drop off their children, and at their places of work while killing them or the protestors who object to their abductions. The images of detention centres and imprisoning migrant children, and the act of disappearing and separating families, might be closer to Germany’s front doors than we think.
In fact, the AfD mirrors important elements of the MAGA movement: far-right politics wrapped in the language of economic populism, alleged restoration of a national homeland, and allegedly against investment in foreign wars. Like Trump and his movement, the AfD presents itself as a defender of ordinary citizens against elitist, lying bureaucrats and progressive institutions and establishments.
They promise tax reductions, economic benefits, and making Germany German again.
It is also important to note that the AfD, while entrenched in an antisemitic history, is vehemently pro-Israel and, in fact, tells Jewish constituents that it is their party that would treat them the best because of its commitment to stand firm against pro-Palestinians, leftists, and “those who hate Israel.”
Germany’s memory culture and mainstream political discourse have allowed a far-right party to simply claim that they are not antisemitic due to the fact that they are simply Zionist.
The AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt is a warning about what happens when xenophobia becomes mainstream political currency, when deportation is presented as the solution to social and economic problems, and when mainstream politicians compete with the far-right by adopting its rhetoric and policies.
Offering a softer, more palatable version of the same politics only risks legitimising the far right without necessarily winning its voters. If voters want tougher deportation policies, they may ultimately choose the politicians they believe will follow through, rather than those who express similar sentiments in a palatable, politically acceptable vocabulary.
Hebh Jamal is a Palestinian American journalist based in Germany.

An ancient disease is surging in Australia — and it isn't always easy to detect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:41:26 UTC
04:41:26 KST

IN BRIEF
- Gonorrhoea and syphilis notifications have surged by more than half in the past decade.
- Indigenous health experts have warned of a serious need for investment in community-led health projects.
Reported cases of infectious syphilis and gonorrhoea have surged by more than half over the past decade in Australia, as experts warn education and testing urgently needs to improve.
In 2025, there were 42,393 gonorrhoea notifications and 5,986 infectious syphilis notifications — a 10-year increase of 57 per cent for gonorrhoea and 56 per cent for syphilis, analysis from the University of New South Wales' Kirby Institute has shown.
Syphilis was declared a communicable disease of national significance in late 2025, in response to "ongoing and concerning" rises in Australian case numbers.
Chief medical officer Professor Michael Kidd declared that awareness was necessary among all Australians, including healthcare professionals, and urged everyone to get tested.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Syphilis and gonorrhoea are common bacterial infections with ancient origins, now easily treated with antibiotics.
But both infections can present with either mild or non-existent symptoms.
If left untreated, syphilis progresses through stages and can spread to the brain, heart, eyes, and other organs. It can cause neurological problems including paralysis, and dementia, and cause soft, tumour-like growths to appear on the skin, bones or internal organs. Tertiary syphilis can eventually lead to death.
Notification rates for infectious syphilis among women increased 170 per cent in the past decade from 2016 to 2025. In contrast, rates increased just 39 per cent among males.
Syphilis during pregnancy can lead to congenital syphilis, which can result in miscarriage or stillbirth, or severe lifelong health impacts in babies that are born, including prematurity, low birthweight and other physical developmental abnormalities.
Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said congenital syphilis is a persistent issue in Australia, with more than half of deaths in the last decade among First Nations infants. There were 14 cases of congenital syphilis in 2025, and 113 from 2016 to 2025, with 40 resulting in the death of an infant.
"This is an entirely preventable outcome with early diagnosis, testing and treatment of pregnant people," McGregor said.
Better approaches for at-risk populations
First Nations peoples were disproportionately affected by STIs, diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous people and syphilis at more than six times.
Kim Gates, community relations lead in the Kirby Institute's First Nations Point-Of-Care Program, said the disparities in diagnoses between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians were an indication of broader inequities in healthcare.
Australian services needed to be designed better to reflect the experiences of First Nations communities, Gates told SBS News, adding that many First Nations peoples have a complex relationship with the Australian health system and "have good reasons to be sceptical of top-down services and approaches".
"This is why Aboriginal-led services are so important," she said.
Gates said that while the 149 Aboriginal Controlled Community Health Services in Australia provide comprehensive and culturally safe healthcare, "there are areas these don't reach".
For Gates, sustained investment in community-led initiatives, like the First Nations Molecular Point-of-Care Testing Program, was the solution to bringing down STI rates among Indigenous populations.
Improving community awareness is key
Dr Arthur Wong, sexual health physician and conjoint lecturer at the Kirby Institute, said that timely testing, treatment and retesting were "crucial", and that post-diagnosis care was also "essential" to avoid repeat infections.
Wong told SBS News that awareness was already affecting syphilis rates, where evidence shows a decline in incidence among gay and bisexual men.
"We do know that testing has increased in certain populations," Wong said. "Gay and bisexual men who are taking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PReP) are tested more frequently for STIs."
But the data leaves out an often-overlooked section of the population — for homosexual, bisexual and transgender women, rates of syphilis and gonorrhoea remain largely unknown.
LGBTIQ+ Women's Project Lead at ACON (formerly AIDS Council of NSW), Lee Wang, says queer and trans women aren't routinely reported in surveillance data, which has adverse health outcomes.
"When queer and trans women are overlooked, it can create the false impression that STI prevention and testing are not relevant to them," Wang told SBS News.
"This can contribute to lower testing and missed opportunities for prevention and early diagnosis, with recent surveys highlighting substantial gaps in STI testing when compared with gay and bisexual men."
There was a need for targeted sexual health education resources, Wang said, like ACON's Word on the Sheets, a digital sexual and reproductive health resource for LGBTQ+ women, trans and gender diverse people.
"We shouldn't confuse a lack of data with a lack of priority," Wang said. "We need healthcare providers who are equipped to discuss sexual practices without making assumptions about sexuality or gender identity."
Wong said preliminary data from the most recent Australian Study of Health and Relationships show that just 17 per cent of people aged 16 to 49 reported having an STI test in the last 12 months.
Rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 years.
Studies in recent years have pointed to a waning use of condoms among school-aged people in Australia, with findings from a Secondary Students and Sexual Health (SSASH) survey analysis by Victoria University in 2024 stating that condom use in Australia was low and has declined over a decade.
Overall, Wong said, Australia needed a "sustained and enhanced" response to sexual health, "to ensure any gains are experienced equally across all populations."

‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:39:28 UTC
04:39:28 KST

The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.
The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.
A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.
It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.
The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made in Europe, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.
Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, including what tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UK on a mooted “youth experience” programme.
UK sources say that while a food and drink deal and a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.
There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.
One government source said: “We are willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”
The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.
France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.
It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.
One EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed. “The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”
It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.
The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.
Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.
A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”
The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.
Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of a potential loss of 300,000 jobs this year unless incentives were put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.
The EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears that European companies are being cannibalised from within.
In her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.
Her surprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canada demonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third-country partners.
Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”
The EU and Canada are to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.
Carney, who is to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.
Burnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in the EFL Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.
The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.
The Conservatives criticised the UK-EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.
Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.
Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.
“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”

Fed raises US inflation outlook while lowering unemployment forecasts

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US Federal Reserve raised its inflation forecasts for 2026 on Wednesday, while lowering unemployment projections, signaling persistent price pressures alongside a resilient labor market.
The median forecast for core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation was raised to 3.4% for 2026 from 3.3% in June, according to the Fed’s latest Summary of Economic Projections.
The core measure, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is expected to ease to 2.5% in 2027, 2.2% in 2028 and 2% in 2029.
The headline PCE inflation forecast for 2026 was also lifted by 0.1 percentage point to 3.7%. Inflation is projected to fall to 2.3% in 2027, 2.1% in 2028 and reach the Fed’s 2% target in 2029.
The upward revisions came despite upcoming methodological changes by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis that economists expect to mechanically lower measured core PCE inflation.
The changes, set to take effect with annual revisions Sept. 30, concern the measurement of prices for services including portfolio management, legal services and computer software.
The Fed, meanwhile, presented a stronger outlook for the labor market.
Officials lowered their median unemployment-rate forecast for 2026 to 4.1% from 4.3%. The rate is projected to remain at 4.1% through 2029, compared with the June estimates of 4.3% for 2027 and 4.2% for 2028.
Changes to the growth outlook were limited. The Fed raised its real gross domestic product growth forecast for 2026 to 2.3% from 2.2%, and its 2027 estimate to 2.4% from 2.3%.
The projection for 2028 was unchanged at 2.2%, while the economy is forecast to grow 2.1% in 2029.
The revisions accompanied the Fed’s decision to raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of between 3.75% and 4%, its first increase since 2023.

US makes major wartime bet on Ukraine’s largest private energy company with $85 million investment
Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm, DTEK, has secured an $85 million loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation for a critical battery storage project, marking the DFC’s largest wartime transaction, DTEK announced on Sept. 16. 
With Russia continuing to target Ukraine’s energy facilities, particularly power plants, ensuring a reliable energy supply has become a major concern in Ukraine. During the war, Ukraine has increasingly searched for investors to bolster its grid by decentralizing energy generation and supply. 
DTEK, owned by Ukraine’s richest man, Rinat Akhmetov, has positioned itself as an entry point for foreign investors in the energy sector, recently inking agreements with U.S. and European firms. But despite a few deals signed over the last 18 months, Ukraine has yet to see a wave of large-scale foreign investment in its energy sector.
The company's CEO Maxim Timchenko believes the deal with Washington could open the door to further foreign investment in Ukraine and inspire confidence in wartime investing. It could also be a game changer for DTEK, which has had difficulties accessing financing from international financial institutions like the European Bank for Reconstruction over its ownership.
"For me, the financial part is very important, but much more significant is this signal that DFC is ready to support Ukraine and DTEK. They have made an assessment of the risk, understand how to manage it, and are saying that private investors should follow. That's how important this is," Timchenko told reporters.
DTEK opened the battery storage facility last September with American energy firm Fluence Energy Inc., which provided 698 Gridstack batteries. Together, the batteries form a 200-megawatt system that can power 600,000 Ukrainian homes for two hours — reducing blackout risks and helping to stabilize the grid in Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
While the DFC loan will primarily refinance loans initially provided by Ukrainian banks, it will also help DTEK build more battery storage with Fluence, Timchenko said. Most developers in Ukraine purchase batteries with Chinese components, but DTEK wanted American products, creating an opportunity to partner with the DFC, he added.
Under President Donald Trump, the U.S. is investing in projects that strictly exclude Chinese parts to compete with sectors dominated by Beijing. In March, the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund — jointly managed by the DFC and Kyiv — inked a deal with defense-tech firm Sine Engineering, which builds software for drones without any Chinese components.
The DFC has long expressed interest in Ukraine’s energy sector and has been in talks with DTEK for several months, likely because it is the largest private player in a sector dominated by state-owned companies.
The company is preparing for winter and needs to restore 4 gigawatts (GW) of power generation by the heating season, when Russia is expected to launch another mass bombing campaign targeting power plants.
Last winter, all of DTEK’s thermal plants were hit, and energy workers have been repairing the damage around the clock ever since. Timchenko told reporters on Sept. 10 that he is confident the company will be ready for another harsh winter.

Free but not quite yet.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:37:19 UTC

Mikhail Ryumin, Sergey Kanurin, Andrey Merkuryev and Alexander Zaytsev
After a year and four months in pre-trial detention, four Russian truck drivers accused of participating in the 2025 devastating Ukrainian drone strike on airfields across Russia dubbed “Operation Spiderweb” have been released. But their ordeal is far from over.
On September 16, the Moscow City Court released the four Chelyabinsk men from pre-trial detention. According to Kommersant daily, the ruling came after the Prosecutor General’s Office refused to approve their indictment, conceding that the evidence of their involvement was insufficient.
The truckers—Mikhail Ryumin (56), Andrey Merkuryev (62), Alexander Zaytsev (57), and Sergey Kanurin (48)—were arrested after June 1, 2025. They had been hired to transport prefabricated houses across Russia, unaware that their trailers concealed Ukrainian drones. The remotely controlled drones launched from their parked trucks to strike strategic military airbases, including “Olenya” in Murmansk and the Ivanovo airfield.
Initially, there was a fifth defendant in the case. Vasily Pytikov, 62, was killed when his truck exploded on a highway in the Amur region during the drone launch. The Investigative Committee quietly closed the criminal case against the deceased driver in February 2026.
Now, the surviving drivers have been freed under a “ban on certain actions”. A defense attorney who requested anonymity told Mediazona that the men are forbidden from communicating with each other or witnesses, and are banned from using the internet and mobile networks, except for emergency calls. Most importantly, the drivers cannot return to their families in the Urals: because the Prosecutor General returned the criminal case to the Investigative Committee, they must remain in Moscow, ready to be summoned by investigators at any moment.
“Nobody will go to Chelyabinsk, I think, because they need to appear before the investigator; investigative actions will still be carried out,” the lawyer explained. “The criminal case has not yet been closed. We hope it will be, but for now, we have only won, you could say, the first battle.”
The lawyer added that months of imprisonment has “negatively affected the health and psychological state” of the drivers, who had been facing decades in prison on terrorism and explosives charges.
“My client was so moved today, he had stopped hoping for anything,” the defender shared. “All of them were overjoyed.”
In the spring of 2025 the truckers accepted what they believed were routine jobs transporting dismantled prefabricated frame houses to four different regions across Russia. Unbeknownst to them, the cargo concealed Ukrainian drones primed for an attack.
On June 1, 2025, those hidden drones emerged from the trucks to unleash coordinated strikes on major Russian military airbases deep within the country. The targets included the “Olenya” base in the Murmansk region, “Belaya” in Irkutsk, “Dyagilevo” near Ryazan, and an airfield in Ivanovo, which houses Russia’s rarest A-50 “flying radar” reconnaissance aircraft.

France picks exiled Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev’s ‘Minotaur’ as its international Oscar entry. The Russian-language film previously won Cannes’ Grand Prix.
France has submitted Andrey Zvyagintsev’s film “Minotavr” (“Minotaur”) for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film, Variety reports.
The French Oscar committee chose the film after meeting with the producers, international sales agents, and U.S. distributors of the five shortlisted films.
“Minotaur” was co-produced by Charles Gillibert’s French companies, CG Cinéma and MK Productions. It follows the director of a company as he prepares for mass layoffs when he is ordered to send 14 people to war. Meanwhile, he learns that his wife is having an affair.
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will announce a 15-film shortlist for Best International Feature Film on December 15. The nominees will be announced on January 21, and the 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on March 14, 2027.
Last year, France submitted Iranian director Jafar Panahi’s “A Simple Accident,” which had won the Palme d’Or at Cannes and later received a nomination.
“Minotaur” is Zvyagintsev’s first film in nearly 10 years. His previous film, “Nelyubov” (“Loveless”), was released in 2017. Zvyagintsev became seriously ill with COVID-19 during the pandemic and underwent a lengthy rehabilitation abroad. He did not return to Russia after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In May 2026, “Minotaur” won the Grand Prix at the 79th Cannes Film Festival.

Demonstrations thanking Türkiye continue for a second day on Wednesday, as crowds in Wajid and Barawe take to the streets carrying Turkish and Somali flags.
Thousands of demonstrators filled streets and avenues in Wajid, carrying banners describing Türkiye as Somalia's elder brother that had always stood by the country in difficult times, and declaring that Somalia and Türkiye were bound by an ancient bond of brotherhood.
In Barawe, one of the main towns of the Lower Shabelle region, large crowds also gathered in the streets to show their support for Türkiye.
Demonstrators marched through the town carrying messages of support, and participants carried Turkish and Somali flags side by side as an expression of the relationship between the two countries.
Those taking part said Türkiye had provided important support to Somalia over many years and had done a great deal for the country.
‘Thank you, Türkiye’
Nasra Bashir Ali, Deputy Director of Communications and Public Relations at the Somali Prime Minister's Office, posted footage of the Wajid demonstration on her official Facebook account.
"The people of Wajid today held a large demonstration showing their support for the fraternal relationship and strategic cooperation between Somalia and Türkiye, praising Türkiye's role in Somalia's development and stability," Ali wrote, closing her post with a message of thanks written in Turkish: "Teşekkürler Türkiye" — Thank you, Türkiye.
Footage shared by Ali showed demonstrators carrying Somali and Turkish flags.
Participants in demonstrations that began a day earlier in various Somali towns had likewise pointed to Türkiye's contribution to the country's security, development and humanitarian assistance, sending messages in favour of maintaining the relationship between the two countries.
Ankara’s largest overseas military base
The rallies came after Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications held a panel in Mogadishu on September 10 examining the countries’ deep-rooted ties, strategic partnership and opportunities to expand bilateral cooperation.
Türkiye has expanded its presence in Somalia since Erdogan's 2011 visit to Mogadishu, providing humanitarian aid and investing in infrastructure and security forces.
Its largest overseas military base, used to train the Somali army, sits in Mogadishu alongside its largest embassy in Africa.
Cooperation now spans energy, fisheries and maritime security. A 10-year defence and economic pact was signed in 2024, followed by an April 2025 hydrocarbon deal giving Turkish Petroleum rights across three blocks totalling roughly 16,000 square kilometres. Türkiye's OYAK group signed a fisheries cooperation deal last year, and Ankara began building a space port in Somalia this year.

After four matches, it’s hard not to be impressed by Maccabi Tel Aviv’s play so far this season.

Kenny Miller has his squad running on all cylinders, and Maccabi appears to be a clear step above the other “big” teams in the league.

Stav Turiel was sent off after receiving a second yellow card, as the referee once again had too much influence on the game, just as the officials did the previous week in Beersheba. Unlike Beersheba’s Ran Kozuk, who had some choice words for the officiating, Hapol Tel Aviv’s Elyaniv Barda did not want to criticize the referees, instead saying that both of Turiel’s yellow cards could have been avoided.
Back to Maccabi, however, the team sits comfortably atop the table with a perfect 12 points. The yellow-and-blue will have a chance to head into the international break with five wins from five when it visits Maccabi Netanya on Saturday night. Netanya is coming off a brutal 2-0 loss to newly promoted Hapoel Ramat Gan in a game in which the Diamond City squad never quite looked right.
But what has really helped Miller’s squad has been the addition of Gaby Kanichowsky, who has changed the complexion of Maccabi’s gameplay. That was especially evident in his first two games back in the Holy Land after spending last season abroad in Hungary with Ferencvaros. Gaby Kanichowsky’s Impact on Maccabi Tel Aviv
Miller had plenty to say about his new midfielder Kanichowsky and how he sees No. 16 fitting into the team with such ease.
“It’s an incredible season. Gaby’s come in and he’s obviously really familiar with the club. He’s played with a lot of these players as well before he left, and he’s fitted seamlessly into that midfield. What it does is it gives us a really, really good balance within the three players that we’ve got [in the midfield].”
As for Tavernier, it’s rare to have such a talent and an established star come to Israel, but here he is, thanks in part to his former teammate and current Maccabi bench boss, Miller. Tavernier explained why he decided to sign with the State Cup holder while also sharing warm words about his new home.
Players of Tavernier’s caliber coming to Israel should never, ever be taken for granted. Even in a good and quiet season, it would be rare for a player of his stature to be playing in Israel, and that was made crystal clear to the former Rangers star by the warmth he has received from the fans, the club, and those around him.
Having players such as Kanichowsky and Tavernier also helps the rest of the squad, whether it’s taking advantage of Kanichowsky’s incredible vision and passing ability or Tavernier’s leadership and the quality he brings to the team. That, in turn, has allowed Miller to heap praise on other players, including Osher Davida, who scored Maccabi’s second goal and continues to create havoc on the right flank – as well as in front of the Hapoel Tel Aviv fans with an Eran Zahavi-inspired goal celebration.
“As a staff, we know the qualities that Osher has. They kept telling me that two seasons ago he had a wonderful season and he had good numbers and goals and assists, and we want him to get back to that level. I think our two wingers are right at the top of their game at the moment. They’re always contributing goal chances, assists, and it was another really, really positive performance from both our wingers, as it was for everybody. The team performances over the last few weeks have been excellent. But in terms of Osher, he’s in a really good place.”
“We need to keep pushing him,” Miller continued. “We need to keep working with him to make sure he keeps that level up. He said to me about two seasons ago that he was better than he is at the moment, then he’s a very, very good player. So we’ve got him in a good place, as we have the whole group, and it’s about keeping it up. It’s about keep pushing, enjoy it, understand why we’re winning, and then move on to the next game. We’ll enjoy this, we’ll move on, as it’s about going and making sure it’s five out of five.”
Young star Noam Ben Harush elevating his play
Noam Ben Harush, who shifted from right back to left back with the arrival of Tavernier and the departure of Roy Revivo, has been a revelation as well. After spending time with both Maccabi Haifa and Hapoel Haifa, the 21-year-old was also part of the youth national team program. As a coach, you want players to take the jersey, keep the jersey by performing and doing the work, again, not just in games.”
“We see the performances that the players are putting in, but that’s down to the work that we put in every single day. And Noam, at the moment, he’s taking that opportunity to play left back. It’s not his position, but he’s been really, really good in that for the last two or three games. The jersey at the moment is his, and it’s up to someone else to show they’re better.”
Of course, getting up for a big game – especially a derby – should be easy. Even Miller wanted to get out onto the pitch and turn back father time.
“It’s a fantastic fixture, it really is. The one thing I would say about our fans at home and away, to be honest, but particularly at home, is when you’ve got 30,000 there supporting you, they create an incredible atmosphere for the team and for the players to go in. What player wouldn’t want to play in front of that type of atmosphere and environment tonight? It’s an incredible place to be. I would much rather be on the field where you can actually impact it!”

Maccabi Tel Aviv aim to remain undefeated against Netanya
Next up is Netanya, and Miller wants to get that fifth win and go into the break with a big smile on his face. Sure, there is still plenty to do, but getting off to such an incredible start against the teams Maccabi has already faced and defeated is exactly what the club wanted. Now it’s on to the next one in what is a marathon, and Miller is well aware that the championship isn’t won after just a handful of games.
“It’s a long, long way to go. We’re really, really happy with the start, and I said it before, it looked a tough start on paper. But we’ve come through the first four games with maximum points, and again, for me, you move on to the next game now. That’s it. All eyes go on Saturday. It’s as simple as that.”

Israel considering additional steps against Netherlands over trade ban against West Bank products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:36:20 UTC
04:36:20 KST

Israel is considering additional steps against the Netherlands over its decision to ban trade in Israeli products from the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights after a court in The Hague rejected a legal attempt to stop the measure, a diplomatic source said on Wednesday.
According to the source, Israel's policy on the matter has not changed: Israel has acted, is acting, and will continue to act against those who act against it, and diplomatic and economic measures taken against Israel will be met with a response.
The Dutch ban is expected to take effect on September 22. Jerusalem views it in the context of a series of measures promoted by the Netherlands in recent months that Israel has described as hostile. The Dutch government itself has said it intends, through the move, to increase pressure on the Israeli government and avoid economically contributing to the continued expansion of Israeli settlements.
Before adopting the measure nationally, the Netherlands sought to advance similar steps at the European Union level. After failing to secure the required majority, it decided to act independently.
Israel already responded with a practical step when the decision was made in The Hague. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's approval, decided to remove Dutch representatives from the international support center for Gaza in Kiryat Gat.
Sa'ar's announcement at the time said the decision was made following a "series of anti-Israel measures by the Dutch government," the latest of which was the trade ban. The Dutch Embassy in Israel and the United States, which plays a central role in the Kiryat Gat mechanism, were informed of the decision.
The original announcement also said that the representatives had been asked to leave Israel within a week. The Dutch side later clarified that the two would not be required to leave their other diplomatic posts, but that their participation in the Kiryat Gat center would end.
The Kiryat Gat center, which involves the United States and other countries, coordinates on Gaza and issues related to stabilizing the Gaza Strip and its future. The removal of the Dutch representatives also highlighted one of the tools Israel can use in response to diplomatic measures against it: restricting foreign countries' participation in regional mechanisms that require Israeli consent.
Sa'ar said at the time: "Our clear message: Anyone who acts against Israel will have no foothold in the region. Israel will not allow measures against it to go unanswered."
The Foreign Ministry statement linked the Dutch government's policy to what it described as an "unprecedented wave of antisemitism and boycotts" in the country.
After the court rejected the request to prevent the ban from taking effect, a diplomatic source said Israel is now considering additional measures against the Netherlands beyond the decision already taken regarding Kiryat Gat.
The source did not specify which measures were under consideration, and no additional decision has been announced so far.
Israel considering retaliatory measures against more countries
The Netherlands is not the first country whose representatives have been barred from the mechanism. Israel previously prevented Spain from participating in the Kiryat Gat center amid the diplomatic crisis with Madrid.
Reports later said Israel was considering using the same measure against additional countries. A diplomatic source denied at the time that Israel intended to take action against Germany and Italy, which the source described as friendly countries, and said reports to that effect were "fake."
Israeli officials said at the time that a disagreement with a friendly country does not, by itself, lead to retaliatory measures like those taken against the Netherlands and Spain.
Despite concerns that the Dutch precedent could encourage other governments to follow suit, Israeli diplomatic officials do not currently expect an automatic "domino effect" across Europe.
They said decisions on such matters are largely shaped by domestic political circumstances, including the composition of the government, the balance of power in parliament and the pressures exerted on political leaders in each country.
In their assessment, therefore, the Dutch ban's entry into force does not in itself indicate that other European countries will follow the Netherlands.
Jerusalem is continuing to monitor similar initiatives in other countries and within EU institutions. The volume of trade directly affected by the Dutch ban is relatively limited, while Israeli officials are more concerned that other governments could adopt the approach chosen by The Hague: after failing to secure agreement for the measure at the EU level, the Netherlands decided to impose the restrictions independently.
Pro-Israel demonstration expected on Thursday in Amsterdam
A demonstration in support of Israel and the Jewish community is expected to take place in Amsterdam's Dam Square on Thursday, where opposition to boycotts and sanctions against Israel is also expected to be voiced.
The event was planned before the court decision, but its organizers had already addressed the expected ruling and the trade ban, linking the rally to the public and political climate surrounding Israel in the Netherlands.
Organizers are preparing to bring participants from across the country through a network of about 35 bus pickup points.
Among the announced speakers are SGP party leader and member of parliament Chris Stoffer, Interprovincial Chief Rabbi Binyamin Jacobs, and Jewish and Christian representatives.
The event is also expected to include the unfurling of an Israeli flag covering about 600 square meters and the singing of "Hatikvah." At the same time, a call has been issued for a pro-Palestinian counter-demonstration expected to begin about half an hour before the pro-Israel rally.
The Dutch ban is set to take effect on September 22 unless a legal or diplomatic development changes the situation before then. Israel is also awaiting the completion of discussions over the nature of its response.

Israeli team to compete in Texan 'Meat Up' with kosher Wagyu shawarma - with all the fixings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:36:02 UTC
04:36:02 KST

A 14-member Israeli team will make its debut at the Texas Open Fire Meat Up in October, aiming to win over judges and barbecue fans with an unlikely centerpiece: a roughly 200-kilogram kosher Wagyu beef shawarma cooked entirely over open flames.
The competition, held at Quail Crossing Ranch in Hondo, Texas, brings together pitmasters, chefs and barbecue personalities from around the world. Organizers say more than 30 teams will cook over live fire, with hundreds of pitmasters and influencers expected to attend.
The Israeli team’s entry will include a giant shawarma spit weighing about 440 pounds, mounted on a specially built iron cooking structure and roasted over coals. An Israeli from Or Yehuda, now living in Miami, is building the equipment, which will be transported to Texas for the competition.
The beef will come from a kosher Jewish supplier in Texas, making the shawarma fully kosher. Team captain Ruben E. Maislos, an Israeli meat blogger with around 600,000 Instagram followers, said the choice was intended both to distinguish the Israeli entry and accommodate members of the team who keep kosher.
“This is a great opportunity to represent Israeli and Middle Eastern cuisine,” he told Ynet. “Our twist is kosher Wagyu, because they’re not familiar with that there. Half of the team keeps kosher, so we wanted to respect them and the occasion because we’re representing Israel.”
Wagyu beef has increasingly appeared in the kosher culinary world, including in Israel. For Maislos and his team, however, the challenge will involve far more than simply putting premium beef over a fire.
“In the United States, anything kosher is considered higher quality, and with meat, that’s critical. You don’t want to end up with low-quality meat. We have to plate it Michelin-style, because you can lose points on color and appearance too. It has to look like a photograph. Everything has to look like a million dollars. It’s not only about whether it tastes good.”
The Israeli team will also include chef Charlie Fadida and chef Yehuda Amar, a former contestant on Israel’s Master Chef who now lives in Miami, alongside grilling enthusiasts, meat lovers and content creators.
Competitors are expected to be evaluated on presentation, technique and flavor, with cooking centered entirely on live fire rather than gas or electric equipment.
The team's menu will lean heavily into flavors familiar from Israel's street-food culture. Tahini, amba, zhug, and spices will be brought from Israel and used to prepare the shawarma's seasonings and accompaniments.
Maislos said the current plan is to serve the shawarma with a shot of mint-flavored arak and, if possible, provide an Israeli soundtrack with singer Omer Adam playing in the background.
Asked about criticism that could arise from presenting shawarma as Israeli cuisine, Maislos argued that the dish had become firmly embedded in the country's culinary identity.
“First of all, we’re a Levantine country, and Israel is made up of people who came here from many different countries. We also have an Arab chef on the team,” he said.
“Shawarma became part of Israeli culinary identity a long time ago, even if the Turks or Greeks tell a different story. The Turks will say it’s theirs and the Greeks will say it’s souvlaki. Everyone says something. There are arguments about asado too, and in South America everyone thinks it belongs to them.”
Campaigning in Jewish communities through United States and showcasing Israeli symbols
Maislos plans to campaign among Jewish communities in the United States ahead of the event to draw supporters to the Israeli stand.
“I’ll start a campaign in America telling people to come buy kosher shawarma,” he said. “This isn’t just another version of what they already know. What we’re bringing is completely different from the other teams, which are making steaks, wings, lamb cuts and sweet sauces.”
“We’re no suckers. Israel is fourth in [beef] consumption in the world. No Israeli doesn’t think he’s the world barbecue champion. I don’t want to lose. We’re coming to put on a show.”
The team is also preparing to compete openly under Israeli symbols, with plans to display Israeli flags throughout its stand.
Maislos said he was not overly concerned about possible hostility, citing his experience as a visitor at the event last year.
“I didn’t compete last year, but I visited the festival and competition, and I saw how warmly everyone received me and how impressed they were that I had come from Israel,” he said. “So from my perspective, we need to amaze them with our food, and everything will be fine.”
“Maybe someone will come and say something, because we’re going to put our Israeli flag everywhere. But it’s Texas. They like us there, and I hope they like Mediterranean flavors too. I just hope there won’t be a protest, but whatever happens, we’ll deal with it.”

04:36:00 KST

Ukraine's air defense forces have put another Western-supplied system to work as the country prepares for a fifth winter of Russian aerial strikes on its energy grid, Militarnyi reported. The 38th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment released the first public footage of the Italian-Swiss Skyguard/Aspide on combat duty.
Ukraine enters the 2026-2027 heating season with an interceptor gap that keeps widening. Patriot deliveries fell from 675 in 2023 to 364 last year and 264 projected for 2026, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. F-16 pilots have resorted to gun-only sorties when missiles run out. Every additional short-range system that covers drones and cruise missiles frees scarce high-end interceptors for the ballistic threats Russia keeps sending.
Ukraine just showed the system in action
The Ukrainian unit posted a video of crews loading missiles onto the launcher and the system standing watch.
The system arrived through two European pipelines. Spain delivered the first batch in November 2022, then-Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov confirmed. A month earlier, 19 Ukrainian troops had trained on the system at Spain's Zaragoza base. Madrid also asked Switzerland for re-export permission, Texty reported, since the Swiss firm Oerlikon Contraves — now Rheinmetall Air Defense — built the Skyguard fire control unit the missiles are paired with.
Italy pledged additional Skyguard units in February 2023. The Italian launchers differ from the Spanish ones. They carry a target-illumination radar and a TV tracking unit mounted directly on the launcher.
A Cold War-era missile in a drone war
Skyguard/Aspide, a related variant of Italy's Spada, is a short-range air defense system built to guard military sites and critical infrastructure from aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. It pairs a Swiss fire control unit with Italian Aspide missiles derived from the American AIM-7 Sparrow, a radar-guided weapon the US Navy developed starting in the late 1940s to shoot down jet bombers during the Cold War. The system can engage targets at distances up to 12–25 km and altitudes from 15 m to 6,000 meters.

FBI chief Kash Patel warns online radicalization fueling threats to synagogues, public officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:58 UTC
04:35:58 KST

The ability to turn online activity and organization into real-world violence, including attacks against synagogues and elected officials, is the most serious domestic threat currently facing the United States, FBI Director Kash Patel told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.
The hearing was the Judiciary Committee's annual FBI oversight hearing, with Patel appearing as the bureau's sole witness. Asked by Republican Sen. Darlin Graham of South Carolina about the leading domestic threat, Patel said the primary mechanism was the "cyber landscape," adding that "the single greatest threat" was the ability to carry out violence through online spaces, whether against children, houses of worship or elected officials.
Patel stressed that he was not necessarily referring to cyberattacks in the sense of hacking computer systems, but rather to the use of the internet, social media and encrypted applications for radicalization, planning and coordinating acts of violence.
One example he cited was a plot foiled in June against the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House. The US Justice Department said at the time that five people had been arrested and charged with planning an attack against elected officials and participants at the event.
According to the indictments, those involved moved their communications to encrypted chats and planned to use explosive-laden drones to create chaos, followed by snipers who would fire on people fleeing the scene. In some of their communications, the suspects also discussed harming members of Congress whom they claimed were connected to the pro-Israel lobby.
Patel's emphasis on houses of worship is particularly relevant to the Jewish community in the United States following several significant incidents this year in which the internet played a role in either the threat itself or the radicalization process.
On March 12, 41-year-old Ayman Mohammed Ghazali of Dearborn Heights attacked Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan. Following an investigation, the FBI determined that the incident was "an act of terrorism inspired by Hezbollah" aimed at the Jewish community and the large Michigan synagogue.
FBI: Ghazali searched online for synagogues, Jewish institutions prior to attack
According to the FBI's findings, Ghazali began consuming pro-Hezbollah and Iranian content online as early as January. In the days before the attack, he searched online for synagogues and Jewish institutions in the Detroit area, and later searched phrases including "largest gathering of Israelis in Michigan," "Orthodox synagogues," and "Israelis near me." He also looked up planned events at Temple Israel.
On the day of the attack, Ghazali arrived at the synagogue in a Ford F-150 pickup truck containing commercial fireworks and containers filled with flammable material. He rammed the entrance door, opened fire from inside the vehicle and exchanged gunfire with security personnel.
Children and staff were evacuated from the building, and no worshipers or employees were killed. The attacker died during the incident.
During the investigation, the FBI found that minutes before the attack, Ghazali sent videos to his sister in which he described the synagogue as "the largest gathering place for Israelis in the state of Michigan," said he had prepared his vehicle for the attack, and that he intended to "kill as many of them as possible."
The bureau said it found no evidence that he had accomplices and concluded that the attacker had been inspired by Hezbollah ideology.
Other incidents this year have also highlighted the connection between antisemitic threats and online activity. In March, a Chicago resident was indicted after, according to the Justice Department, posting on X/Twitter that he intended to "shoot inside a synagogue." The information was forwarded to the FBI's National Threat Operations Center.
In April, a US soldier stationed at Fort Polk was charged after authorities said he threatened in Discord conversations to enter a synagogue with an AK rifle and kill Jews. According to the Justice Department, the investigation was opened after the FBI received an online tip.
Lone extremists, small groups most difficult to identify, FBI warns
The FBI has previously warned that extremists acting alone or in small groups who become radicalized online and target "soft targets" such as houses of worship are among the most difficult threats to identify in advance.
In June 2025, the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security issued a joint warning about heightened threats to Jewish and Israeli communities in the United States, cautioning that foreign terrorist organizations could exploit events in the Middle East to encourage violence inside the US.
Patel stressed during the hearing that confronting the threat requires closer cooperation between the FBI and state and local police departments. Following the Michigan attack, the FBI also called on houses of worship and schools to work with law enforcement authorities and participate in training for responding to shooting incidents.

Saudi Arabia facing growing pressure on multiple fronts as Houthis escalate in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:54 UTC
04:35:54 KST

Saudi Arabia is facing growing pressure from multiple directions as the Houthis in Yemen expand their capabilities and Iran threatens vital infrastructure, and that is causing “great anxiety and pressure” in Riyadh, a source close to the Saudi government has told The Jerusalem Post.
“They’re surrounded from the south and the north and the east,” the source said, adding that the Houthis and the Iran-backed Hashd al-Shaabi in Iraq are major security concerns.
At the same time, Iran poses a different kind of threat, with Riyadh concerned that a direct confrontation could expose critical infrastructure, including desalination facilities, to Iranian missile and drone attacks, the source said, adding: “They definitely thought that they were vulnerable, and they were against the war between Israel-US and Iran.”
Nevertheless, the Saudi approach has been markedly different toward the Houthis, whom Riyadh appears to have initially underestimated.
“I think they miscalculated,” a diplomat in the region told the Post. “They really thought that they had Yemeni forces who could really stand up to the Houthis.”
Riyadh has adopted two fundamentally different approaches toward its adversaries.
With Iran, the preferred strategy is negotiation and mediation rather than direct military confrontation. That is largely because of concerns over the potential consequences of an Iranian attack on Saudi infrastructure.
Houthis progressing along Red Sea coast
The calculation is different regarding the Houthis.
“When it comes to the Houthis, they have a much more aggressive, forward-leaning, military solution,” the source close to the Saudi government said.
Saudi Arabia is supporting Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis while also providing air support.
But Riyadh’s initial reluctance to employ air power more aggressively allowed the Houthis to make significant gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The Tihamah coastal plain is largely flat rather than mountainous, making it particularly vulnerable to air power.
“It could have easily been stopped with air power,” the diplomat said, citing platforms such as Apache helicopters and C-130 gunships.
Instead, Riyadh initially relied on anti-Houthi Yemeni forces to halt the advance.
“They had confidence that the Yemeni anti-Houthis would stop them, and there was a kind of hesitancy or reticence to get involved,” the diplomat said.
That hesitation gave the Houthis crucial time to consolidate their position.
“That gave the Houthis the 24 hours they needed to take over the entire coast,” the diplomat said, adding that the decision was a “huge mistake.”
The Saudis, it seems, are deeply disappointed with the performance of forces led by Tariq Saleh, which failed to prevent the Houthi advance despite receiving training, funding, and weapons from Gulf states.
The forces were initially supported by the United Arab Emirates and later by Saudi Arabia, the source close to the Saudi government said.
“In hindsight, they think that the Tariq al-Saleh forces who didn’t fight, despite being paid and trained and armed,... must have disappointed them,” the source said.
Riyadh is now making greater use of air power. The Houthis have claimed more than 40 airstrikes over the past 24 hours.
The shift in approach has so far helped prevent the Houthis from expanding eastward toward Marib and capturing additional territory around Taiz and other parts of Yemen.
Trump refuses to strike Houthis
US President Donald Trump has refused to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. While CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper did visit Saudi Arabia over the weekend, US officials also met in Oman with Houthi representatives, who reportedly gave them a commitment not to target US ships.
So, why is the US not assisting with the Houthis?
“If it’s for technical, strategic, and military reasons, I can understand,” the source close to the Saudi government said. “If it’s a political chasing away of America, then that’s really problematic.”
Trump’s approach toward Riyadh could be influenced by a number of factors, including disagreements over Saudi support for US-led regional security initiatives.
Trump might believe the Saudis have not been sufficiently supportive, or he could view the US military presence in the region as overextended.
Trump’s strategic thinking is often difficult to predict, the source stressed.
“He’s very capricious,” the source said, adding that a decision to reduce US support could have consequences beyond the immediate political dispute.
Israel assisting Saudi Arabia against Houthis, diplomats say
Despite the growing pressure, Saudi Arabia remains pragmatic in its foreign and security policy, including publicly seeking greater assistance from Israel, the source said.
Israel is assisting Saudi Arabia, with CENTCOM mediating the sharing of intelligence on the Houthis, diplomats in the region told the Post.
“If it gets really bad for the Saudis and they need help, and they’re not going to get it from anyone else,” Riyadh could potentially reconsider its current positions, the source said, adding that its decision-making would ultimately depend on the nature and severity of the assistance required.
“It depends on the nature of the help they need and how desperate they get,” the source said. “The Saudis are ultimately very pragmatic. Regime survival comes before anything else.”

US Federal Reserve hikes rates, sees more tightening in search of 'timelier' drop in inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:35:32 UTC
04:35:32 KST

The US Federal Reserve (Fed) raised interest rates on Wednesday and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the coming months, with new US central bank chief Kevin Warsh joining a unanimous decision that effectively acknowledges the Trump administration's so-far inability to control inflation.
While US President Donald Trump had promised to lower prices on his watch, the combined impact of his global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom has kept price pressures intense enough that the Fed felt it needed to raise its benchmark overnight interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range.
New policy projections showed 16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-percentage-point hike by the end of this year, with only two seeing rates remain stable from here. Warsh apparently again did not submit a rate projection.
US dollar rises against euro following Warsh's first policy shift
This is the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after Trump selected him with the expectation that he would cut rates.
The US dollar rose against the euro after the Fed's announcement, while US Treasury bond yields held largely steady, having already weakened in anticipation of the hike. After hitting a 19-year high above 5% on Monday, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading at 4.958%, compared to 4.946% just before the announcement.
The 30-year bond yield dipped to 5.312% after trading at 5.327% just before the announcement. Stocks were mostly higher, with the S&P 500 index up 0.3% and the Nasdaq Composite up 0.7%.
Market bets on a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in late October ticked up to 56.5% from 54% before the hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool.
"The Federal Reserve's decision today to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point reflects its continued focus on addressing persistent inflation. While inflation has moderated from peak levels, it has remained elevated enough to prompt additional action from the Federal Open Market Committee," said Michele Raneri, head of US research and consulting at TransUnion in Chicago.
The Fed's new policy statement and economic projections, by contrast, show the central bank opening the door to tighter monetary policy through next year, with the policy rate rising to the 4.00%-4.25% range by the end of this year and ending 2027 at the same level.
"Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2% goal," the central bank said in its policy statement after the end of a two-day meeting.
While the statement withheld forward guidance on upcoming policy decisions, as is Warsh's preference, the decision is likely to ease doubts that the Fed chief would hold off on tighter policy out of deference to Trump, a lingering question during his first months in office.
The statement dropped a previous reference attributing current elevated inflation to "supply shocks," particularly in the energy sector, a nod to concerns among policymakers, including Warsh, that price pressures were too broad to be comfortable with.
Warsh is scheduled to hold a press conference beginning at 2:30 p.m. local time to elaborate on the decision.
Rate increase to determine results of upcoming US midterm elections
The rate increase was announced less than two months ahead of midterm elections that will determine whether Trump's Republicans maintain control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency. The Republicans are facing an uphill battle with voters angry about gasoline prices that are about a third higher than a year ago and interest rates on home mortgages that have been rising steadily this year. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is approaching 7%.
Policymakers' new quarterly economic projections raised inflation estimates, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, to 3.7% versus the 3.6% projected at the Fed's June meeting. Inflation is not projected to return to the 2% target until 2029, a year later than previously expected.
Economic growth was raised slightly from 2.2% to 2.3%, while the unemployment rate is expected to end the year at 4.1%, versus the 4.3% projected in June.
Warsh's characterization at his press conference of the logic behind the rate increase and the likelihood of further action will be important in shaping the reaction in financial markets that have been raising yields on long-term US Treasury bonds. The rate hike on Wednesday was widely expected, but investors will look to the Fed chief for more information on what might prompt further increases in borrowing costs.
Warsh has pledged to lower inflation back to 2% "clearly and at sufficient speed" by raising rates as needed.
Trump calls for interest rates of 1% or lower
US President Donald Trump called for sharply lower interest rates on Wednesday, saying rates in the United States should be 1% or lower.
"Interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less," Trump said.
Trump also called for rates to be lowered quickly, saying, "Lower interest rates for the United States of America, and fast."

Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:34:37 UTC
04:34:37 KST

The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.
Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.
The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.
Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”
The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.
“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”
Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.
If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.
The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.
USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.
New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.
Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.
IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.
A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.
“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”
The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.
“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.

Strong economy, sticky inflation, geopolitical risks drove Fed rate hike: Warsh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:33:48 UTC
04:33:48 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
- US central bank unanimously raises federal funds rate by 25 basis points after holding it steady in July
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that a strengthening economy, persistent inflation and heightened geopolitical risks prompted the central bank to raise interest rates after keeping them unchanged at its previous meeting.
Asked what had changed during the seven weeks between meetings, Warsh said recent data, particularly labor market indicators, showed that the US economy had strengthened.
Inflation trends during the summer, meanwhile, failed to demonstrate sufficiently rapid progress toward the Fed’s 2% target, while the geopolitical outlook also changed, he said without referring to the US-Iran war.
“All three of those things lent themselves to a firm, unanimous decision today,” said Warsh.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) unanimously raised the federal funds rate Wednesday by 25 basis points to a range between 3.75% and 4%, following its decision to hold rates steady in July.
Inflation ‘too high’ for ‘too long’
Warsh said the unemployment rate remained low at 4.1%, with job openings and average weekly hours increasing, allowing the Fed to concentrate on the price stability side of its dual mandate.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” he said. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
Based on the latest consumer and producer price data, annual headline personal consumption expenditures inflation was likely around 3.6% in August, while core PCE inflation was running at approximately 3.2%, he said.
Too many categories continued to register price increases above 3% on six- and 12-month bases, Warsh added.
Financial conditions not restrictive
The rate increase removed “a dose of accommodation,” said Warsh, adding that he and other policymakers were “hard-pressed” to describe broad financial conditions before the meeting as restrictive.
He dismissed suggestions that the Fed had followed financial markets, which had largely priced in the increase.
“We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation,” he said, citing the employment trajectory and the economy’s underlying strength.
Warsh declined to signal whether the move would begin a series of increases, saying he was “not in the forward guidance business.”
He also said estimates of the neutral interest rate had no operational effect on the Fed’s decisions.
Fed forecasts growth, inflation above target
Median projections released after the meeting showed real gross domestic product expanding 2.3% this year and 2.4% next year.
Headline PCE inflation was projected at 3.7% this year before easing to 3.2% next year, while unemployment was expected to remain around 4.1%.
The median policymaker forecast placed the federal funds rate at 4.1% at the end of this year and next.
Warsh said he did not submit his projection and emphasized that the forecasts belonged to his 18 colleagues.
Higher Treasury yields reflect economic strength
Warsh attributed rising long-term Treasury yields partly to stronger economic activity, increased competition for capital amid heavy technology-sector investment and geopolitical tensions.
The Fed also established an artificial intelligence task force that is expected to report by year’s end on the technology’s implications for the economy and monetary policy, he added.

The action came a day after the committee voted unanimously to recommend that the House hold Black in contempt. Wednesday’s House vote passed under unanimous consent, meaning there was not a formal roll call, but no member objected to the contempt resolution.

Congress held former attorney general Merrick Garland in contempt in 2024, but the justice department did not act on it. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities.
