Palestinian elections: Why canceling the vote in November would be a mistake - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Palestinians are supposed to vote in legislative elections on November 28. After years without national elections, the importance of that date is difficult to overstate. But there is already growing concern that Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas might cancel the elections as he did in May 2021.
The reasons being discussed are familiar: uncertainty over voting in east Jerusalem, the practical difficulties of holding elections in Gaza, internal Palestinian political calculations, and the fear among established factions that the voters may produce a result they do not like.
None of these concerns should become an excuse to deny Palestinians the right to choose their leadership. Palestinian politics has suffered for years from a deep crisis of legitimacy.
The Palestinian Authority has governed without a renewed democratic mandate. The political system remains divided between the West Bank and Gaza. Fatah and Hamas continue to dominate institutions that many Palestinians increasingly regard as ineffective, unaccountable, or disconnected from their lives.
That is precisely why elections are necessary.
The election is not important because it will automatically produce good government, moderation, or peace. Elections can produce bad outcomes as well as good ones (as we have seen in Israel). They can strengthen extremists as easily as reformers.
But without elections there is no legitimate way to renew leadership, test public support, bring new political forces into the system, or give Palestinians a government that can credibly claim to represent them.
Canceling the elections would send the opposite message: that Palestinian political institutions are prepared to speak in the name of the people but are afraid to ask the people what they want.
The question of east Jerusalem will be one of the most difficult issues. Israel has repeatedly objected to Palestinian political activity in the city and could refuse to permit normal voting arrangements there. That would create a serious problem.
But Israel must not be given a veto over Palestinian democracy, and there is no legitimate reason why the Palestinians should even ask Israel for permission for Palestinians in Jerusalem to vote. Jerusalem, with its 400,000 Palestinian residents, is the largest Palestinian city between the river and the sea.
If Israel blocks the traditional arrangements for voting in Jerusalem, Palestinians and the international community should find other ways to ensure that Palestinian residents of the city can participate. Polling stations can be established outside direct Israeli control. Alternative voting arrangements can be developed, such as electronic voting. Technology can also provide possibilities that did not exist in earlier elections. International diplomatic missions can assist.
The principle should be clear: Israeli obstruction must not become the justification for canceling an election for millions of Palestinians.
The same principle applies to Gaza. Holding an election in Gaza after years of war, destruction, displacement, political division, and the weakening of public institutions will be extraordinarily difficult. But Gaza cannot simply be excluded from Palestinian political life.
If Palestinians are serious about rebuilding one political system, Gaza and the West Bank must eventually be governed by one legitimate authority. That cannot happen if the people of Gaza are denied a voice in choosing that authority.
The practical problems are enormous, but they are problems to be solved, not reasons to abandon democracy.
There is another reason why these elections matter so much. Palestinian politics may be changing. For decades, the political system has largely been defined by the competition between Fatah and Hamas. But there is growing frustration with both.
The plurality of Palestinians – the largest group in Palestinian polls – do not want Fatah or Hamas. Younger Palestinians, independents, reformers, women, professionals, local activists, and new political movements are increasingly questioning whether the old factions can provide the leadership Palestinians need.
That uncertainty may frighten those who already hold power. But elections are not supposed to protect the people in power. They are supposed to give citizens the ability to replace them. If new political movements emerge, if younger leaders win support, if independent candidates challenge the traditional factions, that should be welcomed as evidence that Palestinian politics is alive.
Those who claim to believe in Palestinian self-determination cannot mean only self-determination in relation to Israel. It must also mean the right of Palestinians to choose their own leaders.
There is also an Israeli interest in these elections. For years, Israelis have repeated the claim that there is “no Palestinian partner.” Sometimes that argument has reflected real frustration with Palestinian leadership. But Israelis cannot simultaneously demand a legitimate Palestinian partner and accept a political reality in which Palestinians are denied the opportunity to elect one.
A Palestinian leadership with a genuine democratic mandate would not automatically become a partner for peace. But it would have far greater political legitimacy to make difficult decisions, reform institutions, confront armed factions, negotiate with Israel, and implement agreements. That matters enormously.
Any future agreement will require Palestinians to make painful choices. It will require one government, one legal system, and one legitimate security authority. It will require political movements to choose between democratic participation and independent armed power. It will require leaders who can tell the Palestinian public difficult truths and still claim to speak in its name.
That cannot be achieved indefinitely through presidential decrees, aging institutions, and political arrangements created decades ago.
Giving the Palestinians a voice
The timing is also striking. Israelis are approaching their own election. They will be asked to choose not only who should govern them but what direction Israel should take after October 7 and the wars that followed. Palestinians deserve the same opportunity.
In fact, the two elections should be understood as connected. Israeli politics affects Palestinian politics every day.
Settlement expansion, military occupation, settler violence, restrictions on movement, and the absence of a political horizon strengthen those Palestinians who argue that diplomacy has failed. Palestinian violence and rejectionism strengthen the Israeli Right and those who insist that permanent control is the only way to guarantee security.
For years, extremists on each side have helped strengthen the extremists on the other. Elections offer at least the possibility of breaking that cycle.
That is why the international community, and particularly the United States, Europe, and the Arab states, should be saying clearly now that the Palestinian elections must take place.
They should offer practical assistance for voting in Gaza and east Jerusalem. They should provide election observers. They should support the independence of the electoral institutions. And they should make clear that political pressure from any Palestinian faction or outside government to cancel the elections would be unacceptable.
The November election will not solve the Palestinian national crisis. But canceling it would deepen that crisis immediately.
Palestinians cannot build a state with institutions that are permanently afraid of their own voters. And Israelis cannot continue asking where the Palestinian partner is while Palestinians are denied the opportunity to choose new ones.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

Texas adopts anti-Muslim curriculum amid backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:58:00 UTC
03:58:00 KST

Texas education officials have approved a sweeping rewrite of high school social studies standards that Muslim students, civil rights advocates and some academic advisers say embeds anti-Muslim bias into public school classrooms, including language linking so-called “radical Islam” to the 9/11 attacks and portraying early Islamic history through warfare and slavery.
The Republican-controlled State Board of Education finalized the standards after days of contentious debate, brushing aside calls from Muslim Texans to revise language they warned could stigmatize students and reinforce stereotypes about Islam.
Among the most disputed provisions is a requirement for students to learn that “radical Islam” motivated the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
Muslim speakers urged the board to focus more specifically on al-Qaida, Osama bin Laden and the terrorists responsible for the attacks rather than language they said risks associating Islam itself with terrorism.
The objections also highlighted that Muslims were among the victims and first responders killed on 9/11, including Muslim-American emergency medical technician Salman Hamdani, who died while trying to help others at the World Trade Center.
Another provision directs students studying early Islam to examine Prophet Muhammad through descriptions of military campaigns against Jewish and Christian tribes, slavery and the taking of female captives.
Muslim Texans told the board that such a presentation singles out Islam for hostile treatment while stripping events from their wider historical context.
Some of the board’s own appointed experts also questioned the historical basis for the wording.
Andrea Hutchison, a social studies curriculum coordinator for Prosper Independent School District, warned that elements of the portrayal did not hold up under close historical scrutiny.
Robert Koons, a philosophy professor at the University of Texas at Austin, also questioned the reliability of sources underlying some of the claims.
“I would warn us about including things that are not based on well-established secular sources,” Koons told the board.
Despite the objections, the Republican majority retained much of the disputed language, including rejecting an effort to remove the word “brutal” from a description of early Islamic military campaigns.
The board also did not restore previously proposed material addressing Muslim contributions to fields such as algebra and astronomy.
That omission became another major point of criticism among Muslim students and parents, who argued that Texas classrooms would present students with negative portrayals of Islam while giving far less attention to the contributions of Muslim civilizations to science, mathematics and global history.
“I feel attacked, as if my religion doesn’t belong,” 15-year-old Habiiba Quresh told the board. “I shouldn’t have to defend my religion in the middle of history class because of one sentence someone on this board wrote.”
The Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) strongly condemned the adopted standards, saying the revisions would institutionalize prejudice in classrooms.
“The board has turned our classrooms into a place where prejudice is taught as fact and entire communities are written out of their own history,” CAIR-Texas said.
The organization said the dispute extended beyond Muslims, arguing that the standards also reduce or reshape coverage of Black and Palestinian history.
Board Chair Aaron Kinsey rejected criticism that the overhaul unfairly targeted communities, defending the final framework as balanced.
“There’s been a lot said out of this room, particularly to sensationalize all these topics and to make them seem more divisive than they actually are,” Kinsey said.
He said the 15-member board worked through the competing proposals democratically and described the overall result as an “exceptional job.”
The controversy over anti-Islam propaganda forms part of a much broader conservative restructuring of social studies education in Texas.
The board previously approved revisions for younger students and a required reading list that includes biblical stories. The new framework also places greater emphasis on Christianity, Western civilization and the ideas the Republican majority says shaped the United States.
Under the high school standards, students will be expected to study connections between biblical imagery, principles of equality and justice in the Declaration of Independence and Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech.
Critics argued during public testimony that such treatment presents Christianity primarily through its positive influence while Islam is disproportionately discussed alongside warfare, terrorism and slavery.
Some speakers also challenged what they saw as an uneven treatment of slavery.
An 11-year-old student identified as Sarah reminded board members that slavery existed across civilizations and argued that emphasizing slavery in Islamic history without comparable discussion of Christian justifications for the transatlantic slave trade creates a distorted picture.
“Slavery existed for thousands of years before Islam,” she said. “It is unfair to label slavery as Islamic without also discussing the Christian role in the slave trade to the Americas.”
The U.S. history standards have generated separate criticism over their treatment of American slavery.
The framework describes slavery as an institution that “existed in many societies throughout history,” wording Democratic members and some advisers said could obscure the distinctive racial system of slavery that developed in the United States.
“Slavery is foundational to this country,” Democratic board member Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz said, arguing that students should spend considerably more time studying its impact on the development of the U.S.
The new standards also require students to examine arguments against the modern welfare state that developed through the expansion of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s Great Society programs, which were launched in the 1960s to combat poverty and racial inequality.
Teachers, Democratic board members and civil rights groups have criticized the broader revision process, saying conservative activists wielded disproportionate influence while educators were marginalized.
Critics also raised concerns over transparency surrounding the drafting process and the outside groups that helped shape elements of the curriculum.
Republican members reject that characterization, arguing that the overhaul restores greater emphasis on U.S. history, Texas history, Western civilization and the country’s founding principles.
The restructuring also eliminates the existing sixth-grade world cultures course, a decision some educators fear will leave students with less exposure to societies and traditions outside the Western world.
Supporters say the opposite approach is necessary, arguing that Texas students should first develop a stronger understanding of their own state, country and the historical forces that shaped them.
The overhaul concludes years of political battles over how Texas schools teach race, religion, national identity and American history.
The board postponed an earlier social studies rewrite in 2022 after conservative lawmakers objected to proposed lessons involving race and gender.
The Republican majority has since pushed the curriculum in a more conservative direction, saying schools should not teach children to view the United States primarily through its historical failures.
Muslim organizations and other critics, however, say the mistreatment of Islam illustrates the risks of allowing ideological battles to determine how religions and minority communities are portrayed in public classrooms.
The new high school social studies standards are scheduled to begin being phased into Texas schools during the 2030-31 academic year.

Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:57:14 UTC
03:57:14 KST

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.
But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.
To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new links among allies in “an openly hostile world”.
The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, though it remains “deliciously vague”.
But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit.
The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.
New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.
Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.
It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.
The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.
Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.
Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.
Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.
After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.
Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.
“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.
In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and is keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.
The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.
The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.

Trump praises PM Modi for curbing ‘illicit opium cultivation’ as India stays on US ‘drug transit’ list

The US president also said Washington would continue working with New Delhi on counter-narcotics efforts (File photo)
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday welcomed Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to curb illicit opium poppy cultivation in India, even as Washington included India among 23 countries designated as major drug transit or illicit drug-producing countries.In a Presidential Determination submitted to the US Congress, Trump said he looked forward to continued cooperation with India under the United States-India Drug Policy Framework. “I welcome Prime Minister Modi and the Government of India’s efforts to address illicit opium poppy cultivation and bolster supply chain integrity,” Trump said in the directive made public on Wednesday.
India’s inclusion on the list does not, however, amount to a US finding that its government is failing to tackle the drug trade. The determination said countries are designated because of a combination of geographic, commercial and economic factors that allow illicit drugs or precursor chemicals to be produced or moved through their territory.The US document specifically noted that being placed on the list does not necessarily reflect a country’s current counterdrug efforts or the extent of its cooperation with Washington.Along with India, the countries identified by the US include Afghanistan, The Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Burma, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Laos, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Pakistan, Peru, Venezuela and China.
The designation comes as Washington continues to focus on disrupting international drug supply chains, including the movement of precursor chemicals used to manufacture synthetic drugs. The White House’s 2026 National Drug Control Strategy has also called for stronger bilateral counterdrug cooperation with countries including India.
Trump highlights US-India cooperation
Trump said the US and India would continue working together on counter-narcotics efforts. The two countries established a Drug Policy Executive Working Group earlier this year, with discussions focused on illicit narcotics trafficking, precursor chemicals and the security of pharmaceutical supply chains.The US president also pointed to what he described as “historic progress” by his administration in tackling drug trafficking and narcoterrorist organisations.He cited tighter border security, lower drug seizures and a decline in overdose deaths as evidence of progress, saying seizures of fentanyl and other drugs along the US southern border had fallen by more than half after what he called four years of “open border chaos”.“After four years of open border chaos, seizures of fentanyl and other drugs being smuggled into the United States have been reduced by more than half, and drug overdose deaths have plunged,” Trump said.Trump presses China over drug precursors
Trump separately called on China to take stronger action against the flow of precursor chemicals used to manufacture fentanyl, methamphetamine and other synthetic drugs.“The PRC continues to be the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used to illicitly produce fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other deadly synthetic drugs,” Trump said.He said he had raised the issue directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping and noted that Beijing had introduced licensing requirements last year for companies exporting designated precursor chemicals to North America.The US has made disruption of precursor-chemical supply chains a central part of its broader counter-drug strategy, which calls for international cooperation to prevent legitimate trade channels from being exploited for illicit drug production.

Russian Strikes Kill 6, Wound At Least 17 Across Ukraine

Lithuania’s air defense capabilities

“Yes, incidents still happen that sometimes cause anger, sometimes a smile, like that unfortunate case involving birds,” he added.
Just two days prior to the drone incident, on Sept. 13, a NATO fighter jet was scrambled and a Vilnius Airport closed due to a suspicious object in the air. The object turned out to be a flock of birds.

Era of US global dominance over — media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:55:21 UTC
03:55:21 KST

WASHINGTON, September 16. /TASS/. The era of US dominance on the world stage has ended, American historian and political scientist Phillips Payson O’Brien argued in an op-ed published by The Atlantic.
O’Brien, a professor of strategic studies at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, wrote that "the American age" that followed World War II was inevitably going to end, adding that "what’s shocking is how suddenly" that moment arrived.
According to O’Brien, America’s military strength, global network of bases and logistics systems, and military and diplomatic partnerships around the world proved insufficient to defeat Iran. He stressed that the erosion of US capabilities was not solely the fault of President Donald Trump. However, he argued that the war with Iran had revealed how profoundly the dynamics of global power had shifted and how far American strength had declined.
In the expert’s view, a key reason Washington refrained from escalating the military conflict with Iran over the summer, despite its threats against Tehran, was the loss of its operational base in Bahrain. The facility had served as a crucial logistics hub and housed the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. O’Brien noted that US officials had reportedly considered not rebuilding US military bases in the Persian Gulf that sustained extensive damage in Iranian strikes. He believes that the US military is currently unable to defend some of its key facilities even against a less technologically advanced adversary such as Iran.
O’Brien described the weakening of US power as having a "cascading effect" that had already undermined the Pentagon’s position in the Asia-Pacific region. He called Washington’s transfer of military equipment from the region to the Middle East a "desperate move," saying it demonstrated that US military resources, despite being vast compared with those of most other countries, were "not infinite."
The expert also said the erosion of Washington’s long-standing alliances would be "devastating to America’s global position." Other countries are "already adjusting" to the newly exposed weaknesses of the United States, he added
O’Brien predicted that US global influence would continue to decline. The conflict with Iran demonstrated that the American age had "come to an end," he concluded.

‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:54:48 UTC
03:54:48 KST

Bonnie Greer, who has died at the age of 77, moved to the UK from New York in 1986. She grew up in Chicago with six younger siblings. Her father worked in a factory and her mother “kept house”, she said once – in a tone so elegantly ominous, she conjured an image of a woman holding up a full dwelling with seven children in it, with her bare hands. Greer was ambitious and, academically, a high flyer, but abandoned her law degree, facing baked-in sexism from professors. Yet, given she started writing plays aged nine, arguably she was only hastening a creative career that was inevitable.
The Actors Studio was what drew her to the West Village in Manhattan in the late 70s, and she was there at the height of the Aids crisis, a brutal time of mass bereavements and poisonous prejudice. She lost about 35 of her friends, and later told the Sunday Times: “I owe those people my life. If I hadn’t met my gay friends I would be a suburban SUV-driving granny. They taught me the value of insurrection and fun. Nearly 30 years on, I’m still that 25-year-old, on top of some bar, in one of those vintage dresses, dancing with those guys.” But when she arrived, touring, at the Edinburgh festival, it felt like a release, from the “shadow of death”, and a New York theatre scene bereft of its heart. She stayed in the UK permanently.
Greer was a remarkable talent as a playwright: witty, dry, serious, unflinching. She was playwright in residence at the Soho theatre in the late 80s and was writing plays for Radio 3 and 4 by the early 90s. Marilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, in 2005, is perhaps the most famous, and was later adapted as a stage musical. It dramatises the solidarity between the actor and the singer – Monroe persuaded the club to book Fitzgerald, with the promise that she (mid-1950s, the height of her fame) would sit in the front row every night. Fitzgerald later said she never had to play a small jazz club again thanks to this intervention, and it redrew the boundaries of what was acceptable, in racism, in jazz, in Hollywood. In Greer’s telling, there is no white saviour narrative, only a dynamic creative symbiosis between two geniuses.
Bonnie Greer was a joiner. She was on the board of everything, from the Women’s prize for fiction to the British Museum, she was president of the Brontë society – she got stuck in. An unusual mix of originality and authority, she was in high demand as a cultural critic, particularly in broadcasting. She was a regular contributor to Newsnight Review on BBC Two, as well as a critic for Time Out and a political commentator for newspapers, including this one.
Out of all that came her appearance in 2009 on Question Time with Nick Griffin, then leader of the BNP. It was a frankly bizarre, though not uncharacteristic, bit of political curation from the BBC, since Griffin was a holocaust denier and racist, tried three times and once convicted (in the late 90s) for inciting racial, Islamophobic or antisemitic hatred. Many wondered why the BBC felt such a duty to platform so toxic a figure, and Sayeeda Warsi, also on the panel, asked Greer before whether she was OK to sit next to him (Greer replied: “I’m from Chicago, I’m not scared of this guy”). She said later to the Evening Standard that it was “probably the weirdest and most creepy experience of my life”, but onscreen she was unruffled and effortlessly in command, and she later turned that weird creepiness into an opera for the Royal Opera House, on whose board she also served, along with the London Film School’s.
She was very generous on a panel, receptive and softly spoken while absolutely trenchant, and vividly engaged; she was never without a view. She wrote two novels, Hanging by Her Teeth in 1994 and Entropy in 2009, but her more natural metier was in the discursive, collaborative arts and broader culture. She was once called “Newsnight’s kindest critic”, and said of her stage writing: “I was taught that theatre is supposed to slow the world down so it can be looked at, and the person who looks is not supposed to be the same when they walk out. Otherwise, there’s no fucking point. Art is not a leisure activity. It’s about engagement.”

‘Defend the Ecosystem’: USAF, Experts Want to Up Cyber Defense for Critical Infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:53:17 UTC
03:53:17 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force is shoring up its cyber defenses both on and off base for critical infrastructure such as water and electrical power, and industry experts are calling for more, even specialized, dedicated microgrids offsite to support USAF operations in case of a total blackout caused by cyberattacks.
“We have spent years protecting and defending the tip of the combat spear, but right now, ladies and gentlemen, our adversaries have decided to focus time, resources, and interest on the hand that wields the spear, and that’s where we have to focus,” retired USAF Lt. Gen. Chris “Wedge” Weggeman said Sept. 16 during a panel discussion at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Weggeman, now working in cybersecurity with Deloitte, also said that while the issue is new, the process of mission assurance is well esablished.
“We really don’t need a new playbook. It’s really the same playbook,” Weggeman said. “You’ve just got to know: what does this capability do in terms of enabling my mission? What happens when an adversary takes it away from me, and how long does it take me to recover? And do I have the ability to fight?”
For a long time, the military’s cybersecurity efforts have focused on information technology, or IT—the software and computers that manage data. Increasingly, though, experts are worried about operational technology, or OT—the tech that controls physical equipment and systems.
Airmen from the 16th Air Force at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, recently announced partnerships with research centers, government entities, and private sector organizations to help defend their OT where it touches Air Force assets.
“We are getting after it—workforce development, capabilities, intelligence, and everything else we need to execute this mission,” Brig. Gen. Jason Christman, 16th Air Force OT lead, said in a release.
The move delivered an OT Certification Joint Qualification Record in a two-month timespan. Next steps call for the 16th Air Force team to push the certification across the joint force and share “threat telemetry and defense strategies” with program partners.
The work also included standing up an OT Cyber Defender Schoolhouse within the 16th Air Force, according to the release.
Identify and Defend
The first challenge the service has, Weggeman told Air & Space Forces Magazine after the panel, is “to earnestly and quickly determine the critical mission resilience or redundancies and resiliencies and dependencies we have with [operational technology], and a lot of that OT lives outside of our fence line.”
“We can’t just say there’s a fence line, so I don’t do anything about it,” said Weggeman, former Air Forces Cyber commander and director of strategy, plans, and policy at U.S. Cyber Command.
Another panelist, retired Army Col. Candice Frost, pointed to a recent project that could help model efforts to protect public works OT from cyberattack. Project Watershed 250 in Texas, which launched in August, is combining state assets with the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director to prevent water and wastewater facilities from cyber-attacks.
Future work must include ways to segregate services such as water and electrical, provide backups, and potentially build offsite electrical “microgrids” to keep bases powered if their main power feed is “cut” via a cyberattack, said Frost, now vice president for mission engagement with Parsons.
“Defend the ecosystem, not just the base, because the base is the stronghold, but the ecosystem supporting it is the area that we see in industry that needs the most support,” Frost said.
Identifying critical OT is the first step; then leaders must work to make it resilient. Older equipment, what Weggeman calls the “hand-carved wooden shoe problem,” is somewhat protected from cyberattack because it’s old and not connected.
But increasingly, the retired three-star said, much of the OT supporting a base is being connected to the internet, “which is good because we know how to do that, but also terrifying because an adversary can get in now.”
Weggeman said that while great strides have been made in improving recovery time on the IT side, ways to quickly recover when OT goes down are lagging.
“We have less operational readiness to derive the mission back to where it needs to be from the OT perspective,” Weggeman said.

A little more than two years passed between the delivery of the first prototype in April 2024, the start of ground testing in April 2025, its first flight in October that year and the signing of a contract for serial production in June 2026.
The FQ-44 Fury is being developed as a relatively inexpensive and scalable unmanned aircraft that can be produced in significant quantities.
Its architecture is designed to use artificial intelligence and autonomous systems to perform complex tasks with minimal direct control by an operator.

US inflation expectations tied to Strait of Hormuz

In a post on X, Ghalibaf questioned whether the US Federal Reserve could reopen the Strait of Hormuz or increase oil production simply by raising interest rates. He suggested that changes in borrowing costs would not address the supply-side shock caused by disruptions at strategic energy chokepoints, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb.
Ghalibaf argued that inflation expectations in the United States were being affected by what he described as the closure of key energy routes rather than by interest rates alone. He said the associated “Strait of Hormuz risk” was a factor determining interest rates and claimed that control over that risk was currently in Iran’s hands.
The parliament speaker’s comments challenged the conventional use of monetary policy to anchor inflation expectations. He argued that relying solely on demand-side tools such as interest rates was no longer sufficient under current conditions and that geopolitical factors could have a stronger influence on economic indicators such as inflation.
Under normal conditions, central banks seek to anchor inflation expectations around an inflation target or a credible long-term inflation rate, generally using interest-rate adjustments in response to inflation and economic activity.
Ghalibaf argued, however, that the current situation required financial markets and policymakers to incorporate additional variables, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, into their calculations. He suggested that, in his view, US inflation expectations would remain difficult to anchor as long as the geopolitical risks surrounding these waterways persisted.
Ghalibaf referenced a modified version of the Taylor Rule, adding variables related to the Strait of Hormuz and what he termed the associated risk premium. He said the purpose was to examine whether an interest-rate increase could reduce such risks or increase oil supply.

was as warm-blooded as humans, new study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:48:27 UTC
03:48:27 KST

For years, paleontologists have been piecing together clues that suggest Tyrannosaurus rex may have been quite unlike modern reptiles—including the possibility that it may have been warm-blooded.
But you can’t stick a T. rex on a treadmill or put a thermometer in its mouth, so scientists must resort to more indirect methods to gauge dinosaurs’ metabolisms and internal temperatures—such as the chemical composition of fossilized teeth. And now, for the first time, researchers say they have pinpointed an exact body temperature for T. rex.
“The enamel chemistry is truly recording the temperature at which it formed, and 66 million years later, we can read it using those measurements on a mass spectrometer,” says Aradhna Tripati, a geoscientist at University of California, Los Angeles, and a co-author of the paper. “It’s the next best thing to sticking a thermometer up a T. rex’s ‘butt,’ which we wouldn’t have wanted to do anyway.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Using tiny remains of T. rex tooth enamel found in modern-day Montana, scientists measured isotopes within the sample to estimate the dinosaur’s temperature . They found that T. rex likely ran at around 36 degrees Celsius—similar to the internal body temperature of modern-day humans.
Researchers have estimated dinosaur metabolism and growth rates before, but Tripati says the new study’s method is especially precise at estimating internal temperature because tooth enamel and thermodynamic estimates aren’t as sensitive to confounding factors such as environmental temperatures.
Robert Eagle, a co-author of the study and a geobiologist at University of California, Los Angeles, pioneered this approach to measuring prehistoric body temperatures. He says the findings are a culmination of some 15 years of work. Eagle hopes to use the same technique to suss out the body temperatures of avian dinosaurs and ancient mammalian ancestors next.
“I’m excited that it worked so well because we’ve tried a lot of things with this technique, but this really seemed to be a clear result,” Eagle says. “This gives me optimism that it’s going to be useful looking at other exciting questions.”
The findings add to the growing body of research into how dinosaurs functioned. For example, a 2022 study showed that dinosaurs likely had a range of metabolisms and estimated T. rexes that were on the lower end of endothermy. This new paper, which finds T. rexes’body temperatures to be more similar to those of large mammals than those of smaller, hotter animals such as birds, complements those findings, says Jasmina Wiemann, a paleobiologist at Johns Hopkins University and lead author of the 2022 study.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Science Advances, is “absolutely mind-blowing” and “impressively precise,” Wiemann says. The findings suggest that, based on their temperature, T. rexes likely could have lived anywhere on Earth—even the Arctic, she says.
“It has been really, really exciting to be a young scientist in the field and watching how the collective evidence that we have from different isotope data is converging toward the same picture, suggesting that most nonavian dinosaurs were probably warm-blooded,” Wiemann says.

During her testimony on Wednesday, Saphier tried to create distance between herself and positions taken by both Trump and U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert Kennedy, Jr. Saphier told lawmakers that she does not know what causes autism, and she has “not seen reputable evidence that would suggest that vaccines cause autism.”
On supporting science journalism

When questioned about Trump's recent claim that the mumps, measles and rubella vaccine may be “lethal,” Saphier responded by describing the shot as “our greatest tool for combating measles.”

At today’s hearing, Saphier stressed the importance of Americans personally taking steps to reduce their chances of becoming ill and added that providing more information to the public on prevention will be a priority if she’s confirmed.
“There are small, tangible lifestyle modifications that people can do,” Saphier said. “That doesn’t mean that you have to become a nutrition expert or a someone who’s at the gym every single day. But there are small modifications that people can do that will drastically reduce their risk of illness.”
Wednesday’s confirmation hearing also featured testimony from two other nominees. Chris Klomp, former chief executive of patient data technology company Collective Medical and former director of the Center for Medicare, has been nominated for deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, while Timothy Westlake, an emergency medicine physician, has been tapped to lead the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant producing missile components
An agent of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh sabotaged the power supply to an electronics plant in the Russian city of Voronezh, the group said on Sept. 16.
The facility produces components used in Kh-101 and Iskander-K missiles, as well as Pantsir-S1 air defense systems, according to Atesh.
"Our agent, after a long study of the facility, detailed planning, and searching for weak points, managed to infiltrate an electrical substation near the VZPP-Sborka plant," Atesh said. "After bypassing security, he destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the enterprise and safely left the city."
The sabotage caused a voltage surge and cut power to the plant's workshops, the group said. Atesh also claimed that restoring full electricity supplies took several weeks, disrupting deliveries of key electronic components and delaying the production of Russian missiles and air defense systems.
Atesh did not disclose when the operation took place, saying it delayed publication to protect its agents.
Voronezh, a city in southwestern Russia, lies roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
VZPP-Sborka is a Russian manufacturer of semiconductors, integrated circuits, and power modules whose components are used in several Russian weapons systems, according to Ukraine's military intelligence.
40% of Ukrainians ready to relocate if conditions deteriorate 'significantly' this winter, poll reveals
Some 40% of Ukrainians are prepared to relocate this winter if conditions in the country deteriorate significantly, according to a new poll released by the Gradus agency on Sept. 16.
The survey, conducted by Gradus on Sept. 4–7, polled 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18–60 living in cities with more than 50,000 residents, excluding the occupied territories and areas with active hostilities.
In the lead-up to winter, Ukrainians are preparing for Russia to once again target the country's energy infrastructure in an attempt to make the country unlivable.
Russia has already escalated its attacks on Ukrainian businesses in recent weeks, targeting supermarket distribution centers, postal facilities, gas stations, warehouses, railway infrastructure, industrial plants, and Black Sea ports.
According to Gradus polling, safety is the main factor that would prompt Ukrainians to relocate. However, only one in five respondents said they would consider going abroad — the rest would look for temporary relocation within Ukraine.
"Most" respondents said the decision to relocate would not be prompted by a "single inconvenience" but by multiple factors, such as infrastructure disruptions, safety concerns, and lack of access to healthcare, education, and other essential public services.
"There is an important shift in how Ukrainians are approaching the coming winter: they are increasingly less likely to see resilience as the ability to endure any hardship indefinitely," sociologist Evheniia Blyzniuk, Gradus' CEO, said.
"People are not panicking about possible difficulties, but nor are they relying on the assumption that things will somehow work out. They are assessing risks and preparing backup options."

Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion
Russian authorities plan to build a new prison complex in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast under a program to construct seven such facilities across Russia and occupied Ukraine by 2035, The Moscow Times reported on Sept. 16, citing a Russian government program.
The new facilities will combine pretrial detention centers with penal colonies of different security levels and will have a combined capacity of more than 20,000 people, according to The Moscow Times. The capacity includes 5,380 places for pretrial detainees and 15,120 for prisoners serving sentences.
Apart from the occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Russia plans to build the complexes in Kaluga, Astrakhan, and Tyumen oblasts, Buryatia, and Zabaykalsky Krai, while the first is expected to open in Tatarstan by 2030.
Each facility is expected to cost between 13 billion and 20 billion rubles (around $154 million and $237 million), The Moscow Times reported.
Russia's Justice Ministry estimated that concentrating detention centers and penal colonies in the same complexes could reduce the cost of holding prisoners and detainees by 25-30%, allowing the projects to pay for themselves within about a decade.
Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense
Eighty-one companies are now authorized to form private air defense units amid near-constant Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly Kyiv and the surrounding area, the Defense Ministry said on Sept. 16. 
As Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, more businesses are joining the program, bringing the number of units up by 30 since July.
The ministry said the program is designed to protect workers and facilities while reducing pressure on military air defenses, which now face increased strain beyond concentrated overnight barrages.
Established by the Cabinet of Ministers in November 2025, the private air defense program allows businesses to voluntarily form and finance air defense groups staffed by trained and certified civilian employees. Eligible companies include providers of essential services such as electricity, water, transport, and communications, alongside security firms protecting other businesses.
Companies apply to the Defense Ministry for authorization, then agree with the Air Force command on their units' operations. Under rules introduced in March, participating businesses can also temporarily receive military air defense equipment and ammunition unused by combat units, with Air Force approval.
Private air defense is just one component of Ukraine's multi-level system of airspace protection.
The first successful interceptions under the program were announced in March, when a company's unit downed Russian drones in Kharkiv Oblast. In April, the ministry reported a private group's first interception of a jet-powered Shahed-type drone.
By mid-July, private air defense had downed more than 50 Shahed and Zala drones, according to the ministry.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday that strengthening national unity and extending the state’s sole authority across the country would bolster Lebanon’s position in negotiations with Israel, which has continued its attacks since early March, state news agency NNA reported.

Salam said his government seeks “one people in one state, protected by one army,” and rejects turning Lebanon into an arena for competing regional blocs.

Nato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK.
Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting prime minister Andy Burnham – but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future.
“It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire.
It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, about £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending.
Britain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.
Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.
But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.
Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.
Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.
The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.
Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.
“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.
Citing “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.
Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.
The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.
The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.
Meanwhile, Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties away from the US, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition, prime minister Mark Carney’s office said on Wednesday.
The a grouping of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states is a rapid response military partnership.
Canada, already a Nato member, is seeking closer military cooperation with Europe.
The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK.

The Kentucky Republican read eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor shortly after the chamber convened on Tuesday, citing the war secretary’s violation of multiple provisions of the 1973 War Powers Resolution in launching and waging the war against Iran.
Massie said that Hegseth unlawfully initiated the war, defied the Congress order to withdraw US forces from the war and incurred unnecessary civilian casualties.
“By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement.
Under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, a president generally must end unauthorized US military hostilities within 60 days unless Congress has authorized the action, with an additional 30-day period allowed for an orderly withdrawal.
He added that “Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran.”
Referring to the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro during a US military invasion of the country in early January, Massie said Hegseth “is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders.”
“In all of this, Secretary Hegseth abused the powers entrusted to him as Secretary of Defense by subordinating the constitutional limits on the use of military force and the laws governing the conduct of hostilities to his own policy objectives,” he added.
Congress, Massie said, “must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.”
The impeachment push marks a high-profile challenge to a senior Cabinet official by a member of President Donald Trump’s own party. The resolution would need a two-thirds majority in the Republican-controlled Senate to convict Hegseth and remove him from office.
The House is required to act on Massie’s impeachment proposal by Thursday, giving lawmakers little time to consider the measure before leaving Washington for an extended recess that will last through the November midterm elections.
Massie’s push for impeachment vote came as the Pentagon’s inspector general released the first formal assessment of losses and operational disruptions stemming from the war on Iran, reporting that Iranian retaliatory strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military bases across West Asia and contributed to shortages of key munitions.
Citing communications with US Central Command (CENTCOM), the special report said Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan between February 28 and June 30.
The assessment also acknowledged the depletion of key US munitions stockpiles during the war, while noting that earlier attacks had destroyed critical military assets, including missile-defense radar installations.
The report said the Iranian strikes forced CENTCOM to alter the way US forces operated across the region, as the command “shifted personnel, assets and storage facilities” in response to attacks by Iran and allied forces.
The report warned that some of the changes to the US military presence in West Asia could become permanent, as American military and intelligence officials have discussed the possibility of long-term reductions in personnel and facilities across the region.

Ukrainian border unit’s HIMERA B1 relay took 10 strikes from Russia’s FPV drones and guided bombs. Last one leveled building and tower, and relay kept working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:42:55 UTC
03:42:55 KST

A Ukrainian-made radio repeater survived 10 Russian drone and bomb strikes and a building collapse, and kept transmitting from under the rubble. The HIMERA B1, used by border guards on a telecom tower in Kharkiv Oblast, held its communications link through FPV drones and guided bombs, the manufacturer said.
On what Ukraine's soldiers call the most heavily jammed battlefield in the world, keeping a radio link alive is one of the hardest problems there is, and a cheap, rugged device that outlasts direct hits is a real advantage.
The B1 in Kharkiv Oblast worked in tandem with a second one 10.5 kilometers away, each covering roughly 5 kilometers, until it took 10 strikes. The account is the maker's, HIMERA, but it fits the company's story: a Kyiv firm whose encrypted, frequency-hopping radios were built to survive Russian electronic warfare.
The relay outlasts 10 strikes
The B1 is an autonomous repeater, a box that extends the range of a mesh radio network. This one sat on a telecom tower used by the 1st Border Guard Detachment. During one attack, its power system was destroyed, HIMERA said.
Later strikes partly collapsed the building, and the repeater fell and was buried under debris, yet it kept working.
"Even after that, the repeater remained operational and continued to stay connected," the company said.
Soldiers went in and pulled it from the rubble precisely because it was still transmitting.
The signal beats the jamming
The device is built for a battlefield where Russia listens for radio traffic and uses it to aim, so a poorly protected link can give away a unit's position. HIMERA's radios use AES-256 encryption and pseudo-random frequency-hopping to make a signal hard to intercept, locate, or jam.
A volunteer's frustration built the firm
HIMERA grew out of the front's own shortcomings. One of its co-founders volunteered with the territorial defense in Kyiv Oblast early in the full-scale war and ran into a critical shortage of reliable tactical communications, the company said.
The idea was to build something hard to detect, resistant to jamming, simple to use, and cheap enough to mass-produce, using encryption and frequency-hopping that make a signal difficult to find or suppress.
Within months, the company said, the idea became a team and the team a product, one now fielded widely enough that its repeaters are sometimes dropped into forward positions by drone.

Bloomberg: Germany is preparing hospitals for a possible Russian attack on NATO. Its military says as many as 1,000 wounded troops could need care each day.

Bloomberg: Germany is preparing hospitals for a possible Russian attack on NATO. Its military says as many as 1,000 wounded troops could need care each day.
Government agencies across Germany are inspecting the country’s infrastructure and health care system to assess how well they could function under martial law, according to Bloomberg.
In a report modeling possible scenarios for a Russian attack on NATO, the Bundeswehr estimated that Germany could receive as many as 1,000 wounded service members a day. The country’s five military hospitals would quickly become overwhelmed. Civilian hospitals are required to provide wartime care, putting the health care system under unprecedented strain, Bloomberg notes.
The government’s challenges reportedly include finding enough hospital beds, strengthening medical supply chains, and improving coordination between military and civilian hospitals.
Training enough medical personnel is another pressing challenge. Only a few hundred doctors in Germany have experience treating combat trauma and gunshot wounds. Civilian surgeons are now being offered specialized courses.
Private companies in the health care sector are concerned that their employees could be called up as reservists or volunteer for military service — affecting as many as 20% of their workers in some regions. The companies are also considering how to maintain uninterrupted production of critical medicines if demand surges and assessing whether adequate physical security measures are available.
Germany has seen a surge in hybrid attacks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg. One of the latest incidents involved the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Germany blamed Russia for the sabotage and responded by closing the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russia responded by closing the Goethe-Institut.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has said Russia could start a war with NATO in 2029, though some analysts believe it could happen even sooner. In that event, Germany would be obligated to defend the alliance and, because of its geographic location, would likely become a key transit hub for military personnel, according to Bloomberg.

The copies of the Dutch-language edition of “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister” were taken while being transported from a printing facility to the Dutch publisher’s warehouse, the BBC reported.
A source familiar with the incident said the driver had stopped in a car park for a mandatory rest period and was sleeping in the truck’s cab when the books were stolen.
The precise location of the theft has not been disclosed. Dutch police are aware of the incident and are investigating, according to the report.
The Daily Mail, which first reported the theft and is serializing the book, said it occurred earlier this week in the Dutch countryside.
The truck was reportedly carrying thousands of copies, but only four were taken. It was not clear whether the thieves deliberately targeted the unreleased memoir or took the copies without knowing what they contained.
British publisher Penguin Michael Joseph, part of Penguin Random House, and Dutch publisher Overamstel were approached for comment.
The book is scheduled to be published in Britain and internationally Sept. 22. It recounts Diana’s life from the perspective of her younger brother, Charles Spencer, and includes his memories of their childhood, her marriage and the period surrounding her death.
Spencer announced the memoir ahead of the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death, explaining that repeated interview requests had persuaded him to put his memories into writing rather than continue reading accounts shaped by other people.
“The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral,” he said when the publication was announced. “I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.”
Diana died at the age of 36 following a car crash in Paris on Aug. 31, 1997. Her sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, were 15 and 12 at the time.
At her funeral in Westminster Abbey, Spencer described his sister as the “very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty.”
He also criticized the media’s treatment of Diana, calling her the “most hunted person of the modern age,” and pledged that her family would help protect her sons from suffering a similar fate.

Leaked emails reveal plans to ‘double up’ prisoners in one-person prefab cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:41:00 UTC
03:41:00 KST

The Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show.
Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis in England and Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”.
The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems.
Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour.
According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476.
Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public.
The plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors.
“As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote.
“The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed.
“Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.”
The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantial narrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme, blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed.
According to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60).
Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire.
The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels.
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said.
“Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.”
Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred.
“RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said.
“Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.”
Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation.
“Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said.
There are 87,111 people in prison in England and Wales. Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people.
Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places.
“As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said.
“Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.”

South Korea “cannot afford” to slow the development of artificial intelligence as it seeks to catch up with global leaders and create new markets, the country’s science minister said Wednesday.
“It is an entirely different matter for a country already ahead to adjust its pace, than for a nation that is catching up while simultaneously having to create new markets to slow down,” Science Minister Bae Kyung-hoon said in a social media post, according to Yonhap News.
“We cannot afford to slow down the pace of AI development,” he added.

China has also pushed back, saying “fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would hamper global AI governance, and calling instead for open and inclusive development of the technology.

Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:37:34 UTC
03:37:34 KST

The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandab Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of U.S. protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced U.S.- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the United States nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defence coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
Allies collapse, partners hesitate
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declined to directly intervene militarily.
Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt said Riyadh wanted Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source said MbS asked President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
A Saudi source said the meeting was scheduled long before the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran began in February and "while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss."
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandab — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilise the region via a détente with Iran, has unravelled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defence coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
The Yemen trap
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and U.S. strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen."
