Centre-left Democratic Party (PD) Tuscany Governor Eugenio Giani on Wednesday slammed what he called Premier Giorgia Meloni's "reckless level of electoral demagoguery" after she abolished road tax for small and medium-sized cars and all motorbikes in what he said was a clear ploy to gain favour with voters ahead of the next general election, currently scheduled for next September. 
    Giani complained that the government was not fully making up the shortfall to regional budgets from the abolition.

    Regarding the reimbursements the premier announced for Italy's regions, he went on, "it is falsely claimed that these constitute compensation.

Meloni denied the abolition was an electoral gambit aimed at the 2027 elections saying it was a structural measure.
She also said that her government, which recently became the longest-lasting in Italian history, would serve out its full five-year term until next September, denying any desire for early elections.

EU chief proposes a European Security Council with partners including Ukraine, Canada, and the U.K. — plus a threat-alert system independent of NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:52:47 UTC
02:52:47 KST

EU chief proposes a European Security Council with partners including Ukraine, Canada, and the U.K. — plus a threat-alert system independent of NATO
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed creating a European Security Council that would bring together EU leaders and their counterparts from partner countries such as Canada, Norway, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom. She unveiled the proposal during her annual address to the European Parliament.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders’ format focused on the security of our continent with partners like Ukraine, the U.K., Norway, Canada and others involved,” von der Leyen said. “This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play — this is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality,” she said. “The urgency is clear.”
The European Commission president also called for Europe to create an alert mechanism independent of NATO to coordinate responses to security threats that fall short of armed aggression. Under the proposal, all 27 EU countries would be required to begin consultations if one member state activated the mechanism.
Von der Leyen said the mechanism would complement NATO’s Article 4, which allows allies to request emergency consultations over incidents that do not constitute armed conflict but may threaten their security or territory.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said, adding that there was an urgent need for consensus on how to respond to certain incidents. The number of cyberattacks, acts of sabotage and arson, and drone incursions into EU territory is increasing every day, she said, according to Deutsche Welle.
Von der Leyen also called for Canada to be granted associate membership in the European Union. The proposal drew applause in the European Parliament, according to Reuters.
“I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said, addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in the chamber.
According to DW, EU treaties do not provide for associate membership, though the possibility has been discussed more frequently in recent months. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, among others, has proposed the idea for Ukraine.
Von der Leyen said the EU would provide Ukraine with “the most extensive support” this coming winter, which she said would be the most difficult for the country since the start of the Russian invasion. Specifically, the EU will provide humanitarian aid, bolster Ukraine’s electricity and heat supplies, and strengthen its air defenses.
In recent months, concerns have grown in Europe that Russia could attack a country on NATO’s eastern flank, such as one of the Baltic states. Vladimir Putin has said Russia has no intention of threatening European countries, contrary to claims by “European elites.” He also warned European countries against deploying troops to Ukraine, saying that “this would mean war with Russia.”

Babcock to explore building Ukraine-proven ground robots
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:52:37 BST
02:52:37 KST

Babcock has signed a memorandum of understanding with Ark Robotics to explore manufacturing uncrewed ground vehicles in Britain, bringing a platform already in use on the front line in Ukraine to British and allied forces, the company stated.
The agreement was signed at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the biennial land warfare exhibition, and covers joint exploration of British manufacturing, systems integration and payload integration, along with the development of a full support solution taking in training, logistics, infrastructure and operational support.
The two will also examine opportunities for Ark Robotics’ Frontier system, which gives robots autonomous navigation and allows a single operator to control several vehicles at once.
Louise Atkinson, Chief Executive of Babcock’s Land and Mission Systems sector, said: “In a more volatile and unpredictable world, our customers need the latest and most innovative solutions to ensure they maintain the operational edge. As a business, we connect people, platforms, technology, information and operations across every domain, and by partnering with Ark Robotics, we can leverage our expertise in autonomy, manufacturing and systems integration to deliver next-generation uncrewed ground systems for the UK and international customers.”
Achi Takagama, chief executive of Ark Robotics, said: “Ark Robotics has been at the forefront of the development of unmanned systems in Ukraine. We are building infrastructure for a future in which militaries field many times more unmanned systems than soldiers. Meeting that shift requires more than technology. It requires the manufacturing capacity, systems integration and through-life support that turn a proven platform into a sovereign capability. Partnering with Babcock, a global defence leader, is how we bring what we have learned on the frontline to the UK and other allies at scale.”
The A1, the vehicle at the centre of the agreement, is deployed with the Armed Forces of Ukraine and has a range of up to 20km per charge, a top speed of 40kph and a payload capacity of 15kg. At the exhibition the two companies are showing it fitted with a Concept smoke generator, which lays a smokescreen automatically where and when it is needed.
According to Babcock, uncrewed ground vehicles are taking on a rapidly growing share of front line tasks, resupplying teams with ammunition, weapons and equipment, laying smokescreens and evacuating casualties, keeping people out of the most exposed positions.
That last function has become the most visible of them in Ukraine, where casualty evacuation across ground under constant drone observation has cost stretcher parties heavily, and where a vehicle that can carry a wounded soldier out without exposing four more has an obvious appeal. Ark Robotics describes itself as a European technology company building the infrastructure layer for mass robotics, with its technology deployed across more than twenty military units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and improved continuously through operational feedback.
The agreement follows a series of similar arrangements Babcock has entered this year. It announced a collaboration with Supacat to enhance its General Logistics Vehicle offering for the British Army’s Light Mobility Vehicle programme, intended to replace the retiring Land Rover fleet, and is working with HII and Arondite through ARMOR Force on autonomous systems, modular technology and digital innovation in support of the hybrid navy.

200 nights, one flag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:50:40 UTC
02:50:40 KST

200 nights, one flag
People across Iran took to the streets for the 200th night, protesting U.S.-Israeli aggression
TEHRAN — Night falls differently across Iran.
On Kharg Island, the darkness settles over the humid waters of the Persian Gulf. In Shiraz, the lights of the squares come on beneath the evening sky. In Sanandaj, people make their way toward Azadi Square. In Birjand, families gather in the cold. In Tonekabon, on the Caspian coast, an elderly war veteran walks slowly toward the crowd.
And in Arak, beneath the lights of Martyrs Square, a woman sits behind a sewing machine.
Her name is Zahra Fattahi.
For almost 200 nights, she has brought the machine with her, repairing damaged Iranian flags and preparing them to be raised again.
That image — a woman, a sewing machine, a piece of torn fabric and a square filled with people — may say more about these nights than any official statement.
Two hundred nights have now passed since nightly gatherings began in cities across Iran following the outbreak of war. What started in the immediate aftermath of the conflict has, according to reports by Mehr News Agency correspondents, continued through heat, humidity, rain and winter cold.
The gatherings have been different from city to city. Some have centered on mourning. Others have included cultural programs, Quran recitations, music, children's activities, food and tea booths, speeches and family gatherings.
But beneath the differences is one recurring image: people returning to the same public spaces night after night.
For many participants, these nights have also carried a second, more intimate meaning — the absence of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, the former Supreme Leader who was killed during the war.
His absence is visible in photographs, banners, conversations and moments of silence. For some of those interviewed by Mehr, the nightly gathering has become a place where grief and public presence exist side by side.
On March 12, 2026, in his first wartime message, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei called on people to help one another during difficult days. On April 9, he said that the announcement of negotiations should not lead people to conclude that public presence in squares, neighborhoods and mosques was no longer necessary.
The 200 nights that followed have now become a vast collection of local stories.
The following is a journey through some of them.
Arak: Three generations beneath one flag
In Arak, capital of Markazi Province in central Iran, the camera finds a mother holding her child.
There is nothing spectacular about the image at first glance. No speech. No stage. No dramatic gesture.
Just a mother, a child and a crowd gathered at night.
Yet that is precisely what gives the photograph its emotional weight.
For 200 nights, the square has seen families arrive together. Parents have brought children into a public space where different generations stand side by side.
Arak: A mother holds her young child during a nightly gathering at Martyrs Square in Arak, where families have been among the recurring participants over the past 200 nights.
Another photograph tells a different version of the same story.
Women from different generations stand together beneath a banner. Older women and younger women occupy the same frame, their faces separated by decades but brought together by the same night.
Arak: Women from different generations stand together at Martyrs Square in Arak, creating a single frame that spans generations of Iranian women.
Then comes the sewing machine.
Every night, Zahra Fattahi brings hers to the square. She repairs flags damaged during the gatherings and prepares them to be raised again.
She told Mehr that she had attended almost all 200 nights.
Her contribution is small in physical scale: thread passing through cloth, a needle moving back and forth, a torn edge being joined.
But repeated night after night, it has become a symbol in the visual record of Arak.
Arak: Zahra Fattahi brings her sewing machine to Martyrs Square almost every night, repairing damaged Iranian flags and preparing them to be raised again.
There is something quietly mournful about the image, too.
A flag can be repaired.
A torn piece of cloth can be stitched.
But a person who has been lost cannot be brought back.
For some participants, that is the deeper emotional landscape of these nights: continuing to gather while remembering a leader whose absence has changed the meaning of the gathering itself.
Shiraz: A city that remembers
In Shiraz, the capital of Fars Province in southern Iran, the night begins with lights.
Imam Hussein Square, Moallem Square and Vali Asr Square gradually fill with people. Families arrive. Young people stand beside older residents. Flags rise above the crowd.
Mehr's account describes a city whose nightly gathering has been repeated for 200 nights.
The scene has its own rhythm.
People arrive.
The lights brighten.
Programs begin.
Voices fill the square.
And eventually, late at night, people go home.
Then the next night comes.
And they return.
The emotional force of such repetition is not necessarily in the size of the crowd but in the passage of time. A single night can be an event. Two hundred nights become a memory.
Kharg: Heat, humidity and the lights of the Gulf
On Kharg Island, the story takes place against one of Iran's most important oil landscapes.
The island lies in the Persian Gulf, in Bushehr Province, and is closely associated with Iran's oil export infrastructure.
It is also hot and intensely humid.
Yet the local account describes residents continuing to gather during the 200-night period.
At night, the oppressive heat does not disappear completely. The humidity remains in the air. The sea remains beyond the lights of the gathering.
And still, people come.
There is something elemental about that scene: an island surrounded by water, a city accustomed to heat, and people gathering after dark.
Kharg: Residents gather at night on Kharg Island in Bushehr Province, where the 200-night gatherings have continued despite the island's intense heat and humidity.
Birjand: A teenager among the generations
In Birjand, capital of South Khorasan Province in eastern Iran, the gatherings have been held in Maalem, Abuzar and Modarres squares.
Children stand beside adults. Older people watch the programs. Flags and cultural booths become part of the nightly landscape.
Fourteen-year-old Maedeh Fayazi is among those reported to have attended most nights.
Mahdi Rahimabadi, 42, was present on the 200th night.
Their ages are separated by almost three decades.
But the photograph of them in the same story captures something repeated throughout the country: the coexistence of generations in the same public space.
We will trample America underfoot
From the first night of the ‘Ramadan War’ to the 200th night of nightly gatherings across Alborz Province, residents of Karaj have continued to gather through heat and cold, rain and, in the early days of the war, amid bombings and missile attacks.
In Gohardasht, residents make their way to the nightly gathering along familiar routes. In Azimiyeh, people follow another established path, while Karaj, the provincial capital, has hosted the largest gatherings night after night.
Mahmoud Moradpour, a Karaj resident holding a handwritten sign that reads, “We will trample America underfoot,” says the people will stand by the Islamic Republic, their Islamic identity and their Iranian identity to their final breath.
Mr. Akbari, another participant, who says he has attended the neighborhood and street gatherings for exactly 200 nights, describes the period as “200 nights of estrangement and separation from our beloved Imam.”
Mehdi, a 20-year-old participant, says that throughout the 200 days during which Iranians have taken to the streets, a sense of national honor has risen above differences in beliefs and backgrounds.
For those gathered across Karaj, the passage of 200 nights has become a record of continued presence — shaped by the changing seasons, difficult circumstances and a shared determination to remain together.
Sanandaj: When a square becomes a memory
In Sanandaj, capital of Kurdistan Province in western Iran, Azadi Square has become one of the most recognizable settings of the 200-night story. It is the square that was once simply a square becomes a place people remember because they have returned to it so many times.
The gatherings have included children, teenagers, young people and families.
But the square has also become a cultural space.
Student anthems, Quran recitations, daf music, public booths and other activities have accompanied the gatherings. On some occasions, wedding ceremonies have also been held there.
Thirty-five-year-old Mortaza Sharaf-Bayani told Mehr that he had attended all 200 nights and had helped with programs and Quran recitation.
Mohammad Hassan, an 11-year-old boy from Kurdistan who had attended the gathering with his family, told Mehr correspondent: “I have come to this gathering to seek justice for the martyred leader and to express my support for this demand.”
Zahra Jafari a university student in Sanandaj, another participant in the nightly gathering said that students cannot remain indifferent to events unfolding in their country. The younger generation must understand political issues and be able, under different circumstances, to distinguish between various issues and political currents.
Sanandaj: Zahra Jafari a university student :The younger generation must understand political issues and be able, under different circumstances, to distinguish between various issues and political currents
"Steadfastness is not a habit, but a belief"
In Shirvan, North Khorasan Province in northeastern Iran, the story has unfolded around Imam Khomeini Mosque and Revolution Square. As the seasons changed and summer heat gave way to winter cold and rain, the nightly gatherings continued.
For Fatemeh, a teacher and mother of three, taking part has become far more than simply attending a nightly gathering. She recalls that the gatherings initially began in an atmosphere of mourning and remembrance, but gradually took on a different character.
“Every night, I saw more women joining us and the voice of solidarity growing stronger,” she says. “What began as small groups of just a few people has now become a regular nightly gathering. I feel that we have become one large family, coming together every night to raise our voices in solidarity and steadfastness.”
One of her most vivid memories is of a cold, rainy night when she expected the heavy downpour to keep many people away.
“I thought to myself, ‘Perhaps no one will come tonight,’” she recalls. “But when I arrived at the mosque, I saw that our gathering was just as full and as warm as ever.”
For Fatemeh, that night gave a deeper meaning to being present. As she later told Mehr, “Steadfastness is not a habit, but a belief.”
Around Revolution Square, tea and food booths have remained open, while exhibitions, children’s drawing stations, books, photographs, and cultural programs have filled the surrounding space.
On cold nights, warm tea has become part of the visual memory: steam rising from cups, people gathering around the booths, children staying close to their parents, and the lights remaining on as the square prepares to welcome another night.
Qom: Grief and continuity
In Qom, one of Iran's major religious cities in central Iran, gatherings have taken place in several locations, including Mofid Square, Tawhid Square, Army Square and Imam Khomeini Square, as well as routes toward the shrine of Hazrat Masoumeh.
Samira Zangi, 33, told Mehr that she had attended from the first night.
She spoke of attending with her family despite heat, cold and having a young child.
Her account reflects one of the recurring themes of the 200-night reports: the gathering as a family experience.
But Qom also carries another emotional layer.
For many people there, as elsewhere, the gatherings have taken place in the shadow of mourning.
The faces in the crowd are not only faces of participation. Some are faces of remembrance.
Tonekabon: The veteran who still comes
On Iran's northern Caspian coast, Tonekabon in Mazandaran Province offers perhaps one of the most poignant images of the entire story.
A 69-year-old man stands among the crowd. His name is Abolfazl Mirzaei. He is a 50-percent disabled war veteran. He has lived long enough to carry the physical memory of one war into another period of conflict.
Yet night after night, he makes his way toward Imam Khomeini Square.
Tonekabon: Abolfazl Mirzaei, 69, a 50-percent disabled war veteran, attends a nightly gathering at Imam Khomeini Square in Tonekabon despite his physical condition.
The photograph needs little explanation.
The man's age tells one story.
His disability tells another.
His presence tells a third.
The 200-night story is therefore not only about young faces or large crowds. It is also about people carrying memories from decades past into the present.
What does it mean to be proud?
The word “pride” is often used loosely when discussing nations.
But in the Iranian case, it has a deeper historical and cultural context.
The Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that a strong sense of pride in Iran's cultural heritage, with Persian literature at its core, together with a consciousness of historical continuity and the belief that Iranians can survive recurrent periods of upheaval, has served as a cohesive force in Iranian identity.
That idea can be found across centuries of Persian literature.
Ferdowsi's Shahnameh preserved stories of kings, warriors, loss, endurance and the survival of a cultural memory across generations. Simin Behbahani, discussing Ferdowsi, described the Shahnameh as having helped revive a sense of pride and unity among Iranians.
Saadi, writing centuries earlier, reduced the idea of shared humanity to one of the most enduring images in Persian literature: human beings as members of one body.
These are literary traditions, not political instructions.
But they help explain why words such as dignity, endurance, homeland and memory carry such emotional weight in Iran.
Modern observers have noticed that characteristic as well.
On May 6, 2026, US President Donald Trump, speaking about negotiations with Iran, said of Iranians: "should raise the white flag of surrender" but that it is "too arrogant to do so."
He added that they can fight or cry when wounded and described their pride as particularly strong.
It was a striking acknowledgment from an American president of a characteristic frequently associated with Iranian national identity.
Two hundred nights
The 200 nights can be read in many ways.
Government officials have described them as a demonstration of national resolve. Critics of the gatherings may interpret them differently. The reports from Mehr, however, provide something more concrete: photographs and conversations with people who repeatedly returned to public squares.
A mother holding a child.
Women from several generations standing beneath one banner.
A woman repairing a flag with a sewing machine.
Children drawing.
A teenager returning to the same square.
A 35-year-old man helping with Quran recitation.
A 69-year-old veteran walking into the crowd despite his physical limitations.
And, everywhere, the night.
There is also grief.
The photographs contain smiles, flags, and gatherings, but they cannot entirely conceal the absence around which much of this period has been emotionally organized.
For some participants, the squares have become places to remember Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei.
His name appears on banners.
His image appears in the visual landscape.
And for those who came to regard him as their leader, his martyrdom left behind a form of absence that cannot be filled simply by another speech or another gathering.
That may be why some of the photographs feel quieter than the slogans surrounding them.
A mother holds her child.
An old veteran stands among younger people.
A woman bends over a sewing machine.
The flag is torn, and someone repairs it.
The night grows late.
Then people begin to leave.
The square becomes quieter.
But the story does not end there.
Two hundred nights are not two hundred identical nights.
They are two hundred evenings of changing weather, changing faces, changing emotions and repeated memories.
They are 200 nights in which a country at war has watched its people return to the same public spaces.
Whether viewed as political expression, mourning, communal ritual or a manifestation of national identity, the gatherings have produced a remarkable visual archive.
And perhaps the most powerful image is still the simplest one:
the lights of an Iranian square at night,
people slowly arriving,
and a flag — sometimes worn, sometimes torn, sometimes repaired by hand — rising once more above the crowd.

'Altogether these acts amount to treason' Israeli culture minister says after asking Shin Bet to investigate NAZA filmmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Miki Zohar asks Shin Bet to investigate Yuval Abraham, Rachel Szor for alleged treason
Zohar said "it is very possible" that following a Shin Bet investigation, more serious crimes could be uncovered and that the NAZA filmmakers may end up in prison
Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar told i24NEWS on Wednesday that he asked the Shin Bet to investigate NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor over alleged treason.
"I think these two committed an act of treason," Zohar said. "I began taking action today by contacting the head of the Shin Bet and asking him to investigate the matter."
Zohar said the Shin Bet would be investigating how the pair acquired the information in the film and, in particular, whether they received information from Hamas or from soldiers in violation of their security clearances.
"Taken together, all of these things amount to acts of treason," he said. "These creators essentially acted in a way that we would describe as a breach of loyalty to the State of Israel."
Zohar said he believed this justifies revoking their citizenship and that neither could remain Israeli citizens.
Zohar continued, saying that "it is very possible" that following a Shin Bet investigation, more serious crimes could be uncovered and that they may end up in prison.
He pointed to Section 11 of Israel’s Citizenship Law, which describes the process of revoking citizenship. He tempered this by saying, "Of course, we need to prove that they did so, and I think there is a way to prove it."
Zohar said that in his view this was an open-and-shut case but that he would wait for the full Shin Bet investigation.

Punjab Govt constitutes 7-member coordination committee over Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Amendment) Act, 2026
Chandigarh: The Punjab Government on Wednesday constituted a seven-member coordination committee regarding the Sri Guru Granth Sahib (Amendment) Act, 2026, in accordance with the directives of Sri Akal Takht Sahib.According to the Punjab Government, the newly formed panel includes former Jathedar of Sri Akal Takht Sahib GiRaghbir Singh, Head of Damdami Taksal Sant Giani Harnam Singh Khalsa, Sant Baba Sewa Singh Rampur Khera, retired Justice Jaspal Singh, retired Justice Gurbir Singh, retired IPS officer and PPSC Chairman Jatinder Singh Aulakh, and Law Officer Preet Inder Paul Singh.The state government stated that this committee will maintain continuous coordination with the committee constituted by Sri Akal Takht Sahib.Earlier, on April 20, the Punjab Government notified the Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026, which aims to provide a framework governing the protection and sanctity of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and penalise acts of sacrilege.
The notification followed Punjab Governor Gulab Chand Kataria granting his assent to the amendment bill on April 17. The amended legislation introduces stringent penalties for sacrilege, prescribing imprisonment ranging from 10 years to life along with fines between Rs 5 lakh and Rs 25 lakh for anyone involved in or supporting such acts.
Punjab Finance Minister Harpal Singh Cheema declared that the enactment reflects the firm commitment of the Bhagwant Mann government to uphold the supreme honour and dignity of Guru Sahib. (ANI)"Government of Punjab has today notified the Sri Jaagat Jot Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026, passed in the recent Punjab Vidhan Sabha session and assented to by the Hon'ble Governor on 17th April. This reflects the firm commitment of the @BhagwantMann Government to uphold the supreme honour and dignity of Guru Sahib. Those involved in any act of sacrilege or dishonouring Guru Sahib will face the strictest consequences," said Cheema. (ANI)

Türkiye condemns Houthi drone attack targeting Mecca
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:45:18 UTC
02:45:18 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Türkiye on Wednesday strongly condemned a Houthi drone attack targeting the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia, reaffirming support for the kingdom's security.
"We strongly condemn the Houthis' drone attack targeting the holy city of Mecca," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Türkiye, the ministry said, reaffirms its "support for Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and security," and stressed its “solidarity with Saudi Arabia.”
"We reiterate our call for these attacks, which also threaten regional stability and security, to end immediately and for all actions aimed at further escalating tensions to be avoided," the statement said.
Yemen has been gripped by war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
The rebel group has been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since July, when it declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh, and has recently claimed advances along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition said early Wednesday that Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by Yemen’s Houthi group south of Mecca before it entered the holy city's restricted airspace.
Mecca's peace and security is a shared priority
Turkish Communications Director Burhanettin Duran also condemned the attack in a post shared on the US social media company X, saying: “I strongly condemn the despicable attempted drone attack targeting the sanctity and security of Mecca.”
Duran said any attack targeting Islam's holy sites wounds the collective conscience of the Muslim world, and stressed that protecting Mecca's peace and security is a shared priority.
Echoing President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's calls for dialogue and lasting peace, he said the Islamic world needed common sense and diplomacy rather than new conflicts.
He also reaffirmed Türkiye's support for Saudi Arabia.

UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:41:00 UTC
02:41:00 KST

UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
September 16, 2026
An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom, in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby.
Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday.
They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A).
What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote?
The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%.
Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination."
Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot.
Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington."
"For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"
He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through."
An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests.
The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online.
How did the government react?
The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029.
This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum."
But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country.
Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation.
One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources.
Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour.
The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month.
What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester?
In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community."
It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape.
It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first."
It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65.
The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said.
Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage.
It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said.

UN chief calls for urgent Security Council reform, blames major powers for 'paralysis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:40:48 UTC
02:40:48 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Wednesday that the "paralysis" of the Security Council stems in part from the conduct of major powers, some of which he said violate international law while holding seats on the body, as he called for urgent reform of its composition.
Responding at a news conference to a question about why calls to respect international law have gone unheeded, Guterres pointed to geopolitical divisions among major powers.
"We have geopolitical divides, and in these geopolitical divides, we have powers that themselves violate international law and sit in the Security Council," he said.
"And that has been paralysing the Security Council, as we know. That is why the reform of the Security Council must be an absolute priority," he added.
Guterres said the council's composition no longer reflects the current international order.
Outdated council
"It is unacceptable to have a Security Council with a composition that reflects the world of many decades ago instead of reflecting today's world, and that is a factor of paralysis," Guterres said.
Warning that the dysfunction has emboldened countries to act without restraint, Guterres said the conduct of major powers was setting a damaging precedent.
"Because the example coming from the biggest powers is not a good example, every country around the world feels that they are entitled to do whatever they want," he said.
"And they know that they will do it with impunity because the Security Council, that is the organisation that is supposed to maintain peace and security in the world, is paralysed," he added.
Guterres said the underlying issue was ultimately one of how global power is distributed and exercised.
"The question is a question of power, and the question is that the way power is distributed and power is used in our world does not allow multilateral institutions to act effectively," he said.

Belarus frees 25 political prisoners in return for US sanctions relief
The Trump administration said more releases would be secured soon amid improved US-Belarus relations.
Belarus on Wednesday freed 25 political prisoners as the United States lifted sanctions on two of the reclusive country’s companies, US envoy John Coale announced after his latest visit to Minsk.
The release on Wednesday marked the culmination of a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Ukraine decimates Russian logistics, bringing chaos to Crimea

Those freed include human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where the freed prisoners were taken, Coale said he expected to return in about a month when he hopes to see “hundreds” freed.
The US envoy praised US President Donald Trump on social media, saying his “commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results” and that the administration would continue to “improve US-Belarus relations”.
Coale had been tasked by Trump with securing the release of hundreds of people. In March, the government of Belarus released 250 prisoners following a pardon.

Journalists, musicians among those arrested

Alyaksandrau told Viasna he had lost 30kgs (66 pounds) while in captivity “for the motherland” but was “in a good mood”. He added that he was “very glad that these almost six years are over” and that he hadn’t seen Zlobina – whom he married in a pre-trial detention centre in 2022 – in four years.
Alongside Alyaksandrau, three other journalists – Dzmitry Navazhylau, Kiryl Pazniak and Liudmila Chekina – were released and immediately deported to Lithuania. Reporters Without Borders said it was “delighted” by their release but denounced their expulsion.
Exiled political opposition leader Svetlana Tsikhanouskaya said she was happy for the relatives of the 25 freed prisoners “who have been waiting for this day”. Her husband, Siarhei Tsikhanouski, was freed last year after spending five years in jail.
“Every release requires tremendous effort, and it is clear that [Lukashenko] does not want to release all political prisoners,” she wrote on X, noting that hundreds more remain behind bars.

Major South African party loses court fight over barred candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:37:39 UTC
02:37:39 KST

Major South African party loses court fight over barred candidates
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa’s party has lost a court bid to place 181 candidates on the ballot for local elections in November, leaving it at risk of being shut out of two longtime strongholds.
The Electoral Court on Wednesday dismissed an appeal by the African National Congress (ANC) against an Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) decision to reject candidate lists from six municipalities.
The dispute arose after the ANC failed to complete the final electronic submission of the nominations before an August 28 deadline. The party argued that the candidates’ details and supporting documents had been uploaded before the cutoff, but technical problems had prevented officials from finalizing the process. It said pressing the system’s “submit as final” button was an administrative step rather than a legal requirement.
Ahead of the ruling, Ramaphosa called the problem “containable,” saying technical glitches affecting several parties should not deprive voters of their preferred candidates. The IEC rejected the argument, saying information that had merely been captured, uploaded or saved did not constitute a formal submission.
Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo told the court that the online system had recorded no downtime during the period in question. He said the ANC had also successfully finalized lists for other municipalities shortly before the deadline. The 181 candidates are from six municipalities across the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State. They include 130 proportional-representation nominees and 51 ward candidates.
The ruling could shut the ANC out of both ballots in its Ingquza Hill and Port St Johns strongholds, where it won 46 of 64 and 31 of 39 council seats respectively in 2021. In Mangaung, uMshwathi, Walter Sisulu and Sundays River Valley, its ward candidates remain, but its proportional-representation lists have been excluded.
The Democratic Alliance (DA), South Africa’s second-largest party, opposed the ANC’s application after being allowed to join the case. It argued that accepting the candidates would disadvantage parties that had met the deadline.
The ANC has said it respects the ruling but will pursue further legal action, insisting that it sought recognition of information captured by the IEC system before the deadline rather than an extension or preferential treatment.
The November 4 vote will test whether the ANC can reverse its declining support. Its share of the municipal vote fell from 53.91% in 2016 to 46.04% in 2021, leaving 66 councils without a majority.
The ANC also lost its parliamentary majority in 2024 and formed a Government of National Unity with former rivals, including the DA.
The ANC faced a similar failure in 2021, when it failed to complete all its nominations by the deadline, affecting 93 municipalities. It was later allowed to register the candidates after the Electoral Commission of South Africa reopened submissions under a revised Covid-era election timetable.
The Constitutional Court rejected a DA challenge to the reopening but stressed that parties must comply with electoral deadlines once they are formally set.

Aircraft carrier arrives at on the Clyde in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:36:57 BST
02:36:57 KST

HMS Queen Elizabeth has arrived in Scotland, sailing up the Firth of Clyde and into Loch Long to the jetty at Glenmallan, the Royal Navy has confirmed to the UK Defence Journal.
Commander Adrian Visram, a Royal Navy spokesperson, told us: “HMS Queen Elizabeth is currently in Glenmallan completing a short logistics and engagement stop before continuing on operations.”
The 65,000-tonne carrier sailed from Portsmouth earlier this month for three months of training and operations around the United Kingdom and northern Europe, in her role as NATO’s command ship for the Allied Response Force, a role she assumed in July and one neither Queen Elizabeth-class ship had performed before.
Glenmallan sits on the western shore of Loch Long in Argyll, and its jetty is the only facility on the west coast able to take a ship of the carriers’ size alongside, which is why both Queen Elizabeth-class vessels have called there repeatedly since it was rebuilt.
The jetty itself underwent a £67 million upgrade under a contract awarded to VolkerStevin in 2019, with Jacobs as managing agent and Arch Henderson as designer. It had last been upgraded in the 1970s and had reached the end of its economic life. Around £20 million of that work went to local suppliers and small and medium-sized enterprises in Scotland, and the project extended the jetty’s life by an estimated fifty years while making it accessible to the carriers.
The work involved installing four new navigational aids to allow safe passage through the confined waterway, two modular fender spacer units that move with the tide to keep the flight deck clear of the jetty, and dolphin mooring points to hold a ship of that size securely.
As we reported at the end of April, the last Queen Elizabeth-class carrier to make the trip was HMS Prince of Wales, which called at Glenmallan ahead of Operation Firecrest. That deployment, announced by the Prime Minister at the Munich Security Conference in February, took the carrier strike group across the North Atlantic and the High North, with Prince of Wales leading the force.
Firecrest was designed to deter Russian aggression, protect critical undersea infrastructure and demonstrate the ability to project force at scale within a NATO framework, against a background of a 30 per cent increase in Russian naval vessels threatening British waters over the preceding two years. It included activity under NATO’s Arctic Sentry mission and exercises alongside Standing NATO Maritime Group One, which Britain has led throughout 2026.
Queen Elizabeth’s own programme runs on a different track from her sister’s, and she will undertake advanced training under Flag Officer Sea Training, exercising across the spectrum of modern naval warfare, and will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together in a crisis. The programme continues into next year with participation in major NATO exercises, preparing her to take over from Prince of Wales as fleet flagship and high readiness strike carrier in late 2027.
The Royal Navy has linked the deployment to the £240 million committed in the Defence Investment Plan towards developing drones for a Hybrid Carrier Air Wing, including jet-powered types intended to operate alongside the F-35B.
The first visit by a Queen Elizabeth-class ship to the upgraded jetty came in March 2021, when Queen Elizabeth called there during final preparations for her maiden operational deployment, the first time she had visited western Scotland after becoming a familiar sight on the Forth during her assembly at Rosyth.
On the way up the Clyde the ship paused over the wreck of HMS Dasher, the escort carrier lost on 27 March 1943 with 379 of her company, and laid a wreath. The ship posted afterwards that “the lessons from the tragedy improved the safety of carrier aviation. We still benefit from those lessons.”
Dasher was a converted merchant hull operating in the Firth of Clyde when an internal explosion sank her within minutes, and the inquiry that followed changed how aviation fuel was stored and handled aboard carriers.

The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:36:16 UTC
02:36:16 KST

Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait.
The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia had painfully extracted itself from a war with the Houthis which it recklessly spearheaded – nominally in support of the internationally recognised government – at astounding cost to its own coffers and Yemeni civilians. It apparently hoped that it could calibrate its response to a flight from Iran to Houthi-controlled Sana’a in July, the first in over a decade, sufficiently to save the 2022 truce. But bombing Sana’a airport gave the Houthis the opportunity to escalate while blaming Riyadh.
The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned, thanks to Donald Trump’s unlawful war on Iran. They need to maintain Iranian support and the strait of Hormuz crisis has created a new opportunity to exert economic pressure, and perhaps create a new income stream, via strategic gains along the coast. The forces ranged against them, including the government and southern secessionists, are more fractured than ever. The United Arab Emirates, which has clashed with its former close partner Saudi Arabia, withdrew its troops at the turn of the year.
Saudi strikes alone will not be enough to push the Houthis back. But Mr Trump has rebuffed requests for help. The Houthis have been canny enough to say that they are targeting only the Saudis, though that message reinforces the fact that their leverage could be used more broadly in future. They are also closer than ever to Djibouti, home to US, Chinese and other military bases.
The Saudis face a choice between negotiations with an emboldened enemy now making increasingly maximalist demands – or returning to the kind of full-scale war they previously regretted, with little support this time. Turkey and Pakistan are not rushing to act on the new Mecca defence pact the three countries signed in August.
Yemen’s recent history amply demonstrates the futility of seeking a military solution. Ultimately, its citizens deserve a government not dependent on either Riyadh or Tehran. Outside parties should concentrate on promoting a political process within the country. They should stress that both sides must protect civilians, and support humanitarian efforts. Their priority, however, should be a resolution to the Iran war, without which danger in the region, and broader instability, will only grow.

The Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squander | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:35:23 UTC
02:35:23 KST

European progressives searching for reasons to be cheerful have been finding them hard to come by this autumn. In Germany, the dramatic rise of the Alternative für Deutschland party is threatening the liberal values that underpin the identity of the federal republic. In France, polls continue to point to a likely Marine Le Pen victory in a presidential election, which is months away. Across mainland Europe, centre-left parties are failing to muster an adequate response to nativist movements that have colonised swathes of the working-class support that they once relied on.
In such an ominous political landscape, the outcome of a cliffhanger Swedish election provides a much‑needed source of optimism – albeit one that comes with heavy caveats. Prior to last Sunday’s poll, the outgoing prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, was explicit that if his rightwing alliance won the largest number of seats, he would invite members of the far-right Sweden Democrats party (SD) to become ministers in the next government.
That would have meant the formal end of the SD’s pariah status in Swedish politics, after four years in which its parliamentary votes have propped up Mr Kristersson’s minority administration. In a Europe where firewalls and cordons sanitaires against the far right have never seemed less secure, another significant threshold would have been crossed.
Voters appear to have instead handed the narrowest of victories to the Social Democratic leader, Magdalena Andersson, and the progressive bloc of parties. The SD’s share of the vote fell for the first time since it began its political journey as an openly neo-Nazi party in the late 1980s, and it slipped from second to third place behind the conservative Moderates.
So much for the good news. As in Germany and France, the Swedish far right has not needed to win power for its agenda to become normalised and partially implemented. Mr Kristersson’s reliance on the SD resulted in a government that behaved with performative cruelty towards migrants, and enacted much of its draconian programme on deportations and citizenship restrictions. Ms Andersson has responded by offering a milder version of the same approach to immigration and asylum. As it leaked support on the left accordingly, her party recorded its lowest vote share for over a century.
Unless traditional powerhouse parties of European social democracy are more courageous in seeking to shift the dial of political debate, the far right will continue to set its terms. The SD’s chosen slogan for its campaign was “Make Sweden Sweden again” – varying the usual Maga trope in order to stress the core ethnocentric message. From the sidelines its rhetoric will become still more extreme, and the defeat of the rightwing bloc is already being invidiously attributed to foreign-born voters.
Should Ms Andersson eventually succeed in forming a centre-left coalition government, she should counter the forces of division by channelling the best of her own party’s traditions. The Social Democratic party historically dominated Swedish politics through the idea of the Folkhemmet, or People’s Home, which encapsulated the inclusive ethos of a welfare society admired around the world. Locating the resources and ambition to develop a similarly attractive politics of the common good for the 21st century is the urgent task for progressives, in Sweden and beyond.

Von der Leyen blindsides EU with Canada ‘associate member’ pitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:33:51 UTC
02:33:51 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney greets European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the official welcome ceremony during the G7 Leaders' Summit on June 16, 2025 in Kananaskis. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen wanted to make a splash in her big speech. Instead, the European Commission president’s audacious offer of making Canada the EU’s first “associate member” has created a major diplomatic headache.
The idea was not run past European capitals in advance and has caused considerable confusion, four diplomats told POLITICO. Ottawa also appears to be distancing itself from the label — hours before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to give his own speech to the European Parliament.
Von der Leyen dropped the bombshell proposal during her State of the Union address Wednesday, directly addressing Carney from the floor of the Parliament.
Advertisement
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” she said, drawing thunderous applause from MEPs and an embrace from Carney.
There is another big problem: No one seems to know exactly what associate membership would entail.
And within hours, Canada was tamping down expectations.
“We’re not there,” Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s incoming ambassador to the EU, told reporters in Strasbourg when asked about associate membership. “What we’re focused on is actually driving results.”
That leaves von der Leyen having publicly offered up a new status that the EU hasn’t agreed to create or settled on a definition for — and which Canada itself doesn’t appear exactly eager to embrace.
A 'dangerous' strategy
The idea didn’t come out of nowhere. As U.S. tariffs and Donald Trump’s “51st state” threats strain ties, Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on its neighbor, which receives roughly 70% of its exports, by deepening economic and security ties with Europe.
Advertisement
Ottawa has been exploring whether it can establish an unusually close relationship with the EU, the Wall Street Journal first reported last week. Carney publicly confirmed the broader ambition on Sunday, saying Canada was not seeking EU membership but rather a “unique alliance” with the bloc.
But von der Leyen’s decision to announce the proposal, at the biggest annual set piece of her political calendar, caught EU member countries off guard, according to four European diplomats who said their governments were not informed. They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about their reactions to the proposal.
One diplomat slammed the secrecy as “dangerous” and “unwise,” pointing out that von der Leyen had not even raised the idea at a recent lunch with EU ambassadors. Another diplomat said the copy of the speech their government received in advance did not include the words associate membership.
Mark Carney said last week he wanted a “unique” partnership with Brussels but shied away from using the words associate membership. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
And a different diplomat with knowledge of the discussions with Canada raised a different issue: “Nobody really knows what it [associate membership] means.”
While the Commission president is under no obligation to flag any of the speech's content to capitals in advance, they would need to approve any formal plan to grant Canada an exceptional status.
The idea has also raised questions about whether Britain could seek a similar deal. But EU officials have moved quickly to rule that out, stressing the model is intended for countries that cannot join the bloc. “Unlike Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Norway and the U.K., Canada is not in Europe,” one senior EU official said. “It cannot join the EU.”
Advertisement
Under the EU treaties and the bloc’s established institutional practice, there is a sharp distinction between membership and partnership. The EU has close relationships with many non-member countries, but only its 27 members have a seat in the bloc’s core political institutions and a formal role in making EU law.
A new model of membership “would actually require a treaty change,” German Socialists and Democrats MEP René Repasi told POLITICO.
The lack of wide consultation was visible inside the Commission, too, with an official involved in enlargement telling POLITICO their team had not been involved in any discussions about the proposal and that they knew nothing about it.
In the hallways of the Parliament, the proposal drew mixed reactions. “No one was aware of this special membership granted to Canada,” right-wing ECR co-chair Nicola Procaccini told POLITICO, adding it's "not entirely clear what this membership actually entails" but that the United Kingdom should be the first to benefit from such an arrangement.
Von der Leyen’s announcement should be read as a branding exercise to package a set of deeper ties across certain sectors that Canadians seek, as there is no legal basis in the treaties for such membership status, argued two centrist MEPs and one Parliament official.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola’s office put out a statement following a meeting with Carney that, tellingly, avoided mentioning the topic at all, saying the two leaders talked about “areas with big potential for even closer cooperation,” from critical raw minerals to defense.
Advertisement
The Commission's spokesperson's service did not immediately respond to request for comment.
Ottawa hits the brakes — ish
The response from Canada was hardly an unequivocal embrace.
Carney’s office welcomed Brussels’ broader push to deepen ties, saying after von der Leyen's speech that Canada wanted to strengthen its relationship with the EU and move beyond the existing free-trade relationship to a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance.”
But Ottawa has been careful, at least publicly, to distinguish that ambition from any form of EU membership. Carney himself said last week he wanted a “unique” partnership with Brussels but shied away from using the words associate membership.
Even if Canada eventually warms to the idea, there is a much bigger question: What would associate membership actually mean?
It’s not hard to imagine what quasi-membership could entail, based on privileges extended to other non-members.
Advertisement
Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein all participate in the EU’s single market via the European Economic Area and are in the Schengen passport-free zone, despite not being part of the EU. Moldovans and Ukrainians can make calls and send texts in the EU without additional charges thanks to the bloc’s “roam like at home” program.
Without treaty change, “what one could rather imagine is looking in the direction of the EEA,” Repasi said, calling it “essentially an associate form of membership.”
But the EEA model comes with its own complications. EEA countries are deeply integrated into the EU's regulatory system while having no vote when EU legislation is passed.
Associate membership wouldn’t simply be about rebranding the EU's existing relationship with Canada or a euphemistic catch-all for a closer relationship, but creating a new category of partners for enhanced free trade and cooperation on areas including defense, AI and high-tech science, according to an EU official with knowledge of talks.
There would be no political rights or free movement, at least for now. Canada would be the first, but potentially not the only, country in the club: Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Japan have all been mentioned as possible future members, the official added.
But a fifth diplomat was skeptical about what the result of such an arrangement would be and how it would materially differ from the close partnerships the EU already has with its allies.
Advertisement
A different diplomat pointed out that 10 EU countries have not yet even ratified the bloc's free trade agreement with Canada, CETA, which was signed almost a decade ago, while three have yet to approve the Strategic Partnership Agreement. A more daring pact would likely require the political enthusiasm of EU governments.
Germany also struck a cautious tone at a press conference on Wednesday.
“Canada is an especially close partner for Europe. That is why we are open to discussing new models of partnership,” government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said. But on the “associate member” label, he added: “I think we should give that some more thought.”
Camille Gijs contributed reporting from Brussels. Zoya Sheftalovich contributed reporting from Strasbourg. Oliver Noyan contributed reporting from Berlin.

One of Ukraine's key industries almost disappears from GDP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:30:00 EEST
02:30:00 KST

One of Ukraine's key industries almost disappears from GDP
Before Russia's full-scale invasion, the metals industry accounted for up to 7% of Ukraine's GDP. Metinvest, an international mining and steel group headquartered in Ukraine, now estimates its contribution may be close to zero.
Source: Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko in an interview with Forbes Ukraine
Quote from Myronenko: "The metals industry as a whole used to account for up to 7% of Ukraine's GDP. Now it may be close to zero. Those are the losses."
Details: He said that, of the group's mining assets in Ukraine, only the Central and Northern mining and processing plants are currently operating, though at about 50% of capacity. They produce iron ore pellets and concentrate for export to the EU.
The Southern mining and processing plant is idle because seaports are effectively closed. The Inhulets plant has been shut since 2024 because of high electricity prices.
At Zaporizhstal (Zaporizhzhia Steelworks), Russian strikes have effectively broken the production chain. Myronenko estimated that restoring the damaged equipment would cost tens of millions of hryvnias.
For reference: Ukraine's mining and metals sector has traditionally been one of the country's largest industries. GMK Center, a consulting company focused on the European iron and steel market, estimates that it accounted for 10.3% of Ukraine's GDP in 2021 and 5.5% in 2025. Last year, mining and metals products also accounted for 15.2% of Ukraine's total goods exports, worth US$6.2 billion.
Background:
- Following a Russian ballistic missile strike on 11 August, Zaporizhstal completely halted operations. In late August, Metinvest said it is not yet possible to determine when the plant could resume operations.
- Ukraine's steel production halved in August. In September, Zaporizhstal was hit by four ballistic missiles, with the damage described as critical.

Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election has no meaningful competition. Independent observers still plan to document how paper and online results diverge.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:28:43 UTC
02:28:43 KST

Russia’s 2026 parliamentary election has no meaningful competition. Independent observers still plan to document how paper and online results diverge.
In the summer of 2026, Yabloko — the only party representing Russia’s anti-establishment opposition and one that had campaigned against the war — was barred from the State Duma elections. Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts also faced obstacles, and the authorities managed to remove some from the race. There is no longer any meaningful political competition in the upcoming vote, especially because Moscow and dozens of other regions use remote electronic voting, which the authorities have used in previous years to rig the results. Even so, independent observers still plan to monitor the elections. The Kremlin has spent years making it harder for them to enter polling stations, but they can still do so. Meduza asked one observer why it is worth monitoring an election whose outcome has already been decided.
Why is our source anonymous?
Russian authorities may treat a comment or interview published by Meduza as participation in the activities of an “undesirable” organization. A first “offense” can result in a fine of 5,000 to 15,000 rubles. Another “offense” within a year may lead to criminal prosecution and up to four years in prison. We trust our source completely and have no doubts about his expertise.
— Why did you decide to become an election observer?
— I’ve been monitoring elections in Moscow for more than 10 years. I’ve seen every change in election law unfold firsthand.
In the early 2010s, there was a huge surge in election monitoring and grassroots civic activity in general. Some people I knew invited me to join. Even then, like many people, I didn’t like what was happening in the country. I wanted to change something.
The person who invited me stopped doing this a long time ago, but I’m still at it.
— It seems that many longtime observers have burned out and that election monitoring is no longer as popular as it once was. Is that true?
— Some people really do burn out because you’re very rarely able to get a result overturned — to challenge fraud, that is — even at your own polling station.
Then, once the online votes are counted, the winners aren’t the candidates who came out ahead in the precinct election commission’s final tally but completely different ones. When people see all this, many decide that monitoring is pointless and leave.
On top of that, a great many people left the country in 2022 out of concern for their safety. Others simply got tired.
— Why do you keep monitoring elections? There’s essentially no political competition in this election, and the authorities are using remote electronic voting…
— First, we never know what might suddenly make a difference or when. Suppose Yabloko had not been removed from the race for some reason. That would have been a huge incentive to try to protect Yabloko’s vote count. Not all polls can be trusted, but even those we saw suggested that Yabloko would have made a significant showing.
In any event, by being present at polling stations, we keep the machinery of fraud from expanding. The process is still cleaner with oversight than without it. If we aren’t there, absolute madness will unfold at polling stations. Our presence at least helps keep it in check.
In some local elections in regions without remote electronic voting, there is a very good chance that observers at polling stations will be able to protect votes cast for anti-war candidates.
Moscow, where I work as an observer, is a different matter. Remote electronic voting will be used in these State Duma elections and will most likely upend the results. But even in Moscow, some Yabloko candidates remain in the race [candidates in single-member districts]. And even if online voting reverses the results, we’ll be able to see a huge gap between the paper ballots counted at polling stations and the online vote. That will be revealing, too. It will show people that remote electronic voting clearly distorted the results and misrepresented how they voted.
— So you no longer see your role as forcing the authorities to overturn potentially fraudulent results, but rather as documenting the fraud?
— Sometimes we do manage to get the results overturned. There were cases like that in Moscow during the last parliamentary elections, in 2021. But ultimately, remote electronic voting decided everything there, too.
— How have you managed to avoid burning out over more than 10 years?
— That’s a very difficult question. Maybe it has something to do with my personality.
— The authorities do not welcome independent election monitoring. The clearest example is Grigory Melkonyants’s sentence. How do you assess the risks you face?
— To some extent, anyone in Russia faces risks right now. I don’t think mine are any greater than anyone else’s. I can recall only one case, in 2017, when a member of an election commission faced persecution for his work.
The system is still trying to preserve the appearance of legality, and I can’t recall any cases brought against observers specifically for their work.
Some neighborhood activists even deliberately seek appointments to election commissions in their districts. They do this not only to protect election results but also because the federal law “On Basic Guarantees of Electoral Rights and the Right of Citizens of the Russian Federation to Participate in a Referendum” still says that a court may impose administrative penalties on an election commission member only with the approval of the regional prosecutor. So to some extent, the position actually offers protection.
— How is independent monitoring at polling stations organized these days?
— Political parties and candidates appoint observers. We’re still able to reach agreements with parties represented in parliament, including A Just Russia and the Communist Party. I’ve heard that in some parts of Moscow, even the Liberal Democratic Party does this. It all depends on the local party organization.
We can also have candidates appoint observers [candidates running in single-member districts]. If a Yabloko candidate is running, the easiest thing is to have that candidate appoint the observers. If there is no Yabloko candidate, we have to negotiate with the parliamentary parties.
— Why are the parliamentary parties themselves interested in this?
— Some of them still retain a little independence at the grassroots level. Every State Duma deputy votes as instructed. But in some districts where parties have municipal deputies, they have to work with the public. Regional branches are still willing to make small compromises.
And some parties may still hope they can come to power someday. Parties also have an interest in preventing fraud because the more votes they receive, the more government funding they get. That’s where our interests overlap.
Sometimes observers are dropped when the list is handed over to the party, so only some of them ultimately make it into polling stations. But that’s still better than nothing.
Overall, the authorities have severely curtailed independent election monitoring. For some time now, only someone eligible to vote in the same election has been allowed to serve as an observer. In Moscow City Duma elections, for example, only a Moscow resident can serve, while in municipal elections, observers must even come from the same Moscow district. This has made it much harder to recruit observers for local elections.
— These days, polling stations may also have representatives from pro-government organizations that only purport to monitor elections — the autonomous nonprofit Dialog, for example. Have you encountered them?
— At polling stations, you’re most likely to encounter observers from the Civic Chamber. They try to cover almost every polling station, and they’re a total crapshoot.
Sometimes a relative of the precinct commission chair arrives as the Civic Chamber observer. Other times, someone shows up who immediately starts acting like an observer rather than a bystander and genuinely helps the independent observers.
I don’t really understand how the Civic Chamber selects them, but because there are so many, you do occasionally find honest people among its “observers.” Unfortunately, that’s rare. More often, they turn a blind eye to fraud. Obviously, a relative of the commission chair will side with the commission, not the law.
— What else should people know about voting this year?
— Ever since the COVID era, voting has taken place over three days. It’s best to vote on the last day, Sunday, because the ballots are placed in sealed storage bags between voting days. After the last election, there were reports that these bags had been opened at night and the ballots inside replaced — despite the observers’ best efforts.
So it’s best to come on the third day. Unfortunately, a number of regions use remote electronic voting, which is best avoided. It’s better to go to a polling station and vote on paper. Ideally, you should cast a paper ballot at the polling station where you’re registered on the third day. You’ll receive two ballots there: one for a candidate in your single-member district and one for a party.
But if that isn’t possible — if voters are abroad, for example — then remote electronic voting is acceptable. It is being used in 33 regions this time.
— Is there no way to reverse the effects of fraud in remote electronic voting?
— I have no idea how it could be done. During the last State Duma elections, candidates filed complaints in court — but we know how the courts work. So unfortunately, nothing can be done for now.
In theory, if an enormous number of people suddenly came to polling stations and voted on paper, the prearranged, manipulated online results might not outweigh the paper-ballot vote. I don’t rule out that possibility. But is that likely to happen in this particular election? Probably not.
Still, we know in advance how many voters there are at each polling station, and that number cannot change dramatically during the election. If, after the paper and online results are combined, we see an anomalous increase in the number of voters, that will be the clearest possible sign that a huge number of fraudulent votes were added to the online tally.
— Who is signing up as an independent observer these days?
— Mostly neighborhood activists and young people. I’m speaking only from what I see in my own district. I can’t say what it’s like elsewhere. After all, 2022 dealt an enormous blow to the civic movement. As I said, a great many people left the country.
The influx of young people doesn’t make up for the losses in the election-monitoring movement. Overall interest is declining. Few people stay involved year after year.
— But you still find it meaningful?
— I’ll quote a good song: “In my city, the hardest job is loving someone, but somebody has to do it.” In other words, if we aren’t there, no one will ever know what happens at the polling stations.
No one will ever know what the country’s citizens really think. This is a very subtle point. I very much want the government in this country to change, but I really don’t want anyone to die. I don’t want a bloody regime change. Elections are the only realistic way for power to change hands without bloodshed. And if a window of opportunity ever opens when we can actually make a difference, it will have been worth all the time we had to spend waiting.
In any case, even now, we make things difficult for the authorities at polling stations. I believe it is right to make things difficult for the system of government that has emerged in our country.
Finally, if we all live to see the government truly change someday, elections will still have to be held. You might say we’re keeping the knowledge of how to conduct fair elections from being lost.
Here’s an example that comes to mind: Scientists today are trying to understand how the Egyptian pyramids were built. We shouldn’t let things reach a point where people in the future have to figure out how to hold elections. There should be people who know and remember how to conduct them and what to do to ensure they are fair. The more people like that there are, the easier things will be in the future.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
