US pays $725 million to UN, easing its debt dispute with the world body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:28:01 UTC
02:28:01 KST

US pays $926 million to UN, easing its debt dispute with the world body
- The US paid US$725 million to the UN, reducing its debt and securing its voting rights at the upcoming General Assembly.
- The Trump administration criticised the UN and cut funding, demanding reforms before releasing payments.
- The UN is undergoing reforms and cost-cutting amid financial challenges, with China also making significant contributions recently.
AI generated
UNITED NATIONS - The Trump administration paid US$725 million (S$926 million) to the United Nations (UN), the organisation said on Sept 16, reducing Washington’s large debt and ensuring it keeps its vote at the UN General Assembly convening in New York next week.
US President Donald Trump has criticised the global body for not living up to its potential and slashed funding to many UN agencies. When asked about the planned payment in August, a US official said any payments will be contingent on continued reforms of the UN.
“We received US$725 million yesterday from the United States for the UN regular budget, and we also received US$102 million from the US for peacekeeping on Friday,” said UN spokesperson Farhan Haq.
“The US still owes US$1.312 billion to the regular budget,” he said, adding that, “with these payments, the US is no longer in jeopardy of falling under Article 19 for 2027”.
Under Article 19 of the UN Charter, a member state loses its voting rights in the General Assembly if its arrears exceed two years in annual fees, although grace periods are possible.
The Trump administration has carried out an unprecedented shrinking of its federal government, saying it was bloated and has significantly cut back on domestic and foreign grants in an effort that it says was to put money into causes that aligned with US taxpayer interests.
The US is the biggest contributor to the UN budget, but under the Trump administration it has slow-walked mandatory payments to regular and peacekeeping budgets, and has slashed voluntary funding to UN agencies with their own budgets.
The second-biggest contributor, China, also paid US$641.4 million on Sept 1 in its regular budget contributions, according to the UN website.
The UN has been undergoing a reform and cost-cutting exercise known as “UN80” amid its financial crisis. REUTERS

Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:17:49 UTC
02:17:49 KST

Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted?
Because wealthy nations do not want to take responsibility for their role in the current climate crisis.
It has been three weeks since the collapse of a glacier and rock mass from the Langtang Lirung mountain triggered devastating floods in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys. Officials have confirmed the loss of more than 1,380 precious lives, while around 5,100 remain missing. The disaster shattered thousands of homes and wiped out vital infrastructure.
Nepal government’s rapid assessment estimates that full recovery and long-term reconstruction will need $4.7bn. That is roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s annual gross domestic product (GDP), and more than a third of its federal budget.
And yet, despite considerable media and public attention, the international political response has remained strikingly muted.
We have heard some condolence messages from foreign governments, along with emergency supplies and pledges of help. These matter. But the response mainly targeted immediate humanitarian aid. For instance, the United States pledged $3.6m, the United Kingdom $6m, and the European Union $2.3m. But these meagre funds cannot meet the needs of affected communities and provide them with the shelter, food and infrastructure to survive the winter.
Why has the response been so inadequate? Why have so few political leaders spoken up about this disaster with the urgency its scale demands?
Part of the answer may lie in an uncomfortable question Nepal has now put directly on the table: who should pay for climate loss and damage?
Nepal is increasingly framing the floods not simply as another weather-induced catastrophe, but as a consequence of a climate crisis to which the country contributed almost nothing.
This points to a deeper inequality of climate crisis.
For over a century, wealthy countries have consumed a vastly disproportionate share of the atmosphere’s capacity to absorb carbon dioxide. They grew their economies through industrialisation driven by fossil fuel consumption. Meanwhile, countries like Nepal got little chance to use anything approaching an equivalent share of that atmospheric space.
The result shows a stark divide between those who benefitted disproportionately from burning fossil fuels and those who face growing consequences.
Nepal has argued that international support to deal with climate catastrophe is not a charity. It must be climate justice. It has asked the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for urgent support, and the fund’s board is now considering how to respond.
That changes the political conversation. And it takes us back to the bargain struck in Paris a decade ago.
Developing countries fought hard for the international climate regime under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change to recognise “loss and damage” or the destruction that cannot simply be prevented through mitigation or adapted to. They secured its recognition in Article 8 of the Paris Agreement.
But wealthy countries drew a line around what that recognition could mean. The decision text adopted alongside the Paris Agreement states that Article 8 “does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation”.
It was a strange political bargain: the world could acknowledge climate-related loss and damage, but that acknowledgement could not lead to demands for compensation.
Nepal is now testing the limits of that bargain.
The legal picture is more complicated than simply saying that the Paris Agreement prohibits climate compensation. In 2025, the International Court of Justice ruled that countries have a legal obligation to protect the climate system; if they fail their obligations, they are liable for reparations or compensation for the damage they have caused. The decision sparked renewed attention to the questions around state responsibility under international law.
In the case of Nepal and other developing countries disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, the state does not need to prove that one particular country caused a specific flood before the international community can recognise a responsibility to address the consequences of climate change.
But there is another issue: the traditional international system for supporting developing countries is itself shrinking. At precisely the time climate losses are mounting, official development assistance is falling. It plummeted by 23.1 percent in 2025, the largest annual contraction on record. Humanitarian assistance also fell sharply.
And the problem is not simply that there is too little aid.
For decades, the global economy has transferred enormous amounts of wealth and resources through unequal economic ties between the Global North and the Global South. Climate finance won’t fix that imbalance if it simply returns a fraction of that wealth as loans or private investment options.
A country should not have to borrow its way out of a climate disaster it did little to create.
Nor can compensation substitute for mitigation. Wealthy countries cannot keep consuming a disproportionate share of the world’s energy and material resources while ignoring the consequences elsewhere. They must rapidly reduce their own emissions and ecological overconsumption.
The muted response to the floods in Nepal therefore raises a larger question about international cooperation.
Perhaps the world is comfortable acknowledging the growing cost of the climate crisis. It is much less comfortable when countries affected ask whether the costs should be borne by those who contributed most to creating the crisis.
The avenues for changing this already exist: the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, the UN climate negotiations, and the evolving body of international law on climate responsibility.
What is missing is the political recognition that the costs of climate destruction cannot indefinitely be treated as somebody else’s problem.
If climate justice means anything, it must eventually include reparations for the damage caused by an unequal appropriation of the atmospheric commons.
That conversation can no longer be postponed.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

How Israeli commandos hunted Hezbollah underground for 3 months before blowing up Ali Taher Ridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:15:40 UTC
02:15:40 KST

Three months of exhausting ambushes, close-range fighting and underground warfare on southern Lebanon’s Ali Taher Ridge culminated last Thursday night when Israeli commandos and combat engineers blew up what the IDF described as a major strategic Hezbollah underground complex.
Commanders from Maglan, the IDF commando unit specializing in operations deep behind enemy lines, and Yahalom, its elite combat engineering unit, told ynet how their troops gradually tightened control over the ridge, forced Hezbollah terrorists out of underground positions and destroyed the network just before the Rosh Hashanah holiday.
“Soldiers slept outside in the brush, spending hours in ambushes, in the cold and the heat, to hunt the terrorists,” said Lt. Col. R., commander of Maglan.
The operation followed months of fighting north of the Litani River, including at Beaufort Ridge, before Israeli forces moved toward Ali Taher.
“We reached the ridge about three months ago,” R. said. “The unit captured the village of Mazraat Ali Taher together with Egoz, and then we began taking control of the ridge. We engaged Hezbollah terrorists, began moving into the ridge through ambushes and movement in the brush, built an intelligence picture and started to ‘choke’ the area.”
Lt. Col. D., commander of a Yahalom company, said the mission was part of a series of operations known as “Merom Harim.”
“First at Beaufort Ridge, we found many strategic underground routes intended to defend the ridge, prevent the IDF from crossing the Litani and provide Hezbollah with command and control,” he said. “When we arrived at Ali Taher Ridge about three months ago, our mission was to locate, investigate and destroy the infrastructure. It was an extremely complex mission, the most complex I have carried out in my military service and probably the most significant.”
Fighting through brush, boulders and explosive drones
The terrain made the operation particularly difficult.
“It was very hard to reach the mountain and work there,” D. said, describing thick vegetation, boulders and the distance from other Israeli forces. “We were in terrain that was not operationally held, about a kilometer and a half from where the troops were positioned.”
The topography complicated casualty evacuation and logistics, he said, while dozens of Hezbollah terrorists operated in the area and repeatedly targeted Israeli troops with drones and indirect fire.
The early fighting was costly.
During the battle for the village, Sgt. First Class Nir Ben Ari was killed by a rocket and several other soldiers were wounded.
“I will never forget one moment,” R. said. “The incident in the village was very difficult, and you saw everyone moving forward, soldiers running into the fire to save their friends.”
One badly wounded soldier survived because of the actions of those around him, R. said.
“The doctor at the hospital told me he was one of the most seriously wounded soldiers of the war. Today he is rehabilitating. That is the fighting spirit. The next day after that incident, they got up and continued the operation to capture the same village.”
Cameras in the brush and weapons underground
As Israeli forces advanced, they began discovering the scale of Hezbollah’s preparations on the ridge.
“We put together the intelligence picture on the ground and realized there was a fortified site that had been prepared for a very long time, a strategic asset,” R. said.
Troops found terrorists inside infrastructure, surveillance cameras, booby traps, explosive devices, rocket launchers, Grad rockets, drones and unmanned aircraft, he said.
“Suddenly we found cameras inside the brush. Some were closed-circuit cameras and some were intelligence-gathering cameras,” R. said. “Only when you move through the brush do you discover them and understand there is an enemy there.”
The Israeli troops settled into a routine of prolonged concealed ambushes.
“Every soldier would prepare for an ambush lasting several days, move covertly, reach the position, remain there hidden with special equipment and wait patiently,” he said.
Food and cigarettes delivered by drone
The biggest challenge was figuring out Hezbollah’s underground system.
“We faced a puzzle: How do you crack Ali Taher Ridge and the underground infrastructure beneath it?” D. said.
The IDF brought specialists from across the military and formed teams to devise methods to force Hezbollah terrorists out of the tunnels, according to the officer.
Israeli forces cut off supplies being delivered by drones and conducted foot searches for shafts, using clues such as metal beneath rocks, openings in the ground and weapons positioned near suspected exits.
Two underground routes were discovered at roughly the same time, D. said. One was penetrated after about a month and the second after roughly six weeks.
The long ambushes eventually led to close-range encounters.
“When you push deeper into the ridge, you see the enemy starting to shrink back,” R. said. “One day we took down a camera, and then you see terrorists fleeing and others trying to stick their heads out of shafts.”
Israeli soldiers also saw Hezbollah trying to resupply those underground.
“You see a drone above you and then a package drops,” R. said. “You open it and find food and cigarettes.”
He said troops encountered two kinds of Hezbollah fighters.
“One type came from outside and tried to help those underground. They came in uniforms with weapons and combat vests, and some tried to disguise themselves with blankets or camouflage suits. It was very professional equipment.”
During the operation, he said, dozens of Hezbollah terrorists were killed either by drones or in close-range fighting.
“The second type was the enemy fleeing from underground wearing civilian clothes and carrying Kalashnikov rifles,” R. said. “We applied tremendous pressure. Either the enemy abandoned the area or we killed them.”
Forcing Hezbollah out of the tunnels
Yahalom troops used a series of classified measures aimed at making it increasingly difficult for Hezbollah terrorists to remain underground, D. said.
“Once we had a precise grip on the area and a full picture of who was inside, we carried out various classified actions that ultimately caused the enemy to leave the underground infrastructure,” he said.
“We carried out actions that disturbed them and made them uncomfortable, to the point where it became almost impossible to remain on those levels. We brought them above ground in order to eliminate them.”
The troops also used loudspeakers and attempted negotiations with those inside, he said.
Once inside the tunnels, the soldiers found what commanders described as an unusually sophisticated complex stretching for several kilometers.
“There were operating rooms and medical equipment, command rooms and operations centers, as well as toilets, ventilation systems and kitchenettes,” R. said. “There was important intelligence material and weaponry, and above all we saw that they had really planned for these moments of war, so they could attack and command from there.”
He said the underground command infrastructure had been intended to support Hezbollah forces targeting northern Israeli communities and Israeli troops crossing the Litani.
D. said the operating rooms were among the most striking discoveries.
“It wasn’t a clinic,” he said. “It was a room with surgical equipment, medications, anesthetics and beds, something I had not seen elsewhere.”
‘An incredible generation’
The officers said maintaining the operation for months required soldiers to remain in harsh field conditions for prolonged periods.
“The morale in the unit is among the most exceptional I have ever encountered,” D. said. “The soldiers of the company did not go home for three months. They didn’t wash their faces and didn’t eat like normal people. They slept outside in the brush, in the cold and the heat, for hours during long ambushes.”
“They did what was needed to complete the mission because they understood its importance. They did not complain.”
R. said the campaign had tested the unit after commanders were wounded and Ben Ari was killed.
“We have an incredible generation,” he said. “Soldiers and commanders were wounded, returned and were wounded again during this round.”
He said Maglan’s approach was built around finding ways to outmaneuver the enemy through concealment, patience and sustained pressure.
“That is the spirit of Maglan, how do I get around the enemy,” he said. “That is what allowed us to move forward, camouflage ourselves and find the enemy through very long, painstaking work.”
‘We’re not leaving until we blow it up’
The operation reached its climax with the destruction of the underground infrastructure just before the holiday.
Ahead of the demolition, R. took the soldiers to Beaufort, where they could see northern Israeli communities from the commanding heights.
“You see everything from there,” he said. “You see the communities in the north, and you don’t need much explanation about what that commanding position means.”
The soldiers were told the demolition might take place before or after the holiday.
“They said, ‘Rosh Hashanah or no Rosh Hashanah, we don’t care about being home for the holiday. We are not leaving here until we blow it up,’” R. recalled.
“In the end we made it and got out right at the buzzer. It was a battle that will be etched into the history of the unit.”

No matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go further | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:15:37 UTC
02:15:37 KST

Some things you can set your watch by. Like every time small boats are in the news, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, will manoeuvre himself in front of a camera to suggest that all male migrants are either murderers or rapists. Probably both.
But some things feel older than time itself. Like Liz Truss trying to persuade the world she was right all along. Most former prime ministers leave Downing Street relatively quietly. Lord Big Dave, the Maybot and even Boris nurse their grudges in private. Rishi lives in semi-retirement – almost a recluse – and only attends parliament when it suits him. Keir has been almost totally airbrushed out of history in a couple of months.
Liz, though, is the outlier. She refuses to give up. The last cockroach alive after a nuclear apocalypse. Even now, she probably has a platoon of nuns locked up in her basement in south-east London where they are being forced to embroider a 70-metre tapestry dedicated to a revisionist history of her 49 days in office. One in which an old monarch dies and a new king ascends the throne. As one Elizabethan era ends so another Elizabethan era begins and a grateful nation bows down to her genius.
You have to wonder if this obsession is healthy. Most normal people might be slightly embarrassed to be remembered as the UK’s shortest serving prime minister. And by far and away the dimmest in living memory. But Truss seems devoid of affect. No sense of shame. If anything she seems proud of her 49 days. That long! In Liz’s mind, she was simply too good for us. We weren’t ready for her. Give it a thousand years and her tapestry will be on show in the British Museum.
One thing you can guarantee: offer Liz a platform to speak and she will bite your hand off. No matter how deranged and delusional it may be, Liz is confident she can be yet more deranged and delusional. She is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. Not only is she guaranteed to say yes, she will also make everyone else seem almost normal. Win-win. She’s done all sorts of weird stuff in the US, and in the UK she has her own podcast where she pretends to be interested in someone other than herself on Mike Graham’s YouTube channel. Graham, you might remember, is the man who thinks you can grow concrete. And Liz is sure he’s right.
The new kid on the podcast block is the former Tory Brexiter Steve Baker. So who else would he get as his first guest than the Trusster. If anything, Steve has got even more weird in the two years since he lost his seat. These days he has the look of a far-right survivalist holed up in a hut somewhere in the Montana wilderness. And his podcast surroundings have the same feel. All very basic, just a table and chairs. The table probably has a cache of semi-automatic rifles underneath it. Every so often, Steve will interrupt the recording to do an ad for gold. He no longer trusts traditional currencies.
And up steps Liz. Doing what only someone as half-witted as she can: talking non-stop nonsense. Often with a weird half-smile on her face. At times you are tempted to believe that she is in on the joke that she is the joke. But then you realise she’s deadly serious. She hasn’t quite understood that people aren’t laughing with her, they are laughing at her. There’s something almost unbearably sad about this. So much so you almost feel guilty for indulging her insanity. Then you remember that only 2,000 people are going to watch this. And only we dedicated few are going to make it to the end.
Labour has ruined the country, she says. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown had a secret plot to dismantle British civilisation and nothing has been the same since 1997. At which point, even Steve has to remind Liz that the Tories were in power from 2010. The Trusster doesn’t miss a beat. She is rushing on her run, her onboard computer set to auto-pilot. The Tories weren’t really the Tories. They were socialists in disguise. All of them. They were all part of the woke establishment. That’s why they were anti-Brexit. And austerity never happened.
At this point it would have been a kindness to wrap the podcast up. To remind Liz that antipsychotic help was available. Because to the best of my knowledge, Liz had been a minister in successive Tory governments since 2012. She had also been a vocal supporter of Remain.
Only it turns out that was a different Liz. A doppelganger. She had been temporarily captured by the wokerati and made to do and say a lot of things against her will. It was only when she became prime minister that she could self-actualise into her truest state and then she was thwarted by the Bank of England getting tough on quantitative easing. All a deliberate plot to destabilise her mini-budget. Nothing to do with the mini-budget being riddled with unfunded tax cuts.
There were only two trustworthy people left in the world, she said: Donald Trump and Javier Milei. It was time to disband the judiciary, the prisons and the civil service. The whole world order needed to be rebalanced. Steve readily agreed. He reckoned the NHS should also be included on the grounds that it had almost killed him and a friend of his. Not even Liz was going that far. But together the revolution was possible.
Then the big question. What next for Liz? Would she stand for election again? Maybe, she said. But who for? She’s long since been too mad for the Tories and might even be too bonkers for Reform. All she knew was that she would never go away. Not while there were still things to talk about that no one was talking about except her. Poor Liz. The problem isn’t that no one is talking. It’s that no one is listening. Steve chucked her a nugget of gold and they both ran for the hills. You’ll never take them alive.

EU to ban social media for under 13s, curb access until 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:15:15 UTC

EU to ban social media for under 13s, curb access until 15
STRASBOURG, France - The European Union will ban social media for children under 13 and allow only limited, supervised access until the age of 15 under plans unveiled on Sept 16 by EU chief Ursula von der Leyen.
A global backlash against social media has piled pressure on policymakers, with a rising body of evidence showing negative impacts on children’s physical and mental health.
“It is time for Europe to act,” von der Leyen said during her annual keynote address to the European Parliament. “It is we who decide our rules, not big tech,” she warned.
Australia in 2025 became the first country to ban social media for under-16s, triggering similar moves elsewhere, but the European Commission chief said the 27-country bloc would take a more “gradual” approach.
“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she said. “That means from 13 to under 15, only mini accounts, set up and supervised by parents or guardians, with limited features and time restriction to one hour a day.”
“And between 15 and 18, safe design will be an obligation for the platforms.”
Before outlining the EU’s approach, von der Leyen paid tribute to a 14-year-old girl in Belgium, named Olea, who killed herself one month ago after being bullied, and whose mother she quoted as saying: “I am convinced that without these omnipresent networks, my daughter would still be here.”
Von der Leyen made no reference to online games or AI chatbots, which according to draft legislation seen by AFP would also be hit by the restrictions.
The commission president and tech chief Henna Virkkunen will formally present the proposed “KIDS Act”, including the tiered age limits in Strasbourg, France on Sept 17.
Children’s rights and parents groups welcomed moves to make online platforms safer.
“The devil is of course in the detail. Tomorrow’s proposal must be coherent, comprehensive, future-proof and robustly enforceable,” the 5Rights Foundation advocacy group’s Leanda Barrington-Leach said.
“Finally, Europe is sending a clear signal: it’s time to act against the harmful design of platforms to protect our children from toxic algorithms and features,” said Arnaud Ducoin, part of a group of French families who have filed a complaint against TikTok over teenagers’ self-harm and suicides.
‘Arbitrary age threshold’
The new EU law will also ban addictive design features such as so-called infinite scrolling where children are concerned, according to a draft document.
If platforms break the rules, they face fines of up to six per cent of annual turnover, draft details show.
“We do not have to accept addictive features,” von der Leyen warned, saying “platforms will have to prove that they are safe”.
The “risk” is not limited to children, she noted. “Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone,” she said, telling EU lawmakers that Europe needed more rules that will be proposed in the autumn.
Simeon de Brouwer of digital rights group EDRi said making platforms safer across the board was an urgent necessity, telling AFP “if the design is harmful at 13, it does not magically become safe on their 15th or 18th birthday”.
Pressure from EU states
Von der Leyen had faced pressure from members including France, Denmark and Greece for action across the 27-nation bloc to limit online harms for children.
France, which has proposed its own legislation, welcomed the announcement. Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said it was “a step in the right direction”.
The EU has sought for years to rein in Big Tech, empowering itself with a strengthened legal armoury, but it believes additional tools are needed to limit online harms.
The bloc has already told Meta platforms Facebook and Instagram as well as TikTok to change their “addictive” design through its content law known as the Digital Services Act, but changes have taken longer than Brussels wants.
Digital and consumer rights groups have meanwhile raised concerns over a related age-check app due to be rolled out later this year which Brussels says will keep children off social media.
“Age verification is not a silver bullet and would raise serious privacy and data protection concerns,” said European consumer organisation BEUC’s Agustin Reyna.
The proposal on Sept 17 will only become law after negotiations between EU capitals and the European Parliament, which could take months. AFP

Houthis claim shootdown of Saudi jet (VIDEO)
Yemen’s Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet, releasing a video of the burning wreckage of the warplane. If verified, the video is the first ever evidence of a Saudi jet downed by Houthi air defenses.
In a video statement, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that the jet was shot down over Yemen’s Marib Governorate using “a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile.” Saree then claimed that Houthi fighters successfully repelled two waves of Saudi F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoon jets that were scrambled to search for the wreckage.
Saree did not say when the incident took place, and the Saudi military has not yet confirmed the loss of the jet.
Video footage released by the Houthis showed a missile crew locking on to the jet and opening fire. A missile could then be seen impacting the jet, which plunged to the ground in a fireball. It is unclear whether the pilot managed to eject from the burning airplane.
Footage from the crash site showed Houthi fighters lifting the tail of the aircraft, which bore the Saudi flag. The militants posed in front of the tail section chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
Before Wednesday, the Houthis, also known as the Ansar Allah movement, claimed to have shot down three Saudi fighters, one in 2017 and two in 2018. The group also claimed to have damaged – but not downed – a Saudi jet in 2018. Riyadh denied ever losing a warplane to Houthi fire, and without clear video evidence, these previous claims were impossible to verify.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Violence between the Saudis and Houthis erupted again this July, when the Saudi-backed government in Aden struck an airport in Houthi-controlled Sana’a. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen. Last week, Houthi forces swept across Yemen’s western coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and solidifying their control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
The Houthi offensive threatens Saudi Arabia’s vital oil exports. The Kingdom recently shifted its exports from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the West, as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut due to the US war on Iran. With the Houthis in control of the west, Saudi exports are now threatened from both sides.
According to Saree, Houthi forces also struck a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait and Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu with drones and ballistic missiles on Wednesday.

Belarus has set up checkpoints with anti-drone nets at entrances to Gomel, including on roads leading toward Ukraine.
The Belarusian publication Flagstock reported this.
The checkpoints include concrete blocks, sandbags, structures fitted with anti-drone nets and road signs requiring drivers to reduce their speed.
Their installation coincided with large-scale training exercises involving territorial defense forces in the Gomel region.
One of the checkpoints was set up at the entrance to Gomel from Chernihiv, on the M-10 highway toward the settlement of Novobilichi. Another appeared on Korenovskoye Shosse, a road leading toward Zyabrovka.
The work began in early September. Concrete foundation blocks and sandbags were delivered to the sites.
Later, structures with anti-drone nets began to be mounted on poles, while road signs requiring drivers to reduce speed were installed along the road.
Flagstock drew attention to a photograph published by the Gomel territorial defense Telegram channel. It shows participants in the current military training exercises posing near one of the checkpoints equipped with an anti-drone net.
Based on local landmarks, the journalists determined that the photograph was taken on the M-10 highway opposite the Chabarok restaurant. This made it possible to link the construction of the checkpoints with the territorial defense exercises currently taking place in the region.
The checkpoints are likely part of practical exercises by Belarusian territorial defense forces rather than newly established permanent checkpoints.
Scheduled training for reservists in the territorial defense forces is taking place from Sept. 1 to 25 in Gomel, Svetlogorsk and Oktyabrsky districts of the Gomel region. The Gomel region borders Ukraine, while the M-10 highway, where one of the checkpoints was installed, leads to Gomel from the south.
Military infrastructure in the region is also continuing to expand in 2026. Recently, Belarus began construction of a railway serving military facilities near the borders of Ukraine’s Kyiv and Chernihiv regions.

South Africa slams planned US visa curbs over alleged racial discrimination
Trump administration falling for misinformation from ‘fringe groups’ alleging discrimination against white Afrikaners.
South Africa has called the United States’s plans to impose sanctions on individuals there for alleged discrimination against white Afrikaners a result of “mischaracterisations” being promoted by “fringe groups”.
“We remain committed to addressing these challenges through our constitutional institutions, democratic processes and the rule of law, with the objective of building a more equal and inclusive society for all South Africans,” South African Minister for International Relations and Cooperation Ronald Lamola said in a statement on Wednesday.

Lamola was responding to an announcement made on Tuesday by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Washington would be enacting a new policy aimed at South Africans involved in what he called “race-based” discrimination against white Afrikaners.
Rubio said the US would restrict visas for individuals “responsible for, or complicit in the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa”.
Afrikaners are a minority in South Africa that descends from mostly Dutch colonial settlers, who formalised a system of apartheid in the country that saw land and resources seized from the majority Black population, who were largely relegated to live in enclaves called “Bantustans”.
The apartheid system persisted until 1994, when the country’s first democratic elections brought Black Africans into power.
A 2017 South African government report found that whites, who make up about 7 percent of the population, owned disproportionately large amounts of land, including 72 percent of the individually owned farmland.
South Africa has undertaken programmes to buy land and redistribute it, and in 2025 passed a law that would allow expropriation of land, including in some limited cases without compensating owners.
US President Trump has been lobbied by Afrikaner groups decrying that law and what they say is government-backed discrimination and violent attacks against them, claims that the South African government says are misinformation.
South Africa has also been targeted by Trump for its filing of a case in the International Court of Justice accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
The Trump administration has allowed white Afrikaners to receive asylum in the US, and last year froze most foreign assistance to South Africa.

Satellite data shows major ice losses for Greenland and Antarctica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:13:06 UTC
02:13:06 KST

Satellite data shows major ice losses for Greenland and Antarctica
New research based on satellite data going back to the 1970s has documented major polar ice losses in Greenland and Antarctica — home to Earth’s two great ice sheets — that have contributed to rising global sea levels.
Between 1979 and 2023, according to data from 27 satellite missions, Greenland and Antarctica lost a combined 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice, adding 3.14cm to the worldwide sea-level rise.
The study, employing the longest satellite data record of changes in ice sheets ever gathered to give the most complete account to date of ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica, was conducted by the Ice Sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise team, an international group of polar scientists.
The findings, they said, offer fresh evidence of the effects of human-caused global climate change.
“To put this very large number into context, 11.3 trillion tonnes of ice is enough ice to fill in a cube that would be 23 kilometres in height,” said climate scientist Ines Otosaka of Northumbria University in England, lead author of the study published on Sept 16 in the journal Scientific Data.
Of the ice loss documented in the study, about 60 per cent came from Greenland and 40 per cent from Antarctica, even though Greenland is about one-eighth the size of Antarctica.
“When ice sheets melt, they contribute to rising global sea levels. And with every additional centimetre of sea-level rise, about 2 to 3 million people are put at risk of annual coastal flooding. The ice sheets are now a major driver of sea-level rise, accounting for about 25 per cent of all sea-level rise,” Otosaka said.
“We have extended our satellite data record backwards in time to the 1970s, and this confirms that ice losses started in the 1990s and have increased since then. Our assessment shows that the pace of ice loss increased by a factor of four between the 1980s and 2010s,” Otosaka said.
The study documented a slowdown in ice loss between 2020 and 2023, though the researchers said this appears to represent a short-term variation and not a reversal of the long-term trend.
Unusually high snowfall across East Antarctica provided enough ice to offset some of the losses from glaciers elsewhere on Antarctica, while relatively mild summers in Greenland substantially lowered surface melting, they said.
Some 84 per cent of the ice lost came from glaciers flowing more quickly into the ocean rather than from ice melting at the surface, showing that the long-term trend is being driven by the response of the ice sheets to a warming ocean, Otosaka said.
The researchers said the total sea-level rise attributed to the ice losses at Greenland and Antarctica may not sound like a huge number, but it puts another 6 to 9 million people at risk of coastal flooding and erosion globally.
“These findings have implications for coastal planning, showing that we urgently need to develop plans for protecting coastal communities around the world from the impact of ice sheet melting,” Otosaka said. REUTERS

Emory University launches new academic center intended to counter rising antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:12:19 UTC
02:12:19 KST

Emory University launched a new academic center earlier this month focused on developing practical, government-level strategies to combat rising antisemitism.
The Emory Policy Institute on Countering Antisemitism, known as EPICA, was founded and is led by Ambassador Deborah Lipstadt, a University Distinguished Professor, Holocaust historian, and former US special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism under the Biden administration.
Funded by private donations, the institute is designed to bridge rigorous academic scholarship with public policy, operating under the belief that anti-Jewish hatred poses a fundamental threat to democratic societies.
Reflecting on her transition back to academia after nearly three years in diplomacy, Lipstadt told The Jerusalem Post, “When I finished at the State Department, a number of people, both from within universities and from the world of diplomacy, said to me, ‘Deborah, you have a unique perspective on the issue of antisemitism, anti-Zionism, and Jew hatred, which is a term I prefer nowadays, in that you bring to it decades of scholarly experience, you also bring to it a face-to-face encounter in the lawsuit that you faced with David Irving, and you’ve now been in the diplomatic world for close to three years, so you understand how diplomacy works, what governments can do and what governments can’t do, what are the limits, what are the possibilities. Don’t just squander that or write a book and think that’s enough.’ So I turned to Emory University, Emory College, and they were enthusiastic about my building something that would address this issue, that would involve students as well, but also have a research element.”
EPICA to include undergraduate fellowship program
The institute’s core mission centers on conducting interdisciplinary research, facilitating public dialogue, and training the next generation of policy leaders. A key component of EPICA’s educational programming is an undergraduate fellowship starting in January 2027.
The fellowship will allow third- and fourth-year students in good standing to engage directly with policymakers, participate in study trips to Washington, DC, and complete summer internships on Capitol Hill and at policy think tanks.
Student fellows will produce research related to the Global Guidelines for Countering Antisemitism, an international framework introduced by Lipstadt in a 2024 speech in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and endorsed by dozens of countries and multilateral organizations.
The framework includes recommendations for governments and international bodies, including adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism as a framework.
Institute will support ongoing fight against antisemitism 'virus'
Lipstadt emphasized to the Post that the institute deliberately chose the word “countering” instead of “combating,” explaining that “combats would just suggest a winner, and I don’t think that there’s a winner in this.” Instead, she views the initiative as supporting an ongoing fight against a virus that extends far beyond immediate horizons.
“It’s a counter-effort, it’s an ongoing fight,” Lipstadt noted. “This is a virus that mutates and lives long beyond and beyond anywhere we can look at today.”
Lipstadt stated that through the institute’s efforts, “I would hope that the research that would come out, that the students’ experience, that the work that they will do, would compel increasing numbers of universities to take this issue seriously.”
Lipstadt added that addressing governments also means looking broadly at institutional policies.
“When I say governments, I’m not just talking about federal governments, but even universities, how can they address this? How can they counter this? How can they recognize that this is a dangerous and serious issue? And so that’s what we will be working on,” Lipstadt concluded.

Iranian drone and missile attacks on US bases in the region during Operation Epic Fury might have been aided by Russian spy satellites, CNN reported on Wednesday.
The report, which cited two US officials, said these satellites may have passed information to Tehran after flying over areas with a US military presence, such as Prince Sultan Air Base, which was struck by Iran on March 27.
According to the report, Russian satellites played a "vital role" in the Prince Sultan Air Base attack, which injured 12 US soldiers.
CNN analyzed the tracking data of the satellites in question, revealing that they passed over targeted areas just prior to Iranian operations against said targets.
The satellites included those used for detailed imagery, all-weather radio signal detection, infrared imaging, and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which is used to locate high-value targets.
According to CNN, one of these high-value targets was a US Air Force Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, which was destroyed during Iran's attack on Prince Sultan Air Base.
The report noted the accuracy of such strikes as evidence of Iran's use of Russian satellites, saying that the precision would be impossible without them.
Other targets in question by the report include a CIA facility within the US embassy complex in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
Iran's use of Russia's satellites 'monumental,' Saudi expert says
Saudi expert Dr. Nawaf Obaid told CNN that Russia's capabilities used by the Iranians are the reason for the state of the US-Iran conflict as it stands today.
He noted that Russia's reasoning for helping Iran is due to the US similarly assisting Ukraine in its efforts to strike Russian targets.
"This is Russian payback with interest," said Obaid. "It's monumental in terms of the consequences of what this has done, not just to the US's standing in the region, but to the security architecture of the region going forward."

Israeli AI English-learning startup Loora raises $22m. in Series B
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:11:45 UTC
02:11:45 KST

Israeli AI language-learning company Loora has raised $22 million in a Series B funding round, bringing its total funding to more than $43 million, the company announced Tuesday.
The round was led by Union Tech Ventures, with participation from vgames and existing investors Emerge, Hearst Ventures and QP Ventures.
Loora, which uses artificial intelligence to provide personalized English-speaking practice, said it would use the funding to expand research and development and accelerate growth in the US, Europe, Asia, and Latin America.
The company also plans to roughly double its workforce over the next six months, primarily by hiring for AI research and development and learning-science positions.
Founded in 2020 by CEO Roy Mor and CTO Yonti Levin, Loora has more than 15 million users worldwide, according to the company.
Mor and Levin met during their military service and served together in Sayeret Matkal, the IDF’s elite special operations unit.
The company previously raised $9.25 million during its seed round and $12 million in Series A funding in 2024. The latest investment brings its total disclosed financing to approximately $43.25 million.
AI as an English tutor
Loora’s app lets users practice spoken English through conversations with an AI tutor and receive feedback on grammar, pronunciation, and fluency. The system adapts conversations to a user’s proficiency level and interests.
The app is aimed primarily at adults seeking to improve their spoken English, including for job interviews, professional presentations, and workplace conversations.
Loora said users have held more than 200 million conversations with its AI system. It said revenue has more than doubled during the past 12 months, with annual recurring revenue now in the tens of millions of dollars.
Those financial figures were provided by the privately held company and are not independently disclosed.
Loora also said it had built a business-to-business operation over the past year and now works with more than 100 companies, governments and universities.
According to Loora, 72% of its users say career advancement is a primary reason for learning English, while its typical user is between 25 and 55 years old.
Loora targets limits of traditional language apps
The company is betting that conversational AI can address one of the central limitations of conventional language-learning software: giving users frequent opportunities to speak rather than primarily completing vocabulary and grammar exercises.
Loora says its system uses information from previous conversations to adjust lessons and identify areas where an individual learner needs more practice.
The company says its database now includes more than 200 million learner interactions, which it uses to analyze engagement and refine the way the AI tutor responds.
Some users appear to be treating the AI less like a conventional language course and more like a conversation partner.
One German user spent roughly 40% of his conversations discussing politics, according to data released by Loora. An Indian user discussed 38 subjects over 49 conversations, ranging from water sports to philosophy.
Another user logged practice sessions on 1,377 consecutive days.
English proficiency as a path to economic opportunity
Mor said the company sees English proficiency primarily as an economic and professional issue.
“People who already know English tend to underestimate the scale of the opportunities it creates,” he said. “For most of the world, English is the most significant gateway to advancement, a better job, a place at university or an entirely different future.”
Loora says its service costs about $10 a month in some markets, compared with substantially higher rates for one-on-one instruction.
Roxanne Horesh, a partner at Union Tech Ventures, said the investment firm was attracted to Loora’s combination of AI personalization and repeat usage.
“What stood out to us was the combination of mission and execution,” Horesh said.
She said the challenge extended beyond creating an AI capable of holding a conversation to developing a system that could track individual learners, measure their progress, and adjust instruction over time.

02:11:39 KST

The EU is militarizing the Arctic. Here’s how it plans to do it
The EU’s Arctic policy is becoming increasingly important amidst global competition driven by both climate change and the region’s strategic significance. Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime transport routes, facilitating access to abundant natural resources, and creating conditions for expanded economic activity. Consequently, the Arctic is becoming an arena for rivalry among the leading global powers. For Brussels, the Arctic holds not only regional significance but is also a tool for achieving foreign policy and geopolitical objectives.
Adopted in October 2021, the EU’s current Arctic policy is titled ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’. It focuses on three ‘soft’ priorities: climate and environmental protection, sustainable development, and peace and cooperation. Essentially, in this document, the Arctic is viewed as a low-tension zone, and the primary focus is on the environment and scientific exchange.
However, a lot has changed in the world since 2021, from the Ukraine crisis to the paralysis of the Arctic Council, Trump’s bid to acquire Greenland, Chinese container ships traveling via the Northern Sea Route, and attacks on undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. In January 2026, at the Arctic Frontiers conference in Tromsø, Norway, Kaja Kallas said, “It is time for a fresh EU Arctic policy, one that reflects the times we live in.”
A new phase of the EU’s Arctic agenda after 2022
The EU Arctic policy stands at the intersection of geopolitical, economic, and environmental interests. In recent years, Brussels has sought to adapt its strategy to the shifting international landscape shaped by a sanctions-driven confrontation with Russia, China’s expanding regional presence, and the growing role of the US in security matters. The Ukraine conflict and the region’s growing militarization have pushed the EU to revise its Arctic agenda. The EU must shape its Arctic policy by balancing a normative agenda focused on sustainable development against tangible economic interests and security demands from NATO allies.
In July 2025, the president of the European Commission announced a revision of the EU’s Arctic strategy to ensure that it addresses new challenges. Meanwhile, the EU is strengthening cooperation in the fields of energy, raw materials, and security and defense partnerships with several non-EU Arctic nations – notably Canada, Iceland, Norway, and self-governing Greenland.
Historically, Europe’s cooperation with the Arctic states has developed along three key lines: economic engagement (energy, transport infrastructure, and resource extraction), the environmental agenda (climate change, sustainable development, and biodiversity conservation), and scientific research (meteorological and oceanographic studies, as well as research on glacial melting). However, the current geopolitical situation has significantly altered these areas of cooperation, particularly when it comes to relations with Russia.
The EU joined other Arctic Council member states and “key like-minded partners” in suspending Russia’s participation in various regional cooperation bodies following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Consequently, the EU issued three joint statements concerning the Northern Dimension joint policy, the Barents Euro-Arctic Council, and the Council of the Baltic Sea States. On November 12, 2025, the European Parliament adopted a new resolution on the Arctic that addresses the buildup of military capabilities and emphasizes the need for cooperation with Northern European partners (including Norway) to prepare for the upcoming geopolitical competition in the region. The resolution was passed by an overwhelming majority, with 510 votes in favor, 75 against, and 80 abstentions.
The resolution outlines a comprehensive strategy for the EU’s diplomatic engagement in the Arctic, covering areas such as environmental protection and security. The adopted document signals a shift in Brussels’ Arctic policy, envisions deeper cooperation with Arctic states, particularly Norway, and underscores the region’s significance for Europe’s energy security and geopolitical stability.
To safeguard European interests – including freedom of navigation, the protection of maritime infrastructure, and environmental security – the European Parliament calls for active cooperation with NATO, joint exercises, and coordinated surveillance and defense efforts.
Furthermore, the EU Parliament encourages multilateral governance in the Arctic through the Arctic Council and regional forums; this includes supporting efforts to grant the EU permanent observer status, engaging with Arctic institutions (such as the Arctic Economic Council), and expanding its presence in the region (for example, by means of the recently opened EU office in Nuuk).
The resolution also reaffirms the Arctic’s status as a region of strategic importance to the EU (considering its direct impact on European security), and notes that the EU must move beyond the concept of ‘Arctic exceptionalism’ and integrate High North priorities into its broader foreign, security, and energy policy strategies.
By adopting this resolution, the EU Parliament has signaled that the Arctic is no longer a remote outpost but a strategic frontier vital to Europe’s energy supply, security, digital infrastructure, and environmental sustainability.
The next step will be to integrate this non-legislative resolution into the EU’s updated Arctic policy. A step toward this was taken at the EU Arctic Summit, held September 13-14, 2026, in Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland.
Key outcomes and decisions of the EU Arctic Summit
The summit was attended by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas, European Council President António Costa, the heads of government of Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Romania, and representatives of France, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland, and Sweden.
The primary goal of the meeting, convened at the initiative of the Finnish prime minister, was to formulate a common EU strategic approach to the Arctic, a region that has become critically important to European security.
Following the EU Arctic Summit, a joint communiqué was adopted, outlining the path toward an updated EU Arctic strategy set to be presented in October 2026. Key highlights of the document include:
1) Adoption of a new Arctic strategy. Kaja Kallas announced the preparation of an updated Arctic strategy, set to be presented in October. Security takes center stage in this strategy; in her view, Russia’s growing military activity and China’s strategic investments in the Arctic compel the EU to shift toward ensuring collective defense. The participants of the summit urged the EU to maintain a more active strategic presence in the region. EU Council President António Costa stated that the increase in military spending in the Arctic would be factored into the next long-term EU budget.
2) A unified EU icebreaker fleet. The concept of jointly owning an EU icebreaker fleet was reflected in the adopted communiqué. Kallas spoke of the need to create such a fleet in light of climate change and the geopolitical situation. Finland proposed building the vessels at its own shipyards, leveraging its expertise in the field and sharing experience.
3) Investments in cross-border infrastructure. The participants emphasized the need to develop infrastructure capable of serving civilian purposes (such as supplying remote settlements) and facilitating the rapid deployment of troops. Leaders called for increased investment in military mobility, cross-border transport links, satellite infrastructure, and other facilities in the North. The discussion focused on allocating funds to reinforce roads, railways, and bridges in Finland, Sweden, and Norway – ensuring they can withstand the weight of heavy NATO armored vehicles in extreme cold – as well as modernizing deep-water ports in Northern Norway and setting up POL storage warehouses along the Barents Sea coast. The summit supported the expansion of the European satellite constellation to facilitate navigation and maritime surveillance.
4) Balancing priorities. The statement noted that, despite the strong emphasis on security, issues like climate protection, sustainable development, and peaceful cooperation remain among the priorities of the EU’s Arctic strategy. Particular importance was placed on the situation of indigenous peoples and the need to cooperate with local communities in developing the region.
5) Hybrid threats. Finland’s Petteri Orpo noted that while climate change is opening up new shipping routes, it simultaneously renders the region vulnerable to hybrid influence. The document underscored the need to enhance capabilities for responding to such challenges.
Overall, the summit in Rovaniemi marked a fundamental shift in how European leaders approach the northern territories. The Arctic is no longer seen as an environmental conservation zone and has been officially recognized as a front line in the geopolitical confrontation.
Moreover, the Arctic is no longer discussed as an isolated region; it is being integrated into what analysts call the ‘Northeastern arc’ of European security policy.
Overall, the EU’s forthcoming updated Arctic policy represents an attempt to transform the Arctic from merely an ‘environmental issue’ into an integral component of the European strategy on security, economy, and technological autonomy.

The Jerusalem District Court convicted four residents of Jerusalem’s Beit Safafa neighborhood on Wednesday in a case involving an alleged Iranian-directed plan to kill an Israeli nuclear scientist and his family, the State Attorney’s Office said.
The four pleaded guilty under a plea agreement to offenses concerning their own roles in the case; none was convicted of planning the killing. Proceedings against three other defendants, including the man prosecutors say received the assassination assignment, are continuing.
Mamdouh Khader and Omri Abu Hamida were convicted of failing to prevent a terrorist act. Mahmoud Khader and Muhammad Taha were convicted of helping another defendant maintain contact with a foreign agent.
According to the amended indictment, a person acting on Iran’s behalf contacted defendant Rami Alyan in September 2024 and offered payment for assignments. Prosecutors allege that Alyan was later told to form a cell to kill the scientist and his family.
Khader and Abu Hamida joined a drive to the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot. During the journey, another defendant told the passengers that the trip was part of an assignment from the Iranian contact, the indictment said.
Convicted for failing to take steps to prevent assassination plan
Security personnel refused the group entry, and two other defendants filmed the entrance. After they returned to Jerusalem, Abu Hamida asked why the Iranians wanted the footage and was told that someone at the location was a person they wanted to kill. Khader and Abu Hamida took no steps to prevent the plan, according to the indictment.
Mahmoud Khader admitted helping to spray and photograph writing in Jerusalem. He also drove another defendant to collect two stun grenades and helped obtain a fake police license plate intended for footage that would appear to show an attack on a patrol car.
Taha admitted arranging for a stun grenade to be thrown at an empty home in Katanna (Jerusalem) and filming it to make it appear that a Jewish home had been attacked. He sent the footage to the defendant in contact with the alleged Iranian operative. Taha also held the phone used for that contact to make it harder to locate, the indictment says.
Arguments on their sentences will be heard on a date yet to be set, while the cases against Alyan, Abd al-Rahman Alyan and Muhammad Khatib continue.

Von der Leyen fleshes out Carney’s vision to paint Europe as leader of world’s middle powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:10:29 UTC
02:10:29 KST

BRUSSELS ― Ursula von der Leyen used a major speech on Wednesday to pitch Europe as the leader of a group of like-minded countries that want to hold their own against rival powers such as Russia and China.
Not invited to join this EU-led coalition? Donald Trump’s United States.
Speaking before an audience that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has publicly fallen out with Trump, the European Commission president spelled out her vision of Europe as a geopolitical leader with plans for new partnerships and closer relationships — the most notable of which was offering to explore possible “associate EU membership” status for Canada, in what would amount to a major first for the EU.
Advertisement
“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in the speech at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. She added that the EU wanted to “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies. And here too only Europe ― with its size and power ― can take the lead.”
For the head of the EU’s executive branch, who’s now two years into her second five-year term, the speech amounted to a declaration of geopolitical legacy.
Coming one year after she declared Europe’s “independence moment” from the same platform, von der Leyen expanded on that idea in a speech that seemed to echo Carney’s own address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for the world’s “middle powers” to stand together against autocrats.
Ursula von der Leyen delivers her annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
In addition to offering Canada associate member status, von der Leyen suggested bringing the leaders of the U.K., Norway, Canada and Ukraine together in a newfangled “European Security Council” that would exist outside of NATO, offering a platform to discuss hybrid threats without the United States.
She also proposed that, with Europe in the role of coordinator, like-minded countries could jointly address challenges ranging from climate change to Chinese industrial overcapacity to the risks of frontier AI models.
“This speech was all about the big threats occupying European leaders: Russia and China, and to a lesser extent the United States,” said Mujtaba Rahman, Europe director at the Eurasia Group political consultancy. “It was all about how the EU can organize itself amid an imperialist Russia, a withdrawing America and a materialist China — it’s an attempt to draw those dots together.”
Advertisement
Yet for many of those watching, the speech was heavy on lofty ideas like associate membership for Canada — which faces considerable obstacles to become a reality — and light on practical new proposals to deal with Europe’s immediate challenges.
“Dr. von der Leyen is at her best when she diagnoses the ills of our time and of our Europe,” said French centrist lawmaker Nathalie Loiseau, who sits on the European Parliament’s security and defense committee. “We’re still waiting for the prescription that will help Europe regain its health.”
Skating over the issues
At a time when the EU economy is struggling with anemic growth and high inflation linked to runaway energy prices, the Commission president reiterated previously announced policy proposals on the economy, rather than pitching new ideas.
For example, the speech did not address how to meet Ukraine’s immediate financing needs — a pressing concern at a time when Kyiv has said it needs an additional €23 billion before the end of the year and the EU is its main financial benefactor.
It also included tough language on trade imbalances with China and the toll they are taking on Europe’s economy, but included no new policy proposal aside from doubling down on ongoing dialogue with Beijing.
It also skated over some of the major foreign policy issues dividing EU capitals, namely the Middle East and Israel’s relationship with the Palestinian territories in the West Bank and Gaza.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen made headlines last year by proposing to suspend the EU’s Association Agreement with Israel over humanitarian violations in Gaza. But this time she disappointed lawmakers who’d hoped she might offer a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements, an implicit recognition that her proposal from last year had floundered amid divisions between capitals.
Instead, she lamented the situation in Israel’s illegal West Bank settlements — and urged governments to overcome their disagreements.
Most of all, however, it was von der Leyen’s implicit suggestion that the EU should forge on without relying on the U.S., striking up new partnerships and setting up its own Security Council — outside of NATO — that seemed to unnerve some of the diplomats, lawmakers and officials watching her speech.
“I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras. | Denis Lomme/EP
“I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras, an Estonian member of the conservative European People’s Party and former commander of his country’s armed forces. “Putin is talking about recreating the security infrastructure in Europe and now the European Union starts to do it itself by attacking NATO.”
The Security Council was “a dead-born idea,” said Željana Zovko, vice-chair of von der Leyen’s EPP.
Indeed, many watchers pointed to the reality that in areas ranging from technology to pharmaceuticals to defense procurement, the EU remains heavily dependent on the U.S.
“So much of what we need for Europe’s defense and our economy is done with the United States,” said a diplomat from an eastern EU country who was granted anonymity. “Why alienate them?”

Why Netanyahu is trying to erase Arab parties before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:08:03 UTC
02:08:03 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is trying to get Arab-majority parties banned a month before the national election on October 27.
It has asked Israel’s Central Elections Committee to disqualify the Ra’am party – led by Mansour Abbas – and the Joint List, which is an alliance of Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad groups.
Netanyahu’s party, already the country’s longest-serving prime minister, has demanded the ban, saying there is “no room in the Knesset for those who harm” members of the Israeli forces.
Pre-election public polls show Netanyahu’s ultra-right bloc is unlikely to win a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset to form a government.
The Zionist opposition, led by former chief of Israeli forces Gadi Eisenkot and ex-premier Naftali Bennett, is also expected to fall short of the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government.
This means either political bloc will need support from Arab parties – typically backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who comprise one-fifth of the country’s population of 10.3 million – to form a government.
Experts say the latest disqualification drive led by Likud is not merely an attempt to achieve a legally sanctioned clean-up of the electoral field.
Rather, they view the move as an effort to shrink Arab political power, thus paving the way for Netanyahu’s return to the government.
Arik Rudnitzky of the Moshe Dayan Center for Middle Eastern and African Studies at Tel Aviv University tells TRT World that Likud’s move serves two purposes.
One, it seeks to delegitimise Arab parties – “particularly Ra’am” – as potential partners in an Eisenkot-led government. It will become “more difficult” for the former chief of Israeli forces to assemble a governing coalition without Arab parties in the electoral field, he adds.
Two, it may be meant to discourage Arab citizens from voting at all.
“The calculation is that if an Arab party is disqualified, some Arab voters may boycott the election,” he says.
Lower Arab turnout would improve Netanyahu’s chances of remaining in power.
“The effort is not only about keeping Arab parties off the ballot. It is also part of a broader strategy to obstruct the formation of an alternative government,” Rudnitzky says.
Suppression of voter turnout
Israeli elections use nationwide proportional representation, which means voters don’t vote for a particular member of the Knesset.
Instead, they vote for a “list”, which is the official slate of candidates that each party submits to the election-holding body. Sometimes, multiple parties form an alliance and contest elections under a “joint list”.
Two main Arab-majority lists are contesting the October polls, and Likud wants the election-holding body to ban both.
Rudnitzky says that this cycle is different from earlier attempts to ban Arab parties precisely because Palestinian Israelis are being pulled towards the polls, not away from them.
“The current political discourse within Arab society encourages (Palestinian Israelis) to vote and emphasises the importance of electoral participation,” he says.
Many Palestinian-Israeli citizens see the coming election as “crucial to their future in the country” as polls point to higher turnout than in 2022.
“They may also seek to undermine the perceived legitimacy of Arab parties as potential coalition partners and discourage both Arab parties and voters from supporting a new government led by the current Jewish opposition parties,” he says.
Ra’am is under attack especially because it is a plausible Palestinian-Israeli partner for a non-Netanyahu government.
Abbas’s party joined the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid coalition, the first time an Arab list sat inside an Israeli cabinet. It focused much of its work on crime and civic needs in Arab communities.
Rudnitzky says the targeting of Ra’am “should not come as a surprise” because the party is seeking to establish itself as a legitimate partner in a potential new “government of change”.
Interestingly, Ra’am has placed a Zionist candidate second on its list – meaning he is more likely to enter the Knesset than candidates lower down the slate.
“The more relevant Ra’am becomes to the formation of an alternative coalition, the stronger the political effort to challenge its legitimacy as a governing partner,” he says.
A changed electorate post-2018
Ozden Zeynep Oktav, head of the international relations department at Istanbul Medeniyet University, tells TRT World that Likud has lost legitimacy among Israelis. As such, a weakened Netanyahu is likely to “follow more racist policies”.
In her view, the latest ban attempt is “quite different from the previous ones” because Netanyahu and his family are “fast losing their legitimacy”.
Oktav links Abbas’s growing confidence to the protests against Netanyahu.
As those protests grow, the Ra’am leader “feels more confident” to call on Israel to recognise an “independent Palestinian state”, she says.
That helps explain why a party once admitted into government is now being painted as unfit for the ballot.
Zahide Tuba Kor, a scholar of Middle Eastern studies, tells TRT World that Palestinian-Israeli electoral participation is the structural fact that lies beneath the years-long political deadlock in Tel Aviv.
One reason Israel has remained without a stable government since 2018 is that Palestinian Israelis have abandoned their boycott and turned out to vote en masse.
Once Arab parties began winning 10 to 15 seats, forming a government of Jewish parties alone became far harder, she says.
Israel then set a record of five parliamentary elections in three and a half years, from April 2019 to November 2022.
“Arab parties played a significant role in the failure to form a stable coalition government composed of Jewish parties between 2019 and 2021,” she says.
Netanyahu tried a different tactic before 2021: encouraging Arab voters to back Likud, while splitting the Arab vote so that lists would fall below the threshold of 3.25 percent of total national votes required to enter the Knesset.
“All these tactics backfired,” she says, adding that his opponents were able to form the coalition government with support from the Ra’am party.
That success is exactly what the current campaign is trying to make unrepeatable.
After October 7, 2023, no political party can afford to seek external support from Arab parties, as was done in 2021, Kor says.
“The definitive solution (for Netanyahu) is to ban Arab parties, and redistribute the parliamentary seats currently held by them among Jewish parties,” she says.
Rudnitzky warns that if the Supreme Court overturns the proposed ban, Likud and its partners will still harvest the ruling.
Such an intervention would reinforce Likud’s claim that the judiciary acts against the “will of the people”.
“It could also intensify criticism of the judiciary’s authority to make consequential decisions on politically controversial matters,” he says.

‘Nowhere to go’: Gaza’s damaged buildings turn deadly
A war-damaged building collapses in Gaza City, killing at least 21 Palestinians and exposing fears of unsafe ruins.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Leaning heavily on the arm of a relative, Hayat al-Ajlah moves slowly between the hospital beds, scanning the faces of the injured.
She is looking for her eight-year-old daughter, Dalia.
Recommended Stories
