- list 1 of 3Israeli ‘double-tap’ air strike responsible for killing schoolboy in Gaza
- list 2 of 3Egypt’s el-Sisi rejects displacement of Palestinians from Gaza
- list 3 of 3Norway’s sovereign wealth fund profits from Israeli holdings amid genocide
Hayat has not seen her since they were pulled from beneath the rubble of the al-Saada building in western Gaza City early on Wednesday, when the war-damaged structure collapsed over their heads.
“I woke up to check my phone,” the 37-year-old Hayat said. “Suddenly, I heard a sound like something cracking. It felt like something was falling from underneath us.”
Moments later, the building came down, killing at least 21 Palestinians.
Hayat found herself trapped beneath the rubble, surrounded by dust and darkness, with family members screaming for help.
“I heard my 74-year-old father calling for my 12-year-old son Yasser. ‘Yasser, Yasser,’ he was calling, and then his voice disappeared,” she said. “I panicked and started screaming for my four children.
‘We survived by a miracle’
For nearly an hour, neighbours and civil defence workers worked to pull Hayat, her children and some of the other residents from the rubble. But Hayat knew that others were trapped deeper inside the building.
“My father and mother’s voices disappeared because they were in the part where the floors collapsed on top of each other,” she said through tears. “We were closer to the side of the building that tilted, so we survived by a miracle.”
Nine members of Hayat’s extended family were killed, she said, including her parents, four of her siblings, and three of her nephews and nieces.
Her four children survived, although her daughter Dalia was taken to hospital with a serious head injury.
The collapse had come suddenly, but Hayat said there had been warning signs.
“My mother was afraid of the building, and my father was planning to find another place,” she said.
The family had been displaced from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood to Deir el-Balah, in central Gaza, during an earlier phase of Israel’s genocidal war, before returning about two months ago.
With few alternatives, and many in Gaza still living in tents because of Israeli restrictions on reconstruction, the family moved into an empty apartment on the third floor of the damaged residential building after a friend of Hayat’s father told him it was available.
“My father’s friend told him there was an empty apartment on the third floor. It was severely damaged, but my family wanted to get out of the tent and escape its harsh conditions,” Hayat said.
Many members of her extended family were in the building when the tragedy struck because they had been preparing for a celebration – a family wedding planned for next week.
“We never expected this tragedy. The whole family is either dead or injured,” Hayat said.
Families wait at al-Shifa
At Gaza City’s al-Shifa Hospital, relatives of the victims have gathered in grief and shock, waiting for the lengthy recovery operation to continue and for news of those still missing.
Among them was the Saada family.
Umm Mahmoud Saada, in her 70s, stood crying for her son Mahmoud, his wife and their children.
Mahmoud, 38, was the father of six girls and a boy. Neither Mahmoud nor his family survived.
He had been living displaced in southern Gaza and only returned to Gaza City a month ago, she explained.
“He had a tent in the middle of the street and was exhausted [living in it], and his financial situation was very difficult,” his mother said. “A relative showed him this place, so he settled there temporarily. We did not know it would be his end.”
She recalled seeing her son the day before.
“Yesterday, he visited me. We prayed the noon prayer together, ate together and then he left,” she said. “All our loved ones are leaving us, and our hearts are breaking day after day. Why is all this happening to us?”
Rescue with little equipment
The search operation has been prolonged by a severe shortage of heavy machinery and other essential equipment, a direct result of Israeli restrictions on imports into Gaza and reconstruction.
Palestinian Civil Defence said its teams had worked for hours to reach people trapped beneath the building, but had been forced to rely on limited and basic tools. The shortage made it difficult to clear the large amounts of concrete and rubble and reach those still underneath.
Mansour Bakroun, 56, had been sitting in front of his tent when the building collapsed before dawn.
“The building is around 150 metres [about 500 feet] away. At first, I ran back, calling for my family to flee,” he said.
Once the dust began to settle, he ran towards the building, where residents were already trying to rescue those trapped.
Mansour said the building had been visibly damaged since the beginning of the war.
“Every day, something would fall from it … a piece of a wall, a stone,” he said.
“People left, but those who stayed had nowhere to go,” he added. “They had no other place.”
Another man living nearby, Huzaifa Mohammed, said that he had long been afraid of a collapse.
“Every day, I imagine these buildings collapsing,” he said. “Every day, pieces of stone and walls are falling, and people ask: Where should we go?”
Huzaifa said the sight of children being pulled from the rubble had left him struggling to understand what he was witnessing.
“When I see a little girl brought out with her head crushed, I ask myself: What if this were my daughter or my son?” he said.
Huzaifa said people had spent years living among damaged buildings and warnings of danger, with few places to go.
“How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said. “Are we only going to come out and condemn what is happening? We need solutions. We need someone to look at our situation and ask: How much longer can this continue?”

Ebola transmission declining in DR Congo’s hard-hit Ituri province: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:07:49 UTC
02:07:49 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Ebola transmission is declining in parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) hard-hit Ituri province, the World Health Organization (WHO) chief said Wednesday.
He warned that the epidemic continues to grow overall.
“We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters in Geneva.
Tedros said transmission is declining in the most affected parts of Ituri, while South Kivu has reported no new cases since May and more than 1,700 people have recovered.
After four months, the epidemic has also remained largely contained to northeastern DRC, apart from a small outbreak in Uganda that was “swiftly stopped,” he said.
Tedros warned, however, that more than 7,200 cases and over 3,500 deaths have been reported in seven provinces.
In Ituri, around 300 new cases and 160 deaths were recorded in the last week, accounting for nearly half of the national total.
Cases are also rising rapidly in North Kivu, where weekly infections have nearly doubled in the last two weeks, from about 100 to more than 200.
“The key indicators are not yet improving as they must,” said Tedros. "The response will need to be sustained and strengthened over many demanding months."

The encounter took place at 2:22 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 14, while the Russian vessel was operating in international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea, the ministry said.

Poland reportedly surprised by Brussels plan to use remaining SAFE funds for Ukraine
Poland and several other EU countries have been caught off guard by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's remarks about the EU's plans to use remaining funds from the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme to create a separate scheme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies.
Source: European Pravda citing RMF FM, a Polish radio station
Details: Poland previously said it wants to take part in a second round of applications under the SAFE programme and use funds left unclaimed by other countries for its own defence projects.
However, following von der Leyen's words, it is unclear whether the funds Warsaw were counting on in the second SAFE round and intended to use for its own defence projects will in fact be available.
"There was no such discussion with the European Commission," an EU diplomat in Brussels told an RMF FM journalist, expressing irritation over von der Leyen's remarks.
Quote: "For now, it is we – the member states – who are repaying this loan, not the European Commission."
More details: The diplomat said EU member states were not consulted on the issue. SAFE provides loans taken out by EU countries which must later be repaid. Some capitals therefore believe that member states themselves should have the decisive say over how any remaining funds are used.
Another RMF FM source in Brussels said the Commission wanted to direct unused SAFE funds towards joint projects with Ukrainian companies, including Freyja, the anti-ballistic coalition.
RMF FM reported that, at working-level meetings, the European Commission has so far only hinted that it was considering changes to the way the remaining funds could be used. Member states responded that any such changes would first have to be agreed with them.
The surprise is all the greater because it is not yet known how much money will actually remain in the fund. Member states have until the end of October to provide the commission with information on the implementation of their projects. Only then will it be possible to calculate how much money will in fact remain unused.
Until recently, unofficial estimates put the amount at around €10 billion. Italy was allocated almost €15 billion but has still not signed an agreement for the full amount reserved for it. Rome is considering the impact the loan could have on its budget deficit. In Hungary's case, around €16 billion has been allocated, but it also remains uncertain whether the country will manage to sign its agreement in time.
Only after this stage is completed will it be possible to determine how much money will actually return to the common fund.
RMF FM reported that EU countries participating in SAFE have so far used only a small share of the funds for joint programmes with Ukraine. The European Commission, meanwhile, is seeking additional funding for Kyiv, which has warned of a shortfall in its defence budget.

Israeli 'antiquities looting' exposes wider West Bank annexation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:04:27 UTC
02:04:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli officer’s 'antiquities looting' exposes wider West Bank land grab
An Israeli police officer and settler has entered an archaeological site in the Palestinian-controlled Area A of the occupied West Bank and removed antiquities from Palestinian-administered areas, in what experts have told The New Arab is part of a wider Israeli effort to use archaeology to seize control of Palestinian land and heritage.
Meir Rotter, an Israeli police officer and amateur archaeologist, entered a burial cave in Area A accompanied by Israeli soldiers, according to Haaretz, despite archaeological authority in the area resting with the Palestinian Authority under the Oslo Accords.
Rotter has previously been accused of removing an archaeological artefact from the Palestinian village of Kafr Dhaba in March.
Alon Arad, executive director of Israeli archaeology and heritage organisation Emek Shaveh, told The New Arab that the removal of antiquities should be understood as part of a broader campaign in which archaeology is being used to strengthen Israeli control over the occupied West Bank.
“This is part of the greater trend of weaponising heritage and archaeological sites in order to cement the Israeli grip over the West Bank, whether through official annexation or de facto annexation,” Arad said.
He said Rotter’s case was unusual because the police officer appeared to be operating independently of the Israeli authorities responsible for antiquities in the occupied territory.
“The case of Meir Rotter is unique in the sense that he's operating without any authorisation. He's doing it on his own,” Arad said.
Antiquities removed from Palestinian areas
Rotter is also a settler living in the occupied West Bank, according to Arad, although his role in the Israeli police is unrelated to archaeology in the territory.
“He's just going into Area A or Area B, doing whatever he wants, and then the authorities are not even investigating it,” he said.
Under the 1995 Oslo II agreement, responsibility for civil affairs, including archaeology and antiquities, in Areas A and B was transferred to the Palestinian Authority.
Israel’s Civil Administration retained authority over such matters in Area C.
Arad said Israel’s obligations as an occupying power to safeguard cultural property did not give Israeli authorities or individuals the right to remove antiquities from Palestinian-administered areas or conduct archaeological activity there independently.
“When Meir Rotter takes materials from Area A to Area C, that's a violation,” he said. “That's a violation of both international law and the Oslo Agreement.”
The removal of artefacts from Palestinian territory is therefore not simply a dispute over who controls archaeological sites. Arad said archaeology is increasingly being used as a tool to take physical possession of land while reinforcing an Israeli historical claim to it.
Archaeology and annexation
Rotter’s activities come as the Israeli government has taken steps to expand its authority over archaeological and heritage sites beyond Area C.
In 2024, the Israeli cabinet authorised the Civil Administration to take enforcement action at antiquities sites in Area B, despite Palestinian responsibility for archaeology there under the Oslo agreements.
The government went further in February this year, approving enforcement measures at archaeological sites in Area A.
A separate bill progressing through the Knesset would establish a civilian heritage authority under Israel’s Heritage Ministry to assume powers over archaeology and antiquities currently exercised by the military-run Civil Administration.
Critics say transferring those powers to a civilian Israeli government body would amount to extending Israeli governance directly into occupied territory and further advancing de facto annexation.
The moves have increasingly focused attention on archaeological sites including Sebastia, Mount Ebal and, more recently, Solomon’s Pools near Bethlehem, where Israeli politicians and settler groups have pushed for greater Israeli control.
Arad said archaeology provides both a physical mechanism for asserting control over territory and an ideological justification for doing so.
“Archaeological sites are first and foremost land,” he said.
By emphasising Jewish remains while marginalising other periods of the region’s history, Arad said archaeological sites can also be used to promote the idea that the occupied West Bank is “exclusively Jewish land”.
“It works both on the public narrative, but also in the field as a way to expropriate land and limit Palestinian development,” he said.
Whose heritage?
The cave entered by Rotter reportedly contains Jewish graves dating from the Roman period, the kind of ancient Jewish heritage that has increasingly been invoked by Israeli officials and settler groups to assert claims over archaeological sites in the occupied West Bank.
Arad rejected the argument that ancient cultural or religious connections to an archaeological site can confer modern territorial rights.
“We don't set up borders based on the cultural affiliation of archaeological sites,” he said. “If we start doing so, we dismantle the entire world order on how we determine borders.”
He compared such a claim to modern Italy asserting sovereignty over parts of Britain because they once formed part of the Roman Empire.
Arad stressed that Jewish history in the occupied West Bank was undeniable, but said it represented one part of a much longer and more diverse human history that also includes Palestinians as the natives of the land.
But archaeology, he argued, is increasingly being deployed by Israel’s religious right to construct a physical and historical map in which Palestinian connections to the land are diminished while Jewish connections are emphasised.
“We have 1.5 million years of human presence in Israel and Palestine,” Arad said. “We have lots of stories, and the attempt to tell only one story about this land is destructive.”

Von der Leyen risks fresh EU-NATO turf war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:03:06 UTC
02:03:06 KST

BRUSSELS — European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed the EU take on a stronger role in security and tackling hybrid threats, reigniting a long-running turf battle with NATO over Europe's defense.
Speaking at her annual policy address in Strasbourg, von der Leyen pitched a new leaders’ crisis decision-making forum together with Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the U.K. She also floated a new urgent consultation procedure for hybrid attacks modeled on NATO’s Article 4.
“Our systems were made for a different world — they are driven by well-intentioned attempts at consensus and compromise,” she said. “But we need to consider whether they are still fit for purpose.”
The pitch is already stirring unease within NATO, which has bristled at any attempt by the EU to tackle military-adjacent threats and has warned against “unnecessary duplication.”
“I have seen many initiatives at the EU level during the recent years — none of them yet are really protecting member states,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Of course, any initiative has to be assessed on its merits, but I do feel that NATO has delivered much more in concrete terms for collective security.”
The EU proposals underscore a growing sense that Europe is failing to deal with proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness,” von der Leyen said.
The security council is supposed to help the EU react more decisively. NATO itself has struggled with how to respond to Russian provocations below the threshold of direct military attack.
Advertisement
The last time Article 4 was invoked — a formal request to consult allies due to a security threat — was by Estonia last year after three Russian fighter jets violated the country's airspace. No other capital has invoked it since.
Duplication drama
There are few details on von der Leyen’s ideas. Earlier European security council proposals — which the EU has rejected — include the idea of capitals delegating some defense decision-making powers to a smaller group of leaders in a crisis.
An Emergency Security Protocol, meanwhile, would allow one capital to convene all fellow EU members in a crisis “to coordinate a European response, to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact,” von der Leyen said — almost identical to NATO’s Article 4 procedure.
Mark Carney listens to Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union speech to Members of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
In theory, a security council could help in “coordinating quick action” between the EU, NATO and other partners in a crisis that is “flexible across institutions,” said Giuseppe Spatafora, an analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies. The emergency protocol, meanwhile, could protect non-NATO countries like Ireland, he said.
But the alliance insists it should take the lead on security. “NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the alliance.
Not all NATO allies are skeptical. On hybrid attacks, the “EU is better placed to put in place a mechanism to react, because it has more diverse tools than NATO,” said a second senior NATO diplomat.
Advertisement
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said von der Leyen's schemes were not intended to replace NATO.
“In order for Europeans to take primary responsibility for European defense, we need to have our own defense architecture,” he told POLITICO, “and we shall do that, not undermining NATO — keeping NATO structures as they are.”
But von der Leyen's ideas pose a risk of duplication, two NATO diplomats warned, adding that allies were not formally briefed by the EU on the proposals in advance.
Countries near Russia also fret that it could worsen their security situation. “It gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said MEP Riho Terras, Estonia’s former chief of defense. “It is a very bad idea … which I hope will not have a future.”
The move also risks alienating some non-EU NATO members such as the U.S. and Turkey.
“The idea of a ‘European Security Union’ not including Türkiye, a major capable ally and a pillar of stability, security and peace at NATO’s southeastern flank, would be fatally flawed from the outset,” said one Turkish official.
Advertisement
The White House did not respond to a request for comment from POLITICO.
Setting up new EU bodies and holding consultations will not fix Europe’s underlying lack of political will to confront Russia and the need to match talk with action, said Oana Lungescu, a former longtime NATO official.
“Nations … should be talking about real capabilities and trying to harness real political will to impose costs on Russia,” she said. “How can you do that by focusing political energy and some resources ... towards yet another body?”
NATO’s “Article 4 works because it sits inside [its] Article 5” mutual defense clause, added a third NATO diplomat. “An EU ‘Article 4’ without an EU ‘Article 5’ is a consultation forum with a flattering name.”

English far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailed

2026-09-16

02:01:54 KST

A rightwing extremist who discussed poisoning Jews and Muslims and called for the killing of migrants and minority communities has been jailed.
Ivan Jennings, 46, called for the murder of hundreds of people he labelled “subhumans”, saying it was “justified and actually needed”, in extreme far-right groups over a period of three months in 2024.
The father-of four from Stafford had pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat between 15 August and 14 November that year and dissemination of a terrorism publication, namely a manifesto by the Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik, on 21 August 2024.
Jennings, who worked at a warehouse, was jailed for five years and three months and handed a further five years on extended licence at Leicester crown court on Wednesday.
Daniel Oscroft, prosecuting, told the court that Jennings had been an “active participant” in at least seven extreme rightwing groups on the social media platform Telegram.
Jennings, who joined the far-right organisation Patriotic Alternative in early 2024, told one of the groups that he was in touch with a man “who wanted to go in a boat and make a difference to the amount of people coming into the UK”, the court heard.
In another post, when asked if he supported murder, the defendant wrote: “It’s not murder because we are at war. If it’s subhumans, it’s justified and actually needed.”
On 22 August that year, he searched online for motorboat chartering services at Dover and how much it cost to hire a boat in the UK. A week later, another user shared a video of a boat, on which Jennings commented: “We need one of those to take out the dinghy divers.”
He told another chat group “something needed to be done soon” and each person “needs to take out at least 200 and stop the constant influx [of migrants]”.
The defendant also shared a post about an event in Manchester celebrating Pakistan’s independence day, identifying it as a target with the message: “We need to start acting.”
He made reference to the 51 people killed in the Christchurch terror attacks, a mass shooting at two mosques in New Zealand on 15 October 2019, adding: “We need a bigger impact.”
The court heard that another user commented on the post about the Pakistan independence day event: “It disgusts me to see that in the UK.” Jennings replied: “Exactly, we need to start acting to turn the tables.”
In another comment about the Pakistan event, he wrote: “If I go to prison for anything, it’s going to be for making a real change.”
Oscroft told the court: “In a smaller group of eight participants, there was discussion about the most poisonous mushrooms and how to get them into the food of Jews or Muslims.”
The defence barrister Oliver Renton said Jennings was “struggling with deep existential fears about himself” after he collapsed at work in 2023 in cardiac arrest, and that he descended into “fear and isolation” and became susceptible to “nihilistic, bleak worldviews”.
In his sentencing remarks, Judge Lockhart KC said Jennings had “deeply held abhorrent and racist views”.

Neturei Karta: Opposing Zionism
Inside Neturei Karta, the ultra-Orthodox Jewish group that rejects Zionism and the modern state of Israel while supporting the Palestinians fighting occupation.
An ultra-Orthodox Jewish group, Neturei Karta, rejects Zionism and refuses to recognise the State of Israel while marching under the Palestinian flag. This documentary traces its story from early 20th-century Jewish opposition to Zionism to today’s street protests in Jerusalem and New York. Told through Neturei Karta’s own voices and critical historians, the film revisits the Balfour Declaration, the assassination of Jacob Israel de Haan, the Holocaust-era split that gave birth to the movement, and the group’s marginal but defiant stance after Israel’s creation in 1948. Facing police crackdowns, death threats and isolation from mainstream Jewry, Neturei Karta has deepened its ties with Palestinians – from the streets of Mea She’arim in West Jerusalem to Yasser Arafat’s inner circle and solidarity with Gaza under blockade. Its story challenges assumptions about Judaism, Zionism and resistance in a region locked in conflict.

The horizontality of the landscape, the warm climate, and the strong presence of agricultural activity form the context for an architecture that seeks to respond to its location through shade, open spaces, and an essentially single-story layout. The house occupies a narrow and deep lot. Originally designed as a speculative residence for sale, the house is organized longitudinally, articulating the different sectors of the program and establishing direct relationships between the internal spaces, the garden, and the pool.

EU ambassadors advance major defense projects plan, with Ukraine featuring prominently
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:59:51 UTC
01:59:51 KST

EU ambassadors advance major defense projects plan, with Ukraine featuring prominently
BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU ambassadors on Sept. 16 approved plans for five bloc-wide projects potentially worth tens of billions of euros each to beef up Europe's defense capacity.
The projects were proposed by the European Commission in July 2026 to address "urgent strategic capability shortfalls in key areas including air defense, maritime security, space, drone, and counter-drone capabilities, and monitoring of the EU's eastern flank," a European Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists.
Ukraine is included in four of the five projects, with the space project being the lone exception.
Ambassadors also endorsed the European Commission's proposal to provide 60 million euros ($69 million) to each of the five projects, known as European Defense Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), to get them up and running.
But 60 million euros is only a fraction of the cost of the EDPCIs, which, as presented, would roll out over years. One of them is expected to last until 2045, and taken together, the projects come with a price tag of 281 billion euros ($324 billion).
"The (European) Commission will be the ones to facilitate the funding for each project," a Council Presidency spokesperson said.
The next step to formally bring the projects into existence is for EU defense ministers to vote on them, which is expected at their next meeting scheduled for Sept. 28.
Introducing the projects
The first of the five proposed projects is dedicated entirely to drone and counter-drone technology, where Ukraine is expected to play an important role, and all EU countries are taking part except for neutral Malta.
DECODER, as it is known, is expected to cost between 3.5 billion euros and 5.5 billion euros ($4 billion to $6 billion), making it by far the cheapest of the five projects. That money will fund a network of drone technology hubs to facilitate testing and innovation, and improve interoperability.
read also
Of likely more immediate interest to Ukraine is the air and missile defense project (EU-FIAMD), expected to cost 55-80 billion euros ($63-92 billion) by 2040.
While Ukraine is a world leader in drone warfare, the country's weakness lies in anti-ballistic missile defenses. This gap has been exploited in recent weeks by Russia, with repeated strikes against civilians in Kyiv and the destruction of cultural heritage — all war crimes.
The project aims to ensure countries have "the required quality and quantity" of integrated air and missile defenses, as well as solid early warning systems.
The scope of the newly proposed projects also ventures out into space, where Ukraine is not participating, and into the sea, where it is.
The "integrated maritime and seabed defense" project envisions bringing together military and civilian personnel, as well as drones, to monitor all types of sea-based infrastructure, such as fuel pipelines, wind turbines, and internet cables.
Rounding out the list of the five projects is its most expensive, the Eastern Flank Watch, estimated to cost between 60 and 100 billion euros ($69-115 billion) by 2036.
Unlike the other four projects, the Eastern Flank Watch cuts across combat domains and is instead geographically restricted, though the proposal argues that "it benefits all member states against concrete security threats and is open to extend its geographic area of interest."
It is also the project that has already begun work without waiting for full EU approval, with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announcing in December 2025 that his country would co-lead the group with Poland.

Two German air force Eurofighter jets fly through the sky over the air base in Wittmund, Germany on July 13, 2026. | Focke Strangmann/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany will deploy Eurofighter jets to Latvia to help protect its airspace during next month’s parliamentary election as repeated drone incursions have raised security concerns along NATO’s eastern flank.
Four German Eurofighters will be sent to the Lielvārde Air Base in central Latvia for about a week from late September into early October, Germany’s defense ministry said Wednesday. The ministry added that Latvia had requested additional support from its NATO allies to secure its airspace ahead of the Oct. 3 vote.
The Latvian defense ministry did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
Advertisement
Latvia has experienced several drone incidents this year. NATO fighters shot down a foreign drone over the east of the country in June, while another drone was destroyed in August. Authorities later said the August aircraft was Ukrainian and had likely entered Latvian airspace from Belarus after being affected by Russian electronic warfare.
Latvia’s defense ministry has warned that further foreign drones could infringe on its airspace as long as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
The German jets, from Tactical Air Wing 74 in Neuburg an der Donau, will operate under NATO’s enhanced Air Policing North mission, which forms part of the alliance’s integrated air and missile defense system. Germany will also deploy several dozen personnel.
Germany separately announced that five Eurofighters and around 120 troops will deploy to Ämari in Estonia from December through March for a regular NATO air policing rotation. That will be Germany’s seventh such mission to that part of Estonia.

Switzerland drops in the WEF’s gender equality index
Switzerland has fallen 10 places this year in the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) Gender Gap Index, dropping to 27th place. Globally, at the current rate, it will take 120 years to close the gender gap, the organisation said on Wednesday in Geneva.
Switzerland has not featured in the top 10 countries on this issue since 2021. Among the 145 countries analysed, Iceland remains in first place, ahead of Finland and Norway. Namibia has entered the top five, in fourth place.
Among the concerns is that the proportion of countries led by women has fallen back to the level of 10 years ago. Fewer than 20% of CEOs are women and fewer than 10% of the ministerial portfolios held by women are considered influential.
Whilst artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming one of the most important issues, fewer than one in five engineers working on this topic is a woman.
Overall, the gender gap has been closed by nearly 70%, an increase of 0.4 percentage points.

Syrians take to the streets as empty Western pledges leave them starving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:53:36 UTC
01:53:36 KST

Syrians take to the streets as empty Western pledges leave them starving
TEHRAN — Streets across Syria erupted this week in the largest wave of civil unrest since the fall of the central government in Damascus in December 2024.
Demonstrations flared from Aleppo and Idlib to Hasakah and Deir ez-Zor after the regime of Ahmad "al-Jolani" al-Sharra announced an abrupt 40 percent price hike on diesel, along with steep increases on gasoline and cooking gas.
Protesters burned tires, blocked the strategic M5 highway linking Damascus to Aleppo, and intercepted crude oil tankers moving through eastern provinces.
Angry crowds demanded the immediate dismissal of Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir.
The ruling clique in Damascus cited global market volatility and maintenance at the Baniyas refinery. That explanation offered no comfort to a population enduring systemic collapse.
A cascading collapse of basic survival
Fuel represents only the newest burden on an exhausted population.
Across major cities and rural towns, everyday survival has become nearly impossible.
Bread prices have soared following the government's move to dismantle state wheat subsidies.
A standard bundle of bread now costs up to 15,000 Syrian pounds in regions like Hasakah, representing a massive surge since late 2024.
Electricity infrastructure has fared no better. The government recently shifted generator pricing to dollarized rates, prompting private operators to shut down units.
Some neighborhoods now sit in total darkness for up to 21 hours a day. Healthcare services have undergone aggressive and predatory privatization, locking impoverished families out of basic care.
More than 90 percent of Syrians live under the poverty line, facing a daily battle against hyperinflation.
In May and June alone, over 200 demonstrations hit agricultural regions, where farmers protested unpaid wheat harvests and rising input costs.
The recent fuel shock simply pushed public tolerance past its breaking point.
Empty Western pledges and the Visa card elite
During the transition of power in Damascus, Western powers promised rapid economic integration, foreign investment, sanctions relief, and removal from international blacklists.
Washington and its allies presented these measures as a framework for national recovery. Almost two years later, none of these commitments have reached ordinary citizens.
Instead, economic privileges remain concentrated among the new ruling class.
While ordinary Syrians queue for hours to purchase single loaves of bread, al-Jolani wears tailored suits, pays for his coffee with an American Visa card, and publicly thanks Washington for easing sanctions.
Now as the picture of Syria’s new path has become increasingly clear, many have concluded that Washington’s strategy was never designed to rebuild Syria or improve living conditions.
The primary objective appears to be geopolitical dominance over opponents of the U.S.-Israeli order and control over Mount Hermon.
 
 U.S. forces remain entrenched near primary oil installations in eastern Syria, extracting up to 66,000 barrels per day.
 
 Syrian resources flow outward to sustain foreign military outposts, while local refineries run dry and domestic consumers face artificially inflated prices.
Capitulation to Israel
Security conditions across the country reflect total fragmentation.
The al-Jolani regime has abandoned national sovereignty in exchange for foreign backing.
In the south, Israel maintains military control over Jabal al-Shaykh (Mount Hermon) and has fortified an expanded security zone stretching toward Yarmouk River.
Tel Aviv regularly conducts hostile military patrols and exercises within Syrian territory without meeting any official resistance from Damascus.
Top Israeli officials recently visited troops occupying Mount Hermon, delivering clear warnings just 35 kilometers from the capital.
It appears that the regime in Damascus has quietly agreed to keep southern border areas disarmed and defenseless, effectively transforming Syrian soil into a passive and humiliating buffer zone for Israel.
The illusion of liberation
The "constitutional framework" enacted by al-Jolani granted his office broad judicial and legislative authority without institutional oversight.
Minorities and tribal groups in the east face systematic exclusion from local governance and resource distribution.
Reconciliation pledges made to civil servants remain unfulfilled, while figures linked to previous corruption scandals operate freely under new political banners.
Public anger goes beyond isolated economic grievances.
Demonstrators in Khan Sheikhoun, Maarat al-Numan, and Raqqa have raised fundamental questions about national independence.
The accumulated evidence suggests that swapping one political structure for a Western-aligned regime brings neither stability nor self-determination.

Italy's Meloni says she aims to remain in office until end of term
ROME, Sept 16 - Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Wednesday she intended to remain in office until the end of the legislature, dismissing media speculation that she might seek an early election before her term expires next autumn.

Europe's oldest man has died in Italy at the age of 112
Kyiv • UNN
Vitantonio Lovallo, a 112-year-old war veteran and farmer, has died in Italy. Portuguese man Joaquim Varela has become Europe's new oldest man.
Italian Vitantonio Lovallo died the day before in his hometown of Avigliano in southern Italy. He was born in March 1914 and was considered the oldest man in Europe, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Lovallo worked as a farmer for many years, tended sheep and cultivated his own vineyard. Even after turning 100, the Italian continued working in the vineyard.
During World War II, Lovallo served at the front, and from 1943 to 1945 he was held captive by the Germans. He was married and had four children. His wife died several years ago.
Following Lovallo's death, the oldest man in Europe became 111-year-old Portuguese national Joaquim Varela. At the same time, he ranks only 32nd in the ranking of Europe's oldest residents, behind 31 women. According to this list, the oldest person in Europe and the world is considered to be Britain's Ethel Caterham, who is 117 years old.

French seeks lifting of EU sanctions on billionaire after pressure by Azerbaijan, diplomats say
PARIS, Sept 15 - France has been urging the EU to lift sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov after coming under what it says is pressure from Azerbaijan as Baku holds two French nationals, three European diplomats familiar with the matter said.
European Union envoys extended the deadline for renewing Russia sanctions listings by seven days on Monday after failing to agree on a six-monthly rollover of the sanctions, which requires the unanimous approval of the 27 member states.
EU diplomats said France had joined Slovakia in calling for the lifting of sanctions imposed on Usmanov after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The metals and mining mogul has launched multiple lawsuits in Europe with the ultimate goal of having the sanctions lifted, and his lawyers have contested statements in the media that were used as grounds for the sanctions.
French diplomatic sources said the decision by Paris to call for sanctions on Usmanov to be lifted was driven by national security considerations, and that France was responding positively to approaches from international partners regarding the Usmanov case.
The European diplomats said Paris had indicated in private that Baku was using Usmanov to "blackmail" it over the case of two French citizens held in Azerbaijan, one of whom Paris has said is being held arbitrarily. Baku has sentenced the French national on espionage charges.
The link to Azerbaijan was first reported by the Financial Times on Monday. It was not clear why Azerbaijan was seeking Usmanov's delisting although President Ilham Aliyev has previously lobbied for his delisting.
The diplomats said France believed Baku's move was supported by Qatar and Kazakhstan.
Several other leaders in the region and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, have previously called for Usmanov to be taken off the EU's sanctions list.
The foreign ministries of Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Qatar did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
France's Foreign ministry spokesperson declined to comment on the Azerbaijan connection.
DIFFICULT TIES
Ties between Azerbaijan and France have long been strained, and worsened in 2023 when Azerbaijan regained control of the Nagorno-Karabakh region in a move that triggered an exodus of 120,000 ethnic Armenians living there. Baku reacted angrily to French military support for Armenia, with which Azerbaijan has fought two wars in the past three decades.
France has accused Azerbaijan-linked groups of carrying out disinformation campaigns over the last year, and said Baku has been seeking to fan the flames of riots and independence demands in France's Pacific island of New Caledonia.
The EU sanctions designations, which target nearly 3,000 companies and individuals with asset freezes and travel bans, had been due to expire on September 15. The expiry date has been pushed back to September 22.
One diplomat said member states were now watching to see how Paris would seek to break the impasse before next week or risk undermining both its credibility as a supporter of Ukraine and the EU's sanctions process. REUTERS

It also highlighted the escalating death toll in Gaza, calling for the allegations raised in the film to be thoroughly investigated and for independent journalists to be granted access to report from the devastated territory.
The latest statement follows a separate petition signed by more than 1,000 Israeli filmmakers in support of the NAZA directors amid pro-Israelbacklash over the film’s claims.
The petition said: “We filmmakers and creators call on everyone who is still fighting for freedom of expression and artistic freedom to join us in expressing support and solidarity with Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, the creators of the film NAZA.”
The filmmakers also warned that the continuing backlash and hostility could threaten the physical safety of the directors, as they stressed the importance of independent journalism in Israel.
“The central role of art and journalism is to hold up a mirror to the society in which they exist and to generate discourse and debate without giving anyone a pass, even when the reality is difficult.”
What is NAZA about?
NAZA is based on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel, most of whom spoke anonymously, and examines systems and practices used during Israel’s war in Gaza.
The filmmakers say the documentary builds on investigations previously published by +972 Magazine, Local Call and The Guardian.
The film takes its name from a military acronym reportedly used to indicate the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike on Gaza.
After receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the 80-minute documentary won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.

EU Chief Pledges Strongest-Ever Winter Support and Air Defense for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:52:15 UTC
01:52:15 KST

- Category
- World
EU Chief Pledges Strongest-Ever Winter Support and Air Defense for Ukraine
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged to provide Ukraine with its strongest-ever support package to help the nation navigate the harsh upcoming winter during her annual State of the European Union address to the European Parliament on September 16.
“Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and strengthen Ukraine’s supply of electricity and heat,” von der Leyen stated, emphasizing the critical need to fortify the country’s decentralized power grid and centralized heating systems against Russian aerial bombardment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
She added that the European Union would also rapidly expand its support for Ukrainian air defenses.
The European Commission president underscored the urgent necessity of accelerating the delivery of American Patriot interceptor missiles to Kyiv. However, she also stressed the strategic importance of curbing the continent’s dependence on single-source military suppliers.
To achieve this, von der Leyen announced that Brussels and Kyiv are collaborating to engineer an “affordable modular missile-defense platform.” A key element of this joint initiative is Project FREYJA, which aims to pair Ukrainian combat experience with European industrial manufacturing to build a sustainable, homegrown air defense network.
Project FREYJA is a pan-European, multi-layered anti-ballistic missile defense initiative designed to create an affordable, open-architecture alternative to interceptor systems, similar to the US Patriot. Initiated by Ukraine and backed by a coalition of ten European nations, the project integrates NATO-standard radars with domestic interceptors to build a decentralized continental shield capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic threats.
Looking beyond immediate battlefield requirements, von der Leyen outlined a wider geopolitical vision by pitching the creation of a “European Security Council.” Under this proposed framework, EU leaders would establish an emergency security protocol to regularly convene with the heads of key partner states—specifically naming Canada, Norway, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom—to address hybrid threats and coordinate continental defense.
EU High Representative Kaja Kallas had recently warned that the rise of far-right political movements, such as Alternative for Germany, threatens to undermine continental defense against Moscow. As Kremlin sabotage and hybrid operations draw closer to EU borders, Kallas cautioned that parties taking a passive stance on Russian aggression are creating dangerous security blind spots across Europe.

US charges five as alleged Kremlin assassination network reaches American soil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:52:09 UTC
01:52:09 KST

A US-based recruit was promised up to $1,500 to surveil a prominent Russian dissident before being offered $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target, the US Justice Department (DOJ) said on 15 September.
The charges connect that alleged plot to what prosecutors describe as a wider Russian assassination network operating since at least 2024 against dissidents, defectors, and countries perceived as supporting Ukraine.
A federal grand jury in Manhattan indicted five alleged members of what prosecutors call the “RIS Network”:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63: A Russian national and former colonel in the Russian intelligence services who allegedly recruited people to kill Russian dissidents.
- Kirill Khrameev, 27: Yuri Khrameev’s son and an officer in the FSB, Russia’s principal security service and a successor to the Soviet KGB.
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35: A Cuban national living in Russia who allegedly coordinated attacks and arranged travel for operatives.
- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35: A Cuban national accused of recruiting people in the US for surveillance and murder.
- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22: A Venezuelan national accused of helping Suarez recruit US residents to spy on and kill a Russian dissident.
Suarez sent the US resident two locations associated with the dissident, according to the indictment. After the resident delivered photographs and videos, prosecutors say, Suarez and Castro made the $40,000 offer. When the resident declined to carry out the killing, they allegedly asked whether he knew “someone [who] can do the work.”
In 2025, the indictment alleges, Kirill Khrameev recruited a US citizen to photograph a target in Lithuania for a promised $200. Yuri Khrameev then offered approximately $25,000 to kill the man. When the recruit refused, Khrameev allegedly proposed a “simpler job”: burning a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. He said the purpose was to target countries helping Ukraine, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors also allege that Durruthy coordinated travel and logistics for attacks in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and in Lithuania that September. The Justice Department did not specify what either attack involved.
All five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, carrying up to 20 years in prison. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro also face a murder-for-hire conspiracy charge carrying up to 10 years.
All five remain at large. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow saw no need to comment without “credible evidence,” Reuters reported. An indictment is an allegation, and the defendants are presumed innocent.
From military espionage to alleged murder plots
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, its covert campaign against Ukraine’s Western allies has combined intelligence gathering with escalating sabotage. CSIS found that suspected Russian attacks in Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024, often using locally recruited agents against infrastructure and industries supporting Ukraine.
In August 2025, US prosecutors charged active-duty soldier Taylor Adam Lee with trying to transmit Abrams tank information and deliver hardware to someone he believed represented the Russian government, allegedly in exchange for Russian citizenship. That case involved an American insider allegedly offering military secrets, not a proven Russian recruitment operation.

Moscow court frees four truck drivers unwittingly used by Ukraine in 2025 ‘Operation Spiderweb’ drone attack on Russian military airfields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:52:06 UTC
01:52:06 KST

Moscow court frees four truck drivers unwittingly used by Ukraine in 2025 ‘Operation Spiderweb’ drone attack on Russian military airfields
The Moscow City Court released four drivers whose trucks Ukrainian security services used to launch drones at Russian military airfields during Operation Spiderweb, Kommersant reported.
At a hearing on September 16, the court denied an Investigative Committee representative’s request to extend the detention of Andrey Merkuryev, Alexander Zaitsev, Mikhail Ryumin, and Sergey Kanurin. The four have been charged with carrying out a terrorist attack and transporting explosives as part of an organized group.
Investigators allege that the drivers belonged to a group established by Ukrainian-born Artem and Ekaterina Timofeyev, who were recruited by the Security Service of Ukraine to carry out terrorist attacks in Russia and have been placed on a wanted list. Some of the drivers worked for a business registered as a sole proprietorship in Artem Timofeyev’s name. The Investigative Committee alleges that he approached the others as an ordinary customer seeking transportation services.
The Investigative Committee completed its investigation and sent the case to the Prosecutor General’s Office, but First Deputy Prosecutor General Anatoly Razinkin declined to approve the indictment. According to Razinkin, investigators had found no direct evidence of the defendants’ guilt, and the circumstantial evidence was insufficient to bring the case to court. Investigators disagreed and appealed the decision. The Moscow City Court then denied the Investigative Committee’s request to extend the defendants’ detention and ordered their release.
On June 1, 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spiderweb, using drones to attack military airfields in four Russian regions. The drones were hidden inside wood-frame houses transported by five long-haul truck drivers. One driver, 62-year-old Vasily Pytikov, was killed in an explosion during the operation. It later emerged that authorities had arrested the other four truckers — Merkuryev, Zaitsev, Ryumin, and Kanurin. Ukrainian officials said the drivers were unaware of the drones hidden in their trucks.
The defendants deny any wrongdoing. They said they called law enforcement themselves after the drones flew out of their trucks and also tried to bring the drones down.

Kallas urges European Parliament to “open its eyes”: Russia is the only obstacle to peace

Kallas urges European Parliament to “open its eyes”: Russia is the only obstacle to peace
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said this during a debate in the European Parliament on the urgent need for EU support for Ukraine amid the escalation of Russia’s military aggression, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
““I know that there are people in the European Union — in particular, I have heard some Members of the European Parliament — who for some reason believe that Ukraine is an obstacle to peace. So I tell you: open your eyes — Russia is the only obstacle to peace,” she stressed.”
She recalled the brutality of the latest wave of Russian escalation in Ukraine.
“July and August were the deadliest months for Ukraine’s civilian population since the beginning of this war. As the Russian army has become bogged down in ground fighting, Russia is killing civilians from the air. If Russia’s initial plan was to invade a sovereign country and seize someone else’s territories, its goal today is even more unacceptable. Russian troops are now attacking Ukrainians indiscriminately and brazenly,” she said.
As an example, she cited the fact that Russia has destroyed about 90% of Ukraine’s food storage infrastructure over the past several months, adding that the EU is currently helping Ukraine increase its grain storage capacity.
“We already know what Russia is preparing for this winter: intensifying attacks on energy facilities to make life even more unbearable for ordinary Ukrainian families,” Kallas stressed.
She noted the EU’s ongoing efforts to prepare Ukraine for the cold season.
“This year, the European Union has allocated €75 million to repair and insulate homes, as well as to provide essential items, including warm clothing, blankets, mobile water purification stations, and generators. Preparing for winter is a priority second only to military support and strengthening air defense,”Kallas said.
The High Representative also recalled the Kremlin’s attempts to sow fear among Europeans in order to undermine their support for the Ukrainian people.
“Whether it is attacks on trains carrying foreign senior officials or attacks carried out as close as possible to NATO borders, Putin’s goal is to intimidate the West,” Kallas said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen commented on an incident in which a Russian frigate fired signal flares at a Danish helicopter, as well as the downing of a drone over Lithuania. She said that the EU is strengthening collective deterrence and defense together with NATO, while also increasing pressure on Russia.

Cash for chaos: Israeli gets 13 years for Iran-linked arson, spying missions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:50:56 UTC
01:50:56 KST

An Israeli man was sentenced Wednesday to 13½ years in prison after admitting that he carried out a series of paid assignments for an entity acting on behalf of Iranian intelligence, including setting nine vehicles on fire, spraying politically divisive graffiti and photographing the neighborhood of former IDF chief Benny Gantz and energy infrastructure.
The Central District Court in Lod sentenced Alexander Granovsky under a plea agreement after he admitted to contact with a foreign agent, providing information to an enemy that could benefit it, nine counts of arson and multiple counts of defacing property. A separate case in which he admitted to threats and assault was also incorporated into the proceedings.
According to the indictment, Granovsky’s contact with the Iran-linked operative began in late November 2024 and continued until his arrest on Dec. 15. The two communicated through the Telegram messaging app, and Granovsky received payments for some assignments through a digital wallet.
His initial tasks involved spraying graffiti in public places with slogans including “We are all against Bibi” — using Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s nickname — and “We must put Netanyahu in prison,” as well as an internet address with an Iranian domain. He received payments worth hundreds of shekels for the graffiti.
The assignments then escalated. The operative offered to pay Granovsky to set fire to vehicles and police cars and obtain the addresses of senior military officers and government ministers.
Granovsky said he knew the neighborhood where Gantz, a former IDF chief of staff who later entered politics, lived but did not know his exact address.
Granovsky agreed to set vehicles on fire and received instructions on how to carry out and document the attacks. He ultimately torched nine vehicles, according to the indictment. On some, he spray-painted the words “Children of Ruhollah,” an apparent reference to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, founder of the Islamic Republic of Iran. For some of the arson attacks, he received 900 euros in cryptocurrency.
The operative also instructed Granovsky to buy a handgun. Granovsky said he was unwilling to kill or wound people but indicated he would be prepared to fire at homes.
He later photographed Gantz’s neighborhood and sent the images to the operative. Granovsky also photographed from a distance the smokestacks of the Reading power station in Tel Aviv.
At the operative’s request, he traveled to the power station in Hadera, north of Tel Aviv, but said the heavy security made it difficult to complete the photography assignment and demanded additional payment. When the request was rejected, he left.
In another instance, Granovsky bought an IDF uniform at the operative’s direction but later reported that the clothing had been stolen.
He also agreed to make Molotov cocktails but said he could not carry out the assignment because an instructional video sent to him was in Ukrainian, a language he does not speak. Granovsky also provided the operative with information about two people with criminal records.
The Central District Attorney’s Office asked the court to approve the parties’ agreed sentence of 13½ years.
A prosecutor emphasized that the offenses were committed during wartime and as part of Granovsky’s relationship with an Iranian-linked operative, a connection she said Granovsky understood. She argued that deterrence should be given significant weight because of a growing phenomenon of Israeli citizens being recruited to carry out assignments for an enemy state.
Prosecutors also cited mitigating factors, including Granovsky’s full admission to the charges, his mental health and the relatively short period during which the offenses were committed. They pointed, however, to his criminal record and the seriousness of his crimes.
Granovsky’s public defenders, Anat Yaari and Frida Wall, argued that his case differed from other Iran-linked cases because his actions were not motivated by nationalism or ideology.
They described Granovsky as living on the margins of Israeli society, struggling with drug addiction and complex mental health issues. They said he acted for financial gain to fund his drug use.
The defense stressed that Granovsky was “not the classic spy” and had refused to harm innocent people. Granovsky expressed remorse and said he had not intended to harm Israel.
Judge Merav Greenberg approved the plea agreement, describing the agreed sentence as “heavy and severe, but appropriate to the seriousness of the acts and warranted under the circumstances.”
She described the case as “a serious series of offenses that severely harm the security of the state and its citizens,” committed for financial gain.
The court took into account Granovsky’s confession, acceptance of responsibility and expression of remorse. Greenberg said his admission reflected “genuine and meaningful acceptance of responsibility” and noted that without it, he would have faced an even longer prison sentence.
Although Granovsky refused some assignments and declined to harm innocent people, Greenberg said he nevertheless carried out numerous actions at the operative’s direction.
“Even if the defendant committed the acts for financial gain, with outrageous indifference to the consequences of his actions, that does not diminish their great severity,” she wrote.
The judge said some of the assignments were intended to damage Israel’s social fabric and create chaos and agitation. She said the timing made the offenses particularly serious because they were committed during Israel’s war following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Greenberg also addressed the growing pattern of Iranian efforts to recruit Israelis in exchange for money.
“The phenomenon is gaining momentum, and the courts have a significant role in stopping it,” she wrote. “The need to deter others is the imperative of the hour.”
‘Threw a grenade — and sent the footage to the Iranian operative’
In a separate case Wednesday, the Jerusalem District Court convicted four residents of the Beit Safafa neighborhood of Jerusalem — Mamdouh Khader, Omri Abu Hamida, Mahmoud Khader and Mohammed Taha — of security offenses connected to assignments for an operative acting on Iran’s behalf.
The four pleaded guilty to charges stemming from activities for which they received payment from the operative.
According to the amended indictment, the operative contacted another defendant in the case and assigned him tasks intended to harm Israel's national security. Those assignments included forming a terrorist cell and working to assassinate a nuclear scientist and members of the scientist’s family, obtaining weapons and grenades and producing staged footage purporting to show attacks on a soldier’s home and a police vehicle.
Prosecutors said Mamdouh Khader and Abu Hamida were convicted of failing to prevent an act of terrorism after joining a trip to the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, one of Israel’s leading scientific research institutions.
During the trip, they were told that the visit was part of an assignment received from an Iranian operative, prosecutors said. After the group was prevented from entering the institute, they filmed its entrance and the videos were sent to the Iranian operative.
Abu Hamida later asked why they had filmed the site and was told that a person the Iranians wanted to assassinate lived there, according to prosecutors. Neither man acted to prevent the alleged plot.
Mahmoud Khader and Taha were convicted of assisting in contact with a foreign agent.
Khader helped spray and document graffiti in Jerusalem, drove another defendant to collect two grenades and helped obtain a fake police license plate intended for use in staged footage purporting to show an attack on a police vehicle.
Taha proposed throwing a stun grenade at an empty house in the village of Qatanna to create footage that would appear to show an attack on a Jewish person’s home.
He arrived at the location with the grenade, asked his friends to throw it, filmed the act and sent the video to the defendant who was in contact with the Iranian operative, according to prosecutors.
In another incident, Taha kept possession of the phone used to communicate with the operative in an effort to make it more difficult for authorities to locate it.

Türkiye enters era of domestically produced aircraft in Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:50:39 UTC
01:50:39 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
- ‘As commander of Turkish Air Force, nothing could make me prouder than flying an aircraft produced by our own country,’ says Gen. Rafet Dalkiran
Türkiye’s new-generation basic trainer aircraft Hurkus-II is preparing to enter the Turkish Air Force’s inventory, marking the beginning of a new era for the country’s military aviation.
Haluk Gorgun, head of Türkiye’s Defense Industries Secretariat, and Turkish Air Force Commander Gen. Rafet Dalkiran participated in flights aboard the domestically developed Hurkus-II and Hurjet aircraft.
Gorgun said Türkiye’s first Hurkus-II aircraft would be delivered to the Air Force Command shortly.
“When you sit in an aircraft’s cockpit, you feel much more closely the immense effort extending from the design table to the production line, and from testing to flight,” he said on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal.
“Now, this effort is about to yield another result. We will deliver our first Hurkus-II aircraft to our Air Force Command very soon,” he added.
In a video shared after the flight, Gorgun described the impending delivery as a milestone for Türkiye.
“For the first time, Türkiye is delivering a domestically produced aircraft to its own armed forces. It was very, very meaningful,” he said.
“These were also the final tests today. Being part of these final tests was an additional source of pride for us.”
Dalkiran also highlighted the significance of flying aboard a Turkish-made aircraft.
“As commander of the Turkish Air Force, nothing could make me prouder than flying an aircraft produced by our own country,” he said.
After the flight, Gorgun asked Dalkiran whether the aircraft had passed the test and whether its acceptance had been completed, to which the commander responded: “Excellent. Done.”
 
- Hurjet demonstrates domestic capabilities
Gorgun and Dalkiran also participated in a Hurjet test flight during which the aircraft demonstrated Türkiye’s domestically developed radar capabilities.
During the flight, the Hurjet P2 aircraft used Aselsan’s domestically developed MURAD active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar to detect and lock onto the Hurjet P1 aircraft.
Gorgun said the Turkish Air Force’s personnel would receive their initial training aboard the Hurkus before completing advanced training with the Hurjet.
“The HURJET flown by our commander, which was equipped with the AESA radar developed by Aselsan, locked onto the HURJET we were flying from a certain distance,” he said.
“This was a first. Experiencing this, witnessing a historic moment and walking this path together with our entire team and valuable personnel is immensely meaningful,” he added.

Houthis deny Yemen military claim they laid mines in Bab al-Mandeb

The Iran-aligned group effectively took control of the strait last week after routing Saudi-backed forces, threatening renewed disruption through the vital maritime corridor.
The Houthis have also reportedly begun fortifying their positions in the mountains overlooking the strait in anticipation of a counter-offensive by pro-government forces.
Hussain Al-Bukhaiti, a pro-Houthi Sanaa-based journalist, told The New Arab that the report was “false news”.
“Why do we need to put mines in the Red Sea or in Bab al-Mandeb if we have anti-ship ballistic missiles? We can launch attacks against any ship we choose,” he said.
Since taking control of the area, the Houthis have said they would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but continue to impose a blockade on Saudi ships.
Arab and European countries have expressed alarm over the advance, which consolidates Houthi control over the strait and comes as the waterway has become increasingly important for Saudi oil shipments since the US-Israeli war on Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil markets have been on edge over the past week as the Houthis' gains and a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have triggered fresh concerns about global supply.
The attack, which Saudi authorities said was launched from Iraq, has taken the pipeline offline, forcing the kingdom to rely exclusively on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military. Oil prices surged to their highest levels since May following the news.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
US-Houthi talks
US officials held talks with Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend, a few days after their advance on the Red Sea coast, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The meeting was reportedly arranged by Oman and held at the US embassy in Muscat.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a terrorist organisation in March 2025 but later entered negotiations with them to end the two-month conflict.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has appealed to the US and UK to provide military support in its fight against the Houthis. The Trump administration reportedly told Riyadh it would not get directly involved.
Bin Salman travelled to Cairo on Tuesday to discuss the situation with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
A statement by Egypt's presidency said the two leaders called for freedom of navigation through the Red Sea to be maintained.
Drone over Mecca
The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, triggering condemnations across the Muslim world.
A coalition spokesperson said its forces had allegedly intercepted a drone over the holy city.
Houthi armed forces spokesperson Yahya Saree denied the claims, calling them “fabrications and lies”.
“Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,” he said.
The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, saying that “the security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line”.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a bloc of 57 Muslim countries, denounced the “heinous attacks... against the city of Mecca and the Madinah region”.
The Houthis also said on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi warplane.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's help and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military buildup in the skies of Marib province,” Saree said in a statement.
Saudi warplanes have launched more than 450 airstrikes in Yemen this week, he said.

Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
September 16, 2026
Before taking off for Europe, CanadianPrime Minister Mark Carney had set the tone for his visit, saying he was seeking to build a "unique alliance" with the EU. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported that Canada was considering becoming an "associate member" of the EU, while not aiming for full membership.
In her State of the European Union address on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated that she was indeed open to such an expanded partnership.
"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," she said, addressing European lawmakers and Carney in Strasbourg, France. "That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."
Von der Leyen said a EU-Canada partnership would cover a broad range of areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
Carney is expected to outline his vision for future relations between the EU and Canada during a speech at the European Parliament on Thursday.
What degree of collaboration could be possible between the EU and Canada?
EU member states are closely integrated economically, sharing a common market, trade and customs policy. When it comes to establishing ties with non-EU countries, a list of different options present themselves. They range from free trade agreements that scrap tariffs and trade barriers, to association agreements which may include political elements, to far-reaching economic arrangements such as participation in the common European market, as is the case for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
The EU has already negotiated association agreements with Turkey, Israel and Ukraine. These have different objectives and may or may not mark a preliminary step toward full membership.
Patrick Leblond, an expert on international economic relations at the University of Ottawa, urges a little more caution around the term "association agreement." He considers it unlikely that Canada would adopt European laws or join the EU single market or customs union, which would mean imposing common external tariffs.
Leblond says Carney is likely more interested in forming a kind of alliance that deepens cooperation on issues of economic security and defense.
Closer defense cooperation?
"We have, in a way, taken the US [security] umbrella for granted on both sides. We have underinvested in our militaries," Leblond told DW.
He added that the focus was now on joining forces, for example in the production of military equipment and the development of new technologies.
Security analyst Anand Sundar of the European Council on Foreign Relations also sees great potential for European-Canadian cooperation when it comes to defense. Canada spends about 70% of its defense budget on US-made equipment, according to Sundar. Carney wants to change that, the analyst said, as it would pay off for Canadians to be part of European defense projects to get "more bang for their buck."
Canada has joined the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program. It provides EU member states with up to €150 billion ($173 billion, CA$ 241 billion) in loans for the joint procurement of military equipment. To qualify for funding, no more than 35% of the cost of the components can come from countries outside the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or Ukraine. Yet because Canada joined the SAFE program by paying a fee, more lenient procurement rules apply to its companies.
Nevertheless, Canadian companies still face significant hurdles for producing and purchasing weapons in partnership with European firms, Sundar told DW. The big question is how far the EU is willing to relax its own rules, the expert says, which could also have implications for non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom or Norway.
'Underrated defense power'
"But the biggest draw for the European Union is really the fact that that Canada is an underrated defense power," Sundar told DW.
Canada, the expert added, spends more on defense than the 14 smallest EU member states combined.
The North American country invests 2% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, Sundar said, with an increase expected in the coming years. Canada, like other NATO countries, has committed to spending a total of 5% of its GDP on defense by 2035, of which 3.5% will go towards military equipment and the remaining 1.5% towards other defense-related areas.
Protecting critical infrastructure
The EU and Canada also intend to discuss potential cooperation in the field of critical infrastructure expansion, such as the joint operation of space satellites or maintenance of fiber-optic cables in the North Atlantic, Leblond told DW. The goal here, too, is to become less dependent on the US and its companies. Moreover, Canada has oil and gas reserves that could meet some of the bloc's energy demands.
Trade relations between both have already been codified through the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force on a provisional basis in September 2017. The agreement eliminates nearly all tariffs between the EU and Canada, while also ensuring mutual market access for industrial goods, agricultural products and services. It even enables European companies to participate in public tenders in Canada.
Economic analyst Leblond, however, believes that CETA's potential has not yet been fully realized. He says many Canadian companies still tend to focus on the US and less on Europe. He believes it is the government's responsibility to provide more information about CETA and the opportunities it offers, saying the level of exchange envisaged in this format could also be intensified.
Why is Carney seeking closer ties with Europe?
In January, Carney delivered a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in which he warned of a "rupture in the world order," calling on the middle powers to act together.
"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said.
Indeed, in recent weeks, the US-Canda trade war has continued escalating.
Even though it is clear that Canada cannot sever ties with the US, there is a growing belief inside Canada that the country needs additional allies, Leblond told DW. And the Europeans are considered trustworthy, he added.
Ultimately, the Canadians would want to see such an alliance, whatever form it may take, translate into concrete initiatives and projects through which Europeans and Canadians can help one another.
