Russians Prepare for an Election With Less Choice Than Ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:03:00 UTC
01:03:00 KST

In the hit 2007 Russian political satire “Election Day,” a group of radio executives is sent to a provincial region as it elects its new governor. Their task is to manufacture a candidate, win over voters and make sure the right person gets elected.
One song from the film’s soundtrack, sung by punk rocker Sergei Shnurov, would become a national catchphrase: “Elections! Elections! All the candidates are motherf***ers!”
But what was once political comedy now feels like a glimpse into a different era. Elections at that time may have been cynical and manipulated, but they still involved a semblance of genuine competition.
Nearly two decades later, as Russia prepares to elect a new State Duma for the first time since invading Ukraine, the question is how much of that competition remains.
Wartime elections
When Russians head to the polls on Sept. 18-20, they will elect 450 lawmakers in the lower-house State Duma as well as regional legislators and governors across the country’s 11 time zones.
Among the major political parties contesting seats in the Duma — Russia’s most important election this year — are the ruling, pro-Kremlin United Russia party, the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), A Just Russia, New People and Yabloko.
Experts say these parties’ platforms are broadly similar and largely back the Kremlin’s policies. The only exception is Yabloko, which is campaigning on an anti-war platform but was barred from the State Duma’s party-list vote, the nationwide contest in which voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate.
United Russia, which currently holds 321 of 450 seats in the State Duma, is widely expected to win a majority of the vote. Even so, experts say that the elections remain an important gauge of public sentiment.
The election will also be held in the four partially occupied regions of Ukraine that Moscow claims to have annexed and where fighting continues.
Voting will be spread over three days, while 33 regions will offer electronic voting — two measures that critics say could make it easier to manipulate the results.
'Electoral authoritarian system'
Experts differ on how and when exactly Russia’s elections lost their competitiveness, but they agree that the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 marked a major turning point.
Political scientists now describe Russia as an electoral authoritarian system: an autocracy that continues to hold elections while tightly controlling the conditions under which they take place.
“You can't openly call for an end to the war and you can't openly challenge [President Vladimir] Putin's legitimacy,” said Ora John Reuter, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and expert on Russia’s electoral politics.
“Beyond that, the candidates and parties that are running have a little bit of freedom to debate other policy issues within those constraints,” he told The Moscow Times.
Exiled political commentator Ekaterina Schulmann said that by 2011, the authorities were already shaping the composition of successive Dumas by “the desired degree” and that they “did not differ significantly from one another.”
For the Kremlin, United Russia “must always have a constitutional majority,” while the other parties must know their place and “not interfere with the smooth and energetic legislative process — essentially the rubber-stamping of bills sent over from various branches of the executive government,” Schulmann explained.
It would be wrong to believe that “there were some remnants of freedom before, which have only now been completely stamped out,” she added.
But the range of political alternatives available to voters has narrowed sharply, even by formal measures, experts say.
“Over the past 10 years, the number of legally registered political parties has dropped from 75 to 17,” said Vadim Ternovoy, an expert with the Election Atlas project.
For the first time since 2012, “only parties that are exempt from collecting voter signatures were able to nominate candidate lists for the State Duma elections,” he said. Under Russian law, parties must collect 200,000 voter signatures to appear on the ballot unless they are already represented in the State Duma or have won seats in at least one regional legislature.
The number of candidates in elections at all levels has fallen by around 20% since 2022, Ternovoy said. This figure refers to those who put themselves forward, rather than those who were ultimately registered — which suggests that even the willingness to participate in elections is declining.
Experts linked the decline in interest to the growing imbalance between the risks and benefits of being in politics. Repression has affected not only civil society activists and anti-war Yabloko candidates, but also members of the Communist Party and LDPR in some regions, Ternovoy said.
Even prominent United Russia members have complained of pressure from within their own party during primaries and some have faced criminal charges, he added.
“As a result, many people who might take part in elections with a realistic chance of doing well simply choose not to run. This leaves voters with fewer opportunities to hear different views and make their own voices heard,” he said.
Transition
The erosion of Russia’s political and electoral system began in the mid-2000s as the Kremlin tightened its grip on the media and moved against oligarchs who had amassed political influence. But at times, this decline slowed, and some reforms briefly opened space for political competition.
Direct gubernatorial elections were abolished between 2004 and 2012, though this restriction remains in some regions. Direct mayoral elections have also been scrapped in regional capitals and major cities, while regulations governing political parties have been tightened.
More recent measures include rules barring “foreign agents” from running for office and greater restrictions on independent election observers.
The independent election watchdog Golos, which had documented election violations since 2000, was forced to close last year after its co-chair was jailed in what supporters called an attempt to silence the group.
These restrictions were “in fact a response to growing public demand for greater political participation and accountability from the authorities,” Ternovoy said, pointing to late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny’s attempt to mount a presidential campaign in 2018, as well as mass protests over the exclusion of opposition candidates from the 2019 Moscow City Duma elections.
Is there any competition left?
The fate of Yabloko, the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform, is perhaps most illustrative of the 2026 campaign’s limitations.
In its decision to bar Yabloko from the party-list vote to the State Duma, a court cited alleged violations involving foreign funding, campaign materials distributed through restricted foreign platforms and copyright rules. The party denies wrongdoing.
Yabloko still has registered candidates running in single-member districts, a defined geographic area that elects one lawmaker to the State Duma, as well as in regional legislative elections.
In total, at least 36 opposition candidates were barred from the State Duma and regional legislative elections, according to the exiled outlet Vyorstka. More than half of those cases involved Yabloko candidates, Vyorstka said.
Seventeen of these candidates were disqualified over online posts mentioning Navalny, who is on Russia’s federal list of “extremists and terrorists.” Seven others were barred for sharing links to Facebook and Instagram, which are banned in Russia, or for displaying the platforms’ logos.
Nikolai Bondarenko, a prominent Saratov politician running for the State Duma with the Communist Party, was disqualified after being fined 1,000 rubles ($12) over a photo of Navalny posted in 2024 on a Telegram channel bearing his name. Bondarenko denied having a connection to the channel.
Boris Nadezhdin, whose anti-war presidential campaign in 2024 drew long lines of supporters before the authorities disqualified him, is another would-be candidate this year.
He was barred from running for the State Duma as an independent after being fined for displaying alleged “extremist” symbols in a photo of Navalny, briefly detained and designated a “foreign agent.” He left Russia in August.
Amid these restrictions, the public’s interest — and even interest from candidates themselves — appears limited.
While televised debates are formally part of the election campaign, Putin has never participated in one and many United Russia candidates have followed suit.
In Ryazan, the state broadcaster Rossia 1 spent two consecutive days unsuccessfully trying to assemble State Duma candidates in its studio. Both times, the presenter ended the program shortly after the introduction because no one had shown up.
Sixty-six percent of Russians do not know when the State Duma elections would be held, while 28% said they do not plan to vote, according to a survey published in June by the independent pollster Levada Center.
Among those who do not plan to vote, 41% said their vote would make no difference, while 24% do not believe the elections will be fair.
Yet Ternovoy said the initial registration of anti-war party Yabloko — even without any particularly recognizable party leaders — nonetheless triggered “a largely spontaneous mobilization of part of the anti-war electorate.”
And when Yabloko was barred from the party-list vote in the Duma, Election Atlas documented an 80-fold surge in interest in the party across social media.
Ternovoy compared this to Nadezhdin’s brief 2024 presidential campaign, which coincided with a decline in support for the war in opinion polls.
“Had Yabloko remained on the ballot [for the State Duma party list], it would, under the law, have been entitled to free airtime on the country’s largest television and radio stations starting in late August ... which could have had a significant impact on public opinion,” he added.
He pointed to Election Atlas’ monitoring of social media, which last month showed that people were more concerned with the growing restrictions on political competition than with what officials including Putin were up to.
“To me, this looks like an important shift in public opinion and, quite possibly, the main outcome” of these elections, he said.

Unknown

2026-09-16

01:02:34 KST

Ethem Emre Özcan and Gizem Nisa Demir
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) has delivered 2,000 tons of flour to Palestinian refugees and displaced families in Lebanon.
A ceremony marking the delivery was held on Wednesday at the Port of Beirut, attended by Türkiye's Ambassador to Lebanon Murat Lutem, Lebanese Higher Relief Council chief Bassam Nabulsi, and the director of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in Lebanon, Dorothee Klaus.
The flour will be distributed to Palestinian refugees and families displaced by Israeli attacks.
Türkiye is expected to continue providing assistance to people in need across Lebanon.
 
- 'Our solidarity with Lebanon will continue'
Speaking to Anadolu, Ambassador Lutem said Türkiye's assistance to people in need in Lebanon was ongoing.
He recalled that the Health Ministry had recently sent medicine to Lebanon and said Türkiye had also supported efforts to meet the shelter needs of families displaced by Israeli attacks.
In addition to tents, Türkiye has sent food, clothing, and other humanitarian supplies, Lutem said.
"We see that the aid we have provided over the past 2 1/2 years has exceeded 4,000 tons as of today," he said.
Lutem said Lebanon had endured suffering it did not deserve and noted that around 300,000 Lebanese people remained unable to return home due to destruction caused by Israeli attacks.
"Our country's support will continue. Our president has said very clearly: The security of our country does not begin at our borders; it begins in Damascus and Beirut," he said.
Highlighting Türkiye's historic ties with Lebanon, Lutem added: "Our solidarity with Lebanon will continue."
'Sincere expression of solidarity, friendship, and humanitarian partnership'
Nabulsi said the delivery represented a continuation of Türkiye's longstanding support for Lebanon through state institutions and humanitarian organizations, particularly AFAD.
"This meaningful initiative is a continuation of the support and humanitarian assistance that Türkiye has provided to Lebanon for many years through its state institutions and humanitarian organizations, particularly AFAD," he said.
Nabulsi emphasized that Turkish institutions had stood by Lebanon during difficult periods and crises, adding that Lebanon placed great value on cooperation with Türkiye.
He identified Türkiye and UNRWA as two key partners in addressing humanitarian needs in Lebanon.
The flour was particularly important for meeting families' basic needs and supporting food security, Nabulsi said.
"We do not view this contribution merely as material assistance. It is a sincere expression of solidarity, friendship, and humanitarian partnership," he said.
Nabulsi thanked Türkiye for its longstanding support and continued cooperation with Lebanon.
'Assistance will ease families' expenses'
Klaus thanked Türkiye and AFAD for the aid during her address at the ceremony.
She said the assistance would help ease families' financial burdens.
"This shipment will provide flour and bread to Palestinian refugees and displaced Lebanese people who have been affected by the economic consequences of the latest conflicts affecting Lebanon," she said.

EU states join growing list mulling social media ban for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

The European Union proposed banning children under 13 from social media on Wednesday, joining a growing push to curb minors’ access to the platforms.
More than 20 countries around the world have now taken steps to block or restrict children going online on social media, according to an Agence France-Presse (AFP) tally.
Seven have measures already in place or set to be implemented, with their policies targeting children under the age of 15 or 16.
Australia was the first country to introduce a blanket ban on social media for under-16s, at the end of 2025.
The U.S. state of California has also recently moved to tighten restrictions on minors' access to social media.
Under plans unveiled Wednesday by EU chief Ursula von der Leyen in the European Parliament, the bloc will also only allow limited, supervised access until the age of 15, after months of considering ways to protect minors from features designed to keep users hooked.
Social media has been banned for under-16s in Australia since December 2025.
However, the ban so far appears to have been widely circumvented by teenagers, according to data released in August.
Brazil began implementing measures in March requiring platforms to link the accounts of users aged under 16 to those of their parents, while also requiring platforms to verify users' ages.
In China, where the internet is tightly regulated by the state, minors' access to social media has been restricted progressively since 2019.
Initial measures imposed time limits and curfews on online gaming, before similar restrictions were extended in 2023 to social media and streaming platforms.
Indonesia has banned social media for under-16s since March.
Malaysia has taken a similar approach, with legislation coming into force in June excluding under-16s from major platforms.
Türkiye is set to join the list after passing legislation to bar under-15s from social media in April.
The law is expected to take effect in late 2026.
The United Arab Emirates announced a ban on social media for under-15s last month, with implementation set for around in a year's time.
The governor of the U.S. state of California, Gavin Newsom, signed around a dozen laws on Sept. 10 aimed at protecting children online, including one banning platforms from offering addictive features to under-16s. The law will take effect in early 2027.
Across the 27-nation EU, the Greek government announced in early April that it intends to ban social media access for under-15s from January 2027.
In Germany, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz supports restricting or even banning social media for children, an expert commission has proposed two options: gradual restrictions by age, or platform-specific restrictions.
Austria and Slovenia are also preparing legislation to prohibit access for under-14s and under-15s, respectively.
A similar debate is under way in Sweden, where a government commission has proposed banning social media for under-15s by early 2028.
In Denmark, the government announced in October 2025 that it would propose banning "several social media platforms" for under-15s.
The Irish government has warned that it is considering legislating in the absence of an EU decision.
Outside the EU, the Norwegian government will present a bill by the end of the year to ban access for those under 16.
Britain is looking to ban social media for under-16s by early 2027 under a measure planned by its former prime minister, Keir Starmer.
A curfew would also be implemented for children aged 16 and 17 as part of the plan.
Canada unveiled a bill on June 10 that would also set the minimum age at 16.
New Zealand followed Australia's lead in August with a bill that would ban social media platforms from offering their services to under-16s.
In Portugal, lawmakers from the ruling right-wing party introduced a bill in February that would set the age of "digital majority" at 16 for independent access to social media platforms, online services, games and apps.
In Spain, a bill unveiled in March 2025 and now under consideration would raise the minimum age for opening a social media account to 16.
Italy is also considering legislation that would ban social media for under-15s.
In France, parliament approved legislation this summer to ban social media for under-15s, but the Constitutional Council, the country's highest constitutional authority, struck it down on freedom-of-expression grounds.
President Emmanuel Macron has pledged to introduce a new "legally robust" law by spring 2027.

Von der Leyen’s call for talks on pausing AI can’t quell extinction risk fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:01:43 UTC
01:01:43 KST

STRASBOURG — Ursula von der Leyen has declared herself an AI “optimist.” Yet in the face of rising warnings of the technology’s threats to humanity, the European Commission president on Wednesday sounded far more like a realist — and one with limited room for maneuver.
Von der Leyen didn’t shy away from the topic in her State of the European Union address, calling AI one of the “two tipping points of our time” and acknowledging the dangers it poses.
"The warnings about the future of AI should make us more serious about safety," said key European Parliament AI lawmaker Axel Voss after the speech, touting von der Leyen's focus on "Europe's human-centered approach to AI."
Advertisement
Still, the Commission president's most concrete response to recent calls by top Silicon Valley bosses to pause AI development was a cordial invitation to join her in a “discussion” on the matter.
And while citing the EU’s standing AI rules as a possible building block for global regulations, von der Leyen didn’t use her much-anticipated speech to call on fellow world leaders — particularly U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping — to come together to act.
Her diffidence risks turning Europe into a bystander amid a global scramble over calls to regulate frontier AI, which the U.S. leader has dismissed as a “hoax” — just ahead of a high-level summit between Trump and Xi that will likely explore how to set global standards on AI safety.
Von der Leyen identified “the right diagnosis” in her speech, said Max Reddel, CEO of the Arq Foundation, a Brussels-based think tank focused on AI. But, he added, “the question is whether we can move at the speed and decisiveness she calls for.”
In her speech, von der Leyen had to cater to two demands: that Europe stay competitive in the global AI race while also meeting the moment on global AI safety — a frenzy sparked by a warning from a former Anthropic engineer that AI could lead to the end of the human race.
Von der Leyen said she was an “optimist” that AI could benefit humanity, but noted that “risks have sharply come into focus.”
Advertisement
Europe also finds itself in a bind in addressing AI safety because it is playing catch-up on the business and tech fronts, without a real frontier-lab competitor to U.S. and Chinese firms.
Brando Benefei, an Italian MEP, noted that Europe has regulation knowhow but is playing catch-up with the U.S. and China in the race to build out the technology. “Von der Leyen rightfully says that the AI Act positions Europe to lead on AI safety,” he said of the dilemma, while “Europe must [also] now build capacity.”
In her 73-minute address von der Leyen devoted a notable portion to AI risk scenarios, citing an incident this summer in which OpenAI-powered agents hacked another AI company, and issuing warnings regarding “recursive" self-improvement, which is when AI models create a smarter version of themselves, leading to an unstoppable loop.
The Commission president held the line that the EU executive has been repeating for a week in the face of such threats: We have a law for that. Under the bloc’s four-year-old Artificial Intelligence Act, she said, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic must address the risk of losing control of a model.
Von der Leyen largely sidestepped giving her own assessment of whether the development of frontier AI models should be paused, citing calls from tech CEOs to do exactly that.
“I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier,” she said.
Advertisement
But that part of the speech didn’t include an appeal to AI frontrunners U.S. and China, and their leaders Trump and Xi, to act on it — only an offer to middle powers like the U.K. and Canada “and others” to team up on testing the models.
Von der Leyen received good marks from MEPs and AI safety experts for her comments on what is within Brussels’ remit, which highlighted the limits on the actions the EU can take.
“Finally, the Commission is addressing the frontier risks,” said German Greens lawmaker Sergey Lagodinsky in a statement shared with POLITICO. He praised the “middle powers alliance and dialogue with AI labs” as “the right step.”
But he also urged the Commission to “limit the risks” by implementing the AI Act “ambitiously.”
Daniel Privitera, executive director of the Berlin-based KIRA Centre AI think tank, commended von der Leyen for acknowledging the risks, but said more is needed than just a meeting.
“Inviting CEOs to talk about how Europe can help with efforts to pace the frontier is a first step, but Europe can and should do more to help with a safe transition to transformative AI,” he said.
Advertisement
He added that her pitch to team up with the U.K. and Canada to test models is “promising,” as it gives the middle powers “strategic leverage vis-a-vis the two AI superpowers in the world.”
But mentioning the testing of models is one thing; promptly creating a mechanism for doing so is quite another. “We urgently need these things,” Privitera said, “as catastrophic risks from frontier AI become more salient.”

France: TotalEnergies cut-price fuel spikes controversy among rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:00:54 UTC
01:00:54 KST

TotalEnergies service stations are accused of distorting competition as they display France's lowest-priced fuel. Supermarkets that usually sell fuel as a loss leader to pull in customers are furious, along with independent service stations.
French motorists are clogging TotalEnergies service stations to fill up with discount gasoline, but its rivals are crying foul, accusing the energy giant of distorting competition with the encouragement of the government.
TotalEnergies, which pumps crude oil and refines it into gasoline, also has an extensive network of filling stations throughout France, where retail sales are usually dominated by supermarkets selling gasoline at or near cost in order to pull in customers.
But as oil prices shot higher this spring due to the US-Iran war, the highly profitable company announced a cap of €1.99 per litre of E10 (€2.25 per litre for diesel), considerably less than the national average of around €2.15 per litre — and up to nearly €2.50 in other areas, including Paris.
The cap, which has been in place intermittently for the past five months, has already cost the company 250 million to 300 million euros.
While it is a hefty expense, higher oil prices helped the French company double its first-half profit to 11.2 billion euros.
TotalEnergies introduced the cap when political pressure was building to introduce a tax on windfall profits being made by energy companies.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called on the company in May to put in place "a generous cap".
Its chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, has made clear it will abandon the cap if a special tax is put into place.
"There's nothing forcing us" to keep the cap in place, Pouyanné said recently.
"If a tax is introduced, we'll draw our conclusions and TotalEnergies won't have any more price caps," he added.
Fear of widespread protest
With a presidential election seven months away and France's economic situation worsening, the government is keeping close watch.
"Today, the public authorities are quite happy a private company is doing the job, perhaps in their place," said Jacques Goisque, head of the FF3C trade association that represents a thousand independent service stations.
But there are limits to how much relief TotalEnergies can provide.
The most recent jump in fuel prices has prompted calls to demonstrate, reminiscent of the so-called yellow vest movement in 2018.
At the time, a plan to increase fuel taxes sparked widespread protests from low- and middle-income workers who stood to take the biggest financial hit, snowballing into a challenge to the economic policies of President Emmanuel Macron.
Macron called on the government on Wednesday to tackle the questions about fuel supplies and prices.
Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon noted that around one in ten filling stations in France lacked at least one fuel, with the vast majority of them being TotalEnergies stations.
She said the government would seek to ensure sufficient supplies and gain some regulatory flexibility on refineries.
The goal is "to push prices down as much as possible, or at the very least to keep their increase under control", she said.
'Distortion of competition'
The FF3C group of independent petrol stations lodged a complaint in mid-July with France's competition regulator for unfair competition.
"There is an upstream player with a dominant position that takes advantage of it to set very aggressive prices that are below market levels," said FF3C's Goisque.
"We can't sell at a loss."
The supermarkets that usually sell gasoline as a loss leader to pull in customers are also furious.
Michel-Edouard Leclerc, head of the leading supermarket chain E.Leclerc, said "refiners are lining their pockets" while it is impossible for retail distributors to compete.
"We can't go any lower than what our prices are today," he said. "We don't have a cent of margin in our filling stations."
More than a dozen filling stations closed over the past weekend on the island of Corsica.
"Despite the efforts of our supplier, our purchase price exceeds Total's retail price by several dozen cents," the stations said in a statement.
They denounced "the state failing to regulate prices", which "allows an integrated group that benefits from considerable upstream margins to dictate, to blackmail, leading to this distortion of competition."
While the price cap has financial costs for TotalEnergies, it pays well in terms of public image for a company that has frequently faced criticism for the low amount of taxes it pays in France in comparison with the profits it earns globally.
The price cap has "above all earned the company a large amount of goodwill among the French," Pouyanné, the chief executive, said recently.

Higher emotional intelligence is tied to vigorous exercise in women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:00:15 UTC
01:00:15 KST

A large new study reveals that emotional intelligence is linked to distinct physical activity habits in women, but not in men. Women with higher emotional intelligence scores tended to engage in more vigorous exercise and spend less time sitting, while these associations were absent among male participants. The research was published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences.
Emotional intelligence refers to a person’s ability to perceive, regulate, and effectively use their own emotions as well as the emotions of others. High emotional intelligence is often associated with better psychological well-being, social functioning, and resilience to stress. Emerging evidence suggests that these emotional skills are also tied to biological aging and daily habits, including how people manage their health.
Regular physical activity is widely recognized as a foundation for both mental and physical health across the human lifespan. Health behaviors like exercise, sleep, and sedentary routines influence emotional regulation through shared biological pathways in the brain and the endocrine system. Specifically, the autonomic nervous system and regions of the brain involved in processing emotions respond to the physiological demands of exercise.
Despite this recognized connection, researchers have lacked detailed information on how emotional intelligence relates to specific intensities of exercise. Most previous epidemiological studies have focused on general mental health outcomes or moderate-intensity activities. Vigorous physical activity, such as running or heavy weightlifting, presents unique regulatory demands because it repeatedly induces acute physical stress followed by recovery. This cycle of stress and recovery is thought to strengthen the body’s overall stress-adaptation mechanisms.
Public health researchers Albertas Skurvydas, Daiva Majauskiene, and their colleagues at Vytautas Magnus University and Klaipeda University in Lithuania designed a study to examine these relationships. They aimed to determine how emotional intelligence relates to various physical activity intensities, sedentary behavior, sleep, and body mass index. The research team also wanted to see if these behavioral associations varied by age or sex, given that men and women often display different patterns in both emotional processing and exercise habits.
The researchers recruited a large sample of 6,368 adults in Lithuania, ranging in age from 18 to 64. Women made up about 71 percent of the survey participants. The researchers used a cross-sectional design, meaning they collected data from the participants at a single point in time rather than tracking them over months or years. Participants completed questionnaires distributed through social media platforms, providing self-reported data on their daily routines and demographic backgrounds.
To measure emotional intelligence, the participants completed the 33-item Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test. This widely used psychological tool asks individuals to rate their agreement with statements about how they manage their own feelings and react to the emotions of others. Higher total scores indicate a greater capacity for emotional perception and regulation.
The research team assessed exercise habits using the Danish Physical Activity Questionnaire. Participants recalled their activities over an average 24-hour period within the previous week. The researchers categorized these activities by intensity using metabolic equivalents, a standard metric that estimates the energy expenditure of different physical tasks compared to a resting state.
Activities were grouped into categories ranging from sedentary time to light, moderate, and vigorous physical activity. The researchers also calculated each participant’s body mass index based on self-reported height and weight.
After analyzing the survey responses, the researchers identified distinct age and sex patterns. Emotional intelligence scores increased with age for both men and women. Overall, women exhibited higher emotional intelligence scores than men and engaged in more light-intensity physical activity. Men, on average, had a higher body mass index and reported substantially more time spent engaged in vigorous physical activity.
The researchers then used statistical models to look for independent associations between emotional intelligence and specific health behaviors. Among women, higher emotional intelligence scores were linked to a greater amount of time spent doing vigorous physical activity. Women with higher emotional intelligence also reported less sedentary behavior. These associations held true across the entire adult age range studied.
The behavioral results for men were entirely different. Among male participants, age was the only factor positively associated with emotional intelligence. The researchers found no statistically significant links between a man’s emotional intelligence and his sleep duration, sedentary time, or participation in any intensity of physical activity.
When comparing the two groups directly, the statistical models confirmed that the association between vigorous physical activity and emotional intelligence was markedly stronger in women than in men. The data showed no corresponding interaction with age. This indicates that the relationship between intense exercise and emotional regulation in women did not fade or intensify as they got older.
The study relies entirely on cross-sectional data, which means it cannot determine the direction of the relationship between emotional intelligence and physical activity. Individuals with higher emotional intelligence might be more motivated to engage in demanding exercise, or the repeated physiological stress of vigorous activity might help train emotional regulation systems over time. It is also possible that a bidirectional relationship exists, where both factors continually reinforce one another.
The use of self-reported questionnaires introduces the possibility of reporting bias. Participants might have overestimated their physical activity levels or provided answers that they believed were socially desirable on the emotional intelligence assessment. This shared method of data collection can sometimes inflate the apparent associations between different variables.
The authors note that the observed associations, while present, were small in magnitude. The behavioral factors measured in the study explain only a limited portion of the total variance in emotional intelligence scores. Additionally, the recruitment method via social media may have attracted individuals who are already more health-conscious than the general population. Because the study was conducted entirely in Lithuania, the results might not fully generalize to populations in other cultural or socioeconomic environments.
Future research will need to employ longitudinal designs to track how changes in physical activity habits influence emotional intelligence over time. Experimental studies could also help determine whether modifying a person’s exercise routine directly alters their emotional regulation capabilities across the adult lifespan. Such studies would clarify whether behavioral interventions can effectively support emotional functioning.
The study, “Higher emotional intelligence is linked to greater vigorous physical activity and lower sedentary behavior, specifically among women across adulthood,” was authored by Albertas Skurvydas, Ausra Lisinskiene, Aiste Barbora Uspuriene, Egle Kemeryte-Ivanauskiene, Dovile Valanciene, Asta Sarkauskiene, Jurga Bucaite-Vilke, and Daiva Majauskiene.

He thought Ukrainian army uniform would hide what he did under occupation. It didn’t. Man who guarded Kherson’s Russian-run prison drew eight years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:00:06 UTC
01:00:06 KST

A man who guarded a Russian-run prison in occupied Kherson, where captured members of the Ukrainian resistance were held, has been sentenced to eight years. After Ukraine retook the city, the collaborator tried to disappear into a Ukrainian army unit before the Security Service of Ukraine caught him, the SBU said on Telegram.
A real prison term for a collaborator is less common than it sounds. Ukraine has opened hundreds of collaboration cases since 2022, but many have halted due to their location in occupied territories or Russia.
He guarded the occupiers' prison
After Russian forces seized Kherson in 2022, the man agreed to serve as a "junior inspector" in the administration of a Russian prison set up in the regional capital, the SBU said. In the post, he guarded the cells and the facility's perimeter, which the occupiers used to hold people from the resistance movement in south of Ukraine. Kherson's right bank was under Russian control from March until Ukraine liberated it in November. The left bank remains under occupation.
He hid inside the army
When the right bank was freed, the collaborator initially stayed put, staying in his apartment, the SBU said. He then mobilized into a Ukrainian military unit, where the service said he hoped to lie low. Instead, SBU officers detained him in March 2025 at one of the army's training centers.
A real term is the exception
The court found him guilty of collaboration under the criminal code's article on the offense and, taking his cooperation with investigators into account, sentenced him to eight years, with a ban of up to ten years on holding posts in state bodies or law enforcement.
The case was built by the SBU in Mykolaiv and Kherson oblasts in cooperation with the National Police, under the Mykolaiv specialized defense prosecutor's office.

The Royal Air Force has launched Exercise Cobra Warrior 26-2, the largest test of the UK’s homeland defence.
RAF and NATO forces are being put through demanding training designed to rehearse joint warfighting capability and provide a deterrent to our adversaries.
Running from 14 September to 2 October 2026, the exercise brings together aircraft, personnel and command-and-control specialists from the UK, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the United States to rehearse the rapid integration, resilience and combat effectiveness required to deter threats, defend the homeland and, if necessary, fight as part of a NATO force.
“The return of great power competition across the globe and the significant, and growing, threat posed by Russia to the UK and NATO makes this, by far, the most dangerous period in my 35 years of military service. This is why the RAF is investing in our People and our capabilities – to defend the UK, deter our adversaries and, if necessary, defeat them across the Air and Space domains. Cobra Warrior gives us the opportunity to practise our response to aggression, ensuring we are testing our defences and ability to operate alongside NATO partners during a real conflict.”
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth
Chief of the Air Staff
Cobra Warrior showcases the breadth of RAF capability with Typhoon, F-35 Lightning, P-8A Poseidon and Air Mobility Force aircraft, including Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, operating alongside German, Italian and American aircraft and personnel. The exercise is a practical demonstration of the RAF’s Warfighting Ready and NATO First priorities. It tests how the RAF protects and operates from the home base, integrates with allies at speed, sustains complex missions and develops the warfighting mindset needed to fly, fight and win in contested airspace.
Cobra Warrior also marks the culmination of UK Qualified Weapons Instructor courses, the RAF’s pinnacle post-graduate warfighting qualification. By training at scale with NATO allies, the exercise strengthens collective defence, improves interoperability and demonstrates how the RAF is preparing for the demands of modern conflict.
"We are truly honoured and excited to be here at RAF Waddington to train alongside our NATO allies and international partners. Cobra Warrior represents the premier tactical training environment, offering an invaluable opportunity to enhance our interoperability, refine joint tactics, and strengthen our collective readiness. Participating with our aircraft and personnel allows us to test our capabilities in complex, contested and high-threat operational scenarios. The integration and shared expertise between our nations are what make the Alliance so strong. We look forward to a productive exercise and to flying shoulder-to-shoulder with our partners and qualifying Weapons Instructors."
Major Valerio C.
Italian Deployment Commander
RAF Cranwell is welcoming German Air Force personnel participating in the exercise, underlining the RAF’s commitment to NATO interoperability and strengthening the professional relationships that enable allied air forces to operate together in crisis and conflict.
"RAF Cranwell is delighted to welcome our German Air Force colleagues to the Station for Exercise Cobra Warrior. This Exercise provides an opportunity to strengthen our long-standing professional relationships, train alongside one another and build lasting friendships. Visits such as these are invaluable and we are incredibly proud to welcome them to RAF Cranwell."
Wing Commander Mathew Thornton
Station Commander RAF Cranwell

Poland Builds Border Fortifications After Russian Drone Strikes 2 km From Its Territory
Unknown

00:59:14 KST

- Category

Poland Builds Border Fortifications After Russian Drone Strikes 2 km From Its Territory
Polish military engineers are constructing fortified security posts near border crossings with Ukraine following recent Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure close to the Polish border.
The announcement was made by Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz on X on September 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Poland’s Armed Forces General Command, engineers from the 4th and 18th regiments are building observation and security positions near the border crossings at Dorohusk, Medyka, and Korczowa.
The fortifications are being constructed using HESCO barriers, collapsible wire-mesh containers that can be filled with sand or soil to provide protection.
The measures come after a Russian attack reached infrastructure just kilometers from Polish territory. On September 13, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region, roughly two kilometers from the Polish border.
Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia reported that no one was injured, adding that its monitoring team had warned the train crew of the threat in advance.
The same Russian attack also damaged infrastructure near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk international border crossing, a key transport route connecting Ukraine and Poland.
The strike near Poland came just days after another Russian attack targeted a Ukrainian border crossing with Moldova. Overnight on September 9, Russian forces struck the Starokozache border crossing in Odesa region, killing two civilians and injuring three others.
Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper reported that the two people killed were civilians who were near the checkpoint when the strike occurred. The attack also damaged infrastructure at the crossing and in the surrounding area.
In the aftermath of the strike, emergency crews evacuated another 16 people by bus to a safer location.

====================================================================================================

Shock and anger in Kosovo as former president convicted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:59:00 UTC
00:59:00 KST

Shock in Kosovo as Hague convicts former President Thaci
September 16, 2026
The announcement of the verdict was greeted with shock and profound disappointment in Pristina.
Thousands of citizens had gathered in the main square of Kosovo's capital, many waving flags of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to follow the announcement live on large screens. Similar gatherings took place across the country in Kosovo's main cities.
When it became clear that the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague had found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes — along with former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi — the crowd fell silent.
The silence was followed by calls for justice and chants of support for the four men.
Groups of citizens began trying to demolish sections of the perimeter wall surrounding EULEX, the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo, which was deployed in Kosovo after the country's declaration of independence from Serbia in 2008 and continues to operate to this day.
Large numbers of Kosovo police officers and special units intervened to prevent further damage and incidents.
Political leaders in Kosovo respond
It wasn't just the people on the streets who were disappointed: Kosovo's political leaders were quick to respond to the news from The Hague.
"The conviction of the former KLA leaders is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war," said Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, who was present in the courtroom in The Hague when the verdict was announced. He called it "a major blow to the state and to the domestic narrative."
"Kosovo experienced the war itself. We know what the KLA war was about, and we know that there was no criminal mechanism to harm any population. It is a sad, unjust and undeserved decision," he said.
Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti called the verdict an "unacceptable injustice."
"The conviction and such a severe sentence for four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army is an unacceptable injustice, a great and harmful punishment," Kurti said on Wednesday.
The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which was founded immediately after the war by Thaci and several other former KLA leaders, described the guilty verdict as an "unjust and unacceptable judgment," stressing that "the battle for justice continues until the very end."
"In The Hague, the right of our people, who fought for freedom, survival and liberation from the Serbian state regime that killed, expelled and terrorized Kosovo Albanians, was dealt a severe blow," the PDK said in a statement. "For us, this judgment represents a major injustice because it is based on allegations and material that we consider fabricated and which, over the years, have been promoted by the Serbian state apparatus and propaganda in an effort to criminalize the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army."
The response from Kosovo's acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, was similar. She described the convictions of the four men as "a severe blow to their families, deeply shocking news for the Republic of Kosovo and a grave moment for the Albanian nation wherever it lives."
"On a day like this, the weight of this decision cannot be separated from the history from which we have emerged," Haxhiu wrote in her statement. "Kosovo experienced firsthand the violence of a state apparatus that killed civilians, committed massacres, expelled hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes and left behind thousands of people killed or missing. This experience is an indelible part of the memory of Kosovo and the Albanian nation."
Charges of crimes against humanity dismissed
The panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague handed down the guilty verdicts over three years after the start of the trial and nearly six years after the four men were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 1998–99 Kosovo War.
Though the three-judge panel dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity, the four men were convicted of war crimes against civilians and political opponents who did not support the KLA during the war.
Thaci, who was indicted while serving as president of Kosovo, was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Jakup Krasniqi, who served as a KLA spokesman and later as speaker of Kosovo's parliament on several occasions, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison. Kadri Veseli, who headed the KLA intelligence service during the war, was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Rexhep Selimi, who served as chief inspector of the KLA military police, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.
Defense lawyers for the men said they would appeal the verdict.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which was set up by the Kosovo Assembly (parliament) in 2015, is staffed by international judges and based in The Hague. It deals exclusively with cases relating to allegations of crimes committed by members of the KLA during the Kosovo War.
Before returning to join Kosovo's struggle for independence in 1998, Thaci had been a student in Switzerland.
As a political leader of the former KLA, he received support from Western leaders, who invited him to participate in the 1999 peace talks in Rambouillet, France. At the time, Thaci was seen in Kosovo as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.
About 13,000 civilians — most of them Kosovo Albanians — were killed, and more than 1 million people were displaced during the war, which saw Kosovo, at the time a Serbian province, fighting for independence.
Following NATO's intervention against Serbian forces and their withdrawal from Kosovo, Thaci founded his own political party and came to power, first as Kosovo's prime minister and later as president.
In 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia, a move rejected and still not recognized by Belgrade, Moscow and Beijing. Kosovo's statehood is, however, recognized by over 100 countries.
Relations between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense after over 15 years of negotiations between the countries, mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.
Thaci, who, like the other three men, denied the charges against him, resigned as president of Kosovo in 2020 to face the charges and defend himself in The Hague.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

A drone came down beside a Bundeswehr air base, weeks after Berlin blamed Moscow for the Leipzig airport attack

15:58:55 UTC
00:58:55 KST

A large-scale police operation is underway after a drone of unknown origin crashed 1 kilometer from a Bundeswehr base, German media outlet Bild reported on 15 September.
Drones have repeatedly flown over German military bases, and German prosecutors are already treating one August find near Ukraine-bound cargo as attempted sabotage. Germany's military counterintelligence has tied repeated sabotage on German soil to Russia, with high probability. Neither the owner nor the origin of this drone is known. Russia has denied involvement in earlier incidents, some of which Germany has officially attributed to it.
Discovery near airbase triggers large-scale search
Parts of the drone were found east of Lake Steinhude, the media outlet said. The crash site is one kilometer from the Bundeswehr's Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, the German military confirmed to the outlet. The drone crashed in an open, uninhabited area, the state criminal police office said. After the debris was discovered, authorities launched a large-scale search operation in the area to find additional parts of the UAV, according to Bild.
Investigators do not yet know who owns the drone
The search continues, and the state criminal police office says there are so far no indications of a danger to the public. Investigators learned about the discovery on Monday and want to analyze any other drone parts they find to determine its origin, the media outlet reported. Only then could more be said about the circumstances of the crash, it added.
Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
Drones have been spotted over Bundeswehr bases many times
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the number of reports of drone sightings has "increased significantly" and become "more consistent," a spokesperson for the Bundeswehr Operations Command told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) in August.
"Overall, several hundred suspected drone overflights have been reported in the area of the German Armed Forces in recent years," the command spokesperson told RND.
What came before this crash
Germany is the busiest front in Russia's covert campaign in Europe. A Semtex-laden drone turned up beside a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, and investigators this month named a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal. Berlin blamed Moscow and ordered Russia's Bonn consulate closed.
Two Bulgarians were arrested over a September arson at a Munich building site between two defense-tech headquarters, a day after two attempts to sabotage the power grid that Germany has not attributed. Germany suspects a planned assassination of a Bavarian drone maker's boss, watched by agents hired for single jobs.
The throwaway agents Moscow sent after a Bavarian drone boss arming Ukraine—and how Germany stopped them
Not every strand leads to Moscow. German military counterintelligence this week attributed part of the drone activity over Bundeswehr sites to Chinese intelligence.
Elsewhere the tempo holds: Polish prosecutors have opened more than a hundred espionage cases in 20 months, and in the Netherlands a former commander of US Army forces in Europe said Russian saboteurs attacked the rail network and tried to kill him, which Dutch Railways said they knew nothing about.

Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:58:50 UTC
00:58:50 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on September 16 that an armed Russian drone recovered from a beach at Rusinowo carried a live warhead, neutralized on site, and preliminarily identified as a Gerbera 2.
Col. Bartosz Okoniewski, deputy district prosecutor for military affairs at the District Prosecutor's Office in Poznań, informed the agency that the recovered aircraft had been armed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"It contained a fragmentation-high-explosive warhead together with a fuze," Okoniewski stated to PAP. "We managed to separate the warhead from the aircraft itself, and then, for safety reasons, the warhead was neutralized right there on the beach."
He added that the warhead was detonated on the evening of September 15. The airframe, now stripped of its warhead, was moved to a military site for detailed inspection, where preliminary findings indicated it was a Gerbera 2 type produced and used by Russia.
The drone was located on September 14 near Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec, in Poland's West Pomeranian region. Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the recovery that day, describing the object as a Russian military unmanned aircraft.
On September 16, Poland's Military Gendarmerie reported that soldiers had extracted, examined and neutralized components that could pose a threat, then secured the drone for laboratory analysis.
The on-site inspection, as Okoniewski detailed to PAP, was led by a prosecutor from the military division of the Szczecin-Niebuszewo District Prosecutor's Office. The Military Counterintelligence Service, military and police sappers, gendarmerie officers and the fire service also took part.
The prosecutor's office has opened a case under a preliminary classification of causing an event that threatens the life or health of many people, or property of great value, through an explosion. Investigators are additionally examining the use of an aircraft to cross the state border without the required permission.
The Gerbera is a cheap Russian drone typically fielded as a decoy and a reconnaissance platform alongside heavier Shahed-type strike aircraft, though armed and reconnaissance variants also exist.
Built largely from plywood and foam, the type carries a standard range of roughly 700 kilometers, with examples recovered abroad fitted with extra nose fuel tanks to stretch that reach.
Ukrainian estimates have put the production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, enabling the drones to be launched in numbers that force defenders to expend far costlier interceptors.
According to PAP, Kosiniak-Kamysz linked the recovery to the downing of a Russian drone over Lithuania on the night of September 15. He suggested that the aircraft found in Poland might also have flown over Lithuania on September 13, where it was tracked and targeted for an attempted neutralization.
The drone then, in his account, "crossed the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region and most likely operated over the Baltic." He indicated that Poland and Lithuania would investigate jointly, with the services of both countries cooperating.
The recovery followed a run of similar incidents across the Baltic in September. On September 13, an object that crossed from Lithuania into Russia's Kaliningrad region was identified as a drone.
Around the same time, a resident near Finland's Pellinki archipelago found an unmanned aircraft assessed as a Russian-made Geoscan 701. Two weeks earlier, on August 31, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea roughly 30 kilometers north of Łeba.

Legal aid caseload reaches 154,552 files as debt, family disputes dominate report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:56:13 UTC
00:56:13 KST

The Justice Ministry’s Legal Aid Department opened 154,552 files in 2025, with family and debt matters accounting for most of its caseload, according to its annual report published on Wednesday.
Personal status matters made up 35% of the files opened, and debts accounted for 30%, the report’s breakdown shows. Civil matters accounted for a further 10%, and National Insurance matters for 7%. The figures describe files opened during the year, rather than the number of people represented or the outcomes of their cases.
The report also describes legal work arising from the October 7 attacks and the ensuing Israel-Hamas War. It says the department opened over 3,500 files for bereaved families, families of hostages and returnees, and families of those murdered in the attacks between October 2023 and the second half of 2026.
The department says it assists eligible immediate family members with benefits, inheritance, banking, housing, and insurance matters, among others. Returned hostages can also seek help with legal needs connected to their captivity or the war. Assistance under this program is provided without a financial means test.
Some families are pursuing recognition as victims of hostile acts after witnessing attacks on relatives by telephone, messages, or video.
Dozens of bereaved and hostage families appealing decisions
The department says it represents dozens of bereaved and hostage families appealing decisions by the approving authority. It argues that relatives who witnessed the attacks remotely should also be eligible for recognition; according to the report, the appeals remain pending before an appeals committee at the Tel Aviv District Court.
The report also points to a 2025 Supreme Court ruling in a debt case handled by legal aid. A woman whose actual earnings were below minimum wage challenged a monthly payment set during her debt proceedings. The court held that minimum wage could not simply be treated as proof of what she earned or could earn and sent the matter back for an assessment of her individual circumstances. The ruling did not itself set a new payment amount.
In another development, a law passed in December 2025 allows people aged 65 and over to seek legal aid in specified cases of alleged financial exploitation, without a financial means test. The exemption applies to those cases, rather than to every legal matter involving an older person.
The wartime recognition appeals remain an open question. Their outcome will determine whether the families bringing those claims qualify for recognition on the basis of what they witnessed remotely.

Middle Eastern states have been too dysfunctional for years, and they were unable to respond to the scale of the threats posed by the Iranian axis, Alkhuzaie said.

Syria parliament votes to abolish Assad-era terrorism court, nullify rulings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:55:50 UTC
00:55:50 KST

Syria's parliament voted on Wednesday to abolish an Assad-era terrorism court and nullify the legal effects of its rulings, state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV reported, in one of the first significant legislative moves by the country's new assembly.
The Counter-Terrorism Court was established in 2012 as then-president Bashar al-Assad sought to suppress an uprising against his rule, and it was used to prosecute thousands of Syrians for terrorism-related offenses.
The move formalizes the court's abolition after Syria's new authorities had already treated it as defunct. In June 2025, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served in what he described at the time as the "abolished Counter-Terrorism Court."
Syria's March 2025 constitutional declaration had also called for abolishing the effects of what it described as unjust rulings issued by the court, including returning confiscated property.
The United Nations Human Rights Committee said in 2024 that the 2012 law establishing the court failed to adequately provide key judicial guarantees and raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, and the court's independence. It also noted that the court could depart from ordinary procedures during prosecution and trial.
UN: Assad government used court to prosecute tortured detainees
The UN's International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism said in a 2024 report that the Counter-Terrorism Court formed part of the judicial system through which detainees held by Assad-era security agencies could be prosecuted. The report documented widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment across the government's detention system.
Wednesday's vote came during the opening weeks of the first parliament formed since Assad was toppled in December 2024. The chamber convened for the first time in July.
The vote is among the assembly's first major legislative decisions after it spent its initial sessions establishing its internal rules and committees. It held a hearing this week with Syrian Education Minister Mohammad Abdul Rahman Tarkou over the state of the country's schools and is due to question the energy minister on Thursday over a sharp rise in fuel prices.

00:55:26 KST

Saudi Arabia faces a potential two-front conflict as it weighs what to do about the Houthi advance. The Houthis swept down the coast of the Red Sea and took islands near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Meanwhile, the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq attacked the key East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis then attacked Saudi Arabia as well and even threatened Mecca on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia has been in talks with US Central Command, other Gulf states, and partners about what to do next. Reports even suggest Israel and Saudi Arabia could have new interests in common. However, it doesn’t appear the US will challenge the Houthis.
The US is monitoring the situation, and the Houthis are spreading messaging to the White House that they are not seeking confrontation. Riyadh now appears more alone than before. The other Gulf states were considering a meeting in Oman with Iran. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has praised Oman, months after US President Donald Trump had threatened Oman.
What comes next?
Reuters reported that the Houthi advance represents one of Saudi Arabia’s most serious setbacks in Yemen in years. The offensive illustrated weaknesses in Saudi Arabia’s assessments and the command structure of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters in Yemen. Saudi Arabia’s crown prince went to Cairo this week. Egypt could back a Saudi response.
The Houthis maneuvered tens of thousands of fighters into position last week around September 8 before their offensive. Media in the region initially suggested Houthi setbacks.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces subsequently collapsed during the offensive on the Red Sea. Riyadh knows it will not get major Western backing. It is in the same position it was in 2019 after the Iranian attack on Abqaiq.
The Houthi gains also have broader strategic implications. Control of territory overlooking Bab el-Mandeb could enable the group to threaten shipping and Saudi energy exports while expanding connections toward the Horn of Africa. Currently, the Houthis have not done much, but their presence means they can strike easily. This is a Sword of Damocles hanging over the Bab el-Mandeb.
The Houthis have launched attacks on Saudi Arabia over the last month. Over the last two months, they also sought to invite Iranian regime members to Sanaa, provoking Saudi Arabia. Iran is showing that although isolated by a US blockade they can strike elsewhere.
As such, the Iranians now put Saudi Arabia in a multi-front bind. Saudi Arabia is a wealthy country, and it has many strategic sites. It has more to lose than the Houthis or Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Recently, the Houthis said they fired dozens of drones and missiles at the kingdom, prompting the Saudi Civil Defence to issue brief alerts in the neighboring cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha, according to reports at Arab News and Al-Arabiya.
“Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told reporters on Monday. They claim the Houthis are “entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests.”
Houthi strikes target air hangars, radars, ammunition
The Houthis are upping their rhetoric. The Houthis’ military spokesman Yahya Saree said this week that the group’s strikes targeted “fighter jet hangars, radars, runways, ammunition depots” at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait. The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia has carried out 300 air strikes.
The Houthis have shown they can weather the storm and make advances in the past. Formerly known as Ansar Allah, they emerged from Yemen’s Zaydi Shi’ite community in the north of Yemen. The movement fought a series of wars against Yemen’s government between 2004 and 2010.
After the upheaval of the Arab Spring, the Houthis expanded beyond their traditional stronghold in Saada and seized Sanaa in September 2014. Yemen’s President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi eventually fled, setting the stage for regional intervention.
In March 2015, Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition of Arab countries, including the United Arab Emirates and Egypt, to intervene in Yemen.
The war initially pushed the Houthis back from southern Yemen, but the group retained Sanaa and much of the northern highlands. Years of air strikes and ground fighting failed to dislodge them. However, there was a crisis with Qatar in 2017, and the Saudi focus on Yemen shifted.
The Houthis developed increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities. Iranian technology and weapons transfers helped transform their capabilities.
UN investigators have documented Iranian-origin missile components and UAVs and concluded that the Houthis could not produce many of their more sophisticated systems without foreign support. By 2017-2021, the Houthis were often launching ballistic missiles and drones deep into Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-UAE coalition increasingly fractured over the last two years. Abu Dhabi backed southern forces, called the Southern Transitional Council, while Riyadh continued supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
The UAE reduced its direct military presence beginning in 2019. A UN-mediated truce beginning in April 2022 largely ended Houthi cross-border attacks on Saudi Arabia. Beginning in late 2023, the Houthis launched missiles and drones toward Israel to back Hamas.
Israel carried out strikes on the Houthis as well. The US tried to protect shipping in the Red Sea. In March 2025, the Trump administration even carried out strikes on the Houthis. However, the Houthis have shown, time and again they can emerge from these blows.

French Prosecutors Seek Up to 5 Years in Prison for Sons of Ex-Yemeni President Saleh Over Ill-Gotten Assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

Reported by
Two sons of late Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh could face up to five years in prison as a Paris court hears charges against them for allegedly laundering tens of millions of euros in embezzled state funds and corruption proceeds.
The trial, which opened September 7 at the Paris Criminal Court, follows a 2019 investigation launched by France's National Financial Prosecutor's Office (PNF) based on a tip-off from Swiss authorities, the PNF confirmed to OCCRP on Wednesday.
Brothers Ahmed Ali Saleh, 54, and Khaled Ali Saleh, 39, are accused of laundering proceeds from corruption and laundering embezzled public funds as part of an organized criminal group. Both men are being tried in absentia and are believed to be residing in Dubai.
Their father, Ali Abdullah Saleh, ruled Yemen for 33 years until his ouster during the Arab Spring in 2012. The former president was accused of plundering billions in state funds throughout his long tenure to enrich his family and inner circle. He was killed by Houthi rebels in 2017.
Judicial investigations resulted in the seizure of more than 36,80 million euro ($42,45 million) in illicit assets, according to the PNF. The frozen assets include “seizures of bank accounts and of several real estate (apartments and private mansions in Paris).” The seized real estate alone is valued at 22,6 million euro (over $26 million), “plus a 10 million euro ($11,53 million) receivable representing the outstanding balance from the sale of one of the properties,” explained the press officer of the PNF.
French prosecutors are asking the court for a five-year prison sentence and an arrest warrant for Ahmed Ali Saleh. For his younger brother Khaled, the PNF requested a four-year prison term, also accompanied by an arrest warrant.
In addition to prison time, prosecutors requested the formal confiscation of two Paris real estate properties, $3 million held in Swiss bank accounts, and nearly 3 million euro ($3,5 million) held in real estate holding companies. The French prosecutor also requested prison sentences for two other co-defendants involved in the brothers' alleged scheme.
A Sanaa-based NGO called the Awtad association has joined the case as a civil party, aiming to see the assets and money confiscated by the courts returned to the local population, France24 reported.
When contacted, the defense lawyers for the two brothers stated that their clients did not wish to comment.
However, the attorneys explained that, during the hearing, they emphasized that the prosecution's case relies on fundamental weaknesses
"First, because the fraudulent origin of the funds invested in France has not been proven; it stems solely from vague, general allegations found in open sources, with no tangible evidence to corroborate them,” one of the defense lawyers explained. “Second, because our clients' acquisition of real estate in France was carried out with total transparency and with the full knowledge of the French authorities.”

Some of the drivers were formally employed by a sole proprietorship registered to Timofeyev, while others dealt with him simply as a customer who ordered routine freight transport.
The case materials indicate that the defendants left Chelyabinsk driving trailers trucks carrying prefabricated frame houses. However, unbeknownst to the drivers, Ukrainian drones that had been concealed in the roof of each structure.
On June 1, 2025, when the trucks were positioned near military airfields in the Ivanovo, Murmansk, Irkutsk, Ryazan and Amur regions — where drivers had been instructed to make their deliveries — SBU personnel remotely activated the drones, which then attacked the Russian military facilities. The investigation estimated the damage to Russia’s Defense Ministry at 2 billion rubles ($23.7 million). The investigation lasted more than a year and ultimately filled more than 90 volumes before being sent to the Prosecutor General’s Office. The Insider previously reported on the claimed damage.
Kommersant reported that last week First Deputy Prosecutor General Anatoly Razinkin refused to approve the indictment, saying that investigators had failed to find direct evidence of the drivers’ guilt and that the circumstantial evidence was not enough to send the case to trial. He returned the case to the Investigative Committee for further investigation. The Investigative Committee disagreed and appealed Razinkin’s decision to Prosecutor General Alexander Gutsan.
While the dispute between the agencies remains unresolved, the Moscow City Court ruled that there were no longer any legal grounds to keep the defendants in pretrial detention, and the four drivers were released Sept. 16. The men deny any wrongdoing and describe themselves as “Russian patriots,” adding that after the drones emerged from their trucks, they themselves called the police, tried to shoot down the drones, and attempted to minimize the damage caused to the airfields.

Turkey Calls Militarization of Greek Aegean Islands a Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:53:27 UTC
00:53:27 KST

Turkey considers the militarization of Greek islands in the Aegean Sea, which Ankara considers subject to demilitarization under international treaties, a threat to its security.
Hakan Fidan, Turkish Foreign Minister, made the statement while speaking with Anadolu Agency journalists.
During a visit to Syria on September 13-14, the minister said Ankara had “very serious concerns” about the deployment of weapons and military infrastructure on the islands.
“The arming of islands that have demilitarized status is a threat to us,” Fidan said.
He noted that Turkey had repeatedly conveyed its position to Greece through bilateral diplomatic channels and had also raised the issue with NATO and the United Nations.
According to Fidan, the dispute over the islands’ status has remained a key element of Greek-Turkish disagreements in the Aegean Sea since the 1960s.
The Turkish minister also called on Greece to comply with its treaty obligations and avoid creating additional security problems amid instability in the region. At the same time, Fidan said Turkey was interested in good-neighborly relations with Greece and continuing positive momentum in bilateral relations.
Turkey considers several islands in the eastern Aegean to be subject to restrictions on military presence under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty.
Ankara includes Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Ikaria, Lemnos, Samothrace, and the Dodecanese islands among them. The Turkish Foreign Ministry claims that Greece is violating its obligations by deploying military forces and weapons there.
Greece rejects this interpretation of the international treaties. On September 4, Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis said that Athens would not give up its “sovereign right to have whatever defense force structure it chooses” and does not consider the defense of the islands a subject for negotiations with Turkey.
Athens maintains that the status of Lemnos and Samothrace changed following the adoption of the 1936 Montreux Convention, while the Treaty of Lausanne does not require the complete demilitarization of Lesbos, Chios, Samos, and Ikaria, but only imposes specific restrictions on military infrastructure and troop numbers.
Regarding the Dodecanese, Greece recognizes the demilitarization provisions of the Paris Treaty but points out that Turkey is not a party to it. Greece also invokes its right to self-defense in the face of threats to its territory.
On January 12, 2025, Greece strengthened its air force with the final of 24 Dassault Rafale fighter jets it had ordered. These aircraft form the backbone of the Greek Air Force’s 332nd Squadron, the only unit responsible for patrols in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean areas within its area of responsibility.

Govt scraps road tax for small and mid-sized cars, and motorbikes
We are getting rid of one of the taxes Italians hate most says Meloni
ROME,
16 September 2026, 21:37
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
Meloni, abolizione del bollo pensata per chi usa auto e moto ogni giorno - ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The government on Wednesday abolished road tax for small and medium-sized cars as well as motorbikes, with Premier Giorgia Meloni saying cabinet had done away with one of the taxes Italians hate the most. The cabinet approved the abolition of the vehicle ownership tax (bollo auto) for small and medium-powered cars—the types largely used by families for daily commuting, Palazzo Chigi sources said. The exemption also applies to motorcycles, though each citizen is entitled to the benefit for only one vehicle. The measure covers all motorcycles and over 70% of cars currently on the road, amounting to approximately 14.5 million vehicles in total. The move aims to lighten the tax burden associated with owning a car or motorcycle for a vast number of Italians. "Today, the Government is scrapping one of the taxes Italians hate most," commented Meloni. In 2027, the car tax exemption will apply to vehicles with a power output of up to 80 kW, according to the decree approved by the cabinet. The exemption also extends to mopeds, provided the same owner is not already claiming it for a car.
Meloni said that while the opposition talked about wealth taxes, the government was abolishing a property tax.
"While others talk about wealth taxes, we are removing a property tax," she said on social media.
"Today in the Council of Ministers," she wrote, "we approved the abolition of the vehicle tax for small and medium-power cars—up to 80 kW—and for motorcycles, with an exemption applying to just one vehicle per citizen."
She said the vehicle tax abolition would especially benefit daily car and motorcycle users.
"We have chosen to repurpose some of the funds used until now to combat high fuel costs into a simple, structural measure designed primarily for those who use cars and motorcycles every day—whether for work, taking their children to school, or getting around.
"It is a concrete step: we are abolishing one of the taxes Italians dislike most and continuing on the path of reducing the tax burden."
The tax burden in Italy is around 43%, and has risen slightly in recent years.
