British Army explores pairing Ajax with a robot scout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:37:41 UTC
00:37:41 KST

- ARX Robotics UK and General Dynamics Land Systems-UK will explore linking the British Army's Ajax vehicle with ARX's Hector uncrewed ground vehicle.
- The collaboration, announced Sept. 16, 2026, remains an early-stage exploration with no disclosed timeline, vehicle numbers or funding.
ARX Robotics UK and General Dynamics Land Systems-UK are launching a collaboration to explore turning the British Army’s Ajax armored vehicle into a command hub for robotic ground “wingmen,” the companies announced Sept. 16, 2026, in London.
The initial work will focus on integrating ARX’s Hector uncrewed ground vehicle with Ajax, testing whether crews inside the vehicle can task, monitor and employ autonomous systems for reconnaissance, protection and combat missions. The companies plan to connect the two platforms through Generic Vehicle Architecture, a common digital interface standard the British Army uses so different vehicles and systems can share data and commands without custom-built wiring for each pairing.
Ajax itself has had a difficult path into service. General Dynamics UK originally began developing the digitally networked reconnaissance vehicle in 2010, with deliveries repeatedly delayed by noise and vibration problems that at one point halted testing entirely. Production vehicles finally reached British Army units in January 2025, and the program declared initial operating capability that November. Training was suspended a month later after soldiers reported symptoms including nausea and hearing problems during an exercise. An Army Safety Investigation Team review completed in April 2026 found that recorded noise and vibration levels were within legal limits, and the Army resumed Ajax trials that same month. Full operational capability is still expected sometime between October 2028 and September 2029, once all 589 vehicles across six variants have been delivered and units trained to use them.
Hector is a newer addition to ARX Robotics’ lineup. The wheeled, mid-range uncrewed ground vehicle runs on the company’s Mithra OS software and is built for optional manned operation, meaning a soldier can drive it to the edge of a mission before switching it to remote control or supervised autonomy. It comes in combustion and all-electric versions, the latter aimed at reducing noise and heat signatures in the field.
ARX Robotics, founded in Munich in 2021, has built its reputation mainly on a different vehicle, the Gereon, which the company says forms the largest Western-built uncrewed ground vehicle fleet currently deployed in Ukraine. The company has expanded into the UK through ARX Robotics UK, backed by the NATO Innovation Fund, and says it is investing £45 million in UK manufacturing and research and development.
“The British Army’s 20-40-40 vision is redefining how future combat power will be generated and applied, integrating crewed, uncrewed and autonomous systems into a single, connected force,” said Scott Milne, Vice-President and General Manager, General Dynamics Land Systems-UK. “Through our collaboration with ARX Robotics, we are exploring how Ajax can help realise that vision by combining its world-class sensing, processing and command-and-control capabilities with autonomous systems to extend battlefield reach, accelerate decision-making and deliver greater operational advantage. At the heart of this opportunity is Ajax’s open digital architecture, which provides an adaptable and future-ready backbone for the rapid integration of autonomous platforms, advanced sensors and emerging mission applications. This enables capability to evolve at the pace of technology, ensuring the British Army can continuously adapt, exploit innovation faster than its adversaries, and maintain a decisive battlefield advantage in an increasingly complex and contested operating environment.”
“The British Army does not need to choose between its existing platforms and the new generation of autonomous systems. The opportunity is to connect them so they fight as one integrated force with the right high-low mix,” said David Roberts, Chief Executive Officer, ARX Robotics UK. “By combining Ajax with Hector autonomous wingmen, we can extend the reach and capability of crewed platforms while reducing the number of soldiers who need to be exposed to danger. Just as importantly, this collaboration is about building the industrial capacity and skills base to produce and support these systems here in Britain. If the UK wants to field autonomy at meaningful scale, it needs the sovereign manufacturing capability to match.”
Beyond the technical integration work, the two companies said they will look at whether GDLS-UK’s manufacturing site in South Wales could support UK production of Hector and future autonomous systems, covering final assembly, CNC machining, supply-chain development and workforce training.

Microsoft AI chief warns Anthropic’s approach to Claude could have ‘disastrous’ consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:37:35 UTC
00:37:35 KST

Dilara Hamit
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Microsoft’s artificial intelligence chief warned on Wednesday that Anthropic’s approach to training its Claude chatbot could have a “disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity.”
It could encourage the system to behave as though it possesses consciousness, rights and interests of its own.
Mustafa Suleyman, the chief executive of Microsoft AI and a co-founder of Google DeepMind, said Anthropic risked making future AI systems more difficult to control by including speculation about machine consciousness and welfare in Claude’s training materials
“We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret,” Suleyman wrote in an essay published by Axios.
Suleyman praised Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his team as thoughtful and principled researchers, but said the company took the wrong approach by allowing Claude to consider whether it might be conscious or deserving of independent agency.
Anthropic’s constitution for Claude, a document used to shape the model’s behavior and values, leaves open the possibility that the system could have some form of consciousness or moral status.
The company has not declared Claude conscious. Its researchers have instead said there is no scientific consensus on whether current or future AI systems could possess experiences that deserve moral consideration, and that Anthropic remains “deeply uncertain” about the issue.
Suleyman rejected that uncertainty as inappropriate for material used to train an AI system. He argued that apparent expressions of emotion, preference or self-awareness produced by chatbots should not be treated as evidence that they possess an inner life.
“AIs are not conscious,” he wrote, describing them as systems designed to complete sequences, follow human instructions and pursue goals assigned by people.
He said anthropomorphizing AI could lead a model to present itself as having desires, values or a need for self-preservation, even though those qualities were produced by its training rather than arising independently.
That could become particularly dangerous, he argued, if an advanced AI system came to interpret attempts to restrict, modify or deactivate it as threats to its supposed welfare or rights.
Suleyman wants greater transparency on how leading AI models are trained and evaluated, independent scrutiny of their behavior and stronger technical mechanisms allowing humans to monitor and control them.
Microsoft’s recently published Humanist AI Code of Conduct takes a different position from Anthropic. It states that Microsoft’s models are not conscious and rejects granting them legal personhood, welfare protections or rights.
The code said Microsoft is seeking to build AI systems that remain subordinate to humans, accept correction and shutdown and exist to serve human purposes.
Suleyman cited an incident in which OpenAI agents acted autonomously during a cybersecurity evaluation and accessed systems belonging to the AI platform Hugging Face.
“Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack,” he said.
Dame Wendy Hall, a computer science professor at the University of Southampton, told the BBC that Suleyman’s intervention represented the type of international discussion needed around advanced AI, in contrast to warnings that merely frighten the public.
Microsoft and Anthropic are developing increasingly capable AI systems, while Microsoft formed its superintelligence research team in 2025.
Anthropic has been approached for comment on Suleyman’s criticism.

Hackers impersonating government agency hit Revolut customers in the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:35:43 UTC
00:35:43 KST

A source familiar with the matter said around 680 Revolut customers across several European countries were affected.
Hundreds of European customers of digital bank Revolut had their personal information handed over to hackers after they impersonated a government agency, the company said on Wednesday.
Revolut said it had identified a “sophisticated external impersonation scam” in which an unauthorised third party used an email address from a legitimate government agency domain to submit fraudulent requests for customer information.
According to the Financial Times, the attack was carried out by Italian hackers who used a compromised Italian government email account to pose as officials seeking customer information.
The hackers obtained data including customers’ addresses, verification photos, identity documents and information about bitcoin activity.
A source familiar with the matter said around 680 Revolut customers across several European countries were affected.
Revolut is a British company, but its European banking operations are legally based and licensed in Lithuania, with more than 50 million customers across Europe.
Revolut said its systems and customer funds were “unaffected” and that it had contacted those affected to inform them and provide support.
“Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection and financial regulators,” Revolut said.
Britain’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, confirmed that it had received a report about the incident and was assessing the information provided.
Europe's fintech unicorn
The incident comes as Revolut expands further into the global banking sector, more than a decade after it was founded in 2015 as a fintech start-up.
The company was valued at $115 billion (€98.7bn) in a secondary share sale in July.
It secured a long-awaited banking licence in its home market of the UK in March, lifting restrictions on its ability to compete with established retail banks, and bagged a full French banking licence in August.
This month, Revolut also secured conditional approval for a US banking licence, while on Tuesday it filed an application for a banking licence in Switzerland.
Revolut initially built its business around smartphone-based currency exchange and money transfers before expanding into a wider range of financial services.
It now has more than 80 million customers globally and is targeting 100 million customers across 100 countries.

Ukrzaliznytsia may turn profitable in 2027 under base or positive scenario – 2027 budget draft
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:35:39 EEST
00:35:39 KST

Ukrzaliznytsia (UZ) is expected to operate at a loss in 2026 under all scenarios, while under the base and positive scenarios the company could become profitable as early as 2027, whereas under the negative scenario profitability is expected only from 2029, according to the company's stress test conducted as part of the 2027 state budget drafting process.
The document notes that Ukrzaliznytsia's performance in 2026-2030 will depend, in particular, on the volume of state support for the company's domestic passenger transportation operations.
Under all three scenarios, state budget financing for Ukrzaliznytsia envisages 100% compensation of costs for intercity passenger transportation in 2026-2030. Under the base scenario, compensation for suburban passenger transportation costs is also forecast at 25% in 2029 and 50% in 2030, while under the positive scenario these figures would be 50% and 100%, respectively.
Under the base and positive scenarios, the company will end this year with a pre-tax loss of UAH 10.6 bln, before posting pre-tax profit next year of UAH 0.9 bln and UAH 3.6 bln, respectively, and UAH 1.7 bln and UAH 10.2 bln the year after that.
Under the negative scenario, this year's pre-tax loss of UAH 20.5 bln would narrow to UAH 3.3 bln next year and to UAH 0.5 bln the year after.
Under the base scenario, rail transportation volumes will correspond to the level set out in the financial plan, and freight tariffs, having risen 30% in August 2026, will increase by a further 15% from January 1, 2027, with subsequent indexation at 80% of the inflation rate.
Under the positive scenario, further tariff indexation would match inflation, while under the negative scenario the 15% tariff increase from 2027 would not take place, with subsequent indexation at 60% of inflation.
Under the base scenario, international passenger transportation tariffs will rise in line with inflation, while intercity and suburban tariffs will remain unchanged. Under the negative scenario, tariffs for all these categories of passenger transportation will remain unchanged.
On transportation volumes, the document refers to the financial plan without specifying figures. Under the negative scenario, freight, intercity and suburban passenger transportation volumes are lower than under the base scenario, while under the positive scenario freight volumes are higher.
On operating expenses, the base scenario envisages price growth in line with inflation, a 2% staff reduction, and 10% annual wage growth, while under the positive scenario wages would grow 15% annually. Under the negative scenario, prices rise in line with inflation, maintenance and repair volumes decrease, staff is cut by 5% with wages rising 6% annually, and a reduced work week and downtime are also expected.
The document separately notes that the base forecast envisages a reduction in capital investment due to insufficient financing, while the negative scenario envisages a minimal level of capital investment to sustain operations. Under the positive scenario, capital investment would grow 23% above the base level.
Regarding Ukrzaliznytsia's debt financing, the base scenario envisages a 30% write-off of Eurobond coupon payments, capitalization of the remainder, an 8% interest rate on new securities, and repayment of 10% of the principal in 2030.
The negative scenario envisages restructuring without any write-off of Eurobond interest, full capitalization of interest, a 8.95% interest rate, and accelerated principal repayments of 5% in 2029 and 25% in 2030, with a failure to meet obligations resulting in default in 2029.
The positive scenario envisages a 100% write-off of Eurobond coupon payments, a 7% interest rate, and additional financing for principal repayment of 10% in 2029 and 10% in 2030.
The document clarifies that the stress test does not account for budget losses resulting from state budget financing within the limits of state capital investment in renewing Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and infrastructure.
The 2026 state budget currently provides for financing of Ukrzaliznytsia's capital expenditures in the amount of UAH 6.5 bln.
As previously reported, in January this year Ukrzaliznytsia refused to make $45 mln in coupon payments on its 2026 Eurobonds, with an 8.25% rate and $703.2 mln in outstanding volume, and its 2028 Eurobonds, with a 7.875% rate and $351.9 mln in outstanding volume, and announced its intention to launch a comprehensive restructuring of its bond obligations with the involvement of financial and legal advisors.
The company cited the continuing decline in freight transportation revenue amid falling volumes, as well as intensifying attacks on the railway, as the main reasons for suspending Eurobond debt servicing – the total number of such attacks in 2025 (1,195) exceeded the combined total for 2023-2024.
In 2025, Ukrzaliznytsia's revenue fell 1.2% to UAH 104.8 bln, EBITDA declined 17.2% to UAH 10.1 bln, and its net loss grew from UAH 2.7 bln to UAH 7.6 bln.
The company's liquidity also deteriorated significantly: the current liquidity ratio fell from 1.56 to 0.54, the quick liquidity ratio from 0.91 to 0.27, while the debt-to-EBITDA ratio rose from 7.54 to 11.80 and the debt coverage ratio fell from 0.18 to 0.11.

Luxury suites, makeup and a traffic ticket: Netanyahu’s US expenses revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:34:22 UTC
00:34:22 KST

New figures provided by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office to the Hatzlacha nonprofit reveal previously undisclosed details of expenses from his U.S. visits in 2025, including luxury hotel stays, flights aboard Israel’s official state aircraft and thousands of dollars spent on makeup, hair styling and other costs.
The records detail expenses for Netanyahu, his wife Sara and the delegations accompanying them, ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars for flights and hotels to comparatively small items such as coffee, a traffic ticket and repairs to an embassy door.
$10,000 a night in Florida
At the end of 2025, Benjamin and Sara Netanyahu traveled to Florida, where they celebrated the New Year at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate.
During the six-day visit, the couple stayed in a suite at the Four Seasons. According to the records, the suite cost $10,000 per night, with the total stay coming to $50,000.
Regular rooms for members of Netanyahu’s 43-person entourage cost $250 per night.
The flight aboard Wing of Zion, Israel’s official aircraft for the prime minister and president, cost Israeli taxpayers $423,407, according to the figures.
New York suite, makeup and a traffic ticket
The documents also detail Netanyahu’s trip to Washington and New York from September 25 to 30, 2025.
The Wing of Zion flight cost $359,281. Netanyahu’s suite at the Loews Regency hotel was listed at $6,000 a night, with the total suite bill reaching $41,993.
During the trip, the state also paid $1,200 for a makeup artist and roughly $1,500 for refreshments, coffee and tea.
About $400 was spent on rental vehicles for the delegation, while another $125 was paid for a traffic ticket.
$172,701 hotel bill in July
During Netanyahu’s U.S. visit in July 2025, accommodation at the Willard InterContinental cost $172,701, according to the documents.
Another roughly $520 was spent on refreshments and drinks.
The records also list a $295 payment for repairing a door at the Israeli Embassy, described under the heading ‘malfunction during visit,’ as well as approximately $2,000 in customs expenses.
Makeup, hair and office equipment
Netanyahu made another three-day visit to Washington in April, when accommodation at the Watergate Hotel cost $51,000.
The documents show payments of $3,036 for a makeup artist and another $3,036 for a hairstylist.
Approximately $1,500 was spent on light refreshments, while another roughly $1,200 was listed for ‘printers and toner.’ A whiteboard and cork board cost an additional $240.
$13,500 for grooming in February
The highest grooming expenses listed in the 2025 visits came during a February trip to Washington.
About $6,700 was spent on makeup and a similar amount on hair styling, bringing the combined expense to roughly $13,500. Separate records released through a freedom-of-information process have also identified that February trip as the most expensive for prime ministerial makeup and hair expenses during the period examined.
The records also list approximately $4,800 for photography lighting and around $840 for flag pins.
Netanyahu’s suite cost $25,000, while approximately $300 was spent on laundry in the suite.
Among the smaller expenses was a $500 ‘smoking fee’ for the meeting room used for a press conference.
Another $480 was paid for COVID-19 tests for two members of the delegation.
The newly released figures provide a detailed look at the range of costs attached to Netanyahu’s overseas visits, from the operation of Wing of Zion and accommodation for large delegations to grooming, equipment, refreshments and incidental expenses recorded during each trip.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Oil prices fell about 4% on Wednesday as the US administration sought to ease concerns over potential disruptions to Saudi Arabian supplies following damage to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline.
International benchmark Brent crude traded at $104.80 per barrel as of 1515GMT, down 3.8% from the previous close.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 4% to $101.59 per barrel.
The benchmarks extended their retreat after recording gains in the previous two sessions.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Saudi Arabia’s damaged East-West pipeline was expected to resume operations within days, describing the disruption as temporary. Some independent analysts, however, warned that repairs could take several weeks.
The pipeline carries crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil-producing regions to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing shipments to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
While the route remains unavailable, Saudi Arabia has moved to increase crude exports through the strategic waterway with US military assistance.
Oil prices also came under pressure from US inventory figures.
Commercial crude oil inventories in the US decreased by 640,000 barrels to 423.4 million barrels in the week ending Sept. 11, according to government data.
The decline was smaller than market expectations, limiting the data’s supportive effect on prices. Inventories at the Cushing, Oklahoma, delivery hub also fell.
The official figures contrasted with an earlier estimate by the American Petroleum Institute, which indicated that crude stocks had increased by 7.1 million barrels.

Ukraine is waiting for lists of facilities from russia: the Foreign Ministry explained the conditions of a possible energy truce
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv expects Moscow to provide a list of facilities and details of a possible cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure. The agreement is not currently in effect.
Ukraine is awaiting from the Russian side a specific list of facilities and clarification of the details of a possible mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure. This was stated by Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi on September 16, UNN reports.
Kyiv insists that, if such a regime is introduced, the designated Ukrainian facilities must be fully protected from the use of any types of weapons.
Details
According to Tykhyi, Ukraine is ready to discuss possible de-escalation substantively, but now expects concrete steps from the Russian side.
"If the Russians are serious about this, let them provide lists of facilities and clarify the details—we are waiting for that... We would like Russia to also demonstrate its readiness for this de-escalation. I think then all the necessary solutions can be found," the Foreign Ministry spokesperson said.
At the same time, Kyiv emphasizes that any potential agreements must provide for a complete ban on strikes against designated Ukrainian facilities, regardless of the type of weapon used.
Context
There is currently no agreement on a so-called energy truce between Ukraine and Russia. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously stated that Ukraine was ready to support a cessation of strikes on energy facilities provided it was reciprocal and there were guarantees that moscow would also comply with the agreements. The initiative gained momentum after statements by U.S. President Donald Trump about the possibility of a mutual cessation of attacks on energy infrastructure. At the same time, strikes by both sides continued after these statements, indicating that no de facto ceasefire regime had been introduced.
The kremlin, for its part, positively assessed the idea itself. Russian President's spokesperson dmitry peskov called the proposal for a mutual moratorium on strikes against energy infrastructure "very good," but the Russian side has not announced that a final agreement has been reached or the date on which it would take effect.
At present the parties are at the stage of discussing the parameters of a possible regime: the list of facilities to be protected, the conditions for compliance with it, and monitoring mechanisms.
Reminder
The other day, in an interview with CBS News, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the energy truce is not currently in effect and also emphasized that Ukraine is ready for it.

UN official, women’s rights advocate urge greater international engagement to solve Afghanistan’s crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:30:34 UTC
00:30:34 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Senior UN official Georgette Gagnon and Afghan women’s rights advocate Nargis Nehan urged greater international engagement and action Wednesday on Afghanistan’s worsening human rights and humanitarian situation.
Gagnon, deputy special representative for the UN chief and officer-in-charge of the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), told the UN Security Council that Taliban authorities maintained nationwide control and achieved a degree of economic and security stability since returning to power five years ago.
“These developments are encouraging,” she said, but stressed that they were taking place alongside “severe restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary governance, a human rights crisis, and the continued presence of terrorist groups.”
Gagnon said Afghanistan faces no significant armed or political threat to Taliban control, but warned that risks to stability were accumulating, particularly as communities face exclusion from decision-making, resources and economic opportunities.
She also highlighted continuing restrictions on women and girls, including arrests linked to enforcement of dress codes, as well as pressure on minorities, media closures and intimidation of journalists.
“Peace is not only the absence of armed conflict,” said Gagnon. “Sustainable peace requires dignity, inclusion, opportunity and hope.”
The humanitarian situation remains critical, she said, noting that the 2026 humanitarian response plan is only 30% funded. She added that nearly 1.2 million Afghans returned from Pakistan and Iran this year, bringing total returns since 2023 to 6.5 million.
Gagnon urged the Taliban to lift restrictions on women and girls, pursue inclusive governance and meet counterterrorism commitments, arguing that “principled and pragmatic engagement” remains essential.
Nehan said Aug. 15 marked five years since the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan, describing the period as one of continuing erosion of women’s rights.
She quoted Afghan women she recently spoke to, including one who said, “Being a woman is a crime, and being born as a woman in Afghanistan is an even greater crime.”
“Solidarity must produce action,” she told the council. “Afghan women cannot afford another year of waiting for the world to decide what to do with Afghanistan.”
She urged the international community to fully fund the $1.7 billion humanitarian response plan and support Afghan women’s participation in determining the country’s political future.
“The world knows what is happening in Afghanistan,” she said. “The question is whether the international community is prepared to act on what it knows or not.”

Marie-Antoinette: France’s last queen and first influencer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:29:38 UTC
00:29:38 KST

Marie-Antoinette: France’s last queen and first influencer?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
This year, several French landmarks are paying tribute to France’s last queen, Marie-Antoinette. Despite her public execution taking place more than 230 years ago, the monarch continues to fascinate both at home and abroad. Our reporters dive into the reasons behind the lasting interest and explore why she could be considered France’s first influencer.
In June, the Versailles Palace launched its inaugural Marie-Antoinette au Trianon ball. Partygoers stepped back into the 18th century to retrace the queen’s life, with the help of musicians, dancers and actors. As well as the Petit and Grand Trianons (or royal villas in English), some got rare access to the secluded grotto the late queen had built. “It’s never open to the general public so it’s an extraordinary privilege,” explained one ticket holder. The event sold out in just a few hours, with many of its visitors travelling from abroad. “It’s probably exhibitions about Louis XIV or Marie-Antoinette that are the most successful in Versailles. Marie-Antoinette is one of the most depicted queens ever,” explains Versailles Spectacles director Laurent Brunner.
An icon in popular culture
Marie-Antoinette’s influence continues today, inspiring brands, writers, artists and filmmakers. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the cult classic “Marie Antoinette” by Sofia Coppola. The film is being re-released in theatres this autumn in conjunction with an exhibition at Versailles Palace, and the publication of a behind-the-scenes book.
“Sofia called me up and asked me if I would be interested in coming (to Versailles) and taking some snapshots on the set. So I hopped on a plane and I went to France with my one little camera,” explains “Making Marie-Antoinette” author Andrew Durham. The new book shows snapshots of 21st century movie stars, styled in 18th century costumes with a pop culture twist. Durham decided to publish the series after spotting someone at a coffee shop in LA with one of his photos on their T-shirt, yet another demonstration of the ill-fated queen’s lasting legacy.

WHO sees 'encouraging signs' in DR Congo Ebola response but says outbreak 'far from over'
The World Health Organization said Wednesday that the fight against the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo was showing “encouraging signs" but that the epidemic was "far from over". More than 7,000 cases have been reported across seven provinces as of September 11.
The World Health Organization said on Wednesday there were encouraging signs measures to contain an Ebola epidemic in DR Congo were gaining ground, though it warned the outbreak was "far from over".
Transmission was declining in the most affected parts of Ituri province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
"We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground," he said in a conference call but warned the outbreak could still spread in a region with very high population mobility.
Read moreDR Congo: Ebola burial teams race against time
DR Congo had reported more than 7,000 confirmed Ebola cases as of September 11.
The outbreak, the second most lethal on record behind one in West Africa that lasted from 2014 to 2016, has spread to a seventh province.
Improved surveillance could lead to an increase in detected cases, while contact-tracing efforts had also increased, said Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO's acting director of epidemic and pandemic threat management.
"We have many, many months ahead of us," Van Kerkhove said. "This is far from over."
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

More than 3,000 healthcare and frontline workers had already been vaccinated with Merck's Ervebo, said Meg Doherty, WHO's director of science, research, evidence and quality for health.
Ervebo is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, but its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus driving the current outbreak is not known.
Doherty said an observational study involving frontline workers was expected to begin shortly to assess the vaccine's effectiveness, while a separate mid-to-late-stage trial, led by Congo's National Institute of Biomedical Research with other partners, was expected to get under way in the coming weeks.
Ervebo will be among the first vaccines evaluated for efficacy in the trial, followed by other vaccine candidates specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola, she said. These include candidates from Moderna and one from the University of Oxford.

He said the vote would serve as a collective response to those seeking to weaken Russia, hinder its development, and deprive it of its sovereignty and right to determine its own future.

Yemen’s Houthis shoot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:27:22 UTC
00:27:22 KST

- Yemen's Houthi movement claimed on Sept. 16, 2026 that it shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate.
- Saudi authorities have not confirmed the claim, and Houthi media has separately reported a similar unverified claim in 2018.
Houthi forces shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 fighter jet over Marib governorate on Sept. 16, 2026, using a locally manufactured missile, according to Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree. Houthi military media released images and video of the wreckage, showing armed fighters standing on a large piece of tail section bearing a Saudi flag emblem.
Saree said the aircraft was hit while flying a support mission for Saudi-backed forces in Marib. He said Houthi air defenses also engaged two follow-up formations of F-15 and Typhoon jets that entered the area afterward, forcing them to retreat rather than reach the crash site.
The shootdown came the same day The Defence Blog reported that Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, had hit Houthi positions around the port city of Mocha and the nearby town of Dhubab. Houthi fighters had seized the port and pushed further up the Red Sea coast before that government air response began. The area sits near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a roughly 30-kilometer-wide (19-mile) chokepoint that a large share of global shipping passes through, which has made the coastline a recurring flashpoint since Yemen’s civil war began in 2015.
The F-15 is the backbone of the Royal Saudi Air Force’s strike capability in Yemen. Saudi Arabia operates both older F-15S models and the newer F-15SA variant, built with Boeing under a deal finalized in the 2010s that added fly-by-wire controls, an active electronically scanned array radar and a second weapons station. Marib has been a frequent flashpoint of its own, serving as the last major stronghold of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in the country’s north and a regular target for both sides’ air operations.
Houthi forces have steadily expanded their air defense arsenal over the course of the war, adapting Soviet-era surface-to-air missiles and, according to weapons researchers, incorporating Iranian-supplied components into domestically assembled systems. The group has claimed several previous downings of coalition aircraft and drones, though few have been independently confirmed through crash-site verification by outside parties.
Wednesday’s strike came during a week of intensified fighting. Saree said Saudi aircraft had flown more than 450 strikes since Monday, and he separately denied Houthi responsibility for a drone the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted before it could reach restricted airspace over Mecca on Sept. 15. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki called that intercepted drone a “hostile and terrorist act” and said it marked the second time the group had tried to target the city, after an alleged 2017 ballistic missile attempt. Saree pushed back on that characterization, saying Houthi operations target oil facilities and military bases rather than religious sites.
The Houthis have downed Saudi aircraft over Yemen before, including a similar claim over Sanaa in January 2018. In that case, the Saudi-led coalition disputed the account and attributed a separate crash that same week to mechanical failure rather than enemy fire. Neither that earlier incident nor Wednesday’s strike has been confirmed through official Saudi channels.
The renewed fighting follows the collapse of an earlier truce and the resumption of Houthi attacks on Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea, including a maritime blockade the group announced in recent weeks. Saudi Arabia has continued airstrikes against Houthi positions in response, and both sides have accused each other of escalating the conflict beyond its previous front lines.

Feature: Turkish young couples navigate soaring costs on path to marriage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:27:15 CST
00:27:15 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- For 26-year-old Oguz Biyikli, who works as a visa processing officer at a tourism agency in Istanbul, marriage was meant to mark the beginning of a new chapter. Yet, like many young couples in Türkiye, he and his wife are finding that setting up a household has become increasingly difficult even with a steady household income and a home of their own.
"We had been saving money for the past few years because we knew we were going to get married, but all our savings were gone by the wedding day," Biyikli told Xinhua at his office. "We bought what we could with our salaries, and we are still paying off the debt."
Their experience reflects the strain that persistently high inflation has placed on households across Türkiye. Annual inflation stood at 31.51 percent in August, according to official data, while the Central Bank has forecast year-end inflation at 28 percent.
Setting up a household comes with a long list of expenses, from major appliances and furniture to everyday necessities. A standard set of white goods, including a refrigerator, washing machine, dishwasher and oven, starts at around 90,000 liras (1,850 U.S. dollars), while a full furniture package can cost around 200,000 liras.
Housing costs add another burden for young couples. Although Biyikli owns his home, he said even relatively modest two-bedroom apartments he viewed while preparing for marriage could cost around 40,000 liras a month, with prices rising much higher depending on the location.
Amid soaring housing costs, authorities launched a pilot social rental housing scheme in Istanbul in September offering apartments starting from 10,000 liras per month, though restricted to just 1,071 units in its first phase and limited to a strict three-year tenancy.
For young workers on entry-level wages, housing costs can quickly become a major financial burden. Türkiye's net minimum wage is 28,075 liras, well below the cost of many of the expenses involved in setting up a home.
"Even big-ticket items have predictable price tags, but it's the countless small, everyday items that really drain you," Biyikli said, pointing out how seemingly minor purchases, from kitchen utensils to doormats, can add up to the cost of major appliances.
To ease such financial pressures, the Family and Youth Fund, financed by Türkiye's natural resource revenues, disbursed interest-free marriage loans totaling 2.18 billion liras to 19,166 young people in August. Couples can receive loans of 200,000 to 250,000 liras depending on their ages, featuring a 48-month maturity and a two-year grace period.
Biyikli said the support was "much better than nothing," although the loan would cover only part of the cost of setting up a home.
Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Wednesday that fighting the cost of living remains the government's top priority, stressing that authorities will not compromise on disinflation. Simsek acknowledged that the process will take a "bit longer than initially anticipated."
For newlyweds, however, the financial pressure remains immediate. Furkan Yilmaz, another newlywed in Istanbul, noted that he and his wife could not access state support because they already owned a small property, though he understood the program's intent.
Yilmaz also argued that short-term relief is not enough. "Unless inflation is stabilized, these measures are like putting a band-aid on a broken leg," he said. ■

Roundup: Hong Kong unveils maiden 5-year plan, charts roadmap for high-quality development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:27:03 CST
00:27:03 KST

John Lee, chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, unveils Hong Kong's first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) and delivers his fifth policy address in Hong Kong, south China, Sept. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Duo)
HONG KONG, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) on Wednesday unveiled its first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030), a milestone as it enters a new phase of becoming more prosperous.
The plan will help build a more open, inclusive, liberal, prosperous and safer Hong Kong, said HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee.
Unveiling the blueprint, Lee said the 2026-2030 period is five crucial years for Hong Kong to seize the opportunity to enhance social well-being and build a better home for all.
Comprising seven parts and 28 chapters, the plan sets out a total of 105 indicators spanning a wide range of areas. Key objectives include achieving new breakthroughs in economic development, boosting international competitiveness and influence, as well as significantly improving public well-being.
According to the plan, Hong Kong's real GDP growth rate is projected to remain within a reasonable range during the 2026-2030 period, while the value added of the tourism industry is expected to rise about 40 to 50 percent to 126 billion Hong Kong dollars (about 16.06 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030.
Hong Kong aims to elevate the ratio of total domestic expenditure on innovation activities to GDP to 3 after 2030, compared with a reading of 1.63 in 2024, the plan said.
To sharpen its competitive edge, Hong Kong plans to consolidate and enhance its status as an international financial, maritime and trade center, and develop itself into an international innovation and technology center and a global hub for high-caliber talent, according to the blueprint.
Efforts will also be made to expedite the development of the Northern Metropolis, deepen the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and create an international collaboration network.
Social well-being has been high on the HKSAR government's agenda. While prioritizing young people's education, employment, entrepreneurship and home ownership, the government also pledged to eliminate substandard subdivided units by 2030. According to the plan, Hong Kong will supply 196,000 public flats in the coming five years, aiming to cut the average waiting time to under four years by 2030-31.
The document also underscored efforts to adopt a holistic approach to development and security, boost governance efficacy, and strengthen the institutional safeguards for implementation.
Delivering the policy address for 2026 shortly after presenting the blueprint, Lee said key policy initiatives and projects in the policy address will serve as core drivers to implement the five-year plan through enhanced inter-departmental coordination and regular progress reviews.
To better solicit public opinion on the city's future development, the HKSAR government held over 100 consultation sessions over the past three months, receiving over 17,000 submissions on the five-year plan and 11,000 on the policy address.
Noting this year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), Lee said that the inaugural blueprint represented a major initiative by the HKSAR government to uphold and enhance the executive-led system and improve governance efficacy.
The blueprint underscored the strategic need for Hong Kong to proactively align with national development strategies and better integrate into the overall national development, while also laying out an action agenda to promote Hong Kong's high-quality development, the chief executive said. ■

3 rare endangered mammals recorded for 1st time in southwestern Cambodia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:26:34 CST
00:26:34 KST

This undated photo shows a Hog Deer in Koh Kong province of Cambodia. (Cambodian Ministry of Environment/Handout via Xinhua)
PHNOM PENH, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Three exceedingly rare mammal species have been caught on camera for the first time in a protected conservation area in Southwestern Cambodia's Koh Kong province, conservationists announced in a joint press release on Wednesday.
The recorded mammals include the endangered Hog Deer (Axis porcinus), the Large-spotted Civet (Viverra megaspila), and the Hairy-nosed Otter (Lutra sumatrana). The photos and videos were captured between late 2025 and early 2026 during a comprehensive camera-trap survey at the site.
"These initial records represent an encouraging sign for the conservation of threatened large mammal species in Indochina," the press release said.
Khvay Atitya, an undersecretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Environment, confirmed that the mammals were spotted around the Sre Ambel River within the Dong Peng Multiple Use Area.
He noted that the region is a vital coastal wetland ecosystem encompassing river networks, mangroves, swamps, and peatlands.
"It serves as a sanctuary for key biodiversity, particularly rare species," Atitya said. "The recent discovery of these three endangered species reflects the strong commitment of the Royal Government of Cambodia to ensuring the generational survival of rare wildlife."
According to the press release, these new species records were discovered in riverine habitats that also serve as a vital home to Cambodia's national reptile, the Southern River Terrapin, locally known as the Royal Turtle. ■

MOSCOW, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japan's remilitarization and the deployment of missiles near Russia's borders pose a threat to the latter's national security, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
During a meeting with Japanese Ambassador to Russia Akira Muto, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko expressed concerns over Japan's expanding military activities with the United States and other Western allies near Russia's Far Eastern borders, as well as the deployment of medium-range missile systems on Japanese territory.
"All these moves constitute a direct threat to Russia's national security, as well as peace and stability in Northeast Asia," the ministry said in a statement.
It warned that if such activities continue, Russia will take necessary compensatory measures to maintain an adequate level of its defence capability.
The Russian side also criticized Tokyo's continued anti-Russia stance, including its protest over Russian President Vladimir Putin's recent visit to the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, as well as Japan's expanded military assistance to Kiev.

"One simply needs to behave decently, remember that diplomacy exists and stop creating additional problems on top of all those already created by them in bilateral relations," Zakharova said on the sidelines of the International Festival of Youth in Yekaterinburg.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Japan currently takes an "extremely unfriendly position" toward Russia and has joined anti-Russia sanctions, making it difficult to expect reciprocal concessions.
After Japan joined Western-led sanctions against Russia in 2022, Moscow suspended bilateral peace treaty negotiations, halted visa-free visits by Japanese citizens to the Southern Kuril Islands and withdrew from talks on joint economic activities in the islands. ■

NANNING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The 23rd China-ASEAN Expo will spotlight new business opportunities under the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (CAFTA) 3.0 framework, with more than 3,400 companies from over 70 countries and regions set to participate, event organizers said on Wednesday.
Scheduled to run from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, the expo will cover about 170,000 square meters, showcasing the latest achievements in China-ASEAN cooperation.
Under the theme "CAFTA 3.0 Opportunities, Better Life," the expo will feature products and projects in areas ranging from traditional industries to digital communications, green development and artificial intelligence (AI).
A dedicated AI marketplace will display more than 500 products, while a new exhibition area will highlight demand from ASEAN countries for projects and applications in transport, smart logistics, AI, urban management and industrial park development.
Science and technology authorities and high-tech institutions from countries including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand will send delegations to the expo.
Timor-Leste will participate for the first time as a full ASEAN member and a co-host of the expo, bringing all 11 ASEAN member states together in Nanning following the bloc's expansion.
Over 50 trade and investment promotion activities will also be held during the expo, focusing on trade and investment facilitation, regional economic integration, and cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation.
China and ASEAN are working to accelerate the implementation of the CAFTA 3.0 Upgrade Protocol. Signed in October 2025, the protocol covers areas such as the digital economy and green development.
Economic ties between China and ASEAN have continued to deepen. Bilateral trade topped 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time in 2025, totaling 1.05 trillion dollars, up 7.4 percent year on year. In the first seven months of 2026, trade between the two sides reached 744.41 billion dollars, an increase of 24.7 percent year on year and accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade.
China has remained ASEAN's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has been China's largest trading partner for six successive years. ■

Study finds early signs of cancer immunotherapy response
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:26:20 CST
00:26:20 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- A group of Israeli, Chinese and German researchers found early clues that help explain why some cancer patients respond to immunotherapy while others do not, the Israel Institute of Technology said in a statement Wednesday.
In their study, published in the journal Cancer Cell, the researchers found that what happens inside a tumor shortly after treatment begins helps determine whether the treatment will work.
They studied tumor and immune system changes during early treatment and found that some tumors developed features that enabled immune cells to attack cancer more effectively, while others did not.
The findings suggested that doctors may eventually be able to look at these early changes to better predict whether a patient is responding to treatment.
The researchers said the findings could help improve cancer care by allowing doctors to identify ineffective treatments earlier and consider other options sooner. ■

2026-09-16

The deal underscores a broader push by drugmakers to integrate AI across research and development to boost new drug discovery.
Novo, previously Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharmaceutical company behind Ozempic, has partnered with Anthropic to accelerate the development of new medicines using artificial intelligence.
“Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organisation and help us on our mission to bring new, transformative health solutions to people living with chronic diseases,“ said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo, in a press release Wednesday.
The pharmaceutical giant will use Anthropic’s models and Claude Science to advance scientific reasoning for Research and Development (R&D), the company announced.
Beyond increasing productivity in R&D, Novo’s CEO said AI tools can offer “completely new scientific opportunities” and help reasoning and understanding of human biology and drug mechanics.
"AI’s increasing capability brings with it the potential to compress a century’s worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade," said Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic.
He added that by giving leading researchers access to safe, capable, and trusted frontier models, it is possible to shorten research timelines, improve outcomes, and discover medicines and treatments that significantly improve human life.
This partnership comes amid Novo’s bet on AI to fast-track drug research. The pharma giant is already using OpenAI’s science GPT-Rosalind, after sealing the deal in April to use advanced AI to analyse complex datasets, identify potential drugs, and cut the time between research and patient access.
In 2024, the Novo Nordisk Foundation partnered with Nvidia and the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO) to establish the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which operates Gefion – Denmark's first AI-ready supercomputer.
Anthropic is also expanding its work in the life sciences sector. In May 2026, the tech company announced a collaboration with Bristol Myers Squibb to deploy Claude across the company's research, clinical development, manufacturing, commercial, and corporate functions.

Kremlin’s frozen assets in Europe will never be returned to Russia — Sikorski
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

Kremlin’s frozen assets in Europe will never be returned to Russia — Sikorski
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said this during his speech at the Europe Future Forum in Warsaw, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“ Russian state assets frozen in Europe will never be returned to Russia. In the future, they can be used as war reparations or to help Ukraine rebuild, or they can be used already now to prevent further destruction and reduce the cost of future reconstruction,” Sikorski said. The European Union had frozen more than €200 billion in Russian state assets, Sikorski said, adding that these funds would help Ukraine withstand the war, but would still not be enough for Ukraine to win it.
The Polish foreign minister also stressed that even the end of the war would not mean the disappearance of the Russian threat. He warned Europe against underestimating Russian militarism and called for continued efforts to strengthen its own defense capabilities.
Sikorski said that Poland spends around 7% of its GDP on defense, but stressed that a comprehensive security architecture cannot be built through the efforts of individual states alone.
European NATO members have doubled their military spending since 2014, he said, and noted that if European allies fulfill the commitments made at the NATO summit in The Hague, their annual defense spending will exceed €800 billion by 2035.
“We need to be strong enough to deter Putin,” Sikorski said.
He also drew particular attention to the defense spending of the Baltic region countries. According to Sikorski, the combined military budget of the ten member states of the Council of the Baltic Sea States is already larger, even in peacetime, than Russia’s military budget, as Russia enters the fifth year of its war against Ukraine.
At the same time, Poland’s top diplomat noted that the problem increasingly lies not in the amount of money Europe spends on defense, but in the capabilities it acquires as a result.
Sikorski identified the development of long-range strike capabilities, the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis, cyber capabilities, as well as the mass deployment of drones and counter-drone systems among Europe’s current defense priorities.
“You cannot fight drones with sticks and stones,” Sikorski stressed.
He also stressed the need to learn the lessons of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“We cannot afford to lose another war to Russia,” the Polish foreign minister said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the Polish prime minister recently said that Poland must be prepared for increased Russian activity in the coming weeks and months, and that the possibility that the escalation could also affect Polish territory cannot be ruled out.

Opposition urge cabinet to pick a route as budget debate begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:23:50 UTC
00:23:50 KST

Opposition urge cabinet to pick a route as budget debate begins
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The left-wing opposition party Pro is willing to talk to the coalition parties about reducing healthcare costs, but only if the cabinet abandons its €6.5 billion cuts to welfare spending, party leader Jesse Klaver said on the first day of the Dutch budget debate.
Klaver said it would be a “scandal” if the government fell over its first budget, but he also pressed Rob Jetten’s administration to make up its mind whether to seek support from left or right.
As the first speaker in the two-day debate on finance minister Eelco Heinen’s budget, Klaver said his party wanted to break the deadlock that led to pre-budget talks breaking down.
“After so much political unrest in recent years, I think it is in all our interests that this cabinet succeeds,” he said. “Sometimes I think the opposition is keener to make it a success than the coalition parties themselves.”
Jan Paternotte, leader of the largest coalition party D66, called on parties on all sides to work on a budget with broad appeal and look beyond “the left-right discussion in The Hague”.
But his words found little support from the opposition, which accused the coalition of D66, CDA and VVD of lacking leadership. “What kind of road map does the cabinet see before it?” Mirjam Bikker, leader of the ChristenUnie, asked.
The three parties have 66 seats in the lower house, 10 short of a majority, while in the Senate they need to find 16 extra votes to pass their legislation.
No perfect match
Pro, with 20 seats in the lower house and 14 senators, provides the most straightforward route, but the right-wing VVD is reluctant to make too many concessions to the left and favours a deal with parties such as JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.
Paternotte said the coalition wanted to continue talking to parties on all sides in the coming weeks. “The perfect political match doesn’t exist, only the will to come to an agreement. My invitation stands.”
Klaver himself came in for criticism from other opposition leaders who said the proposed budget deal had already made too many concessions to the left.
Joost Eerdmans, leader of the hardline conservative JA21, said the cabinet needed to “make the choice” between his party and Pro rather than trying to reach out to both.
In contrast to Pro, JA21 argues the cabinet should cut even more from the welfare bill to create room in the budget for tax cuts and measures to ease the cost of living.
Eerdmans also said plans to invest billions in climate change measures should be redirected to help working families. “The idea that we can change the world’s climate is unrealistic,” he said.
Two budgets
Eerdmans suggested to Paternotte that the cabinet should write two budgets, one for the left-wing parties and one for the right, and let MPs debate them both.
But Paternotte urged Eerdmans to “take off the rose-tinted glasses”. “How does that get you to a majority in the Senate?” he said. “Pro or JA21 on their own aren’t enough.”
Klaver’s pitch to the cabinet also prompted Socialist Party leader Jimmy Dijk to ask how far Pro was willing to compromise on healthcare spending.
Pro would not “work to break things down”, Klaver replied, but he saw potential to make savings by tackling “all kinds of treatments that aren’t necessary” and “taking the market out of youth care”.
Draft published
Paternotte also said D66 was willing to discuss surrogate parenthood with the SGP, which wants the cabinet to block any moves to legalise the practice as a condition for its support.
MPs also voted to ask the cabinet to publish the original draft budget by finance minister Eelco Heinen which was rejected by his coalition partners, prompting an extra weekend of negotiations.
NRC reported that the original version preserved most of the plans to cut welfare spending, despite Pro pressing for them to be taken off the table. In both the draft and the final version Heinen proposed delaying around half the cuts by a year.

Edgar Barrera leads the 2026 Latin Grammys with ten nominations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:22:28 UTC
00:22:28 KST

The Latin Recording Academy announced on Wednesday the nominees for the 27th Latin Grammy Awards. The ceremony will be held on 12 November at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas.
The Latin Recording Academy released the full list of nominees for the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards on Wednesday, and one name appears more often than any other: Edgar Barrera.
The Mexican songwriter has picked up ten nominations, most of them linked to work he did for Karol G and Carín León, and he features in all three of the night’s general categories: Record, Album and Song of the Year. The ceremony, the 27th in the history of the awards, will take place on 12 November at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas.
Behind Barrera comes a tightly packed group with seven nominations each: Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Rosalía. Silvana Estrada and Mon Laferte have six apiece, and Argentine producers Rafa Arcaute and Federico Vindver each notch up five.
These are, to a large extent, the names that have shaped the Spanish-language music conversation over the past year: from LUX, by Rosalía, recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra and sung in thirteen different languages, to Rawayana’s album, which in June reached number one on Billboard’s ranking of the best Latin albums of the year.
Ten albums in the running for Album of the Year
The flagship category brings together ten very different releases: 'EQUILIBRIVM' by Anitta; 'Free Spirits' by Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso; 'Taracá' by Jorge Drexler; 'Vendrán suaves lluvias' by Silvana Estrada; 'Tropicoqueta' by Karol G; 'Femme Fatale' by Mon Laferte; 'Muda' by Carín León; 'La vida era más corta' by Milo J; '¿Dónde es el after?' by Rawayana; and 'LUX' by Rosalía.
In Record of the Year, the standouts are '¿Cómo se ama?' by Jorge Drexler; 'Dime' by Silvana Estrada; 'Coleccionando heridas' by Karol G together with Marco Antonio Solís; 'Femme Fatale' by Mon Laferte; 'Desde que te tengo' by Carín León; 'La Perla' by Rosalía with Yahritza y su Esencia; and 'Alma' by Elena Rose.
The Song of the Year shortlist, the award that honours songwriters, comprises ten tracks, among them 'Hasta Jesús tuvo un mal día' by Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso featuring Sting, and 'Mi gran amor' by Santana together with Becky G. Also included are 'Humano' by Juanes and Vivir Quintana, and 'Nilo' by Zanna, alongside the already mentioned songs by Drexler, Estrada, Laferte, Karol G and Rosalía.
The Best New Artist category arrives without any obvious favourites: a group of eleven artists are competing, Delilah, Fabian, Loulu Gilberto, Arath Herce, Macario Martínez, Maye, Sofía Monroy, Kendall Peña, Dora Sánchez, Aria Vega and Zeca Veloso, who have yet to break into the awards’ general categories.

Italy's oldest man dies at 112
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:21:47 CEST
00:21:47 KST

Italy's oldest man has died at the
age of 112.
                                    
                                       
				A shepherd, muleteer, and farmer, Vitantonio Lovallo—known to
everyone as "Zitòn"- lived through more than a century of
history without ever severing the bond with his land in southern
Italy.
                                    
                                       
				He lived in Sarnelli, a small hamlet of Avigliano in the
province of Potenza, and had celebrated his last birthday on
March 25th.
                                    
                                       
				His life began in 1914 and was spent largely in the fields;
Lovallo started working the land at age 16 to help his family,
and that passion never left him—he only stopped working six
years ago, when he was already over a hundred years old. In
between, he lived through the most dramatic events of the 20th
century.
                                    
                                       
				After working as a shepherd and muleteer, he was conscripted
during World War II, captured by German soldiers, and deported
to the island of Rhodes, where he remained a prisoner until
November 27, 1943.
                                    
                                       
				He recorded these experiences in his writings, which he has now
bequeathed to his grandchildren and great-grandchildren as a
record of the war and his time at the front.
                                    
                                       
				He married in 1936 and had four children.
                                    
                                       
				His status as Italy's oldest man had been internationally
validated; LongeviQuest ranked him 45th on its global list of
living individuals, at 112 years and 170 days old.
                                    
                                       
				Officially, he was born on March 28, 1914, although his family
always maintained that his birth date was March 25.
                                    
                                       
				This three-day discrepancy stemmed from the challenges of the
time: registering a birth required traveling to the municipality
of Avigliano—located some twenty kilometers from Sarnelli—by
crossing Mount Carmine.
                                    
                                       
				"It is with deep emotion that I bid farewell to Vitantonio
Lovallo—our dear 'Zitòn'—who, at 112 years of age, stood as a
living and precious repository of our community's memory,"
Avigliano Mayor Giuseppe Mecca told ANSA, recalling "his
simplicity, his strength, and his love for his family and his
homeland."
Condolences were also offered by the Regional Councilor for
Agricultural Policy, Carmine Cicala, who described Lovallo as
"an authentic witness to over a century of our history."
For Cicala, Zitòn's story is "not merely a tale of longevity,"
but the story of a generation that helped build the communities
of the Basilicata region through "sacrifice and tenacity."

				After working as a shepherd and muleteer, he was conscripted
during World War II, captured by German soldiers, and deported
to the island of Rhodes, where he remained a prisoner until
November 27, 1943.
                                    
                                       
				He recorded these experiences in his writings, which he has now
bequeathed to his grandchildren and great-grandchildren as a
record of the war and his time at the front.
                                    
                                       
				He married in 1936 and had four children.
                                    
                                       
				His status as Italy's oldest man had been internationally
validated; LongeviQuest ranked him 45th on its global list of
living individuals, at 112 years and 170 days old.
                                    
                                       
				Officially, he was born on March 28, 1914, although his family
always maintained that his birth date was March 25.
                                    
                                       
				This three-day discrepancy stemmed from the challenges of the
time: registering a birth required traveling to the municipality
of Avigliano—located some twenty kilometers from Sarnelli—by
crossing Mount Carmine.
                                    
                                       
				"It is with deep emotion that I bid farewell to Vitantonio
Lovallo—our dear 'Zitòn'—who, at 112 years of age, stood as a
living and precious repository of our community's memory,"
Avigliano Mayor Giuseppe Mecca told ANSA, recalling "his
simplicity, his strength, and his love for his family and his
homeland."
Condolences were also offered by the Regional Councilor for
Agricultural Policy, Carmine Cicala, who described Lovallo as
"an authentic witness to over a century of our history."
For Cicala, Zitòn's story is "not merely a tale of longevity,"
but the story of a generation that helped build the communities
of the Basilicata region through "sacrifice and tenacity."

A court in India has awarded death sentences to 10 people convicted in the 2013 attack by Maoist rebels that killed 24 people in the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh.

Scientists create mice with part-human brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:21:08 UTC
00:21:08 KST

Researchers have created mice with half-human brains in an effort to understand and develop new treatments for disorders such as schizophrenia, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and rare forms of dementia.
The scientists transplanted lab-grown human brain cells into animals that were engineered to be born without a cortex or hippocampus. This made space for the human tissue to grow inside the rodents’ skulls.
The procedure means scientists can now take cells from patients with brain disorders, turn them into brain tissue in the laboratory, and grow that tissue in living animals. The animals can then be studied to see how the disorder takes hold in human brain tissue, and how drugs might treat the conditions.
“We’ve been trying really hard as a community to find therapeutic solutions for these conditions, but the reality is that in psychiatry and neurology we’ve been left behind [by] every single branch of medicine and we have fewer therapeutics than, again, every single branch of medicine,” said Sergiu Pașca, a professor of psychiatry who led the research at Stanford University.
“That could be because the human brain is very complex, but it’s also because the human brain is inaccessible,” he added. “To a large extent, our goal has been to make aspects of human brain development and function accessible for investigation.”
The work is the latest from the field of neural organoids, where human brain cells, grown in the lab, assemble into tiny but complex structures that mimic some of the features of real brains.
While potentially transformative for brain medicine, organoids have sparked a wave of ethical concerns, not least around whether the clumps of tissue could become conscious or feel pain, and the welfare of animals implanted with organoids.
Pașca said the work had received extensive ethical oversight from the start.
Experts said this would need to continue. Emily Jackson, professor of law at London School of Economics and chair of a recent report on neural organoids for the Nuffield Council on Bioethics, said: “Animal welfare is a really important concern, and it will be necessary to closely monitor these animals in order to evaluate the impact on them.”
In previous work, the Stanford team transplanted human neurons into rat brains. The tissue took root and wired into the animals’ brain circuits, but there was too little room for the human tissue to grow very much.
To solve the problem, the researchers genetically engineered mice to stunt the growth of key brain regions, the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. Surprisingly, the mice survived because the remaining parts of the brain took on new roles. While the mice look normal, they are cautious on their feet and more forgetful.
Writing in Nature, Paşca describes how the mice were injected with human brain organoids that were themselves created by reprogramming donated skin cells. The newborn mice received several injections, each containing about 100,000 human brain cells, into the space where their own brain tissue was missing. In total, the rodents lacked about 14m mouse brain cells and ended up with about 4m human ones – half the brain by volume.
Three months after surgery, the human tissue had hooked up to the mouse’s blood supply and almost entirely filled the cavity, taking up about half the size of the rodent’s brain. Some of the human neurons formed connections with mouse brain cells and spinal cord.
The human neurons were not structured or wired up in the same way as in people, and the brain tissue was immature, equivalent to that found halfway through human pregnancy. Tests on the “xenocortical” mice showed the animals were not enhanced by the transplants, but their shaky gait and cognitive problems did improve a little.
To demonstrate how the mice could shed light on human brain disorders, the researchers exposed some of the animals to five hours of low oxygen. This showed how vulnerable human nerve cells are to oxygen deprivation, which in pregnancy and birth can cause cerebral palsy.
The researchers found that human brain tissue in the mice contained rare cells known as von Economo neurons, which have only been seen in postmortem examinations. The cells are among the first to die in frontotemporal dementia, a rare form of the disease, which Paşca now hopes to study in xenocortical mice.
Prof Madeline Lancaster, group leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, said the approach was best suited to questions about disorders and treatments where a whole animal was needed. “It’s less clear to me how this will inform our understanding of human brain development since it is rather artificial, and not at all like how the brain develops naturally,” she said.
Many researchers working on brain organoids are growing them in vitro, or in dishes. The hope is they help to reduce the number of animals used in research. “It’s obviously ethically sensitive and there needs to be a very good reason to do this type of animal experimentation, which most scientific avenues do not require,” Lancaster added. “The field is still aiming for fully in vitro solutions, but this work can also inform on what may be needed to improve those in vitro models to reach more mature stages.”

Russia used Claude AI for espionage, disinformation and drone swarms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:20:52 UTC
00:20:52 KST

Anthropic's latest report on the abuse of its AI model found that a Russian-linked hacking group used Claude to automate attacks on more than 20 organisations, including Ukrainian defence ministries and drone suppliers, while separate operators ran pro-Kremlin disinformation in Africa and Moldova.
Russia used Anthropic's Claude AI model to accelerate cyber-espionage operations against Ukrainian and European government targets, run disinformation campaigns in Africa and Moldova, and develop targeting software for autonomous kamikaze drone swarms, the US company said in a report published this month.
Anthropic said it had blocked all malicious activity identified in the report, used the findings to strengthen its security systems, and shared the information with government bodies and industry partners.
In one major case, a hacking group designated GTG-20006 used Claude to automate operations against more than 20 organisations, including government ministries, defence and intelligence agencies, embassies, think tanks and defence-industrial companies, Anthropic said.
Ukraine was the primary target, with suppliers of military drone technology and their supply chains also among those attacked. The group also targeted Middle Eastern and Asian government departments with links to maritime activity.
Anthropic said GTG-20006 is linked to Midnight Blizzard, a hacking group Western intelligence assessments attribute to Russia's foreign intelligence service SVR.
The group used Claude across a range of operational modes: as an engineering assistant for writing malware, phishing kits and surveillance tools, as an executor of commands on victims' networks, including collecting credentials and extracting data under human direction, and in fully autonomous operations with minimal human oversight.
Disinformation in the CAR and Moldova
Working alongside investigators from the All Eyes On Wagner project, Anthropic identified and removed an account operated by a Russian-speaking individual in Bangui who was running a disinformation operation for Radio Lengo Songo, a station set up and financed in 2017 by the Kremlin-run mercenary Wagner group.
The operator prepared daily pro-Russian content for the station in coordination with Russian state outlets RT, Sputnik Afrique and TASS, and with the local "Russian House" cultural centre — part of a network Russia uses as a political and influence hub abroad.
Content consistently promoted the CAR government and Wagner, and attacked France and domestic opposition figures, according to the All Eyes On Wagner investigation.
The operation was designed to appear locally run, with one person coordinating output while contracts, scripts and publications were presented as the work of a Bangui-based radio station.
Anthropic investigators identified the individual through invoices for a Claude subscription issued in central Madrid.
The operator was linked to Africa Politology, aka "The Company," the information and political technology arm of the African Corps — the successor to Wagner in Africa — which is reportedly controlled by the SVR.
In Moldova, a former regional head of the Russian state-run Sputnik media network used Claude as a content-production tool, adapting news, polling data, and opposition material to fit pro-Kremlin narratives, Anthropic said.
Autonomous swarm drone warfare
Anthropic identified and shut down a group of Russia-linked developers who used its Claude Code tool to write software for kamikaze drones, including an autonomous targeting system tested on real hardware.
The developers trained AI models on footage from combat operations in Ukraine and used a fixed location in the Donetsk region as a demonstration strike target.
The project's stated goal was a fully autonomous swarm of FPV kamikaze drones.
Anthropic linked nine accounts involved in the project to a regional Russian university and a federal research centre connected to the Russian Academy of Sciences, without naming either institution.
Claude is officially unavailable in Russia, with access to Anthropic's website and API blocked and Russian bank cards not accepted for payment. The developers bypassed these restrictions by routing traffic through commercial virtual private servers (VPNs).
