Swiss lower house of parliament signs off Mercosur trade deal
ZURICH, Sept 16 - Switzerland's lower house of parliament on Wednesday approved a trade agreement with the South American bloc Mercosur days after the upper house had given its backing to the corresponding bill, which also contains financial support for Swiss farmers.
The lower house initially rejected the Mercosur deal in June, but approved it after lawmakers included financial aid for farmers worth 517 million Swiss francs ($631 million) over six years to cushion the effects of the agreement.
Farming is a sensitive policy area in Switzerland and the trade accord is likely to be put to a referendum under the country's system of direct democracy.
The deal between member states of the European Free Trade Association, or EFTA, and the core Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay passed the lower house with 118 votes in favour and 66 against. There were 10 abstentions.
Switzerland is the biggest economy in EFTA, which also includes Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. REUTERS

The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.
The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president, JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.
The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.
A former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between the Trump administration and the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”
In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki.
Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.
The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one.
The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.
The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.
Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.
“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”
Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper.
Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.
A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.
In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.
Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi east-west pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.

Space Development Agency Aims for Two More Launches This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:55:55 UTC
23:55:55 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Space Development Agency wants to wrap up its Tranche 1 launch campaign by the end of spring 2027, flying six more batches of satellites to build out its tracking and data transport constellations, according to Director Gurpartap Sandhoo.
The agency is aiming to complete two of those launches by the end of 2026—one in the next month or so and the second in December, Sandhoo told reporters Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space, and Cyber Conference.
“The focus in the next six to eight months is trying to get those up there,” Sandhoo said.
SDA was created in 2019 to disrupt the Pentagon’s traditional practice of buying small numbers of exquisite satellites and taking years to field them. Central to its approach is to regularly refresh its constellation with new tranches of satellites as technology advances and requirements evolve, a concept called spiral development.
Supply chain issues, technical challenges, and last year’s historically long government shutdown have slowed down those plans; the agency had hoped to have all 154 of its first operational satellites, dubbed Tranche 1, on orbit by this summer. To date, it has fielded 63.
Sandhoo said the agency has addressed some of the challenges that contributed to earlier delays. After its first two launches, SDA and its vendors struggled to make contact with all of their satellites and confirm they were operating as intended—an issue that contributed to a monthslong launch pause that stretched from last October to this July. The latest batch of satellites that launched in mid-July, the second Tranche 1 “plane” built by York Space Systems, moved through that process much faster, he said, due to hardware and software upgrades.
“The time it took to check out the second plane was two or three times faster,” Sandhoo said. “The teams learned. They got things done much, much quicker. And I do expect the same as we do multiple launches as we go forward.”
But some of those old hurdles have persisted—namely, supply chain hindrances. SDA vendors and their suppliers have struggled to scale things like focal plane arrays and optical communications terminals, or OCTs, which use laser links to transmit data.
Sandhoo said that while there’s been some improvement in the supply chain, manufacturing throughput is still an issue, particularly for capabilities like OCTs that were not previously produced in large numbers. He also cited quality control issues with those same components.
That means staying on schedule will likely still be a challenge for SDA, and Sandhoo said there’s some risk that the first missile tracking satellites, slated to fly in December, could get pushed to early next year. He told Air & Space Forces Magazine the risk is linked to flight software issues and OCT delays.
These delays have been a setback to SDA’s goal of demonstrating a mesh network on orbit, which Sandhoo previously said he expected to accomplish by the end of September. Now, he’s aiming for the end of the year, naming it as a top priority for the agency over the next three to four months.
“We should be there already, but I push on the team every week that the next step is to get that done,” he said.

More than 104,000 displaced in Yemen as West Coast fighting continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:53:58 UTC
23:53:58 KST

More than 104,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen as fighting along the country’s West Coast continues, the UN migration agency said on Wednesday.
A total of 104,796 people from 17,461 households have been displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) latest Displacement Tracking Matrix.
Taiz remains the epicentre of displacement, with more than 63,000 people displaced across its districts, including 21,018 in Jabal Habashi, 12,642 in Al Ma'afer and 8,250 in Ash Shamayatayn.
Nearly 26,400 people have been displaced in Lahj, while Aden has recorded more than 3,500, the IOM said.
Displacement is also rising in Al Abyan, Hadramawt and Ma'rib as fighting spreads, according to the agency.
“Yemen is a country torn by war, displacement, poverty, and climate impacts,” IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement.
“Overlooking the suffering of civilians is not acceptable as needs continue to rise,” Pope added.
The agency said families were moving under fire, often at night and with few belongings, while the pace of displacement was outstripping aid workers’ ability to track movements in real time.
The IOM also said 2,776 people had crossed from Yemen into Djibouti, where the agency is providing emergency assistance.

Iran war has cost the US $38bn: How will it impact US economy, politics?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:53:51 UTC
23:53:51 KST

Iran war has cost the US $38bn: How will it impact US economy, politics?
High energy costs at the pump and strategic setback for US in the Iran war will likely cost Trump in the midterm elections.
The United States war on Iran has cost the country $38bn so far, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) said this week, adding that an estimated $3bn will be added every month if the conflict continues, placing strain on the country’s finances and economy.
The report, which was released on Tuesday, revealed that the protracted war is straining US munitions stockpiles and fuelling inflation as the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil export chokepoint, remains under Iranian blockade. The shortage of munitions poses a major security risk in the event of a new conflict.
The findings of the inquiry will likely add fuel to the wave of criticism about the six-month-old war, which the US launched alongside Israel on February 28, and which US President Donald Trump claimed would only last a few weeks.
The conflict has rattled the global energy market and contributed to rising prices as US voters express concern about the cost of living in the run-up to the November US midterm elections.
The CBO’s report also comes on Monday’s report from the Pentagon’s official watchdog about the losses the US has incurred throughout the war – including the first admission by the body of low weapons stockpiles.
Here’s what we know about how the war continues to affect domestic US politics, as well as its economy.
What did the congressional report find?
The $38bn cost cited is close to the $37.5bn shared by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a Senate hearing on July 21.
It does not include the costs of recent US strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz or of Iranian attacks on US military installations in the region. Nor does it count borrowing expenses, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.
Dwindling weapons stockpiles have made up the bulk of the costs – $25bn of weapons have been used up so far – with the budget office estimating it could take five years to restore expended US stockpiles.
The conflict is likely to fuel inflation, which is expected to rise by 0.5 percentage points in the first three months of 2027, said the Congress’s nonpartisan bookkeeper.
The rising cost of the war will also act as a drag on US fiscal health as the country’s national debt topped a record $40 trillion last month.
The top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, requested the inquiry into the US’s war expenditure. The Department of Defense did not cooperate with the inquiry, he said.
“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded,” Boyle said in a statement.
How does this compare to the Pentagon watchdog’s report?
On Monday, a separate report by the Pentagon’s Office of the Inspector General also outlined US losses in the war – the first such public acknowledgement by US authorities.
That report found that the war had cost $33bn between February 28 and June 30 – with an estimated $22bn spent on expended munitions.
In a turnabout from the Trump administration’s repeated assurances that US stockpiles of weapons remain healthy, the Pentagon admitted it is indeed running out of munitions – particularly defensive systems – and is facing “bottlenecks” in supply chains.
US officials have continued to publicly reject US media reports about the shortage of munitions and missile interceptors as the war, which Trump initially said would last “four to five weeks”, has entered its seventh month. Trump has claimed that Washington has “virtually unlimited” ammunition.
The White House and Pentagon disputed the findings of the CBO on munitions shortages.
Monday’s Pentagon report also found that up to June 30, the war had caused $184m in damage to US facilities in the Gulf and killed at least 18 US military personnel.
Iranian attacks, the report said, destroyed or damaged dozens of aircraft, including at least 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones.
What has been the political opposition to the US war on Iran?
Opposition to Trump’s war on Iran is mounting, with several Republicans joining the Democrats on Tuesday to vote for a third time to end the conflict.
Seven House Republicans backed the resolution, including three voting in favour for the first time, joining all House Democrats who are opposed to the war. It will likely fail to pass in the Senate, where the Republicans hold a majority.
Even if it were to clear the Senate, Trump can still veto it.
Congress has the authority to declare war, but the president, as the commander in chief, can authorise military actions. Trump started the war before getting approval from Congress.
Past US presidents from both parties have done the same – from Democrat President Harry Truman in 1950 when sending troops to the Korean War, to Republican President Richard Nixon before the US invaded Cambodia.
Meanwhile, public approval for the war is at an all-time low. Just 31 percent of Americans support US military action against Iran, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from late August, down from 37 percent in March.
How has the war impacted the US economy?
The most salient effect of the war for everyday Americans throughout the conflict has been soaring fuel prices. On Tuesday, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US hit a new record high of $6.27 ($1.66 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association.
US consumers paid an additional $100bn for petrol and diesel in the first six months of the war, according to a tracker from Brown University’s Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs.
Across the country, the added cost amounts to roughly $763 per household, based on an estimated 131 million households nationwide.
Higher fuel costs are also driving up the cost of food – with the shortages of oil and gas affecting nearly every stage of the food-supply chain.
In line with his dismissive statements on dwindling weapons stockpiles, Trump has also made flippant remarks about fuel prices, telling the Reuters news agency earlier this month: “If they rise, they rise.”
Democrats have made the cost of living a key issue in the approaching midterm elections in November, which appears to have resonated with voters. The party registered wins for a number of progressives this year, from Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary to Peggy Flanagan’s Minnesota win, also in the Democratic Senate primary.
On Tuesday, several Democratic lawmakers pressed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the state of the economy, inflation and the rising cost of living – tying these issues to the Iran war and the rise in global oil prices. Bessent blamed inflation on the previous Biden administration and claimed Americans are better off under Trump.
The war is also affecting US fiscal health. National debt surpassed $40 trillion in August, and the 30-year treasury yield jumped to 5.32 percent that same month, the highest cost of borrowing for the US government in nearly two decades, according to the Center for American Progress.
How will the cost of the war impact the US midterm elections?
Opinion polls suggest that the Republican Party could struggle to hold onto control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate when voters go to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections.
The rise in oil and gas prices due to the war has also become a major issue for Republicans in the lead-up to the elections.
According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from Monday, Democrats were leading over Republicans by 44 percent to 37 percent in congressional vote preference.
On Sunday, Trump, who has promised to pay every adult $5,000 if the Republicans hold onto their majorities in both houses of Congress, said the war would end after the elections. He also shrugged off concerns that the Iran war will hamper his standing in the upcoming vote.
“I don’t believe in the word ‘regret.’ You can always question yourself a little bit,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News last week.

Ebola response making progress in Congo, but outbreak 'far from over,' WHO says

Ebola response making progress in Congo, but outbreak 'far from over,' WHO says
Sept 16 - The World Health Organization said on Wednesday there were encouraging signs measures to contain an Ebola epidemic in Democratic Republic of Congo were gaining ground, though it warned the outbreak was "far from over."
Transmission was declining in the most affected parts of Ituri province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
"We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground," he said in a conference call but warned the outbreak could still spread in a region with very high population mobility.
Congo had reported more than 7,000 confirmed Ebola cases as of September 11.
The outbreak, the second most lethal on record behind one in West Africa that lasted from 2014 to 2016, has spread to a seventh province.
Improved surveillance could lead to an increase in detected cases, while contact-tracing efforts had also increased, said Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO's acting director of epidemic and pandemic threat management.
"We have many, many months ahead of us," Van Kerkhove said. "This is far from over."
More than 3,000 healthcare and frontline workers had already been vaccinated with Merck's Ervebo, said Meg Doherty, WHO's director of science, research, evidence and quality for health.
Ervebo is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, but its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus driving the current outbreak is not known.
Doherty said an observational study involving frontline workers was expected to begin shortly to assess the vaccine's effectiveness, while a separate mid-to-late-stage trial, led by Congo's National Institute of Biomedical Research with other partners, was expected to get under way in the coming weeks.
Ervebo will be among the first vaccines evaluated for efficacy in the trial, followed by other vaccine candidates specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola, she said. These include candidates from Moderna and one from the University of Oxford. REUTERS

In April, 24 Ukrainian companies ran their own air defense. By mid-September, 81 do — about one new firm per day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:51:29 UTC
23:51:29 KST

Ukraine has authorized 81 private companies to run their own air defense against Russian drones, letting the factories and infrastructure sites that Moscow hits daily shoot back, Ukraine's Defense Ministry says. The firms have been provided "authorized" status under an experimental program, a count that has climbed from 51 in mid-July, according to ArmyInform.
The idea is to let the targets defend themselves. Russian drones strike Ukrainian factories, warehouses, and power sites so relentlessly that the state cannot shield everyone, so the Defense Ministry is enlisting the companies being hit to form their own drone-defense teams.
Ninety-two firms have already applied, among them operators of critical infrastructure and businesses from across the country's industries and regions. The teams are not freelancers: they fold into Ukraine's layered air defense under the command of the Air Force, so they do not fire into a shared sky blind.
The count climbs fast
The program has grown quickly since it began in late 2025, from 24 companies in April to 30 in June, 51 in July, and 81 by mid-September. The units are made of trained, certified civilian staff, some running mobile fire teams with heavy machine guns, others flying interceptor drones.
By June, they had already shot down more than 20 Russian attack and reconnaissance drones, the ministry said, including one jet-powered Geran, the faster variant that has strained Ukraine's defenses.
Russia's drones drive the demand
The Defense Ministry launched the project at the end of 2025 to add a layer of protection for workers and production sites that had become routine targets.
The goal the ministry set for the wider effort is stark: detect every aerial threat and destroy 95 percent of them. The steady climb in members, roughly one company added per day since July, suggests that demand is not slowing.

GFCN experts emphasize importance of fact-checking in deepfake era

YEKATERINBURG, September 16. /TASS/. Experts with the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) told the International Festival of Youth (IFY), currently underway in Yekaterinburg, how fact-checking is becoming an essential skill amid the spread of deepfakes.
Yulia Ablets, Deputy Director General of the ANO Dialogue Regions and founder of the New Media Workshop, who moderated a panel discussion titled "Truth in the Era of Viral Content: Challenges, Threats and Opportunities in the Digital Environment," said the world is currently facing a confidence crisis aggravated by the growing number of fakes.
She cited a recent survey by ANO Dialogue Regions showing that even as 71% of respondents said they can tell authentic information from fakes, the number of those who give in to disinformation and spread it has continued to grow. "We can see how an emotion-laced post can spread faster than a dozen substantiated refutals. Therefore, broader media literacy, the culture of using media content, and fact-checking become as important for the layman as for media specialists and owners of media platforms," the expert argued.
In turn, another GFCN expert, Ilya Rybin, who leads nofake.kz and specializes in communications, pointed to the issue of uncontrolled spread of content: "Doing fact-checking on only a large-language model just won't cut it." "The Share button, not the Generate button, is the most dangerous thing on the Internet now," he explained.
Analysts also noted that in the era of pipeline-like deep fake generation with a low entry threshold not only upgrading the algorithms but also boosting media literacy among masses serves as a response to these challenges. And it is "youths who play a central role in these efforts as they shape the culture of fact-checking as an everyday norm," they insisted.
Yekaterinburg is hosting the IFY under the motto "Follow Your Dream" through September 17. As many as 10,000 youth leaders from 191 countries, including 5,000 delegates each from Russia and overseas, are expected to attend the global event. A thousand teenagers aged between 14 and 17 will take part in the festival’s program.
TASS is the general media partner of the event.

Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:50:26 BST

Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future
- Published
The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.
The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening and taking political action, not in debates over personnel".
Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability.
He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership.
Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September.
The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state.
It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government.
Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers.
The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims.
The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU.
The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, Germany's political landscape needs stability".
"Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia.
- How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? 
  - Published7 September
It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz.
An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses.
However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls.
In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority.
The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament.
Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely.
No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors.
Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage.
But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany.
This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted.

Union claims victory as ministers agree to fully fund pay rise for teachers in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:49:46 UTC
23:49:46 KST

The UK’s biggest education union is claiming a significant victory after the government bowed to pressure and agreed to fully fund a forthcoming pay increase for teachers in England in a sudden U-turn.
Members of the National Education Union (NEU) were due to vote in a ballot for strike action next month over the government’s recent pay offer which provided for a 3.5% increase from this month, with an additional 3% from next September.
While the offer was a significant improvement on initial proposals from the then education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, there was concern among teachers and unions that it was not fully funded and schools would have to find almost a third of the wage increases from existing budgets.
After weeks of negotiation over the summer with the NEU general secretary, Daniel Kebede, Phillipson’s successor, Lucy Powell, confirmed on Wednesday in a letter to the union that the entire pay offer would be fully funded, using funds from recent revaluations of the local government pension scheme.
Kebede said it was a “significant” step and would result in an estimated additional £500m of funding for schools this year, which otherwise would have been spent on the pay rise.
“Finally, we have a government that accepts the reality that any teacher pay award must be fully funded,” he said. “Plugging the £460m black hole in school budgets signals a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community.
“Schools have been running on empty for far too long. Leaders simply could not afford to fund the pay award as set out by the previous education secretary. The new administration has accepted that it is wrong to force schools to make cuts to education just to make ends meet.”
Although the NEU national executive is yet to decide on the fate of the national ballot, the government will be hoping its latest gesture – which it regards not as a change of policy but a change in affordability – will lift the threat of strike action and possible school closures.
In a snap poll before the summer break, 97% of NEU members who participated said it was “unacceptable” that their school would have to find the funds to make up the 1.1% shortfall in government funding of the pay rise, and 89% were prepared to take strike action to ensure the teacher pay award was fully funded.
In her letter to Kebede, Powell said: “I understand you are concerned the funding available in 26-27 is insufficient to cover the costs of the recent pay award.
“I am therefore pleased to be able to update you that recent revaluations to the local government pension scheme will see a 4.9ppt reduction in employer contribution rates and deliver significant savings on schools’ pay bill for support staff.
“We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.”
She added: “Given the material change to the affordability position, I would ask that the NEU revisits its proposed ballot of members planned for October and moves away from strike action.”
Luke Sibieta, a research fellow at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the government’s announcement amounted to a £500m boost to school funding in England, which equated to a permanent increase of just under 1%. “Coming on top of other funding increases, this means that from next year schools will be £1.6bn better off than they had expected to be this summer.”
A spokesperson for Powell said later that the education secretary “has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities.
“High-quality teaching is the single most important in-school factor in improving outcomes for children, which is why this government has backed the profession with a pay award that recognises teachers’ vital role.”
Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the NASUWT teachers’ union, said: “Finally the government has seen sense and started to address the issue we have been raising for months around the funding of the teachers’ pay award.”

Germany’s rearmament push runs through America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:48:21 UTC
23:48:21 KST

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stands alongside German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius during an honor cordon welcome ceremony at the Pentagon in Washington on Sept. 15, 2026. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
WASHINGTON — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius came to the Pentagon on Wednesday with a dilemma: Berlin wants a stronger, more self-reliant European military, but much of what it needs comes from the United States.
Pistorius is in the U.S. this week after earlier being rebuffed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Berlin is seeking direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.
"Germany is strengthening its defense capabilities and acts as a driving force in Europe," Pistorius said at the Pentagon alongside Hegseth. "We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the U.S. and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe over time."
Advertisement
He said Germany has increased its defense spending to $147 billion this year — up by 25% compared to 2025 — and has almost tripled it over the last decade.
The two signed a statement of intent on defense-industrial cooperation covering joint production, licensed manufacturing, maintenance hubs and supply-chain resilience. What the document did not contain were concrete projects, timelines or investment commitments.
Despite efforts by Germany and other European countries to build up their defense industries and reduce dependence on the U.S. in areas such as long-range missiles and satellites, much of the new defense spending is ending up with American companies.
On Friday, Pistorius will travel to Fort Worth, Texas, for the rollout of Germany’s first Lockheed Martin F-35A fighter jet, arguably the most significant weapon in the Bundeswehr’s modernization drive. Berlin has ordered 35 aircraft, with pilot training beginning next year in Arkansas and deliveries scheduled through 2029. Officials are already discussing a potential follow-on order of 15 more jets.
The F-35 is more than another procurement program. It secures Germany’s role in NATO nuclear sharing, unlocks new operational capabilities and ties the Luftwaffe into the alliance’s rapidly growing community of F-35 operators.
And it is only one example of reliance on U.S. arms-makers.
Advertisement
Germany’s rearmament increasingly runs through American production lines: CH-47F Chinook transport helicopters, P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, Patriot air-defense systems and key technologies for the future F127 air-defense frigate.
Hegseth praised Germany's higher defense spending and said it was a key step toward what he calls "NATO 3.0" — the idea that European allies will bear more of the burden of defending the continent while the U.S. pivots to other areas of the world.
“Europe must assume primary responsibility for its conventional defense,” he argued.
Transatlantic divide
But the views of Berlin and Washington are diverging.
Pistorius underlined that the major danger facing the continent is Russia, calling it “the greatest threat to the alliance, the West, and our way of life since the height of the Cold War.” He also cited challenges from Iran, North Korea and China.
The German minister stressed Berlin's continued support for Ukraine. The Trump administration has halted almost all new military aid to Kyiv since taking office.
Advertisement
Hegseth identified no specific threats and underlined that President Donald Trump's main mission was "American manufacturing, American made, American jobs."
For now, Germany's rearmament drive dovetails with that vision. Pistorius said: "Germany is investing and buying in the U.S., adding up to about $50 billion, creating growth and jobs in the United States of America."
But Germany is using its own resources and teaming up with other European countries on defense projects. Berlin is also increasingly frustrated that the U.S. is favoring its own needs — boosting production of Tomahawk missiles to rebuild its own stocks depleted by the war against Iran — which is delaying potential deliveries to Germany.
Berlin sees the Typhon launcher system and Tomahawk cruise missiles as essential for deterrence against Russia. The acquisition would give Germany something it has never possessed: the ability to strike targets deep behind enemy lines with conventional land-based precision weapons. The problem is that the capability Germany wants depends entirely on American production.
“I made it very clear that the timelines previously discussed are too slow from our perspective,” Pistorius said after raising the issue with Hegseth. The Americans, he added, had “taken note of this positively.”
Hegseth is leading a rethink of U.S. force posture in Europe, and the Trump administration has already pulled troops out of Germany. Asked after their meeting whether he had gained greater clarity about future U.S. deployments, Pistorius was blunt: “No, not yet.”
Advertisement
Pistorius insisted that buying more U.S. weapons would not undermine Germany's effort to boost its own capabilities.
Instead, Berlin wants German firms integrated into American supply chains, maintenance networks and licensed-production arrangements. Throughout the visit, Pistorius emphasized that German industry could help relieve production bottlenecks and expand capacity on both sides of the Atlantic.
"NATO needs to become more European in order to stay transatlantic," he said.

Scientists turn seawater into fresh water without harmful brine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:44:50 UTC
23:44:50 KST

Scientists turn seawater into fresh water without harmful brine
A new solar-powered desalination system could turn seawater into fresh water while eliminating brine waste and even harvesting valuable lithium.
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Rochester
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a solar-powered desalination system that turns seawater into fresh water while removing nearly all of the leftover salt as a solid instead of producing harmful brine. The self-cleaning technology could also recover valuable minerals such as lithium, potentially turning desalination waste into a useful resource.
- Share:
Around the world, billions of people still lack reliable access to safe drinking water. The United Nations estimates that 2.2 billion people do not have safely managed drinking water, while regions from California to the Middle East increasingly rely on desalination plants to turn ocean water into fresh water.
Desalination can provide a critical water supply, but today's most common methods come with significant drawbacks. Reverse osmosis forces water through specialized membranes to remove salt, while thermal distillation uses heat to separate fresh water from seawater. Both approaches can consume large amounts of energy, often require water treatment before and after the process, and generate a highly concentrated salty waste known as brine.
When that brine is discharged back into the ocean, it can increase local salinity and reduce oxygen levels, creating harmful conditions for marine organisms.
A Solar-Powered Alternative to Conventional Desalination
Researchers at the University of Rochester have developed a different approach that could help address several of those problems at once.
Scientists at URochester's Institute of Optics created a solar thermal desalination system designed to produce fresh water efficiently without generating liquid brine or requiring chemical additives to pre-treat the incoming water. The method is described in a paper published in Light: Science & Applications.
The research was led by Chunlei Guo, a professor of optics and physics and a senior scientist at URochester's Laboratory for Laser Energetics.
At the heart of the technology are solar panels made from black metal that has been treated with femtosecond lasers. A femtosecond is an extraordinarily short unit of time, equal to one quadrillionth of a second. Pulses from these ultrafast lasers can precisely alter a material's surface, creating microscopic structures that dramatically change how it interacts with light and water.
The laser treatment makes the metal extremely effective at absorbing sunlight and also gives it superwicking properties, meaning water spreads rapidly across the surface instead of beading up.
How the Self-Cleaning Surface Works
Each panel contains a laser-treated active region that draws a very thin layer of seawater across its surface. The dark metal absorbs nearly all of the incoming solar radiation, heating the water and causing it to evaporate.
That evaporation leaves salts and other dissolved minerals behind. Rather than allowing those materials to accumulate where evaporation is taking place, the panel directs them toward untreated areas along its sides, known as the passive region.
This movement is important because salt buildup is one of the biggest challenges facing solar desalination systems. If minerals form a hard layer across the active surface, they can block water movement and eventually stop the system from working.
Why Real Seawater Is Much Harder to Desalinate
Guo says previous solar thermal desalination systems have often performed well in laboratory experiments using simplified artificial seawater made from water and sodium chloride.
When sodium chloride crystallizes as water evaporates, it tends to form a relatively grainy and porous structure. Water can continue moving through those crystals, helping dissolve accumulated salt and making the surface easier to clean.
Real seawater is far more complicated.
In addition to sodium chloride, it contains magnesium, calcium, and many other dissolved substances. Some of those compounds can crystallize into hard, dense deposits that are much less porous.
It is similar to the mineral scale that gradually builds up inside a shower head or tea pot. In a desalination system, however, the challenge is much greater because seawater contains hundreds of times more dissolved salts than ordinary tap water.
As those deposits accumulate, water can no longer flow freely across the surface, reducing efficiency and eventually clogging the system.
Using the Coffee Ring Effect to Move Salt
To overcome that problem, Guo's team carefully designed microscopic grooves in the black metal so salts and minerals would be pushed away from the active region instead of forming a stubborn crust.
The researchers also took advantage of a familiar physical phenomenon called the coffee ring effect.
Anyone who has spilled coffee and watched it dry has probably seen it. As water evaporates, suspended particles move toward the edge of the droplet, leaving behind a dark ring.
"If you drop coffee on a surface, eventually the water evaporates and there's a ring left at the outer edge that is the concentrated coffee particles," says Guo. "We use that same principle to advance the salts to the passive region."
Instead of allowing minerals to build up where sunlight is driving evaporation, the system guides them toward the edges of the panel.
The researchers tested the technique using actual seawater collected from the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans. In those experiments, the surface effectively cleaned itself while producing fresh water, directing the remaining salts into the passive region where they could later be collected.
Importantly, that mineral buildup did not reduce the panel's desalination efficiency.
Turning Desalination Waste Into Useful Materials
Another major advantage is what happens to the salt after the water is removed.
Rather than producing concentrated liquid brine that must be treated or discharged, the system extracts nearly 100 percent of the dissolved salts in solid form.
That material could potentially become a resource rather than a waste product. Some of it could be used as table salt, while more valuable minerals could also be recovered.
One particularly important target is lithium, a key material used in lithium-ion batteries that power electric vehicles, smartphones, laptops, and many other electronic devices.
In a related study published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, Guo and his colleagues demonstrated that the same superwicking solar panels can be modified to separate lithium from the other salts produced during desalination.
The researchers embedded nanoparticles made from hydrogen titanate into the microscopic grooves of the black metal. Those particles selectively isolate lithium from the mixture of salts and minerals.
"Mining lithium from the earth has proven to be very taxing from an energy and environmental standpoint, so pulling lithium directly from saltwater could be a very important future route," says Guo.
Recovering Lithium From Saltwater
Using samples from Great Salt Lake, the team was able to recover about 50 percent of the lithium contained in the salts left behind after desalination.
That result points to a possible future in which desalination facilities could do more than produce drinking water. They might also recover commercially valuable materials that would otherwise remain trapped in waste streams.
The technology is still at an early stage. So far, the researchers have demonstrated the superwicking desalination approach in proof-of-concept experiments using relatively small devices.
Guo says the basic design is inherently scalable, however, and could eventually contribute both to expanding access to fresh water and to creating more sustainable sources of valuable minerals.
If successfully scaled, the approach could address two major challenges at the same time: producing more fresh water for a growing global population while reducing the environmental burden associated with both desalination waste and mineral extraction.
The research was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and Worldwide Universities Network. Guo's colleagues from the Institute of Optics who contributed to the research include Senior Scientist Subash Singh, alumnus Ran Wei '24 (PhD), PhD students Luheng Tang and Tainshu Xu, and Mingjiang Ma.

- Luheng Tang, Subhash C. Singh, Mingjiang Ma, Chunlei Guo. Rapid lithium extraction via solar-thermal interfacial evaporation with zero liquid discharge. Journal of Materials Chemistry A, 2026; 14 (25): 16023 DOI: 10.1039/D5TA08968A

Earlier this month, the High Court of Justice unanimously struck down a law shielding haredi yeshiva students from arrest, investigation, and other proceedings over draft evasion, finding that the coalition had used a fundamentally defective legislative process to deprive the IDF of central enforcement tools.
Eight of the nine justices went further in the verdict, ruling that the law’s substance was also unconstitutional because it protected one group from criminal enforcement while leaving intact the legal obligation to report for military service to the group’s members.
This law never took effect. Justice Ofer Grosskopf froze it on July 15, one day after it passed, and the full nine-justice panel maintained that freeze following a hearing later that month.
Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

Gaza rug maker revives 300-year-old family craft in ruins left by Israeli war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:44:25 UTC
23:44:25 KST

In a cramped room beneath his home in eastern Gaza City, Palestinian craftsman Hussein Mahmoud al-Sawwaf turns a wooden wheel by hand as strands of wool and acrylic stretch across a simple loom, gradually taking the shape of a handmade rug.
There is no electricity, no modern machinery and no trace of the large factory where al-Sawwaf worked before Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip.
All he has are simple tools, yarn salvaged from the destruction and hands that know the craft well.
At his modest home in the Tuffah neighborhood, near the “Yellow Line” where Israeli forces are deployed, al-Sawwaf has converted a small space into a workshop for making handmade carpets and rugs after his factory was destroyed and its warehouses burned during the war.
With carpets, rugs and floor mats scarce in Gaza’s markets and the few available products increasingly expensive, al-Sawwaf has revived a craft his family has passed down for about 300 years.
For him, rug-making is no longer simply about preserving his ancestors’ profession. It has become a way to provide a cheaper product for Palestinians exhausted financially by the war while restoring a source of income for some of the workers who lost their jobs when his factory was destroyed.
Demand for such products has grown as widespread destruction of homes and businesses has stripped Palestinians of livelihoods and household belongings.
Large numbers of people have also been forced to live in tents, shelters and temporary accommodation after their homes were destroyed, damaged or rendered uninhabitable.
 
A craft born again out of necessity
Several men who worked with al-Sawwaf before the war now sit beside him in the small workshop. The craft has brought them back together after the war scattered them and deprived them of work.
They operate a manual wheel designed by al-Sawwaf himself to cope with the prolonged electricity shortages that have affected Gaza since the war began.
Al-Sawwaf, the son of the late carpet maker Mahmoud Husni al-Sawwaf, said he was forced to stop working during the first weeks of the war and flee from northern Gaza to the south amid Israeli attacks.
As the war continued and carpets, mats, fabrics and raw materials disappeared from local markets, he decided to resume the family trade with whatever resources remained.
“After fabric, carpets and mats were no longer available, I began renovating the shop and resumed work so we can meet some of our people’s needs, especially those displaced in tents, given the continuing blockade and restrictions on the entry of materials,” he told Anadolu.
 
 
Factory reduced to rubble
Returning to work was not easy. The factory that had supported al-Sawwaf, his family and dozens of workers no longer existed.
He said Israeli attacks completely destroyed the facility and burned its stocks of raw materials, finished products and machinery. Only one machine and a small number of tools could be salvaged.
Al-Sawwaf estimated that 80% to 85% of the yarn and other materials stored in his warehouses were burned.
Another portion of his stock remains in a warehouse in an area under Israeli military control, and he does not know what condition it is in.
Among the materials that survived were wool and acrylic yarn imported before the war, which have now become a rare form of capital that he is using to keep the craft alive.
“We work with whatever resources we have available,” he said.
 
Back to basic tools
The workshop reflects the scarcity surrounding it. There is no regular electricity, modern equipment or steady supply of raw materials.
To overcome those limitations, al-Sawwaf designed a hand-operated wheel inspired by a machine used during his grandfather’s time and adjusted his looms so they can function with basic tools.
With repeated movements, he winds the yarn and turns the wheel as workers arrange and secure the threads around him, gradually forming each rug strand by strand.
The devastation in Gaza has extended far beyond homes, damaging factories, workshops, stores and other economic facilities and leaving many Palestinians without jobs or income.
At the same time, Israeli restrictions on the entry of goods and raw materials have contributed to shortages and higher prices, while many families have little purchasing power left after years of war.
 
A cheaper alternative
Against that backdrop, handmade rugs have become a practical response to a growing need.
Al-Sawwaf said demand for his products has been noticeable, particularly because handmade rugs are cheaper and better suited to what families can currently afford.
“I have seen significant demand from people for handmade rugs because of their low price and because they are affordable,” he said.
The rugs he now produces differ from traditional carpets in price and design but offer families a practical way to cover the floors of homes and tents.
Their light weight and ease of cleaning and transport have also made them attractive to customers, al-Sawwaf said.
 
A 300-year legacy
For al-Sawwaf, however, every rug carries meaning beyond its practical use. Each thread represents the continuation of a family profession that he fears could disappear because of the war.
He said his late father used to tell him that the craft had been inherited from earlier generations. He later learned that his family’s history in carpet-making stretched back roughly 300 years.
“This is the profession of our fathers and grandfathers, passed down to their children,” he said. “I remember my father telling me that it had been his grandfather’s profession many decades ago.”
Al-Sawwaf has brought several former factory workers into the small workshop in hopes of restoring at least part of the income they lost when the factory was destroyed.
 
Working near ‘Yellow Line’
Al-Sawwaf’s workshop is located near the Sanafor junction in Gaza City’s Tuffah neighborhood, close to the so-called “Yellow Line” marking areas where Israeli forces remain deployed under the ceasefire arrangements.
“I insisted on living and working despite the Israeli army forces being nearby,” he said. “We have to continue the journey after my father.”
The “Yellow Line” was established as an Israeli military deployment line following the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. However, Israel subsequently expanded its control to encompass areas estimated at approximately 70% of the Strip's territory.
Al-Sawwaf hopes conditions will eventually allow raw materials and machinery to enter Gaza again so he can expand production and rebuild the factory he lost.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza began in October 2023. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 73,000 Palestinians killed and over 174,000 injured, mostly women and children.

117 journalists displaced from Yemen’s western coast amid escalation: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:43:37 UTC
23:43:37 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Ikram Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 117 journalists and media workers have been displaced from Yemen's western coastal city of Mokha and surrounding areas amid a military escalation since the beginning of September, the Yemeni Media Freedoms Observatory said Wednesday.
The nongovernmental organization said in a statement that the journalists and media workers fled Mokha, in southwestern Taiz province, and nearby areas amid recent military developments and the entry of Houthi forces.
It said the displacement was sudden, with several journalists leaving their homes in the hours before Houthi forces entered Mokha, amid fears of arrest or detention because of their journalistic work.
Some journalists were forced to leave without taking their personal belongings or professional equipment, it added.
The observatory quoted journalists who fled Mokha as saying that “Houthi forces raided the homes of journalists and looted their belongings.”
Others said they left in haste and were able to take only a limited portion of their belongings and equipment.
The group also reported the death of journalist Zakaria Dahman, a staffer at at Al-Jumhuriya TV, owned by Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh, in the southern port city of Aden after his health deteriorated during the fighting and displacement from Mokha to Aden, according to his colleagues.
Information blockade from conflict-hit area
The organization said the departure of journalists and correspondents from Mokha had “reduced access to independent, firsthand information from inside the city, making it more difficult to verify developments on the ground and provide information to the public.”
It called on international and local organizations, donors and press freedom partners to “urgently support displaced journalists, including through temporary financial assistance, housing, psychological support, professional assistance and the equipment needed to continue their work safely.”
The western coastal areas of Yemen have witnessed a major escalation in recent days, coinciding with advances by Houthi forces and their reported capture of positions and areas previously held by government forces. The developments have reshaped the control map along parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces have announced advances in the northern Al-Jawf province bordering Saudi Arabia. They have also said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
Government forces have also announced airstrikes on Houthi targets in and around Mocha and in parts of Taiz, Lahej and Al-Dhalea provinces, saying they destroyed military vehicles and weapons and repelled a major attack on Marib.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has intensified since early July 2026 after years of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Sweden's centre-left opposition wins election, SVT says
STOCKHOLM, Sept 16 - Sweden's centre-left opposition has defeated the incumbent right-wing governing bloc by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday, after 99% of the votes in Sunday's parliamentary election had been counted.
Only 26,169 votes separated the two blocs at 1647 GMT, but with fewer than 1% of districts left to count, parties led by opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats looked set to win 175 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, signalling a change of government.
"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," SVT said.
The right-wing governing bloc of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, was meanwhile on track to win 174 seats, data from Sweden's election authority showed.
The agency is now counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, and has said this process may go on until Thursday before all votes are accounted for. REUTERS

14:42:47 UTC

At a meeting following the presentation ceremony, Ambassador Auväärt and Governor General Arbour discussed the close and practical alliance between Estonia and Canada, as well as cooperation on security, support for Ukraine and economic affairs.
“Canada’s role in ensuring the security of our region and supporting Ukraine cannot be overstated. We greatly value the presence of Canadian forces in our neighbouring country Latvia and Canada’s significant contribution to NATO’s collective defence,” Auväärt said.
The Ambassador noted that economic ties between Estonia and Canada have grown increasingly close in recent years. Cooperation between the two countries encompasses, among other areas, critical minerals and global supply chains, including rare earth production and the magnet factory opened in Narva last autumn by the Canadian company Neo Performance Materials.
The Ambassador also highlighted the Estonian community in Canada, which is one of the most vibrant Estonian communities outside Estonia. A testament to this is KESKUS, the international Estonian centre that opened in Toronto a month ago.
“Amid the tragic events of the 20th century, Canada gave thousands of Estonians the opportunity to build a new home and a future, for which we are deeply grateful. We also greatly value Canada’s decision to be among the first countries in the world to recognise the restoration of Estonia’s independence,” the Ambassador said.
Gert Auväärt was born on 22 August 1980. He holds a master’s degree in law from the University of Helsinki and has undertaken further studies in cybersecurity at the Marshall Center and the European Security and Defence College. Since 2004, he has held various positions at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, including as Legal and Economic Adviser at the Estonian Embassy in The Hague and Legal Adviser at Estonia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations. From 2017 to 2018, he was Head of International Relations at the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA), and from 2018 to 2021 he served as Deputy Permanent Representative at Estonia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, where his responsibilities included successfully completing Estonia’s first campaign for a seat on the UN Security Council and coordinating Estonia’s substantive work and presidencies during its membership of the Council.
From 2021 to 2026, Auväärt served as Deputy Director General of RIA and Director of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-EE). For the past five years, he also represented Estonia on the Management Board of the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and was a member of the European Cyber Crises Liaison Organisation Network (EU-CyCLONe).

====================================================================================================

China’s Free-Trade Offer to Africa Won’t Solve the Trade Imbalance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:41:00 UTC
23:41:00 KST

In Abuja on August 14, 2026, nearly 500 government officials, diplomats, scholars, and business representatives gathered for a seminar on China’s new zero-tariff policy and what it means for African economic transformation. Nigeria’s minister of state for agriculture, Aliyu Sabi Abdullahi, used the occasion to strike a cautious note. “Zero tariffs alone do not guarantee success,” he told the room. “The question before us, therefore, is not, can Nigeria export more? The question should be, can Nigeria export better?”
Since May 1, China has extended zero-tariff treatment across 100 percent of tariff lines to the 53 African countries with which it holds diplomatic relations. That gives nearly all of Africa (with the lone exception of Eswatini) duty-free access to one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The early results look encouraging: Chinese imports from Africa reached $28.7 billion in May and June, up 23.5 percent from a year earlier. During the seminar in Abuja, China’s ambassador to Nigeria reported that Chinese imports from Nigeria specifically had already grown more than 40 percent year-on-year in both May and June.
African governments have good reason to welcome China’s new zero-tariff policy. The problem is that lower tariffs alone cannot resolve the deeper imbalance that has built up in Africa-China trade.
Africa-China merchandise trade hit a record $348 billion in 2025, but the flows were badly lopsided. China sold Africa $225 billion in goods, Africa sold China $123 billion. For every dollar of goods Africa sold China, it bought back roughly $1.83. The resulting deficit, $102 billion, was 64.5 percent above 2024’s figure. In the same period, Chinese exports to Africa grew 25.8 percent, while African exports to China grew just 5.4 percent.
Market access – like China’s new offer to African countries – can change the volume of trade, but not necessarily the structure of trade. What is actually being exported by each partner matters more than the size of the deficit itself. Research from the Boston University Global Development Policy Center and the African Economic Research Consortium found that from 2000 through 2022, 89 percent of African exports to China came from extractive industries: oil, copper, iron ore, alumina. Over the same period, 94 percent of African imports from China were manufactured goods.
A 2026 update from the same researchers showed that not much had changed. Extracted natural resources still dominate Africa’s exports to China, while agriculture and manufacturing each account for a small share of export value.
Most African countries have clearly stated ambitions to move up the value chain. Lower tariffs alone will do little to accomplish that goal. The rising volume of Africa-China trade is easy to measure and just as easy to celebrate, but the overall numbers are less important than the composition of trade.
The tariff opening still matters, of course. African exports of avocados, apples, and oranges to China have risen sharply since implementation. Market access of this kind can pull real investment toward certification, cold-chain logistics, and packaging, some of the obstacles holding producers back. But that won’t happen automatically.
Take copper as an example. Copper can be exported from Africa as raw ore, or it can be refined and worked into components before it ships. Currently, that work – and the added value – happens almost entirely outside the continent. China’s zero-tariff policy doesn’t care whether the copper is raw or refined; the tariff line is the same either way.
Two recent examples show what greater processing and value capture inside Africa can actually look like. At a processing plant in Kenya’s Athi River Export Processing Zone, locally grown avocados are ripened, sorted, and cold-pressed into extra virgin avocado oil bound for China. In Rwanda, a company that began exporting dried chilies to China in 2022 shipped its first batch of pickled chilies in June – a deliberate move toward a higher-value semi-processed product made only after the tariff change. In both cases, more processing is happening before the goods leave the continent, which means more of the value is captured in Kenya and Rwanda rather than downstream in China.
African countries do have the capability to move up the value chain, and intra-Africa trade proves it. UNCTAD reported that 61 percent of trade happening within the continent consists of processed and semi-processed goods, far above Africa’s share of processed exports to the rest of the world. The opportunity is to pair China’s external market with the regional value chains the African Continental Free Trade Area is meant to build. Cotton grown in Mali or Burkina Faso can be baled and shipped directly to China for processing, or it can move first through mills in Cote d’Ivoire or Ghana and leave as finished cloth.
It’s not tariffs that are holding back African manufacturing. China’s zero-tariff policy won’t solve problems like unreliable electricity, expensive financing, inefficient ports, thin transport links, certification bottlenecks, or customs delays. UNCTAD estimated that road transport alone accounts for about 29 percent of the price of goods traded within Africa, compared with 7 percent for goods traded beyond it. According to UNCTAD, non-tariff barriers constrain intra-African trade roughly three times more than tariffs.
African governments need to treat China’s opening as one input into a larger industrial policy, not as a substitute for having one. Africa-China trade will likely keep setting records, but that alone won’t help African economies climb global value chains. The real test will show up in the breakdown of those trade statistics: whether Africa is still mostly exporting raw materials like crude oil and copper ore or refined metals and finished goods.

Celebrated playwright and novelist Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:39:35 UTC
23:39:35 KST

Greer was known for incisive TV and radio appearances and for her novels, plays and essays which delved into politics, culture and identity.
American and British playwright-novelist Bonnie Greer has died aged 77.
Her husband David Hutchins announced the news, saying: "It is with profound sadness that I announce that my beloved wife, Bonnie Greer, has died aged 77 after a brief illness."
"Bonnie was an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."
Hutchins added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her. Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."
Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer moved to Britain in 1986. She became a familiar face on British television, including as a panelist on shows like Newsnight and Question Time.
Greer was awarded the Verity Bargate Award for Best Play for "Munda Negra" and she was also the author of the novels "Hanging By Her Teeth" (1994) and "Entropy" (2009).
Other works include the biography "Langston Hughes: The Value Of Contradiction" (2011) and the play "Marilyn And Ella" (2008) about actress Marilyn Monroe and singer Ella Fitzgerald.
Greer was appointed to the British Museum's board of trustees in 2005 and later served as deputy chairwoman. She also served on the boards of the London Film School and Royal Opera House, and was appointed a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2022. She also served as Chancellor of Kingston University in Kingston upon Thames, London.
In 2010, Greer was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for her services to the arts.
RIP Bonnie Greer 1948 - 2026

EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:39:26 UTC
23:39:26 KST

The EU will move forward with plans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed.
Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products.
She promised a draft law for a total ban on social media for under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps.
The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law.
Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which she said was “harming everyone”.
The commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address. In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants in response to events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August.
Von der Leyen also made an unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK.
The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version of Nato’s article 4 – an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents – those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.”
Nato’s article 4, which is separate from the collective defence clause, article 5, means members of the alliance can consult when one of them believes their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.
European nations have recently faced a series of hostile acts attributed to Russia, including sabotage, incursions by jets into European airspace and a drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Warning that Ukraine faced a tough winter, von der Leyen suggested the EU may have reached its limits on economic restrictions against Russia. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said.
After 21 rounds of measures, EU member states have found it increasingly difficult to agree sanctions on the Kremlin’s war machine, wary of the cost to their own economies.
Von der Leyen also touched on Europe’s divisions over whether or not to introduce restrictions on trade with Israel and its illegal settlements in the West Bank. “When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she said.

More than 104,000 people displaced inside Yemen as fighting continues: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:38:56 UTC
23:38:56 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
More than 104,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen as fighting along the West Coast continues, the UN migration agency said on Wednesday.
A total of 104,796 people from 17,461 households have been displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) latest Displacement Tracking Matrix.
Taiz remains the epicenter, with more than 63,000 displaced in its districts, including 21,018 in Jabal Habashi, 12,642 in Al Ma'afer and 8,250 in Ash Shamayatayn.
Nearly 26,400 people have been displaced in Lahj, while Aden has recorded more than 3,500. Displacement is also rising in Al Abyan, Hadramawt and Ma'rib as fighting spreads, said IOM.
"Yemen is a country torn by war, displacement, poverty, and climate impacts," said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “Overlooking the suffering of civilians is not acceptable as needs continue to rise.”
The agency said families are moving under fire, often at night and with few belongings, while the pace of displacement is outstripping aid workers' ability to track movements in real time.
The IOM added that as many as 2,776 people have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti, where the agency is providing emergency assistance.
20M need health assistance
Nearly 20 million people in Yemen need health assistance as escalating violence places further strain on the country's already fragile health system, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said.
"The recent escalation of violence is compounding an already severe health and humanitarian crisis," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters in Geneva.
Tedros said fighting has caused a sharp increase in casualties and displacement, while attacks on health facilities, shortages of supplies and fuel, and disruptions to referral services are pushing the health system “closer to collapse.”
He warned that risks from cholera, measles, polio and dengue, as well as malnutrition, are growing, particularly among displaced communities living in overcrowded conditions with limited access to safe water and sanitation.
Tedros said the WHO is providing emergency medical supplies and working with partners to strengthen frontline response capacity. However, humanitarian access remains "severely constrained," while funding shortfalls threaten efforts to sustain and scale up the response.
He called for the protection of health workers and facilities, unhindered humanitarian access and increased international support to address rapidly escalating needs.
