Sniffing out trouble: Customs dogs remain vital in the age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:26:22 UTC
23:26:22 KST

From synthetic drugs to concealed cargo, trained dogs can detect what scanners may miss. At a WCO forum in Tashkent, experts showed how canine units and new technology are increasingly working side by side.
As artificial intelligence and advanced scanning systems transform border controls, customs services still rely on one of their oldest detection tools: trained dogs.
AI can analyse images and data, identify patterns and help customs officers decide which shipments or containers warrant closer inspection.
But customs officials, dog handlers, and other specialists from more than 50 countries gathered at the World Customs Organisation's 7th Global Canine Forum in Tashkent argued that this does not remove the need for dogs trained to detect scents.
Antonio Lo Parco, head of the WCO's Regional Office for Capacity Building for Europe, told Euronews that dogs possess detection abilities “that AI cannot substitute”.
Information from canine detection can also feed into AI systems, he added, helping customs authorities identify patterns and emerging trends.
Oliver Stolper, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's regional representative for Central Asia, also sees the two tools as complementary.
AI can help customs services identify containers that require additional scrutiny and analyse images for signs of illicit cargo.
“But a dog cannot be replaced,” Stolper told Euronews. “Customs organisations continue to rely on them and for good reasons, as we can see in everyday work.”
Experts explained that technology can help narrow the search, while a trained dog provides an additional form of detection.
The role of detection dogs is also evolving as illicit drug markets change.
Jonibek Yusupov, an officer at Uzbekistan's Agency for the Control of Narcotic Drugs and Firearms, said authorities had recorded a significant rise in synthetic drugs since the pandemic.
Canine units are now training dogs specifically to recognise the scents associated with synthetic narcotic substances.
“If we rely solely on artificial intelligence or technology, we can only analyse images,” Yusupov told Euronews. “But narcotic substances have a smell.”
How a service dog is trained
Uzbekistan's National Canine Centre has been training dogs and handlers for three decades.
Established in 1996, it trains canine teams for customs and other law-enforcement agencies. It was granted WCO Regional Canine Centre status in 2008.
Its dogs are trained for tasks including the detection of narcotics, psychotropic substances, weapons, ammunition and explosives, as well as search-and-rescue and tracking operations.
But not every puppy is suitable.
At around four months old, dogs bred at the centre begin working with instructors and are assessed for characteristics including their response to noise, unfamiliar environments and heights.
“Not every dog can become a service dog,” chief instructor Captain Ahmadjon Goyibov told Euronews.
The centre primarily works with German and Belgian Shepherds, Russian Spaniels and Labradors.
Dogs that pass the selection process are gradually introduced to environments they may encounter during operations, including vehicles and railway carriages.
Specialised training begins around eight months of the dog's age and normally lasts six to seven months. Training is adapted to each dog's temperament.
Dogs are also taught how to signal a detection to their handler, for example by sitting, lying down or remaining still.
Goyibov rejected a common misconception that drug-detection dogs are made dependent on narcotics or otherwise forced to perform their work.
“We never use force against the dogs,” he said. “We train them solely through positive reinforcement. We give them their favourite toy or their favourite food as a reward, but we never use force.”
Toys, including ones with food or treats inside, are used as rewards during exercises, teaching the animal to associate a successful detection with something positive.
For Goyibov, however, technique alone is not enough.
“To become a good canine specialist, first and foremost, you need to love service dogs and animals and be able to show them care and affection,” he said.
A regional training centre
Uzbekistan's centre also trains foreign canine teams.
In recent years, 220 handlers from countries including South Korea, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Armenia and Mongolia have received training or professional development there.
More than 200 service dogs have also undergone specialised training, with some later deployed by customs authorities outside Uzbekistan.
Elpida Kasapi of the Greek Customs Service said the forum gave participants the opportunity to study WCO criteria for canine training centres and consider how to apply them at home.
“What we are doing here will be extremely useful for us,” Kasapi told Euronews, “as it will allow us to gain knowledge and information that we can then apply to the Greek context and to our practices in Greece.”
According to Uzbekistan's Customs Committee, between 2023 and the first half of 2026, service dogs trained at the centre helped intercept more than 12 tonnes of narcotic substances.

====================================================================================================

China is building the machinery of a post-Western order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:25:51 UTC
23:25:51 KST

China is building the machinery of a post-Western order
The latest SCO and BRICS summits offer a glimpse of a world no longer organized around a single center of gravity. As governments from Asia, Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere seek greater room to maneuver, the old architecture of global governance is under pressure – not necessarily because it has become irrelevant, but because the distribution of power around it has changed.
That is the backdrop against which China’s Global Governance Initiative, or GGI, enters its second year.
When President Xi Jinping unveiled the initiative at the SCO Plus meeting in Tianjin on September 1, 2025, it could easily have been dismissed as another diplomatic cliché. A year on, and China has begun translating the GGI into institutions dealing with mediation, data, and artificial intelligence, while embedding its principles in its longer-term economic and diplomatic planning.
A different map of globalization
The GGI starts from a proposition that the institutions of global governance have not kept pace with the distribution of global power. China’s preferred answer is not to abandon multilateralism but to dilute what it sees as its concentration in the hands of a small number of established powers. Sovereign equality is central: Every state, in principle, should have a voice regardless of its size, wealth, or political system.
This is where the GGI connects with China’s overall foreign policy. The Global Security Initiative emphasizes common security and strategic stability; the Global Development Initiative promotes development and economic integration; and the Global Civilization Initiative stresses dialogue across different civilizational traditions. The GGI provides an umbrella under which these ideas can be linked to the institutions of international governance.
China has little interest in a fragmented world economy. It is the main trading partner of more than 160 countries and regions and has concluded 24 free-trade agreements with 31 countries and regions. At the same time, Beijing rejects the idea that economic integration must entail political convergence on Western terms.
The post-Cold War model of globalization was built around the neoliberal ‘Washington Consensus’ and institutions whose center of gravity was largely Western. China’s alternative is a combination of economic openness with political sovereignty and strategic autonomy over development choices.
This is why Beijing’s opposition to trade wars, technology blockades, unilateral sanctions and protectionism sits comfortably alongside its advocacy of globalization. China wants interdependence to remain an economic asset without allowing it to become a political instrument of coercion.
The politics of the five deficits
The GGI also reflects China’s view of a world entering what might be called a polycrisis. Wars and geopolitical confrontation coexist with trade fragmentation, climate pressures, sovereign debt, and technological inequality. Beijing describes the result as five deficits: deficits of peace, development, security, governance, and trust.
For Beijing, today’s problems cannot be solved by reproducing yesterday’s hierarchy. A system designed when the global economy was dominated by the US and Europe, the argument goes, cannot indefinitely give those same actors disproportionate influence while countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East acquire greater economic and political weight.
Chinese scholar Wang Yiwei has put it bluntly: Global governance should not mean governance by the US or the West, but governance by all countries, particularly the Global South, which represents about 80% of mankind.
That is the GGI’s most politically significant claim. It is also the one most likely to encounter resistance.
For the established powers, greater representation can sound like a euphemism for reducing their influence. For many developing countries, however, reform of global institutions has long been a matter of practicality, not ideology. The question is why their economic and demographic importance is not already better reflected in institutions governing finance, trade, technology, and security.
From slogans to institutions
During the GGI’s first year, Beijing has tried to give the concept institutional form.
In October 2025, the International Organization for Mediation began operations in Hong Kong. It is the first intergovernmental organization dedicated specifically to resolving international disputes through voluntary, non-binding mediation. Thirty-three countries became founding members. ‘Mediation’ fits China’s longstanding emphasis on negotiation and non-interference while addressing a genuine weakness in the international system: the growing difficulty of resolving disputes when major powers themselves are parties to them.
Two months later, China helped establish the Group of Friends of Global Governance at the United Nations, with 43 founding member states. This places the GGI inside the UN’s multilateral environment, rather than trying to establish a parallel system.
In March 2026, Beijing became home to another novelty: the World Data Organization. And in July, the World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai produced an agreement by 29 countries to establish the World AI Cooperation Organization, headquartered in Shanghai.
Mediation, data, and artificial intelligence are all governance gaps. Existing institutions were largely created before digital platforms, generative AI, and data flows became strategic assets. Whoever helps write the rules in these fields will have influence well beyond the conference room.
The United Nations is still the arena
The fact that China advocates a more multipolar order while simultaneously insisting that the United Nations remain at its center may seem like a paradox, but there really is no contradiction here: Beijing does not want to replace the existing system, but to change its internal balance.
China’s contribution to the UN regular budget rose from less than 1% in the year 2000 to more than 20% in 2025, making it the organization’s second-largest contributor after the US. Beijing has also placed implementation of the UN Pact for the Future at the heart of its diplomatic agenda.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026-2030 calls for China’s participation in reforming global economic and financial governance, defending the multilateral trading system centered on the World Trade Organization, opposing protectionism, and expanding China’s network of free-trade agreements. That’s not the rhetoric of a country preparing to withdraw from the existing order.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) offers a model and a testing platform for Beijing’s project. At the Tianjin summit that coincided with the GGI’s launch, member states inaugurated four security centers and agreed to establish an SCO Development Bank.
An idea with deeper roots
The GGI isn’t China’s first attempt to articulate a theory of international order.
The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, developed in the 1950s, placed sovereignty, non-interference, and equality at the center of China’s diplomatic thinking. In the 1970s, Mao Zedong’s Three Worlds theory offered a different interpretation of the global balance: Two superpowers dominated the international system, while developed and developing countries formed distinct political constituencies, with China identifying itself with the developing world.
The circumstances have changed radically. China’s own position has changed most of all. But the underlying concern with hierarchy and great-power dominance has survived.
There is an older Chinese intellectual reference point as well: Tianxia, or ‘all under Heaven’, imagined political order as extending beyond the boundaries of a single state. It was not a theory of modern sovereign equality and should not be projected mechanically onto today’s international system. Still, its emphasis on order, coexistence, and harmony provides part of the intellectual background for Beijing’s ideas of a global community.
The modern version is not a hierarchy centered on China, but a world conceived as an interconnected whole in which civilizations can cooperate without becoming identical.
The hard part begins now
The GGI’s first year has demonstrated that China can mobilize diplomatic support and help create institutions. The harder task is demonstrating that these institutions can produce international public goods. That will require more than conferences and declarations.
Can mediation prevent disputes from escalating when the interests of major powers collide? Can new institutions for data and AI produce rules that countries outside China’s political orbit genuinely accept? Can the SCO and BRICS convert their growing membership and economic weight into effective collective action? And can China persuade countries that a more multipolar order will mean not simply a redistribution of power among great states, but greater agency for smaller and developing ones?
The GGI does not offer a fully worked-out alternative world order, and that may ultimately be its strength. Its ambition is to make an existing system more representative, more inclusive and, crucially, more capable of delivering results.
China’s underlying bet is that the international order is already moving toward multipolarity and that institutions will either adapt to that reality or lose legitimacy. As the Chinese government has put it, mankind is destined to move “from confrontation to cooperation, imbalance to balance, division to coexistence.”

All cargo entering Gaza is subject to strict Israeli approval, including essential items as well as heavy machinery and other items Tel Aviv classifies as "dual-use."

Firefox teams with Mistral for AI browsing
- Mozilla’s Firefox launched an AI assistant called "Smart Window" powered by French start-up Mistral, focusing on strict privacy and no personal data selling or retention.
- The AI assistant uses open-source models and promises not to save chatbot prompts or responses, addressing global concerns about AI privacy and control.
- Mistral, backed by €3 billion funding, partners with Firefox to offer private, user-controlled AI browsing, with rollout starting in North America and France, expanding to the UK and Germany in 2026.
AI generated
PARIS – Mozilla’s web browser Firefox unveiled on Sept 16 an AI assistant powered by the French start-up Mistral, promising strict privacy protections as worries grow about artificial intelligence’s capabilities.
The “Smart Window” on Firefox will rely on open-source models, and the non-profit group said it would not sell personal data or “use your conversations to train models”.
Alarm is growing worldwide that artificial intelligence capabilities are progressing faster than developers can control, prompting calls for stronger government regulation.
“We are bringing privacy, control and choice to AI-powered web browsing,” Mistral chief executive Arthur Mensch said in a statement.
Chatbot prompts and responses will not be saved on Mozilla servers, and Mistral has promised there will be no retention of private data – a key feature for a growing number of corporate AI clients as developers roll out more powerful models.
“A browser shouldn’t be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next,” Mozilla’s chief executive Anthony Enzor-DeMeo said in the statement.
Mistral said last week it had raised €3 billion (S$4.4 billion) in what it called the largest-ever European tech fund-raising, propelling its overall value to €21 billion.
It remains much smaller than AI giants such as OpenAI or Claude maker Anthropic, but positions itself as offering models that clients can run themselves with their own data.
“This partnership represents two open source advocates working together to bring Mistral’s scientific innovations to Mozilla’s consumers around the world,” Mensch said.
The Smart Window assistant will first be available in North America and France, and rolled out to Britain and Germany later in 2026. AFP

Canada buys a training system

Both sides gain from the deal

The problem the program targets is one every modern army now faces: technology evolves so fast that training has to keep pace, or fall behind.

India rejects the so-called Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission
NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday rejected the so-called Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, saying it has no legal basis and reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of India.Responding to media queries, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson said, "We have seen reports in this regard. The MEA said the entire Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh "have been, are and will always remain integral and inalienable parts of India"."Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," it said.India also reiterated that it has never recognised the so-called "China-Pakistan Boundary Agreement" of 1963 and has consistently maintained that it is "illegal and invalid".

Govt set to abolish road tax for small and mid-sized vehicles
We are scrapping one of the taxes Italians hate most says Meloni
ROME,
16 September 2026, 16:23
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The government is set to abolish road tax for small and medium-sized vehicles including cars and motorcycles, Premier Giorgia Meloni said Wednesday saying cabinet would do away with one of the taxes Italians hate the most. The cabinet is set to approve the abolition of the vehicle ownership tax (bollo auto) for small and medium-powered cars—the types largely used by families for daily commuting, Palazzo Chigi sources said. The exemption also applies to motorcycles, though each citizen is entitled to the benefit for only one vehicle. The measure covers all motorcycles and over 70% of cars currently on the road, amounting to approximately 14.5 million vehicles in total. The move aims to lighten the tax burden associated with owning a car or motorcycle for a vast number of Italians. "Today, the Government is scrapping one of the taxes Italians hate most," commented Meloni.

Sahin Demir
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Iran has “no trust” in International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi for what Tehran considers his politicized handling of the country’s nuclear file, a senior Iranian nuclear official said on Wednesday.
“We have no trust in the director general unless he wants to make a fundamental change in his approach,” Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), told state news agency IRNA.
Kamalvandi accused Grossi of acting politically rather than professionally, saying his reports and public remarks have fueled political pressure on Tehran by European countries, the US and Israel.
“The agency must return to its place, where its work is professional and technical, not political,” he said.
Kamalvandi defended Tehran’s restrictions on IAEA access to nuclear facilities damaged during the war, citing war and security concerns.
He said Iran’s adversaries were seeking information that could be used for additional attacks, making the protection of information on nuclear facilities particularly important.
Kamalvandi also raised concerns about the confidentiality of information provided to the agency, arguing that Tehran should not be expected to provide all information if it cannot be adequately protected.
Iran has restricted IAEA access to nuclear facilities damaged during the war with the US. At the same time, Grossi has stressed the need for inspectors to access the sites to verify Iran’s nuclear material and activities.
Kamalvandi also briefly addressed AEOI chief Mohammad Eslami’s planned attendance at the IAEA General Conference in Vienna, saying Austria had already issued him a multiple-entry Schengen visa before signaling that the visit should not take place.
He accused Vienna of changing its position under US pressure.
Iran subsequently summoned Austria’s charge d’affaires in Tehran and lodged a formal protest for the reversal.

Iran’s date production exceeds 1.9m tons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:21:21 UTC
23:21:21 KST

Iran’s date production exceeds 1.9m tons
TEHRAN- The Head of the Center for Development of Mechanization and Agricultural Industries of the Ministry of Agriculture, stating that more than 1.9 million tons of dates are produced in the country, said: Iran is among the top four countries in the world in terms of production of this product.
According to a Wednesday report by IRNA from the Ministry of Agriculture, Karim Zolfaghari, on the occasion of National Date Day, added: The future of Iran’s date industry depends on moving beyond raw selling and developing the production chain, and processing and complementary industries can be the link connecting producers to domestic and international markets.
The Head of the Center for Development of Mechanization and Agricultural Industries of the Ministry of Agriculture considered dates one of the strategic and export products of the agricultural sector and stated: Strengthening Iran’s presence in target markets requires improving quality, appropriate packaging, standardization, and producing products suited to the needs and tastes of consumers in these markets.
Zolfaghari, stating that dates, in addition to high nutritional value, have significant capacity for foreign exchange earning, employment creation, and development of food industries, emphasized: Moving toward processing and producing diverse products can significantly increase the economic value of this product.
The Head of the Center for Development of Mechanization and Agricultural Industries of the Ministry of Agriculture Jihad, referring to the capacity of date processing industries in the country, said: Currently, 654 date processing and complementary units have operating licenses from the Ministry of Agriculture Jihad, with a nominal capacity of more than 820 thousand tons.
He stated: The production of products such as date paste and syrup, liquid sugar, chocolate and combined products, compote, lavashak, vinegar, and alcohol shows that dates are not just a raw agricultural product and can become the raw material for a wide range of industries.
Zolfaghari emphasized: Development and completion of export infrastructure, support for knowledge-based companies and startups, creation of specialized towns and export terminals in production hubs, as well as reconstruction and renovation of worn-out processing units, are among the most important priorities in this field.
He added: Dates can turn from a traditional agricultural product into the axis of development of food, pharmaceutical, and new products, and investment in processing, technology, and market-making, while increasing the income of palm growers, creates sustainable employment and enhances Iran’s position in the global date trade.
Iran is among the world’s leading producers of dates, and the steady growth in exports highlights the product’s importance in the country’s non-oil trade basket.
The country is renowned for its diverse range of date varieties, with major production centered in the provinces of Kerman, Sistan-Baluchestan, Hormozgan, Khuzestan, Bushehr, and Fars.
Domestically, Iranians consume about 70 percent of the harvest, with a significant surge in demand during the holy month of Ramadan. The remaining 30 percent or roughly 350,000 tons, is exported annually, generating substantial revenue of around $400 million.
Key international markets for Iranian dates include India, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey, Russia, and countries in East Asia and the European Union.
To further enhance the sector's value and reduce post-harvest losses—historically estimated at 30 percent—there is a growing focus on processing dates into value-added products such as syrup, paste, and chocolate for both domestic use and export.
Iran's agriculture sector is a cornerstone of its economy and a key player in its non-oil exports. The country produces a vast array of crops, thanks to its diverse climate zones, and is making significant strides in boosting its international trade.

Taliban seeks US ties, cites Afghan war legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:20:36 UTC
23:20:36 KST

The Taliban wants formal diplomatic relations with the US but said Washington must first address the legacy of its two-decade war in Afghanistan, Taliban spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News in an interview.
Five years after the Taliban returned to power following the US withdrawal, Balkhi portrayed the end of the invasion as the administration's main achievement, while acknowledging persistent unemployment, economic difficulties and public dissatisfaction.
“The greatest achievement obviously Afghanistan has had is the end of occupation,” said Balkhi, arguing that the country had since seen improvements in security, trade, investment and infrastructure.
He claimed Afghan exports rose from $750 million in 2020 to nearly $2 billion, while the number of factories increased from 1,500 to 6,000. He also said the government had been able to pay civil servants and attract billions of dollars in investment.
Balkhi acknowledged, however, that “there are areas where we haven't met the expectation of the general population,” citing widespread unemployment and other challenges.
Diplomatic isolation
The interview on Tuesday also highlighted Afghanistan's continued diplomatic isolation. Russia is the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government.
Balkhi argued that Afghanistan was already engaging diplomatically with several countries and questioned the practical meaning of formal recognition.
On relations with Washington, he said Kabul wanted diplomatic ties with “every single country of the world, including the United States,” and would welcome the reopening of the US Embassy and American investment in sectors such as minerals and gas.
He also rejected calls by US President Donald Trump for Afghanistan to return billions of dollars worth of American-funded military equipment left behind after the 2021 withdrawal. CBS reported that roughly $7 billion in US military hardware remained in Afghanistan.
“That’s the assets of the state of Afghanistan,” said Balkhi, rejecting any deal linking the equipment to the release of Afghan funds frozen abroad.
Asked about the argument that American taxpayers paid for the equipment, Balkhi responded, “The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?”
Demanding frozen assets
Balkhi demanded the release of Afghan central bank assets frozen by Washington, saying the funds belonged to the Afghan state rather than the Taliban government.
On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Balkhi said the Taliban condemned attacks on civilians and reiterated its commitment under the Doha agreement that Afghan territory would not be used to attack the US or any other country.
The interview also focused on restrictions on women and girls. Regarding the suspension of public schooling for girls from seventh grade onward, Balkhi said alternative forms of education remained available and rejected reports of girls attending clandestine classes despite the restrictions.
“There is no such thing as secret schools,” he said, describing the arrangements as homeschooling or madrasa, or Islamic, education.
Looking back at the war that followed the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, Balkhi said Afghanistan had learned that conflicts should be resolved through diplomacy.
“War is not the solution, and occupying Afghanistan certainly isn't to your benefit,” he said, urging greater cooperation for Afghanistan's reconstruction and development.

Berlin’s ‘Mamdani’ eyes mayor’s office as supporters call for a ‘Palestinian Tel Aviv’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:19:20 UTC
23:19:20 KST

Berliners head to the polls on Sunday in an unusually tight election that could put the left-wing Die Linke at the center of the German capital’s next government and propel its lead candidate, Elif Eralp, into contention for the governing mayor’s office.
The latest surveys show anything but a certain victory. An Insa poll published this week puts Die Linke and the conservative CDU level at 20%, while an Infratest dimap survey gave Die Linke a narrow 21%-20% advantage and a ZDF poll put it at 23% against 21% for the CDU. The AfD, Greens and SPD trail behind, leaving coalition negotiations likely to determine who ultimately governs the city.
Even so, Die Linke’s rise has been striking. The party won 12.2% of the second vote in Berlin’s 2023 repeat election, according to the official results, meaning current polling would represent a substantial gain.
At the center of that campaign is Eralp, 45, a lawyer and Berlin state lawmaker whose parents fled Turkey as socialist and trade-union activists. Her political work has focused heavily on migration, discrimination, civil rights and housing, and she has become the party’s candidate for governing mayor.
Berlin’s ‘Mamdani’
Eralp has increasingly been compared with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Die Linke itself has embraced the parallel. After Mamdani’s victory last year, Eralp said that if a leftist could win in New York, there was no reason the same could not happen in Berlin, calling his affordability-focused campaign an inspiration.
The resemblance is most visible in the issues Eralp has chosen to emphasize. Rather than building her campaign primarily around national or international ideological battles, she has focused on rents, housing and the cost of living, backed by intensive social-media outreach and door-to-door campaigning. German reporting on Die Linke’s strategy has explicitly described Mamdani’s New York campaign as a model for the party’s Berlin operation.
Housing is at the heart of the pitch. Eralp backs implementing Berlin’s 2021 referendum on bringing large corporate housing portfolios into public ownership, a proposal that would affect about 220,000 apartments. She also supports a rent cap for municipally owned housing and a state tenant-protection office.
The strategy is aimed at voters beyond Die Linke’s traditional base. Berlin’s housing shortage and soaring rents have pushed affordability to the forefront of the campaign, allowing Eralp to present the party’s program as a response to an everyday economic problem rather than simply an ideological project.
Recognition of ‘genocide’ and rejection of Oct. 7 celebrations
But the campaign has repeatedly been pulled back toward another issue: Israel and Gaza.
At its federal party conference in June, Die Linke formally adopted the position that Israel’s conduct in Gaza constitutes genocide, endorsing the assessment cited by international organizations, rights groups and legal experts. The same party debate also stressed the security, self-determination and dignity of both Israelis and Palestinians, illustrating the effort by the leadership to combine its fierce criticism of Israel with opposition to antisemitism.
Eralp has herself tried to draw that line. In May she published a five-point plan aimed at protecting and strengthening Jewish life in Berlin, warning that antisemitism had intensified since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack and saying Jews must be able to live openly and safely in the capital.
She also distanced herself from an incident at a Die Linke event in Neukölln where a rapper performed lyrics calling for the destruction of the IDF. Eralp said antisemitism must be confronted immediately and called for consequences over the episode.
Yet some activists associated with the party’s pro-Palestinian wing have gone considerably further. Hannah Bruns, a Die Linke member associated with its Palestine solidarity group, was documented declaring that Palestinian liberation would not be complete until Tel Aviv was “in Palestinian hands.” Die Welt has separately reported that party members sought her expulsion and described her as advocating an “Intifada until victory.”
The rhetoric places Eralp in a difficult position. Young and pro-Palestinian voters have been an important part of Die Linke’s recent growth, and reporting on the party’s campaign strategy has identified Gaza as one of the issues that helped it mobilize younger activists. At the same time, Eralp has publicly insisted that Jewish life must be protected and that antisemitism has no place in the party.
Party activists defend Oct. 7 as ‘resistance’
The internal dispute intensified again this week after Die Welt reported on an audio recording from a meeting of Die Linke Berlin’s Palestine solidarity working group.
According to the report, individual party members portrayed Hamas’ Oct. 7 massacre as “resistance” and “self-defense.” One participant, discussing a proposal in support of armed resistance, said: “Was Oct. 7 a brutal act of terrorism? We have to say clearly: No, it was an act of resistance.” The proposal was ultimately rejected.
Those remarks directly contradict the Berlin party leadership’s stated position. In an October 2024 resolution, Die Linke Berlin declared: “Our solidarity ends where the massacre of Oct. 7 is celebrated as an act of resistance,” while also condemning Israeli war crimes and pledging to combat antisemitism in its own ranks.
The party subsequently adopted additional measures against antisemitism, including dialogue with Jewish and Israeli communities, outside expertise and procedures for responding when members violate party principles.
Those tensions have become part of the larger argument over what kind of Die Linke would enter government if the party performs strongly on Sunday: one centered on Eralp’s campaign against high rents and the cost of living, or one repeatedly forced to answer for the rhetoric of its most radical pro-Palestinian activists.
For Eralp, the final days of the campaign therefore involve two very different political battles. One is over who can make Berlin more affordable. The other is over whether she can maintain Die Linke’s pro-Palestinian positioning while enforcing the boundaries her party leadership says it has drawn around antisemitism, political violence and the Oct. 7 massacre. Berlin elects its new House of Representatives on September 20.

Four years on, Iranians reflect on impact of ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’

Mahsa Amini death four years on: Iranians reflect on ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’
Amnesty International says Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during the 2022-23 protests.
Tehran, Iran – Four years ago this week, Mahsa “Jina” Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman, was leaving a metro station in Tehran with members of her family when she was detained by the Guidance Patrol, Iran’s morality police, for perceived noncompliance with Iran’s mandatory hijab laws.
Amini’s headscarf had slightly receded from her forehead, so two female and two male members of the morality police put her in a van and transported her to a so-called re-education centre, where she would receive guidance on how to dress in a way deemed appropriate by the authorities.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4As fuel prices rise again, Iran’s government urges citizens to cut back

- list 3 of 4‘War on terror’: How 9/11 changed the language of conflict
- list 4 of 4A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
Security camera footage released by the government showed Amini in the downtown Tehran re-education centre collapsing onto the ground, as a chador-clad policewoman scolded her. She was taken to a nearby hospital and pronounced dead three days later on September 16, 2022.
Authorities claimed Amini had pre-existing health conditions and denied any wrongdoing. But her father, Amjad Amini, said fellow prisoners told him her daughter had been beaten inside the police van.
Two female journalists, working for local newspapers, helped break the story and grabbed the attention of the nation. The reports included a heart-wrenching image of her parents embracing in front of the intensive care unit where Amini died. The journalists were later imprisoned on national security charges.
Small demonstrations took place in front of the hospital, and then in her hometown of Saqqez, in the western province of Kurdistan, after her funeral. Within several weeks, protests had spread across Iran, calling for greater freedoms for women and Iranians in general. The protests lasted into early 2023 and received support from across the globe.
The United Nations’ Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran later corroborated reports by foreign-based rights groups that at least 550 Iranians were killed during the protests, including 68 children and 49 women in 26 of Iran’s 31 provinces.
A Kurdish saying, “Woman, Life, Freedom”, became the slogan of this unprecedented movement, which has significantly altered how Iranians dress and think.
“I thought we would never be able to choose the way we want to dress, but the movement created massive cultural change and a more progressive identity that can never be taken away now,” Bahar, a 26-year-old woman living in Tehran, who used just her first name for security reasons, told Al Jazeera.
Bahar said she never believed in the mandatory hijab and always wished she could choose what to wear, as most women across the globe do, including in almost all other Islamic countries.
For months after the protests died down, she would keep a headscarf around her neck for fear of reprisals by the authorities. Despite the lingering risks, she no longer carries that headscarf, either.
Setareh, another young resident of the capital, has the support of more family members for her choice of what she wears and how she looks. She faces fewer instances of verbal abuse on Tehran’s streets for how she dresses, and is rarely turned down by ride-hailing drivers for not wearing the hijab.
“People and families, especially men, are now more accustomed to women dressing more naturally, even if they don’t like it,” she told Al Jazeera.
Many Iranians have reflected on the movement online, with one post recalling the time two young women took the then-unprecedented step of eating breakfast in a traditional downtown Tehran restaurant without mandatory hijabs.
They were arrested and later released, but their actions opened the way for countless others after them to do the same.
What are the authorities saying?
Wearing a hijab has remained mandatory for women in Iran since shortly after Iran’s 1979 Islamic revolution, and authorities have frequently attempted to reinstate it where possible.
When the protests started in late 2022, the government tried to push its own narrative by staging counter-demonstrations. State-linked and more traditional voices continue to criticise and attack those who ignore the dress code required by the state.
A harsh hijab bill was passed in late 2023 that envisioned tougher punishments for offenders, but President Masoud Pezeshkian said he could not enforce it since most people rejected the law and it could lead to more unrest. This was happening at a time when Iran was facing eternal pressure from the US and its allies, he added.
Mai Sato, special UN rapporteur on human rights in Iran, said in a statement on Wednesday that even though that law was suspended, numerous cafes, restaurants and shops continue to be closed by authorities and some staff or customers are arrested for breaking the hijab rules.
This week, local reports said several women were arrested over the hijab laws and put into vans and buses by armed security forces in the city of Isfahan. Reports of other crackdowns have emerged in Rasht and Mashhad, although the authorities have not confirmed or commented on the incidents.
Videos circulating online on Wednesday showed that some businesses were closed in Saqqez and other Kurdistan cities to mark the anniversary of Amini’s death, with security forces present in main squares and streets, likely anticipating protests.
Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, a senior official and the father-in-law of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, told local media this week that a “decadent Western lifestyle” was being propagated by Iran’s “enemies” inside the country through women’s unveilings.
Iran remains in a state of war since the United States and Israel launched strikes on February 28, killing much of the Iranian leadership and 120 children at a school in Minab.
“Due to war conditions, for now we can’t enter the arena of hijab the way we should,” he said, indicating that police had been lax on enforcing the law due to the current situation.
Hossein Taeb, head of the Basij paramilitary force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and another figure close to the office of the supreme leader, said the authorities must deal with hijab through unity.
“We must not allow such issues to disturb our domestic cohesion,” Taeb said during a speech this week to a group of Basij commanders.
In an extensive report released on Wednesday, Amnesty International reiterated its previous findings that Iranian authorities had committed “crimes against humanity” during the Mahsa Amini protests, and called for accountability.
It named 87 Iranian officials who it said should be criminally investigated, spanning national, provincial and local command structures, including the IRGC, police and Interior Ministry authorities.
Names included Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and armed forces commander Mohammad Bagheri, both of whom were killed during the war, as well as Ahmad Vahidi, the incumbent commander-in-chief of the IRGC, who was interior minister at the time.

Gaza: At least 21 dead in building collapse
September 16, 2026
At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.
"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.
"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."
The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.
Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse
"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people are digging with their bare hands."
With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.
"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."
According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.
"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian Coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he added.
Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery
Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.
Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.
More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

European parliament calls for hybrid attacks to be recognized as form of warfare, names Russia as greatest threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

European parliament calls for hybrid attacks to be recognized as form of warfare, names Russia as greatest threat
As Ukrinform correspondent reports, this is stated in a resolution on hybrid warfare and protecting the EU's territorial integrity and critical infrastructure in the area of security and defence, adopted in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
The resolution was supported by 470 MEPs, while 129 voted against and 62 abstained.
"Hybrid operations are deliberate, combined, intelligence-led and coordinated acts by states – including through non-state actors, intermediaries and proxies – spanning multiple domains simultaneously; stresses that they are designed to appear as isolated incidents and remain below the threshold of armed conflict, while having the potential to produce effects comparable to conventional aggression, thus making attribution and an effective response significantly harder; calls therefore on the EU and the Member States to recognise that hybrid acts can constitute a form of warfare regardless of whether conventional force is employed," the text states.
The European Parliament named Russia, acting directly or through controlled actors and intermediaries, including Belarus, as the most serious state-sponsored hybrid threat to the European Union and its member states.
The document also refers to hybrid campaigns by China, Iran and North Korea, as well as activities by terrorist and criminal groups, private military companies, oligarchic networks and other non-state actors.
According to the MEPs, Russia seeks to weaken European unity and democratic institutions, deepen political divisions, spread fear and distrust, reduce the EU's defence readiness, and undermine support for Ukraine.
The European Parliament called on the European Union to shift from a reactive to a proactive strategy that would make it possible to disrupt hybrid operations, deter their organizers, and increase the costs of hostile actions for them.
"Any violation of the Member States' sovereignty must be met with effective, proportionate and coordinated retaliation measures," the document states.
The MEPs propose developing a cross-sectoral plan to counter hybrid warfare, including strengthened civilian-military cooperation, clear response protocols, and calibrated countermeasures proportionate to the severity of hostile actions.
They also propose establishing a single coordination centre between the European Commission and the European External Action Service.
The resolution calls for the preparation of a mechanism for applying the mutual defence clause under Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union, not only in cases of armed aggression but also in particularly serious hybrid scenarios.
The document states that some Russian hybrid attacks against the EU and its member states may bear the characteristics of state-sponsored terrorism. In such cases, countries are encouraged to use all available legal instruments, including the solidarity clause under Article 222 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
The European Parliament called for the immediate creation of a separate horizontal EU sanctions regime to counter hybrid threats. It would operate alongside the sanctions regime targeting Russia's destabilizing activities and would allow organizers of hybrid campaigns to be sanctioned more quickly.
MEPs also condemned systematic incursions by Russian drones and cross-border provocations against countries on the EU's eastern flank, describing them as a deliberate campaign to intimidate civilian populations.
The European Commission was urged to provide, in the EU budget for 2028–2034, dedicated funding for protecting external borders, modernizing surveillance systems, and deploying drone detection and counter-drone capabilities around airports, energy facilities and transport hubs.
Member states were also urged to systematically adopt Ukrainian practices for countering hybrid threats:
The European Parliament said that strengthening cooperation with Ukraine, Moldova, Armenia and partners in the Western Balkans was a strategic necessity, as these countries were facing persistent Russian attacks. It called on EU member states to draw on their experience and establish structured mechanisms for systematically exchanging best practices and operational expertise, including Ukraine's experience in maintaining essential services, ensuring continuity of government, protecting critical infrastructure, conducting strategic communications, and maintaining societal resilience during prolonged attacks.
The resolution was prepared on behalf of the European Parliament's Committee on Security and Defence by Lithuanian MEP Rasa Juknevičienė.
As Ukrinform reported, Lithuanian MEP and European People's Party representative Rasa Juknevičienė previously said that the EU's fear of escalation only encourages Russia to test new boundaries.

Merz abandons UN trip amid sinking approval – Reuters

Merz abandons UN trip amid sinking approval – Reuters
German Chancellor Freidrich Merz has reportedly canceled his planned trip to the UN General Assembly in New York, as his political future hangs in the balance after a landslide loss to the right-wing AfD in state elections.
Merz was scheduled to travel to New York next week, where high-level meetings between world leaders kick off at UN headquarters. However, a German government source told Reuters on Tuesday that the trip had been canceled, as the chancellor’s “presence is required in Berlin.”
According to another source, Merz’ Christian Democrats (CDU) have called a special meeting for Sunday.
The CDU is reeling from its state election loss to the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt last week. The AfD secured 43.8% of the vote, with the CDU a distant second at 17.2%. Merz’ party has been trailing the AfD in opinion polls for over a year, and an equally dismal performance is expected in elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin this weekend, where the CDU is polling at 7% and 20%, respectively.
Just over a year into his chancellorship, CDU members and the German public are losing confidence in Merz. Both Merz and his center-left predecessor, Olaf Scholz, have presided over a country in rapid industrial decline, with Germany’s largest manufacturers – including Volkswagen and BASF – closing plants due to spiraling energy costs, a direct result of Berlin’s self-imposed embargo on Russian oil and gas.
Merz has poured money into an ambitious rearmament program, promising last year to build “the strongest conventional army in Europe.” Meanwhile, ordinary citizens have been told to work more and warned that the “welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed.” In May, Merz’ government announced new social spending cuts and plans to raise the retirement age from 67 to 70.
Merz loses at home and abroad
Over the weekend, an INSA poll found that a majority of CDU voters no longer support the chancellor, while 78% of the general public disapprove of his leadership.
As Merz’ approval rating tanks at home, Germany’s standing at the UN has diminished. In June, the country lost a bid for a temporary seat on the UN Security Council for the first time in history. Critics blamed Berlin’s iron-clad support for Israel – with the German government going as far as describing Israeli strikes on Palestinian schools as “self-defense” – coupled with fierce opposition to Russia, a position that appeared hypocritical to the Global South.
“When it comes to Russia, international law counts, but when it comes to the USA and Israel, it doesn’t,” left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht told the Berliner Zeitung at the time. “This double standard was voted out by the international community yesterday.”
Back in Germany, Merz has vowed to stay the course. After promising to unveil measures to lower fuel costs “very soon,” the chancellor said on Tuesday that he was “elected for four years, and I would like us to use these four years to steer the country out of this difficult period.”

Dubai also set out new figures for its media sector. "It's not just attracting the companies to have Dubai as their home, but to retain them," Badri told Euronews.
Badri has worked in the sector for more than 20 years and opened the council's programme with an address titled From Dubai: The World Films, Plays and Streams.
"The narrative was always other countries telling our stories,” she said. "Now you have institutions that can tell their own stories from Dubai."
The definition of media has widened too. The event began as the Arab Media Forum, small and regional. It now runs eight forums covering film, gaming, podcasting and influencers alongside journalism.
"We had journalism, multimedia and graphic design only," Badri said. "Now you have gaming, you have films."
Film, television and diplomacy
The Games Forum heard from Saifi Ismail of Yalla Group, the first UAE technology company to list on the New York Stock Exchange, and from a panel with the UNDP on the social uses of games.
A television panel brought together the Gulf drama actors Samira Ahmed, Dawood Hussain and Mohammed Al Mansoor. An exhibition of early Gulf broadcast equipment, much of it still working, drew steady traffic from younger delegates.
Dr Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the defence affairs, interior and foreign affairs committee at the UAE Federal National Council, said coverage of international relations concentrated too heavily on governments.
"What we need is to invest in people-to-people diplomacy, and the media should take a lead in playing that role," he told Euronews.
He cited the UAE relief operation in Nepal, where flooding and landslides have affected thousands and where the UAE has flown in successive aid consignments since early September. "We have here in the UAE a community of more than 500,000 Nepalese," he said.
On regulation, Al Nuaimi said the UAE, home to some 200 nationalities, asks for one thing. "We don't ask people to change. The only thing we ask them to respect is the rule of law," he said.
Mona Ghanem Al Marri, vice chairperson and managing director of the Dubai Media Council and president of Dubai Press Club, said foreign direct investment in the sector reached $1.62 billion in 2024, writing for Euronews on opening day.
The summit runs until Thursday.

The comments Zuckerberg posted on social media followed a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that quickly found support from tech leaders including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk at SpaceXAI.
Warnings from researchers about the technology's potential threats to humanity have sparked a debate among industry leaders over how best to rein in the technology before it could escape human control.
AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said.
“Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens," he wrote on X.
Zuckerberg, who didn't name Anthropic or any other companies, posted days after Amodei outlined a three-step plan to ensure AI safety, including a proposal for companies and countries to coordinate a slowdown in its development.
Zuckerberg said Meta delayed releasing its Muse AI agent for several months to ensure its safety and security.
“We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said.
Companies should prioritise building safe AI models instead of systems that can automatically improve themselves, a function known as recursive self-improvement, Zuckerberg wrote.
“Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely.”

Pentagon’s Iran war costs hit $38 billion in five months – budget office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:14:26 UTC
23:14:26 KST

Pentagon’s Iran war costs hit $38 billion in five months – budget office
The US war with Iran cost the Pentagon approximately $38 billion in its first five months, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). The bill could rise by another $2 billion to $3 billion for every additional month of fighting – and by more if hostilities intensify.
In a report released on Tuesday, the CBO estimated Defense Department expenses from the start of US combat operations on February 28 through August 1. The figure includes the estimated cost of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, as well as additional flying hours, military operations, and higher fuel costs.
The office said its estimate was “subject to considerable uncertainty” because the Pentagon did not provide the requested information, forcing analysts to rely on government databases and publicly available reports. The estimate also excludes the cost of repairing damaged US bases, military casualties, future veterans’ care, and expenses borne by other federal agencies.
Another month of conflict would cost about $2 billion if violence remains at the “low and sporadic” levels seen in May and June, the CBO estimated. If operations return to their July intensity, the monthly bill would rise to about $3 billion. Costs could be higher still if the conflict escalates further.
Billions of dollars’ worth of US weaponry has been used up in the conflict. The CBO estimates that replacing munitions used through August 1 would cost $21.7 billion, including $7.3 billion for land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for missile-defense interceptors and $1.2 billion for other weapons.
The Trump administration asked Congress in June for $87.6 billion in supplemental funding, including $67.1 billion for the Defense Department. The CBO assessed that $42.3 billion of the overall request appeared directly related to the Iran war.
The report was released as CBS News published photographs showing extensive damage caused by Iranian missile and drone strikes on US positions across the Middle East. The images were provided anonymously by active-duty service members because of military restrictions on contact with the media.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told CBS News.
The photographs showed a destroyed E-3 Sentry surveillance aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, along with damaged buildings and burned-out vehicles at US facilities in Kuwait.
The Pentagon inspector general separately reported that US forces had suffered $3.7 billion in equipment losses through late June. Nearly 60 manned and unmanned aircraft were damaged or destroyed, according to the watchdog.
Trump said last month that the conflict was costing the United States “relatively little.” His remark came as fighting continued, despite his repeated declarations of victory. Trump proclaimed “total and complete victory” in early April and has since repeatedly claimed that Washington won or was close to ending the conflict.
The war has faced mounting domestic opposition and criticism over the administration’s decision to conduct hostilities without congressional authorization. The House voted for a third time this week to limit US military involvement, approving a war-powers resolution by 220 votes to 204. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure.
Separately, International IDEA reported that key measures of US democracy have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years. The organization said the Trump administration’s actions had weakened the rule of law both domestically and internationally, while warning more broadly that democratic erosion increases the risk of conflict.

Northern ports; driver of Iran’s trade development with Eurasia

Northern ports; driver of Iran’s trade development with Eurasia
TEHRAN- CEO of Mazandaran Free Zone Organization Amin Ofoghi stated: The Mazandaran Free Zone, whose establishment began last year, is considered a valuable gift from the 14th government to the people of Mazandaran Province and has created new hope in the province.
Ofoghi added: Today I am speaking about the northern free zones and the northern ports of the country. In this region, Amir Abad Port, Nowshahr Port, Babolsar Port, as well as the separated area between Juybar and Babolsar, include an area of about 460 hectares, which in the future will be connected to the trade, tourism, and technology sectors.
Referring to the share of northern ports in the country’s maritime exchanges, he stated: About 65% of Iran’s maritime exchanges in the Caspian Sea take place in Amir Abad and Nowshahr ports, and another 27% takes place in Anzali and Caspian ports; therefore, about 92% of the country’s maritime exchanges are carried out in the ports of free zones.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: These ports are either sovereign or ownership-based, and what we hope to resolve today with the presence of officials is the issue of integrated management and unified governance in these ports; because integrated management can play a very important role in developing exchanges and using existing capacities.
Goal of the northern free zones; developing relations with Eurasia
Ofoghi, referring to the philosophy behind the establishment of the northern free zones, said: The goal of establishing the northern free zones is to develop relations with Eurasian countries, and our plan is to turn the northern free zones into a hub for transit and goods exchange in the CIS and Eurasia by developing logistics infrastructure, both in hardware and software, activating economic diplomacy, and international corridors.
He added: One of the tasks the government assigned to the northern ports during the recent war events and conditions was supplying essential goods, and fortunately the Mazandaran free zones succeeded in supplying about 70% of the essential goods needed by the north of the country through the northern ports.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization, referring to the unused capacities of the northern ports, stated: Today we are talking about a capacity of about 30 million tons for which investment has been made, but in the best case, about 9 million tons of it is operational. That is, the infrastructure has been created and the laws also exist, but we need integrated management to activate this neglected capacity.
Ofoghi stated: We believe the northern ports can directly, by eliminating intermediary countries, conduct exchanges related to food and needed goods with Russia and Kazakhstan, which are among our most important partners in the Caspian Sea.
Referring to the experience of free zones in creating direct trade routes, he said: During the time of the late Engineer Torkan, a project was carried out in the free zones to supply goods from China without intermediaries, and we were able to import 15,000 containers through the China and Kazakhstan route into Caspian Port.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: I have had the honor of working in free zones for 23 years, and at that time our view was to create routes as economic defense so that we could supply goods, raw materials, and intermediate inputs.
Ofoghi added: In Anzali there were two ports; Caspian Port and Anzali Port, both of which were within the free zones. 15,000 containers with two-way cargo entered Caspian Port, but not even one container went to Anzali Port. The reason was clear; in Caspian Port, integrated management and free zone laws were applied, but in Anzali Port we were sovereign and ownership was in the hands of another body.
He said: This experience showed us how much integrated management in ports can help the development of trade exchanges.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization stated: I hope today we can give the northern free zones at least one year to activate existing capacities by applying Article 65 and integrated management, and show the results in practice.
Ofoghi added: We have problems in the tanker and maritime transport sector with the Iranian flag. Many times we have taken cargo to Chabahar, the northern free zones, Solyanka Port in Astrakhan—the only port more than 50% of which Iran owns outside the country—and even toward European ports such as Hamburg, but these routes have not continued.
He considered the reason for this to be the necessity of applying the incentives and exemptions of free zones and said: For an investor and a foreign company, it is very important that the company’s activity be carried out in a free zone and benefit from legal exemptions and incentives.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: If we can regain the trust of investors and cargo owners, there is great capacity to activate trade routes. Two weeks ago, on the same China–Kazakhstan route, cargo entered Amir Abad Port.
Ofoghi, referring to the legal capacity of free zones, said: In free zones, we can accept ships entering from around the world under different flags without waiting and more quickly; because the law has defined free zones as enclosed customs areas.
He added: Naturally, other bodies should operate within their legal boundaries, and customs, quarantine, and standards affairs can be carried out within the free zones themselves.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization said: In the current war conditions, goods must be able to enter the free zones, and the cargo owner should have a tradable warehouse receipt, and customs, quarantine, and standards should also be carried out in the same area.
Ofoghi stated: In Article 14 of this matter, permission for the entry of goods into free zones is foreseen, and in Article 24 there are issues in this regard, but in the discussion of determining duties, the legal authorities of free zones must also be considered.
Stating that cost, time, and security are the three main factors in activating trade corridors, he said: We believe that with the authority the law has given to free zones in determining tariffs and costs, we can be influential in reducing the time and cost of routes.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: The routes we have tested so far are very important for cargo owners, and the route must be reliable for the foreign cargo owner. We believe that if the northern free zones can reduce the multiplicity of decision-making bodies and the existing bureaucracy, the advantages of free zones can provide the basis for their role-playing; especially in the area of the country’s logistics resilience.
Ofoghi, referring to the late Torkan’s view, said: The late Engineer Torkan always emphasized that in free zones, projects should be implemented as models. If we succeed, we are ready to implement the integrated management plan for the northern ports, which the law has foreseen and the government has approved, and if successful, to apply the same model in other free zones as well.
Emphasizing the capacity of the northern ports to become third-generation ports, he said: We can turn the northern ports into third-generation ports. All over the world, production units are located in the hinterlands of ports, and this significantly reduces logistics costs.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization added: In this model, raw materials are imported, production takes place, and the final product is prepared for export or entry into the mainland or target countries. We can do this in the northern ports as well, but the authority issuing the license, production certificate, and value-added certificate must be one organization.
Ofoghi stated: The law has given this permission to free zones, and we ask the government to help free zones implement this legal capacity.
Referring to the capacity of free zones for developing joint transport companies, he said: In banking, fuel, and other services, we can also succeed. Many times in joint commissions, the creation of joint transport companies has been approved, but in the past 15 years this phrase has been repeated many times, and ultimately very few of these companies have been formed, and no successful joint logistics transport company has been created.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: I believe that in free zones, because it is possible to register a company and a foreign investor can own 100% of the company’s shares, and there is also the possibility of land ownership and capital entry and exit, we can also launch joint logistics companies if we have management of the ports.
Ofoghi, referring to the importance of Amir Abad Port, said: Amir Abad Port is one of the very important ports of the Caspian, but unfortunately we do not have enough ships and tankers under the Iranian flag in the Caspian Sea, and for more than 20 years, a pier opposite Amir Abad has not been fully used.
He added: Today we need this capacity more than ever. The private sector investor is ready to carry out the rail project, bring it into operation, and even hand it over to the government.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: Two important Caspian ports, namely Amir Abad Port and Caspian Port, are connected to the rail network, but the share of rail transport is very low, especially in the north of the country, which faces traffic problems.
Ofoghi said: If the management of this matter is in the hands of free zones, we can transfer cargo from road to rail. For the foreign investor, it is also very important that regular and planned transport lines exist in Iran.
Referring to the experience of regular shipping lines, he said: We have experience with liner routes. With a shipping company on the Kazakhstan route, we had liner lines for three years, and the cargo owner anywhere in Iran knew that if he delivered his goods at a certain time, the goods would go to Kazakhstan and return at a certain time.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization added: Today there are no liner lines in the Caspian Sea, while free zones have this possibility and the law has allowed them such activities.
Ofoghi further referred to the capacity for joint production with third countries and said: We have a joint request to be able to create joint production for the market of third countries.
He added: In the past, with four CEOs of free zones, we visited the free zones of other countries, and they were very interested in having joint production for the market of third countries.
The CEO of the Mazandaran Free Zone Organization continued: In this model, raw materials and technology can enter through our ports, use Iran’s laws, workforce, and energy, and foreign investment can also enter this cycle; but in some cases even the possibility of using land faces obstacles, because the Ports Organization does not agree and states that it will act according to existing regulations.
Ofoghi in the end emphasized: Our request is that a unity of command be created for the northern ports, and that the multiple decision-making bodies, instead of being stationed at the entrance of the free zones, operate within the framework of integrated and coordinated management, so that we can use the capacity of the northern free zones for the development of trade, logistics, economic diplomacy, and the economic resilience of the country.

You pay 40 paise for transaction worth Rs 100.

No, but you need to run businesses on a self-sustainable basis,” he said.He also compared the proposed charge with other banking services.“You will get used to it. US retail sales increased more than expected in August, recording their strongest monthly gain in five months, according to Census Bureau data released Wednesday.

Sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and bookstore sales increased 1.2%. Furniture store sales advanced 0.9%.
Sales rose 0.7% at clothing retailers and general merchandise stores. Motor vehicle and parts dealers registered an increase of 0.6%.
Food and beverage store sales gained 0.4%, while building material and garden equipment retailers were the only major category to record a decline, falling 0.2%.
A closely watched measure excluding food services, automobile dealers, building materials stores and gasoline stations, which feeds into calculations of gross domestic product, jumped 1.4%, sharply exceeding expectations for a 0.4% gain.
