Israel ambassador says Kuwait could join Abraham Accords within six months
Israel’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates has claimed that another Gulf state, potentially Kuwait, could join the Abraham Accords within the next six months, despite Kuwait’s longstanding refusal to normalise ties with Israel.
Yossi Shelley made the claim in an interview with Israeli public broadcaster KAN on Tuesday, saying Kuwait could join the US-brokered agreements within four to six months.
The comments come as Israel seeks to expand the network of Arab states formally establishing relations with it, six years after the UAE and Bahrain became the first signatories to the Abraham Accords.
But Kuwait has remained a prominent holdout, with opposition to normalisation deeply rooted in the country’s political and public spheres.
Unlike most other Gulf monarchies, the country has a politically influential parliament, where Islamic and Arab nationalist forces have traditionally opposed normalisation with Israel.
While Kuwait’s emir retains ultimate authority over foreign policy, public and political resistance to Israel remains a major factor shaping the country’s position.
Trump pushes for wider Abraham Accords
Shelley’s comments came as US President Donald Trump has called for the Abraham Accords to be expanded further across the region.
Trump has previously urged additional countries to join the agreements, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt and Jordan, alongside existing signatories the UAE and Bahrain.
In comments cited by the Israeli media, Trump argued that the countries should sign the accords simultaneously after extensive US efforts to advance the initiative.
The renewed push comes against a backdrop of major regional tensions and the continuing fallout from Israel’s war across the region.
Shelley also described Israel-UAE relations as strengthening, saying there had been “dramatic growth” in bilateral ties and cooperation.
He claimed the UAE and Israel were now “true partners at the moment of truth”, while acknowledging that some aspects of their relationship remain sensitive and are not publicly reported.

Taliban seeks US ties, urges Washington to address legacy of Afghanistan war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:57:32 UTC
22:57:32 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The Taliban wants formal diplomatic relations with the US but said Washington must first address the legacy of its two-decade war in Afghanistan, Taliban spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News in an interview.
Five years after the Taliban returned to power following the US withdrawal, Balkhi portrayed the end of the foreign military presence as the administration's main achievement, while acknowledging persistent unemployment, economic difficulties and public dissatisfaction.
“The greatest achievement obviously Afghanistan has had is the end of occupation,” said Balkhi, arguing that the country had since seen improvements in security, trade, investment and infrastructure.
He claimed Afghan exports rose from $750 million in 2020 to nearly $2 billion, while the number of factories increased from 1,500 to 6,000. He also said the government had been able to pay civil servants and attract billions of dollars in investment.
Balkhi acknowledged, however, that “there are areas where we haven't met the expectation of the general population,” citing widespread unemployment and other challenges.
The interview on Tuesday also highlighted Afghanistan's continued diplomatic isolation. Russia is the only country to have formally recognized the Taliban government.
Balkhi argued that Afghanistan was already engaging diplomatically with several countries and questioned the practical meaning of formal recognition.
On relations with Washington, he said Kabul wanted diplomatic ties with “every single country of the world, including the United States,” and would welcome the reopening of the US Embassy and American investment in sectors such as minerals and gas.
He also rejected calls by US President Donald Trump for Afghanistan to return billions of dollars worth of American-funded military equipment left behind after the 2021 withdrawal. CBS reported that roughly $7 billion in US military hardware remained in Afghanistan.
“That’s the assets of the state of Afghanistan,” said Balkhi, rejecting any deal linking the equipment to the release of Afghan funds frozen abroad.
Asked about the argument that American taxpayers paid for the equipment, Balkhi responded, “The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?”
Balkhi demanded the release of Afghan central bank assets frozen by Washington, saying the funds belonged to the Afghan state rather than the Taliban government.
On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Balkhi said the Taliban condemned attacks on civilians and reiterated its commitment under the Doha agreement that Afghan territory would not be used to attack the US or any other country.
The interview also focused on restrictions on women and girls. Regarding the suspension of public schooling for girls from seventh grade onward, Balkhi said alternative forms of education remained available and rejected reports of girls attending clandestine classes despite the restrictions.
“There is no such thing as secret schools,” he said, describing the arrangements as homeschooling or madrasa, or Islamic, education.
Looking back at the war that followed the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, Balkhi said Afghanistan had learned that conflicts should be resolved through diplomacy.
“War is not the solution, and occupying Afghanistan certainly isn't to your benefit,” he said, urging greater cooperation for Afghanistan's reconstruction and development.

Announcing Hong Kong’s first five-year plan on Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also revealed the official names of the three Northern Metropolis developments: San Tin University Town, Hung Shui Kiu University Town and Ta Kwu Ling University Town.

According to the five-year plan, authorities will step up efforts to attract world-famous institutions or first-class scientific research institutes to establish a presence in the towns.

Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:11 UTC
22:56:11 KST

Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
Trump lashes out at justices who rejected his federal mail-in ballot plan, raising questions on his next electoral moves.
US President Donald Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court for rejecting his push to curb mail-in voting, raising fears that the US president might use federal powers to meddle in November’s midterm elections.
“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president lashed out after the court verdict on Monday. The justices “are merely a shell of their original selves, a court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Selling the war: Purges, polygraphs and propaganda
- list 2 of 3Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 3 of 3Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
The ruling means states can continue administering mail-in voting under their existing procedures. Mail-in and absentee ballots have been used in the United States for decades and now account for roughly a third of votes cast nationwide.
Despite the ruling, political analysts and some officials fear that Trump may not let the electoral process proceed as planned, and might pull some other strings to tilt the election in his favour.
So what voting rules exactly has Trump tried to change – and what other powers could his administration seek to use in the run-up to the midterms?
Can Trump use federal powers to tilt the elections in his favour?
Election officials across the country are concerned about the prospects of interference, from the potential for ballot seizures to voter-fraud investigations.
A Reuters investigation based on interviews with dozens of state and local election officials showed that they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and intimidation tactics.
According to the report, more than a dozen local and state election officials said they are hiring outside lawyers or seeking legal training for themselves and their staff to prepare for potential demands by the administration for access to sensitive voting records or election equipment.
Nearly twice that many said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation, including the false claims made by Trump and Republican allies that voting machines are unreliable and mail-in voting is inherently corrupt.
What have the opposition and campaigners said on Trump’s electoral agenda?
Campaigners have fiercely resisted Trump’s executive actions attempting to dictate federal voting procedures. Groups including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Brennan Center for Justice have sued the administration, arguing that the Constitution gives authority over federal elections primarily to states and Congress, rather than the president.
The pushback has also come from Capitol Hill. A bipartisan group of 261 current and former members of Congress filed a brief with the Supreme Court challenging Trump’s executive order and the subsequent Postal Service rule. They argued that the measures violated the separation of powers by taking authority over federal elections that the Constitution grants to states and Congress.
“The Constitution is clear that the states and Congress make the rules for federal elections, not the President,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, one of the lawmakers leading the effort, said.
As per the US Constitution, elections are conducted by local authorities working under the states.
Raskin described Trump’s attempt to use the US Postal Service to regulate mailed ballots as “a naked power grab”, accusing the president of seeking “to inject confusion and chaos into our elections in a last-ditch effort to keep his party in power”.
Senator Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate Rules Committee, similarly argued that neither the president nor the Postal Service had the authority to determine how states administer elections. He said restricting voting by mail could particularly affect military personnel, people living in rural areas, and Americans living abroad.
The White House rejected accusations that it is seeking to interfere in the midterms, saying its measures are aimed at preventing illegal voting and ensuring confidence in the electoral system.
Why does Trump oppose mail-in voting?
This is not the first time Trump has cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, citing debunked claims of widespread election fraud associated with it. Trump falsely blamed his presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud in 2020. Back then, he called the voting system “the greatest scam in the history of politics”. He and his supporters opposed changes made during the COVID pandemic to expand mail-in voting.
Trump and his supporters also claim that the mail-ballot plan enables a large number of non-citizens to register and vote illegally, corrupting elections. For this, he has pushed for the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act (SAVE Act) that would require citizens to provide “documentary proof” that they are American citizens when they register to vote. The legislation is stalled in the Senate over concerns that millions of voters will be disenfranchised.
Studies show that voter fraud is extremely rare. The Heritage Foundation, the conservative-leaning think tank behind Project 2025 – which inspired many Trump administration policies – documented 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time.
What has he done to change election rules?
Trump has been explicit about his desire to assert more federal control over the election, saying in early February that “Republicans ought to nationalise the voting”. The White House has dismissed concerns that federal actions could disrupt the midterms, arguing that the administration is enforcing election laws and safeguarding confidence in voting.
In March 2026, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail-in voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters.
For the midterms, that move would force all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time.
The order also required states to provide the Postal Service with a list of eligible voters before elections. Several government departments, including Homeland Security and US Citizenship and Immigration Services, would also have the voters’ lists.
The postal agency was additionally empowered to deny mailed ballots if they did not comply with new standards or were not associated with registered voters on the states’ lists.
The attorney general has demanded that 47 states and Washington, DC, a federal district, hand over their complete voter registration lists, according to a tally from the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan policy group. Eleven states have complied or agreed to comply. The Trump administration has launched lawsuits against the 20 others that refused.

Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population may have been far larger than estimated: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:06 UTC
22:56:06 KST

Beril Canakci
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Australia may have had a much larger Indigenous population before European colonization than previously estimated, with new research putting the median at 2.22 million people.
The study, published Tuesday in the journal Nature Human Behaviour, used archaeological and genetic evidence, historical observations and computer modeling of the continent's environmental capacity to reconstruct the population before British colonization.
Previous estimates have generally placed Australia's pre-colonial Indigenous population between 250,000 and 1 million people. Researchers said earlier figures were affected by the lack of systematic population records and by disease and violence that had already reduced Indigenous communities by the time early colonial estimates were made.
The research estimated that about 93% of the pre-colonial Indigenous population was lost in less than 80 years after the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, with researchers attributing the demographic collapse to the effects of colonization, including disease and frontier violence.
The study estimated that about 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861 would be needed to reconcile its population estimate with historical census records.

How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:56:00 UTC
22:56:00 KST

How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
September 16, 2026
Any and all ships may pass, at least at first. That was how the spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis rebel militia put it. Transit through the Red Sea would be safe, with one exception: According to the Houthi spokesperson, ships from Saudi Arabia would not be allowed to pass this stretch of the sea.
The comments came during a time when the Houthi militia has been fighting to increase its presence at the southern entrance to the ocean passage. The Houthis now control the tiny volcanic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, at the entrance to the Red Sea, as well as other parts of the Yemeni coast and some small islands.
With these moves, pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia, the country that opposes the Houthis and previously fought a war (unsuccessfully) with them.
But pressure is now also increasing in Egypt. Every decrease in shipping traffic through the Red Sea also impacts one of that country's most important sources of national income, the Suez Canal.
As yet, maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not been significantly reduced. According to news agency Reuters, last Saturday 24 ships passed through it and on Sunday, 27 did so. That is around the same as the 10-day average. The Houthis appear to want to signal that their plan is not stop traffic altogether. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a chokepoint between Yemen and and the Horn of Africa. Ships have to pass it to enter the Red Sea.
In general though, maritime traffic has decreased here, according to maritime intelligence organization Kpler. On Monday, 21 ships went through the strait. But in the middle of July, the average number of ships passing through was 47.
How will things develop from here?
"The Houthis could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe," says Stephan Roll, a senior fellow with the Africa and Middle East division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, or SWP, in Berlin. "So first we have to wait and see how big the actual disruption to the Suez Canal will be."
Even complete control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait doesn't automatically mean control of the Suez Canal. But it does give the Houthis a further opportunity to indirectly threaten traffic.
For Egypt, this new disruption comes at a particularly unwelcome time. Houthi attacks at the end of 2023 had already disrupted business at the Suez Canal. According to the International Monetary Fund, earnings at the canal in 2024 fell by around $6 billion (€5.2 billion). Before the current security crisis, Egypt had been making between $9 billion and $10 billion from the Suez Canal annually.
More recently things had actually been improving again.
"The situation is certainly problematic compared to 2023," Roll told DW. "But it is not so clearly negative compared to the situation one, two or even three months ago."
Thanks to rising oil prices and the resulting higher cost of circumnavigating Africa, shipping companies had been using the Red Sea as they travelled between Asia and Europe.
The Suez Canal's finances had recently improved. The Suez Canal Authority, which manages the passage, reported that during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, revenues had risen by 23% to $4.67 billion (€4.5 billion). Despite the various conflicts in the region, this actually represented a recovery for the Suez Canal.
Houthi offensive could change all that
There is also a second critical factor. After recent drone attacks that the Saudis blamed on Iraqi groups, Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline to the coastal city of Yanbu will be out of service for at least several weeks. Between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil were going through the 1,200 kilometer pipeline per day as the Saudis attempted to circumnavigate the Strait of Hormuz, blocked due to the US-Iran war. This latest damage could put as much as 4% of global supply at risk, according to Reuters.
An analysis by Qatar-based think tank, the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, warns of a scenario where the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are both likely to become more precarious. The East Asia Institute, a think tank based in Korea, has also written about the dangers of dual choke points.
Neither route can be seen as an independent alternative because flows of oil and trade depend on secure connections at several points.
Certainly for Egypt, this will increase economic pressure.
What can Egypt do about this?
In geopolitical terms, there is not a lot that Egypt can do. The Houthis in Yemen have only impacted the country indirectly.
"Egypt's military capabilities are very limited," Steffen Krüger, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Cairo office, explained.
Egyptian interventions in Yemen in the 1960s are still remembered in Cairo — back then, the country sent thousands of troops to support a new government in Yemen, in a war that would eventually last years — so Egypt would prefer to exercise restraint there.
"Although Egypt formally remains a member of the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, its participation is largely symbolic," Krüger told DW.
And there is no doubt that Egyptian officials have noted the lack of success other countries like Saudi Arabia and the US have had in their attempts to rein in the Houthis.
"The Egyptians simply have no real alternative," argues the SWP's Roll, adding that Egypt is likely to try diplomacy first. "Basically they have to try to put a positive spin on a bad situation and somehow negotiate appropriate arrangements with the Houthis."
London-based media outlet The New Arab wrote that the Houthis offered to talk directy to Cairo about shipping security via the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) in London. But the ICS rejected that claim and said that "no such request was ever made to ICS" and that the chamber hasn't had direct communications with the Houthis.
On Tuesday, Saudi Arabian leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Cairo to try to get Egypt's support against the Houthis.
"The Egyptians are likely to wait and see," says Roll of the SWP about the next steps for Cairo.
Egypt has a difficult balancing act to perform. The country is closely allied with Saudi Arabia but is also bound to suffer economically in any further escalation between the Saudis and the Houthi group.
A decisive factor will depend on if, and how, the Houthis restrict maritime shipping, and if they go beyond vessels with Saudi Arabian ties, or whether they are just using their currenty improved military position to exert pressure on their enemies.
This story was originally published in German.
Editor's note: A previous version of this article mentioned a story in The New Arab that claims the Houthis offered to speak with Egypt via the International Chamber of Shipping. The ICS has rejected this claim; we updated our story accordingly.

Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:54:03 UTC
22:54:03 KST

Eighty-one companies are now authorized to form private air defense units — up from 51 in mid-July — the Defense Ministry said on Sept. 16, as the country, and particularly Kyiv and the surrounding area, come under near-constant Russian attack.
As Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, more businesses are joining the program. The ministry says the program is designed to protect workers and facilities while reducing pressure on military air defenses, which now face increased strain beyond concentrated overnight barrages.
Established by the Cabinet of Ministers in November 2025, the private air defense program allows businesses to voluntarily form and finance air defense groups staffed by trained and certified civilian employees. Eligible companies include providers of essential services such as electricity, water, transport, and communications, alongside security firms protecting other businesses.
Companies apply to the Defense Ministry for authorization, then agree with the Air Force command on their units' operations. Under rules introduced in March, participating businesses can also temporarily receive military air defense equipment and ammunition unused by combat units, with Air Force approval.
Private air defense is just one component of Ukraine's multi-level system of airspace protection.
The first successful interceptions under the program were announced in March, when a company's unit downed Russian drones in Kharkiv Oblast. In April, the ministry reported a private group's first interception of a jet-powered Shahed-type drone.
By mid-July, private air defense had downed more than 50 Shahed and Zala drones, according to the ministry.

Catherine Ringer dies: grief in music and political circles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:53:55 UTC
22:53:55 KST

Catherine Ringer died at 68 from cancer on 14 September. Since then, artists, politicians and cultural figures have paid tribute to the voice and freedom of the music icon.
Some voices you recognise in a split second. Catherine Ringer’s was one of them. A voice that could laugh, rasp, scream, sing of love, desire or madness. A voice that never wanted to be put in a box.
The announcement of her death has triggered a wave of emotional reactions. Among them, French President Emmanuel Macron, who paid tribute to a personality he called "unclassifiable, irreverent, profoundly French".
On X, the president accompanied his message with a clip from 2024 in which the artist sang 'La Marseillaise' during a ceremony marking the enshrining of the right to abortion in the Constitution.
The Élysée also paid solemn tribute on Wednesday in an official statement. The text traces the journey of this "all-round artist", born in 1957 in Suresnes and immersed from childhood in an artistic family environment. After her first steps on stage at the Café de la Gare and then at the Palace, as well as "darker, more painful experiences" from which she managed to break free, 1979 marked a major turning point when she met Fred Chichin.
Together, they created Les Rita Mitsouko, a duo with an art "free and impossible to categorise", which broke through to the general public in 1984 with the resounding success of the song 'Marcia Baïla'.
Following the death of her partner in 2007, Catherine Ringer carried on her career "with deeply moving dignity", alternating solo projects with returns to the stage to revive the band’s cult tracks. Described variously as "a diva, a popular singer and an avant-gardist", she leaves, according to the presidency, "a singular, flamboyant artistic legacy" that has left a lasting mark on musical life in France.
Across the political spectrum, voices have spoken up to stress that she was also a tireless activist, but without a party label – feminist through her actions long before the word became a slogan – standing up to sexists on TV shows as much as to right-thinking orthodoxies. Among them, Dominique de Villepin on X (source in French) and France Insoumise MEP Manon Aubry (source in French).
Her peers pay tribute and thank her
Rock musicians, pop artists, rappers or icons of French chanson: all are mourning the loss of a "big sister" of the stage.
On social media, the music world seemed to freeze in order to salute the woman who injected a punk streak of madness into mainstream French pop.
Singer-songwriter Benjamin Biolay posted a powerful tribute on Instagram (source in French), recalling the formative shock of the album 'The No Comprendo', and honouring the memory of an extraordinary voice and the poetry of the mythical duo she formed with Fred Chichin.
Singer Étienne Daho (source in French), meanwhile, posted a photo with Catherine Ringer and simply her first name.
And then there are the words from legendary band Sparks, with whom Les Rita Mitsouko worked. The American band spoke of an artist that was "one of a kind", a "true force of nature", and a friend whose path they know they were lucky to cross.
Tributes are also coming from far beyond the world of music. Actors and performers like Josiane Balasko, Nikos Aliagas, Michèle Laroque, Julie Gayet, Flavie Flament and Alain Chabat, among others, have shared their memories and their emotions on social media.
One particularly beautiful tribute from a user spotted on X shows that the artist touched many generations, including the youngest, and will continue to do so.
Finally, there is no better way to end this article than with music. The music of Catherine and Fred, the soundtrack that accompanied and lulled a large part of this writer’s life. This song in particular is forever tied to a vivid memory: a concert in October 2000, in a venue in Lyon. Seeing them play that night and hearing this track live is etched forever.
'C'est comme ça' – Les Rita Mitsouko – album 'The No Comprendo' – video directed by Jean-Baptiste Mondino in 1986.

Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
ANKARA, Sept 16 - The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has dealt Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of U.S. protection.
A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, has also left the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.
Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources said the Houthi breakthrough reflected various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaced Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.
The diplomat said the Houthis had quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: "Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis' intentions.”
Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, described the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: "They just weren't picking up the signal. They just weren't seeing the signs."
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi added: "The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen."
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces handed the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced U.S.- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.
The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group's military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries' equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
"The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn't resist. Completely. Completely," said Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.
The setback has also exposed how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials said neither the United States nor European countries were prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies had not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defence coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials did not respond to a request to comment for this article.
ALLIES COLLAPSE, PARTNERS HESITATE
With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) went to Cairo to seek help containing the fallout after Washington declined to intervene.
Two regional sources said Riyadh wanted Egypt to play a role in Red Sea operations, recalling Cairo's intervention in 2015 when its naval and air forces helped secure Bab el-Mandeb. There was no immediate word on whether Cairo would agree.
Egypt's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS had asked for Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.
Former U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross said the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"I don't think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they're making," Ross said.
A Gulf official said Saudi Arabia now faced a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risked turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
"If you don't inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them," the official said.
Control of territory around Bab el-Mandeb — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis' regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.
Combined with Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.
MbS's foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilise the region via a détente with Iran, has unravelled since the start of the U.S.-Iran war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom's de facto ruler.
The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defence coalition, exposed the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.
THE YEMEN TRAP
The Houthi offensive revealed a blind spot in Saudi and U.S. strategy: while Washington and its allies focused on containing Iran directly, Tehran widened the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.
The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran's influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it's a "win-win-win," said Farea Al-Muslimi.
Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington's reluctance to come to its ally's aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh's leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi described Washington's refusal to help defend Saudi territory as "the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement" in decades.
"The Americans are saying No," he said. "That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now."
Yemen's long record of defeating foreign powers - from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia - helps explain why Riyadh's search for partners may yield only limited results.
Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
"Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it," Muslimi said, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers were humbled.
"The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen," he said, adding in reference to Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: "The Egyptians failed in Yemen." REUTERS

Germany checks hospitals’ readiness to treat the wounded amid warnings of a possible attack by the russian federation - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:49:50 EEST

Germany checks hospitals’ readiness to treat the wounded amid warnings of a possible attack by the russian federation - media
Kyiv • UNN
Germany assesses hospitals’ readiness for war amid threats from Russia. The Bundeswehr forecasts up to 1,000 wounded military personnel daily.
An inspection of healthcare facilities was initiated in Germany to determine whether they could withstand the strain in the event of an armed conflict amid threats from russia, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
In Germany, government authorities are inspecting the healthcare system and infrastructure to determine whether they could withstand the strain in the event of an armed conflict.
Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, hybrid attacks have become more frequent in Germany: in particular, an attempted drone strike involving explosives was recorded at Leipzig Airport last month, and a series of cyberattacks on hospitals also took place. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius warned that by 2029, Russia could be capable of attacking NATO territory. In that case, Germany would be obliged to come to the Alliance’s defense, and given its location in the center of Europe, the country would likely become a key transit hub for military personnel and a place where they could receive medical care.
In a report modeling potential scenarios for a Russian invasion of NATO territory, the Bundeswehr estimated that up to 1,000 wounded soldiers could arrive in Germany each day. Since the country’s five existing military hospitals would quickly reach their limits — and the law obliges civilian hospitals to provide assistance during wartime — the system would likely face unprecedented strain, and medical personnel might have to prioritize care between military and civilian patients.
The publication notes that ensuring a sufficient number of hospital beds is only part of the challenge. Germany’s leadership also needs to strengthen medical-supply chains and establish better coordination between the military and civilian healthcare systems. Another problem is personnel training: estimates suggest that only a few hundred doctors in Germany have experience treating combat injuries. To improve the situation, the Bundeswehr and the German Trauma Society (DGU) are offering civilian surgeons courses on providing care during mass-casualty emergencies and treating war injuries.
When this cooperation was formally established in 2017, the world was a very different place, recalls Sasha Floge, secretary-general of the DGU. "At that time, we still believed that we lived in a safe world — if one disregarded Islamist terrorism," he said. — "No one believed that the security situation would change fundamentally or that we would be discussing collective-defense scenarios." Today, demand is high: the governments of some federal states reserve entire weeks of training, and getting into the courses is not easy. The most intensive programs, which use the bodies of deceased people and anesthetized pigs, can train only 50 to 100 surgeons per year.
If war broke out, the Bundeswehr’s medical services would provide care to wounded soldiers at the front and then transport them to Germany, where the authorities of the federal states would direct them to civilian hospitals. This strategy was tested in March, when the military held its largest medical exercise in decades, simulating an attack on Lithuania and the transportation of soldiers to hospitals in Berlin and parts of Brandenburg. According to Floge, the exercise was successful, but additional practice is needed to ensure effective cooperation between the two systems in an emergency.

More than 800 'excess' deaths recorded in France during latest heat wave period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:45:41 UTC
22:45:41 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
France recorded 817 “excess deaths” between July 27 and Aug. 20 during a period of high temperatures, with at least 751 involving those aged 75 and older, the Health Ministry said Wednesday, according to the Le Monde newspaper.
Sante publique France, the country's national public health agency, said that “this excess all-cause mortality concerns almost exclusively people aged 75 and over, with at least 751 excess deaths.”
It added that “all regions were affected,” except Normandy and Occitanie.
The figure brings the number of excess deaths during heat-wave periods since late May to more than 7,300, according to Sante publique France.
The agency recorded 1,243 excess deaths between July 3 and 22 and 5,764 between June 17 and July 2.
“The final estimate of consolidated excess all-cause mortality for the entire summer, broken down by heat wave, will be presented in the summer assessment produced after the surveillance period,” said Sante publique France.
The agency also recorded 300 deaths during the first heat wave episode of the year, between May 24 and 28.
Its previous assessments were based on preliminary, unconsolidated mortality data.
For the June 17 to July 2 heat wave, those aged 75 and older accounted for about two-thirds of the excess deaths, while they represented three-quarters of the total during July 3 to 22.
Sante publique France concluded that “these impacts highlight the importance of implementing management and prevention measures to reduce the impact of heat on populations, without waiting to observe health impacts.”
France experienced an exceptionally hot summer in 2026, with the season described as the hottest ever recorded in the country, according to data from Meteo-France.

'Starship Troopers' director confirms Donald Trump's space uniforms are Nazi-inspired

“I don’t know if this president is aware that the movie says these [characters] are fascists without knowing that they’re fascists. That’s the point,” said Paul Verhoeven, the director of 'Starship Troopers' - which was the direct reference cited by Trump when posting about Space Force uniforms.
If the Jackboot fits...
On 6 September, Donald Trump bulk-posted a series of AI-generated images, in which he renamed New Mexico as “New America”, declared the Moon as US territory, and portayed himself as the Green Lantern.
During this AI slop rampage, Trump proposed new uniforms for the United States Space Force – which was established in 2019 during Trump’s first term in office.
The image Trump posted was a design mockup for a new “service dress uniform” that was “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper Uniform.”
Many were quick to point out that this was a curious choice of inspiration, as Starship Troopers is a 1997 sci-fi war movie which is a cautionary tale about the dangers of fascism.
The cult film by Dutch director Paul Verhoeven is about a group of friends who enlist in the military and get swept up in an intergalactic war. Beyond fight against space bugs, Starship Troopers explores themes of misplaced patriotism, colonialism, xenophobia and violence decrying from fascistic rule.
The movie was based on the novel by Robert A. Heinlein, which Verhoeven interpreted as fascistic, nationalistic and in favour of military rule. The director used his film to deconstruct these elements and undermine the themes, using Nazi iconography to further his point. For instance, officer uniforms in Starship Troopers are similar to those worn by the Gestapo...
Verhoeven has gone on the record many times to state that he directed the film in order to turn a “right-wing book” into a film that was a dark satire about the dangers of fascism.
Now, Verhoeven has said that Donald Trump's administration should be aware that the film’s heroes are all "fascists without knowing that they’re fascists”.
“When [the Trump administration] talks about Starship Troopers, they should be aware that it’s based on the style of Leni Riefenstahl," Verhoeven told The Hollywood Reporter - referring to the German filmmaker who was closely associated with the Nazi regime and glorified it through films including 1935's Triumph of the Will.
“I don’t know if this president is aware that the movie says these [characters] are fascists without knowing that they’re fascists. That’s the point,” continued Verhoeven.
Once again, a potent reminder that the Trump administration should really think twice before co-opting cinematic references.
Trump has previously appropriated several pop culture touchstones, including Superman, Hannibal Lecter, Jedis and Spider-Man, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks display a lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.
That being said, Verhoeven said that he is used to Starship Troopers’ satirical intent being misread and that the film has been challenging for audiences “because its heroes are, without knowing, Nazis."
"I thought people would understand and laugh about it. But that was not the case,” he added. “I’m a Dutch citizen, and I cannot vote. I’ve been here in this country [US] for 40 years and it’s still difficult for me to understand the political culture here in America.”

YEKATERINBURG, September 16. /TASS/. Russia does not intend to enter into any contracts or agreements with the EU on issues of its national security, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the International Youth Festival.
"In areas that affect the security of the state, we will not and do not intend to conclude any contracts or agreements with Europeans," he said.
The foreign minister pointed out that it was Europe that severed relations with Russia, rather than the other way around.
"We are now fully provided with markets and partners, and despite the hybrid war against Russia, everything is going as acceptably and positively as possible given all the circumstances," Lavrov stressed. "When and if any European country wants to resume a serious dialogue, we will first listen to what they have in mind and what they can offer, and then we will decide whether it suits us or not. But there will be no more returns to the embrace that took place at the end of the Soviet Union and in the 1990s."
The International Youth Festival is being held in Yekaterinburg from September 11 to 17 under the slogan "Follow Your Dream." The festival is expected to be attended by 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries: 5,000 from Russia and 5,000 from other countries. The program will include 1,000 teenagers aged 14 to 17.
TASS is the event’s general information partner.

Amazon says unable to reactivate UAE, Bahrain data centers
Unknown

2026-09-16
13:44:11 UTC

Breadcrumb
Amazon says unable to reactivate data centers in UAE and Bahrain
Several Amazon data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain hit by drone strikes in March cannot be reactivated, the company's cloud arm said on Tuesday.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) said it was unable to restart several sites in Bahrain and one in the UAE. AWS has three sites in Bahrain, according to its website.
"After a thorough assessment, we have determined that we are unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted exclusively in this Region," it said in a status update.
AWS said in early March that drone strikes damaged two of its data centers in the UAE and a facility in Bahrain.
The incidents, which occurred a few days after the United States and Israel began attacking Iran, were "a result of the ongoing conflict" in the Middle East, AWS said at the time.
AWS is the world's leading cloud computing provider, competing with rivals including Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud to offer infrastructure that underpins popular apps and websites, as well as powering generative AI.
AWS said on Tuesday that it was still working to restore its "resources" at two sites in the UAE.
"Since the disruption began in March, most customers have been able to re-establish their operations in other Regions by restoring backups or copying data that remained accessible," AWS said, referring to its infrastructure in the UAE.
In the case of Bahrain, the company said it had "exhausted every option for restoring data and resources that had not been migrated before the Region became unavailable."

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China, Japan, South Korea and Iran advanced to the men's basketball semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games after winning their respective quarterfinals on Wednesday.
China held off Saudi Arabia 87-78 despite forwards Zhu Junlong, Zhao Jiayi and Li Hongquan being sidelined by injuries. China took a 48-39 lead into halftime, but Saudi Arabia fought back to tie the game at 62 at the end of the third quarter.
The fourth quarter remained tight before two free throws from Hu Jinqiu gave China an 83-75 lead with 2:04 remaining. Mohammad Alsuwailem then made a free throw and a layup to cut the deficit to 83-78 with 1:29 left, but consecutive baskets from Cui Yongxi and Liao sealed China's victory.

On Bahrain's last possession, guard Mustafa Rashed missed a three-pointer from the corner. He was then ejected after receiving his second technical foul of the game for disputing the call, ending Bahrain's hopes of a comeback.
In the other two quarterfinals, Lee Hyun-jung scored 28 points and grabbed nine rebounds, while veteran Choi Jun-yong added six points on his return as South Korea routed Jordan 114-80; Host Japan defeated Chinese Taipei 85-78, with Kotetsu Kurokawa scoring 23 points.

Asia-Pacific Community: CPEC project helps Pakistani women break barriers, scale new professional heights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:44:02 CST
22:44:02 KST

by Raheela Nazir
ISLAMABAD, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Wearing a smart navy blue uniform and looking all primed and equipped to operate a massive train, 26-year-old Nida Saleh could barely contain her excitement while mounting herself into a cabin of the Orange Line Metro Train (OLMT).
The metro train is the first modern rail transit system in Pakistan's eastern Lahore city under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), jointly constructed by China Railway Group Corporation and China North Industries Corporation.
"I used to think why I could not get to choose the field of my choice and prove myself in the workplace and challenge traditional gender stereotypes," Saleh said.
"A few years on, here I am working blissfully as Pakistan's first female metro driver." Saleh joined the project as a transport engineer before deciding to take on a more demanding role as a train operator under the guidance of Chinese engineers.
"Initially, my family was concerned, but witnessing my passion for opening a way for other women, my parents were at ease. My main purpose is to bring about social change and improve the well-being of Pakistani women while becoming a source of hope, encouragement and inspiration for other women," she said.
Saleh believed that the journey to become the country's first female metro operator was not possible without the Chinese colleagues who went the extra mile to train her and impart world-class technical knowledge and standard operating procedures.
"The gesture of women's empowerment through the Chinese projects symbolizes the great friendship between Pakistan and China," she said, adding that CPEC projects in Pakistan are not only empowering local women and helping them grow, but also playing a pivotal role in transforming the country's economic landscape.
After Saleh's resounding success, another batch of 10-15 women were trained to enhance women's participation and promote professional independence for them in Pakistan.
"Never in my wildest dreams have I thought of becoming a train driver, said Hijab Aziz, another female train operator.
"I was a bit nervous initially, but thanks to my seniors, Chinese and Pakistani colleagues who taught us the nitty-gritty of train operations and passenger handling," she added.
Aziz takes pride in sharing that she is one of the pioneers. "During my training, I completed my theoretical and practical courses in which we studied safety protocols, passenger safety, fault handling and train operations to become certified train operators," the 25-year-old explained.
"We also learned about pressure handling as we are handling huge locomotives. We have been put through several tests and practice before actually hitting the rail track. This project is first-of-its-kind in providing opportunities to females in such fields," she added.
Being part of Pakistan's public transport system, which is considered the backbone of urban mobility, providing essential services that support economic activity as well as social equity, Aziz said she feels a sense of achievement as she transports people to their workplaces, educational institutes and day-to-day activities.
The OLMT in Lahore developed a new working space for the female segment of society to excel professionally, said Qamar Mehboob, deputy general manager at the OLMT.
"Modern systems do not differentiate between genders, and technology is gender-neutral if mastered. The orange line project is committed to women's empowerment, which will be offering more opportunities for women in various departments, including maintenance and operations in the coming days," he added.
Wang Zhiwen, acting director of operations and maintenance at the OLMT project, said that highly experienced subway drivers from China are involved in teaching Pakistani female train operators according to Chinese standards.
"From theoretical learning to handling emergencies on main lines, female train operators were quite proficient," he said, adding that Chinese supervisors intend to train more female drivers as well as engineers to do maintenance and repair and deal with malfunctions in the future.
The OLMT is catering to more than 260,000 people daily with reduced travel time, having a substantial effect on the lives of people, especially those who could not afford to travel frequently. Considering the high demand for a cheap mode of transportation in Lahore, the capacity of the service is being increased to 500,000 people daily with additional train sets, according to Bilal Akbar Khan, Punjab minister for transport and mass transit.
Many projects under the CPEC and joint ventures between Pakistani and Chinese companies are bringing about socio-economic benefits to Pakistan, transforming the lives of locals, and furthermore, many projects are proving to be game-changers for Pakistani women.
"The Orange Line is one such example where women's participation is being encouraged by creating a conducive environment, making them feel respected, valued and supported, leading to higher job satisfaction and productivity," Khan said.
"Enabling women professionally at workplaces and providing them an appropriate mode of transportation is the country's top priority, and the Chinese people are helping us in this regard," he said.
Sadia Ahmed, an electrical engineer working at the rolling stock department of the OLMT, said that since her recruitment she has excelled in professional skills and learned the latest technology, with the privilege of having a happy and supportive working environment.
"When I joined this company about two years ago, I knew this was exactly what I was looking for -- a chance to jumpstart my career and better future -- build a successful and accomplished life for my family and myself," Ahmed said enthusiastically. ■

Kosovo Ex-President Thaci Gets Jailed 25 Years for War Crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:44:00 UTC
22:44:00 KST

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Wednesday, Sept. 16, after a tribunal in The Hague convicted him of war crimes committed during Kosovo’s conflict with Serbia in the late 1990s.
According to Reuters on Wednesday, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers found the 58-year-old former commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) guilty of murder, torture, cruel treatment, and arbitrary detention.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The court held Thaci and three other former KLA commanders criminally responsible for the arbitrary detention of 385 people, cruel treatment of 49, torture of 303, and the murder of 96.
None of the victims were actively participating in hostilities when the crimes occurred, the court said.
“The plan was as simple as it was harmful,” presiding judge Charles Smith said.
Judges found that the four defendants had participated in a joint criminal enterprise targeting people perceived as opponents of the KLA’s political and military objectives.
Court details killings and detention network
According to an official statement from the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the defendants helped establish detention facilities in KLA-controlled areas and identify, arrest, and imprison alleged opponents.
The victims included Kosovo Albanians associated with rival political or military organizations, people accused of links to Serbian or Yugoslav authorities, and members of ethnic minorities, including Roma and Serbs.
4 Years Since the Discovery of the Izyum Mass Graves
Judges said the vast majority were innocent civilians who had been labelled collaborators or spies, often without evidence.
Detainees were held in inhumane conditions, beaten, confined in small cells, and denied adequate food and medical treatment, according to the judgment.
The court found that Thaci played a central role in developing and implementing the policy of targeting perceived KLA opponents while serving on the organization’s General Staff and leading its Political Directorate.
It also found him personally involved in the arrest, interrogation, and arbitrary detention of 13 parliamentarians, as well as the arrest, transfer, and murder of Behajdin Allaqi.
Thaci stood silently as the sentence was announced. He had denied all charges and may appeal the verdict.
Prosecutors had requested a 45-year prison sentence.
Three other KLA commanders convicted
Three other former KLA commanders were also convicted of war crimes.
Kadri Veseli, the former head of the KLA’s intelligence directorate, received an 18-year sentence. Rexhep Selimi, a former KLA inspector general, was sentenced to 13 years, while former KLA spokesperson and deputy commander Jakup Krasniqi received 25 years.
All four will receive credit for the time they have spent in detention since their arrests in November 2020.
However, the court acquitted the defendants of six charges of crimes against humanity. Judges said prosecutors had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the offenses formed part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population.
The panel emphasized that the trial did not concern the legitimacy of the KLA’s campaign for Kosovo’s independence or crimes committed by Serbian forces against Kosovo Albanians.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 under international pressure to investigate alleged crimes committed by former KLA members during and immediately after the 1998-99 war.
Although it applies Kosovo law, the court is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors.
Protests follow verdict
The ruling triggered protests among Thaci’s supporters in both The Hague and Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, where he remains a national hero to many ethnic Albanians.
Several hundred demonstrators briefly clashed with police outside the tribunal after attempting to march toward the court building, Reuters reported.
Hundreds of people also marched through Pristina, where riot police were deployed amid concerns over possible unrest.
“This verdict is shameful. From today, there will be no peace in Kosovo,” former KLA fighter Raif Pllana told Reuters during the demonstration.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama also criticized the verdict, posting an image of barbed wire drawn across a map of Europe with the word “Unbelievable.”
Thaci served as Kosovo’s prime minister before becoming president in 2016. He resigned from the presidency in November 2020 after the tribunal confirmed the indictment against him.
Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but Belgrade continues to reject its sovereignty. The legacy of the war and the status of Kosovo remain major sources of tension between the two sides.

China Focus: China's railway construction gains strong momentum as Jan.-Aug. investment rises
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:56 CST
22:43:56 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's railway construction endeavors maintained solid momentum in the first eight months of 2026, with significant progress made on a number of key projects, the national railway operator said on Wednesday.
Fixed-asset investment in the railway sector totaled 511.8 billion yuan (about 75.68 billion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of the year, up 1.5 percent year on year, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
This steady progress in railway construction has helped boost related industries and employment, injecting new momentum into the expansion of domestic demand and stable economic growth, the company said.
A number of key projects have recently made positive progress. For instance, the Wenling-Yuhuan section of the Hangzhou-Shaoxing-Taizhou high-speed railway in east China's Zhejiang Province opened to traffic, putting Yuhuan, a city in southeastern Zhejiang, within 1 hour and 47 minutes of the provincial capital Hangzhou by direct high-speed train.
Construction also advanced on several technically challenging projects.
Railway construction teams have pushed tunnel construction forward in cold and difficult mountain terrain, finished tunnels through complex and risky ground conditions, started building beams on major railway bridges, and begun laying tracks on the country's longest high-speed railway bridge under construction.
The company said it will fully implement the railway construction tasks set out in the outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), coordinate the planning and construction of new lines with the upgrading and capacity expansion of conventional railways, and continue to improve the quality and efficiency of railway investment to support high-quality economic and social development.
China has built the world's largest high-speed railway network. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
According to the company, the country's operational railway mileage is expected to reach 180,000 km by 2030, with high-speed rail amounting to roughly 60,000 km.
Railway construction boasts a long industrial chain and wide spillover effects, driving demand for steel, cement, construction machinery and equipment manufacturing, while creating local jobs.
In the first seven months of the year, China's railways recorded 2.8 billion passenger trips, up 4.1 percent year on year and a record high for the period. Over the same timeframe, the network carried 14.85 million trips by foreign passengers, a surge of 32.5 percent.
China's railways carried 2.35 billion tonnes of cargo in the first seven months of 2026, rising 0.7 percent from a year earlier, lending solid support to logistics cost cuts and sustained stable economic performance.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. When fully built, the network will cover major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

The recovery reflects growing cooperation between Egypt and Switzerland in protecting cultural property and combating illegal trafficking of antiquities, the ministry said.
The Embassy of Switzerland in Cairo said the ancient funerary mask dated back to the Ptolemaic period, more than 2,000 years ago.
The return marks another milestone in the longstanding cooperation between Switzerland and Egypt to protect cultural heritage and fight the illicit trafficking of cultural property. Since 2011, Switzerland has returned around 80 cultural objects to Egypt, the embassy added. ■

China to bolster opening up with better legal framework for foreign-related affairs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:25 CST
22:43:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China will further strengthen its foreign-related legal framework over the next five years to improve its "legal toolkit" for relevant affairs, Vice Minister of Justice Wu Yanjun said Wednesday.
The move comes as the country seeks to better support its opening up and manage risks arising from the increasing overseas activities of Chinese citizens and businesses, Wu told a news conference.
Efforts will also be made to guide legal responses to foreign-related civil and commercial disputes and better protect the personal and property rights of Chinese citizens and businesses, Wu said.
China has introduced several sets of regulations in response to practical needs in foreign-related areas this year, including rules on countering foreign long-arm jurisdiction, regulations on industrial and supply-chain security, and rules governing outbound investment.
The rules on countering foreign states' unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures, which were issued in April this year, stipulate that the Chinese government has the authority to take countermeasures in response to such actions. The regulations also state that no organization or individual shall enforce or assist in enforcing such unlawful jurisdiction measures.
Under the new rules, Chinese authorities carried out an investigation after the European Commission announced an investigation into Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com's proposed takeover of German retailer Ceconomy in May.
In August, the Ministry of Justice announced that the EU's cross-border investigation constituted unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction, and that no organization or individual may comply with or assist in implementing relevant measures.
In May, citing the same set of rules on countering foreign unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction, the ministry said the EU's probe into Chinese security check company Nuctech constituted unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction.
As some legal experts pointed out, China's efforts in pursuing high-standard opening up require a stable international environment, yet some foreign countries' unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures have brought about serious uncertainties.
Analysts believed that the new regulations also carry direct implications for Chinese companies seeking to safeguard their overseas-related rights and will significantly boost companies' confidence in responding to external bullying.
At Wednesday's media conference, Wu said the ministry has also worked to provide more efficient and higher-quality legal services to Chinese companies and citizens operating overseas.
According to Wu, the ministry will further coordinate legislative work on international judicial assistance in civil and commercial matters, overseas labor cooperation and overseas contracted projects. Measures will also be taken to develop international commercial arbitration centers and support more Chinese law firms and arbitration institutions in expanding their operations overseas.
Moreover, China will play a more constructive role within the framework of international platforms, including the United Nations, in the area of the rule of law and actively participate in international cooperation to combat cross-border crimes such as telecom and online fraud and money laundering, Wu said.
At the same media conference, Jiang Shan, a ministry official in charge of legislative affairs, said the ministry would step up legislation in key areas affecting people's livelihoods and strengthen safeguards for basic work and living conditions.
It will conduct studies on laws and regulations covering oversight of social insurance funds, security of grain reserves, protection of the rights and interests of older people, elderly care services, and food safety, Jiang said. ■

CANBERRA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Australia had a much larger Indigenous population before European arrival, with far greater population losses from colonization than previously thought, new research shows.

DR Congo Ebola outbreak remains "uncontrolled" as transmission trends diverge: WHO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:19 CST
22:43:19 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains "uncontrolled" despite an overall decline in cases and deaths, as the epidemic follows increasingly different trajectories across affected parts of the country, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Wednesday.
"The outbreak remains uncontrolled and increasingly heterogeneous," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in its latest weekly situation report.
For much of the outbreak, the eastern province of Ituri has been the epicenter of transmission and still accounts for almost 80 percent of confirmed cases. Infections there have been declining since mid-August, helping drive down the national caseload.
"The peak is behind us (in Ituri). We are already on the downward slope," Jean-Jacques Muyembe, a veteran Congolese virologist heading the country's National Institute of Biomedical Research, said late Tuesday in Kinshasa, noting "a clear improvement" in the fight against Ebola in Ituri.
That modest national decline, however, masks what the WHO described as "a pronounced geographic redistribution of transmission." Over the latest three-week period, confirmed cases fell by about 6 percent nationwide, driven largely by a 25-percent drop in Ituri, while cases surged by more than 76 percent in neighboring North Kivu.
North Kivu, the second-most affected province after Ituri, is now moving in the opposite direction. The WHO described a "sharp and sustained increase" there, with the province recording its "highest incidence" since the outbreak began, as the flare-up in North Kivu has been broad-based rather than confined to a few hotspots.
North Kivu now accounts for about one-third of new cases and more than one-third of new deaths nationwide, as its worsening outbreak increasingly offsets the gains made in Ituri, according to the WHO.
Muyembe nevertheless cautioned that progress in some areas did not mean the epidemic was over, as transmission remains uneven and continues to intensify elsewhere. He stressed the need to further strengthen contact tracing and other response measures.
At the same time, researchers are moving closer to results from several experimental vaccines and treatments, as no vaccine or specific therapy has yet been approved for disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, the strain behind the current outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved against Zaire ebolavirus, is being used in the DRC under a compassionate-use framework and research protocols to determine whether it can offer some protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. A total of 2,307 health and frontline workers had received the vaccine by Sept. 13, about 20 percent of the targeted group, according to the WHO.
Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Tuesday that laboratory findings and field observations had provided grounds to investigate possible cross-protection, but stressed that they did not yet amount to proof. Clinical studies are now underway to assess whether the vaccine can reduce infection, severe disease or deaths.
Research on treatments and prevention is also advancing. Mbala said a clinical trial evaluating post-exposure prophylaxis for people at high risk of infection has been moving forward, with an initial analysis potentially available by the end of this month.
Separately, the WHO said 128 people had received investigational treatment or prophylaxis, including 16 confirmed patients and 112 high-risk contacts receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial is testing the experimental monoclonal antibody MBP134, remdesivir and their combination in confirmed patients.
"Although the response has been unprecedented in its scale, the epidemic continues to expand," said Olivier le Polain, head of epidemiology and analytics for response at the WHO, Tuesday at a UN briefing in Geneva, warning that the high caseload and wide geographic spread meant it would take "many, many months" to bring the outbreak fully under control.
Muyembe did not give a new deadline for containing the outbreak, saying only that response teams should "do everything possible so that we can celebrate the New Year under better conditions."
The DRC government's latest situation report, with data through Sept. 13, showed that the country had recorded 7,258 confirmed Ebola cases, including 3,510 deaths, across 62 health zones in seven provinces.
The current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

A thinktank linked to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is preparing an influential policy plan that is reportedly going to call for substantial tax cuts for the rich.
The Centre for a Better Britain (CFABB) is due to publish the 200-page document next week, giving insight into the economic and financial policies that are likely to form part of Reform UK’s platform before the next election.
The thinktank proposals are said to benefit some of the UK’s wealthiest taxpayers, by abolishing inheritance tax and phasing out capital gains tax, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.
That would mean depriving the Treasury of a lucrative source of funding. The UK’s inheritance tax raised £8.5bn last year, while capital gains tax brought in a record £24bn in 2024-25, for public and government operations.
CFABB – founded by the former Reform chief operations officer Jonathan Brown – is also expected to propose cutting rules and regulation for the UK’s financial services sector, in what is being called “big bang 2.0”, a reference to Margaret Thatcher’s City deregulation drive in the 1980s.
That is on top of calls to break up the Treasury and move its economic growth responsibilities to a different department, the news outlet reported.
A spokesperson for CFABB said Bloomberg appeared to have been briefed on an “early draft of the report” that did not reflect what would be released next week. They also insisted that there would be “no unfunded tax cuts” proposed in the report, and “no suggestions that we go pre-2008” in terms of regulatory reforms.
The spokesperson said the Bloomberg story included inaccuracies, but said they would not be drawn into discussing which points were incorrect.
The prospective tax proposals come as Reform UK faces questions over the motivation of two crypto billionaires – Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne – who each donated £36m to the party within 24 hours last weekend. The donations, totalling a combined £72m, amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics. Harborne and Delo have denied seeking to buy influence over the party’s policies.
CFABB has notable ties with Farage’s party, with its operations based in Millbank Tower near Reform’s headquarters.
It formally launched as CFABB in September last year, after raising fresh funds under its previous guise, Resolute 1850. The original name is said to have been reference to the Royal Navy ship, HMS Resolute, whose timbers were used to make the US president’s desk in the Oval Office.
In an interview with the Financial Times last autumn, Brown – the thinktank’s founder – said he planned to look at ways to weaken the authority of Britain’s courts and civil service, in what some said echoed “Project 2025”, the US project drawn up in the run-up to Donald Trump’s second presidency to help him deliver radical conservative policies with greater political power.
CFABB currently has five staff, and previously counted James Orr – Reform UK’s former head of policy – as the chair of its advisory board.
Orr was suspended from Reform UK earlier this month after being filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to help orchestrate a plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. Orr denies wrongdoing.
A spokesperson for CFABB said Orr stepped down from the thinktank role when he took a job at Reform in February, and was not replaced.
