- list 3 of 3Ed Sheeran blames US tour promoter for dropping Macklemore
Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, drew criticism after saying “Free Palestine” and making other pro-Palestine comments while on tour with Sheeran at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey earlier this month.
He was ultimately dropped from the remainder of Sheeran’s tour, partly under pressure from the billionaire owner of one of the venues, the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, Robert Kraft. On Tuesday, Sheeran blamed the tour’s US promoter.
“I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of this message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said,” Sheeran wrote. “I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge.”
Who are the musicians and bands who have also quit the tour?
Which artists are pulling out and why?
In statements on their social media platforms shortly after Sheeran’s announcement, American singer-songwriter Finneas, Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Irish band Beoga and Danish pop band Lukas Graham announced they would be dropping out of the tour, which is scheduled to begin on September 19 in Philadelphia.
Sheeran is set to kick off his North American tour at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Saturday.
Finneas, US singer-songwriter
Finneas, who was scheduled to open for Sheeran in some American cities during the tour, announced on Instagram on Tuesday that he had decided to withdraw from the tour after Macklemore’s expulsion.
He and his sister, the multi-Grammy and Academy Award-winning pop singer Billie Eilish, have talked about their Irish family roots and have been outspoken about their support for Palestine before.
“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” he said on Instagram on Tuesday.
“I stand with Palestine and its people,” he added.
Aaron Rowe, Irish singer
On Tuesday, Rowe, who performed as part of Sheeran’s Australian leg of the tour earlier this year and was to do 10 more dates in the US, said he has also decided to withdraw.
“I don’t take the decision lightly,” he said on Instagram.
“Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this,” he acknowledged.
“But as Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal,” he added.
Beoga, Irish band
Beoga is Sheeran’s backing band. Yet on Tuesday, the group announced on Instagram that it would also quit the US leg of the tour “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”.
“We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us. We have been friends with Ed for over 10 years now and will continue to be. We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people,” they added.
Lukas Graham, Danish band
Announcing their withdrawal from the tour in an Instagram statement on Tuesday, lead singer Lukas Forchhammer wrote: “It’s hard to watch families in other parts of the world burying the people they love. We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”
“Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge,” he said.
How did the Macklemore controversy start?
Macklemore opened a Sheeran show at the New Jersey MetLife Stadium earlier this month with a speech about Palestine.
He said: “The people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them. I say free Palestine. I say free Lebanon. Free Cuba to the Congo to Sudan to Iran.”
The speech triggered an immediate backlash, and the Israeli-American Council started a petition to have Macklemore dropped from the tour.
Macklemore defended his statements, and also his performance of the song Hind’s Hall – dedicated to Hind Rajab, the five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces while stranded inside a car in Gaza – by stating that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial”.
Hamilton Hall, one of the main buildings on the campus of Columbia University, was the site of a student protest in 2024 against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The students occupied the hall and renamed it “Hind’s Hall”.
How did Robert Kraft get involved in the row?
In an Instagram post, Macklemore told fans: “Ed [Sheeran] told me that [Robert] Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium.”
He also claimed that Sheeran told him Kraft had rallied other stadium owners, who collectively issued an ultimatum: “If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”
Kraft defended his involvement in preventing Macklemore from performing at his own stadium in a statement. He said, “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf.”
“But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas … whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.”
Kraft’s public statement on the issue did not address the claim that the billionaire lobbied other stadium owners. He did say he would be happy to sit down with Macklemore and talk in person.
What has Ed Sheeran said?
Sheeran posted his response to the row on Instagram on Tuesday, confirming that Macklemore had been removed because of his pro-Palestinian stance, but denying that he was responsible.
He wrote: “I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated. Macklemore asked to join my tour last year and I agreed, because I respect him as an artist. As with all my support acts, I agree that they play a setlist of their choosing.
“After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting. I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said. I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.
“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision; it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
“I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”
How did others react?
While Sheeran and the tour’s operators have yet to comment on the supporting acts quitting, Macklemore, climate activist Greta Thunberg, the musicians, fans and supporters of Palestine and Gaza, have all lauded the artists for their decision to quit the tour.
Macklemore has commented on each of their Instagram posts with a heart and the Palestinian flag.
Some Instagram users who had not heard some of the artists, such as Rowe, before left comments such as, “You’ve gained a fan.”
Commenting on Finneas’s post, the Europe Palestine network, a civil society initiative, said: “What is happening is HUGE !!! Artists turning their back to billionaires !!! I am so happy and proud !!!!”
Sheeran has faced criticism on social media for allowing Macklemore to be barred from performing.
In a video rant against Sheeran, Belgium-based filmmaker and activist Thomas Maddens said that one of Sheeran’s songs, “What Do I Know” in 2017, includes the lyric, “The Revolution is coming, it’s a minute away. I saw people marching in the streets today.”
Maddens noted that, despite this song, Sheeran apparently sided with the people who are not marching [for Palestine].
Addressing Sheeran in his video, he added: “When it is white people you march with them. But when it is brown people, you don’t seem to care very much.”
While Macklemore did not blame his longtime friend Sheeran for the debacle and described him as “apolitical”, the latter has performed at a charity concert to raise money for Ukraine, and he has also recorded a music video with the Ukrainian military rock band Antytila.
Pink Floyd cofounder Roger Waters, who has also been vocal about his support for Palestine, said on his social media: “There are two kinds of people in this world.”
“Some people do the right thing. That rapper, Macklemore, would be one of those people.” he said.
Referring to Sheeran, he said: “And there are people who are p***ks, like you, who do the wrong thing. Goodbye.”

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at DVD 2026
Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen the capabilities of the British Army and boost economic growth.
Good afternoon. It’s nice not doing a speech in a suit, I have to say, and actually be able to get out there and get some mud going on, which is, I think, one of the great benefits of this event here. So good afternoon.
It is a real privilege to be here at DVD 26. I want to thank Rupert, our new National Armaments Director, and his team, for the work they’ve put in, their colleagues in the British Army for all the work that they’ve done. And my thanks to industry for what is a fantastic showcase of the warfighting abilities of our British Army, but also the potential of what could come next as well.
Strengthening that connective tissue between defence, industry and what is to come is an important part of delivering not just the Strategic Defence Review that was delivered last year, but also the Defence Investment Plan that was delivered only a few months ago. Now land is an essential domain, integral to the government’s mission to re-arm and reindustrialise the UK and it’s this domain that is one of the cornerstones of our deterrence as a nation.
And as an industrial sector, the land domain not only underpins the fighting power and lethality of the British Army, but also reinforces the argument that defence is an engine for growth.
Now, although I’m now supposed to say reindustrialisation, every time I say engine for growth due to the swapping Prime Ministers, the great advantage of that is both are true: that if we spend an increasing defence budget more with British companies, we create more good, decent jobs at home. We increase our industrial capacity, which increases our deterrent ability, as well as getting the latest kit and equipment into the hands of our warfighters.
And that’s why the land domain is so important, because this is not just a factory based in one part of the UK. The companies that work in the land domain make huge contributions to every single region of our country and the supply chain furthermore, in every single part. It is a success story that we don’t talk about enough, and it is one that is integral to defence’s contribution to reindustrialising the country. And that is an essential part of delivering on the increased defence spending that the Treasury is making available for defence.
And we can see that whether that’s from Merthyr and Oakdale, Telford, Stockport and Newcastle and across the nationwide network of suppliers, not just big companies but increasingly more SMEs getting involved in defence supply chain. This is a good thing, and this exhibition here allows us to talk about the ingenuity, the technology being brought forward and the people behind it, and that essential partnership between the public sector and the private sector that we need more of.
And as we reform defence procurement to be faster, because I think it’s fair to say that everyone in this room, regardless of what kind of clothing you are wearing today, will know that defence procurement is not as fast as we would all like it to be. We’re speeding it up. And some of the examples I’m going to talk about today are good examples of how we’re accelerating procurements, so we can get more kit and equipment faster and deliver greater value for that increased defence spending.
Now, I’m really grateful for the progress that we have collectively made as an industry and as a government over the past two years. As a government, we’ve delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, and the land warfare sector here has been a recipient of that increased defence spending, and it has a bright future ahead.
Now, our Defence Investment Plan laid out £298 billion worth of spending over the next four years, and we’ve secured a portfolio of land warfare modernisation programs within that Defence Investment Plan that will not only invest in British industry, but also give the British Army the kit and equipment they need, and provide the opportunity possible for those platforms to be exportable as well, working with our allies at the same time.
Now, that model and that funding is vital if we’re going to deliver the Recce Strike model that has been set out so clearly by CGS. That’s built around better targeting, better battlefield surveillance and more lethal long range fire, an increase in lethality of our British forces, to give us a generational upgrade in the abilities of the British Army. That’s not only about long range fire, but if you took long range fire as the example of the upgrades over the next four years, we’re investing £190 million in short range ballistic missiles, £400 million in inexpensive one-way attack drones and weapons, and £220 million in Project Nyx to build an advanced armed autonomous drones to fly alongside our Apache helicopters.
That’s about improving the lethality and delivering against CGS’s 20:40:40 strategy, which has been baked into the Defence Investment Plan. Now, that will be collectively a higher resolution picture of the battlefield and increase the effectiveness and speed of our targeting.
Now we’re investing a combined £4.4 billion to take forward Boxer, Ajax and Challenger programmes over the next four years and £370 million to roll out Project Asgard, which has proven itself as the brains behind the Recce Strike concept. And that has certainly worked in Estonia, we’re rolling it out to more parts of the British Army as well. Now enabling our forward land force to fuse existing capabilities such as armoured vehicles with drones and other new capabilities, is vital to deliver that new type of deterrence that we need in the 21st century.
These programmes sit alongside our new multi-million pound investment in new medium helicopters from Leonardo in Yeovil, uncrewed ground vehicles with more announcements to come in that area, counter-drone technologies and a successor to the venerable Land Rover. You might not have noticed, but apparently there’s some vehicles being exhibited out there. There’s not many of them on the show, so you probably would have missed them on there. But it is good to see such a competitive option.
So much of the stuff that we buy that I sign off as the Minister comes from single source procurement. That’s the right thing when we’re dealing with high end procurements, advanced British technologies. But for a Land Rover replacement, having that competitive edge with companies far and wide providing options for defence to choose from, I think shows a market working well and we’re making progress against that.
Now look, over the next four years we’re investing more than £19 billion in land warfare capabilities, as well as £11 billion in weapons and ammunition. So, when we talk about as a politician what we inherited, hollowed out and underfunded forces, we inherited brilliant people, a structure that has at its heart a real desire to renew and rearm. And that is what this increased defence funding helps enable: new technologies being brought forward.
And today, I’m delighted to unveil progress with three of our latest investments in that are vital components of Recce Strike.
First, to equip our soldiers with highly mobile ISR capabilities that will give them round the battlefield tactical awareness. We’ve signed contracts with three British SMEs worth a combined £16 million for more than a thousand small ISR drones.
Second, to replace the ageing Watchkeeper system, I can today confirm that we have placed a contract with Tekever to bring twenty four of their AR5 drones into service by 2029. Together, these systems give us a ‘David and Goliath’ style mix of spy drones, equipping the Army with small, agile, rapidly deployable systems for the frontline alongside sustained high fidelity intelligence from the AR5 over longer range and durations.
And thirdly, I can also announce today that we have awarded contracts to MBDA and Thales to explore how we can develop the tech behind a new beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour weapon system, a capability that the British Army has not had since Swingfire, left service over 30 years ago, a capability that can drastically improve the ability of our land forces to strike and survive on the modern battlefield.
Now, these are just three procurements that will not only demonstrate how we’re evolving operationally in response to the lessons from Ukraine, but they’re programmes that demonstrate how we have reformed our procurement processes in response to what we’ve learned from our friends in Ukraine.
That’s more collaboration and innovation, so that our kit is designed to be built to evolve with the changing threats and technologies, with more focus on developing sovereign capabilities to build our industrial resilience and more backing for UK SMEs and UK-based businesses to create and sustain highly skilled, well-paid – wherever possible I say this as a Labour MP – unionised jobs throughout the UK, backing the men and women that work in our industry with a bright career, whether they’re mid-career, being retrained with the latest technology, or joining for the very first time. There is a bright career ahead in the defence industry.
We have not always been able to be as vocal in saying so, but collectively one of our missions of all of us in this room today, perhaps especially me, but not just me, is to tell the story about this investment and what it brings to our communities. Opportunities, reindustrialisation increased deterrence and warfighting abilities. There’s three priorities that defence has for the next quarter that you’ll hear the new Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, talk about frequently.
Again, all those three things are true. And as defence, we’ve been very good at not telling anyone about the benefits of defence spending here in the UK. Our job now, as we look ahead to a decade of rising defence spending, is to make the case that defence spending delivers good jobs at home, as well as delivering us the national security improvements that keep the UK and our allies safe.
Now, I make no apologies for directing more of that rising defence budget at British-based firms and UK workers, and on the face of it, that could appear protectionist. But it’s not. It’s a strategic decision that we have taken, and a departure from previous decisions taken by previous governments. Because when taxpayers see both a security and an economic dividend from increased spending on defence, it helps us to increase the size, not just of the public coalition in support of that investment, it also increases our ability to defend the nation as well.
Now, that’s why telling our story is so important. And so, I want to challenge you to tell the story of your work as well. I don’t want anyone giving away anything ‘secret squirrel’. But I do want you to talk about how investment in your businesses, in the systems the British Army is using in international collaborations, as well as investment and R&D at home, creates opportunities and good jobs. That is a story that helps reinforce the case for increased defence spending, and helps the public realise that, in the face of increased threats that they can see on their TV screens and on their phones, there is a clear plan being delivered to keep our nation safe.
Now then, stories of innovation and opportunity, and whilst it might sound not always sexy, stories about procurement reform, are vital. We need to tell the story about cutting-edge design, sci-fi like capabilities, and battle-winning kit, much of it actually on display out there. Stories of reindustrialisation that rebuild pride in our industrial base and our communities, and young people succeeding in the communities that they call home. These are the stories that work hard for the taxpayer. That show the taxpayer that defence is working hard for the investment they are making in the MOD and in our national security. Getting more bang for our buck literally in increasing lethality, but certainly value for money as well, and delivering more for our armed forces.
Now, the three contracts that I’ve highlighted today have all three of those elements. They’ll fuel innovation, sovereign capabilities and export opportunities at the same time, and they will help galvanise our industrial base. And in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, they will give the soldiers of our British Army a clearer picture of the battlefield and greater lethality on it.
Now, the government’s guiding mantra are backing UK firms pays us back four times over: in military strength, in industrial strength, in economic growth and in public support for defence. It takes us closer to achieving our objectives of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027, tripling it by 2030 and growing it tenfold by 2035. That’s not just the government’s story. That’s your story as well. And across the British Army, procurement, and industry, it’s one that if we tell, well, we’ll deliver not only added effect but greater support for defence spending.
Now, for my part, this Autumn I’ll be working hard to stimulate more sources of investment in defence. It will talk to how we crowd in private capital, into core defence and into our supply chain, how we use that private capital, both from venture, sovereign and other forms to support our R&D, support our bringing products to market, grow and stabilize SMEs, especially in the Valley of Death, as they go up through the TRL levels for their products.
And it will help deliver via the new Defence Investment Unit that we’ve established in the MOD, something that will get more of that private capital to where it matters. Now for small businesses, growing businesses, start-ups, and the success of the Defence Tech Unicorn Fund, where the MOD has invested a small amount of money helping grow businesses, we have now more defence tech unicorns in Britain than anywhere else across Europe. This is a success story we need to talk about and that will help us build towards the Defence Investment Summit, which will take place in early December, where will be an opportunity for financial institutions and our partners to announce their own investments in defence, both in core defence, the investable opportunities that the MOD is providing for commercial partners to invest in the systems that we use and the products that we use, but also to support our defence supply chain again.
And to each of you in industry, I want to challenge you ahead of that, to tell the story about why defence is a great place to work, why it is a great place to invest, and in particular, why establishing a defence business or growing a defence business in Britain is right, not just to access that growing defence budget here, to provide a market to export to our friends as well.
I saw that firsthand at the recent Guildhall event hosted by the Lady Mayoress of the City of London, seeing the work of the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, bringing together small defence companies with investors to be able to marry opportunity and capital to grow and provide more opportunities. And if we do that, we can not only attract new investment into defence, but we can show our people, our allies and the defence sector that this is an area of our economy worthy of investment, worthy of attention and worthy of good careers that keep us safe, protect our freedoms and support our way of life.
We have a lot of work to be doing, but I’m really excited to see so much of that work that you are all doing here on showing the vehicles and platforms that we have outside. Let’s keep going. Thank you.

Russia's defence minister awards medal to captain of ship that fired flares towards Danish helicopter
Russian Defence Minister Andrei Belousov has awarded a medal to the captain of the Soobrazitelny, a corvette which fired signal flares towards a Danish Armed Forces helicopter in international waters near Gedser.
Source: European Pravda, citing the Russian Defence Ministry on social media
Details: The Russian Defence Ministry said Belousov awarded the Medal for Combat Merit to the captain of the Soobrazitelny for what it described as "skilful and decisive actions in preventing a provocation by a Danish Air Force helicopter".
Russia's Defence Ministry said that at 14:22 on 14 September, the Soobrazitelny, a Baltic Fleet corvette, was operating in international waters in the south-western Baltic Sea when it detected an aerial asset identified as a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter. The ministry said the helicopter was approaching the Russian warship and did not respond to calls on the international communications channel.
Quote: "To prevent a provocation by the Danish helicopter, the corvette commander decided to fire two red signal flares, after which the helicopter left the area where the Russian warship was operating."
Background:
- Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador after a Russian warship fired two flares towards a Danish helicopter on 14 September.
- Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, commenting on the incident, said that Russia had stepped up its hybrid warfare against Europe.
- Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin accused the Danish military of a "provocation" over its manoeuvres near the Russian warship.

OPINION - No rush for peace: Why a broad peace in Ukraine remains elusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:25:48 UTC
22:25:48 KST

Maksym Skrypchenko
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
- Maksym Skrypchenko is the president of the Transatlantic Dialogue Center, a Ukrainian think tank.
Recent trips to Moscow and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, preceded by a visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, marked a new attempt by Washington to jumpstart negotiations on ending the Russia-Ukraine war. However, the intensity of diplomatic contacts currently far outweighs their tangible results. The reason lies not so much in the lack of an acceptable peace formula as in the fundamentally different expectations the parties hold concerning the war's continuation: Ukraine seeks ways to stop the destruction, while Russia hopes that, in the coming months, Kyiv will no longer be able to keep resisting.
This divergence can’t be explained by shifts on the battlefield map alone, as there have been almost none. Russian pressure at the front has not secured the kind of victory that would allow Moscow to dictate terms. At the same time, Ukraine lacks the advantage needed to rapidly liberate occupied territories. To call this balance a stalemate would be to underestimate how the nature of the war itself is evolving. What matters most is the ability to destroy the opposing side's economic foundation.
Targeting the economy
Ukrainian strikes on the Russian oil industry are a good example. They are intended to raise the cost of the war to the point where Moscow sees a practical benefit in mutually limiting attacks. Kyiv is open to a wide range of agreements, from protecting Black Sea shipping and grain infrastructure to halting strikes on energy facilities or even a complete mutual cessation of long-range strikes, as this would allow for de-escalation without waiting for the resolution of all political disputes.
The problem is that Moscow has so far been unwilling to discuss such arrangements; instead, it links any meaningful move toward a truce to Ukraine’s prior withdrawal from the remaining parts of Donbas under its control. By insisting on the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the rest of Donbas, which Kyiv believes it will be able to defend at least for a few years, the Kremlin is demanding what Kyiv considers impossible.
Russia’s reluctance to agree to limits on strikes stems from the conviction that time is on Moscow’s side. In private discussions with American counterparts, the Russian side points to Ukraine’s budgetary difficulties and the uncertainty surrounding future European funding. Upcoming elections in Europe are also presented as an additional sign of weakened support for Ukraine in the future. The Kremlin operates on the assumption that while losses in its own oil sector are manageable, the combination of winter-induced destruction and financial constraints will ultimately force Kyiv to give up.
Ukraine is bracing for attacks not only on its power grid but also on its gas infrastructure, preparing for a massive humanitarian crisis. Under these circumstances, the supply of air defense systems and reliable funding not only help Kyiv defend itself but also undermine Moscow’s confidence that Ukrainian resistance will eventually collapse.
Stalled negotiations
Meanwhile, visits by American negotiators have not brought a breakthrough, and Moscow has linked its willingness to take further steps in the talks to the conclusion of the September parliamentary elections. Both Kyiv and Washington understand that the Russians will likely find new grounds for delay thereafter, allowing them to continue the military campaign into the spring.
The American attempts to offer economic incentives in exchange for de-escalation have not yet resolved the fundamental contradiction. Moscow may well be interested in economic benefits without losing its desire to continue the war.
In the absence of conditions for a broad agreement, the upcoming meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his US counterpart Donald Trump during the UN General Assembly could offer the next opportunity to test the prospects for a limited truce. Draft resolutions calling for an end to strikes on grain infrastructure in the Black Sea are already circulating at the UN. Such an agreement would have significance far beyond Ukraine, mitigating risks to the global food supply and allowing the UN to demonstrate its practical utility after years of criticism regarding its ineffectiveness.
For Trump, a Black Sea truce could also serve as a diplomatic achievement ahead of the midterm congressional elections, particularly as the protracted war with Iran continues to consume American resources. For these reasons, he might be interested in spearheading this process and leveraging American influence to ensure the agreement is upheld. Skepticism over UN mechanisms further reinforces Ukraine’s desire for Washington to assume direct political responsibility for the truce's observance. Ukraine’s readiness for a mutual truce leaves sufficient room for an agreement. To capitalize on this, Washington and Europe must use sanctions, incentives, or both to convince the Kremlin that another winter will not deliver the victory it has so far been unable to achieve on the battlefield.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Iran blocks ‘Bibi’s Kitchen’ Instagram over ‘cutlet’ joke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:24:51 UTC
22:24:51 KST

Iranian authorities blocked the Instagram account of a Tehran restaurant after it posted a play on words that was interpreted as a political jab at the Islamic Republic.
The restaurant, called “Bibi’s Kitchen,” posted an Instagram story reading, “Nothing beats Bibi’s cutlet,” accompanied by Iranian pop star Moein’s song “Bibi Gol.” Shortly after the post went viral, the account was blocked by judicial order for what authorities described as “publishing criminal content.”
On the surface, the post appeared to be promoting a dish on the restaurant’s menu. But in Iran’s political vocabulary, both words carry a double meaning. “Bibi” is an old-fashioned Persian term for grandmother. But it is also the well-known nickname of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and has appeared in anti-government memes and posts expressing support for Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic.
The term “cutlet,” meanwhile, became a political taunt after Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020, mocking the condition of his body after the attack.
Since then, opponents of the Islamic Republic have used the word to refer mockingly to senior regime figures killed in military strikes. The combination of “Bibi” and “cutlet” was therefore interpreted as a reference to Netanyahu and senior Iranian officials killed by Israel, although the restaurant itself did not explicitly make such a political statement.
Iranian authorities have acted against similar uses of the word before. In January 2023, prominent chef Navab Ebrahimi was arrested after posting a cutlet recipe around the anniversary of Soleimani’s killing. His restaurant was shut and his Instagram account was taken offline. Contemporary reports said social media users believed the cutlet post was connected to his arrest, although authorities did not publicly establish that as the reason.
In January 2024, doctor and university professor Mohammad Shoja was detained in the northeastern city of Bojnourd after posting a photograph of a cutlet on the night senior IRGC commander Razi Mousavi was killed.
In June 2024, the Iranian judiciary opened a case against playwright and theater director Hossein Pakdel for allegedly “disrupting the psychological security of society” after he wrote on Instagram that politics turns “stupid men into special diet cutlets.”
Sensitivity surrounding references to Israel has intensified amid the current conflict. Iranian authorities said in March that more than 1,000 people had been arrested on accusations including sharing anti-government material online or cooperating with Israel and the United States. The judiciary has also warned that some forms of assistance to hostile states can carry the death penalty.

IN BRIEF: What is known about incident with Russian warship, Danish Air Force helicopter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:23:11 UTC
22:23:11 KST

MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. On September 14, the Russian Navy Baltic Fleet’s corvette Soobrazitelny fired two red signal flares toward a Danish Air Force helicopter to prevent an incident, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the main information available so far.
Statement by Russia’s Defense Ministry
- On September 14 at 2:22 p.m. [Moscow time] (11:22 a.m. GMT), the Baltic Fleet’s Soobrazitelny corvette was conducting operations in neutral waters in the southwestern part of the Baltic Sea when it detected an aerial target, which it identified as a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- The helicopter was heading toward the Russian warship and did not respond to calls on the international communication channel, the ministry stated.
- The Defense Ministry explained that the corvette commander decided to fire two red signal flares as a precautionary measure. After this, the helicopter left the area where the Russian warship was located.
- Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov awarded the Medal ‘For Military Distinction’ to the commander of the Soobrazitelny corvette for his skillful and decisive actions in preventing a provocation by the Danish Air Force helicopter, the ministry reported.
Russian ambassador summoned to Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs
- On September 15, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen announced that the Russian ambassador had been summoned to the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, allegedly due to the incident involving the Danish helicopter.
- The Danish Ministry of Defense protested about the Russian ship firing flares in international waters toward the Danish Air Force helicopter.
Comment by Russian Ambassador to Denmark
- Attempts by the Danish authorities to explain the provocative actions of the Danish Air Force helicopter toward the Russian ship as "routine practice" raise serious concerns about the possible consequences of such recklessness, Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin said, commenting on the incident.
- He noted that the Russian side will carefully examine all the circumstances of the incident.
- The statement emphasized that this is not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have performed dangerous maneuvers near Russian military ships navigating on the high seas and outside Denmark’s territorial waters.

Up to 1,000 Wounded a Day: Germany Reshapes Medical System for War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:21:20 UTC
22:21:20 KST

Germany is preparing military and civilian medical facilities to operate in the event of a potential large-scale armed conflict and a mass influx of wounded.
Bloomberg reported this in an article about Germany’s efforts to restructure its health care system amid the threat of war in Europe.
According to Bundeswehr estimates, in the event of an armed conflict on NATO’s eastern flank, between 300 and 1,000 wounded service members could be evacuated to Germany each day, with about one-third requiring intensive care.
The Bundeswehr’s five military hospitals would not be able to treat that many wounded on their own, meaning much of the burden would fall on civilian hospitals, which would also have to keep treating the civilian population.
Federal Health Minister Nina Warken said German medical facilities are taking measures to increase their resilience to armed conflict. These include creating additional stocks of medicines and surgical supplies, equipping protected spaces, installing bullet-resistant glass and physical barriers to protect against drones.
At the Bundeswehr hospital in Ulm, officials are considering restoring an underground medical bunker dating back to the Cold War. It is designed to accommodate about 2,000 people and operate independently for 90 days, but its ventilation and power systems would need modernization before it could be brought back into service. Medical facilities are also assessing the use of underground parking garages as long-term shelters and increasing stocks of critical medicines.
Another challenge is preparing medical personnel. Only a few hundred German doctors have practical experience treating combat-related trauma, so civilian surgeons are being trained to handle mass casualties and war injuries.
According to Benedikt Friemert, director of the Bundeswehr hospital in Ulm, Germany’s health care system is not yet fully prepared to operate under such conditions.
The Bundeswehr assumes that, in the event of war, Germany’s geographic position would make it one of NATO’s main rear-area and logistics hubs: troops and materiel would move eastward through the country, while wounded personnel would be evacuated in the opposite direction.
German military officials regard the experience of Russia’s war against Ukraine as a key factor shaping the new system of medical support and civil-military cooperation.
Germany is also developing field medicine. In particular, the Bundeswehr has ordered 149 mobile medical aid stations from Rheinmetall, which Ukraine has been using since 2023.

Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian officer is accused of waging an aggressive war against Ukraine. He organized the supply of missiles, aerial bombs, and drones to the Russian army.
Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General have completed the pretrial investigation and referred to court an indictment against Russian Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko. He is suspected of waging an aggressive war or aggressive military actions, as provided for by Part 2 of Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, Krivoruchko formulated and implemented the aggressor state's military-technical policy, organized the fulfillment of the state defense order, and controlled the supply of weapons.
It was established that Krivoruchko signed state contracts for the production and supply of Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, Iskander-M missile systems, guided aerial bombs, as well as Geran- and Gerbera-type drones. He also controlled the fulfillment of defense orders and reported to the leadership of the Russian Defense Ministry on the expansion of weapons production and supplies for the Russian army
In addition, according to the investigation, the defendant initiated the creation of the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Its units subsequently took a direct part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The evidence collected indicates that the weapons whose supply was organized and controlled by the accused were used by Russian forces during missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian territory, in particular against civilian and critical infrastructure. As a result of such attacks, civilians were killed and injured, and residential buildings and critical infrastructure facilities were destroyed
The article provides for a sentence of 10 to 15 years in prison.
Reminder
The Security Service of Ukraine and the prosecutor's office notified Russian Colonel General Sergei Kuzovlyov in absentia of suspicion over the strike on Kramatorsk in June 2023.

Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:18:08 UTC
22:18:08 KST

Partner content
Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home
A new job, a burst pipe, a divorce, a renovation gone on too long: there are more moments than you’d imagine when you might suddenly need somewhere to live. Here’s how serviced and flexible housing can step in, whatever the reason.
1. The new job or the temporary assignment
 Relocating for work is the classic reason many people need a home in the Netherlands, but it’s far from the only version of it. Travelling nurses posted to a new hospital, researchers starting a fellowship, or consultants sent in for a few months on a project all arrive in the same position: they need somewhere to live, quickly, without signing up for a permanent rental contract.
Corporate Housing Factory (CHF) provides fully serviced apartments across the Netherlands – offering comfortable, home-style living for stays from one week up to a year, combining the convenience of a hotel with the privacy and space of a residence.
You request a quote, the team confirms availability, and in some cases you can get the keys as soon as the next day. Apartments come fully furnished, from kitchen appliances to Wi-Fi, with cleaning included. Companies are invoiced directly, and the booking system is connected to the Global Distribution System (GDS), so travel management companies can book on a client’s behalf just as easily as they could book a hotel.
CHF’s newest property, in Arnhem, is a case in point. The building dates back to 1878 and survived the bombing of the Second World War – one apartment still has a shrapnel hole, deliberately unfilled. It’s since been transformed into an industrial-chic block with high ceilings and top-quality furniture, right by Arnhem Centraal station and a local supermarket. The location was chosen for the wider Nijmegen-Arnhem-Wageningen region, where technology, healthcare, sustainability and logistics employers have long struggled to find decent corporate housing for their staff.
2. The housing emergency
 Then there’s the reason nobody plans for: a fire, a mould problem, a burst pipe or damage that suddenly makes your own home unliveable. It’s the kind of situation that can leave the victim feeling like an emergency bunker is the only option. And after an already stressful event, most people would rather not compromise on comfort.
This is where Thuis in de Stad comes in: “Until recently, we focused on corporate clients, so it was always relocations, work trips or internships,” says Claudia Vrancken from CHF. “With Thuis in de Stad, we’re opening the spectrum more broadly to the other unexpected reasons someone might suddenly need temporary housing.” You can anticipate fully furnished apartments, all utilities included; arrive with a suitcase and the rest is taken care of.
3. The renovation project, or getting caught between selling and buying
 The same goes for two other reasons someone might need to move out temporarily: a renovation that makes the house unliveable for a few weeks, or the gap between selling one home and getting the keys to the next. Neither is an emergency, but both mean needing a comfortable base at short notice, for an unpredictable length of time.
One detail that matters more than people expect in the Netherlands is the ability to register at an address – something most short-term rentals don’t allow, but which is essential for things like getting a BSN number or opening a bank account. (Just don’t forget to deregister when you leave!)
4. The divorce process
 Separation is another situation that can leave someone needing a home almost overnight – often with the condition of staying close to children and family during a period of transition. Flexible, furnished housing means not having to make a long-term commitment while things are still being worked out, while still having a proper place to call home in the meantime.
It’s also worth knowing, whatever the reason for the move, that pets are welcome – unlike with most hotels or holiday rentals. “Our apartments are all located in mixed-use buildings, so you really have the feeling you’re living somewhere with local families, kids and pets, instead of in a hotel,” says Claudia.
5. The sudden business trip elsewhere in Europe
 Not every unexpected need for a home happens in the Netherlands. A consultant might have to jump on a plane at short notice for a project in another European city, with everything needing to be arranged just as quickly as it would be here.
For that, there’s Your Serviced Apartment Agency (YOSAA): a boutique Europe-wide apartments platform. The general idea of YOSAA – connecting living, hospitality and real estate – is the same as CHF and Thuis in de Stad: the convenience of a hotel with the freedom and flexibility of your own apartment.
Whatever the reason – a new job, an emergency or a sudden change of plans – temporary housing isn’t just for expats. Sometimes life itself creates the need for a home between homes. If that sounds like you, contact the booking team via email at bookings@corporatehousingfactory.com to find the right temporary home for your situation.

We could not provide the Dutch News service, and keep it free of charge, without the generous support of our readers. Your donations allow us to report on issues you tell us matter, and provide you with a summary of the most important Dutch news each day.

Ukrainian drone commander says his forces killed decorated Russian general
KYIV, Sept 16 - Ukrainian drone forces killed a Russian general in eastern Ukraine on Saturday, a little over two weeks after he received a Hero of Russia award for his wartime service, Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi said.
Major General Anton Grunis had won praise from President Vladimir Putin earlier this year after reporting how troops under his command helped Russia capture the Ukrainian stronghold of Kostiantynivka, a territorial claim disputed by Kyiv and independent military analysts.
Brovdi, who commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said one of his units had killed Grunis in a nighttime strike on his position in a Russian-held part of Ukraine's Donetsk region.
"General Grunis was eliminated on September 12," Brovdi wrote in a Telegram post on Wednesday, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Reuters could not independently verify Brovdi's assertions.
Russia's Defence Ministry does not routinely confirm battlefield deaths of senior personnel, but Russian commander Apti Alaudinov, in a post on the Telegram messaging app, said Grunis had died, without giving further details.
A solemn-faced Grunis received the Gold Star Hero of Russia award at a ceremony in late August, standing first in a line of officers in dress uniform.
On July 3, he had addressed Putin via video link at a televised security meeting and described in detail how troops of his 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade had participated in the claimed capture of Kostiantynivka.
Putin congratulated him and said: "Luck comes to those who do the work."
At the time, Ukraine denied that Russia had captured the city and said its forces retained control. The U.S.-based Institute for the Study of War said Russian forces had infiltrated but not fully seized the city and said Russia's claim was part of a wider information campaign to "portray the Ukrainian frontlines as collapsing."
Russia’s overall advances have slowed this year, but its forces have continued to press strategic cities such as Kostiantynivka. Moscow wants to control all of the broader Donbas region and has made that a central territorial demand in stalled negotiations with Kyiv. REUTERS

Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant Faces Falling Water Levels, Blackout Risk, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Falling water levels and repeated losses of external electricity are creating an increasingly difficult safety situation at the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency said.
None of the plant’s six reactors is generating electricity, and all remain in cold shutdown, the Military Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said in a statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
HUR said a work shift of about 1,150 employees, described as the minimum staffing level, was maintaining the facility’s safety systems.
The agency said the water level in the plant’s cooling pond had fallen from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 meters in early August and 12.55 meters by the end of the month. It said the level was continuing to decline, while at least 15 meters was required for the facility’s normal operation.
The plant lost external electricity three times in August, on Aug. 1, 4 and 8, because of problems with the Ferrosplavna-1 power line, according to the intelligence agency.
HUR said the facility had experienced between 23 and 25 external power outages since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Backup diesel generators were activated during the August outages. However, their operation placed additional pressure on fuel supplies in the occupied region, the agency said.
“In the event of a prolonged total blackout, the plant would require about 150 metric tons of diesel fuel per day,” HUR said.
Ukrainian Businesses Expect Hryvnia Revenue Growth, Brace for War Through 2027
Nuclear plants depend on a continuous electricity supply to operate cooling and other essential safety systems even when their reactors are shut down.
Backup generators are intended to provide temporary power only if external supplies are lost.
Russian forces also disconnected internet access at the plant on Aug. 13 and 14, disrupting communications, the monitoring of key indicators and international oversight, HUR said.
The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe’s largest nuclear power station, has been under Russian control since the early months of the full-scale invasion. The facility is located near the occupied city of Enerhodar in southeastern Ukraine.
HUR said residents of Enerhodar were experiencing repeated disruptions to electricity, water supplies and communications, as well as severe shortages of food and fuel.
The agency accused Russian forces of deliberately isolating the city’s information environment and mistreating civilians.
HUR also alleged that Moscow was seeking to incorporate the nuclear plant into Russia’s regulatory system by involving inspectors from Rostekhnadzor, the Russian agency responsible for technical and nuclear oversight.
It further accused Russia of using its representatives at the International Atomic Energy Agency to help legitimize the occupation. The intelligence agency cited a visit to the plant by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi on Sept. 4, shortly before the agency’s General Conference in Vienna.
HUR claimed that Mikhail Chudakov, a Russian deputy director general at the IAEA, had secured changes to the agency’s Power Reactor Information System that displayed occupied Crimea as part of Russia and rendered the names of Ukrainian nuclear plants in Russian.
The intelligence agency also said Russian forces continued to use the Zaporizhzhia plant as a military base and shelter for occupation troops.
Russia has controlled the plant since March 2022, but Ukraine and the international community continue to recognize it as Ukrainian territory.

The Power of Baikal (Power of Siberia 2) trunk gas pipeline project from Russia to China envisages supplying 50 bln cubic meters of gas via Mongolia. Following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to China in 2025, Russia and China signed a legally binding memorandum on the construction of Power of Siberia 2 and the Soyuz Vostok transit gas pipeline through Mongolia.

Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant supplying missiles Moscow uses to bomb Ukrainian cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:17:10 UTC
22:17:10 KST

Pro-Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH says it sabotaged the power supply to a Russian semiconductor plant in Voronezh that produces electronic components used in Russia’s missiles and air defense systems.
Targeting such suppliers can hit Russia’s ability to sustain its missile campaign: disrupting production of critical electronic components can slow the replenishment of weapons used to strike Ukrainian cities.
In a statement published on 16 September, ATESH said one of its agents infiltrated an electrical substation near the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Sborka (VZPP-S) and destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the facility. The movement said the agent escaped the city after the operation.
VZPP-S is a Russian producer of semiconductor devices, integrated circuits and power modules. Ukraine’s military intelligence lists the company as part of Russia’s defense-industrial supply chain and says it has produced electronic components for Kh-101 cruise missiles, Iskander-K missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
ATESH claimed the sabotage caused a major voltage surge and shut down production workshops. The movement said full power was not restored for several weeks, causing delays in deliveries of components for Russian weapons and, consequently, delays in missile and air defense production.
The movement’s claims have not been independently verified.
ATESH is a pro-Ukrainian partisan movement operating in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia. It says it recruits local residents and Russian military personnel to conduct sabotage, gather intelligence and pass information to Ukraine. The movement regularly publishes claims of attacks and acts of sabotage against Russian military and defense-industrial targets, though individual operations are often difficult to independently verify.
The plant has already been targeted
The reported sabotage comes after the VZPP-S facility was struck in a Ukrainian attack in June.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says VZPP-S produces components for the Kh-101, including transistor assemblies and matrices used in the missile’s electronic systems. It also says the company supplies semiconductor components for the onboard computer of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K system, as well as components for the Pantsir-S1’s television channel.
The company itself describes VZPP-S as a major Russian producer of electronic components, with more than 900 products in serial production.
ATESH said it delayed publication of its claim to protect its agent.

US-Houthi talks focus on Red Sea shipping and Bab el-Mandeb: Houthis pledge not to target US vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:16:23 UTC
22:16:23 KST

U.S. officials met earlier this week in Oman with representatives of Yemen’s Houthi rebels, just days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic strip along the Red Sea coast in an offensive that defeated forces loyal to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, Reuters reported Wednesday. According to the report, the Houthis told the United States during the meeting that they intended to refrain from attacking American vessels in the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which they have effectively taken control of.
According to Reuters, the meeting was not made public but was confirmed by three sources. It took place Sunday at the U.S. Embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, where the Houthis told American officials they remained committed to the ceasefire agreed with the United States in 2025 and therefore had no intention of attacking U.S. vessels. One source, a Yemeni official, also told Reuters that the militia’s representatives said they would not attack Israeli ships or any other commercial vessels, with the exception of those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis a “foreign terrorist organization” in March 2025, making any support for the group a criminal offense. Washington nevertheless continued negotiating with them afterward, and in May last year, after two months of U.S. strikes aimed at halting Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping lanes, the sides reached a ceasefire. The Houthis continued attacking ships near their coast but appeared to avoid striking American vessels.
Over the weekend, following the Houthis’ territorial gains near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which effectively gave them control of the waterway, questions mounted over whether the United States and other countries would mobilize to help Saudi Arabia drive the Houthis from the area. The concern was that, alongside the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could also be completely blocked, further disrupting global supplies of oil and goods.
But on Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump said the Houthis had “called” his administration and asked the United States to stay out of the war in Yemen. On Monday, Vice President JD Vance said Washington was in direct contact with the group, without elaborating. At the same time, it emerged that Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, had called Trump last week to request U.S. military assistance in light of the Houthis’ dramatic advances, but Washington made clear to Riyadh that it would not intervene directly in the conflict.
Houthis say they did not fire at Mecca, claim to have downed F-15
The current situation has left Saudi Arabia in a strategic bind. Even as the Houthis and other Iranian proxy groups fire into its territory and strike its oil facilities, Washington is not stepping in actively to assist, and neither are Riyadh’s new partners in the so-called “Mecca Alliance,” Turkey and Pakistan. The two countries signed the defense pact with Saudi Arabia only last month but have so far limited themselves to condemning the attacks on the kingdom.
Officials in Turkey and Pakistan said efforts to “institutionalize” the alliance must be completed before it can become operational, and that Riyadh had not, in any case, asked either country for help.
According to Wednesday’s Reuters report, one source who confirmed the meeting in Oman said the U.S. side was represented by embassy personnel and that one member of the Houthi delegation was Mohammed Abdulsalam, a senior official based in Muscat who is under U.S. sanctions. Those sanctions, it emerged, did not prevent the talks from taking place.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and have been fighting for more than a decade against a coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia. More than 100,000 people have been killed in the war, while Saudi Arabia has faced heavy international criticism over its bombing campaign. In recent years, the fighting subsided following the declaration of a ceasefire, but it resumed in July after the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in response to a Saudi blockade of Yemeni ports.
The current wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia has left the kingdom without a secure outlet for its crude oil, in part after pro-Iranian militias in Iraq struck one of its most important oil pipelines.
According to Saudi Arabia, the Houthis on Tuesday launched a drone toward Mecca for the first time in the current round of attacks. Mecca is Islam’s holiest city and home to the Kaaba, with millions of Muslims making the pilgrimage there each year. Riyadh said it intercepted the drone but declared Wednesday that firing toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers from the Yemeni border, amounted to “crossing a red line."
The Houthis, for their part, denied launching an unmanned aircraft toward Mecca. The last time they apparently attempted to attack the city was in 2017, when they fired a ballistic missile in its direction.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Wednesday morning that they had shot down an F-15 fighter jet belonging to the Saudi-led coalition over Marib province in central Yemen. They provided no evidence and did not say when the alleged shootdown took place.

Local sources told the Reuters news agency that the high death toll was due to a lack of safety procedures and rescue equipment.
Sudan Doctors Network, a Khartoum-based medical group, said search efforts were ongoing and the casualty figure could rise, adding that the site was missing basic safeguards for workers.
The group condemned the “negligence” it said put miners’ lives at serious risk.
West Kordofan is held by the paramilitary RSF, which has been fighting Sudan’s army since April 2023. Smuggled gold has been a key source of revenue for the group.
“Mining activities in areas under RSF control, in the absence of safety standards and adequate protection and rescue equipment, turn mining into a direct threat to the lives of civilians,” it said in a statement.
It called for the search to continue and for medical and logistical help to be provided, and urged those in control of the area to end unregulated mining.
Sudan ranks among Africa’s leading gold producers, and most of its yellow metal comes from dangerous, informal mining at disused or unofficial sites.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would work with Canada to become the EU's first "associate member" in her annual speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Wednesday.
"We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," von der Leyen said. "So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU."
She further stressed the need to maintain European independence in various sectors, including energy, raw materials and clean technologies.
To do that, EU countries will not only need to work together, but also have strong partners like Canada, whose Prime Minister, Mark Carney, is in Strasbourg and was warmly applauded by EU lawmakers as he arrived to listen to von der Leyen's speech.
Von der Leyen, now in her second five-year term at the helm of the EU executive arm, walked up to and embraced Carney after mentioning the "associate membership" issue for Canada, and Carney got a standing ovation from the chamber.
Through its partnership with Canada, she called for EU states to tackle climate change, competition from China and other major challenges.
The bloc was dealing with "an openly hostile world", von der Leyen said, setting out priorities for the 27-nation EU for the year ahead.
Von der Leyen: Solidarity among EU states necessary for facing challenges
She said solidarity among member states was the only possible solution. "Our path is clear. Building an independent Europe that has the power to act."
The 27-nation bloc faces war at its borders, with Russia's invasion of Ukraine. On trade and other issues, it also faces stiff rivalry from US President Donald Trump's United States and an increasingly assertive China.
The EU faces major headwinds at home as well, including the increasing popularity of a eurosceptic far-right, seen in regional elections in Germany that have weakened Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Opinion polls see Marine Le Pen as the strongest contender in next year's presidential vote in France.
"The state of our Union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our Union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been," von der Leyen said.
EU to use any means necessary to reduce 'unsustainable' China trade deficit
Turning to trade, von der Leyen said the EU will use every possible means to reduce its "unsustainable" trade deficit with China. She said that the imbalance, with a goods trade deficit of €1 billion ($1.15 billion) a day last year, had reached a tipping point.
"Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good. But deeds are better," she said.
Von der Leyen also said the bloc will need to stay its ambitious course on mitigating climate change but also step up efforts to adapt to it, drawing on experiences from the last three months when the continent was hit by unprecedented heat waves and wildfires.

Will militaries pivot on drone technologies after major Reaper losses in Iran? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:14 UTC
22:13:14 KST

The US lost around 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones in the conflict with Iran. This is according to a new Lead Inspector General Report to the United States Congress. Operation Epic Fury, which covers the fighting from April to June 2026. Since June, more Reaper drones have been lost in the conflict.
These types of drones, the Reaper and the Predator, are legacy US drone platforms. However, they have been lost in larger numbers as they have been pressed into service in places like Yemen and now Iran.
The losses may point to these types of larger drones becoming obsolete. The drones are vulnerable to air defenses. The reason they are so vulnerable is due to their history. They are a legacy of the US global hegemony after the Cold War. The drones are a symbol of American power. Now they could also be seen as a symbol of the changing world order.
The MQ-1 Predator and MQ-9 Reaper helped transform US unmanned aircraft from reconnaissance platforms into strike systems. What that means is that the Predator was first rolled out to do slow intelligence and reconnaissance missions, monitoring areas.
This was considered a dull and dangerous job. Losing reconnaissance planes and pilots has historically been a problem. For instance, Francis Gary Powers was an American pilot whose U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
Hellfire missiles: An early breakthrough in drone warfare
The Predator was an answer to this problem. No need to send pilots. Send drones. America’s General Atomics developed the Predator during the 1990s. The prototype first flew in 1994, and the RQ-1 entered operational use as an intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance aircraft, including deployments over the Balkans.
Then it became clear that the drone can and should be armed. A breakthrough came when the US began experimenting with arming it with the AGM-114 Hellfire missile. The first airborne Hellfire launch from a Predator occurred in 2001.
By October 7, 2001, armed Predators were flying combat missions over Afghanistan. This was too late to take out Bin Laden. However, the drone became a symbol of the war on terror.
The terrorist groups being hunted by US drones in Afghanistan, Iraq, Somalia, and Pakistan did not have air defenses. However, much has changed since then.
The MQ-9 Reaper first flew in February 2001. Reaper entered operational service in 2007. Compared with the Predator, it offered substantially greater speed, payload, and weapons capacity, including Hellfires and bombs. The Reaper was a natural evolution of the Predator.
The challenge in Iran, Yemen, and other places is that the Reapers are being lost at a higher rate than they will be replaced. It’s not clear if they will actually be replaced as the US transitions to other drones. The war in Ukraine and also in Iran has shown the need for large numbers of other drones.
The US knows it not only needs a Reaper replacement, but also needs tens of thousands of other smaller drones. Back in May, Aviation Week noted that the US Air Force had approved requirements for an MQ-9 Reaper replacement. It was supposed to be attritable, meaning it can be lost in larger numbers. Mass production and open architecture with a 1,500 km. range and 20-hour endurance.
Tyler Rogoway at TWZ noted that the requirement was for a drone “cheap enough to risk losing. “The Air Force’s MQ-9 Reaper successor will trade survivability for lower cost, broader missions, and mass production.”
New drones in development for replacement, supplementation
Armed Forces Press recently noted Swarm Aero had unveiled Gamera, a potential replacement. “After the US lost dozens of its MQ-9 Reaper drones to fighting in Iran, newcomer drone-maker Swarm Aero announced Monday that it had developed a drone in the same medium altitude, long-endurance (MALE) class, capable of executing swarm missions and cheap enough to afford losing, even in large numbers.”
It is said to have “a wingspan of about 72 feet, a payload capacity of 2,800 pounds, a ‘Pacific-spanning’ range of 9,000 miles and a combat radius of 2,300 miles with ‘hours’ of on-station time once at its patrol area.
Kitted-out Reapers, which reportedly cost $30-50 million apiece, have a payload capacity of up to 3,800 pounds.” In addition, another report at Aviation International News noted that General Atomics “has unveiled its Wildfire uncrewed air system” as a potential replacement.
The point is that the replacements are coming. In addition, many other drones are being used. The US is worried about munition shortfalls due to the Iran war. However, the lesson will be that the US needs new and cheaper munitions and drones. Rather than try to replace what was lost, the war will lead to major changes, much as World War II and other conflicts have.
The US military is already investing in lower-cost drones and missiles that can be produced and employed in large numbers, reflecting lessons from Ukraine and the 2026 conflict with Iran. One example is the Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS), a one-way attack drone similar to Iran’s Shahed 136.
Cheaper missiles are also a good move to get around the losses of the Reapers. Anduril’s Barracuda-500M is designed as an affordable, mass-producible cruise missile. Another entrant is Covenant’s Anthem, a long-range cruise missile carrying a payload exceeding 200 kg.
The future is clear. Cheaper and mass-produced drones and missiles. The era of the Reaper and Predator as a symbol of American warfare may be ending. Many other countries that use large drones, including Israel, will be learning from this.

Swiss passenger rail traffic reaches record high in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

Swiss passenger rail traffic reaches record high in 2025
In 2025, rail transport volume totalled 23.7 billion passenger-kilometres, according to figures published on Wednesday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO).
In a direct year-on-year comparison, rail demand rose by 3.2% compared to 2024 (22.9 billion passenger-kilometres), representing an increase of 737 million passenger-kilometres in one year. A passenger-kilometre corresponds to the transport of one person over a distance of one kilometre.
This growth is part of an ongoing trend: 2024 had already seen a 3.1% increase over 2023. Over a ten-year period, rail passenger numbers have shown a clear upward trend despite the impact of the pandemic.
Between 2015 and 2025, rail transport volume rose by 16.3%, from 20.4 billion to 23 billion passenger-kilometres. After plummeting to 13.3 billion in 2020 at the height of the health restrictions, rail travel recovered and surpassed its pre-crisis level as early as 2023.
Road transport dominates
Compared with other modes of transport, the rail network remains second behind road transport. According to 2024 data, private motorised transport (mainly passenger cars) accounted for 70.6% of the overall transport market, with 94.6 billion passenger-kilometres.
More
We travelled from Switzerland to Denmark by train – the journey took 24 hours
Railways account for 17.2% of the total volume of travel, ahead of non-motorised transport (5.9% with 7.8 billion) and public road transport such as buses and trams (3.5% with 47 billion). In total, public transport as a whole (rail, road, cable cars and waterways) accounts for 21.1% of passenger travel in the country.
Within this collective transport system, conventional rail accounts for more than 81% of passenger-kilometres travelled, confirming its position as the backbone of public transport in Switzerland.

Kosovo’s former president jailed for 25 years over war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:09:41 UTC
22:09:41 KST

Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders, committed during his time as a senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army during the country’s war for independence from Serbia in the late 1990s.
The European-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers, convicted Thaci, 58, and three other former senior commanders of 96 murders, and counts of torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention directed at political opponents and civilians.
The convictions come at the end of a years-long process, strongly opposed by many in Kosovo, to bring accountability for crimes committed by KLA commanders during the 1998-99 war in which war crimes were committed by both sides.
Thaçi, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face charges, stood in silence in The Hague as the presiding judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.
The former president, who served as the head of political directorate of the KLA’s general staff, faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity alongside the three other former leaders of the KLA who are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
In addition to the murders, Thaçi was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.
Once a hardliner, Thaçi shifted towards a more moderate political identity after being courted by western diplomats who suggested he could be a central figure in Kosovo’s post-war settlement.
At the heart of the prosecution’s case was the degree to which the convicted men had senior operational command over the KLA as a centrally-led armed force and whether the crimes amounted to a pattern of abuse.
The court ruled that Thaçi had “actively participated in and encouraged crimes”. Smith said: “The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious”.
He added: “The so-called intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated.”
Smith said Thaçi “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage crimes but insisted the trial was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army” or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia. Thaçi could appeal the verdict.
Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaçi and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi who had all denied the charges against them.
Krasniqi received 25 years in prison, Selimi 13 years and Veseli 18 years. Thaçi also faces separate charges of intimidating witnesses with judgement in the case still to come. He has plead not guilty.
The three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity and said prosecutors had failed to show these happened as part of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population as a whole.
Known by the nom de guerre of Commander Snake during the war, Thaçi stood out among the KLA leadership as an intelligent and articulate figure who would later charm diplomats – most notably the US secretary of state Madeleine Albright – at the negotiations in Rambouillet that ended the conflict.
But behind the self-assured image he projected as a senior political figure, he was long dogged by allegations of a darker and more ruthless side from his time as a wartime commander.
Thaçi’s defence partly rested on the notion that while serious abuses did occur, the KLA was a not a strictly centralised organisation, claiming that Thaçi’s senior position in the rebel group did not indicate culpability for crimes committed by local units.
“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaçi told judges in February.
The trial was opposed by many in Kosovo. Outside the court, Kosovo foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, told the media: “A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision,.”
Thaçi’s PDK party called the verdict “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army”.
In Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence. Some started shouting “UCK,” the Albanian-language acronym for the KLA.
Thaçi, who was born in Kosovo’s rugged Drenica mountains – the KLA heartland – was a philosophy student who rose through the KLA’s ranks, returning from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence.
Thaçi served in a series of senior political roles after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the The Hague. After the war, Thaçi became a central political figure and was instrumental in Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of Nato airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
