AID Coalition operates a program called Fly & Vote, a program that helps Israeli expats determine whether they are eligible to vote and helps secure seats on flights to Israel.
The petition was also filed against the Democrats party. Likud claims there is evidence linking the Democrats' goal of "undermining public support for Likud" with the other organizations' activities.
An estimated 1 million Israelis live outside Israel, and under Israeli law, citizens cannot vote overseas. Likud, the ruling party led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, threatened to pursue legal action against AID Coalition in May, and Transportation Ministry officials have discussed ways to limit flights to Israel ahead of the election.
According to Likud's petition, filed by attorney Ilan Bombach, the Fly & Vote initiative is intended to help Israelis abroad for political purposes and AID Coalition is affiliated with the fringes of Israel's left-wing camp, a claim the organization denies.
The petition argues that even if participants pay for their own flights, they receive other benefits through what Likud says are prohibited means, including group purchasing power, exclusive or early access to flights, coordination services, accommodation and transportation and assistance with documents.
Likud said it was not seeking to prevent Israelis from voting or to discourage citizens from participating in the election, but rather "to distinguish between general civic activity and organized, funded and targeted election activity."
The party accused the initiative of exerting "unfair influence on participation in the election" and warned that it could "seriously undermine the integrity of the election and the equality and fairness of the electoral process."
AID Coalition said in response that Likud was seeking to prevent Israelis from voting.
"We have received Likud's petition, which seeks to deny those who boarded planes to fight on October 7, who pay taxes and remain involved in the life of their homeland, the right and obligation to take part in determining the future of the State of Israel," the organization said. "We will study the petition and respond accordingly."
Earlier this month, responding to a warning letter Likud sent ahead of the petition, AID Coalition said it operates "completely independently of any party framework" and provides bureaucratic assistance to Israelis seeking to return to the country, rather than financial assistance.
Attorney Omri Segev, who signed the organization's response, also said the project is open to every Israeli citizen abroad, including those intending to vote for Likud.

The organization has also contacted travel agencies in Israel and abroad.
Organizers say more than 30,000 Israelis have registered with the initiative to check their eligibility to vote, while several thousand have already paid a $75 commitment fee.
Dagon said that even Israelis who have lived abroad for many years and ended their Israeli tax residency can remain on the voter rolls. "The process of removing people from the voter registry barely exists," she said.

Four years after Mahsa Amini's death, rights groups warn Tehran's crackdown persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:47:25 UTC
21:47:25 KST

Human rights groups said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus, as Kurdish businesses shuttered across her home region and the UN Special Rapporteur said four years of state violence had failed to extinguish the resistance.
Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody, Kurdish businesses across her home region staged a general strike on Wednesday while international human rights organisations warned that those responsible for crushing the 2022 protests remain in power and continue to use the same methods.
Shopkeepers and businesses in Saqqez, Sanandaj, Mahabad, Marivan, Baneh and Bokan shut their doors following a call by Kurdish political coalitions. Video circulating on social media showed empty bazaars across the region.
Amnesty International, in a report marking the fourth anniversary, said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) said on X that the Parliament would continue to support young Iranians facing execution or imprisonment, singling out the case of twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, sentenced by Tehran's Revolutionary Court after recent protests.
The European Parliament "will keep their light shining until it breaks through the darkness.", Metsola wrote on X.
UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran Mai Sato said that four years of brutal state violence — including lethal force deployed during nationwide protests in late 2025 and early 2026 — have failed to extinguish the resistance.
"Four years on, the resistance Jina’s death gave rise to has not been extinguished," Sato said in a statement on X.
"The women and girls who took to the streets in her name still insist on the right to decide what they wear, where they work and how they live... Those rights will not stay deniable forever."
Sato also noted that despite the Law on Protecting the Family through the Promotion of the Culture of Chastity and Hijab being formally suspended since December 2024, cafes, restaurants and shops have continued to be closed for hijab violations, with arrests reported in some cases.
What happened to Mahsa Amini?
Amini, 22, was detained by Tehran's morality police on 13 September 2022 over compulsory hijab rules and died three days later after being brutally beaten in custody.
The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded she had been subjected to physical violence in custody and that Iranian authorities were responsible for her death. Iranian officials rejected the findings and denied she had been physically assaulted.
Protests spread nationwide in the days after her death. While compulsory hijab and women's rights were central, the movement drew together demands for political freedoms, minority rights, economic justice and changes to the political system.
The UN fact-finding mission documented up to 551 deaths across 26 provinces, including at least 49 women and 68 children, and said some violations — including killings, torture, rape and sexual violence — reached the threshold of crimes against humanity.
Tehran acknowledged detaining more than 22,000 people, according to Amnesty International, which also documented enforced disappearances, unfair trials and death sentences.
Tehran pivots to hi-tech
Compulsory hijab remains law, the political structure is intact, and many participants in the protests are in prison, in exile or under sentence.
The regime has shifted enforcement away from morality-police patrols toward cameras, facial recognition, drones and digital tools. Iran's police announced in 2023 that public cameras would be used to identify women not wearing hijab.
The UN fact-finding mission's 2025 report cited facial recognition being used to monitor students' dress at the entrance to Amirkabir University in Tehran.
A 2025 study published in the journal Iranian Studies at the University of Cambridge described the movement as producing a "cultural revolution" alongside a political one, arguing it weakened the state's ideological hold over public and cultural life.
For instance, images of morality police vans detaining women on the streets were among the most potent symbols of the 2022 protests, prompting Tehran to avoid public confrontation methods.
The growing presence of women without headscarves in public spaces and the central place women's rights and freedoms take in political debate show that the situation has not reverted to where it stood before September 2022 — a direct result of the movement's actions.

Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded the commander of the Russian corvette "Soobrazitelny," whose crew fired two signal flares toward a Danish Air Force helicopter on September 14 in international waters near Gedser. This was reported by Russia's Defense Ministry, UNN writes.
Details

French former minister on trial over alleged Renault-Nissan lobbying
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:38:15 BST
21:38:15 KST

French former minister on trial over alleged Renault-Nissan lobbying
- Published
French former minister Rachida Dati has gone on trial in Paris for corruption, accused of taking money from Renault-Nissan in return for political influence.
Dati, 61, who was justice minister under former President Nicolas Sarkozy and culture minister under Emmanuel Macron, is known to have been paid €900,000 (£770,000) by the car giant between 2009 and 2013.
According to a contract signed in 2009, shortly after she ceased being a minister under Sarkozy and was elected as a member of the European Parliament, the payment was for legal services performed for the company.
But magistrates argue the contract was used to disguise payments for lobbying work. Dati denies the allegations.
Magistrates believe Renault-Nissan's former CEO Carlos Ghosn recruited Dati to lobby on the company's behalf in the European Parliament, and to facilitate contacts with Sarkozy who was head of state until 2012.
Ghosn, 72, is also standing trial and denies any wrongdoing. He will be absent from court, having been a fugitive in Lebanon since 2019.
Dati's lawyers will contest the charges, which if substantiated carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in jail, a large fine, and a five-year ban on holding public office.
This could mean her being forced to surrender the mayorship of the wealthy 7th district of Paris, which she has held since 2008.
Dati returned to national politics in 2024 as culture minister but resigned in February to launch a bid to be mayor of the city of Paris.
She was beaten by the Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire after a campaign in which her forthcoming trial was used as an argument against her.
Anti-corruption groups acting as civil plaintiffs in the trial say stricter legal limits need to be established on political lobbying in France.
"The affair illustrates the risks of public decision-making being captured by private interests," said Patrick Lefas of Transparency International France.

Most surveyed bankers expect NBU to raise key rate to 16%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:38:09 EEST
21:38:09 KST

Most bankers surveyed by Interfax-Ukraine expect the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) to raise its key policy rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 16% per annum, following its September 17 meeting.
"We expect the National Bank of Ukraine to raise its key policy rate by 50 basis points on September 17, to 16.0%. The main reason for this decision is accelerating inflation and intensifying inflationary risks," said Serhiy Kolodiy, chief macroeconomic analysis expert at Raiffeisen Bank's analytical research department.
Inflation accelerated to 8.1% year-on-year in August, from 7.7% in July and 7.2% in June, coming in somewhat above the central bank's forecast. Intensifying Russian strikes on energy infrastructure are creating additional pressure on the supply of goods, widening the currency deficit, and raising inflation expectations among the public and businesses, while supply chain disruptions caused by the attacks are an additional inflationary factor.
Raising the rate would also help preserve the appeal of hryvnia savings and ease pressure on the currency market amid active budget spending and a significant inflow of external financing, according to Kolodiy.
Inna Provotar, head of management accounting and business analysis at OTP Bank, also considers a rate increase to 16% possible.
"Such a step would be justified given the current inflationary pressure and the need to curb further price growth and stabilize inflation expectations. At the same time, in our view, this would be more of a preventive tightening of monetary policy aimed at strengthening macro-financial stability, rather than the start of a prolonged rate-hike cycle," she said.
A-Bank deputy board chairman and risk management head Oleh Trybulkin also expects a 0.5 percentage point rate increase, citing incomplete transmission of the previous rate hike into hryvnia deposit yields, which rose less than the key rate itself.
"An additional argument in favor of a hike is the NBU's own outlook: in its July macro forecast, the regulator projected the key rate rising to 16% in the fourth quarter of 2026 and holding at that level in the first quarter of 2027. Not enough has changed since the last meeting to significantly alter that trajectory," Trybulkin explained.
Trybulkin cited inflation dynamics, deteriorating logistics due to the deliberate destruction of warehouses, the state of the power system, and the situation in the Middle East, given its impact on oil prices, as key factors for the central bank's upcoming decisions.
Despite the arguments in favor of a rate hike, Globus Bank board chairman Serhiy Mamedov currently expects the rate to be held at 15.5%.
Monthly inflation could reach about 1-1.5% in September and 1.5-1.7% in October, according to his estimate, with possible acceleration driven by the effects of Russian attacks, additional business costs for logistics and energy supply, rising fuel and transport costs, seasonal price growth, and the general pressure of the wartime economy on production costs.
"That's why, for now, we're leaning toward the more conservative scenario: the National Bank could hold the key rate at 15.5% in September. This would give the regulator a chance to assess how severe the fall acceleration in inflation turns out to be, what the consequences of the recent attacks will be, and whether the situation will require additional monetary response at upcoming meetings," Mamedov said.
A 0.5 percentage point rate hike could be a preemptive step to curb inflationary pressure and currency demand, in his view, though excessive monetary tightening could constrain lending activity. A possible adjustment to the yield on the NBU's three-month deposit certificates, whose maximum rate currently stands at 19%, will also matter for the deposit market.
Radabank capital markets department director Serhiy Hnezdilov also sees two scenarios — holding the rate at 15.5% or raising it to 16% — but considers the latter more likely.
"The case for a hike has better odds, because inflationary pressure from rising fuel costs has already been present since spring, and now factors like destroyed warehouses, reconfigured logistics, and various risks are adding to that. So we're leaning toward the 16.0% scenario," he said.
The National Bank cut its key policy rate from 15.5% to 15% per annum in late January 2026 and held it there for three consecutive meetings, before raising it to 15.5% per annum on July 30, as previously reported.

Israel's far right seeks to ban Palestinian candidates, parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16

Breadcrumb
Israel's right wing seeks to ban Palestinian parties, candidates from Knesset elections
Israel's far right is seeking to prevent Arab political parties and candidates from standing in next month's Knesset elections, reviving a long-running battle over the political participation of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Disqualification motions have been filed against Ra'am, the Joint List and Balad, as well as individual candidates including MK Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.
The challenges come ahead of Israel's 27 October election and will be heard by the Central Elections Committee later this month.
The official election records show that motions were filed against Ra'am by Likud, Otzma Yehudit and the Choosing Life–Forum of Bereaved Families group.
Likud has also targeted the Joint List and Cassif, while Otzma Yehudit has filed motions against Abu Shehadeh and Balad has been targeted by Orot HaShachar.
The latest moves have once again raised questions over the limits of political participation in a state that defines itself as both Jewish and "democratic".
Under Israel's election law, parties and candidates can be barred from standing if their positions or actions are considered to reject Israel's status as a Jewish and democratic state, promote racism or support armed action against Israel.
Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, says that these grounds are broad enough to have been used against Palestinian political positions in previous elections.
In several prominent cases, the Central Elections Committee approved bans that were later overturned by the Supreme Court. In 2003, for example, the court overturned the disqualification of Balad and MK Azmi Bishara.
In 2022, the Central Elections Committee again voted to disqualify Balad, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the decision and allowed the party to run.
Adalah, which has represented Arab parties and candidates in disqualification proceedings for more than two decades, says the repeated attempts to exclude them expose a fundamental contradiction in Israel's claims to democratic political participation.
The organisation is representing the Joint List, Ra'am, Balad, Cassif and Abu Shehadeh in the current proceedings.
In a statement shared with The New Arab, Adalah warned that "Once again, Israel’s right wing is using the disqualification process to attempt to silence and delegitimise the political representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel".
"In more than two decades representing Palestinian political parties and individual candidates, Adalah has seen such accusations proven baseless and rejected by the Supreme Court time and again, and these attempts are equally baseless," it said.
"However, given the crackdown on the rights to freedom of expression, assembly and association of Palestinian citizens of Israel particularly since October 2023, the current conservative orientation of the Israeli Supreme Court, and rampant public incitement against Palestinians, Adalah has grave concerns about the current round of disqualification motions and their potential outcomes."
The Central Elections Committee is expected to hold hearings on the motions on 23 and 24 September.
The committee's decisions can be appealed to Israel's Supreme Court, with the deadline for appeals set for 29 September and the court expected to rule by 4 October.

US House Advances Major Russia Sanctions Bill Targetting Oil Fleet and Child Abductions
The US House advanced a Russia sanctions bill on September 15, clearing a procedural rule vote that teed up final consideration of the measure rather than deciding its passage.
This was reported by The Hill on September 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The rule cleared 214-211 after two Democrats, Representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, broke precedent to advance it. It marked their second such break in two weeks, following an identical crossover on a rule vote earlier this month, the outlet noted. Rule votes are typically treated as a test of party loyalty, which made the Democratic support unusual.
The tally opened the way for debate and a final vote on the legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. Passing the rule did not enact the bill; it only advanced it toward final consideration on the House floor.
The rule vote handed a victory to the bill's backers, including Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who overcame resistance from within his own party and from Democrats. Ahead of the vote, the opposition had left some predicting the measure was "dead again" after nearly a year and a half of negotiations, according to The Hill
.
At a House Rules Committee hearing on Monday, McCaul framed the vote as a message to the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, over US support for Ukraine. He also cast it as a warning to Chinese leader Xi Jinping against aggression toward Taiwan.
"This is a moral issue that requires moral courage," McCaul declared. "When we look back on this moment, I want us to be able to say that we did everything possible to end this war."
The legislation would grant President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy and would extend existing sanctions on Iran, The Hill reported.
According to Eugene Goncharov, policy director of the American Coalition for Ukraine, the measure also expands sanctions on Russian military figures and foreign suppliers. It bans new US investment in Russia, targets Moscow's shadow fleet of oil tankers, and tightens export restrictions. The bill further carries sanctions authority against those responsible for the abduction of Ukrainian children, he added.
The vote took place during the "Ukraine Action Summit," a weeklong lobbying push that drew more than 600 constituents from 50 states and Puerto Rico, the outlet reported. "The Sanctioning Russia Act is the number one priority for Ukraine advocacy right now," Goncharov stated.
Democratic opponents, while supportive of Ukraine, argued that the bill hands Trump tariff powers the Supreme Court has already curtailed, according to The Hill. Representatives Don Beyer of Virginia, Gregory Meeks of New York, and Richard Neal of Massachusetts warned in a joint statement that the measure would do "more harm than good."
"This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable," they wrote.
Not all critics of the tariff powers wanted the bill defeated. Michael McFaul, a former US ambassador to Russia, argued on the social platform X that its passage carried more weight as a signal than the risks of failure. "If it fails, Putin will cheer & Ukrainians will be disappointed," he wrote.
A final House vote remained pending after the rule cleared. Goncharov predicted the measure would ultimately reach Trump's desk for signature. "This is the bill that is likely to pass and be signed into law, and when that happens, it will make this war harder and more expensive for Russia to keep fighting," he explained.
The rule vote marked the latest milestone in a months-long endeavor to advance the sanctions package through Congress. In late July, the Senate cleared its own procedural hurdle in an 86-12 vote, opening debate on the bill and setting up a final vote, weeks after Graham's death.
The legislation, which he drafted, would authorize tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil and gas, and it advanced as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Capitol Hill.

Venezuela’s People Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:37:02 UTC
21:37:02 KST

Venezuela’s People Problem
A state that spent decades alienating its professional class has lost the capacity to govern.
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
Days after two deadly earthquakes struck northern Venezuela on June 24, killing at least 6,000 people and injuring tens of thousands more, the Venezuelan Seismological Research Foundation, known as Funvisis, made an unusual public plea: Could whoever had taken one of its GPS sensors please give it back?
For 13 years, the high-precision instrument had been bolted to a rocky outcrop in the hills of western Venezuela, quietly tracking the millimeter-scale movements of the Boconó fault, which was the likely source of the first of the two quakes. When Funvisis technicians went to recover the readings the sensor had stored, they found that the machine had gone missing. More than two months after the earthquakes, the organization still does not know who carried it off.
The absent sensor is but one gauge of a state that has lost the capacity to govern. Venezuela once operated 250 to 300 seismic-monitoring stations; today, no more than five still function. Many of the engineers, physicians, nurses, firefighters, and rescue workers a country depends on when disaster strikes have long since left Venezuela—part of a generation-long exodus of skilled professionals from state institutions.
President Trump has said that the oil-rich country will be run “properly” and “professionally,” but the earthquakes exposed Venezuela’s deficits. The highest expectations and fondest hopes—whether of Wall Street, Houston, or Caracas—will not conjure up the people needed to rebuild a country that has thoroughly hollowed out its professional classes.
In just 20 years, Venezuela went from Latin America’s wealthiest nation to one of its poorest thanks to the mismanagement, corruption, and poor governance that began under the populist president Hugo Chávez, who served from 1999 to 2013, and continued under his successor, Nicolás Maduro. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez, who took over Venezuela after the United States captured Maduro in January, inherited a state that cannot marshall the technical expertise to rebuild what the quakes destroyed or to reconstruct an economy that collapsed long before the ground did.
Rebuilding is a matter not merely of money and political will but of human capital. Bureaucrats, planners, regulators, and inspectors turn plans into functioning grids, ports, and clinics. Their absence may be the biggest obstacle facing American policy makers overseeing Venezuela’s reconstruction.
Venezuela is not the first country to suffer brain drain to the point of institutional collapse. Afghanistan has reportedly struggled to stand up its health-care sector and civil service ever since many of its professionals fled the return of the Taliban in 2021. Haiti has been losing doctors, judges, and engineers for decades. But Venezuela’s case is one of particularly deliberate self-destruction, in a country where oil wealth helped produce a sizable middle class.
Hostility toward the professional class was a hallmark of Chávez’s particular brand of socialism from the beginning. Adherents saw professional skills, when they were not explicitly placed in service of the revolution, as advancing the interests of capitalism and imperialism, the Venezuelan political scientist Guillermo T. Aveledo told me. In 2003, Guillermo García Ponce, a director at a pro-Chávez newspaper, went so far as to describe technocrats at state-owned companies as a “fifth column” to be “wiped out.”
“For Chavismo, privilege always comes cloaked in a PowerPoint presentation,” the journalist Francisco Toro wrote in 2007. By dismissing expertise and deliberation as ideologically suspect, Toro added, “Chavismo is left to rely on the will of the leader alone.”
The state’s public utilities were among the first institutions to confront the PowerPoint problem. Chávez replaced their professional managers with loyalists who were more compliant than competent, people who used to work in these companies told me. Jacqueline Faría, a Chavista engineer who took over the state-owned Caracas water company Hidrocapital in 1999, invested millions of dollars in a failed program to clean the Guaire River. Now she leads Rodríguez’s reconstruction efforts.
In addition to Hidrocapital, the Chávez government proceeded to dismantle the corporate-style leadership of the Caracas metro and Venezuela’s largest electricity company, Edelca, and to place these companies under the control of military officers. It eventually did the same with Funvisis. In 2009, Chávez took direct control of the country’s airports and seaports.
Water and power shortages, sometimes nationwide, became commonplace as mismanagement, corruption, and doctrinaire regulations gummed the works of nearly all of Venezuela’s public infrastructure. Consider Edelca’s two dam projects. The company began building the Caruachi dam in 1997, under Chávez’s predecessor, but finished it only after nine long years. It began building the Tocoma dam in 2007 and still has not finished it, despite almost $10 billion in investment. A Brazilian contractor involved in the work later admitted to paying Venezuelan officials and middlemen as much as $98 million in bribes from 2005 to 2016 to secure contracts. A U.S.-Argentine company will now take over the project.
Perhaps no sector was more gravely affected by Chávez’s assault on professionalism than the oil industry. And no industry is more crucial to U.S. plans for Venezuela’s recovery—or more central to Washington’s interest in the country in the first place.
Before Chávez, Venezuela’s oil company, known by its Spanish acronym PDVSA, was owned by the state but autonomously governed as a commercial entity. It set the gold standard for such an arrangement, expanding into international markets and fully acquiring Citgo, a major Houston-based refinery, in 1991. Much of the Venezuelan state ran on clientelism, but the oil company was meritocratic. Its research arm, the Venezuelan Institute of Oil Technology, or INTEVEP, employed about 170 full-time Ph.D. researchers and held roughly 1,200 American patents in the period before 2003, according to Francisco Monaldi, an energy expert.
That was the year Chávez began meddling in PDVSA’s affairs. He fired its board on live television and appointed a military officer to run the company. PDVSA’s workers went on strike in protest. Chávez fired more than 18,000 of them—dismissing, in one stroke, 60 to 80 percent of all provisioning, planning, maintenance, and exploration staff.
The finance team was laid off almost entirely; state cronies took over an office that accounted for nearly all of Venezuela’s foreign-exchange earnings. INTEVEP’s scientists were replaced, Pánfilo Masciangioli, a researcher and manager at the institute from 1982 to 2010, told me, “with people who did not even know how important it was to publish a paper.” The institute’s patents fell to about 100 during the decade that followed.
“The company’s gray matter was lost,” Monaldi told me. In its place came party loyalists and military men, who filled PDVSA’s vacancies and directed its revenues into Chávez’s populist schemes. Former employees scattered abroad. The number of Venezuelans in Alberta—the epicenter of Canada’s oil industry—rose from 465 in 2001 to 3,860 in 2011, and in Colombia, former PDVSA oil experts helped nearly double national oil production by 2011. Meanwhile, across the border, clientelism swelled PDVSA’s payroll from 28,841 in 2003 to 177,770 in 2014.
The effect fully manifested a decade later: Global oil prices fell, and Venezuela’s ruined oil industry collapsed, its output falling from about 3 million barrels a day before Chavez’s PDVSA purge to an average of 512,000 a day in 2020.
Employees of Venezuela’s state institutions came under continual pressure. In 2004, more than 2 million Venezuelans signed a referendum to recall Chávez. A lawmaker close to the president drew up what would become known as the “Tascón List” to identify and fire the petitioners from state institutions and companies. Hundreds lost their jobs. At the National Library, “a clique decided who was leaving and who was staying,” Mario Di Giacomo, an information specialist there for nearly 20 years, told me. “Dissent was not acceptable.” Loyalists replaced the professionals, and the library’s collections descended into neglect. Millions of archival records are decaying, Di Giacomo said.
The Tascón List was but one way of identifying people for firing. At the Venezuelan Institute for Scientific Investigation, the country’s premier scientific-research center, the physicist Claudio Mendoza made a public comment mocking Venezuela’s nuclear ambitions in 2006 (he noted that the country would achieve little so long as it rejected scientific expertise). He was dismissed four days later. The Chavista zoologist Ángel Viloria took over the institute and systematically purged its scientists from 2006 to 2011.
“You were either fired or forced to retire,” Mendoza told me. Venezuela slid from Latin America’s fifth-largest producer of scientific papers in the early 2000s to its 11th by 2022. By 2016, researchers who had emigrated accounted for roughly 33 percent of the country’s scientific publications; at least 68 percent of these scholars held doctoral degrees.
Trump has promised that American investors will spend $100 billion to rebuild Venezuela’s “rotting” energy infrastructure, but he hasn’t said who will do the work. The simple truth is that Venezuela has rid itself of the technocrats who could deliver the recovery Washington has promised. Few will return to the bureaucracy that ejected them. Some have emigrated for good; among those who remain, many distrust the authoritarian government or do not wish to be associated with it.
The United States is currently overseeing talks between the Rodríguez government and the democratic opposition about the country’s recovery and reconciliation. It could use that platform to push for basing appointments to public institutions on relevant expertise rather than political loyalty and, in doing so, help restore confidence among the country’s professionals.
Among the hollowed-out agencies that should be high on the list for rebuilding is Funvisis—not only for reasons of public safety but also because the geophysical data that Venezuela no longer collects are the raw material of modern oil exploration. Companies use seismic surveys to image a reservoir before they spend a dollar drilling into it, and Venezuela’s archives are dated, its instruments are scarce, and the geophysicists who once operated both are now working in Calgary or Houston or Bogotá. A state that cannot say whether the fault lines beneath it are moving is poorly placed to tell an investor what lies within the Orinoco Basin.
Washington can disburse the oil money and lift the sanctions; it cannot staff the ministries. Only Venezuelans can do that. Ultimately, the country’s recovery will be measured less in barrels lifted or dollars banked than in how many of those professionals will go back to work for the state.

Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:33:18 UTC
21:33:18 KST

Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.
- Share:
Scientists have reconstructed short videos using only brain activity recorded from mice, effectively allowing researchers to recreate what the animals were seeing. The study, led by researchers at University College London (UCL), offers a new way to investigate how the brain transforms visual input into an internal representation of the world.
Published in eLife, the findings could help scientists better understand how visual information is processed in the brain and may eventually make it possible to compare how different species perceive the same surroundings.
Decoding What the Brain Sees
Researchers have spent years trying to understand how the brain interprets signals arriving from the eyes. In human studies, scientists have shown people images and movies while recording brain activity with fMRI, then used those measurements to try to reconstruct visual information down to the level of individual pixels.
The new work takes a different approach. Instead of relying on broader brain imaging signals, the researchers used recordings from individual brain cells in mice. These single-cell measurements can provide a more detailed picture of how visual information is represented in the brain.
Using activity recorded from the visual cortex, the team was able to generate high-quality reconstructions of videos that had been shown to the mice.
Lead author Dr. Joel Bauer (Sainsbury Wellcome Centre at UCL) said: "We wanted to have a better way of investigating how the brain interprets what we see. The current methods of understanding what specific groups of neurons are representing are not very generalizable to situations which haven't been specifically tested for. And so, we wanted to develop a method that can capture what is being represented in the brain and compare that to reality."
The researchers are especially interested in the differences between what is physically present in front of an animal and how that information is represented inside the brain. Studying those differences could reveal which visual features the brain emphasizes, changes, or filters out.
Turning Neuron Activity Into Video
To reconstruct the movies, Dr. Bauer and his colleagues used a dynamic neural encoding model originally developed by another research team for the 2023 Sensorium Competition. The model is designed to predict how individual neurons (brain cells) will respond while mice watch movies. It also takes into account other factors, including the animals' movements and changes in pupil diameter.
The UCL researchers then refined the approach using the same dataset. First, they calculated how the neurons were predicted to behave if the mouse had been looking at a blank screen. They compared that prediction with the neurons' actual activity while the mouse watched a movie.
The neural activity had been measured with a microscopic imaging method that identifies which individual brain cells are active by detecting localized increases in calcium levels.
Using the difference between predicted and measured activity, an algorithm gradually changed the pixels of an initially blank movie. With each adjustment, the reconstructed video became more similar to the one that had actually been shown to the mouse.
Reconstructing a New 10-Second Movie
After the model had been trained, the researchers gave it a more difficult test. They recorded a mouse's brain activity while it watched a video that had never been included in the model's training data.
Using only that neural activity, the system reconstructed a 10-second movie resembling the unseen video.
Dr. Bauer added: "Using this approach, we were able to achieve high-quality reconstructions of 10-second video clips. The accuracy of the reconstructions improved with the inclusion of data from more individual neurons, demonstrating the importance of comprehensive neural data."
The result suggests that the method was not simply memorizing previously shown videos. Instead, it was able to use patterns of neural activity to infer visual information from a new scene.
Measuring How Closely the Videos Matched
To evaluate the reconstructions, the researchers used a method called pixel correlation, which compares corresponding pixels in the original and reconstructed movies.
The analysis showed only small differences in the timing of the two videos. However, the researchers say there is still considerable room to improve image resolution and the amount of the visual scene that can be reconstructed.
Future work will focus on collecting data that can support sharper reconstructions and cover a larger portion of what the animals are seeing.
Why Our Brains Do Not Simply Record Reality
The researchers now plan to use the technique to investigate a deeper question about vision: how much does the brain's internal representation differ from the world that is actually in front of us?
Vision is not simply a camera-like recording process. The brain continuously interprets, filters, and modifies incoming sensory information. Understanding exactly where and how those changes happen could reveal important principles about perception.
Dr. Bauer concluded: "We don't have a perfect representation of the world in our heads. The visual processing pipeline skews and warps our representation in a way that modifies information. This deviation between reality and representations in the brain is not necessarily an error but a feature, reflecting how our minds interpret and augment sensory information. We want to explore how this happens in the brain."

Materials provided by University College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Joel Bauer, Troy W Margrie, Claudia Clopath. Movie reconstruction from mouse visual cortex activity. eLife, 2026; 14 DOI: 10.7554/eLife.105081.3

A German Navy warship has been commanded by a woman for the first time

Unknown Publisher

A German Navy warship has been commanded by a woman for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
Ute Niklas took command of the frigate "Rheinland-Pfalz" and a crew of 126 service members. She is to prepare the ship for combat readiness.
Ute Niklas has become the first woman in the history of the German navy to take command of a frigate. She assumed command of the Rheinland-Pfalz from Captain Benedikt Eichhorn. Niklas must now bring the frigate and its crew of 126 service members to full combat readiness after repairs at a shipyard, reports UNN, citing Bild.
The new captain told Der Spiegel that an "exciting but challenging phase" lies ahead. She said she is looking forward to the ship's return to sea.
This is not Niklas's first experience serving aboard the Rheinland-Pfalz: she previously served as the ship's first officer. Most recently, she worked as an operations staff officer at the Bundeswehr's Command of Overseas Operations in Schwielowsee near Berlin.
Women were granted access to all military specialties in Germany only in 2001. More than 25,000 women currently serve in the Bundeswehr — slightly more than 13% of its service members.

Like people in other G20 countries,
Italians want their economies transformed to address inequality
and the climate crisis, but do not trust their leaders to bring
about the necessary change, according to a new survey by Ipsos
on behalf of the Earth4All initiative.
                                    
                                       
				The report said 73% of Italians agree there is too much economic
inequality in their country, a level that is even higher than
the average of 70% for the 17 countries the survey was conducted
in, and up from 61% in 2024.
                                    
                                       
				It said 61% of people here agree with the assertion that the
economic system is rigged to benefit the rich and powerful, and
68% agree that the economic system needs major changes.
                                    
                                       
				Yet while the mandate for change is overwhelming, the trust in
governments to deliver it has deteriorated.
                                    
                                       
				Only 22% of people in Italy believe their government will make
decisions that benefit the majority of people 20 or 30 years
from now, significantly below the global average of 31%, with
40% disagreeing.
                                    
                                       
				That collapse in trust runs through the wider social fabric.
                                    
                                       
				Overall, 66% of the Italian public agreed that the country is
more divided than it was 10 years ago, which is in line with the
global average of 67%. Only 8% disagreed.
                                    
                                       
				Earth4All, which is working to accelerate the systemic changes
needed for an equitable future on a finite planet, says the
study shows it is time for a new kind of social contract, which
takes the scale of change people are asking for seriously and
offers it through fair and democratic means.
                                    
                                       
				"Just 22% of Italians trust their government to act in the best
interests of the majority of people over the long term," Owen
Gaffney, the Earth4All co-chair and one of the report's authors,
told ANSA.
                                    
                                       
				"The Italian result is substantially below the G20 average of
31% - which is already very low.
                                    
                                       
				"It is clear that greater trust is needed to adequately deal
with long-term challenges like climate change.
                                    
                                       
				"We need to re-invent democracies to rebuild trust".

The West has tried everything except ending the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:29:39 UTC
21:29:39 KST

On 6 May 2022, I began using the term tsunami of ripple effects to describe the cost of not intervening in a war that threatens the security of the Alliance. That was NATO's own strategic ambition—right up until the Madrid Summit in June 2022, where it found its political will and military capabilities wanting, deterred by Russia.
The latest wave of that tsunami reached American voters this month, in the price of diesel—and the US President's response shows exactly how the refusal to end the war keeps compounding its costs.
Diesel, and the president who blamed the victim
President Trump has urged President Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel-supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel US diesel prices to a record high, according to CNBC.
"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said during an official visit to Ireland. "Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel because he's causing a shortage of diesel. This isn't done by the Middle East; this is done by what's happening with Russia and Ukraine."
The claim inverts the evidence. The latest IEA assessment is unusually clear: the US-Iran war and the disruption of Middle Eastern flows are the dominant shock, with Gulf refined-product exports down almost 60% since February.
Disruptions to Russia's refining system and the near-halt in Russian product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks, the IEA says, "have compounded these losses." The aggressor is responsible for the dominant shock; the war Trump himself helped start accounts for most of the rest; and the victim's attempt to force Russia toward peace has only reinforced the consequences of that aggression.
Yet Trump singled out Zelenskyy—not Putin for starting the war, not himself and Prime Minister Netanyahu for the war against Iran.
Ukraine has intensified the tempo of its refinery-strike campaign and improved its targeting to cause maximum pain to the Russian oil industry, striking at least 26 different Russian oil refineries since the beginning of 2026, according to ISW. The strikes have put roughly half of Russia's refining capacity offline and prompted widespread fuel shortages, with Moscow recently extending a ban on diesel exports through the end of September to stabilize domestic supplies.
The lie, the contradiction, and the lack of credibility
Trump's statement is an outright lie—the link to the US/Israel war on Iran is clear for anyone to see—and it is in direct contradiction with US and European policy.
As late as early July, Trump noted that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were an escalation capable of bringing the war to an end. The reversal appears driven primarily by the fuel-price shock and its political consequences—not by any change in his assessment of the strikes' military value. US consumers have seen a roughly 20% increase in diesel prices in a matter of weeks, midterms are seven weeks away, and the Republican Party is struggling in the polls.
And Ukraine's strikes aim at the exact effect Western sanctions were designed to achieve: ensuring Russia cannot afford to continue the war by undermining its economy. Neither the US nor Europe is supposed to import Russian crude or refined products—the EU banned them, cutting Russia's share of EU oil imports from 25.8% in 2021 to 2.2% in 2025, and the US prohibited them in March 2022.
"The United States is taking sweeping action against Russia's key source of revenue for funding its brutal and illegal war against Ukraine," Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said in January 2025. That is exactly what Ukraine is doing—with the difference that when Ukraine does it, Trump calls it "hurting the world."
The tsunami of ripple effects
Diesel is only the latest wave. During the year after Madrid, I watched the West take the role of bystander to a war that is all about us—a Russian ever-escalating hybrid war against European NATO members—seemingly accepting the global consequences.
I say seemingly because it makes no sense to sit idle while the tsunami grows to the point where it causes political, economic, and geopolitical chain reactions impossible to predict and difficult to control.
Inaction is not neutral. It is also a choice, and it carries the consequences of engagement with one crucial difference: inaction makes us react to the strategic environment, whereas action lets us shape it.
Aid without an endpoint is not a policy for ending the war; it is a policy for enduring it.
Enduring it is what produced the tsunami: the reverberations that raise the cost of living, undermine food and energy security, and spread famine, recession, inflation, and rising interest rates—increasing the risk of social unrest, extremism, and, ultimately, the fall of governments. Europe is living through the biggest refugee crisis since the Second World War.
he international security architecture is being dismantled, the institutions meant to unite us are discredited, and NATO no longer deters Russia—raising the risk of direct conflict between Russia and Europe.
In June 2023, I argued this would likely change the political landscape in the US and Europe—as in the 1930s—as political forces sought to exploit voters' frustration over the war's global effects. It produced President Trump and a rising tide of right-wing forces across Europe—the leading edge of what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called, at Davos, a rupture the world hasn't yet reckoned with: "We understand that this rupture calls for more than adaptation. It calls for honesty about the world as it is... We know the old order is not coming back." Its consequences for Europe have not yet dawned on us.
How to end it
The only way to end the tsunami of ripple effects is to end the war. Waiting only lets it reach the scale where it produces chain reactions impossible to control.
Since 2014, the West has tried to stop Russia's war through diplomacy, negotiations and ceasefires; sanctions and economic pressure; diplomatic isolation; military aid, training and intelligence; NATO deterrence and reinforcement; and humanitarian and financial assistance. More than 200 negotiations were held to stop the war from happening.
They were all futile, because Russia was never negotiating in good faith—it sees negotiation as a means to defeat its opponents. Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.
For a negotiation to succeed, it must solve the cause of the war: Russia's Great Power ambitions, its pursuit of strategic parity with the US and China at the expense of its neighbours. Until that is checked, there will be no peace—and those ambitions are not negotiable. They can only be denied through military power.
The West has done everything short of military intervention. It is time to employ military power, because the cost of continuing the present path is far too high. If Europe wants to turn the tide, it must become proactive. Instead of waiting for the war more intelligence services are warning about, Europe—or rather a Coalition of Like-Minded European countries—must help shift Russia's appraisal of the strategic environment. We need to intervene militarily to end the war, and the tsunami of ripple effects with it.

In Sweden, many breathe sigh of relief as far right suffers election losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:22:25 UTC
21:22:25 KST

In Sweden, many breathe sigh of relief as far right suffers election losses
The election is tight, but one result is clear: the Sweden Democrats’ bid to turn hate into votes failed.
Stockholm, Sweden – Jimmie Akesson, leader of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), cast his early ballot in Rinkeby, a Stockholm suburb where most residents have a minority background.
“It was a political stunt,” said 18-year-old Sumeyah Ali. “It was meant to provoke.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘I’ll never be Swedish enough’: Far-right campaign upsets minority groups
- list 2 of 3As Sweden heads to polls, Israel and Palestine policies are on the ballot
- list 3 of 3Multicultural Malmo: Swedish city loathed by far right braces for election
After voting, Akesson told reporters Rinkeby “doesn’t look like Sweden … Sweden shouldn’t look like this, I think.”
His provocative comments were designed to fuel the party’s anti-immigration and Islamophobic rhetoric, said Ali at an office space for Jarva i samverkan, a Stockholm-based network of local nonprofits that coordinates free activities and youth programmes.
But his apparent bid failed.
Although the overall general election is too close to call, one result is clear: the SD suffered its first-ever decline in a parliamentary election, falling three percentage points to 17.5 percent and slipping from second to third place behind the Moderate Party.
Anti-Islam threats
The party, which has neo-Nazi roots, has repeatedly targeted Islam.
In 2023, Akesson called for a halt to new mosques and said Sweden should, in the longer term, begin “seizing and demolishing mosques” that spread “anti-democratic, anti-Swedish” propaganda, a proposal rejected by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
Akesson has said he targets Islamism, not Muslims, but senior SD MP Richard Jomshof abandoned that distinction during the campaign.
When asked by the newspaper Dagens Nyheter in August what message he had for Muslims living peacefully in Sweden, he replied: “They can stop being Muslims, for a start.”
Zack*, a 27-year-old resident, told Al Jazeera that many have grown thicker skin in response to the SD, which has also proposed banning the hijab and intimidated people with posters reading “We make Sweden, Sweden again”.
“It was rage-bait, but it didn’t work,” said Sara, a 25-year-old business owner.
She recalled when Rasmus Paludan, the Danish-Swedish far-right politician, burned a Quran in Rinkeby Square in 2022. Riots, as well as peaceful protests, took over several Swedish cities.
“It was chaos then, but people know now we can’t be provoked, as that is what they [the far right] want,” she said.
In the end, there was no response to Akesson’s visit. He enjoyed a seamless visit, reportedly welcomed by a young boy who held the door open and later shook hands with a poll clerk.
A setback for SD
For the SD, once considered a political pariah, this election signalled an opportunity to capitalise on two decades of steady growth and enter government with the right-wing bloc that includes the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
By the early hours of Monday, preliminary results gave Sweden’s centre-left opposition bloc a razor-thin lead of 176 seats to 173 over Kristersson’s right-wing alliance. But the numbers settled little; some votes are still to be counted on Wednesday, and the final results are not expected for several days.
With a margin of just three seats, even a small shift could change the outcome, and even with a majority, the opposition’s four parties would still have to agree on a government.
Analysts warned of a deadlock that could drag on for weeks and possibly end in a snap election.
Young people feel ‘their vote will count’
Voter turnout largely rose in multicultural areas like Rinkeby, but fell across the country overall. With little margin between the blocs, every vote counts.
“Before, young people felt like their vote didn’t matter, but now they feel their vote will count for a united society; even their parents are telling their kids to go and vote,” said Ali.
Sweden’s public broadcaster published a poll showing that voters with a non-European background favour the left bloc, with the Left Party, sitting at the opposite end of the political spectrum to SD, rising from 17 percent of the vote in 2022 to 21 percent this year.
In Rinkeby central, preliminary results show more than half of voters backed the Left Party.
One stop away on the underground is Tensta, an area equally maligned by right-wing politicians; 54.35 percent of voters backed the Left Party, with only six votes for SD despite the party placing a poster in the central square.
The Trump effect
Ali believes the SD election campaign was driven by an “Americanisation” of Swedish politics, where politicians try to emulate United States President Donald Trump’s divisive politics.
In Stockholm’s central station, SD spent about $100,000 on a weeklong summer campaign that included posters that read: “If you commit crimes, live off benefits, don’t learn Swedish or misbehave, you’re not welcome.”
In Skaraborg, western Sweden, SD bus advertisements asking “Missing Mogadishu?” and promoting a grant to help migrants return home were pulled by the transport operator in August after about 20 drivers of Somali heritage called in sick in protest.
Ali remains optimistic as many Swedes embrace diversity and several initiatives are working to reduce segregation.
Stockholm City has launched Fokus Jarva, a project that aims to close the gap in conditions between the district and the rest of the city, with plans for some 15,000 new homes alongside upgrades to schools, services, jobs, safety and public spaces.
Ali suggested that Akesson should look beyond Rinkeby’s beige and grey housing blocks to see its vibrant, diverse and supportive community.
“In the end, that’s what makes a place, however it looks,” she said.
*Some interviewees asked that their surnames be withheld because of the political nature of the interviews.

Explainer-EU chief wants Canada to become an 'associate member'. What does that mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:18:25 UTC
21:18:25 KST

EU chief wants Canada to become an 'associate member'. What does that mean?
BRUSSELS, Sept 16 - European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member".
Earlier this week, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney — who was in Strasbourg to listen to von der Leyen's annual State of the Union address — said Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership.
WHAT MIGHT THE NEW RELATIONSHIP INVOLVE?
There is currently no such status as "associate member" set out in the European Union's treaties — though various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated in the bloc over the years.
Most recently, Germany suggested Ukraine be an associate member as an interim stage to full accession, though the proposal failed to gain traction as some EU capitals pushed back.
WHAT IS CANADA SEEKING?
Carney is seeking new alliances amid repeated threats by U.S. President Donald Trump against Canada's sovereignty.
Both sides want to forge deeper cooperation to counter U.S. and Chinese economic dominance as well as preserve democracy and the rules-based international order, which they see as under threat.
In her speech, von der Leyen said the two sides would create a "common prosperity and economic space". This would include joint work on manufacturing, a tech alliance, integration of defence industrial bases, the Arctic, AI, energy and critical minerals.
WHY MIGHT THE IDEA OF 'ASSOCIATE MEMBER' BE COMPLICATED?
Implementing such an 'associate' status would be unprecedented and may be legally complex.
Von der Leyen was speaking in her capacity as President of the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm. It would fall on the EU member states to decide whether the idea flies.
There is no suggestion von der Leyen is proposing enshrining the status of 'associate member' in EU treaties. That would require unanimity among all 27 capitals and ratification by all domestically.
Canada and the EU already have a trade agreement, called CETA. More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.
If Canada wishes to become locked into the EU's Single Market, Ottawa would need to reconcile Canada's norms and regulations to match EU law.
Canada would become a rule-taker with no say on policy if it entered the Single Market without full membership like Iceland, Norway, and Liechtenstein who are members of the European Economic Area.
Switzerland has select access to the Single Market through trade agreements including the free movement of people, transport and product standards recognition.
Canada's rules have historically been geared towards its biggest trade partner, the United States.
WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR EU CANDIDATE COUNTRIES?
The quest for a deeper alliance between Canada and the EU will not impact the path to accession for European candidate states -- but it may serve as an irritant if Canada is perceived to be getting special treatment.
Accession negotiations and aligning with EU norms is a long process that often requires candidate nations to push through politically sensitive reform.
Full membership can only be granted to European states and provides access to the bloc's €18 trillion ($20.77 trillion) Single Market, voting and representation, EU funding and legal recourse to the European Court of Justice.
Ukraine saw Germany's proposal for "associate membership" as "unfair" as Kyiv would participate but with no voting rights.
The EU has said it could admit new members as soon as 2030. Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova are the most advanced among candidate countries. REUTERS

Swiss AI tech helps determine biological age from retina images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:17:00 UTC
21:17:00 KST

Swiss AI tech helps determine biological age from retina images
A new artificial intelligence (AI) system developed by the University of Lausanne can determine a person’s biological age from photographs of the retina, thereby assessing their risk of diseases such as cancer or dementia.
A significant difference between the biological age determined in this way and actual age indicates increased health risks, as the university announced on Wednesday. According to the study, a higher biological age of the retina is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, cancer and dementia. The researchers published their findings in the journal Nature Communications.
To develop their method, the scientists trained an AI algorithm using images of more than 70,000 people aged between 40 and 79. The model estimates retinal age with an average deviation of less than three years from actual age.
Differences between men and women
The study also revealed clear differences between men and women. In men, a retina that appeared older was more strongly linked to characteristics of metabolic syndrome, such as high blood pressure, diabetes or being overweight. In women, by contrast, retinal age was more strongly associated with vascular factors, such as an increased risk of thrombosis.
More
How AI is used in diagnostics
Menopause also appears to play a role. Before menopause, women’s retinas appeared, on average, younger than those of men. After the menopause, this difference was reversed. The study does not prove a causal link, but it does open up an interesting line of inquiry into the role of hormonal changes, the report continues.
Differences barely perceptible to the human eye
Artificial intelligence detects features that are barely perceptible to the human eye. These include subtle variations in colour or brightness, as well as the density of the blood vessels.
However, the researchers emphasise that a retina that appears older does not necessarily mean that a person is suffering from, or will suffer from, a specific disease.
The observed links to lifestyle, however, suggest scope for intervention. Smoking was identified as the strongest factor contributing to accelerated retinal ageing. Early treatment of cardiovascular problems may also play a role. However, further studies are needed before clinical application is possible.

English village votes to leave UK, newspaper says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:16:41 UTC
21:16:41 KST

LONDON, September 16. /TASS/. Residents of Piddington, a village in England’s Oxfordshire, have voted to leave the United Kingdom in protest against government plans to establish an asylum center near the settlement, The Daily Telegraph reported.
A total of 285 residents voted in favor of leaving the United Kingdom, while 26 voted against. Turnout stood at 92%. The results of the referendum, held on September 15, were announced Wednesday morning. The vote was symbolic and had no legal force.
The UK government earlier announced plans to convert a former military site into an asylum center for people who enter the country illegally by small boats across the English Channel. The facility is expected to accommodate about 1,300 people. The main concern among village residents is that the arrival of new neighbors could lead to an increase in crime.
"This is a message to the government: you will have to change your position and take our views into account," Piddington Parish Council Chairman Tim McNally said. He acknowledged that the referendum was not legally binding but added that Piddington would now consider itself a principality. "We used to be a village called Piddington. Now we are the Principality of Piddington. And we will put up an appropriate sign," he said.
McNally said the campaign had received support from opposition political parties, including the Conservative Party, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats, and had drawn interest from more than 500 lawmakers at different levels who want to hold similar votes in their towns and villages.
Battle for Britain
One of Piddington’s residents, 76-year-old Herbert Owen, compared the referendum with the Battle of Britain during World War II.
"This is about everything our grandparents and parents fought for, and the fate of the country is being decided today. It’s not just about Piddington, it’s about our whole country. The current government is destabilizing the situation," he said.
The newspaper reported that more than 130 women from Piddington sent letters last week to all female members of the House of Commons, warning that their lives "will be destroyed" if the authorities proceed with plans to open the asylum center. "We will not feel safe walking the streets," the letter said.
The newspaper said Piddington residents are now making plans to install a network of surveillance cameras, an emergency alert system and organize patrols to improve security. Local women also plan to take self-defense classes.

New 'spy' drones to give Army greater powers on the battlefield
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:15:07 BST
21:15:07 KST

New 'spy' drones to give Army greater powers on the battlefield
British soldiers will receive new Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) drones, giving them better sight of the battlefield and greater protection against emerging threats in conflict.
- 
    British soldiers will be better protected and gain greater intelligence on the battlefield with new ‘spy’ drones.
- 
    Up to £400 million investment in long-endurance surveillance drones and more than one thousand smaller drones unveiled as part of separate £16 million deal.
- 
    Part of government’s commitment to the Army’s next generation of uncrewed aerial systems highlighted in the Defence Investment Plan.
They range from small, easy-to-use drones that give soldiers real-time awareness on the frontline, to larger aircraft that give commanders detailed intelligence over longer distances and periods of time.
A new contact, worth up to £400 million, has today been awarded to Tekever to bring their AR5 drone into service. The AR5 is a long-endurance surveillance drone that can carry up to 50kg of cameras and sensors, replacing the ageing Watchkeeper system which has been used since 2014.
Meanwhile, more than 1,025 small drones are being delivered as part of a £16 million deal with three UK-based small and medium-sized companies with deliveries nearing completion.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP unveiled the news at this year’s Defence Vehicle Dynamics event – the UK’s biennial land warfare exhibition.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  Our soldiers deserve the best technology, and that’s what we’re delivering. From small drones giving troops eyes on the enemy, to the AR5 offering commanders better intelligence over the battlefield, we’re transforming the Army’s ability to see, understand and act first.
This is defence procurement that backs British industry, creates skilled jobs and keeps our Armed Forces ahead of our adversaries.
Both programmes are creating jobs in the UK. The Tekever contract will help support more than 1,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030 across the company’s UK sites in locations including Bristol, Swindon, Lydd, London, Southampton, Edinburgh, and at West Wales Airport. The small drone deal has created more than 30 new roles so far, with 18 already filled in Hampshire, Surrey, Exeter, including several veterans.
This builds on the government’s commitment to backing business and British industry, creating new jobs and delivering growth in every postcode.
The small drones being delivered include:
- 
    245 FOXE-NATO drones from Evolve Dynamics, based in Hampshire. These weigh less than 250g and include infrared cameras for use at night.
- 
    670 Skydio X10 INTL drones from Marlborough Communications Limited in Surrey. These can be ready to fly in under a minute and reach speeds of up to 45mph.
- 
    110 SONORA drones from a partnership between Brigantes Consulting (based in Exeter) and Harmattan AI. These are designed to help train soldiers before they use similar drones in real operations.
The Tekever AR5 deal starts with an initial order of six drones, rising to up to 24 by 2029. The drones will be built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon and have already been used by Ukraine against Russia.
Tekever UK’s Managing Director Karl Brew said:
  We are proud to be delivering the AR5 to the British Army at this critical moment for national security. This investment allows us to grow our UK operations, create hundreds of skilled jobs and bring cutting-edge surveillance technology, proven on the battlefield in Ukraine, into service with British forces.
The small drone deal was delivered by the UK National Armaments Director Group. It forms part of Project Rapstone, the Army’s programme to bring new technology to soldiers faster, with a goal of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and getting new equipment from industry to the front line within 24 months.
The Defence Investment Plan commits new investment in the Army’s long-range surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, including the next generation of uncrewed aerial systems to replace legacy Watchkeeper drones.

‘No question of rollback’: Govt digs in on UPI charges amid Rahul Gandhi’s attack

No question of rollback of 0.4% MDR charges on UPI transactions over Rs 2,000.
NEW DELHI: The government has ruled out any rollback of the proposed 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions above Rs 2,000, saying the decision has already been taken and will come into effect from October 15.“There is no question of a re-think,” a top government official told news agency PTI when asked whether the Centre was considering withdrawing the proposed MDR on high-value merchant transactions.
The decision comes amid sharp criticism from Opposition parties, traders and sections of the digital payments ecosystem who dubbed the move as 'Modi Tax'. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi accusing Prime Minister Narendra Modi of yielding to US pressure over the new UPI framework, .Earlier in the day, in a video posted on X on Wednesday, Gandhi attacked Modi over the revised UPI framework, alleging that the Prime Minister had taken a different approach.“Modiji has a completely diff concept, he's neither left or right he has decided to completely lie down straight and in front of Donald Trump. He's put a tax on every single Indian person by taxing UPI and giving huge amount op money to the United States,” the former Congress president added.
Also read: New UPI charges challenged in SC; petitioner flags impact on common manGandhi later said: “Modiji, please stop lying down in front of the US. Have a spine, stand up and withdraw the UPI tax. Thank you."The Centre has rejected the allegation that the changes were driven by foreign pressure. The finance ministry said on Wednesday that India’s UPI policy decisions were being taken independently with the objective of creating a sustainable and inclusive digital payments ecosystem.“Debunking the ‘External Pressure’ Myth: Some claims suggest the change is due to foreign influence. This is false. India’s UPI policy decisions are made independently, with the clear goal of building a self-sustaining, inclusive, and affordable digital payments ecosystem,” the ministry stated on X.Government sources cited by PTI said the MDR framework was aimed at strengthening the UPI ecosystem, including its safety and security, while making the system financially sustainable.The finance ministry has also stressed that customers will not be charged for UPI payments. “MDR is a charge within the merchant payment ecosystem. It is not a charge on customers making UPI payments,” it said.Person-to-person transfers will remain free, while merchants receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month through QR codes will continue to have zero-MDR protection, according to the ministry. It said more than 95 per cent of merchant payments are below Rs 2,000.
The move follows concerns raised by Parliament’s Standing Committee on Finance in its 32nd report, over the financial sustainability of the zero-MDR regime. The panel had noted that the government was spending roughly Rs 2,000 crore annually to support the incentive scheme.With the new framework set to take effect on October 15, the government is now expected to focus on implementation, merchant incentives and the expansion of UPI in rural and semi-urban areas.

EU's von der Leyen pitches Canada as bloc's 1st associate member
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants to explore making Canada the European Union’s first "associate member" as allies seek closer ties in what she called an "openly hostile world."
EU lawmakers gave a standing ovation after she made the proposal and then walked over to embrace Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in the European Parliament to hear her annual State of the Union address.
New partnerships were needed "in the cold fragility of today’s world," von der Leyen told the assembly in Strasbourg.
The 27-nation bloc faces war at its borders, with Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Both the EU and Canada have also been facing stiff rivalry on trade and other issues from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump and from an increasingly assertive China.
"I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said.
The EU and Canada "see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defense, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen told the assembly.
It will be up to EU member states, and not von der Leyen alone, whether her proposal goes ahead.
The EU has historically resisted such types of flexible alliances that have no legal status. EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full accession.
One EU diplomat expressed surprise at von der Leyen's proposal, saying "nobody really knows what it means." The diplomat added there were concerns that the European Commission chief "is over-promising and won't be able to deliver."
Ahead of von der Leyen's speech, seven EU diplomats in Canada and Europe had told Reuters there were active efforts toward deeper collaboration on trade, defense and digital security, but no specific plan for a more comprehensive Canadian-EU relationship had been discussed at a high level.
Significant obstacles also remain to ramping up trade. Mark Manger, a professor of political economy and global affairs at the University of Toronto, has said EU officials have been frustrated by Canada’s refusal to open two industries it protects at great expense: telecommunications and dairy.
Canada's Carney said earlier this week Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership. He will make his own address to the European Parliament Thursday.
Carney's European trip follows a historic breakdown in Canada-U.S. relations after trade talks collapsed last month, sparking a series of tit-for-tat tariff measures.
He has pledged to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade in the next decade as the country pivots away from its southern neighbor amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war.
Carney said Tuesday more detailed discussions would begin at the Canada-EU summit in Montreal in late October.
"Our relationship with the EU has become increasingly close, especially over the past year and a half," Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand told Reuters.
In her speech, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada will work together across sectors.
"We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defense industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project," she said.
"Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," she added.
Von der Leyen added, "This is a partnership not against anyone else."

Taiz camps overflow with Yemenis fleeing fighting after Houthi offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
