Taiz camps overflow with Yemenis fleeing fighting after Houthi offensive
Tens of thousands of people have been displaced in the Taiz governorate following the recent escalation in the conflict in Yemen.
Taiz, Yemen – Hajja Fatima Mohammed Saleh, a 70-year-old Yemeni woman, is among the countless people and families displaced from Taiz governorate, southwest Yemen, in recent fighting between government forces and the Houthis.
The Iran-backed rebel group, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), now controls most parts of northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
- list 2 of 4Saudi Arabia promises to respond to Houthi attacks ‘firmly’
- list 3 of 4Can the Houthis hold on to Yemen’s strategic western coast?
- list 4 of 4Saudi Arabia faces high-stakes choices as war with Houthis escalates
Saleh’s village in Maqbanah district, on the border of Yemen’s western coast, is situated at the epicentre of last week’s Houthi assault in which the group captured the whole of the Red Sea coast, including the port city of Mocha.
At least 100,000 people have now fled their homes following renewed fighting between the two sides, according to the United Nations’ refugee agency, most leaving with few belongings due to the speed of the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said she had to leave her wheelchair behind as it was unsuitable for the rugged terrain her family had to navigate to find shelter.
“The attack was massive, we had never seen anything like it before. Shells were falling heavily on the village, and bullets were flying in every direction,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We had no choice but to leave and flee to a safe place. We left everything we owned and walked a long distance on foot. For me, I suffered especially because I am disabled and cannot walk, so I had to crawl – using both hands – for a long distance through rain and floods before we found a vehicle to carry us.”
UN agencies and the internationally recognised Yemeni government say that Taiz governorate has witnessed most of the displacements, with Taiz City among the Houthis’ next targets after their victory on the Red Sea coast. This means the humanitarian situation could worsen even further.
Ali al-Shumairi, director-general of the Executive Unit for the Management of IDP Camps in Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera that 65,845 people were displaced between August 10 and September 15. About 95 percent of those displaced come from the five districts which witnessed the heaviest fighting: Jabal Habashi, al-Maafer, Maqbana, al-Wazi’iyah and Mawza.
Fighting has intensified on several fronts in Yemen as government forces have carried out air attacks on Houthi positions in attempts to retake Mocha, days after the group captured the strategic port city, tightening its grip on the Red Sea – a vital shipping lane.
This development has placed the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the strategic waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean, at the heart of the war between the United States and Iran, and amplifies pressure on global trade routes.
Yemen’s more than 10-year civil war was reignited in July, threatening a United Nations-brokered truce that halted large-scale violence in 2022, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have launched a campaign against the Houthis on a number of fronts since last week. They have retaken some positions and are advancing in the southwestern Taiz province as clashes intensify.
Osama al-Wafi, supervisor of the Mushrifa camp in Wadi Bikhawlan in Taiz governorate and a representative of the Yemeni government’s Executive Unit in Jabal Habashi district, described the situation as “dire and tragic”.
“These people have been displaced and have lost all the basic necessities of life, after having homes, farms, and livestock. Now they are only looking for a shelter to house them,” al-Wafi told Al Jazeera.
He said the number of displaced people arriving at the camp is steadily rising, with more than 1,500 families entering over the past six days, most living in the open due to a lack of shelter.
The al-Munij camp in the al-Bireen area, about 40 kilometres southwest of the semi-besieged city of Taiz, has become a temporary refuge for Yemenis fleeing the area after another bout of conflict between government and Houthi fighters in 2020.
Over the years, al-Munij has extended over a space of two square kilometres to house more displaced families, while other larger camps have been established in the area. Most residents complain they lack access to the most basic services – such as sporadic drinking water supplies and few toilets – in the camps.
Hajj Saif Qaed Thabet, 73, has been living with his wife and four children in an exposed space with no doors since arriving at al-Munij on September 10. He left behind a farm and livestock from his home in al-Kadaha, western Taiz governorate.
“We were displaced because of the war, fleeing bullets and artillery shells falling over our heads. Since arriving at the camp, we have been living like this, waiting for our situation to be addressed and for us to be housed in a suitable place,” said Thabet. “Praise be to God in all circumstances.”
Malouk Ahmed Ali, 55, from the al-Kadaha area in Taiz, said her family of 14 all escaped drones, shelling and gunfire on foot, including five children under her care, seven under her daughter’s care, and her elderly grandmother.
“We fled to an area near our village in the hope that the war would calm down quickly and we would return to our homes, but the clashes expanded until they reached us, so we were displaced again to here aboard a military vehicle that came to transport the threatened homeless people,” she told Al Jazeera.
“When we arrived at this camp, we were received and placed in this small tent as temporary housing for all members of the large family. Although they took all our information, our situation has not improved much so far, and we still hope it will improve.”
Ali hopes the war will end soon so she can return home but believes her family’s possessions, including solar panels and a battery, will have gone.
“As for our livestock, most of them died, some fled to the mountains and valleys, and what remained was looted,” she said.

What von der Leyen’s words reveal about the mood in the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:05:45 UTC
21:05:45 KST

Ursula von der Leyen’s big speech covered a wide range of topics, from closer ties with Canada to climate change, from trade with China to artificial intelligence.
POLITICO analyzed the past decade’s worth of State of the Union speeches to look at what words were used and reused, showing how the focus has changed since Jean-Claude Juncker, von der Leyen’s predecessor as Commission chief, gave his address in 2015.
That year, the key topics included the Greek debt crisis and an upsurge in refugee arrivals. By the time von der Leyen gave her first State of the Union speech, the Green Deal and the post-Covid Next Generation EU recovery program were firmly on the agenda.
Russia and Ukraine had, of course, become key themes in the 2022 speech, months after Moscow’s full-scale invasion — and they have remained so since. Now, with von der Leyen well into her second term, there’s an additional focus on energy, climate, security and defense.
There were no State of the Union speeches in 2019 and 2024, as EU elections were held in both of those years.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wagor International School in Taichung has been recognized as an Apple Distinguished School for the second time, CNA reported Wednesday.
The program recognizes schools not only for their use of devices but also for how technology transforms teaching and learning. Wagor, which first received the designation in 2022, said it has used technology in education since 2014, per UDN.
The school has adopted a one-to-one tablet program and encourages teachers to integrate digital resources into their classes. All its teachers hold Apple Teacher certification, while the school has recently invested in AI teaching materials to strengthen AI literacy among students and faculty.
Wagor also encourages students to move beyond textbooks through self-directed learning, video projects, digital creation, and presentations. The school said these activities help students become active creators rather than passive recipients of knowledge while developing independent thinking and practical skills.
As AI becomes more widespread, Wagor said it aims to teach students not only how to use technology but also how to engage with the world through it while maintaining empathy, social awareness, and independent judgment.

Poland reiterates Ukraine support after Russia drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:04:00 UTC
21:04:00 KST

Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
September 16, 2026
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.
After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.
"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.
"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.
Poland prepares response
Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.
"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.
On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.
"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.
Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train
Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.
Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.
Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.
"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."
"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.
Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.
Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland
Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.
But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.
In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."
Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."
"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.
Polish media sound alarm
The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.
"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."
"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.
Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."
"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.
Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.
"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."
This article was originally published in German.

RoboCup IranOpen competition 2026 underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:03:31 UTC
21:03:31 KST

RoboCup IranOpen competition 2026 underway
TEHRAN – Tehran is playing host to the 20th edition of the RoboCup IranOpen competition, which started on Wednesday and will wrap up on Friday.
Over 400 teams, comprising some 2,000 participants, are competing in 30 specialized leagues, including Rescue Maze, Rescue Line, Design and Construction, Student 2D Soccer, Student Flying Robots, Student Soccer Player, Rescue Simulation, and Soccer Simulation leagues, IRNA reported.
Self-driving car, Rescue Virtual Robot, and Rescue Agent Simulation, creativity, and innovation leagues are among other parts of the competition.
RoboCup is an international initiative covering the areas of artificial intelligence and robotics, with the ultimate goal of developing a team of humanoid robots that is able to defeat the official human World Soccer Champion team by 2050.
The initiative is a platform for testing technologies such as real-time decision-making, multi-agent collaboration, sensor data processing, and navigation in complex environments.
The event was first launched in 1997 and was inspired by the victory of a computer chess player against the then world chess champion, Gary Kasparov.
RoboCup (Originally called the Robot World Cup Initiative) is an international research and education initiative. It is an attempt to foster AI and intelligent robotics research by providing a standard problem where a wide range of technologies can be integrated and examined, as well as being used for integrated project-oriented education.
Recent achievements
Thirteen Iranian students under the age of 12 showcased their scientific, technical capabilities, and creativity, ranking second and third in different leagues of the RobotChallenge 2026 which was held in Beijing, China.
Each year, RobotChallenge, one of the world’s largest artificial intelligence robotic championships, brings together people from all over the world who compete with self-made, autonomous robots in various competitions.
Kicked off on August 8, the event brought together participants from some 48 countries, including China, Russia, Romania, Iran, Japan, Germany, and South Korea, IRNA reported.
Iranian students ranked second in the Technical Report league, third in Robot Rugby senior, and Innovation.
The achievement demonstrates the capabilities and proficiency of Iranian students in constructing and operating robots, the design process, problem-solving, and the effectiveness of technical presentations.
At the Rayan 2025 international artificial intelligence and programming competition, known as the World Finals, Iranian students showcased strong performance in both the AI and programming sections. In the programming section, Ali Safari placed first. China secured second and third place, followed by India, Vietnam, Armenia, Serbia, and Pakistan, respectively, ISNA reported.
In the AI section, Iranian teams, namely No Trust issues here, Pileh, AI Guardians of Trust, AIUoK, red-serotenin, Persistence, and GGWP were placed first to seventh.
The final round of the Rayan international artificial intelligence and programming contest was held on Friday at Sharif University of Technology in Tehran, with participants from 25 countries.
Supported by the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy, the event kicked off on November 25, attracting hundreds of contestants from the U.S., Russia, China, India, Italy, Chile, Australia, Armenia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Belarus, Afghanistan, Ukraine, Taiwan, Romania, Singapore, Poland, Slovakia, Vietnam, Serbia, Argentina, Colombia, Kazakhstan, and Ethiopia, as well as the host, Iran.
The solo programming section was held with 60 Iranian and foreign participants who worked individually to solve nine complicated algorithmic problems within a duration of three to four hours.
The scientific competition aimed to promote knowledge, foster international networking, and establish scientific authority in AI and programming.
Enhancing algorithmic thinking, problem-solving skills, teamwork, developing innovative ideas, starting new businesses, and expanding AI engineering and programming were among the other objectives of the contest.
Iranian robotics team, called Mositto, managed to win a gold medal at the 8th edition of RoboCup Asia-Pacific (RCAP) 2025.
The competition was held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, from November 10 to 15, 2025. Hosted by Khalifa University of Science and Technology, it brought together over 160 teams and more than 700 participants with nearly 2,000 researchers, industry professionals, students, and visitors from around the globe, to witness the competition in AI-driven autonomous robotics challenges, with eight leagues and 15 sub-leagues, including soccer and rescue.
The event highlighted themes like smart mobility, AI for sustainability, and technologies addressing regional challenges.
The team, comprising eight students, secured first place at RoboCupJunior Rescue, Rescue Line, and Secondary League, showcasing Iranian students’ talents and creativity to the world.

Russian Major General Grunis Killed by Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces – Madiar

Russian Major General Anton Grunis, whose death was previously reported without details about how he died, was killed by Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces in the Russian-occupied part of the Donetsk region.
Ukrainian SDF Commander Robert Brovdi said the 427th Unmanned Systems Brigade “Rarog” executed the operation on the night of September 12, 2026.
OSINT analyst Dominik identified the strike site in the occupied city of Horlivka and published the coordinates: 48.306265, 38.203961.4.
The commander released a video showing nighttime drone strikes on buildings. However, the footage itself does not show which building Grunis was in. Brovdi said Grunis was the seventh confirmed Russian military commander at the brigade, division, or army level to have been killed by units of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces.
Previously, the Russian Suvorovskoye Brotherhood Telegram channel reported Grunis’s death but did not provide the cause, date, or location of his death. At the time, Militarnyi reported that the general commanded Russia’s 4th Motor Rifle Brigade.
The formation was created in 2014 from armed groups of the so-called “Luhansk People’s Republic” (LPR), including the Prizrak unit. After being incorporated into the Russian military, the brigade became part of the 2nd Army Corps and later the 3rd Guards Combined Arms Army of Russia’s Southern Military District.
Units of the brigade fought in the Luhansk region near Toshkivka and Hirskе. They were later redeployed to the Donetsk region, where they took part in assault operations near Chasiv Yar and on the approaches to Kostiantynivka.

Russia says there is still time to stop an arms race in space after US orbital weapons admission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:02:58 UTC
21:02:58 KST

Russia says there is still time to stop an arms race in space after US orbital weapons admission
MOSCOW – Russia believes there is still time to prevent an arms race in space by drawing up a legally-binding international treaty to outlaw the deployment of offensive weapons there and called on the United States and other nations to set aside their scepticism about the idea, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Sept 16.
Ryabkov was commenting after the US acknowledged this week that the Pentagon is operating weapons in Earth's orbit, a landmark moment in the militarisation of space.
US Space Force chief Douglas Schiess said that enlisted members of his military branch “operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the Joint Force against space-enabled attacks”.
Speaking at a news briefing in Moscow, Ryabkov said the United States had not notified Russia – one of the world's top three space powers – about its new weapons capability, but said the US statement had not come as a surprise.
“This is nothing new to us; we are monitoring all of this, recording it all, and drawing the appropriate conclusions,” he said, noting that Moscow had long spoken of the need for a treaty that would rule out the use of force in space or the threat of force against objects in space.
“The Americans and other Westerners, in particular the British, have for many years used inflammatory excuses to cover up their unwillingness to move in this direction; they seek out spurious arguments to avoid doing so and attempt to turn the tables by accusing us of activities which, in their view, are destabilising in nature,” said Ryabkov.
“But we believe that it is not yet too late to create an environment that would preclude an arms race with escalating risks of open conflict in outer space.” REUTERS

Hong Kong aims to raise zero-carbon energy share of fuel mix to 30% by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:02:04 UTC
21:02:04 KST

Hong Kong aims to raise zero-carbon energy share of fuel mix to 30% by 2030
Target is one of four binding environmental protection targets revealed in city’s first five-year plan
Hong Kong has pledged to boost the share of zero-carbon energy in its electricity generation fuel mix to 30 per cent by 2030, up from the current 28 per cent – one of four binding environmental protection targets set out in the city’s first five-year plan on Wednesday.
The binding goal aligns with existing climate protection strategies that target a zero-carbon energy share of between 60 and 70 per cent by 2035, as part of the city’s broader push towards carbon neutrality by 2050.
“With these efforts, we strive to strengthen energy security, lower energy generation costs and stabilise electricity tariffs to minimise the impacts of the war in the Middle East, which has driven up liquefied natural gas prices,” a government source said.
Natural gas currently accounts for most of Hong Kong’s electricity generation, making up more than 50 per cent of the fuel mix as of June this year, followed by coal at under 20 per cent, and nuclear and renewable energy at around 28 per cent.

Statement by the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the drone attack on Mecca
16.09.2026
Holy sites of all religions constitute a cultural and civilizational heritage of all humanity. Protecting world heritage sites during armed conflicts has been and remains a priority for Poland.
We consider the Houthi drone attack targeting Mecca to be unacceptable. It is part of a pattern of actions leading to chaos and instability in the Middle East, threatening civilians, civilian infrastructure, and maritime shipping lanes.
We call for respect for the special status of religious sites and symbols—and for refraining from attacks against them—especially given the serious challenges to global security and the economy that we currently face.

European Parliament strips Polish far-right leader of immunity to face Holocaust denial charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years.
The decision marks the sixth time that the European Parliament has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial. Braun is already on trial in Poland for an attack on a Jewish religious celebration in parliament and is facing a number of other legal cases.
Parlament Europejski w głosowaniu w Strasburgu uchylił immunitet europosła Grzegorza Brauna. Sprawa dotyczy negowania przez niego Holokaustu. Więcej: https://t.co/rB3UPUiS8o pic.twitter.com/icRLEqsWmF
— Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) September 15, 2026
In a vote on Tuesday, a majority of MEPs voted in favour of a request, submitted in February by Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, to lift the immunity enjoyed by Braun as an MEP. He has sat in the European Parliament since being elected in 2024.
In his request, Żurek said that Polish prosecutors wish to charge Braun in relation to “denial of genocide crimes committed by functionaries of the Third Reich in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp and the Lublin concentration camp (Majdanek)”.
Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has prosecutorial power, also revealed that the accusation relates to the use of gas chambers at those two camps.
Neither the IPN nor Żurek confirmed at the time what specific words Braun had said that prompted the planned charges against him. However, the IPN noted that they had come at a live event broadcast online on 27 September 2025.
On that date, Braun took part in a discussion with Jan Żaryn, a right-wing historian and former senator for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, titled “The Polish Underground State and the Jewish Issue”. A recording of the event is still available online.
During his remarks, Braun referred to the “fake gas chambers of Majdanek and Auschwitz”, calling them “a dark, monstrous fantasy that has no satisfactory historical or academic support”.
He suggested that the idea of the gas chambers had been invented as part of “propaganda and black PR operations conducted by the Soviet and Anglo-Saxon security services during World War Two”, and that the false claim continues to be exploited by Jews today.
The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026
In actual fact, historians estimate that around 900,000 people were killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The vast majority were Jews, but victims also included Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and ethnic Poles.
Meanwhile, gas chambers at Majdanek were used to kill tens of thousands, again mainly Jews. Today, the ashes of the camp’s cremated victims are preserved in a memorial at the site of the former camp.
Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the veracity of Nazi crimes against Jews. Last month, he was charged with denying Nazi crimes in a separate case over earlier comments in which he called Auschwitz’s gas chambers “fake”.
Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026
In December, Braun went on trial over a separate set of charges relating to four other incidents, including his attack on a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament in December 2023 and his disruption of a lecture by a Holocaust scholar.
“I am standing before this court because I dared to defend myself against oppression and the ritual manifestation of Jewish supremacy,” declared Braun at the start of the trial, which remains ongoing.
Braun is also facing various legal cases relating to his anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT actions. Last week, he posted a video of himself using a hammer to vandalise a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Police are investigating that incident.

“If they say, ‘We are not attacking these facilities,’ then they must put on the table a list of their facilities – those they do not want us to attack,” Zelensky said.

Kyiv defines energy differently from Moscow
Zelensky said US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility of halting attacks on oil refineries and other energy facilities during their recent visit to Ukraine.
“I told them that we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but it is necessary to understand what this means for Ukraine,” Zelensky said.

Oil exports central to Russia’s war budget

The ‘Ossoff angle’: media-savvy senator borrows from Obama as 2028 chatter builds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:20 UTC
21:00:20 KST

Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One.
The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall.
After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance.
This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century.
While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state.
Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television.
“How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’
“You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.”
At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65.
The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities.
While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different.
Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed.
More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.)
Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day.
Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county.
His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail.
Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.”
But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight.
“It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”

Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

This month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule about his extensive reporting on the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.
Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.
The vast geographical inaccuracies of the old map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia. The new projection shows Africa as taking up almost double the ratio of total land area shown on the map. It all feeds into a sense that there is something domineering about it, portraying some countries as not just political and economic powers, but geographical ones as well, and therefore natural hegemons. It is an emotional response more than anything, but a testament to how much our perceptions of the physical world are linked to our estimations of stature.
No, the world map has not gone ‘woke’
The Guardian’s west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule is struck by how, despite its disproportionality, there was still opposition to retiring the 16th-century map. The US was the only country that vetoed the UN resolution, and six other nations abstained. The US dismissed the effort as “superfluous”, but Eromo sees this as a euphemism for “ideological” or “woke”. “I don’t see why it feels so strongly,” he told me. “This is a scientific discussion. It’s not an imposition.”
There is nothing binding about the resolution, and yet, there is something revealing about the world’s superpower opposing it. It suggests that the US would like to preserve that connection between size and status, even when appearances are deceiving. US president Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland was reportedly influenced by its inflated size on the old map, an acquisition that would swell US territory in the political imagination. Greenland is “massive” said Trump – but in actuality, it’s a fraction of its size as shown in the Mercator projection. The old map depicts it as roughly the same size as Africa, despite it being 14 times smaller. Could huge geopolitical tensions, and confrontation with Europe, could have possibly been avoided by simply showing Trump an accurate map?
Do maps really matter?
“It does matter. Make no mistake,” said Eromo. In his view, the significance is in the momentum such a resolution triggers. “There’s two proverbs we have in pidgin,” Eromo said: “every dance begins with a clap” and “it’s grains of rice that fill up a pot”. In other words, this might feel like a small change, but the boost of one successful campaign could pave the way to what Eromo describes as a “multipolar world order”. He points out that this resolution comes on the heels of a separate landmark one – the UN vote to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as a crime and call for reparations, an effort also led by an African country.
There is a growing traction around a particular kind of advocacy: one that uses the procedures of high-profile international institutions to challenge dominant western understandings of history and reality. These interventions in how we make sense of the world may be symbolic – but they are meaningful, and they are gaining ground.
Moving towards a shared reality?
It is staggering that the Mercator map has pretty much remained the unchanged standard for over four centuries. In questioning what was once assumed to be fact, the resolution has not only addressed issues of accuracy. It has also, somehow, punctured the vast and abstract unrealities established throughout history by the west. The theft of resources and people is only one part of what was stolen from many regions of the world during colonisation. Countries were then stolen from, again, in terms of landmass on maps, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed. There is something intangible and deeply political about the map’s significance – which is symbolic and threatening.
Eromo said that this sort of change makes people nervous because it ties in to all the ways in which legacies of literally carving out the continent and enslaving its populations still resonate. Hanging over the resolution are questions of precedent, of the floodgates being opened – the sort of building pressure that has resulted in calls to decolonise curriculums, for example. If the map that hangs in classrooms all around the world is changed, people may ask: “What else are my children going to be taught now?” Eromo said that there is something diminishing about learning that behemoths such as the US, China and Russia “can all fit into Africa with some space to spare.”
There are broader anxieties at stake – about what constitutes our shared reality, one that is increasingly fractured by social media and AI. These make tussles about maps a matter of holding on to the little that we can establish as concrete and true, in the face of vast political and digital forces that are warping our perceptions of the world. Eromo cites a statement that stood out for him, issued by Africa No Filter, an advocacy group that has been a part of the map justice campaign: “If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning?”

Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria through the soil, a five-year multinational research project has found.
The EU-funded project, which has so far resulted in 22 peer-reviewed studies, found microplastics in the soil of all 227 agricultural fields it tested across 11 European countries. The researchers said this poses a global threat, with healthy soils essential for life on Earth.
In many cases, this contamination reflected current farming practices as well as historical land use, demonstrating that plastic pollution can persist for many years.
The researchers also found that microplastics could interact with other agricultural stressors such as pesticides and veterinary drugs.
One study in Switzerland found that fields with the highest levels of tyre-wear particles also had the highest levels of other toxic chemicals and metals.
Microplastics can create new microbial habitats on their surfaces. Known as the plastisphere, these surfaces form a hotspot for interactions between plastics, microbes and agrochemicals, the researchers found.
An increase of antibiotic-resistant genes was found within plastispheres when compared with controls. Pesticides appeared to amplify this effect further.
Edoardo Puglisi, a partner of the project and professor of microbiology at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Piacenza, Italy, said the smaller the microplastics were, the more they tended to adsorb pollutants, microbes and DNA, leading to a “Trojan horse effect that can potentially increase the diffusion of pathogens and antibiotic-resistance genes”.
This Trojan horse effect can have an impact on earthworms and soil organisms by disrupting critical processes such as nutrient cycles, one study found.
Earthworms play a vital role in shaping the composition of the soil microbiome as well as the ecological functions of soils.
The EU-funded Minagris research project, in collaboration with the Countryside and Community Research Institute at the University of Gloucestershire, also found microplastics could affect plant growth and function. One study found that higher concentrations of microplastics reduced leaf area, chlorophyll content, photosynthetic efficiency and plant biomass in lettuce.
When drought conditions were added, these effects became even more pronounced, with plants performing less well than under either stress alone.
Environmental assessments often consider pollutants individually, but the findings show pollutants can behave differently when they occur together. The researchers say policy needs to recognise that plastic contamination is part of a wider picture of soil degradation and pollution.
In an effort to reduce plastic pollution, there has been an increase in the use of biodegradable plastics. However, the project found biodegradable plastics were not automatically safer and could still degrade into microplastics, potentially causing ecological damage.
“Once these plastics fragment into the ground, they’re practically impossible to remove, acting as vectors for agrochemicals and altering critical soil ecosystems,” said Dr Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, a research associate in soil physics at Wageningen University in the Netherlands.
“To protect long-term food production and soil health, policy must catch up. We urgently need standardised plastic monitoring, full manufacturer transparency, and risk assessments that evaluate through different species how microplastics interact with co-pollutants.”

How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:18 UTC
21:00:18 KST

Olive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.
Salade nicoise with olive-brine vinaigrette
Though this one-bowl wonder began life as a simple tomato and anchovy salad with olive oil, it has become more elaborate over time, and the addition of cooked green beans, eggs and even tuna all make sense to me. What’s worth preserving, though, is its Mediterranean simplicity, and the olive-brine dressing adds a lot of flavour without needing loads of extra ingredients.
In the spirit of simplicity, this vinaigrette keeps to just three wonderfully flavourful ingredients: olive brine for salt and depth of flavour, red-wine vinegar for acidity and olive oil for substance and piquancy. It won’t hold a stable emulsion in the way a mustard dressing does, so give it another good shake just before it goes on the salad. I buy whole olives with the pits in and pit them myself. They, and the brine, taste so much better that way.
Serves 4
For the vinaigrette 
2 tbsp brine from a jar of olives
  1 tbsp red-wine vinegar 
  6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  Black pepper, to taste
For the salad
6 eggs
  200g green beans, topped
200g cocktail tomatoes, or cherry tomatoes
1 red pepper, stalk, seeds and pith removed, flesh sliced into rings
½ medium cucumber, skin on and seeds in, cut into large chunks
4 spring onions, cut into 1cm lengths (white and green parts)
1 small jar black olives
  Anchovy fillets, (optional) to taste; I used a whole standard 50g tin
1 small handful basil leaves, to finish
Put the olive brine, vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil in a jar, and add a grind of black pepper to taste. Screw on the lid and shake until the mixture emulsifies. It won’t stay emulsified for long, so shake again just before you’re ready to eat. The dressing will now keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Put the eggs in a pan of cold water and bring to a boil. Once boiling, add the green beans, bring back to a boil and cook for four minutes. Drain, then put the eggs and beans in a bowl of iced or cold water. Once cooled, drain again and put the beans to one side (they can be left whole or cut into pieces). Peel and halve the eggs.
Cut the tomatoes in half, then arrange all the vegetables on a platter. Scatter over the stoned olives and drained anchovy fillets to taste, then finish with the halved eggs, some torn basil leaves and the freshly shaken dressing. Eat straight away.

Army to replace Watchkeeper with Ukraine-proven drone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:00:05 BST
21:00:05 KST

The Army is to bring the Tekever AR5 into service under a contract worth up to £400 million, replacing the Watchkeeper system in use since 2014, alongside a separate £16 million deal delivering more than a thousand small drones, the Ministry of Defence stated.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, announced both at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the biennial land warfare exhibition, on Wednesday.
The AR5 is a long-endurance surveillance aircraft able to carry up to 50kg of cameras and sensors. The deal begins with an initial order of six, rising to up to 24 by 2029, with the aircraft to be built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon. The type has already been used by Ukraine against Russia.
Mr Pollard said: “Our soldiers deserve the best technology, and that’s what we’re delivering. From small drones giving troops eyes on the enemy, to the AR5 offering commanders better intelligence over the battlefield, we’re transforming the Army’s ability to see, understand and act first.
“This is defence procurement that backs British industry, creates skilled jobs and keeps our Armed Forces ahead of our adversaries.”
According to the department, the Tekever contract will support more than 1,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030 across the company’s British sites, which include Bristol, Swindon, Lydd, London, Southampton, Edinburgh and West Wales Airport.
Karl Brew, Managing Director of Tekever UK, said: “We are proud to be delivering the AR5 to the British Army at this critical moment for national security. This investment allows us to grow our UK operations, create hundreds of skilled jobs and bring cutting-edge surveillance technology, proven on the battlefield in Ukraine, into service with British forces.”
The smaller aircraft come from three British small and medium-sized companies, with deliveries nearing completion. Evolve Dynamics of Hampshire is supplying 245 FOXE-NATO drones weighing less than 250g and fitted with infrared cameras for use at night. Marlborough Communications Limited of Surrey is providing 670 Skydio X10 INTL aircraft, which the department says can be ready to fly in under a minute and reach 45mph. A partnership between Brigantes Consulting of Exeter and Harmattan AI is delivering 110 SONORA drones, designed to help train soldiers before they use similar systems on operations.
That deal has created more than 30 new roles so far, with 18 already filled in Hampshire, Surrey and Exeter, including several veterans. The small drone contract was delivered by the National Armaments Director Group and forms part of Project Rapstone, the Army’s programme to bring new technology to soldiers faster, with the stated goal of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and moving new equipment from industry to the front line within 24 months.
Watchkeeper, the system the AR5 replaces, entered service in 2014 after a development programme that ran considerably over time and cost, and was withdrawn from service earlier this year. The Strategic Defence Review identified its replacement as part of a wider shift towards uncrewed systems, and the Defence Investment Plan commits new investment in the Army’s long-range surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities including the next generation of uncrewed aerial systems.

The Russian drone found Monday off Poland’s northwestern coast was carrying a warhead with a detonator, prosecutors handling the case announced Wednesday.
On Monday, the Polish military located and retrieved a drone from the Baltic Sea near the beach in Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec. Authorities neutralized the Russian Gerbera 2 drone on the beach and then moved it for further examination.
The aircraft contained a “high-explosive fragmentation warhead fitted with a fuze,” Colonel Bartosz Okoniewski, deputy regional prosecutor for military affairs in Poznań, said in a televised briefing Wednesday.
Advertisement
Investigators have not officially established where or when the drone was launched, where it entered the sea or what mission it was carrying out.
According to the Operational Command’s spokesperson, Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, the most likely explanation is that the drone drifted from international waters to Poland's territorial waters.
The incident comes amid mounting tensions between Russia and European countries. On Tuesday, NATO jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, and a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish military helicopter.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sunday that “the coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense Russian activity,” adding that “the escalation of the Russian Federation's actions is becoming a fact, and examples of this are getting closer and closer to our border.”

Pope Leo says Middle East conflicts strain Jewish-Christian relations

Pope Leo says Middle East conflicts strain Jewish-Christian relations
VATICAN CITY, Sept 16 - Pope Leo said on Wednesday that recent conflicts in the Middle East had tested relations between Jews and Christians, adding that differing views of the ongoing violence had strained dialogue but not broken it.
In a new decree to mark the Catholic Church's last 60 years of efforts at inter-religious dialogue, the pope also reiterated the Church's condemnations of both antisemitism and Islamophobia.
"The conflicts that have erupted in the Middle East in recent years have ... left their mark on Jewish-Christian dialogue," said the decree, developed by three top Vatican offices and approved by Leo.
"Many channels of communication have been strained," it said. "Nevertheless, the pillars of dialogue among believers, built over 60 years of common effort, have remained firm. Upon these foundations, it is both possible and necessary to continue building."
The decree, issued to mark the anniversary of a 1965 Church document widely credited with improving centuries of acrimony between Jews and Christians, did not mention any specific Middle East conflicts.
Leo, the first U.S.-born pope, has previously criticised the Iran war, drawing the ire of President Donald Trump on social media.
Wednesday's decree described fighting antisemitism as a "shared struggle" for Jews and Christians. It also said attitudes of Islamophobia "fail to distinguish" between cases of extremist violence and the everyday lives of the world's Muslims. REUTERS

Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:58:00 UTC
20:58:00 KST

Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Auditor General Janar Holm told ERR that the scandals that have emerged in the defense sector in recent months do not pose a security threat to Estonia. He said openly discussing problems instead makes the country stronger.
"I know many countries where it is not possible to talk about such things. This only makes us stronger," Holm said in response to a question about whether scandals in the defense sector pose a security threat to Estonia.
At the same time, Holm said the situation in the defense sector is concerning because several of the problems are systemic. He added that the more money that flows into the sector, the greater the confusion becomes.
The National Audit Office found problems with both the acceptance of goods and the awarding of contracts in 64 contracts handled by the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK). "Wherever we looked, there was some kind of problem," Holm said. In his view, a conventional inventory is not sufficient for accounting for Estonian Defense Forces stocks and a more digital system is needed.
EDF needs accounting rules
Holm said the Estonian Defense Forces, like all other government agencies in Estonia, must begin complying with accounting rules. He said this is important, on the one hand, for the Defense Forces itself, so that it has a quick and up-to-date overview of its assets and where they are located. On the other hand, the public must be able to see whether the money allocated to the defense sector has reached its intended destination.
However, because of problems with the accounting records, a situation arose this year in which the National Audit Office went to audit the annual report and the Defense Forces and Ministry of Defense said they had €1.2 billion worth of stocks. The National Audit Office cannot confirm whether the stocks are actually worth €1.2 billion because of the problems with the accounting records. "It seems to us that the figure should be somewhat higher," Holm said.
When there is confusion, it creates fertile ground for someone with bad intentions to take something for themselves at the state's expense. Efforts are now underway to determine what assets should be there in the first place in order to establish what is missing. Holm said there is also confusion surrounding the artillery shell deal, with the information lacking a clear audit trail.
Difficult to place blame without information
When information is lacking, it is also difficult to determine who is responsible. Holm said the parties are shifting the blame back and forth. "From the National Audit Office's perspective, what matters here is something that is often regarded as bureaucracy — namely, documentation," he said.
The National Audit Office has also told the Estonian Center for Defense Investments that the information does not provide a clear audit trail.
"We are now arguing over this and classified information is also creating a great deal of confusion, but presumably there will be clarity at some point," Holm said. He said primary responsibility always lies with the agency that enters into a transaction. In this case, the main responsibility lies with the head of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, who signed the contract.

Not Mumbai, not Delhi: This North Indian city tops India in domestic expenditure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:31 UTC
20:57:31 KST

As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually.
Chandigarh has emerged as India's highest-spending city on a per-household basis, according to The Many Urban Indias, a report by People’s Research on India’s Consumer Economy (PRICE) and Tata Sons. An average household in the city spends nearly Rs 19 lakh a year, putting Chandigarh ahead of India's biggest metropolitan centres on this measure. The study examines how households across India’s 100 leading cities earn, spend, save and borrow.
Chandigarh has the highest average household spending in India
The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
Chandigarh is identified as the city with the highest average household consumption in the report. As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually. The distinction is about average spending per household, not the total amount spent across the entire city. This matters because larger cities have many more households and can generate a much bigger overall consumer market even when their average household spending is lower.The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
It places the city among the country's highest-spending urban centres, alongside Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. The report also highlights Chandigarh's household financial position, noting that it has high levels of savings and low levels of debt.
Chandigarh and Bengaluru have the highest average household income
Chandigarh’s spending figures become more interesting when viewed alongside household income. According to the study, Bengaluru and Chandigarh have the highest average household income in India, at Rs 28 lakh per year. India's six largest metropolitan centres- Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Hyderabad are grouped together as the Big Six in the study. They have more than 10 million people each and account for a substantial share of the country's urban economic activity.
Delhi NCR is a major part of the report’s consumption story. The study says that Delhi NCR has a total consumption market worth $126 billion. This is nearly as much as Mumbai and Bengaluru combined. The report attributes this to two factors: Delhi NCR has around 7.5 million households, compared with 4.6 million in Mumbai. Its average annual household consumption is nearly Rs 15 lakh. This gives Delhi NCR a large overall consumption market, even though Chandigarh leads on average household spending.
Delhi NCR’s transportation spending alone is bigger than some cities
One of the report’s more striking findings concerns transportation. Delhi NCR households spend more than $33 billion annually on transportation, according to the study. That amount is larger than the total consumption market of Pune or Ahmedabad. The report also estimates that Delhi NCR’s annual dairy consumption is around $10 billion.
Mumbai: More high-income households, but not the highest average spending
Mumbai remains one of India’s major consumption centres, but the report places it behind Chandigarh on average household spending. The study says that Amritsar, Ahmedabad and Jabalpur have higher average household spending than Mumbai. At the same time, Mumbai leads the 100-city group in the share of high-income households.
The report defines high-income households as those earning more than Rs 36 lakh annually at 2025-26 prices. Their share across the 100 cities has increased to 12%, from 3% a decade earlier.
Bengaluru: Highest average income, but Chandigarh leads consumption
Bengaluru is another important comparison in the report. The city shares the highest average household income position with Chandigarh, at Rs 28 lakh per year. However, the report says that Chandigarh and Thiruvananthapuram have the highest average household consumption in India. It also identifies Surat as a city where average household consumption is higher than Bengaluru’s. This means Bengaluru’s high average income does not automatically translate into the highest average household spending.The report groups the cities into four categories:
Big Six: Cities with populations above 10 million.
Boomtowns: Cities with populations between 2.5 million and 10 million.
Breakout cities: Cities with populations between 1.5 million and 2.5 million.
Frontier cities: Cities with populations between 0.5 million and 1.5 million.
Chandigarh falls in the Frontier category, while Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are part of the Big Six.

67 killed in gold mine collapse in Sudan’s West Kordofan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:18 UTC
20:57:18 KST

Ikrame Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 67 people were killed after the Al-Zara gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, with search operations continuing for survivors, the Sudan Doctors Network said Wednesday.
“More than 67 people were killed” when the mine collapsed near Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan, which is under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the independent medical network said in a statement.
It said search operations were still underway for survivors or people trapped under the rubble, warning that the death toll could rise due to the mine’s lack of basic safety and protection measures for workers.
The network condemned “the negligence that had put miners’ lives at risk,” saying that mining in areas controlled by the RSF, without safety requirements or adequate protection and rescue equipment, “turns work into a direct risk to civilians’ lives.”
It called for search-and-rescue operations to continue and for the provision of the medical and logistical resources needed to deal with the disaster.
The Sudan Doctors Network also urged authorities controlling the area to “assume responsibility for protecting civilians and mining workers and to halt unregulated mining activities to prevent similar accidents.”
Artisanal mining employs more than 2 million people across Sudan under harsh conditions and accounts for about 80% of the country’s total gold production.
The Sudanese government does not prohibit artisanal mining but has sought to regulate the sector, which provides livelihoods for large numbers of Sudanese despite its risks.
Gold is a major source of foreign currency for Sudan after the country lost three-quarters of its oil revenues following South Sudan’s independence in July 2011, along with about 80% of its foreign-exchange resources.
Sudan has been gripped by war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Returning after unauthorized absence does not mean automatic reinstatement in service - Ministry of Defence
Kyiv • UNN
After a service member returns from unauthorized absence, they may continue their service only through the established procedure. Until the order is issued, duties, payments, and benefits are not restored.
Returning after unauthorized abandonment of a military unit does not mean automatic continuation of military service. This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The ministry noted that, pursuant to Part Two of Article 24 of the Law of Ukraine "On Military Duty and Military Service," service members whose military service has been suspended:
-  are dismissed from their positions; 
-  are considered not to be performing (not carrying out)
the duties of military service; 
-  are not included in the personnel strength of the Armed Forces of Ukraine or
other military formations. 
After returning to the unit, service must be resumed in accordance with the procedure established by law. Only after the relevant order is issued may the service member be assigned duties, and their monetary support, benefits, and social guarantees be reinstated
To remind you
Earlier, the Ministry of Defense stated that Ukrainian service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit while abroad may use a simplified procedure for returning to service.
Service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit, including abroad, through June 12, 2026, inclusive, may use the simplified program for returning to the military.
UNN also reported that a new status has appeared in the "Army+" mobile application for service members returning after unauthorized abandonment of their unit.

Scotland imposes mandatory environmental assessments on new datacentres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:55:33 UTC
20:55:33 KST

Holyrood has voted to pause planning applications for all new AI datacentres for up to a year until the Scottish government has developed a national strategy.
On Wednesday, MSPs backed a Scottish Labour motion to halt new schemes for up to 12 months while rules on hyperscale datacentres are developed in what could be a blow to the British government’s AI strategy.
Scotland has seen a boom in planning applications for large datacentres as global investment in AI infrastructure has exploded, with British officials encouraging developers to include Scotland in the infrastructure buildout. Datacentres are critical for storing and processing data used by AI. One scheme in Auchtertool, Fife, has been billed as the second largest in the world, and is among more than 20 large datacentres proposed so far.
Campaigners have raised concerns about water usage and carbon emissions from large datacentres, and questioned whether Scotland has the capacity to cope with the resulting explosion in energy demand.
On Wednesday, MSPs voted to approve only projects that meet robust environmental impact assessments that consider the impact of neighbouring communities, and to make no decisions on planning for datacentre applications for up to a year until national planning guidance has been formalised by the Scottish government.
Kat Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, who has spearheaded demands for a datacentre moratorium in Scotland, said the vote was a “landmark day for all those communities across Scotland who have been extremely concerned about projects coming forward in their areas.”
“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward and we can all at least take a breath now,” she said. “That means the Scottish government must now urgently call in those applications which are approaching a decision date. The communities will expect nothing less.”
Ahead of the vote, the Scottish government announced that large-scale datacentres would face mandatory environmental impact assessments, as a result of growing concern about the ecological impact of the AI boom.
This month, hundreds from community groups protested outside Holyrood against the construction of large datacentres for AI until clear planning rules and the definition of a “green” datacentre had been formalised.
On Thursday, AI leaders will gather at Dumfries House in Ayrshire for a summit with King Charles on the future of the technology, amid warnings that the speed of its development threatens the survival of humanity.
After the vote, the Scottish Labour economy spokesperson, Daniel Johnson, said the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside the impacts on the environment, communities and energy demand.
“So far the SNP has failed to do the work needed to get this right – that must change. It is right that the SNP government has accepted the need for national guidance before more decisions are made, and I want to see that guidance delivered with the urgency needed,” he said.
“The SNP must put in place the protections needed and ensure that any datacentres work for communities, create good jobs and deliver for Scotland.”
The Scottish government has been contacted for comment.

STRASBOURG, France, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union (EU), as she unveiled plans for closer security cooperation, tighter migration controls and stricter bans on children's social media use.
In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada would seek to upgrade their ties from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) to an "Alliance for the Future," covering manufacturing, technology, defense, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence (AI).
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," she told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who attended the address.
"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics," she said, adding that she wants to bring the relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible."
Von der Leyen also proposed what she called "Europe's own Article 4," modelled on NATO's consultation mechanism, under which EU member states will convene when one country faces a serious security incident below the threshold of armed aggression.
She further proposed creating a European Security Council involving EU leaders and partners including Canada, Norway, Ukraine and Britain.
The State of the Union address sets out the Commission president's priorities for the EU for the coming year and is the centerpiece of the European Parliament's four-day plenary session, which opened Monday. ■

PYONGYANG, September 16. /TASS/. North Korea has warned of the possibility of using nuclear weapons in accordance with the provisions of the law on policy regarding the state’s nuclear armed forces in response to the actions of the US and South Korea, the Korean Central News Agency reported, citing a Defense Ministry spokesperson.
The 2022 law provides for the use of nuclear weapons in the event of an attack on the country’s leadership and nuclear command and control system, as well as in the event of a threat to use nuclear or other weapons of mass destruction against North Korea.
"Such threats involving attacks and the use of weapons of mass destruction against our state by enemies can be considered the most serious challenge to our security, which requires the implementation of the relevant provisions of the law on the policy regarding the state’s nuclear armed forces," the statement said.
The defense official advised the US and South Korea to "analyze what the invocation of the relevant articles would entail and take this as a serious warning."
This statement came after a September 10 meeting of the US-South Korea Counter Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) Committee. According to Pyongyang, the parties agreed to improve information sharing, enhance joint response capabilities, and intensify relevant exercises.
However, the North Korean Defense Ministry viewed this as preparation for the potential use of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons against the country. The statement also noted that similar scenarios were rehearsed during the US-South Korea Freedom Shield joint military drills.

US special envoy John Coale announced that 25 people were released from Belarusian prisons in exchange for the lifting of US sanctions on two Belarusian companies following talks with the country’s longtime authoritarian leader, Aleksandr Lukashenko.
“25 prisoners are free today!” Coale wrote on X on September 16.
"We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," he added in comments to reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk.
The US envoy has been negotiating with Lukashenko since last year, with the talks leading to the release of some 500 people in return for an easing of Washington’s sanctions against Belarus.
In the latest such effort, the United States will lift its sanctions on Belarusian paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry sector group Bellesbumprom, Coale told the state news agency BelTA.
The United States and the European Union hit Lukashenko and his government with major sanctions in the wake of the 2020 presidential election, in which Lukashenko, in power since 1994, claimed victory.
Further restrictions were imposed in 2022 after Minsk allowed Moscow to use Belarusian territory as a launchpad for its invasion of Ukraine.
“We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future,” he wrote on X, having earlier told BelTA that “additional sanctions relief” would continue to be granted in exchange.
Coale later told Reuters in an interview that he expects to return to Belarus in about one month's time, possibly to announce the release of many more prisoners.
"I hope hundreds (are released). I don't know. That's my hope," Coale was quoted as saying.
"I'm confident that we'll get a lot more out."
Following the latest round of diplomacy, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Svyatlana Tsikhanouskaya wrote on X that she was “happy for every person who has finally found themselves free today” and “for their families and loved ones who have been waiting for this day.”
“Every person released is a victory. So today’s release is another humanitarian result,” she said, adding, however, that “it is far from the end of this process,” with hundreds of other prisoners remaining behind bars in Belarus.
According to earlier estimates by the Viasna rights group, which monitors arrests and is banned in Belarus, the country was still holding more than 900 political prisoners, even as Washington negotiated the release of hundreds of detainees beginning in 2025.
While Belarusian opposition figures have largely welcomed US efforts to secure the release of prisoners, experts say Lukashenko is using the issue to “legitimize” his rule internationally and is arresting more people to replace those freed, an assertion denied by the Belarusian leader during his talks with Coale in Minsk.
“For Lukashenko, the most important thing is...strengthening his political agency,” Vadim Mozheiko, director of the Krakow-based Kosciuszko Institute, told Current Time on September 16, adding that this “is especially important given his lack of domestic legitimacy.”
Separately, Mozheiko pointed out that a “significant proportion of those released were forcibly deported from Belarus,” a move he described as “yet another form of repression.”
A September 15 report by the UN experts said that "Belarusian authorities are using the country’s criminal justice system as an instrument of repression, systematically targeting and persecuting individuals deemed to oppose the government."
"Plainclothes officers routinely detain individuals they label as critical of the Government without warrants, subject them to beatings and stress positions, deny access to lawyers, and force them to record humiliating 'repentance' videos under duress and threats against their families," it added.
After Coale released a picture of the people freed on September 16, RFE/RL’s Belarus Service identified several prominent figures among them who had been arrested amid Belarus’s crackdown on anti-government protests and in the years that followed.
Among them was Lyudmila Chekina, the director-general of Belarus’s popular news portal Tut.by, which was shut down amid pressure from the country’s authorities in 2021.
She was sentenced to 12 years in prison on various charges, including “harming the national security of the Republic of Belarus.”
Paval Belavus, a noted art manager and founder of a popular shop selling Belarusian national symbols, was also released. He had previously been sentenced to 13 years in prison on high treason and other charges.
