US court dismisses 4chan’s case against Britain’s media regulator
- A US court dismissed 4chan and Kiwi Farms' lawsuit against Britain's media regulator Ofcom, citing lack of jurisdiction and advising them to defend themselves in UK courts.
- The dispute arose over Ofcom enforcing the UK's Online Safety Act, aiming to protect children and vulnerable users from illegal online content, with fines imposed on 4chan.
- Ofcom received full UK government support, and the court acknowledged its right to regulate, rejecting the forums' claims that enforcement violated their US constitutional rights.
AI generated
US internet forums 4chan and Kiwi Farms’ lawsuit against Britain’s media regulator Ofcom has been dismissed by a court in Washington, DC, which said it did not have jurisdiction to rule on the matter.
The owners of the forums clashed with Ofcom over its enforcement of Britain’s Online Safety Act, legislation which has caused broader tension between US tech companies and Britain.
Critics of the law, which is designed to protect children and vulnerable users from illegal content online, have said it threatens free speech. The British government has “fully backed” Ofcom in taking action.
4chan, an irreverent site that hosts content including pornography and conspiracy theories, and Kiwi Farms had said “threatening communications” they had received from the British regulator interfered with their constitutional rights and operations.
Ofcom had accused both of failing to respond to its statutory information requests.
Ofcom sent 4chan a “provisional notice of contravention” on Aug 12, 2025, that threatened to impose a fine of £20,000 (S$34,200) as well as daily fines of £100 for up to 60 days. 4chan brought its suit later that month.
The regulator imposed the fine – the first under the new regime – in October.
The US court ruling, dated Sept 15, said the plaintiffs could defend themselves in British courts. It added that if Ofcom obtained a judgment, that would most likely have to be enforced in the United States, because the companies had no presence or operations abroad.
At that point they could take their case to US courts, the judgment said.
“Put simply, plaintiffs’ suit fails because they seek to use American courts as a sword against Ofcom rather than as a shield to protect themselves,” District Judge Rudolph Contreras said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: “A US Court has acknowledged that we are within our rights as a UK regulator to investigate breaches of the UK’s online safety laws, and has dismissed claims by 4chan and Kiwi Farms who have sought to stop us doing our job of creating a safer life online for people in the UK.” REUTERS

KHARTOUM, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- At least 63 people were killed in a gold mine collapse in Sudan's West Kordofan State, according to survivors and eyewitnesses on Wednesday.
A survivor told Xinhua by phone that the accident occurred Tuesday at the Al-Zaraa mine in the Al-Riqiq area in West Kordofan.
He said parts of the mine, which consists of about 10 shafts, suddenly collapsed, and estimated that more than 300 people could be trapped inside.
Another survivor told Xinhua that local rescue teams had recovered 63 bodies from the collapsed mine on Wednesday.
"Search operations are still underway for missing people trapped under the rubble," he said. "Search and rescue efforts are facing great difficulties due to the depth of the shafts and the lack of specialized equipment."
Meanwhile, according to an eyewitness at the mine, the collapse affected several adjacent shafts, burying dozens of miners.
Difficulties in reaching the bottoms of the shafts and a lack of appropriate machinery had hampered efforts to recover the victims, the eyewitness said.
Artisanal mining is a major source of income for many Sudanese and produces about 80 percent of the country's gold. The sector operates at more than 800 sites across northern and western Sudan, employing over 1.5 million miners.
Gold is one of Sudan's major sources of foreign currency. According to official statistics, Sudan produced 70 tons of gold in 2025. Accidents are frequent at mining sites due to inadequate safety measures and deteriorating infrastructure. ■

21 dead, dozens missing after war-damaged building falls in Gaza
Unknown

2026-09-16

Breadcrumb
21 Palestinians dead and dozens missing after war-damaged building collapses in Gaza
At least 21 Palestinians, including at least 5 children, were killed and more than dozens injured after a war-damaged residential building collapsed in Gaza City at dawn on Wednesday, with around 100 people still missing or feared trapped beneath the rubble, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health, Civil Defence and eyewitnesses.
The six-storey Al-Saada Building collapsed at around 2:15 a.m. on Al-Sina'a Street, southwest of Gaza City, while residents were asleep, according to local eyewitnesses.
The building had been damaged during Israel's war on Gaza and was sheltering families whose homes had been destroyed or damaged.
The collapse also struck tents belonging to displaced Palestinians that had been erected near the building.
In a press statement, Gaza's Ministry of Health said 20 bodies had been recovered and more than 25 people injured as rescue teams continued searching for survivors and those missing beneath the debris. Gaza's civil defence later updated the toll to 21, according to Alaraby TV.
The ministry said the latest collapse brings to 50 the number of Palestinians killed in the collapse of war-damaged buildings across Gaza since Israel's war began on October 2023.
Gaza Civil Defence said around 100 people were inside or around the building when it collapsed. Its teams, working with the Gaza Municipality, the Egyptian Committee and the International Committee of the Red Cross, rescued 16 people and recovered the bodies, while others remained beneath the rubble.
A man emerged from the rubble, but his family did not
Khaled al-Okka, a father of six, was among those who were rescued and taken to hospital, but his family remains trapped beneath the collapsed building.
From his hospital bed, he has been following reports from the rescue site, waiting anxiously for news of his relatives.
"The collapse happened suddenly as residents slept, leaving us with virtually no time to escape," he recalled the incident to The New Arab.
He found himself trapped beneath the rubble before rescue workers eventually reached him and pulled him out.
"My thoughts have been focused on my children and other family members who remained inside the building," he said.
"My greatest fear now is for my children and my family," he added. "I was pulled out, but they are still under the rubble. I do not know what happened to them or whether they were able to reach a safe part of the building before it collapsed."
He said residents had no warning that the building was about to give way.
"Everything happened in a moment. People were sleeping, and suddenly the building came down on them," he explained.
Al-Okka said he remains unaware of where exactly his relatives may be trapped, leaving him dependent on the rescue teams searching through the wreckage.
Cries for help beneath the rubble
At the site, relatives gathered as Civil Defence teams worked through layers of concrete and twisted metal in an attempt to reach those still missing.
Khader Akila, a resident in the area, told TNA that residents heard cries for help coming from beneath the debris after the collapse.
He said one child remained trapped for more than an hour while Civil Defence workers tried to reach him.
"People could hear voices under the rubble, but reaching them was extremely difficult," Akila added, describing the rescue effort as a race against time.
He said rescuers lacked the equipment needed to lift the massive concrete slabs, forcing them to work with whatever limited tools were available.
Another local resident, Ismail Hana, told TNA that the collapse showed the dangers facing Palestinians who continue to live in buildings damaged during the war.
"There is no safe place in Gaza," he said. "Even sleep is no longer safe."
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza Civil Defence, told TNA around 100 people, including women, children and elderly residents, were inside the building and surrounding area when it collapsed.
He said displaced families were also living in tents nearby, adding that "the building had been damaged during the war and developed structural cracks before collapsing on its residents."
He explained that Civil Defence teams were continuing to search for survivors and recover bodies but were facing major difficulties because of the lack of heavy machinery.
"We urgently need excavators, bulldozers and heavy equipment to remove the rubble and reach those who may still be alive underneath," Basal said.
He accused Israel of preventing the entry of such equipment into Gaza, saying the shortage was not only hampering the current rescue operation but also leaving Civil Defence teams ill-equipped to respond to other building collapses.
2,000 buildings at risk of collapse
Basal warned that around 2,000 damaged residential buildings across Gaza remain at risk of collapse while still being inhabited, raising concerns as winter approaches and already-weakened structures face further deterioration.
He said the collapse of the al-Saada Building could be followed by further incidents if damaged structures remain occupied without proper engineering assessments and urgent repairs or demolition of sections deemed dangerous.
The warning comes as thousands of Palestinian families remain without safe alternative housing after Israel's war caused extensive destruction to homes and infrastructure. Many displaced families have been forced to shelter in damaged buildings or tents erected beside them.
Civil Defence has repeatedly called for heavy machinery to enter Gaza to clear rubble, rescue people trapped beneath collapsed structures and deal with buildings at risk of falling.
Basal said that the provision of heavy rescue and rubble-clearing equipment was included among the humanitarian provisions of the ceasefire agreement, which took effect in October 2025.
He accused Israel of failing to implement the provisions concerning the entry of such machinery into Gaza.
He called on the states that guaranteed the agreement to intervene and facilitate the entry of excavators, bulldozers, and other rescue equipment, warning that continued shortages could increase casualties if further-damaged buildings collapse.

20:54:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Cross-Strait institutional dialogue was suspended because Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities rejected its political foundation, which is the one-China principle, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Previous cross-Strait consultations had been conducted on the basis of the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, said Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, in response to the DPP's claims that the mainland had unilaterally halted institutionalized consultations and restricted travel and exchanges.
The DPP, since coming to power in 2016, has adopted a secessionist line and refused to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which "unilaterally undermined" the basis for cross-Strait dialogue, leading to the suspension of institutionalized talks and communication mechanisms, she noted.
Furthermore, the DPP authorities have restricted cross-Strait travel and cooperation in various fields, she said, adding that such measures had impacted the interests of people and businesses in Taiwan.
"The DPP is accustomed to distorting facts, shifting the blame and turning accusations back on others," she said.
The Taiwan question stems from a full-blown civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, though the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
The two sides had established institutionalized communication channels and reached agreements on a range of issues before the DPP took office in 2016. The mainland has repeatedly called for resumption of cross-Strait dialogue on the basis of the 1992 Consensus.
Regarding the mainland's new regulations governing entry and exit, which took effect on Sept. 15, Zhu said these regulations would provide a clearer legal framework for travel between the mainland and Taiwan.
Repeated warnings from the DPP authorities about the new regulations were only aimed at deterring Taiwan residents from visiting the mainland, to prevent them from seeing through the DPP's disinformation attempts, she said.
About 2.85 million visits to the mainland by Taiwan residents were recorded in the first half of 2026, up 24.9 percent year on year.
"The steady flow of Taiwan people traveling between the two sides is the clearest demonstration of how absurd the DPP authorities' efforts to restrict and obstruct cross-Strait exchanges are," she said. ■

Estonian government agrees on preliminary allocation of next period EU support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Estonian government agrees on preliminary allocation of next period EU support
Estonia plans to use EU funding to upgrade police aviation, strengthen border security and expand shelter capacity as part of efforts to improve the country's internal security and crisis preparedness.
The Cabinet has approved the basic framework for Estonia's national plan for the European Union's 2028-2034 budget period, including an initial proposal for allocating funding. The national plan is the central strategic document that will guide Estonia's use of funding from the EU's long-term budget.
The national plan is based on five priority pillars: the economy and competitiveness, security and resilience, rural development, agriculture and fisheries, education and social cohesion and good governance. The most important reforms and investments for the next period will be grouped under these pillars, helping Estonia achieve its long-term development goals, the government's press service said.
Under the national plan's initial allocation proposal, more than half of the funding would go toward boosting economic competitiveness and strengthening security and crisis preparedness, accounting for 33 percent and 19 percent of funding, respectively. Another 38 percent would go toward rural development objectives, including the Common Agricultural Policy, fisheries and the food sector. Education and social cohesion would receive 10 percent, while approximately 1 percent would go toward good governance.
Under the European Commission's proposal, Estonia would receive approximately €6.5 billion in the next budget period. The initial allocation through 2031 covers €5.5 billion in investment needs. The final amount of funding is still subject to change during negotiations and will depend on an agreement on the European Union's 2028-2034 long-term budget.
The final package of EU funding for the next budget period and Estonia's national plan will be completed after an agreement is reached on the EU's long-term budget and negotiations between the European Commission and Estonia on the national plan's content and funding have concluded. This is expected in fall 2027.
For example, €260 million proposed by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications is intended primarily for strategic industrial investments and research and development, with the aim of establishing new production capacity, expanding factories and supporting the production of higher-value-added goods.
To modernize production, the ministry has also proposed allocating at least another €45 million to the digitalization and automation of businesses and the adoption of artificial intelligence solutions. Funding would also support stronger cybersecurity and reduced bureaucracy, helping businesses cut costs and operate more efficiently.
The proposals also emphasize the importance of ensuring that economic growth is not concentrated solely in and around Tallinn and Tartu. A total of €108 million is planned to support regional businesses and the growth of small and medium-sized enterprises outside the country's major centers. Among other things, the funding would be used to develop industrial and business areas with the aim of creating well-paying jobs across Estonia.
Helicopter procurement planned
In the field of internal security, the government plans to purchase multipurpose helicopters and a surveillance aircraft, strengthen border security, combat serious crime, manage migration and create more shelter capacity, the Ministry of the Interior said.
Police aviation capabilities need to be upgraded to ensure that Estonia can continue to provide round-the-clock border surveillance, rescue people at sea, transport patients from the islands and respond to major emergencies. The upgraded aviation capability must also make it possible to respond to several incidents simultaneously and maintain readiness when some aircraft are undergoing maintenance, being used for training or already deployed on other missions.
EU funding will also be used to strengthen surveillance of Estonia's external border. Various procedures will be digitalized to improve migration management, while digital travel documents and visas will also be introduced.
EU funding will also be used to create more shelter capacity in apartment buildings and healthcare, social services, education and cultural institutions. Public warning systems and crisis communications will also be improved to ensure people quickly receive up-to-date information and act accordingly.

German peace groups vow to mobilize civil society against Israeli arms production at Volkswagen plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:53:32 UTC
20:53:32 KST

- Peace campaigners warn project could pave way for broader Israeli defense industry involvement in Germany, Europe
German peace groups have vowed to mobilize against plans to produce defense systems at Volkswagen’s Osnabrueck plant in cooperation with Israeli company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
“We see an opportunity to channel resistance into civil society against arms production in the city. Our project and main focus is to mobilize civil society for it,” Marie Dominique Guyard, a spokeswoman for the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, told Anadolu.
“We want to put more pressure on the political parties and city officials. Our strategy is to initiate a political discussion on the topic of arms production in the city,” she added.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative has been at the forefront of protests in recent months, urging Volkswagen to abandon plans for defense production at the site.
The group has received support from Germany’s opposition Left Party, which has called Volkswagen’s planned cooperation with Israel’s state-owned Rafael “unacceptable,” citing the Israeli government’s conduct in Gaza.
Rafael, meanwhile, has been expanding its European footprint as governments across the continent boost defense spending and procurement.
Under the controversial plan, Volkswagen has agreed to sell its Osnabrueck plant to private equity firm Aurelius and the state of Lower Saxony, with the site set to be developed into a center for defense production.
Systems and components for air defense are expected to be manufactured at the plant for Germany and other European countries.
Volkswagen decided two years ago to phase out vehicle production at the Osnabrueck site by summer 2027.
‘Direct German subsidy for Israeli arms’
Peace activists and some opposition politicians have repeatedly criticized the plan, arguing that the plant should remain focused on civilian production.
Volkswagen has been grappling in recent years with sluggish demand, persistently high production costs in Germany, the impact of trade tensions with the US and fierce competition from Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers.
Speaking on behalf of her organization, Guyard condemned the planned cooperation with Rafael, saying it amounts to “almost a direct (German) subsidy” for an Israeli arms company.
“Furthermore, this amounts to an almost direct subsidy for an Israeli arms manufacturer, which we find particularly inappropriate and politically misguided, given Israel’s current wars in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and also in Iran. Therefore, we continue to condemn this planned joint venture,“ she said.
“This is, in effect, direct support for the State of Israel’s war policy, and we believe that is wrong,” she added.
Guyard’s criticism was echoed by prominent German peace activist Juergen Graesslin.
“For Osnabrueck, as a self-proclaimed ‘City of Peace,’ this would be a dramatic reversal,” Graesslin said in an interview with the daily taz newspaper.
“For many decades, the city has taken pride in this label, and now it apparently has no problem degenerating into a war-supporting ‘City of War’,” he added.
Graesslin argued that civilian vehicle production was being replaced by cooperation with an Israeli arms manufacturer “which is heavily involved in … activities that constitute the most serious human rights violations, including in Gaza and the West Bank.”
“That is morally extremely troubling,” he said.
Civil society resistance takes shape
Meanwhile, civic resistance to defense production at the Osnabrueck plant is slowly gaining momentum, according to Guyard.
Resistance would mean “forging a broad alliance that already exists. The problem is that so-called left-wing parties like the SPD and the Greens fully support arms production. That’s a major problem,” she said.
“There are already coalition partners in the city who oppose arms production. Unfortunately, the labor unions are not among them, nor is the mayor of Osnabrueck,” Guyard added.
Among the groups involved in the local campaign is the newly created Zukunftswerk Osnabrueck network, an open coalition of individuals, political groups and initiatives.
On its website, the network emphasizes a “clear anti-militarist stance,” while calling for a future based on solidarity, democracy and environmental sustainability for the plant, Osnabrueck and beyond.
Concerns over wider German-Israeli defense cooperation
Guyard also warned that the Rafael project could become a gateway for broader Israeli defense industry involvement in Germany and elsewhere in Europe.
“I think that if the project is successful – and this is no secret, as Rafael’s director himself has said – he sees the project as a stepping stone toward closer cooperation in Germany and Europe.”
Asked whether she was concerned about this development, she replied, “Yes, of course.”
Guyard said the rapid expansion of Germany’s defense industry, backed by rising public spending, was creating opportunities that Israeli weapons manufacturers were seeking to tap.
“Arms production is booming and is also fueled by government debt, and Israeli arms manufacturers want a share of this windfall – and that concerns us.”

Former Kosovo President Thaçi sentenced to 25 years in prison for war crimes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:53:08 EEST
20:53:08 KST

Former Kosovo President Thaçi sentenced to 25 years in prison for war crimes
Kyiv • UNN
The Hague court found Hashim Thaçi guilty of killings, torture and unlawful detention of people during the war in Kosovo. He may appeal the verdict.
On Wednesday, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague found former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi guilty of war crimes, including killings, torture and unlawful detention of people. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Thaçi, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as commander-in-chief of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), which consisted mostly of ethnic Albanians, during the violent separation of the region from Serbia in the 1990s.
The court said Thaçi was guilty of the killing of 96 political opponents and people considered to be collaborators with Serbian security forces, carried out by Kosovo Liberation Army forces during the conflict.
He was also found guilty of the arbitrary unlawful detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of 49 people. The court added that none of the victims was actively participating in hostilities at the time the crimes were committed.
The court said that Thaçi actively participated in and encouraged the crimes as part of a joint criminal enterprise based on a common plan.
The plan was as simple as it was destructive. In particular, it provided for: the creation of detention facilities in all areas controlled by the KLA; the identification of people considered opponents of the KLA; their arrest and detention and, when necessary, their killing
According to him, the victims were held in inhumane conditions, beaten, kept in tiny cells and not provided with sufficient food or medical care.
Thaçi, who stood silently while the judge read out the verdict and sentence, denied all the charges.
He may appeal the verdict.
Supporters gathered in Pristina and The Hague
The verdict was closely followed in Kosovo and Serbia, where the legacy of the 1998–1999 conflict and Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008 remain sources of tension between ethnic Kosovo Albanians and Serbs.
Thaçi remains a respected figure for many Kosovo Albanians, while the tribunal itself is extremely unpopular in Kosovo.
Brief clashes occurred in The Hague between several hundred Thaçi supporters and police when demonstrators tried to march to the court from the place where they had been listening to an audio broadcast of the verdict announcement.
In Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, several hundred people marched through the city after the verdict was announced, while dozens of police officers from riot-control units were deployed throughout the city.
"This verdict is shameful. From today, there will be no peace in Kosovo," said Raif Pllana, a former KLA fighter who came to support Thaçi in central Pristina.
Police said that, in case the protests turned violent, a joint action plan had been prepared with foreign peacekeeping forces. The United States urged its citizens to avoid areas where large crowds were gathering.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama criticized the verdict, posting on social media an image of a map of Europe wrapped in barbed wire and writing one word: "Incredible."
Prosecutors sought 45 years in prison
Prosecutors sought 45 years in prison for Thaçi and three other former senior KLA commanders.
However, the three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity. The judges said prosecutors had failed to prove that these crimes were part of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population as a whole.
Thaçi’s lawyers argued that the charges were unfounded and effectively represented an attempt to rewrite history.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, based in The Hague, were established in 2015 under international pressure to hear cases against former KLA fighters accused of war crimes and crimes committed after the war.
On Wednesday, the judges said that the trial had taken place against a backdrop of serious witness intimidation. They also referred to witnesses who had withdrawn their previous testimony, lied to the court or changed their earlier statements.

Von der Leyen describes ‘horror’ at Mladić funeral but holds off on Serbia measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:52:15 UTC
20:52:15 KST

The Commission chief is resisting calls on the EU to impose consequences on Serbia, which remains a candidate country for membership of the bloc alongside other Western Balkan states.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday that she was "horrified by the images" of covincted war criminal Ratko Mladić's funeral in Belgrade earlier this month, but stopped short of announcing any punitive measures against Serbia.
"The glorification of war criminals simply has no place in the European Union," von der Leyen said during her annual State of the European Union speech. She refrained from directly criticising Serbia despite calls for firmer action from the bloc.
Mladić, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia", died in August while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the Bosnian War in the 1990s.
His body was flown to Belgrade on a state plane, greeted by an honour guard by the Serbian military and various security forces, and commemorated by the public broadcaster and the Serbian Orthodox Church. His coffin was wrapped in a Serbian flag.
Officials in Belgrade had previously denied that he would be given a funeral with state honours.
The images prompted outrage across Europe, with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković criticising the EU's muted response.
The Commission helmed by von der Leyen had been pushing to advance Serbia's bid to become an EU member by unlocking Cluster 3 talks on economic growth.
But EU capitals blocked the move, citing persistent concerns over democratic backsliding – even after the Venice Commission said Belgrade had implemented most of its recommendations on judicial reforms.
Diplomats have told Euronews that the funeral given to Mladić has effectively put Serbia's accession push on hold, with one saying that "anyone even considering opening Cluster 3 will think twice".
Henrik Dahl, a Danish lawmaker for the European People's Party (EPP), told Euronews on Wednesday that "Serbia has put themselves in the back of the waiting line (to join the EU) because they gave a state funeral to a war criminal".
Several EU lawmakers have also questioned the affiliation of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party to the EPP, the centre-right political family to which von der Leyen belongs.
The EU's enlargement chief, Marta Kos, postponed her planned visit to Belgrade in response to the funeral, prompting speculation that von der Leyen could announce similar repercussions.
The Commission chief is widely expected to tour Western Balkan candidate countries including Serbia this autumn, but the executive has refrained from confirming whether the programme for the visit is yet confirmed.

No word from Riyadh on oil delivery cancellations as scale of disruption remains unclear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:50:52 UTC
20:50:52 KST

The pipeline shutdown has put pressure on Saudi oil supplies to Europe as further conflict in the region threatens shipping routes. Riyadh has yet to comment on reports that some refiners face delays until November.
Saudi Arabia has remained silent on reports that it has cancelled or delayed crude oil shipments to European refiners following last week's drone strikes on its East-West pipeline, as the scale of the disruption to European deliveries remains unclear.
Energy pricing agency Argus reported on Tuesday that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.
Saudi Arabia’s state-controlled oil company Aramco told Euronews it "declined to comment" on this and other similar reports in a brief email on Wednesday afternoon.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown last Friday after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.
Saudi and Iraqi authorities said the drones came from Iraq. The ministry said technical teams were checking the pipeline, but did not say when pumping would restart.
The pipeline carries crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
From Yanbu, tankers heading to Europe sail north towards the Suez Canal. Egypt’s SUMED pipeline provides another route for crude to reach the Mediterranean from the Red Sea.
Oil stored at export terminals can keep cargoes moving during a shutdown. How long those stocks last depends on the amount available and how quickly pipeline deliveries resume.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Tuesday that the pipeline interruption would be “measured in days”.
Bab el-Mandeb in Houthi crosshairs
The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday that it had intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca the previous evening. The Houthis denied targeting the city.
Last week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea after seizing the port of Mokha and nearby islands from Yemen's Saudi-supported internationally recognised government.
Bab el-Mandeb lies south of Yanbu, on the direct route to Asia. Europe-bound tankers sailing north from Yanbu do not pass through it, but the strait is a key passage for trade between Europe and Asia.
Qatar warned on Tuesday that losing access to Bab el-Mandeb would worsen the disruption already affecting shipping through Hormuz.
Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told a briefing in Doha that this would be “catastrophic for the entire world," calling for international efforts to keep the waterway open.
Meanwhile, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi discussed the security of regional shipping routes in Cairo on Tuesday.
El-Sisi said Saudi and Gulf security formed part of Egypt's national security, expressing support for Saudi measures to protect the kingdom and calling for a political settlement in Yemen.

Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:50:40 UTC
20:50:40 KST

Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
Rosselkhoznadzor, Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance, has ordered the recall and destruction of batch No. 20 of the “Multikan-8” vaccine, which has been linked to dog deaths. The agency sent the order in a letter (.pdf) to the vaccine’s manufacturer, the company “Vetbiokhim,” and published the document on its website.
The letter directs “Vetbiokhim” to recall and destroy batch No. 20 itself, then report back to Rosselkhoznadzor.
Why Rosselkhoznadzor ordered the destruction of only one batch of “Multikan” remains unclear. “Vetbiokhim” had already recalled four batches of the vaccine amid earlier reports of mass dog deaths following vaccination.
Dog deaths after vaccination with "Multikan"
Dog owners began speaking out in large numbers in mid-August about pets that died after being vaccinated with “Multikan-8,” saying at least 300 animals died across several Russian regions. Those affected asked lawmakers in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, to look into what happened.
No official figures on the number of dogs that died exist, and it’s unclear whether such statistics were ever compiled. Rosselkhoznadzor’s regional office and the prosecutor’s office in the Yaroslavl region, where the first reports of dog deaths surfaced, launched an inspection of “Vetbiokhim,” though no results have been announced.
Some of those affected (1, 2, 3) have linked the deaths to contamination of the “Multikan-8” vaccine with the virus that causes Aujeszky’s disease (pseudorabies), whose symptoms resemble those seen in the dogs that died. Unofficial testing of vaccine samples allegedly also detected the virus, according to those affected, but laboratories soon began refusing to run the tests, citing “pressure from above.”
“Vetbiokhim” claimed its own tests had found no contamination of the vaccine with the Aujeszky’s disease virus.
On September 10, Meduza reported that “Vetbiokhim” had drawn up settlement agreements with those affected. The company did not acknowledge any link between the dog deaths and the vaccine but offered to compensate the owners of animals that died. The agreements, however, required owners to waive any claims against “Vetbiokhim” and to stop discussing what happened to their animals in the media, on social media, or in messaging apps without the company’s consent.
“Multikan-8” is a vaccine that protects dogs against canine distemper, adenovirus infections, parvovirus and coronavirus enteritis, leptospirosis, and rabies.
Imported veterinary drugs, including rabies vaccines, largely vanished from the Russian market after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Western sanctions that followed, leaving veterinary clinics to rely mostly on Russian-made products.

Belgium unveils new AI strategy to strengthen national control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:50:03 UTC
20:50:03 KST

Melike Pala
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Belgium has adopted a new national strategy on artificial intelligence aimed at strengthening the country's capabilities, skills, and policy tools while ensuring greater control over the technology, the government said Wednesday.
Digitalization Minister Vanessa Matz said the strategy seeks to ensure that AI creates value for Belgium while allowing the country to "keep control" of its development and use, French-language broadcaster RTBF reported on Wednesday.
Matz noted that 42% of Belgians are already using generative AI, while 34.5% of Belgian companies have adopted AI technologies, placing Belgium among European countries experiencing rapid uptake of the technology.
The new strategy updates Belgium's first National Convergence Plan, adopted in 2022, taking into account changes in the technological and geopolitical environment.
It aims to build on existing investments in research and innovation, public services, infrastructure, and access to European capabilities, while concentrating resources on priority areas and accelerating the transition from AI experimentation to deployment.
It will now be discussed with Belgium's federated entities to determine how it will be implemented.
Among the measures envisaged is a reform of the Strategic Committee on AI to include representatives of the federated entities and strengthen monitoring of priority projects.
The strategy also calls for greater focus on sectors where Belgium has particular strengths, improved access to data for priority AI projects, and the introduction of a "sovereignty grid" for public procurement involving cloud and AI technologies.

Venus may have swallowed its own moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:49:57 UTC
20:49:57 KST

Venus may have swallowed its own moon
Venus may be moonless today because its slow rotation caused a former moon to spiral inward and crash into the planet.
- Date:
- September 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Riverside
- Summary:
- Venus may have once had a moon, but new research suggests the planet’s incredibly slow rotation could have doomed it. Computer simulations showed that instead of gradually drifting away like Earth’s moon, a Venusian moon would likely spiral inward until it crashed into the planet, with larger moons falling even faster.
- Share:
Scientists have puzzled for years over why Venus, despite being similar to Earth in size, mass, and overall structure, has no moon. New research from UC Riverside suggests a striking possibility: Venus may once have had a moon, only to eventually pull it back into the planet.
Previous explanations generally focused on two possibilities. One suggested that Venus once had a moon that was later destroyed by a massive impact. Another proposed that Venus simply never experienced the kind of collision that could have created a moon in the first place.
A new study published in The Astrophysical Journal offers a different explanation. According to the research, Venus may not have needed a dramatic external event to lose a moon.
"My study shows Venus didn't require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today," said UCR astrophysicist and lead author Stephen Kane. "It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it."
Why Earth's Moon Is Moving Away
Scientists know that Earth's moon is gradually drifting farther from us because the Apollo 11 mission left mirrors on the lunar surface that allow researchers to measure the Earth-Moon distance with extreme precision.
"We know that the moon is slowly moving away from the planet, at a rate of around four centimeters per year," Kane said.
That movement is closely tied to Earth's relatively rapid rotation. Our planet completes one spin in about 24 hours. Some of the energy associated with that rotation is transferred to the moon, helping push it slowly outward over time.
Venus behaves very differently.
A single rotation on Venus takes about 243 Earth days. Because the planet spins so slowly, a moon around Venus would not necessarily migrate outward in the way Earth's moon does. Instead, the combination of Venus' gravity and its sluggish rotation could cause the moon to gradually spiral inward until it collided with the planet.
Simulations Send the Moon Into Venus
To investigate that possibility, Kane developed computer models that simulate how planets and moons interact through gravity.
He first tested the model using Earth and the Moon, reproducing the known evolution of the system to confirm that the simulation behaved realistically.
Kane then applied the model to Venus. He changed the planet's rotation rate and tested hypothetical moons with masses ranging from half the mass of Earth's moon to ten times its mass.
Across most of those simulations, the outcome was remarkably consistent. The moon eventually crashed into Venus.
Larger moons met that fate even faster.
"When I made this discovery, I was shocked," Kane said. "I thought surely the broad range of scenarios I was exploring would lead to a variety of results. But it all went pretty much in the same direction."
The simulations do not prove that Venus ever actually had a moon. Kane thinks it is possible, but whether one formed remains unknown.
What the study does suggest is that if Venus once possessed a moon, that moon may not have been able to survive indefinitely.
Could Evidence Be Hidden Inside Venus?
Finding direct evidence of an ancient moon collision would be difficult because Venus has undergone major geological changes.
Roughly 80% of the planet's surface is similar in age, which scientists interpret as evidence of a large resurfacing event about a billion years ago. That event may have erased much of Venus' older geological record.
Clues could instead be hidden deep inside the planet.
Scientists think Earth's moon formed after a massive collision early in Earth's history. Seismic studies have identified unusual structures far below Earth's surface that could contain remnants linked to that ancient impact.
Comparable measurements of Venus might someday reveal whether the planet absorbed a moon of its own.
A Moon Crash Could Have Changed Venus
Such a collision could also provide clues about another major question: whether Venus was ever capable of supporting life.
If a moon crashed into Venus, it would have delivered enormous amounts of energy and angular momentum to the planet. That could have affected Venus' rotation, geology, and climate.
If the planet once had oceans or other environments that were more favorable to life, a major moon impact could have significantly changed its subsequent evolution.
The possibility is especially intriguing because Venus is Earth's closest planetary neighbor and may once have been far more Earth-like than the extremely hot world seen today.
What Venus Could Tell Us About Other Earth-Like Worlds
The findings may also matter far beyond our Solar System.
When scientists search for potentially habitable planets around other stars, they often focus on worlds that resemble Earth. Whether those planets have moons is one factor that researchers sometimes consider when thinking about their long-term environments.
Earth's moon creates tides, may have contributed to continued geological activity, and has played an important role in the planet's evolution. Still, scientists do not know whether a large moon is actually necessary for life to develop or persist.
"My feeling is there are benefits to having a moon, but it isn't required for habitability," Kane said. "The moon has definitely changed the way Earth has evolved through time, but we don't fully know how important that role is."
Kane's results suggest that forming a moon may be only part of the story. A planet also has to be able to keep it.
Worlds that rotate too slowly could cause their moons to spiral inward, ending in collisions capable of dramatically reshaping the planets themselves.
"When people think about Earth twins around other stars, one question they ask is, 'Does it have a moon?'" Kane said. "My study shows a disturbing scenario for many of those cases. If these planets don't rotate fast enough, the moon will crash to the surface, and that would change the course of history for those planets."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Riverside. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Stephen R. Kane, Franck Selsis, Jérémy Leconte, Sean N. Raymond. Tidal Demise: The Evolution and Fate of a Hypothetical Venus Moon. The Astrophysical Journal, 2026; 1009 (1): 31 DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9d6c

Finland aims to launch direct-to-phone emergency alert system by end of year
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:49:07 EEST
20:49:07 KST

Finland aims to roll out a new emergency alert system before the end of this year, according to a spokesperson from the digital and population services data agency.
The system will use cell broadcast technology to send alerts directly to mobile phones without users needing to download a separate app.
Finland's government submitted a proposal to parliament at the end of last month requesting legislative changes to the Act on Emergency Warnings, which would allow for the introduction of a public warning system based on cell broadcast technology.
"A cell broadcast service would enable the transmission of rapid, prompt and geographically targeted emergency warnings to devices across all mobile networks within the affected area," a statement from the interior ministry explained.
The new system will complement the country's current emergency warning system, which will also remain in place. Currently, emergency warnings are issued through the 112 Suomi app, radio broadcasts, teletext page 112 and, when necessary, on television.
Interior Minister Mari Rantanen (Finns) said in June that building the system was a "priority" for the government, and that funding had been allocated to the project to ensure its swift construction and rollout.
The need for such a system has been heightened by an increase in the number of warhead-carrying drones that have strayed into Finnish airspace. An incident in May saw authorities order people in Uusimaa, the country's most populous region, to move indoors and stay there due to concerns a drone had entered Finnish territory.
Finnish authorities previously estimated that the system would be ready by October this year at the earliest, or by the end of 2027 at the latest.

Congo's Ebola epidemic might have gone unnoticed for months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:49:00 UTC
20:49:00 KST

Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone undetected for months
September 16, 2026
The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.
Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way, with several international organizations highlighting delays in the initial response.
Congo is no stranger to crisis response. The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis, and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.
Early warnings came from WHO, Africa CDC
A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.
They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.
It wasn't until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown illness with high mortality reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.
Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread
Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.
Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the rare Bundibugyo type of Ebola.
Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.
About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.
"This significant delay [...] highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.
According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.
"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.
Red Cross reported 'widespread' public fear 'since March 30'
There were other indications that Ebola was already circulating long before the emergence of this first confirmed case.
A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."
Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state and ultimately death.
The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."
US researchers: February outbreak is plausible
The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.
But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15.
In addition, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.
In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.
An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.
WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak
On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."
Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.
In an August interview, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he said.
Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?
Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.
Villa'sstudy does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.
Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.
In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.
According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.
This article was originally written in French.

A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."
Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state and ultimately death.
The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."
US researchers: February outbreak is plausible
The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.
But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15.
In addition, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.
In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.
An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.
WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak
On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."
Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.
In an August interview, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he said.
Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?
Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.
Villa'sstudy does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.
Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.
In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.
According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.

Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone undetected for months

Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone undetected for months
September 16, 2026
The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.
Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way, with several international organizations highlighting delays in the initial response.
Congo is no stranger to crisis response. The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis, and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.
Early warnings came from WHO, Africa CDC
A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.
They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.
It wasn't until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown illness with high mortality reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.
Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread
Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.
Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the rare Bundibugyo type of Ebola.
Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.
About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.
"This significant delay [...] highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.
According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.
"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.

About 70 percent of electricity generators at hospitals in Gaza have gone out of service due to shortages of fuel, oil, and spare parts amid the ongoing Israeli blockade, the health ministry has said.
Zaher Al-Wahidi, director of the ministry’s Health Information Centre, said during a press conference at al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Wednesday that shortages of fuel and oil threatened to bring critical and life-saving hospital departments to a halt at any moment.
Wahidi rejected Israeli claims that it was facilitating the entry of medical aid and logistical supplies into Gaza, emphasising that there are attempts to “improve the image” of the situation and conceal a campaign of “ethnic cleansing” in the enclave.
He said the supplies allowed into Gaza “represent only a very small amount” and do not meet even the minimum operational needs of health facilities, leaving them “struggling between life and death.”
“The health system in Gaza is being driven toward a systematic and mass execution, going beyond a humanitarian catastrophe to a fully fledged health genocide,” he said.
‘Immediate and urgent action’
Wahidi said the fuel crisis also led public transport companies and buses to announce a complete or near-total halt in operations on Wednesday, preventing hundreds of medical workers from reaching their workplaces and further isolating health facilities and hampering their ability to respond to emergencies.
“Health facilities have turned into isolated structures slowly dying amid the continued comprehensive blockade and the prevention of essential necessities of life from entering,” he said.
He said the situation coincides with an “unprecedented shortage” of medicines and medical supplies, the disruption of diagnostic equipment and the closure of treatment routes abroad for patients and wounded people on waiting lists.
Wahidi urged the international community, the UN Security Council, the World Health Organization, and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs to take “immediate and urgent action” to allow the entry of essential medical and operational supplies.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, nearly 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 wounded, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Air pollution exposure linked to higher risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:42:58 UTC
20:42:58 KST

Short- and long-term exposure to air pollution may contribute to a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and death by suicide, according to a new analysis.
Exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of suicidal ideation and death by suicide both in the short and long term, highlighting the influence of environmental factors on people’s health.
A new analysis, published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health, found evidence that short-term exposure to small particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), as well as long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and PM2.5, increases the risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.
Researchers analysed more than 40 studies examining different types of air, noise, light and water pollution, and their relationship with death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal thoughts.
Over 720,000 people die by suicide globally every year. In the European Union, more than 48,000 people died as a result of intentional self-harm in 2023, according to the latest Eurostat data.
“While there is no one single cause for suicide, reasons have been described as multifaceted and include several individual and biological factors in addition to wider cultural and social factors,” the authors wrote.
These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the role environmental exposures play in suicide risk, the authors noted. Yet, the environmental risks remain not fully understood, they noted.
How does the environment influence health?
The analysis points to possible mechanisms connecting air pollution and suicide. For example, air and water pollution have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and neurotoxicity, which can harm brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.
Traffic and other sources of environmental noise and light pollution have also been linked to higher stress levels via circadian rhythm disruption.
“The main contribution of the study is not to demonstrate that pollution is a causal factor in suicidal behaviour, but rather to remind us that psychological suffering always occurs within a particular context,” said Susana Al-Halabí, a psychology professor at the University of Oviedo in Spain, who did not participate in the study.
She added that pollutants can also be a maker of more vulnerable social environments, such as neighbourhoods with poorer living conditions, lower environmental quality, more everyday stress or higher levels of inequality.
According to the authors, further research should investigate the cumulative effect of these environmental exposures to better understand their role in shaping suicide risk.
“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they wrote.
If you are contemplating suicide and need to talk, please reach out to Befrienders Worldwide, an international organisation with helplines in 32 countries. Visit befrienders.org to find the telephone number for your location.

Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes

Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
- Published
The former president of Kosovo, Hashim Thaci, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes.
A hearing at The Hague on Wednesday sentenced the 58-year-old for crimes during Kosovo's independence war against Serbia in the 1990s, in which more than 10,000 people died.
He was convicted after a three-year trial of crimes including murder, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment. A number of other allegations against him were not proven.
Thaci was a co-founder and commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a group that fought for independence. He is regarded as a hero in Kosovo.
He was accused of killing nearly 100 people and of committing other atrocities including enforced disappearances.
Thaci was facing trial alongside three former commanders of the KLA who faced similar charges.
The Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) was set up in the early 1990s as a militant group of ethnic Albanians, in what was then a province of Serbia, and during the war is alleged to have carried out attacks on the region's ethnic Serb minority.
Thaci became Kosovo's first prime minister when it declared independence in 2008. He later became president but resigned in 2020 to face the charges in The Hague.
Thousands of people gathered in Kosovo to watch the verdict on large screens as they were handed down.
In the capital, Pristina, photographs and videos showed people in tears as they learned of the verdict.

French president directs government to secure fuel supplies amid rising prices

French President Emmanuel Macron has directed his government to step up efforts to secure fuel supplies and contain prices as rising costs put pressure on service stations, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Wednesday.
“About 10% of stations have had difficulty with at least one fuel,” Bregeon said.
She added that about nine in 10 of those stations belong to TotalEnergies.
Bregeon said Macron had called for a “total mobilization” on fuel supplies and price control.
She said TotalEnergies' decision to maintain a price cap on gasoline and diesel had attracted increased demand.
“That creates an influx of consumers, higher volumes sold than usual and a logistics chain that can sometimes come under pressure to restock, particularly after weekends,” Bregeon said.
She said the government had provided the necessary exemptions, including allowing fuel trucks to operate on Sundays and public holidays, and would continue working with the industry.
Bregeon noted that there were no “abnormal difficulties” in domestic logistics chains but that France was stepping up efforts to secure supplies internationally.
“The objective, in the coming days and weeks, is really for the president of the Republic to secure these supplies, secure the volumes,” including through other countries, she said.
She also said the government was working on the possibility of greater flexibility in European regulations, including to “loosen the system a little” for refineries.
Bregeon added that Macron was also holding regular discussions with US and Iranian counterparts and countries in the region to work toward a rapid easing of tensions and the “peaceful reopening” of the Strait of Hormuz.
Fuel prices in France have risen sharply in recent weeks amid disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East, with gasoline and diesel prices reaching record levels.
The rising prices have also prompted protests. About 100 fishermen and their supporters blocked a fuel depot in Frontignan in southern France on Wednesday.
